InnerCube is a puzzle game that has you rolling a cube with six different colors to match the colored tiles on the floor to clear each of the game's more than one hundred levels. It plays simple with the arrow keys and starts out easy enough. Before you know it, you'll have to roll your cube in circles to flip to the correct side to mash down the colored tiles. Each puzzle has its own floor that provides both challenge and constriction.
Its a simple, fun, engaging, soothing and relaxing game all rolled into one. Completing each puzzle makes me want to play another. You have no time limit, but the game keeps track of how many moves you've taken. Each section of the game is broken into fifteen puzzles. To get to the next segment, you'll need to achieve gold status or perfect in five or more puzzles. In other words, there's both replay value and forced replays here.
There's more than strict puzzles here, the game has its own survival mode where colored tiles keep appearing on a big grid. The tiles keep appearing and soon you'll be restricted and stuck without a move to make. This mode has a bomb that will go off if you take too long, but the problem I ran into is you can get stuck long before the bomb goes off. In fact I think there might be a glitch with the bomb. The timer stops being a threat at all. So I ended up stuck with only the menu to quit the mode as my only salvation.
Some of the puzzles you can overthink and its a matter of finding the optimal route to cover the highlighted tiles. You will also find solid colored tiles strewn about certain puzzles. These too require you to roll over them with the correct color of your cube, but they are only a mere barrier or distraction rather than a way to complete the puzzle. You'll see them more in the survival mode.
The background looks beautiful. Its a simple, elegant and colorful in design. The game music is soothing to keep you focused and the menus have more pep to them encouraging you to move along and find a puzzle to play. The more moves you take, the more gray the background will become. There's a nice futuristic voice to congratulate you at the end of each level and she tells you what you've earned or unlocked as well.
The game keeps track of your personal bests for each level along with your score and it gives you quick tips in the earlier puzzles. One puzzle leads to the next in concession without having to return to any menu. It keeps a good flow to the game even if it could be streamlined even more. You still get the choice to replay the level, go to the next or return to the menu.
One complaint that I have about the game is the controls are relegated to the keys, which is fine, but the menus require you to use your mouse. While having the mouse is still a good option, each menu item should be accessible via the keyboard as well. Another issue is the fixed camera so you can only see three sides of your cube, but hey that's part of the challenge. Knowing what's on the other side.
I'd also like to thank someone for my review copy. Who it is I'll never know.

A throwback to the 8bit era of fiendishly tricky platform games, reminiscent of games like Jumping Jack on the ZX Spectrum.
Rating 5/10
The first thing you'll learn about BIT.TRIP RUNNER is that it's a game that requires perfect timing and precision as well having to memorise level layouts and obstacles as there are no checkpoints and that each level has to be completed in a single run as failure returns you to the beginning of the level.
This requirement of a perfect run is both what makes and breaks Bit.Trip Runner. At its best it's a gloriously fluid experience as you meticulously learn the obstacles on a level and the feeling of exhilaration when you manage to pull of a perfect run.
However it's also at times an incredibly frustrating experience. There are a handful of levels that are too long which can lead to extended attempts to the point of quitting and some obstacles require such pin-point precision that means failure towards the end of the level is a maddening experience as you watch your character revert back to the start. However if you stick with it your perseverance is rewarded.
There is much to recommend in Bit.Trip runner, from the visuals, music and the challenge but I would only recommend it to those who like an old fashioned challenge, for those who like their games to be unforgiving and to reward patience and practise as well as precision.

Fun if a bit basic, with not a lot of replay value. Skill points ultimately serve to make the game easier rather than opening up new possibilities (and you can end the game with every single skill if you collect most things), so mess with them as you please. The game locks you out of dungeons after you complete them, so if you're in for getting absolutely everything, take your time with these or look up a guide.
Main issue with the game is that it's mostly trial-and-error, which leads to a lot of deaths. Some parts are unclear as to how you're supposed to progress, partially because some parts of the background look like foreground.
Story is ok if a bit lackluster. Animation makes up for this and the sound design really drives home the intended effect of the story. It's a beautifully designed game, from the UI to the world itself, though the overworld is ultimately a bit bland considering every section looks the same only with different color palettes.
With the exception of finding collectibles such as health, energy, ability, or experience points, the overworlds are fairly empty and serve entirely to get you from one dungeon to another. This game could have used a warp ability between save points, as traveling from one side of the map to the other turned out to be tedious.
The controls are tight and the gameplay itself is fantastic. Maneuverability in this game is just as important as combat, if not more important considering you don't actually have to kill anything to progress.
For the price it's a good game. I got about 7 or 8 hours out of it, and only a small portion of that was spent being frustrated, mostly during dungeon sequences.
Played it once for the story. Then a second time for the flawless mobility/combat system, the stunning visuals and musical score and every delightful corner of this game.

This is probably one of the best games I've played in years. I may be biased, as the Age of Sail is one of my favorite eras in history, but the game is a lot of fun even without the kind of nerdish attention to detail I apply to this genre.
It has a bit of a learning curve, and being this early in development, the UI needs some work, but that's coming. The devs have been very communicative with the community, so we're always in the loop on what's coming next.
If you like sailing tall ships and filling your enemies ships with cannonballs, you can't go wrong with Naval Action.

Yes, this is an early access game that are unfinished. But is it fun to play as it is now? The answer to that is absolutely yes. The core gameplay is there. Trading mechanics is working fine, and battles are fantastic. It runs smoothly too as long as you dont enable AA. There is a lot of things i expect to be improved. But as an early access review i wont deduct points for that. This is not a finished game. Join now, and be a part of the community that shapes a naval warfare game with huge potential.
There is no tutorial, but we are very helpful in "help" chat in the game. There is also tutorial videos on youtube. What you need to know is that it is no arcadish game. You aim and shoot manually, the navigation is done with a map and use of compass. You dont appear as a dot on it. But there is a great community with many good guilds to join and be a part of. The big ones offer voice chat(Teamspeak). And we have great fun warring other nations for ports and control of the high seas.
Conclusion is that the base game is there. And it is absolutely fun, and that i think, is the only thing that should matter in a early access. Its not perfect(yet) but i hope its going to be, and everyone that supports the developers buying in at this stage, will contribute in making it so.

I have bought the game back in November/December 2014. I liked the period, but was a bit sceptical, especially when combined with a paypal payment method and was just willing to try it.
How much was I mistaken. It is my most played game on steam right now. I did hunt AI ships alone. I did chase player ships off the perceived turf with a group. For a time I was the one of lucky few, who were able to build HMS Surprise. I did successfully trade iron, when there was almost none left in the whole carribean. I went to the edge of the world. I met people that were nice and crude, honorable and dishonorable, dauntless captains as well as cowards. Does this appeal to you? If yes, this game might be just for you.
HOWEVER, you have to be willing to overlook some substantial flaws, at least for a time. Terrible UI. No help, if you don't search for it/ask. You have to be willing to accept behavioural standards of the community (courteous, gentlemenly). You have to be willing to learn. You have to be able to think of the battles as battles, not as the grind.
2nd HOWEVER, you get an opportunity to participate in the development of the game you have been waiting for for the last 10-15 years, due to the great devs, who really listen. (I can pinpoint some features that are in the game to originate with specific players and specific posts on the forums).
I will not tell you if the game is right for you. For me, best 40 EUR I spend on a game. For an early access title 9/10.

I've never played a "survival game" before this one. When I saw the description in Steams Summer Sale, I thought that it looked interesting. I gave it a try and bought it.
I decided that for my very first steps I will start on a PVE-only server with low or zero population at that moment. This gave me the chance to get used to the game functions without having to concentrate on other players at the same time. For players liking PVP there are also servers where this is implemented.
For me, buying this game  has definitely been a very good decision. The game caught me instantly and keeps me playing, testing, and very much enjoying.
The game starts on a beach, the character has nothing but a sharp stone in his hand and some minor clothes at his body. This is where the tutorial pops up. First task: Find something to eat. So I started walking and searching, found corn and berries. And  I found pirates soon - which killed me instantly. First survival test failed. Restart at the same location as in the beginning. I wanted to know whether I could survive longer, I knew now where those pirates were and went the other direction.
The tutorial is in my opinion very well done. It leads from finding food to chopping wood and stone, creating a stone axe and building the first base with a builders desk, a bed and a storage chest. I went on with the tutorial and suddenly realized that an hour, two and three hours quickly went and I still was playing and enjoying.
Of course, my character died several times. It looks like that tigers also have the task to "find something to eat". And there I fully realized that when dying, my character looses everything which he had in his inventory. Bags with the content stay where the char died. So, go there again to pick it up. Of course it was hidden in high grass, I had to search a bit (the location of death is luckily shown on the map). And - the tiger was hidden there, too, still hungry!
I learned, running away, as quickly as possible, is a very good way to survive. My previous belongings were "Out of Reach" for me.
Strangely, this didn't push me away from this game, in contrary, I wanted to survive longer. And I have many hours and days which kept me enjoying ingame. I learned how to build huge houses, create a boat and visit other islands.
I won't tell all my adventures in the game, just give it a try yourself.  :-)   And beware of tigers!
What I find to be very positive with this game, is how the developers are active in the forum or reacting on email-feedback given to them. I got quick responses and hints about possibilities which I have. In some other games I'm used to bugfixes taking months and the community is getting no or very late answers and information.
Out of Reach is different: While playing, there might be a message that in five minutes the servers will go down - but ten minutes later I can continue playing. Some minor bugfixes are solved this way immediately. Bigger updates take low time to be downloaded, so playing is not "waiting for hours" but surprisingly I was back ingame quickly.
I am also very pleased about the fact that so far I've never stumbled about a severe bug. This game is Early Access, so bugs and changes are to be expected often. I found minor bugs only and was pleased about the recent changes. For example, the implementation of Events with shipwrecks went smoothly. There was only one location where those wrecks appeared and we players could test whether it worked as intended. It did, at least for me. The locations for shipwrecks will soon be spread over the whole map.
Exactly this behavior of the developers pleases me. We can test and give feedback and it will be taken into account before spreading it map-wide. This is how I love it.
So, developers, please continue with this good work, all my thumps up for this! And players, dare it and test this game! I find it worth playing.
Have fun!    :)

For the love of God, do not buy this game.
The game can literally be beaten in around 20 - 30 minutes. Now, one might argue that the game is still enjoyable for the "art" or "story", but the game has neither that are exceptional. Open Sorcery is a testament to doing an awful lot with very little. First up, there is no music, no voice acting, few images, few sound effects. This is a text based choice game. This doesn't detract from its appeal, but buyers should know what they're getting. The strengths this game has are:
- An excellent and engaging story: The people feel real, their problems feel real, and you will care enough about them to really want to help them. And you'll feel it if you can't. I cried at least once.
- Cerebral game play: Though the game play is limited to pressing the right words you'll need to read carefully and use your head to solve your problems, sometimes while you're under pressure. Getting it right feels relieving.
- Consequential choices:  This game doesn't hold your hand. You'll want to make the right choices, and if you don't people's health, sanity or even lives may be at stake. You might not be able to help everyone.
- Great presentation: Though text is the major medium the game uses, it uses all the tricks possible to convey the story really convincingly and effectively.
This isn't a big budget story, it's a low budget, relatively short (~4 hours), brilliantly executed, minimalist, story of something trying to understand humans, protect humans and become human.

I received a copy of Open Sorcery for reviewing purposes. This has is no way altered my review for this game.
Open Sorcery is a text-based RPG where you play as a Firewall program in a world where magic exists. Each day you're given the task to look at 4 different locations, and if there's a "threat" (aka elemental spirit) then you get to choose how you want to deal with it. Want to just kill it with fire (literally)? Have fun. Would you rather try reasoning with it instead? No problem.
Usually attacking a spirit will make you stronger while trying an indirect approach (like reasoning with it) will allow you to learn more about it. There are different Matters (fire, water, dark, etc.) and Motives (chaos, order, love, etc.)  you can learn about while you play, which you can use in specific situations. You also have a relationship meter with each person you interact with, and in some situations you need a high enough number in order for something to happen. In most cases it's good to go out of your way to become better friends with someone.
The best part about Open Sorcery is its replay value. You won't be able to do or learn everything in one playthrough, so it's a nice way to encourage you to try different tactics each time you start a new game. Overall I give Open Sorcery an 8/10.

Do you enjoy a nice neon-paletted future where corporations rule and humanity is kept down by an oppressive government? Well then you'll like this, provided you don't want the neon palette. This is the vision of a future where humanity is past its' prime and is trying to fend off the slow decay of time; all while fending off hordes of aliens and daemons. The grimness of this universe is a refreshing twist, even after several decades as a series.
Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine puts you in the boots and bulky armour of one of the Imperiums' chapters of Space Marines. If you like sitting behind a wall and occasionally firing over the wall, then just stop there. In this game, there ARE no walls (metaphorically speaking of course)! YOU are the wall. You are a shield for the weak and a sword to be swung by the powers that be. As much as the game preaches that life is the Emperors' currency; you are a sturdy block of gold, in a world populated by pennies and pound coins. So what makes you so valuable, apart from the shiny aspect of your nature?
You are a block of Gold. Let's do a comparison. I want you to drop a penny onto your fingers while they are on a desk. Didn't hurt, did it? Now; drop a big block of Gold. If you actually did, I applaud your delusion of invulnerability, but I'm not going to kiss your boo-boo better. If you didn't; you're smarter than the person asking me to kiss the boo-boo. You see, logical thought dictates that there is a big difference in the damage a penny and a Gold Brick can do. You play the heavier of the two objects; that most delightful bringer of death. You are a big stompy thundering cannon comprised of flesh and muscle, located securely behind an energy shield and a hell of alot of metal. You don't fire a little 9mm pistol as you do in so many other titles. With your bulkier stature, you should be able to wield more mighty weapons and this game will allow you. Ever wondered what happens when a rocket propelled explosive shell (with a diameter of nearly an inch) comes into contact with the face of a 6 foot Ork, armed with naught but a club and a suicidal disregard for the laws of physics and mortality? If you answered "red?" then the klaxons in your room, set to ring with the sounds of victory when you are correct (at least if you're as egocentric as I) should be deafening you in reward for your foresight.
In a world full of games with lots of brown or orange; this game decides that red is still a viable colour. VERY viable. In fact, so viable that often times you will encounter pools of red where once a green enemy stood. If you are discouraged by blood, this game isn't for you. If you like blood, this game delivers it in such vast amounts that even the least sadomasochistic of us would still require the unbuttoning of the jeans to alleviate the tightness the combat produces. While I recommend this game to women as well, this game has an undeniable reek of man about it. I would be surprised if the word "testosterone" was not included once in every five lines of code written for the engine. While there is a brilliant plot behind the title, it isn't one that I'd recommend you buy the game for. The plot isn't what you want in a game, is it? Plot is a nice addition but gameplay is what differentiates a game from a movie or book and this is a shining example of that ideology. You fire rocket propelled shells from a fully automatic death-cannon; when you aren't lobbing balls of corrosive plasma into the faces of a tiny little green fellow. But range is only a part of the game. To regenerate health, you are not allowed to cower. Your health is tied to your efficiency in combat, as it drops when your shield is depleted and raises when you execute an enemy in close combat. To replenish your red goo, you need to turn your foes into red goo, and presumably the splat perks your character up enough to make him healthy again. Still makes more sense than being eaten by a dog in an open world game and healing up by pulling a bullet out of your left arm. It sounds better too. There is a definite booming sound behind your guns and your mighty melee weapons sound vastly different when they smash into metal in comparison to tearing through flesh. Your chainsword revs pleasurably as you swing it and your heavy bolters sound exactly as the name makes you believe. They sound heavy, as if they were firing bolts.
Now let us discuss multiplayer. Six big stompy fellows clash against six big stompy fellows and there are three types of big stompy fellow you can be. You can be a tactical marine, who lumbers across the battlefield with some medium power ranged weapons. The assault marines jet around the battlefield with jump packs, slamming with a mighty force into the ground before spinning their melee weapons viciously to rend the flesh of all who oppose them. If you are more of a heavy fellow, the Devastators will fit you perfectly. Armed with the biggest weapons of all three, they stomp and wield death at range. They are so heavily equipped that instead of shoulder charging an enemy to interrupt the swing of their sword; they kick them. Even as you walk, the camera shakes to give you the true sense that you are heavy, gifted the power of a ton of metal and muscle. The ground never seems to sit still when you introduce twelve armoured Goliaths upon a map.
This is a game of David versus Goliath; except this time, you play Goliath and logic wins over storybook morality. Big stompy fellows don't get stopped by a stone, they club the sling wielder into the ground with fist and foot.

There were also many things about the game that reminded me of The Stanley Parable (some of the mazes with rooms that change as you move through them, and other trippy effects like the "MC Escher" level).
The graphics are very good in my opinion - after all, it (reportedly, I am unable to test this) has VR support. However, there are still some mysteries left in the game even after completing it. I'm really not sure if I missed something, despite getting the "best" ending.
Overall I thought it was a good value for the price - comparing it to going out for a cheap meal or going to the movies, I definitely got much more value for my money and enjoyment from this game.

Update 2016-06-24: There was just a new release, 1.8, with a new game mode (law) that basically eliminates all randomness and makes the game deterministic. Now even people who don't understand probabilities can enjoy the game.
If you like turn-based strategy, wizards, spellcasting, magical creatures and monsters this game might be for you. Randomness plays an important role in the game, so you have to think about tactics and probabilities. If you get easily frustrated because you think a 3% attack from a rat should never be able to kill your draon this game isn't for you.
Gameplay
Each game starts with two (or more in multiplayer) wizards on a small map, and each wizard has a random deck of cards. Those cards are spells that have certain odds to succeed. The odds can be boosted by using mana. Mana is gained by killing creatures, failing to cast a spell, and collecting mana sprites. Wizards with different staffs get different "mega spells" they can "buy" for 60 or more mana points.
All creatures can be cast with a 100% success rate as illusions that behave exactly like normal creatures, except that the opposing wizard can disbelieve them, which makes them vanish and gives the wizard the opportunity to cast another spell in the same round. However, when disbelieve is cast on a real creature nothing happens, and no other spell is possibly this round.
So, additionally to the usual strategic thoughts in games (how to position units, how to attack/defend) you have to make many decisions like:
- Should I create a weak monster with a high probability, or should I try for a big bad one with only a 30% chance of succeeding?
- Should I burn cards I find useless to boost the odds of a hard spell?
- Should I move aggresively to secure the mana sprites?
- Is that dragon my enemy just cast real? Should I risk trying to disbelieve it? Do I even care if it's real or not? (It's a dragon, you probably do)
The last point shows why this game is very much about knowing and reading your opponent. It can be a psychological game of bluffing and calling bluffs.
To me, this game is similar to X-COM but better because:
- The turn mechanic is better, you can move once, attack once, and cast one spell every round, in any order. Your minions can do the same except they can't cast spells.
- In online matches you don't have to carefully explore the map. You always see the entire map, this makes the game faster. Online duels default to a 20 turn limit.
- It has wizards and dragons.
- Oh yeah, I tried online games with X-COM and didn't like them much.

Updated review since recent changes:
Really love this game to bits! Gives me all of the turn based tactical goodness that i could ever want in a format that doesn't demand a whole afternoon to have a satisfying game session. The way this works is through subtle but genious game mechanics...perhaps seemingly obtuse at first. The game teaches you the basics in an indepth tutorial (wizard training) but below what might at first seem "OMFG! TOO MUCH RNG!" will eventually turn into a deep love for the game if you manage to learn the nuances. The nuances come in taking advantage of the smaller details like...A tall unit blocking line of sight, receiving mana for failed casts (the lower the % of success, the more mana given), the engage system, dispelling troops to open up extra attacking opportunities, creatures shifting chaos/law alignment regardless if it's an illusion or not, casting an illusion pegasus to ensure an extra hit can be taken by the paladin's retaliate....Great stuff!
Otherwise with recent additions you have a robust coop system which allows you to tackle harder PVE realms with a pal, or invite them for some crazy 6 wizard action.
Overall it's just a fun game, very unique and worthy of your time. A generous demo is also available on steam, which allows you access to pretty much all that i've been yammering on about (except the realms and coop...PVP is the main attraction of this game though)

I enjoy this game immensely. This review summarizes some reasons why.
At the end of the 14th century, Earth shattered into innumerable fragments in a magic-instigated apocalypse. Powerful magic allows fragments of Earth to endure as habitable, island realms scattered between planes of existence. From a planet called Limbo, wizards and gods engage in eternal conflict over who controls the many, surviving realms of old Earth. Each realm holds the promise of ancient artifacts, lore, and power to fuel the ambitions of wizards and gods alike. It is a feudal, dystopic society of magic users.

is a rebirth and reimagining of
(1985) and
(1990) by their original creator, Julian Gollop. Mr. Gollop is more known for creating the original
(1994), the widely acclaimed classic which inspired
and many other games. The classic
and
games were rooted upon deep, tactical play.
is a true successor to both legacies.
I cannot really do the basic gameplay experience justice in a short paragraph. It has too many tactical layers. But at essence, the game involves duels of up to 6 wizards. Wizards can invoke flamboyantly magical spells and summon creatures. Yet wizards themselves are fragile and must be protected. Imagine a three dimensional, multi-layered game of wizard chess with variable numbers and types of pieces which can come and go, and where each attack has a very real chance of failure. But if you lose the wizard, then you lose the game. Sometimes you will lose despite your best efforts, and sometimes you will win because you were lucky rather than good. That said, this game is tactically deep and, over time, rewards players who come to understand and appreciate all of the many, varied tactical approaches to gameplay.
There is a tutorial labeled “Wizard Training” in the main menu. It comprises a series of gated set-piece encounters which gradually introduce you to the fundamental mechanics and tactics of the game. Having played the game for hundreds of hours before experiencing the tutorial, I still found it enjoyable. It’s not often that I can say that about a tutorial.
Multiplayer wizard duels can be played live or asynchronously with up to 6 players. Matches can be friendly or ranked. And matches can be played Equipped (with custom equipment) or Classic (with standard equipment). Ranked matches allow you to qualify as an "Archmage" at which point you will be given your worldwide rank computed by an ELO scoring method. League standings reset in monthly seasons. Whether friendly or ranked, matches generally go quickly. As for the asynchronous games, these are my favorites. You can have up to 20 asynchronous games going at any time. Each player has many days to complete their turns in a match, but I find matches generally go more quickly than that. After ranked matches were first introduced, I completed 35 ranked async matches in just 3 days, and this was gameplay I managed in bits of free time that I had rather in continuous sittings. (I love, love the asynchronous functionality.) Additionally, players can create custom friendly matches, changing the parameters of the game.
There are developer and player created Realms of Chaos which you can explore online with your wizard. These Realms vary in size and challenge and come with a rating system to help determine which are worth exploring. The essential aspect of this game mode is to explore the map to find and defeat all of the Wizard Lords (AI-controlled mini-bosses) in order to reach and defeat the Wizard King (AI-controlled boss) of the Realm. While you are doing this, the Wizard King and his Wizard Lords summon reinforcements. And if you take too long, the Wizard King can banish you from the Realm. This game mode should not be considered a full-fledged RPG. Think of each of the Realms as puzzles to be solved, and some have stories to tell.
The game creates an internal friends list based upon your Steam friends list. You can also add game-only friends. With these friends, you can invite them to co-op with you in online Realms or in online custom games with up to 6 wizards.
There are offline game modes which allow hotseat gameplay against any combination of human or AI-controlled opponents. There is an offline singleplayer campaign. I have not played much of the singleplayer campaign. I find the online Realms experience superior as it integrates with all of the other online features.
The game uses the Unity game engine, which should be compatible with most computers. The custom art and animations are quite pretty. And the game really does have its own, unique graphical theme. Don’t rely on me for too much input on this, as I was playing the game when wizards and creatures were represented by crude, unanimated placeholder graphics. But if you really care about graphics, the graphics are good.
As-is, the game is a gem. If you like tactical turn-based games, then spending $20 on
will get you one of the more fun games in your Steam inventory. If you’ve read this far and the game still intrigues you, then you should get the game.

(This is my first review on Steam so I may be a bit slapdash) Squirreltopia is a 2D hardcore platformer game created by Surreal Distractions. I got this game as a free key from the developer at the PCMR subreddit.
Plot:
An evil squirrel named Shadow Tail imprisons all of the woodland squirrels. You and an infinite army of squirrels at your disposal go on a suicide mission to stop him. Really that is all there is to it. If you expected some type of plot for a $4 platforming game, you will be very disappointed. Luckily, this game doesn't need it anyway because that is not what you are looking for in this game.
Gameplay:
This is a hardcore 2D platforming game and you will die a lot. Fortunately, you have unlimited lives in this game. There are five worlds in this game and each have ten levels. As you complete each level, you will unlock gems which are used to open the gate to a boss so you can fight him and not only get to the next world, but also unlock levels that were blocked off to you. There are a total of 50+ levels in this game. While Squirreltopia doesn't do anything new to differentiate itself from other platformer games (besides the cute art style), its foundations are very solid and this is very good for a $4 game.
There are two difficulty settings: Easy and Hard. Easy allows checkpoint on each level (except the death wall levels) while Hard mode has no checkpoints and offers a time trial to complete. If you complete the time trial fast enough, you get a time trophy. As much as a completionist I am, Hard mode turn me off as I cannot do most of these levels without a checkpoint, but for those who are platforming gods, this can be a good challenge for you.
The controls are very simple: move left and right and jump. Game can be played on a controller, WASD, or arrow keys and the option of having spacebar as your jump button. The squirrel's movement is based on acceleration, so as you move faster, you can clear longer jumps. When you slow down, the squirrel skids to stop rather than making a complete stop. You can that the game is running on ice physics and to a degree, you are right. Some people thinks this is a problem, however the game was designed that in mind and the levels show. Controlling your acceleration is important as sometimes if you go to fast, you may hit a wall, destroy all of your acceleration, and cannot make the second jump due to you not having enough space to make a long jump. Normally I prefer tight controls in games like Megaman, but I totally understand the semi-loose controls in this game. It takes practice.
The game has a lot of varying levels and it never feels like it is doing the same thing over and over. The level design is pretty creative and well thought out. You will be treated to many different obstacles and hazards like balloons, springs, and bubbles that bounce you up, or bomb tiles that blow in a few seconds, lasers, electric traps, spikes, etc. There is even automatic scrolling/death wall levels in the game. The games does get a bit more difficult as time goes on (and trust me, there are a few levels where you will be spending like an hour trying to complete), but the pacing is excellent. The game doesn't do cheap tricks whatsoever (except for 5-8 and death wall levels. They feel a bit cheap and need to be tweaked but fortunately that is really only 5 levels). If you messed up, it is your fault. Completing difficult levels will feel very satisfying and rewarding.
There are bosses in the game and this is where I feel it is one of the games weakest elements. They are simple; hop on their heads five times and BAM, dead. However, the A.I for some of these bosses are rather unpredictable and makes fighting them more luck based than actual skill based. Boss 2 and the Final boss suffer as they may pull some cheap shots at you.
There are mini-games in Squirreltopia which you can get through by collecting cartridges in the game, but I never really bother with it to be honest I cannot comment.
Graphics:
The game is 2D and is made on Game Maker Professional. While you won't expect something stellar, it is also not dull either. The environments vary a lot and don't feel stale. Each of the five worlds all have a different setting to them like one world would have a desert theme background, another world you are in space. Even the levels themselves all have varying backgrounds so it doesn't feel like you are running through the same area on a different level. It makes each level refreshing and new yet they also fit the theme of the world as well. You play as different squirrels each with different colors and eyes as you die each time or switch areas. It is cutesy to say the least (not a bad thing).
Sound:
The game has a small soundtrack (I believe 8 songs) however each track is very good to listen and match the theme of the world. World 3 and World 4's tracks are my favorite in the game and the boss themes are also very good as well. You can buy the soundtrack for $1 and I don't find that to be a bad investment whatsoever. The music will keep you sane as you die multiple times throughout the game.
Flaws:
I only have small gripes with this game. I think the death wall levels (like 4-10 for example) should be tweaked just a bit. Slow down the walls chasing after you. Some bosses have unpredictable A.I, making some of them luck based rather than skill based. Level 5-8 has an RNG effect (let just say this level is completable on certain outcomes). Also, the game does nothing new. For some reason, the overworld of World 1 and a couple of levels, there is some huge slowdown in the game but that is probably due to the fact I have a crappy laptop instead. I can turn Vsync off to rectify this, but I get screen tearing in return. This only happens in I will say 5% of the game for me. The rest runs at normal speed. I also find that the jump button doesn't always register when I hit it so it leads to some underseving deaths, but I think the keyboard in my laptop is terrible. I doubt you will go through these problems. Otherwise, nothing game breaking I can say.
Verdict:
For $4, this game is actually really good. If you are a fan of hardcore platformers, you will enjoy this game. If not, it may not hurt to try. As of writing this review, there is a 50% off sale for this game. $2 is a good deal for a game that can give you enjoyment for some hours. I recommend this game if you are like platformers.

Remember that it is in early access and is being constantly updated.  Also, bear in mind that most of the recent negative reviews have nothing to do with Fragmented itself.  Fragmented is not The Repopulation, nor was it ever meant as a replacement for TR.
For everyone whining, crying, and throwing tantrums that would do credit to a three year-old because Fragmented isn't TR, I would say that it was never billed to be.  Nor was it meant to replace TR.  During the re-development of TR, which was necessitated by the near-bunkruptcy of Idea Fabrik, pulling the rug out from under ABT's use of the Hero engine, they generated some base code.  This base code was bundled together without the MMO elements to create Fragment.  So, when ABT was working on Fragmented, they were working on TR as well.
Now, however, with all the negative reviews causing a huge slump in sales of Fragmented, ABT has been forced to sell TR to IF, the company that caused all this to begin with.  So I congratulate everyone screaming, "I want my Repop!!!!!" and leaving negative reviews.  You've killed what chance there was of TR ever emerging under ABT.  Now we just have to hope that IF keeps somewhat to the original vision of TR and decides to honor kickstarter pledges.

Ori and the Blind Forest has earned its stripes in more ways than one.
The first ten minutes of the game are a heart-touching series of beautifully animated scenes between two characters that don't need a word of dialog; all set to a soundtrack that's on par with the best of indie composers. While technically there's a narrator speaking through parts of it in vague, riddlish sentences, it still represents a superb example of showing rather than telling.
The game does not simply rest on some status as an artistic, classic-gameplay adventure though. You may have heard mentions that the game is hard; I don't rank it among Super Meat Boy's levels of masochism, but unique platforming challenges and coordination are some of the staples of its gameplay. This would be a lot more annoying were it not for an inventive checkpoint system; you can essentially save anywhere by using up one expandable "Energy" point; as a Metroidvania, there are also true save points that refill both your health and Energy. I really hope for the difficulty not to put people off; at the very least, it will make those reward moments so much sweeter when you finally escape the flooding of the Ginso Tree.
Every room in the game always seems to have the detail of a painting; the fantasy wonder of a game like Trine, but seeminly almost all of it hand-painted instead of 3D (many times, it's hard to tell the difference!) With some of the game's more cinematic set-piece moments, it's almost hard to fathom the kind of work that went into the visuals. You could pretty much hit the screenshot button at any time and have yourself a new wallpaper.
Out of the storytelling, animation, soundtrack, challenge, and overall cinematic presentation; Ori would be a highlight of the year for mastering just *one* of these elements to the degree they've managed. Had I known what I do about this game prior to buying it, I easily would have accepted a starting price of $60. As it is, Moon Studios simply seems to have a whole lot of artistic vision that they now want to share with the world.
I have not even finished this game yet, so for all I know I might have more praise to share about the ending. I'm almost certain they'll manage another tearjerker on par with their prologue.

This is a game that I really want to like. I love sailing ships, I love naval combat. And this game is maybe 75% of the way there.
But here's the thing. There's literally no explanation of any mechanics in the game. I mean not a single one, there's no help page. No tooltips. No explanation of what things on the Worlds Worst UI do. No explanation about settings and things you can toggle on your ship. If you want to find any of this out, you have to go dig around the game forums, and read explanations of things that are out of date or don't help at all.
The players in game don't really answer questions either. I've seen several lost new players asking questions, and being ignored by the veterans in the chat channels. The playerbase obviously isn't putting any effort into helping the new people get a grip on a complex game.
The progression is absolutely glacial. I've played for 8 hours now, and haven't even gotten halfway through the first captain level. Even the gameplay gets glacial, once your ship takes enough damage and your crew takes enough casualties (about 5 maybe, it's insane) everything takes longer to do. Guns reload so slow you could watch a youtube video in between shots. Don't get me wrong, I'm a fan of slower-paced games, and wouldn't like to see this game turn arcadey. But as it stands, the pacing is just painful.
When it's on, it's on. It's great sailing into battle, broadsiding other ships. Until everything slows down. It looks like there's a lot of fun metagame in the faction conflict, but you're gonna spend ages grinding before you get out of your baby ship.
Wait until the developers get a clue before buying this. As it stands it's maybe worth $20, not the asking price.

A cover-based, MMO FPS ( massively multiplayer online, *third person shooter ) set in a post-apocalyptic city. Mostly solo-oriented but there are group fights.
Pros:
- The graphics engine is staggering - the most advanced engine since CryEngine ( Crysis ). I get goosebumps just looking at the snow and fog ( even after playing the main campaign for 112 hours ). The graphical fidelity is so close to photorealistic that the line between "game" and "reality" is blurry. Art and photographs that hang on walls look photo realistic. Posters on outside billboards, are worn and have weathering and moisture damage. The graphics scale well. Using a GTX 780, I've played on Ultra, High, Medium and Low settings.
- The attention to detail in the world-building / level design is amazing. The scope is massive. The designers even decorated the floors with chalk drawings by "children". You feel like you are in a real city.
- The artificial intelligence is the best since "Half Life 2" and "Fear 1", with low level thugs flanking and alternately acting like gangster rappers in a music video or scared children.
- I did enjoy the exploratory, timed missions, where you had to figure out how to get from point A to B, since it was sometimes very puzzling, which is a tribute to great level design. The combat missions were always great. The low level, group missions were crazy fun.
Cons:
- There are only a few different mission types, which is fine for the first 15 levels. I doubt that most people would want to stick around to do the same missions for another 15 levels? The worst mission is a fetch quest where you walk in slow motion, carrying suitcases that contain lead bricks, back to an armored vehicle. At some point you will ask yourself, "Do I really want to fix the city's plumbing problems, at the water works, for the Nth time?". I think that most people could exhaust this game in 2 free weekends?
- Chat channel contained Chinese and Russian characters, which was annoyingly odd. I wondered if the developers wanted people to think that the game is more populated than it is:
- It was difficult to find people to do the group missions at level 18-30. It would not surprise me if people stop playing the game around level 18.
- I get the impression that the population is slowly dying. There's a banding effect where there are a lot of low level and high level players but a black hole of missing players around level 18-29. I had to wait until the weekend to find players for higher level group missions. Sometimes, high level players volunteer to help with missions.
- The free stuff that you get from the Gold edition version of the game, with exception of the cosmetic sets of clothing, is mostly garbage. By the time I got my gear, I was level 5+ and the gear was level 4, so it was already under level. The shotgun is only used by more experienced players, since it is a point blank weapon and only if there is not anything else to use. There's hardly any reason to use a side arm in the game; ballistic shield skill makes it more viable though. The game already contains 3 Walmarts worth of cosmetic clothing in the game. You will run into problems if you dislike the DLC and try to claim a refund on the Season pass through Steam because it does not log hours played in the DLC seperately from the main game. You might have better luck buying the base game and DLCs seperately?
- I noticed a couple of minor glitches in the game that are 8 months old. When you look at the map, sometimes it shows every enemy as level 25, which is not true; it's a temporary display error. I've seen another glitch ( that happened 1 time ) where I was blocked from removing items from my Darkzone stash ( box of stuff ). The glitches are so old that it was a bit worrying that the developers did not seem interested in patching these bugs out.
Miscellaneous:
- The game can be very addictive.
- There is a tonne of solo content. There are group fights that are used to progress the story ( but you can solo them if you have elite gear ).
- You level so quickly that it obsoletes your clothes and weapons. Each level is a DPS / armour jump; that drives the incentive to obtain gear. Some people will like that, some will be "meh" and some people will find that grindy or eventually so. It's easy to be under or over level because the gear scaling can get out of whack sometimes.
- There is a dedicated PVP zone but the PVP is kind of "meh" and seems more dependent on gear than skill, but not always.
- Reviews talk about some enemies being "bullet sponges", which is somewhat true but it's more related to scaling differences between what clothes you are wearing relative to the target and what weapons you are using. There are specific types of weapons for specific circumstances. As an example, assault rifles will strip armour from the target.
- You need to be max level ( level 30 ) in the main campaign to access the DLC. It makes more sense financially, to buy the base game and then figure out if you want to continue playing the game. It's difficult to write a generic review about the DLCs because each one is different and will appeal to different demographics. Chaos Reborn is a fun tactical ‘board’ game in which you can either manage risks in order to get what you want in Chaos Mode or use more traditional rts tactics and spend mana in Law Mode.
Basically in Chaos Mode you have to manage an RNG using verious tools when attacking or casting spells. Equipment, height, cosmic balance and spending mana can all tip the odds in your favour. In Law Mode creatures & wizards have hitpoints and attack causes damage to them whilst you cast spells by spending mana with Equipment giving advantages in combat & spell casting. Both modes have merit and are fun to play & you can select the best one to suit your style of play.
The graphics are great, the creatures are varied and many have special abilities that add to the strategic elements along with the various bits of equipment you can pick up along the way. All this means battles are varied, gripping, and anyone who leans some basic tactics can win.
As for the gameplay itself, there are a number of modes to keep you occupied whether it be friendlies, league matches, or jumping into the more RPG based Realms. You can create Custom battles to fight your online friends, or call them for help in a Realm battle.
So, to conclude, Chaos Reborn really does have something for a lot of gamers and I highly recommend it.

It's amazing how much personality a colored font and some clever placement can provide to plain text...
Basically, you play as a fire elemental spirit quasi-AI tasked with protecting four locations.  The game is broken into game days that involve visiting each of the four locations, solving whatever problems might be in that location on that day.
At first, the game lays on the computer metaphor very heavily, however, it starts to crumble rather quickly, as you, as a supposed program supposedly being kept from showing any signs of emergent AI are given surprisingly free reign to respond to various problems straight out of the gate.  The very first (non-tutorial) spirit you meet, you have the option to destroy it on sight, call for backup, or bargain with it to answer riddles to get it to leave peacefully... and the guy overseeing your actions is more concerned about you learning about the concept of "chaos" than the fact that you just did something so clearly outside the parameters of your instruction to start with...
Gameplay consists entirely of clicking on text prompts.  Some are standard Visual Novel multiple choice, but a lot of them are in the text, itself, where clicking on text results in a different word being shown (as seen in the trailer).  There are no "continue" buttons, however, so most of the time, one of the lines of text is the "continue" text, and others are "more information" text, and sometimes, you're making a choice between which set of text you are functionally asking a question about, and which you are ignoring when you thought it was just going to be a line that changes to a different description when you clicked on it.
The game features several puzzle-like elements, the primary one of which is that you need to guess the elemental affinity of whatever spirit is causing problems to deal with them.  There is a "matter", which is one of the four Classic Greek elements, plus "light" and "dark" thrown in, and a "motive", which is the primary emotion or purpose of the spirit, which includes "order", "chaos", "love", "fear", "life", and "death".  Oftentimes, it's telegraphed pretty clearly, but when it isn't, the game basically just stops until you retry over and over and eventually get it right.  There aren't any additional hints to help you along, outside of closing the game, going to the forums, and asking for help directly.  There was only one instance I had to resort to plugging in permutations until I was told I guessed right, though, but it was still rather annoying.
Different methods of dealing with problems result in different status changes.  You can "learn" new matters and motives for yourself, which basically amounts to a MegaMan-like ability to copy powers from other spirits you interact with.  You also have an affection meter with several important characters, which is tested near the end of the game to have more beneficial ways of dealing with various problems.
There are in-game achievements (but they don't have any on Steam) to encourage playing through multiple times to try every possible path, although I don't really have the will to do so, myself.
As an odd side-note, this game may be the only accidentally "homonormative" game I've ever played.  The only characters actually displayed in relationships with other characters are all in homosexual relationships.  Even Janet (one of your character's creators, and a 16-year-old) lives with a single mother with no other parent ever mentioned.  Of course, I haven't talked to the creator, but I at least presume that's just an accidental quirk of someone wanting to add LGBT stuff in, but forgetting to actually show any other relationships.

Wow. All I can say is wow.
I should just say this game is a horrific piece of garbage and end it there, but no, I'm gonna do my job and tell you why you should stay as far away from this terrible game.
In Gabe Newell Simulator we play as Gabe Newell (DUH). We finally decide to release Half Life 3 and aliens take it away, so it's up to us to get it back.
Apart from the JPEG screenshot of the game story at the start of the game and the final level, there is no dialogue whatsoever. The graphics in the game are some of the worst graphics I have ever seen. All of it is just slapped up unity assets and that's it. The game has massive texture pop ins and sometimes the entire level disappears.
The gameplay is probably one of the worst third person shooters I have ever seen. You have an option of 4 guns which all do pretty much the same damage expect for the UMP which does basically nothing. You can't fire from your hip so you have to aim down sights. Gaben controls like a tank and every movement you make is clunky and unresponsive.
There is no sound effects what so ever. There is one song in Level 4 and gun sounds, but apart from that it's dead silence, so be prepared to be alone with your inner thoughts when you play this game.
The game has 6 levels in total and two endings, but you can see the alternative ending in the level select screen so you don't have to replay the game twice. To complete the entire game it took me 40 minutes and there is no replay value whatsoever so don't expect anything after the first playthrough.
In the end I can safely say Gabe Newell Simulator is the worst game I have played in my entire life and yes it tops my previous contender Slaughtering Grounds. This game is an abomination and proves the fact that there is no quality control in Greenlight. Stay far away from this garbage.

In short, Ori and the Blind forest is a beautiful game, and I mean that in both aesthetically and from a design point. It is a wonderfully enjoyable game all the way through, and if you are a fan of metroid-vania, or games with superb production values you owe it to yourself to buy this game. Even if you aren't a fan of metroid-vania games, it's still worth at least considering.
I'm going to start with the visuals. I expect you've seen the screenshots, but they don't do the game justice. You really have to see the game in motion in all its glory to really appreciate just how good it looks. It's easily one of the best looking games I have ever played, everything is incredibly vibrant and extremely well animated, everything just looks alive and about as real as a 2D "painted graphics) game can.
The gameplay is solid. It doesn't do anything revolutionary, but what it does it does very well. Your character handles extremely well, much like a heavier and less "glidey" Meat Boy. A controller would be ideal, but the game is very manageable with a keyboard and mouse. The combat early is not particularly interesting, although it is useful during the sections while you are platforming and fighting at the same time. Later on though once you get some new abilites the combat becomes much more interesting and engaging.
The production values and overall atmosphere are stunning. For a 2D platformer it is very immersive, most of the story presented in a voiceover that doesn't interrupt gameplay, and the few cinematics that there are very compelling and well placed to give you time to rest after a stressful section. The story is simple, but well presented and engaging. Characters, despite almost none of them talking are still expressive through excellent animations and facial expressions. Finally, the soundtrack is fantastic. It perfectly compliments what's happening on screen and adds a lot of emotion to the whole game. I would gladly purchase the OST if it was for sale.
You'll get somewhere from 7-9 hours of gameplay from your first playthrough. If you are determined to gather every collectable, then it'll probably take closer to 11 hours, although be warned, there are areas that you cannot return to after having beaten. Replay value isn't fantastic unless you like speedrunning or achievment-hoarding, but even so I would still recommend getting this game, at the very least when it's on sale. I have no regrets buying Ori and the Blind Forest, and found it was absolutely worth the $20.

The Warhammer 40K universe is an extremely hostile and angry place. Like a Marketing meeting with no beer budget, everyone is perpetually at war with everyone else. Contrary to expectation, the source of all this rage and conflict is not Asian Telemarketers who like phoning up at dinner time offering the latest asinine mobile phone deal, but mysterious malevolent entities known only as the Chaos Gods who have cursed the universe to eternal enmity.
The Chaos Gods live in an alternate dimension known as the Warp where the Laws of Nature do not apply. For example, real-estate in the Warp is actually affordable and Investment Bankers are honest. From the Warp, Chaos Gods secretly fund all manner of evil projects to induce insanity and corrupt society. Projects such as Uwe Boll movies,
and
. Not to mention truly evil stuff like Electronic Arts, the MPAA and the Republican Party.
The story of Space Marine begins in epic fashion with a massive Ork invasion on the Imperial Forge World Graia. Naturally the Imperials are upset about this because Forge Worlds are not only responsible for manufacturing Titan War Machines it's also where they manufacture items for Imperial Gift Shops throughout the Empire. Best-selling items such as the "I Love The Emperor" bobbleheads and the "Emperor Protects" brown underpants that are extremely popular with the Imperial Guard.
An Ork invasion is no joke. These ornery and irascible Orks are like a force of nature, unleashed on hapless worlds they leave nothing behind but woe, devastation and mountains of insurance claims. Just like an angry visit from the mother-in-law whom you've 'forgotten' to invite to your Christmas Party, but not as bad.
To quell the threat of the Orks, the Imperium send in the Ultramarines Chapter of the Adeptus Astartes aka the Space Marines. And by 'Space Marines' they really mean 'Space Marine'. As the lone hero Captain Titus you get two BFFs who tag along on the mission, but they don't do much fighting and serve mainly to ask silly questions and clarify plot points in cutscenes so you know what's going on.
The Ultramarines have an organisational theme similar to that of the Roman Legions but with some differences. Your companions have names like Sidonus and Leandros but sadly no Bigusdickus. Also, Captain Titus while happy to charge into battles with overwhelming odds fortunately refrains from saying vacuous things like "On my signal, unleash Hell!" and constantly asking people around him if they are entertained every time he kills something. Nor does he resort to childishly throwing Communications Devices when things look grim.
Space Marine would have been an amazing game if not for the poorly designed healing mechanic. Healing is accomplished by 'Executing' an enemy which begins a short but satisfying cutscene of Titus eviscerating his foe, however Titus is not invulnerable during this cutscene which means he continues to take damage and may be dead or almost dead at the end of it. So when seriously low on health, Titus transforms into Sam Fisher and the game goes into stealth mode where you creep around trying to find a careless victim who has wandered away from his friends. This happens more often than it should. Very lame and not honourable behaviour worthy of a Space Marine.
With a mixture of gunplay and melee, an epic storyline and a beloved IP in the Warhammer 40K universe, there are many reasons to like Space Marine. Just played it again, this time without all the excitement I had when it was first released, and some of the game's shortcomings are very much more evident. While gameplay is solid, the shooting to melee transition is smooth, although a little forced. The weapons and tactics are pretty simple and straight forward but fun nonetheless.
My real problem with the game is that if you're a fan of the Warhammer 40k games, the story has major flaws. So obvious that you wonder if who ever wrote the story knew the lore at all, or even had it checked. The game basically takes place in a parallel universe where all the finer points of the Warhammer 40k lore are just wrong. Off the top of my head, mistakes such as:
The Ultramarines (especially the 2nd Company), was a poor choice considering the Chapter's fanatical adherence to the Codex. There is no way Titus or Sidonus would have made it that far up the chain of command. Leandros is the only real Ultramarine.
Drogan shouldn't have been dealing with a "Warp Device" if he was Ordo Xenos, he should have been Malleus or they should not have mentioned any particular Ordo at all.
The final scene with the second Inquisitor, Thrax, who arrives with a Black Templar escort is wrong too. The Black Templar don't get along with the Inquisition. If anything, he should have come with an escort of Sisters of Battle, because he should probably have been Ordo Hereticus.
I know I sound like I'm just whining, but the greatest aspect of Warhammer is the rich and complex lore, and this game doesn't seem to give a damn.

After playing the second installment in the Runner series and loving it to bits, I was enticed to buy the original, and am very sorry to say that this game does not hold up. I'll refrain from comparing this game to the sequel as much as possible during this review in order to keep things fair.
To start off. This game looks bad and sounds boring. I can't comprehend as to why the developer would want to keep commander video as a 2D pixelart sprite, and have the rest of the world in a disgusting looking, 3D, roblox-esque style. It would be much better if it were all just pixelart. To make matters worse, the music,  which is supposed to be one of the game's main features, just doesn't mix well. The best description I can give it is that is sounds flat. The little chimes that play as you surpass every obstacle make it sound like a toddler bashing his xylophone at random, unfitting moments. There are upgrades you collect in each level which increase your mutliplier, and make the music climax, but that's the only redeeming factor about this bad soundtrack. Particularly, during the first boss battle, I was stuck listening to the same loop over and over and over again, for about 20 minutes. This made the battle downright boring.
Whilst I'm discussing the boss battle, I need to bring up something that's downright shamefull about this game: The fact that it breaks the golden rule of good video game etiquette. That rule being "
". During the entire game, you spend your time looking to the right of the screen, watching out for obstacles. The fact that these obstacles move from the right side to the left means you have enough time to react and avoid those obstacles. This boss battle broke that mechanic, and sent obstacles towards me from just a couple of pixels infront of my character. The game stopped being something that could be compared to "The Impossible Game" and more like "I Wanna Be The Guy", where winning was no longer about how skilled you are, but about how you can remember exactly when you need to perform a precise action.
I suggest you purchase the sequel, and forget this game even exists.

If you are looking for a challengeless, but also mostly featureless standard time management game, then Gnomes Garden may be a suitable pick—a lot more so than Gnomes Garden 1 was.
In the world of casual games, it is frequent to meet a sequel that changes little compared to its predecessor. But Gnomes Garden 2 takes it even a step further, as it is practically the exact same game Gnomes Garden 1 was.
Not that the first one was too complex to begin with, they both have the most barebones time/resource management formula: order 1-3 workers to collect four resource types, then spend them on upgrading production facilities or removing various road obstacles.
Other sequels at least pretend to experiment with new additions, but Gnomes Garden 2 doesn’t even try to be anything but a carbon copy. This is most obvious at the last stage: holding a banquet to celebrate restoring your kingdom made sense in the first game, but here it is supposed to be the last battle against an evil queen; the developers didn’t even bother to come up with a new finale.
On the plus side, the other stages have new level design, and I have to admit, they were a lot more fun this time around, mostly because the difficulty in resource placement and in target times was a lot more lenient. This resulted in a more casual, but also more fun game.

Gnomes Garden 2 is a casual strategy game developed by Jerzie and Creobit. For the players familiar with Hercules series, they will feel right at home.
The game plot is about the gnome princess and her attempt to stop the troll queen.
Gnomes Garden 2 essentially focuses on four resources: food, wood stone and magic crystals. All those resources are either found on the map or generated by buildings in each level. The game essentially revolves around the workers that move from their hut to either resources or resource camps.
The game is very simplistic in terms of graphics and the music is enjoyable although it can be quite annoying after a while.
Gnomes Garden 2 is essentially a puzzle. You have limited time to achieve certain objectives while deciding what to build first and how to minimize time spent on tasks since each task can take a couple of seconds. The idea is to complete before the time runs out and achieve three stars during each level. Unfortunately, the issue is that the game has very limited gameplay and after about 12 levels you pretty much lose all the novelty except for the special powers.
The special powers are boosts used during the game to do things such as stop time or make your workers much faster than before.
The game also has steam cards and in-game achievements for certain milestones.
Overall, I would say Gnomes Garden 2 is a nice game but unfortunately originality which makes it dull after a couple of levels. I would recommend it if you can get it at a reduction price, although there are other titles which fit the category much better.

The evil Troll Queen sent the Gnome Princess to a destroyed land. Will she manage to restore everything and show the wrong to the Troll Queen?
I must say that I've bought this game because I enjoyed the first one, the achievements are easy and there is trading cards, though they're not still dropping as not implemented yet. And there is no change in the gameplay for this one, so, don't mind my lazyness, I'll copy/paste that part from the first game review.
Like for 12 Labours of Hercules, the main character isn't helping at all. In other words, it's the servants that are doing all the work. Gnomes Garden 2 is a casual time management game where you have workers that are gathering resources needed (food, wood, stone and crystals), building mines (for the stone and crystals), farms and windmills (for the food), workshop (for the wood), upgrading these for a better production and repairing routes and other objectives (like light a fire or activate portals). However, the servants can be helped by witches (needed for some objectives - they can restore trees, plant them, activate portals, make the trolls or the sleeping golems disappear, grow lilypads) and firemen (helping objective plants to grow or to scare the little monster that will incapacitate your witch or servant from doing their jobs for a few seconds). And you'll repeat that for 50 levels.
However, there are temporary bonus, regenerating over time, that can be activated : run faster (your minions move faster), work faster (less time for the building to give the resources) and stop time (the timer is frozen for a limited time). And these are very handy if you want to reach the three stars. Indeed, you have a timer. If you go past a star, you're loosing it. The less time you spent, the more likely you'll keep three stars. And as it's an achievement, you're also motivated. Nothing is wrong to loose one or two in the first run, so that you can try different strategies for the level. However, keep in mind that sometimes, you need to manage tightly your resources: you may be lacking some of them when they're needed and can't advance anymore (example: no more stones for a hole in the road - the building that could have given you the resource is behind this hole and there is no other road to it - you're doomed to restart). One of the good points is that you're not limited in the tasks done by the servant, if you want to gather 3 woods and 2 foods, you can check them without restriction (compared to 12 Labours of Hercules where you couldn't indicate more than 3 tasks). Also, I found some improvement: the task that will be done is highlighted AND finally, the resplenishing for the bonus isn't no more affected by the use of another. On the downside, the timer bonus is now very slow to be full.
However, I found the levels more easier than in Gnomes Garden, as I only restarted a couple of levels and not many of them. I don't know if it's because I was more aware of how the game worked or not, but well, I finished it much faster if I compare the time: 5,8h against 7,8h. Well, when trading cards will be available, my time will raise.
As you can see, the gameplay isn't hard per se, it's just a matter of being efficient and to make the right choices (no need to upgrade a building to the maximum if the current level is sufficient or to upgrade the house - I've made the majority of the levels with two workers only). However, you don't have any other characters that can help. It's just the minions, not even the princess is present in the level to do something.
I found the graphics being more polished than in the first one. I don't know why but the map looked better, the presentation of the objectives were less harsh and I found the buildings and characters more alive. I don't know if it's a question of colors or a question of being used. However, the objectives in the bottom of the screen is still confusing, though now that I know of it, it seems less inconvenient than in the first game.
The soundtrack is also nice.
But while I preferred Gnomes Garden 2 to the first game, there is still the magic missing from 12 Labours of Hercules. The gameplay didn't improved at all apart for rebuilding a cable car and a statue of the king, the rest is the same as in Gnomes Garden. So, while I'm still recommending this game for any casual time management lover, I would advised you to wait for a real discount or for a bundle.

Squirreltopia Reveiw
48/100
Visuals 14/20
-Art Design 8/10
The art style is great. A semi-minimalistic styling befitting the squirrel theme. Color usage is exciting yet not overly obnoxious.
-Graphics 6/10
The graphics are on the low end to fit the minimalistic retro-call-back art style. There are no real graphic options, as the art style of the game is of greater value than the graphics.
Audio 5/20
-Soundtrack 2/10
The soundtrack is cute and adorable at first, yet repetitive. While it fits the theme quite well, it quickly becomes either unnoticeable white noise or annoying. Sadly, it is hard to tell if there is a soundtrack or simply one song on repeat. If there is a full soundtrack then it sounds all the same.
-Sound effects 3/10
The sound effects are mostly fitting, especially of the minimalist semi-retro theme. Sadly, like the soundtrack, they make little impression and can be summed up as white noise as well.
Gameplay 9/20
-Mechanics 6/10
The game mechanics are fairly simple. Highly basic minimalist platformer calling back to retro gaming. You run, you jump, and you try to stay on the platforms and out of hazards. Nothing too impressive or inivative.
-Controls 3/10
Controls are okay. You move left and right and have a jump button. Overall pretty simple. There is a momentum to the character. The more you move towards a direction the progressively faster you go. Sadly, sometimes the jump button or directional input seemed unresponsive. Mostly the jump button, as the directional input could be summed up with the player needing to adjust to the momentum of the character initially. Sometimes jumps were completely failed simply by the fact the character did not jump when the jump button was pressed.
Story 14/20
-Theme 7/10
The theme is adorable and consistent. Squirrels. Things are trees, enemies are decently understandable by either being nature related or simply adorable.
-Plot 7/10
The plot is simple and summed up instantly with the initial cut scene. An evil squirrel, defined as “Shadow-Tail” in out of game descriptions, uses a machine to steal a bunch of squirrels and gems that you apparently must rescue. On death, your squirrel's color pallet seems to change insinuating a different squirrel.
Design 6/20
-Difficulty 4/10
The difficulty is suppose to be high yet due to being cheap. Sadly, it is low, even on hard. All the difference between easy and hard is hard has no checkpoints and has a timer that appears to count up.
-Level design 2/10
The level design initially is pretty good. Very simple, and the best part is it introduces different gameplay mechanics such as enemies and obstacles very well over time. The hub world looks good, yet a lot of various random worlds are cut off, and inaccessible. Initially it is believed that they are unlocked somehow. Unfortunately this never seems to come as not every level is able to be completed apparently. Levels four and seven both featured gameplay mechanics that were set up in a way as to be theoretically impossible to pass by the implemented game mechanics. There are rumored boss fights, but with only four levels and one minigame available to play with, they are no where to be found. At best, the game and level design are made as youtube-fodder style troll-platformers.
In summery: This game is carried by it's art style alone. Everything else simply kills it. It is a terrible waste of time, money, and harddrive space. Levels at worst feel like they cannot be completed by fault of game design, and at best, feel like an obnoxious bit that you never want to go through twice. Similar to how people discuss the water temple.
