No, just no.
First and foremost, this is not a game; it's an on-rails interactive short story. I knew this prior to purchasing this title (which was on sale at the time), but I was intrigued when I heard how innovative it was with its narrative presentation. However, I discovered that the "innovation" was simply a non-linear story offering virtually no exposition. And here comes the counter argument: "Oh-no! The developer didn't hand you an explanation on a silver platter because you were too lazy and stupid to actually explore what the story had to offer!" Nope. I did a second playthrough with developer commentary enabled, played the prequel Gravity Bone, and was still none the wiser.
Now I'm not saying that these types of narratives can't work, but here's the problem with a lot of these stories: when very little exposition is given about the characters and how they relate to the world around them, this strips away any humanity the characters would have had, which in turn makes it difficult for the audience to have any profound connection with them. Just because a story is intentionally confusing, does not make it good.

Naval Action is a gorgeous game with a lot of potential, some of it front and center and already realised.
The game is an interesting mix of gameplay styles. The ship to ship combat is streamlined but deep. Requiring you to not only use the wind to your advantage, but also the waves of the ocean itself. You must navigate successfully, and command your crew to prioritize tasks onboard. All of this culiminating in an epic and tense battle, with the thunder of cannons and smoke filling the air.
The gameplay itself harkens back to Pirates! as well as elements that remind me of EVE (massive map, crafting and trading).
Players choose a nation to start with, which will determine your starting location (U.S, U.K, Dutch, Sweden, Spain, Denmark & Pirates). Each nation has unique challenges based upon number of ports and geographical location. Interestingly enough I jumped on the French side, and lo-and-behold, most of the players were speaking French!
Once you start in your home port you can grab missions from the admiralty and head out to the open sea (which is an absolutely massive map of the Caribbean). Once in open sea you can engage battles that are under way, other players (if you're on a PvP server) or head towards your mission objectives.
Eventually you gain gold, experience and promotions. Allowing you to build, buy, or capture better ships.
PRO:
- Fantastic looking
- Authentic Historical ships
- Immersive weather and large map
- Crafting (seems decent so far)
- Tactically deep
- Map does not show where you are, requiring you to use visual markers and a compass (I think this could be a PRO or CON)
CON:
- UI is a bit rough at the moment but is fairly functional
- No tutorial on gunnery, crafting or trading
- Somewhat steep learning curve
- Map does not show where you are, requiring you to use visual markers and a compass (I think this could be a PRO or CON)
All in all, the UI is rough but the gameplay is solid. I was extremely skeptical of this title heading in, but after logging a few hours today I can safely say this game is already very fun and once it gets polished and more ships added in, it will be very very good.

This was a kickstarter project!? It is no surprise that the Kickstarter for Original Sin 2 met its goals five times over within 12 hours.
AAA+++ production, major updates to the game on re-release and provided FREE to original owners (other developers take notes!!!)
Not only is this one of the best RPGs I have ever played but I fully support Larian Studios in their future endevaors. They listen to their community, they provide updates to year old games without trying to bilk their customers for more money, and they have made one heck of an amazing game!
PROS:
-Incredible game engine
-Excellent combat mechanics
-NON LINEAR questlines. You can complete most quests via several different methods.
-Almost ALL characters can be attacked/stolen from/killed. This can lead to a variety of methods for completing quests (although on rare occasion you might render a side quest incompletable if you kill everyone involved but this will not hinder your progress in the main story).
-LOTS of content! (My one playthrough, skipping all dialogues, was just over 80 hours).
-Solid graphics
-Solid voice acting
NEUTRALS:
-There seems to be a rich backstory, but I play mainly for the mechanics and not for the plot so I skipped all the dialogue/etc (and still spent around 80 hours for a single playthrough).
-Skill/stat distribution is in need of a complete overhaul (the EE changes did not help much):
--Primary stats are virtually useless (esp past 10 points at which point you can use all related gear).  The only worthwhile stat otherwise is Constitution for HP (or Perception for archers). Mages don't need perception since wands always have 100% hit chance.
--Skills are oddly distributed and severely lacking. Most builds will require 2 or maybe 3 skills total; you will have far more than enough skill points for this leaving a lot of leftover points with no real skills to take. FOR EXAMPLE: An archer build needs 5 bow (or xbow) and 5 marksman.....thats it. No other skill will improve the archers dps, and if you choose to take a school of magic then you are no longer shooting your bow... the only other thing is to take Lucky Charm, but even then it just gives you offense rating which only equates to CHANCE to hit (you won't miss much, but I guess this is a minor dmg buff still)
--The stat/skill/talent system is inherently fine; the problem is with the current layout of abilities and stats. The talents also need a serious overhaul, with particular focus on talents gained at skill levels 3 and 5 to promote more build variety.
***These are issues that would be a major deal in competitive multiplayer, but since D:OS 1 is a single player/coop game these issues are VERY MINOR and will hopefully be fixed for D:OS 2's competitive multiplayer component.
CONS:
-A variety of skills are far too similar, with certain classes simply being better. FOR EXAMPLE: Freezing Touch and Petrifying touch are identical skills, except "Frozen" provides an addition +10 armor to the target which Petrify does not. This means petrify is better in almost all instances over frozen as a status modifier.
Instead, the different schools should be functionally opposites. This is well executed with Cold and Fire magic:  Frozen (unable to act, -10% cold resist, +10% fire resist) -> Chilled (same buffs as frozen) -> normal (no buffs) -> Warmed (-10% fire resist, +10 cold resist) -> Burning (DoT, -10% fire resist, +10% cold resist).  The function of fire magic and cold magic is distinctly different, and one can negate frozen by intentionally firing/heating up the target and vice versa.
Unfortunately, not all schools of magic operate on this principle and consistency would go a long way (especially for competitive mp coming in the sequel).
-Blacksmithing is almost worthless.
-Crafting is boring although it does provide minor stat buffs.
GG!

'Dream' tries to tackle a very ambitious project of exploring the dreams of a struggled (young?) man. He loves to dream and reflect about them, and a big part of the game results in wandering/exploring three dream hubs, each with their own themes and challenges. The more you explore, the more you'll get to know about the character...
While I really do like this concept, I didn't really like the game that much.
For starters, I didn't really like the character in general. He sounds too old (for being a young character), he's bland and overall pretty boring. As for the dream hubs, they might be big, but they are sooo boring and have little actual content. The 6 side dreams are a hit or miss as well (which are smaller levels within the dreams).
Each hub comes with a mandatory (or a series of) puzzles, some of these were just horrible and tedious (just look up the conveyor belt puzzle if you don't believe me).
And don't get me started on the bugs and glitches. Thankfully I didn't encounter gamebreaking bugs, but I did have some serious problems with the key bindings. For some reason (I use an AZERTY keyboard), 'Q' wouldn't work as a primary key for strafing to the left (after a lot of trial and error, it did work as a secondary keybinding).
In conclusion: It's a nice concept, just poorly executed, the music is very good, and is probably the only thing the devs did right... speaking of the devs, after a couple of patches, they were just gone...

Codename CURE is a Source Engine mod, so that means some things are similar to other games that have used this engine (Team Fortress 2, Half Life, GMOD, Portal 1 and 2)
I really like the fact that it legitimately instills the fact that survival is impossible without the help of others.
Most of the things I've seen in my hour of playing it has been teamwork, good mechanics, and a really great game in the making.
What I've seen is that, in my opinion, is that every class has it's strength and weaknesses, and team composition really matters. A team full of Snipers won't do good, because not only is this not TF2, the Snipers are weak on really close range.
Furthermore, some things may need to be changed, such as the melee mechanic, gun animations, and zombie damage.
While this may be on the list of the developers, I can bear with it being in the game for now, because it's in Early Access, and the developers are getting feedback on what the players like and dislike about the game, and act accordingly.
If you're sick of teams of players with little to no cooperation with each other in similar games like these, then Codename CURE just might be the game for you.

is an enjoyable game. But it needs a good amount of work to make it stand out from any of the other numerous zombie Co-Op Survial games out in the market already. As it stands in it's current itteration in February of 2017.
Most of the assests being used from Half-Life 2 have been changed. However, many of the enviormental objects, textures, and sounds have remained stock, and unchanged. Which kills the immersion of this being little more than a Half-Life 2 mod. If the developers have simply changed all of, if not most of the stock Half-Life 2 sounds. It would go a long way into making the game more immersive.
There are some noticible bugs still, which can be forgiven since it's in Early Access and if they address them in the future. So it's to be expected of a constantly updated product, and since the game is completely free, I have even less of a problem with them being there currently.
However, sometimes certain objectives won't activate upon pressing an important button, elevators that are needed to escape an area will not always appear and things like that. Zombies also have very basic path finding AI. If you place a resupply crate or an object in a doorway, for instance. Than zombies will get hung up on them, and rarely be able to navigate around them, making certain waves really easy to survive.
However, these are the only real major bugs that I've encountered in the time I've sunk into the game. And for product in Early Access, it's really comemdable.
The game does get static and boring after awhile, since the classes are all pretty run-of-the-mill typical stuff you'd expect in a zombie co-op game. With gadgets that barely make them distinguishable from their fellow squad mates. And the vanilla maps are very basic, drab city, urban scapes. With very little varity but to go from Point A to Point B type of thing.
All-in-all, I do reccomend the game to anyone looking to find a bit of fun with a group of friends for a few hours, with something a little different than games like
or
.
As it stands, I'd give it a 5/10 rating, mainly because the game is just "
" at best, it's not doing much to stand out from the countless other co-op Survival games out there. However, I do applaud the developers for showing care in their creation, and it is fun no matter what criticims can be lobbied against it. And for that, I commend them whole-heartedly.

No, just no.
First and foremost, this is not a game; it's an on-rails interactive short story. I knew this prior to purchasing this title (which was on sale at the time), but I was intrigued when I heard how innovative it was with its narrative presentation. However, I discovered that the "innovation" was simply a non-linear story offering virtually no exposition. And here comes the counter argument: "Oh-no! The developer didn't hand you an explanation on a silver platter because you were too lazy and stupid to actually explore what the story had to offer!" Nope. I did a second playthrough with developer commentary enabled, played the prequel Gravity Bone, and was still none the wiser.
Now I'm not saying that these types of narratives can't work, but here's the problem with a lot of these stories: when very little exposition is given about the characters and how they relate to the world around them, this strips away any humanity the characters would have had, which in turn makes it difficult for the audience to have any profound connection with them. Just because a story is intentionally confusing, does not make it good.

Thirty Flights of Game Design:
I you are into more modern games that force-feed you story, you probably won't like this game. It takes a quite different approach by explaining the plot through small chunks of information, forcing the player to piece together the events that happen. The result of this is a confusing and interesting series of small levels that  continue the plot. This game is meant to be a ride more than a game I would say, though there are game elements involved through small objectives or the possibility of death.
For five dollars, this game is an interesting experience. I wasn't sure what to think when I beat it, but I liked that feeling. All I can say is that if you are a fan of interesting game design, you must play this game. If not, meh, I enjoyed it a lot. I think it's worth it.

Brilliant, as long as you know what you're getting...
First and foremost this is more a short interactive story than a game, there's not a lot of player input. The game mainly consists of moving from one scene to the next with story unfolding through jumpcuts. Now if "short interactive story" hasn't put you off already than buy this game, granted for 5 euro it may seem steep, you'll get through it in about 15 minutes the first time.
As a story this is incredibly well put together, you'll play through it the first time and kind of know what's going on, and then you'll probably end up playing through it maybe 2 to 3 times more as you try to figure out the sequence of events. Plus the games wacky art style and music are more than worth the price of admission. I'm honestly a huge fan of this game.
On a side it comes with the prequel "Gravity Bone" which is also awesome and features the same type of style, so there's two reasons to buy it. However you can download "Gravity Bone" from the net for free and "test run" how you feel about this type of game if you're nervous about spending the 5 euro. But honestly I'd recommend buying this.

I have to say that this game came out of nowhere for me. As much as I search for gaming news I didn't hear a single thing about this. I have to say it was a pleasant surprise. It's a metroidvania style platformer that is medium difficulty with a couple of difficulty spikes near the end of each dungeon.
First thing that is noticed is the games high production values. Everything from audio to visual presentation is stunning, making the world look and sound gorgeous. Techical wise, for me it takes pretty long for the game to start up or shut down and I had some frame skipping here and there but nothing drastic.
I enjoyed the story for its presentation. It has a storybook feel and they manage to make characters feel more than one dimensional with how little screentime they actually have.
It has the basic structure of its genre, which means, that it gives you an area which you can't complete fully unless you want to backtrack into it with abilities that are given later in the game. The game is over after completing 3 different dungeons in a set order. Ori and the Blind Forest can be finished in less than 3 hours but chances are it is going to take you a bit longer on a first playthrough.
Your primary way of attacking is a homing attack which tracks enemies on a certain proximity. You can upgrade its properties via experience points. Later on Ori can acquire abilities such as double jumps and glide. Most unique ability you get is bash, which enables you to use enemies and projectiles as a free airdash when near them. It also resets air options, making some interesting platforming situations.
Like Super Metroid, this game has a good potential for speed runs since it's comparatitively short and you don't need to grind for experience points if you so choose.
If this game is on sale - buy it. If it isn't? Buy it anyway.

Divinity: Original Sin (Enhanced Edition) is essentially, a revised version of Divinity: Original Sin (Classic). The game's interface has been simplified, the gameplay has subtly been altered and the game input has been optimized for use with a controller. In addition, new game difficulty settings have been added. Those are some key changes to the game. While those may not seem like a big deal, it drastically changes the feeling of the game. Realistically, by playing this version you're getting the console port version of the game but with pc's strong visual options.
What is Divinity: Original Sin? Divinity: Original Sin is a beautiful role playing game featuring strategic turned based party combat in an imaginative medieval setting, all while introducing you to a unique dual-dialouge system between 2 heroes you create at the beginning of the game and play through the game with.
What is a "Dual-Dialogue" System? Imagine playing the game as 2 characters, you prioritize one character as your main character, so you think for him/her and make decisions for them on their behalf but there is what makes it different from other role playing games - your secondary character has a say in your choices, they can agree with you or disagree with you and if they disagree with you, then that choice can change the out come of the quest or the storyline as a whole. You cannot control them but they may change the mind of an npc for example which may make you angry. So think of it as simulating playing co-op with a real human and being able to communicate with them on making choices throughout the game's timeline. Similar to old school dungeons and dragons pen and paper games in that respect.
I feel that is one of the game's main selling features as it makes the game very unique.
The graphics of Divinity: Original Sin are beautiful, it's a modern looking rpg with an old soul and it reflects on the art style it possesses. I love Larian for this.

BIT.TRIP RUNNER is a simplistic music platformer and quite literally one of the best indie games I've ever played. The game essentially involves a few rudimentary controls and your character is continually running forward and you have to work your way past obstacles in order to reach the finish all the while collecting gold bricks (if you are a completionist). The game is very simple and it introduces you to the level design and challenges bit by bit giving great progression and understanding, teaching you things like jumping/crouching/kicking in subsequent stages. The biggest draw to this game is the superb music and how your actions since on a fixed route play a melody making the game one part platformer, and one part musical experience (think timing of the actions akin to hitting the keys for a guitar hero style game only much more creative). I cannot stress how great a game this is, and as indicated by the sequels I am not alone in this sentiment. Its low price tag and easy to get into platforming makes this a full recommendation for fans of platforming genre and those only seeking a casual play of it.

Naval Action is a hard core, age of sail naval warfare pseudo-simulator, emphasis on the Hard Core.
Firstly, it nails the whole alone on the ocean feel (when you get away from busy ports). Part of the gameplay is learning to navigate using only a map and compass. If you're looking for a real Age of Sail feeling type of game, this is it.
What Naval Action is not: easy. Naval Action isn't a Pirates of the Caribbean game and takes basically no cues from the movie franchise. Naval Action is more like Master & Commander than Pirates of the Caribbean. You could hunt a single enemy player for hours before engaging in an hour-long gunnery duel and boarding action.
Speaking of fighting, the combat is challenging, but fair, and the game doesn't try and hold your hand when you start. It takes a while to learn how to fight with the wind dictating your movement and with guns that have poor accuracy and slow moving projectiles, but nothing is as satisfying as landing a complete broadside and watching your enemy's armor become Swiss Cheese.
Notice that I said Pseudo-Simulator. It's hard to be an actual simulator and be fun, so there are some player gimmes, like teleporting between cities, but more complicated sailing manuevers such as controlling your yards individually and the accurate sailing model give a sense of complexity missing from other naval themed games.
However, there are two major caveats that Game-Labs gave up: The first is that you never have to sail at true speed throughout the Caribbean. There's an Open World overmap which you'll probably spend most of your time. In the Open World, the entire map is available for you to journey to but you can't fight in it and can't interact fully with your ship, and time goes faster, which in turn makes it seem like you aren't travelling at a snail's pace across the absolutely massive Open World map. When you reach a battle (either by attacking or being attacked), you'll transfer to a tactical Battle map where you move a true speed at true time and most of the simulator elements become available. If you've ever played Star Trek Online, think Sector Space vs. System Space.
The other caveat is that it is always windy. You'll never get stuck in doldrums or without a breeze, either in the strategic Open World overmap or in an instanced Battles. But that doesn't mean you can go in any direction you please, you still can't travel directly upwind, though fore-and-aft rigged ships will travel faster close-hauled than square-riggers. Yeah, you'll get to (or really, *have* to) learn some nautical sailing terms in this game, too.
The game is hard, and relatively unforgiving if you just think you can walk in and trounce the first enemy you see. Tactical planning is much more important that twitchy skill or APM. That being said, there are a ton of guides on the Game-Labs forums that will help you out on avoiding the major mistakes many players make. For good measure, I'll give you a first bit of advice: Don't go British.
Good Sailing, Captain!

Chaos Reborn has been a pleasant surprize. I picked it up thinking that it might be ok. I was mostly curious. It turns out it is actually a really good game if you like turn-based strategy with some RNG, like you would get by playing certain miniatures type games.
My advice for a new player would be to hope for the best but be prepared for the worst when summoning, moving, etc. So if the giant you summoned kills the paladin then great, but consider what your next move is if that doesn't happen.
I would also strongly recommend jumping into the online realms. I started with the campaign and then discovered the online realms later and have not gone back to the single player campaign yet. Jump into the online realms and request allies and volunteer as an ally. It's a lot of fun.
Also, when you complete a realm you keep the gear acquired and can equip it for the next realm. So as you play you upgrade. If you quit the realm you don't keep anything. The gear breaks down to armor, staves, and talismans that fit into configurations in your armor and staves and add abilities or change them. Your armor has stats for defense and offense as well as other things and your staff determines your special attack.
The online realms are rated and even in part created by players. They have to be approved by moderators though and so far I've been enjoying them. They are so far well done. They have story and very light "choose your own adventure" moments, for example, where you encounter travellers and have to decide what to do.
It is a modern version of chess with story... and of course RNG. This is my review after 58 hours in game.

This game has gotten a lot of mixed reception, so I initially passed it up. Didn't bother looking at it again until it had a free weekend on steam several weeks back.
I'm so glad I did. A year out from release, and it looks like most of the kinks have been ironed out here. Very few bugs, lots of solid gameplay improvement (especially the recent edition of loadouts). All on top of an already sweet concept executed pretty dang well.
It has its flaws - the main story doesn't exactly wrap up with much closure, and only one of the three expansions is truly something I'd recommend flat out. And yeah, if you think about what The Division represents ingame, you really are playing a shadow government agent with way too much power. Everyone you fight in this game is a US citizen, and none of them get a trial. It's touched on very briefly by one or two characters, but the narrative doesn't seriously make you question your actions. Still, as long as you can look past that, there's a lot to enjoy here.
The world that has been crafted - the desolate, frozen ghost town of Manhattan island, is a sight to behold. The little details everywhere are great; there are tidbits of lore and fluff sprinkled all over. The dark zone in particular is a treat; you really feel like it's been completely abandoned and has become a free-for-all for the few who dare enter. And there are hundreds of clothing options to change the look of your agent - all while looking like a badass prepared for anything, including the harsh weather.
The gameplay is very solid; it's your standard cover based shooter, but you still have a lot of freedom to move around, use a big variety of skills and weapons, and tailor your build to a lot of different play styles. Weapons and gear are moddable, and when you hit the level cap you really do start to consider each stat bonus carefully.
It took me about 40 hours to beat the main game and I've already sunk another 100 into the endgame content. And I still love it.
Side note on the expansions: Survival is a BLAST and I highly recommend it. Super fun and tough, games can take up to almost 2 hours, though usually are around 1.5. Underground is alright, if relatively uninteresting. Haven't tried Last Stand but I've heard it's got a lot of balance/meta problems. And I'm not that interested in PVP anyway.

six years after its release.

possibly beginning the trend of users jokingly giving over-the-top positive reviews to bad games
, and became a popular gift to troll other players with.[2] Rock, Paper,

The world of 40k is probably one of my favorites of all time. Close seconds are the worlds of Starcraft, Bioshock, and Fallout. This is a great game to be introduced to the world. You can show up knowing nothing of the world and enjoy a fun shooter. If you are a fan of the franchise then you must or already own this game.
Graphics
Solid. Not going to blow you out of the water, but stands up well enough. The art style is definetly not played with much. It is what you'd expect from a 40k game. Its dark, space apocaliptic, roman catholic, conquistador weirdness. Which is pretty awesome. Come on. You know you're kind of digging it. Oh ya, a ton of space orcs. Like a lot of them.
Gameplay
You shoot a planet, just about all of it. Like you kind of just keep going, and shooting.... and shooting. Combat is fun, and the game makes you choose which weapons you value more. Can't carry them all with you, so youre going to have to choose how you want to play. However you can change weapons almost from scene to scene, to don't be afraid to try stuff.
Sound
Sound is acceptable. I wasn't blow away from it. It did the job, it made the game feel like an action game. But I never really felt like the sound really kicked a scene up a notch. It was there, I didn't hate it. Its meh.
Story
Pretty typical space marine fare. Get dropped on a planet because the bad stuff hit the fan. You go to clean it up and things just go downhill, and downhill, and when you thought you might be close to done, things really just go downhill. I've always really been a fan of the space marine stories. You feel like it really is them against everyone. You show up to a losing fight and win it, and move on to the next fight. No thanks, no glory, you just suck it up and push on. Probably the strength of this game.
Overall score 7/10.
I gave it a seven because I felt it was worth playing even if you just enjoy shooters. The sound is pretty meh, and the graphics arent going to blow you away. But the gameplay is fun, the story is engaging and everything is kept pretty close to 40k art direction and behaviour standards. I enjoyed it and I recommend it.

Any action you try to perform is determined by luck 100% of the time so there isn’t anything remotely strategic about this game.
Want to summon a creature? It’s down to luck.
Want to cast a spell? It’s down to luck.
Want to attack an enemy? It’s down to luck.
Despite what any in-game statistics tell you, everything including your wizard seems to have 1 HP so attacks come down to who is lucky enough to make a successful attack first.
If every possible play wasn’t determined by random number generation (RNG) it could potentially be an interesting game but since it’s not you only end up wasting your time and money on this dreck.
Avoid at all costs.

Outstanding strategy game that I was hooked on from the tutorial. The game is turn based on a hex board, beginning with two wizards. Turns are spent vying for position and building strength, with the ultimate goal of taking down the rival wizard. However, not only do the individual spells have certain probabilities of success, but the casting of spells alters these probabilities. The result is a very deep and satisfying experience (even when a string of bad luck will inspire a decidedly... emotional investment in the game).
What's best is that the game gently eases the player into the complexity through a series of tutorials with optional challenges (recommended both for the challenge and a deeper understanding), which is rare to find even in simpler titles. Rounding out the package is a very attractive look, with a full 360 degree view of the battlefield and the ability to zoom in to see the great artwork on display.
Even so early on, I give this game my highest possible recommendation to anyone with even a remote interest in turn based strategy.

I've only had the privilege of playing Naval Action alpha for the month prior to early access but I've found it to be fun and it's got great potential. It's a slower paced game with moments of high drama. Players that enjoy games like Eve online, POTBS or Elite Dangerous would probably enjoy this.
Sailing the ships is a joy, the devs have really nailed that part of the game. It does take some practice to get any good at it especially the gunnery and manual sail control. You actually have to aim your shots here, there’s no tab target and use ability type stuff.
The graphics are really well done they can be taxing on some systems though and at this point the port UI still is unfinished.
The game world is large and as a result getting from A to B takes time. This gives you plenty of opportunity to chat with other players, plan you next crafting project or plot your next attacks. This may annoy players that expect things to be fast paced, others like me really enjoy a relaxing sail from island to island.
The game supports both PvE and PvP players with both types of servers available, the difference being you can’t attack other players in the open world on the PvE server.  PvP options include fighting on the open world, arena type battles and port battles for territory control.
For the less violent types there is crafting, trade and hunting NPC’s on the open world map. There’s also a rudimentary mission system, currently only simple kill NPC missions but they’re pretty challenging none the less.
One thing I must say is the game is very stable I've not had a single crash in 100 hours of play and the only bugs I've reported have been typos in the test. There’s still a lot of ideas and improvements to be added though so the next few months are going to be exciting.

... and Little Red Riding Hood said; Grandma, what big teeth you have  ....  and so Moon studios and Microsoft have given us Ori and the Blind Forest.
An adorable protagonist and a colorful visually stunning plat-former grace the store page.  What Ori and the Blind Forest truly is, is aggravation incarnate.  Released with an unfortunate number of bugs resolvable only with
.
Ori is also a mixture of well implemented and imprecise controls.   Landing on a thin vertical beam seems imprecise.   The analogue range for the Stomp move, where you press A to jump and hold the analogue stick down feels too restrictive so you wind up missing the move at critical times.
Many areas of the game depend on enemy projectiles in order for Ori to properly navigate environments.   Missing a projectile or sequence of  projectiles will result in death after death after death.  You will die numerous times in Ori and the Blind Forest.  Deaths for the average player will enumerate into the mid to high hundreds.  Ori is not Super Meat Boy and this level of frustration is not welcome.
The best parts of the game occur after obtaining new abilities and revisiting previous areas to claim previously unreachable artifacts.   Plat-forming flows magnificently here.  Entering areas for the first time should play as well but doesn't.  Thankfully the game's save system allows the player to create their own save points.  Moon studios integrated such save points seamlessly.  Save points appear as blue flames and are called soul links as they have the added function of allowing access to ability trees.  The game awards ability points through defeating enemies or like Health and Energy orbs, Ability orbs appear usually in difficult to reach places which brings us to the mapping function.   The map is comprehensive and serves it's purpose.  Not all artifacts appear but the game is a 2D plat-former built for exploring so finding all artifacts is a challenge.
Ori and the Blind forest is not a competitionist friendly game.   Completionists may be locked out from collecting all of the artifacts.  There are three areas in the game where it is possible to leave artifacts behind and never get the chance to reclaim.  That aforementioned third party utility not only allows you to fix your glitched saves but also allows re-entry into any area of the game.  Another mortal sin is showing two paths on the map.  If you go right, you get to explore.  If you go left you get an auto-save and get locked out of going right.
Shame.  Ori and the Blind Forest could of been a magnificent plat-former.  Given the number of glitches and bugs, odd design decisions, an anti-completionist mentality and aggravating game-play Ori cannot be recommended.

This is quite a wonderful game. Ori and the Blind Forest is very similar to other metroidvania games, but it excells beyond them in its amazing art style, music, and design. As far as actual gameplay, the core controls are very tight. This game also implemented some pretty neat and creative ideas I have not seen in side scrolling games previous to this.
To me there are a lot of metroidvania games that have confusing maps or require way too much backtracking in an unfun way. This game however directs you nicely to the next destination without treating you like a dummy. You still figure it out it just isn't convoluted.
This game has some pretty challenging segments but thanks to an absolutely amazing save system, these areas never felt frustrating or overly punishing. On the subject of the save system, you basically can save whereever you want to but it takes up a certain amount of energy to do so. This is a neat mechanic and really helps to make segments more challenging but you get through them pretty fast because you don't repeat the same easy segments over and over. The only issue with this is sometimes you might forget to save and are taken back a good ways. There are automatic save points however, so this system isn't too crazy.
The game is beautiful and worth playing for the music and graphics alone, it is wonderful that the gameplay matches the effort put into the dressings. To some the game might feel short. For me it took about 8 hours to beat, and that might be on the high side. Considering the price though, and the polish of the total product, 8 hours to me makes a solid and satisfying gaming experience.

People who say that the end game is "boiring" or "a grind" and use that to justify a bad review, I think are not RPG fans.
The primary criticism I see for this game is that the story mode, the base game is fun, and when you reach level/gear rating cap it just becomes a grind. People who think this are probably just FPS players who bought the wrong game. Make no mistake:
If you are looking for a fun shooter to play, get a different tom clancy game, this one is not like the rest. The Division is an RPG and is very similar to many others. Now if we are to look at this game from the standpoint that it is an RPG, you'll see why it is not fair to say it is bad because it is 'grindy'. Look at ANY popular (mmo)RPG title (Diablo, Runescape, Borderlands, etc) and you will find every single one is very similar to The Division in how the late game functions, in fact, I might even go as far as to say that
The Division has one of the best end games of any
out there.
Don't believe me? I'll give you an example: Diablo 3, a game considered pretty good in the RPG community has just about two end-game activity. Grinding neph rifts to get gear, and competing on leaderboards for getting fast runs on difficult greater rifts. That's literally it. But you
hear it's playerbase complaining that it is "grindy" or "gets boring" because the playerbase is RPG players, they knew exactly what they were getting into. Compare this to the division, late game activities in the Division include (with the DLCs): Dark Zone pvp loot farming, Incursion missions, survival mode (a battle royal type gamemode which is honestly really fun), large pvp objective based shooter gamemode (very similar to most fps's), Underground randomly generating dungeons, and HVT mission farming. All that and the division community STILL thinks that it is "grindy" and "gets boring beyond the story mode". People who think this game is a boring FPS, are very correct, but people who think this game is a boring RPG,
TL;DR: Buy it if you are an RPG player, don't buy it if you are an FPS player

You don't just play this game, you make a permanent decision.
Once you launch Bad Rats, your life will change forever.
I bought this game during the 2016 Winter Sale, and I thought it would be so funny because it's a meme game. That decision changed my life forever, because launching badrats.exe is basically saying that you want to be hunted down by monsters.
So, a day after I launched the exe file I found a note on the back of my house. It reads, "You will not get away with this, cat." At first I thought it was some stupid prank, but I was wrong. Later that day, at about 9:45 PM, I heard a screech and then a yell. "We're going to find you, cat!" this monster yelled to me, from a distance. I freaked out and immediately uninstalled badrats.exe from my computer, and gave it a report on Steam.
The creature's voice was now extremely angry, saying it would murder me when it found me, but it left.
One day, I was caring for my back yard, I saw this humanoid rat person climb over my fence, it roared, then charged at me. I dodged the charge, and ran into my hosue, and locked the door. The rat man was furious, and kicked down my back door. He screams, "We will find you, cat!" and left.
Haven't seen him since.

Before I even got into a dream I got stuck in a bug where I couldn't put down a painting. Just restarted the game and moved on. A couple more bugs and the relaxing pace of the game turned into confusion and frustration.
Once I did get into the dream I found that the twisting halls of the catacombs and the blurring effects of the dream's desert environment were giving me headaches and making me nausious.
On top of that the gameplay and narration is sub-par as well..
-The narration is uninspired and sometimes seems hokey the way the protagonist talks to himself
-The dream itself seemed really gimmicky - like what people try to tell you dreams are like (with random objects from your real life in random places / for some reason you're alone the whole time [from the dream I experienced]) instead of actually creating a setting that better represents how dream worlds might actually be like..
-The puzzles and dream details are arbitrary and solving them makes no real connection to the character's "journey"
-Small details like your bare feet making shoe clicking sounds on sand (and hard surfaces too), and your entire body moving in a mirror's reflection when you simply turn your head are just a few of those minor details that can really throw your opinion about the game - even though those things are none too important in the grand scheme of things. (The shoe sounds with bare feet really struck a nerve with me for some reason though :P)
I haven't been able to put more time into this game to experience a nightmare or finish the game - I wish I could at least try. I just can't get past the sickness from playing the game, let alone the bugs that break the game and/or force you to redo tasks you've already done. If I somehow get the courage and maybe take a pill for motion sickness and play the rest of this game I might edit my review, but I doubt it would turn into a recommendation. A disappointment.

Disorder has some very stressful gameplay! I just beat it and I do not have all the Steam Achievements (actually, I only have two of them). -- However, I think that my experience is still a valid one. Without any spoilers, I will have to say that the story confused me a little while all the easter eggs kept me intrigued in whatever was going on. The game has a certain ambiance that becomes more prevalent as the game proceeds. Honestly, the last stage took me by surprise and even had me on the edge of my seat! (Definitely bringing on the horror vibe that reminded me a lot of Eversion.)
There are only minor issues like platforms having random paths that make it more difficult to jump at times. As well, I had an issue with some stages that had the bouncing platforms. But, I would have to say Disorder is an experience that a hardcore gamer might love -- all stresses included! I am a casual gamer so I found the gameplay a bit tedious at times. But, having as short a playtime as it does, the torture is not something I regret. The levels built off of one another which is shows good planning on the developer's’ part. I went into this game blind so these are just my honest feelings. As an aside, I really liked the alternate choices offered throughout the levels. (They really helped out when my weak resolve for advanced puzzles kicked in!) I also like the hint of an alternate ending.
TL;DR: I felt some kind of way but I recommend playing it if you love hardcore platformers/ horror/ the indie game element/ and being stressed out of your mind. It isn't terribly long and I recommend putting it in your inventory!

this game is amazing! I'm about 200 hours in and still haven't beat it. I keep starting over looking for the perfect way and then I just change my mind and start again. Do I want to 2 brute warriors with healing mages? Do I want to go the standard Warrior, Thief, Archer, Mage combo? Do I want to run a Tank, Healer, Crafter, Mage? Do I want one mage to specialize in Fire and another specialize in curses? So many combos and party configs. The story is also perfect, the voice acting is perfect, the graphics are perfect. Only 3 things bug me.
1. Targeting: Your archer's turn is up, you target this nasty Ogre with a big club who wants to make mince meat of you. You click to shoot your trusty arrow at him and... OMG he swayed back and forth in his standard idle animation, you clicked the ground instead, your wimpy archer walks over to the Ogre and stands next to him. Oh and now your turn is over since you walked all that way, now it's the Ogres turn to smash the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your archer with his club.... UGH!!!! It happens to often the targeting system is crap. talking to bunny rabbit or a tiny mouse, it's incredibly hard because you can't click on them. Did you want to move forward and attack the next foe in line? No, apparently your warrior wanted to waste his turn looting the dead skelton during a battle. I mean you clicked on the ground where that dead skeleton was, that must have been what you wanted to do. So during battle to act you have to be very patient and move your mouse to the exact spot, then see how the idle animation works, and time your click for when they are under it. You have to move your mouse ever so slowly to the spot and keep it there for 5 seconds to make sure it actually does what you say it will.
2. Hidden clicks. This kind of ties in with the targeting. But the graphics are perfect and hidden in these are some super hidden clicks that if you don't move your mouse to the exact spot you will miss important aspects of the game. For example: There is a room later on in the game you have to click 5 tiny buttons to get into this middle room and fight 6 demons. I moved my mouse meticulously over the entire terrain looking for these hidden buttons, but the only way I could continue was to look up online where it was and even when it told me I had trouble finding it. Early on the characters say stuff like "I spotted something" but later on there are key places where you just drag your mouse all over the terrain inch by inch looking for secrets. This is not fun.
3. Two players max! You have to hack it to get 4 players working and it doesn't work the best. A 4 player group is pretty key in nearly every other game I've played. So we all played through the story mode 1st, and then went back and hacked our 4 player mode so we wouldn't miss anything and could enjoy the game together. But only being able to play with 1 friend really bummed me out. But if you like single player or just one friend at a time you won't notice this.
Other than that though the game is perfect. The spells vary and work together amazingly. Dop oil on bad guys, light oil on fire, use rain to put fire out, use electricity to shick wet enemies, blast fireball in water to make steam cover for advancing shock troops. It's endless and tons of fun. Even the melee you can charge with different effects like fire, earth,  air, and water. It genuis. The quests have multiple ways to solve, you can he honest, you can steal from them, you can just kill them, you can frame them and watch the story unfold. endless replayability. Also the game is really long! I honestly thought I was at the end of it a couple times and had more than gotten my money's worth. but it keeps going and unfolding constantly. I would guess it takes about 80 hours to complete if you don't use hint guides and refrain from crafting (which is kinda OP) and makes the game a bit easy, even on tactical mode.
Highly recommended 9/10

My trouble with Divinity: Original Sin began at the character creation screen.
You have to pick two characters with no explanation as to why. I set about designing a fearsome, burnished bronze-skinned, flame-haired vixen, and I named her Mavis, because old names are brilliant and if I ever get a dog I’ll probably call it Wilf. Mavis looked like she could turn her steely gaze on a field of enemy orcs and they’d burn through fear alone. The other character had hair like Marouane Fellaini, and I called him Barry. This was a mistake.
After the brief introduction from a pirate with a voice like John Lennon about some sauce someone had spilt in Rivellon (I wasn’t sure about that bit if I’m honest), you’re thrown pretty much into the deep end. There’s no type of tutorial beyond a training dungeon of sorts, but the UI is quite straightforward and there’s nothing to frighten anyone who managed to get their head around the countless RPGs of old this game resembles, Point-and-click to move, “I” for inventory, you know the drill.
Immediately the game screams I AM RPG at you, with scrolls and mysterious tales and a corpse on the beach. Your two characters interact with everything in sight, from crates that are invariably empty to NPCs who have a series of odd tales to tell; as you reach land you find the journal of a man joyful at how he can fly who then climbs a nearby cliff and discovers that he really can’t, like those pillocks who hurl themselves off Worthing Pier with experimental wings on their back every year.
You can talk to just about every character in the game, though non-named NPCs have little to say and often ramble over the top of each other like teenagers at a weed-free party. Your adventuring pair even talk to each other in a manner affected by how you’ve chosen their “AI Personality” at the start. I knew no better and chose “random” for both, which turned out to mean “schizophrenic”, as one minute Mavis was complimenting Barry’s grave-robbing skills and the next she was calling him a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for breaking their only lockpick.
In opening zone Cyseal you’ll eventually unearth two additional characters you can co-opt to form a merry band of travellers. And travel they will around this massive world, which seems to stretch out endlessly in every direction with additional zones to teleport to when you’ve accidentally worked out how. Fans of exploration will certainly have a wondrous time in this game.
Unfortunately, it was a desire to see the world that first led to the realisation that Barry was a useless fool, much like the real Marouane Fellaini. Of course I was happy to blame myself for Barry’s first electrocution, wandering as he was through a puddle at least six inches deep. Dangerous business, puddles. There must have been a warning I missed, I think.
But absolutely everywhere poor Barry went, trouble found him. Hordes of zombies would home in on him as the weakest link and he would invariably die after a single round of turn-based combat. His mighty weaponry could only have been rendered even more deadly by the addition of a feather duster to his non-sword hand.
At one point the hapless Barry watched as all three of his colleagues fled a hopeless battle in turn only to realise he was too close to the enemy to get away. Over the course of nine combat turns he tried to use his “action points” to run away, and seemed about to make it to safety when he was ended in a horrifying ball of flame that appeared from Christ alone knows where. As usual, Mavis had to find his sticky pile to resurrect him and escort him back to Cyseal, tail between legs.
At least part of Barry’s problem was that while exploring the world outside the town, you’re given no warning that you’re about to be attacked by a group of six or seven undead or wolves or similar that are of a far higher level than you could hope to cope with. Retreat becomes depressingly useful, though there seems to be little penalty for it (and once you’ve retreated, have fun working out how to re-link your characters so they’re not wandering about alone – it took me about 20 minutes and you’re on your own).
Even Cyseal held terror after terror for our witless hero. The group would find a book with the solid RPG title of Secrets of the Scroll Volume II, and what self-respecting adventurer wouldn’t want a read of that? So Barry picks it up to flick through, but the game mechanics dictate that he’s actually stealing the book and its nearby owner suddenly goes berserk and starts hacking at him with some sort of axe until he is yet again a tragic red mess the book’s owner now has to clean up.
Theft is everywhere, and if you’ve a moral problem with larceny you’ll get nowhere with this game. When no-one’s looking you can trouser whatever’s on offer in someone’s house to sell to any vendor. If the lady of the house pops to the toilet it’s your duty as saviour of the world to have away with that portrait of her husband while her back is turned.
Some aspects of the game are handled a little ham-fistedly, mostly notably the system for convincing NPCs to let you do what you want. I wanted to get through a door; the guard, of a friendly faction I should add, said “No”. I chose the option to try to “reason with him”. This led to an inexplicable game of rock, paper, scissors, which I lost, at which point the guard decided I was a simpleton and started attacking me. “Chip my rock with your scissors will you? Come here!”
The game is about depth, exploration, a very pleasing crafting system, and not graphics. Visually it’s no more than fine, though the magic effects when you’re hurling combinations of the four elements at doomed enemies are quite enjoyable. That said, strangely often I found myself entering a building with windows that was lit (poorly) by torches despite the bright sunlight outside.
Another thing the game is not about, though, is hand-holding. If your favourite flavour of RPG involves a linear story, signposted waypoints and a clear route from start to end via an engaging story, Divinity: Original Sin will not make your 2014. Too often you are left wondering which NPC you haven’t spoken to yet to push things on, trying each one in turn until you’re finally given a clue to one of the (well-written) storylines. It can be quite frustrating if you’re not interested in gradually levelling up and heading off out into the wilds, because without levelling up you will soon find out which of your group is Barry.
Ultimately the key to this game is its freedom. If you’re happy to explore an open world, crafting, looting and delving into the often-excellent game mechanics, this game will delight you. If you’re looking for a serious, story-driven RPG, the narrative of Divinity: Original Sin is unlikely to hold your attention for long enough to justify the purchase. It almost seems to want to be a solo (and co-op) MMO, with its depth and flexibility but without the never-ending concern of “other people”.
Divinity: Original Sin belongs in that curious time between Baldur’s Gate and World of Warcraft, having vastly improved on the former but been, in some senses, neutered by the latter and the genre it helped popularise. As a single-player game, Divinity: Original Sin is almost certainly better than most WoW-type fantasy games, but without a coherent, easy-to-follow storyline it straddles the divide a little unsuccessfully.
Granted, even among its many improvements, Divinity: Original Sin Enhanced Edition is not a perfect experience, but it sure is unique. Pros:
- Great art and music.
- Visuals are clear and easy to understand.
- Game provides good mechanics, maps, and level of challenge.
- Fun squirrel theme gives the game a lot of character.
Cons:
- Controls aren't good, and your control settings are incredibly limited.
- Movement feels slow and clunky.
- Making your character move the way you actually want is very difficult.
- Game feels unpolished in many areas.
- Some things are rather unclear and unexplained to the user such as controls.
tl;dr, As someone who is a strong advocate for platformers, I'd have to say that I do not recommend this game to someone who is looking for a fundamentally 'good' platformer, however this game does provide some solid entertainment for its low price point.
This game looked fun and challenging, and the difficult trial-and-error style platforming looked appealing to fans of games such as IWBTG or Super Meat Boy. In these types of games, much of the difficulty comes in the intense level design which will have you making mistakes and repeating an area until you can perfect it. This works great in the aforementioned games, however in Squirreltopia that sort of enjoyment just isn't there. Instead of feeling like you made a mistake, it simply feels like the game's poor control and physics is what got you killed. Difficult and precise jumps in Squirreltopia simply feel like a mixture of timing and luck, and is not about the precise movement of your character. What should be trial and error while improving your skills and execution instead just feels like brute forcing your way through an area. You will constantly tell yourself "I could have gotten that if I could control my character better", and become quickly frustrated a you miss simple jumps onto small platforms because you held back a split second early and went helplessly falling into a pit without any chance of redirecting your character midair.
The default controls use arrows keys, left and right to move, and up to jump. You have to use the Enter key to enter through doors, but the game never tells your this anywhere so you just sort of have to try stuff out until you figure it out. You can change your controls to another preset configuration on the main menu, however the method of control I would have preferred using, "Arrow keys + space", did not even work. My space key did not do anything, nor did the up arrow, but interestingly the "WASD + space" configuration does correctly work allowing you to jump with space.
Understanding how to open levels that are locked off is unclear and unexplained. Understanding what the collectibles do or what they are for is incredibly unclear to new players, and you are unable to see which levels you have and haven't obtained items in.
That being said, many of the game mechanics such as the bubbles are fun and interesting. Level design over-all is pretty solid, and the game has a lot of charm and character. In a general sense, this game is actually quite good. However, given the terrible control you have over your character in a game where moving your character matters so much, it's difficult for me to genuinely recommend this game to anybody who truly enjoys intense platformer games.

I purchased Naval Action via their website just before the Steam Early Access release. In general I have been pleasantly surprised at the current quality of the game. I have logged 30 hours on this and game has never crashed on me or become unplayable. I have experienced the odd bug but the devs seem to work quickly to resolve them.
The game itself in its current state has plenty to do. The joy of sailing around an Open World Caribbean is there. You join a nation and are essentially at war with all other nations (attacking your own nation’s ships, unless they are carrying contraband, makes you a pirate for life). So whether it’s hunting down a trade ship or a frigate, there are enemies to fight, both PC and NPC. There are also Port Battles which can decide whether a port will change hands to another nation. These often become big organized PvP affairs.
The game was already populated by an active community before it came to Steam. There are active player groups with each nation. The website forum has  many threads on the full range of subjects that a new player will want to know. This is a good thing because the game currently lacks tutorials.
Right now there are two sides to the game, combat (sailing around, accomplishing missions or fighting) and crafting/trade. You can craft basic goods and ship upgrades all the way up to crafting ships, which can then be used by you or put on sale in a specific port. You can also buy/sell goods in different ports.
Please note that in Naval Action, your XP rank limits how many sailors you can command but there is no limit on the ships you can buy. So you start off at 40 sailors (and a Cutter that needs 40 sailors to man it). Thus, even if you have the gold to buy it, you won't be able to man a frigate that require a crew of 200 or more, let alone a Ship-of-the-Line. An undermanned ship often performs poorly in every way. So resist that “buy” button, even when you have the gold to pick up a big warship. Make sure you can crew it (and outfit it with cannons/carronades, with you must buy separately).
The other thing that should be noted is time. It can take a while to sail around in the Open World, especially if the wind is not in your favor. Hitting the seas for a full 30 minutes or an hour is not unheard of if your destination is several ports away. The Open World also has no real navigation tools. From your starting point you really have to look at the map (M), decide on a bearing and sail in the direction you want to go. Once land disappears you don’t know where you are, its pure guesswork and planning. Just sailing off without paying attention to the compass can get you lost. Note that behind the chat window in the upper left hand corner of the screen in Open World Sailing there is another panel that gives you some options, including allowing you to teleport back to the nation’s capital port.
For faster play, there are missions that typically allow you to jump into combat fairly quickly, from a load screen for a simple PvP match, or a mission that sends you to a spot in the Open Worlds near your current port to do battle. These two mechanisms are often the best way to grind up gold/XP but are also the most convenient for players with limited gamer time.
Expect a slight learning curve because of the lack of tutorials and a sometimes not-so-intuitive UI in a few places. I spent a lot of time combing through the forums on Naval Action’s website for the answers to various questions the first week I started playing. I highly recommend spending a lot of time in the starting Cutter (it's free and replacing it is free) to get acclimated to the game.
In general, if you enjoy Age-of-Sail, you'll enjoy this game, even in its current Early Access incarnation.

One of the only games I've gotten via Early Access just because of how interesting it seemed. And of course, it had to let me down.
I understand the premise - I mean, come on, the title - the game is meant to be a collection of off-the-wall areas to explore that escape reality due to your character dreaming. However, the developers seemed to take that premise and pretty much stop there. They ran as far as they could with making it generic odd dreams (and nightmares). In each dream, you find these scrolls which attempt to explain certain dream symbols and meanings, but most of the time they are just very generic meanings (and sometimes they talk about multiple meanings) and do not actually attempt to explain anything relative to your character or the game itself. They are literally as if you had just gone searching the web for dream object meanings, which of course vary all over the place and aren't exactly solidified.
So there is not really much of a story to the game; not much connects together. It's simply the randomness thrown together. You explore places that are basically just meant to say "Hey, the character feels lost or bored or confused!" Nothing is really sensible nor do things link together much. You find a handful of items throughout the dreams but they are entirely useless - you do almost nothing with them. The scrolls are mentioned above. And besides that, you wander around and then solve puzzles.
Now, when it comes to those puzzles, they are all also very boring and nothing exactly fun or interesting to work through. For instance, the entire first dream can be completed very quickly if you stumble upon the mazes and just waltz around in them in a bored manner. You get chased after by some weird mist-like manifestions, but all they do is transport you outside of the mazes and have you go back in. So you just keep running around until you trigger a bunch of lights to turn off - and you repeat for 4 mazes. Once done, the dream is technically over and you can leave. For the second dream, the puzzles there are scattered, like the difficult-to-see laser tile puzzle, or the planet puzzle, but still nothing really fun. Essentially, all of the puzzles are very tedious and boring.
The dreams themselves are also nothing that special really. Graphics-wise, they definitely look really nice in many places, and at first they seem like something interesting to go through (I mean, I got the game based on the looks and general premise mainly - to explore!), but then you realize that there isn't much to them. Same generic areas but with slightly different objects, mainly used to lay things out like the scrolls. Now, there are side dreams that you can actually go into, but for the most part, these are also lackluster. For instance, the roller coaster dream is literally nothing at all. There's one that is like M.C. Escher with stairs that would've probably been way more interesting if you could have changed the gravity/orientation and walked up stairs in different angles. But instead, you just remain on the floor and tediously search for openings in the walls and climb up the highest stairs possible, ignoring nearly everything else in the rooms.
Essentially, most of the dream world is simply boring to go through, even if you try to relax by just wandering. And as said above, while there are some nice graphics in the game, there are also a lot of places where the game simply drops that and turns them into blocky white areas or places that are just bleak, dull, and some single color without actual atmosphere.
Relative to the style of the game, there's also the sound and music, which is alright. Some areas do have some nice music that partially plays, but there are also some that have a lot of annoying noise or quietness (which does not really emit any emotion). You also have the character narrating the game, which actually ended up bothering me a lot, and I did not expect that happening at all. He just says completely random things, or will read text that pops up out of nowhere in the dreams, so his talking serves almost no purpose.
Then you have what a lot of people seem to complain about: bugs/glitches. The performance of the game definitely isn't the best, as I had a lot of lag when I really shouldn't have. Your motion can sometimes noclip through things, and certain places (e.g., the roller coaster mentioned earlier) bounce through objects in unsensible ways. In terms of actual bugs with the gameplay, I encountered some, but not as many as others. I had the computer in the first dream glitch out and freeze up, and I had certain puzzles not mark themselves as complete despite really being finished. Some other random issues here and there occurred, and sometimes I had to exit and restart, but the game didn't entirely prevent me from continuing like has happened for some others.
Even worse, the developers seem to have disappeared and not bothered to do any more work, which many customers are complaining about.
All in all, a lot of things just seemed rather clumsy. The developers seriously took advantage of the "dream" premise itself - way more than they should have - and used it as a reason to just create a random, jumbled mess. The general idea is for a lot of it to have meaning and distinct symbolism, which they only threw around in pieces to seem like they were doing something. There's some very slight context here, but not developed in any way.
A big letdown.

You don't just play this game, you make a permanent decision.
Once you launch Bad Rats, your life will change forever.
I bought this game during the 2016 Winter Sale, and I thought it would be so funny because it's a meme game. That decision changed my life forever, because launching badrats.exe is basically saying that you want to be hunted down by monsters.
So, a day after I launched the exe file I found a note on the back of my house. It reads, "You will not get away with this, cat." At first I thought it was some stupid prank, but I was wrong. Later that day, at about 9:45 PM, I heard a screech and then a yell. "We're going to find you, cat!" this monster yelled to me, from a distance. I freaked out and immediately uninstalled badrats.exe from my computer, and gave it a report on Steam.
The creature's voice was now extremely angry, saying it would murder me when it found me, but it left.
One day, I was caring for my back yard, I saw this humanoid rat person climb over my fence, it roared, then charged at me. I dodged the charge, and ran into my hosue, and locked the door. The rat man was furious, and kicked down my back door. He screams, "We will find you, cat!" and left.
Haven't seen him since.
Still a better lovestory than twilight

Warcraft III takes place in the fictional world of Azeroth. Several years before the events of the games, a demon army known as the Burning Legion intent on Azeroth's destruction corrupted a race called the Orcs, and sent them through a portal to attack Azeroth. After many years of fighting, the Orcs were defeated by a coalition of humans, dwarves and elves known as the Alliance; the surviving combatants were herded into internment camps, where they seemed to lose their lust for battle. With no common enemy, a period of peace followed, but the Alliance began to fracture. The events of Warcraft III occur after a timeskip from Warcraft II. This period was originally intended to have been documented in Warcraft Adventures, but that game was canceled in mid-development.
The game's plot is told entirely through cinematics and cutscenes, with additional information found in the Warcraft III manual. The campaign itself is divided into five sections, with the first acting as a tutorial, and the others telling the story from the point of view of the humans of Lordaeron, the Undead Scourge, the Orcs, and the Night Elves, in that order.
The game opens with the Orc leader, Thrall, waking from a nightmare warning him of the return of the Burning Legion.[20] After a brief encounter with a man who is known only as "the Prophet", and, fearing that his dream was more of a vision than a nightmare, he leads his forces in an exodus from Lordaeron to the forgotten lands of Kalimdor.[21]
Meanwhile, the Paladin and prince of Lordaeron, Arthas, defends the village of Strahnbrad from demon-controlled Orcs.[22] He then joins Archmage Jaina Proudmoore, who aids him in investigating a rapidly spreading plague, which kills and turns human victims into the undead. Arthas kills the plague's originator, Kel'Thuzad, and then purges the infected city of Stratholme. Jaina parts ways with him, unwilling to commit genocide, or even watch him do so. The Prophet, after previously trying to convince other human leaders to flee west, begs Jaina to go to Kalimdor as well.[23] Arthas pursues the dreadlord, Mal'Ganis, who was the leader behind Kel'Thuzad, to the icy continent of Northrend, where he helps his old friend, Muradin Bronzebeard, in finding a powerful sword called Frostmourne. Meanwhile, Arthas begins to lose his sanity after hearing his forces have been recalled by the Emissary. Unwilling to return, he has mercenaries burn his own ships to prevent his men from retreating, then betrays the mercenaries and has his men kill them, much to Muradin's disgust. Arthas and Muradin eventually find Frostmourne. Muradin, however, learns that the sword is cursed.[24] Arthas disregards the warning, and offers his soul to gain the sword. By doing so, Muradin is struck down by a shard of ice when Frostmourne is released, and is presumably killed. Arthas supposedly kills Mal'Ganis, and abandons his men in the frozen north as his soul is stolen by the blade, which was later revealed to be forged by the Lich King. Some time later, Arthas returns to Lordaeron and kills his father, King Terenas.
Now an Undead Death Knight, Arthas meets with the leader of the dreadlords, Tichondrius, who assigns him a series of "tests". Arthas first exhumes the remains of Kel'Thuzad and contains them in the magic urn that holds the ashes of his father, which was protected by Uther the Lightbringer, head paladin of The Order of the Silver Hand as well as Arthas' former mentor and close friend. Arthas kills him too, then sets off to Quel'thalas, kingdom of the high elves. He then later attacks the gates and destroys their capital of Silvermoon. He kills Sylvanas Windrunner, the Ranger General of Silvermoon (only to resurrect her as a banshee), corrupts their sacred Sunwell and revives Kel'Thuzad as a Lich. The Lich informs him of the Burning Legion; a vast demonic army who are coming to consume the world. Kel'Thuzad's true master is the Lich King, who was created to aid the Legion with his Undead Scourge, but in truth he wishes for the Legion to be destroyed. Arthas and Kel'Thuzad open a dimensional portal and summon the demon Archimonde and the Burning Legion, who begins his purging of Lordaeron with the destruction of Dalaran. Arthas and Kel'Thuzad are cast aside by Archimonde, and Kel'Thuzad reveals to Arthas that the Lich King has already foreseen it and is planning to overthrow the Burning Legion.
Thrall the warchief arrives on Kalimdor, meeting Cairne Bloodhoof and the Tauren and clashes with a human expedition on the way to find an Oracle. Meanwhile, the Warsong Clan are left behind in Ashenvale to build a permanent settlement, but anger the Night Elves and their demigod Cenarius by cutting down the forests for resources. To defeat them, the Warsong leader Grom Hellscream drinks from a corrupted fountain of health contaminated with the blood of the Legion's pit lord commander Mannoroth, successfully killing Cenarius, but binding his clan to the Legion's control. Thrall manages to reach the Oracle, in fact the Prophet, who tells him of Grom's doings. Following the Prophet's directions, Thrall and Jaina join forces to purge both Grom and the world of demonic influence. They succeed in capturing Grom and healing him of Mannoroth's corruption. Thrall and Grom begin to hunt Mannoroth and Grom kills him, dying in the process, but in doing so freeing the orcs from the demonic control of Mannoroth at last. Thrall tells the lifeless Grom that he freed them all and lets out a piercing roar alerting Jaina and Cairne to Grom's death.
Tyrande Whisperwind, leader of the Night Elves, is outraged to find the Humans and Orcs violating the forests and blames them for Cenarius' death, so she initially vows to destroy both. However, she soon finds out that the Burning Legion has arrived on Kalimdor. In order to oppose the Burning Legion, Tyrande reawakens the sleeping Elf Druids, starting with her lover, Malfurion Stormrage, and frees his brother Illidan Stormrage from prison, against Malfurion's will. Illidan meets Arthas, who tells him about the powerful "Skull of Gul'dan". Consuming the Skull and becoming a demon-elf hybrid, Illidan uses its power to kill Tichondrius. He is however banished from the forest by his brother as he is now part demon. Meanwhile, the Prophet summons Thrall, Jaina, Tyrande and Malfurion, and reveals that he used to be Medivh, the Last Guardian and the betrayer from Warcraft: Orcs & Humans, returned to make amends for his past sins. The Humans, Orcs, and Night Elves form a reluctant alliance to spring a trap on the Burning Legion, and delay it long enough for many ancestral spirits to destroy Archimonde at Mount Hyjal. Peace once again comes to Kalimdor as the Burning Legion's forces wither away in defeat.[25]

Putt-Putt Saves the Zoo is probably my favourite out of all the Putt-Putt games, and was even as a kid. Of the ones I played back then, this one was also probably the biggest time sink. I just played it in about an hour, which included playing the story, taking photos, and mucking about with the mini games.
The game is pretty self explanatory, but regardless: Putt-Putt has to save the zoo by helping the animals find their places. Of course, this might have some adults raising their eye brows, as you likely come ot realize that not only is the actual zoo keeper oddly unorganized, but the zoo seems fairly hazardous to a visitor's health between the swing entrances, accidents, etc.
Between exploring the areas, clicking on everything, playing the games, and more you could spend quite a bit of time with your child on this game. The main point of the game is teaching about the animals, clearly, along with some problem solving skills (How do you warm something up? How do you fix something that is broken?).
Also, when it comes to the credits, don't exit immediately. Just as with the rest of the game, there are things in the credits for a player to click on, to hear noises, watch animations, and even see the people behind the voices of the game.
Despite the dusty years, Putt-Putt Saves the Zoo, and all games for that matter, continues to shine. The memories left behind gives nostalgia a warm welcome.
