I really would like to give two ratings...because the single player and multiplayer feel like two completely different games.
The campaign is at first, what you would expect from a third person shooter. First a short intro video, then a tutorial, that sends you against some minor enemys, so you can learn the basics of the game.
But soon you will find yourself in an endless tube level, that never ends. Just running straight the obvious only way, the game forces you. I mean, tube levels are common to simpler shooters, like Half Life, Doom or Serious Sam, but these games never gave you the feeling, that you are in one large tube and never be able to choose an own path of running through the game. In Half Life the levels are designed nicely designed and actually gives you the feeling of a big open complex, you are walking through.
In Space Marine you can actually see your way, you are going to walk, like a red carpet with barriers on your right and left. You can obviously see it, but cant do anything about it.
The next part are the two totally stupid followers you have. They are like a walking talking cutscene that is following you, wherever you go....because beside talking they dont do any more. Hitting enemys? Sometimes. Killing an enemy? You should praise the day.
And that is not an AI problem. Imperial Soldiers, you find in your path, are able to kill several enemys before they die like the weak soldiers they are. So even a small soldier, with the life span of a fire in a blizzard, does more kills than your followers in the entire game.
The combat system feels mixed:
Firearms are awesome, with precise shots you can even take out big enemys with your simple bolt pistol, weapons like the plasma cannon rip massive holes into entire armys and splatter them across the map. But your weapons dont look, like they have real impact. Enemys just splatter and fall down. They dont backflip, when hit in the head and dont really behave, like you are shooting them with a real bolter.
All in all your arsenal is still impressive and I praise the day I found out, that you can rip the heavy bolter turrets from their posts and carry them with you.
The melee system is completely dull. You hit an enemy, he hits you. You can do some evasive maneuvers but it doesnt feel like other THQ games like darksiders. Your character feel immobile and heavy, like controlling a tin can filled with lead.
In reality, THQs praised combat system without hide and seek, but directly storm at your enemys at all cost, make the players feel, like they want the opposite. You often find yourself heavily damaged and fleeing, cursing the stupid combat system.
All in all the campaign is a tube filled with dull enemys, places you will forget after seen them and senseless dialogs and cutscenes you never cared about. Oh, and the endboss is a pure quicktime event.
The multiplayer is a different game: You can play versus other players or coop against AI hordes. Fully customizable classes and a decent leveling system with upgrades, give you hours of fun. The best part, the exterminatus Coop is one hard ♥♥♥♥♥ to fight. Have a good team or die trying.
You can choose from 3 classes, who are seperated from their tasks. The melee (with jetpack), the tactical with medium weapons and the heavy weapons guy.
But beside all fun, it is filled with DLC content, not only skins, but two whole game modes.
I personally think, the game could be made with the Starcraft II Editor, where I played 3rd Person Shooter Mods with equal grafics and more Gameplay.

I wont take a refund for this game but as of 27th of december 2015 this game is full of bugs or annoying glitches.
I only have 30 minutes into this game so yes I am still eligeble for taking a refund.
First of all and probably the most annoying of all, screen tearing. Despite vsync, a 980ti and other high end hardware this games gives me an awfull load of screen tearing. Lowering the resolution or overriding nvidia's settings on the game doesn't help. I like smooth gameplay and visuals, screen tearing is something that personally makes me hate a game. However this game has potentional and it looks gorgeous so I will patientfully wait for the updates...
The graphical settings that can be adjusted are just to minimal. They should've given plenty more of options. For example I don't like blur, disabling it still results in a blurry depth in the distance.
The game doesn't deliver much of a guide/tutorial on how to interact with certain puzzles. You just have to try every key to get to know the results, you can ofcourse check out the key bindings, but personally I don't think that a player has to go that far to get familiar with the important keys.
It is also unclear as what to do, you kinda explore and free roam while solving a puzzle so now and then, then you enter a portal and scout out a new place where not everything always work as you'd expect.
Probably the last thing for now that I found rather irritating, is the inventory. After messing with the keys I figured out that scrolling makes me pick an object from my inventory and it slowly materializes into my hand. This slowly.. is awefully annoying. It looks splendid and amazing, but that feeling fades away when you cycle through objects to inspect what they are... waiting for like 10 seconds per object results in a big time waste. If you have to look a small thing on a map you'd wait 10 seconds for it to materialize. So the wait is longer than what you have to look for. In the beginning I thought the game was just broken or so since it took that long.
Apart from the puzzles being rather simple, they are close to unique. You won't find many other games with the same type of puzzles.
I also enjoy the option of making my own choices rather than having a linear gameplay.
As the last pro, the visuals are superb have to hand it out to them.
TL;DR

-hard to get used to basic game mechanics

"When Portal meets Inception."
I think this little sentence summerizes the game at all.

The Story:

As Howard Phillips, you jump into the role of a young man, whose parents want to force him into a lifestyle. He himself wants to become an author, but he keeps staying in the shadow of his uncle. Because of he's not very successfull in his life, he often falls back into his dreams. The mainstory is about his familys past and the last speech he had with his uncle. In the begining you get a short preview of the whole speech. Now it's your turn; discover the dreams of Howard and solve the riddles you get in there, to relive the speech on your own.
Since the story is somehow monotone at some points, I can only give 6/10.

The Gameplay:

Since the story is based on solving riddles, the gameplay is kept pretty simple:
Classic WASD-Controlled walking
Some ducking and jumping
Interaction with objects via left-click or a bound key
But, like in Portal, it is not a negative aspect, because this game is based on solving riddles.
While discovering your dreams, you feel a bit like in the movie "Inception", because in this movie the also use the so called "luzid dreaming", while moving around in the dreams of others.
In addition it is a lot of fun, seeing the dream worlds change, the more you solve the riddles.
All in all I give an 8/10 for the gameplay.

The Graphics:

I don't want to do a graphic analysis, because this game doesn't want to impress with awesome 4K-textures or bombastic real-/quicktime-events. But the graphics part is always a part of a complete review.
The graphics are very balanced at all. The worlds are 67% made of repeating textures, but these are very detailed. The textures, that are important for the riddles, are very lovely designed. A picture frame, that makes an impression of a glass-made front and a wooden backside, or a clipboard, where even the clip is well textured, are aspects that make a game deserve commendation.
All in all, I have to lower one's sight, because of the repeating textures in bigger areas.
Therefore, it is still a solid 7/10.

Pro & Contra:

Pro:
Well done merging of Portal and Inception
One one hand you have relaxing riddles and on the other hand you have very hard ones
Lovely designed (dream-)worlds
Very clear atmospheric difference between the different worlds


Contra:
Gamesound is too low even on maximum, as long as the background music is turned on
Some small collision-bugs
Minimal graphic-bugs in some situations

My Result:

Based on the numbers, I get a 7/10 for this game. But since it has a lot of little aspects, that are very positive, I incline a bit more to 8 so I want to give 7,5/10.

At first I was thrown off because it was completely different than Repop, but after playing a bit I found myself getting into it more and more.  I can't speak for veterans of this genre, but I can tell you I enjoyed this game enough to want to jump into the world when I can.  It also led me to appreciate a new genre of game so how bad could it be.  There are some glitchy moments in the game and it is weird that I can break huge trees with my bare hands, but as a noob I'm not going to complain.  After doing some research on other similar games, Fragmented isn't as polished as ARK for example (my son owns ARK on Xbox), but for the right price I would recommend it.  Now for me the right price is during a Steam sale, but you will have to decide for yourself what it is worth to you.  I find it refreshing that a  developer who was running into issues with their original game (Repopulation), didn't want to screw everyone who supported it by leaving them with nothing.  So in conclusion, Fragmented which is still early access, isn't as polished as other games, but it made me want more.  For someone unsure if the genre is for them, it is better to pay $9.99 for Fragmented than $30 for other similar games.  For me, I will be visiting my character again soon.

Alphabear is one of the best mobile games I’ve ever played, so it’s great to see it ported over to Steam.
If you missed out on the mobile version - it’s a bright, challenging word puzzle game with dozens of cute bears to unlock and collect.  What more could you want?  Seriously, stop being so greedy.
If you’re already familiar with the game, this version is almost identical - though there are a few improvements.  Each chapter contains far more levels.  There’s a new dictionary function - to help convince you that yes, the random combination of letters you desperately punched in really *is* an obscure word, honest.  And there are no time limits on using particular bears - so once you unlock game-changing legendary bears (yes you, Relativity Bear), you can keep using them as often as you like.  Keyboard control makes it much easier to enter words quickly, and when playing typed words the game will helpfully select letter tiles with fewest turns remaining.
It would be great to see the addition of many more achievements (bears unlocked, levels completed, lengths and categories of words played) - hopefully these will come with the next update.  But that’s a tiny complaint, and it’s definitely worth the price tag in its current form.  Overall rating: MANY BEARS

The game is a re-imagening of the old Classic "Chaos" where two Mages are placed in a battle Arena with spells in their deck to duke it out.
The twist on this is that every Spell is basicially not a 100 % success chance, but has the possibility to fail and leave you with nothing but a nice sound effect and a bit of Mana in return.
The Meat of this game is the Multiplayer where you battle up to 3 other Mages in said randomized Arena's to win.
Your Starter Deck of Cards/Spells is randomized but dependend on the game mode, can be favoured by equipment steering the randomness into certain directions with higher chances.
A big part of the game is to manage said chances and mitigate if a spell is worth taking the risk or if you cast a more secure low level spell first to increase the success percentage of the bigger spell, which you can as well Manage with some goold olf fashioned Mana.
You gain Mana either via failing a cast, killing an enemy creature or collecting Mana Flux from the battlefield.
Now while all of this sound rather basic, the Meta level of the battles are quite addicting. You have the possiblity to simply cast any creature as illussion, it will work and function like a real one and the enemy can't tell if it is an illussion or not.
Every Mage starts with a Spell that lets you disbelieve said Creatures, which in case it is an illusion, will simply have it poof into thin air and gain another chance to cast a spell.
If you guess wrong though, the cast for this round is over and you are left in disadvantage. This level of Bluffing your opponent will cause either of you to loose a turn if guessed wrong or dealing with an unnessecary illusion.
Personally I'm having a blast with the Combat System and the quite addicting Meta of bluffs and Strategy involved. Yes it is heavily RNG heavy, but the unpredictability of the Game makes every round unique and never feel old. :)
Thus I can only recommend the game.
As well for those who don't enjoy the PvP Nature of it, there exist Player made Story driven Realms to explore and conquer. Which summarize in a host of PvE battles with nice storied flavour, Cities to visit and buy loot, as well Monster Camps to recruit to breach the Palace and dethrone the King. :D

This game is great fun and an excellent value.
This is the most hybridized game I have ever played. It is a turn-based mixture of...
-Squad tactics (ala X-COM)
-Monster summoning and spell casting (ala Magic the Gathering)
-Exploration and adventure (ala Eador)
-Multiplayer (sort of a slow motion Might and Magic-esque DOTA2...)
If you want to play alone you can, if you want to play with others you can do that either exclusively or as you like. For example, in my first realm I played it completely solo only to request a real person's assistance with the final realm conquering battle. I got a nice, helpful, ally and we won! Yay! (In case you are wondering, you share the loot evenly with your ally if you do this with help)
There is a lot of replayability here. As I understand it the realms that can be player and developer created are potentially unlimited and there are always tournaments. There is ZERO PAY TO WIN, which is great. The game also offers some gear tweaking and development that you can do in the form of outfits, staves, and talismans. The talismans are what you trick your outfit and staff with to boost abilities or add new ones.  These outfits are counter-balanced and designed mainly to augment particular playstyles.
The depth in the game is astounding and the tuturials do a great job of easing you into it. You have:
-Different units that can fly, range attack, counter attack, are undead, etc.
-Different spells that attack, buff, etc.
-Different totems and battlefield walls and such
-Different heights on the battlefield as well as points of interest to contend over (mana power ups)
-Alignments (law and chaos which affect the chance to get off spells of the same or opposing types) along with ways to influence this spectrum in either direction
Very impressed so far and have not begun to scratch the surface. I bought this for under $20 on sale and it is a STEAL!
Thanks developers.

Note: I've had Naval Action since very shorty after the closed beta started. I've played off and on since then, but I'm not an expert by any stretch of the imagination.
Naval Action is a game about the 'Age of Sail' that lasted from the 17th-18th centuries. You take command of any one of a number of sailing vessels, starting from cutters and yachts, to the largest Man-O-War. Most ship classes are named for ships that actually existed (you can't rename them as of now, and I don't know if that's planned), and a few from more realistic fiction also fill the roster. they can hold different numbers and sizes of gun, larger crews, reinforced planking, and all manner of other upgrades to set them up for your tastes. Nothing exists at the moment to change them astecticly, however.
As these are sailing ships, the weather  (naimly the wind) can be your best freind, or worst nightmare. if you have to head northwest, and the wind is coming out fo the northwest, it's going to be a long and slow slog up to your destination. Learning how to use the wind to your advantage will be the hardest challenge you face in Naval Action. You ship can take damage, and if shots hit below the water line, you're liable to start leaking. Masts can be shot off, rudders damaged, and crew can be killed with grapeshot from the ship's guns, Sails can be shredded to ribbons with chain-shot.
The game itself has a map that encompases the whole of the Carribiean, and parts of North and South America. There are ports for a number of nations, all of them currently at war, as well as ports where any ship may enter. There's Pirate ports (I've yet to find Nassau, though D:)  and Pirates coming out of them. You'll start off by sinking (or if you can manage it, capturing) these pirates, before venturing out to wage war with the other nations, or trading valuble (and sometimes illegal) commodities thoughout the world.
It's a game best left for the patient, it takes me a good half hour to get to Cuba from Charleston, and another ten mintues to get to Hati or Jamaica. The overworld map is pretty large, to say the least.
the graphics in this game are top-notch when in combat-mode, though are a bit simpler when in the overworld. The menus are far from complete (though even they have come quite a ways). The sound is suprisingly good for a yet-to-be-finished title. Get yourself a good set of headphones, and you'll be sucked in, with the sounds oc water and creaking wood in between the smoky roar of your deck guns.
Pros:
-The game is quite realistic - Wind makes a difference, and you can use it to your advantage.
-Looks georgious while in combat.
-Sounds georgious while in combat.
-You can sail the Suprise.
-Bigger ships do not always trump smaller ships (get on the stern of a frigate, and have the wind on him, and you can happily rake him in the backside all day long).
-PvE options for people to learn on, but while XP transfers to PvP Gold doesn't seem to (a nice tradeoff IMHO)
-Gives me a reason for having a whole playlist of Sea Shanites (Which I liked before I even knew about the game).
-You can get large numbers of players together for large naval battles, when everyone knows what they're doing, ti's a sight to behold.
-The Developers are really active in the community, and seem to enjoy us enjoying the game, which is nice.
-A large number of nations to choose from, depending on how you want to start out, and what you want your ship's flad to look like.
Cons:
-Realisim means that you can't go directly into the wind like AC4, you'll have to learn how to tack (this isn't as much of an issue for those who have sailed before like myself, but newcomers might want to watch a few tutorials Which I might even make a few myself)
-Larger ships with square-sails are complex to operate for the newcomer.
-No ship insurance built into the game as of yet.
-Not every command can be re-bound. The functions of the number keys come to mind, how I'd LOVE to set up a custom joystick to handle that instead, but it's a bit less conveiniant then I'd like for that.
-the overworld doesn't look quite as pretty as combat, and you will be spending time in the overworld a lot.
-no spyglass in the overworld, where you'd realllllly like to have it
-not optimized, which is to be expected, but those of you who cannot stand anything less then 60 FPS, turn back now.

This is a bad game, hiding behaind a great license. It is very pretty, very repetitive, and presents Space Marines as slightly stronger than your average Ork.
What this game does best, by far, is present a stunningly beautiful graphical display. The Ultramarines, weapons, jump packs, and world at large faithfully recreate the best iteration of a Warhammer 40K universe in any game out there. I believe this is what has led to so many positive reviews.
The gameplay however, is not good. Repetitive to the extreme, hordes of enemies come at you, and you press X a lot. When a larger enemy comes at you, you press Y, then X a lot. Sometimes you press B as a "finishing move" which restores health. Each weapon has two finishing move animations. You will see them a lot.
What is more infuriating however, is how this game does the exact opposite of what we all hoped it would; play a near-invincible juggernaut that is a Space Marine captain. Far from feeling invulnerable however, you will quickly learn that small groups of enemies can take you down very quickly. Individual Orks take 6-8 shots from your heavy bolter to kill. Your two squadmate Ultramarines are borderline useless, and any form of squad tactics are completely absent. And for some reason, Relic decided to use the Halo-style personal shield for the Space Marines. Meaning, as you wade into combat, you will frequently need to run away and duck behind a corner for your shield to regenerate. It is also notworthy that this game has no form of a "cover" system.
Very pretty, very repetitive, makes Space Marines out as slightly stronger imperial guardsmen. If that sounds appealing to you, this is your game.

You play as Howard, a man probably in his mid twenties. You wake upon your sofa having successfully managed to sleep through whatever show it was you were hoping to watch. So you decide the best thing to do is head to bed. When you get to bed your dream is full of floating cubes and a strange gate which you travel through. You now find yourself in a canyon of some kind which you explore until you find a stack of computers. Now in order to progress you must make your way through four mazes, turning off lots of lights whilst being chased by some mysterious ‘smoke’. Confused? So was I…
The basic idea behind Dream is fairly solid. Walk around until you find a puzzle, solve said puzzle and then move to a new area. However it’s a game with no tutorial or even directions of any sort. The puzzles (when you eventually reach them) are fairly good. They’re varied, interesting and at times need some thinking about and highly enjoyable. With one particular puzzle took me a good amount of time to even figure out what I was supposed to be doing and solving it gave me a huge sense of satisfaction.
Whether you’ll like Dream largely depends on how long you think it takes for ‘Exploring’ to become ‘Aimless Wandering’. Returning back to the house I began to look around and found lots of clue to Howard’s life or rather more about his recently deceased author uncle who’s house he now seems to be living in. The other levels also seem to have plenty of these little hints and secrets but finding them quickly becomes a chore and just finding the next puzzle to progress can be frustrating.
There are three acts (four if you include the starting house) and each act offers two ‘Side Dreams’ these are bonus optional puzzles and/or areas adding a little variety to the game. There are also the Nightmare Acts. I’d love to tell you about them but I refuse to play them. I started the level something moved down the corridor a door slammed and messages were scrawled across the mirror in blood. I’m not great with horror even when I’m expecting it so I decided to leave it. However what’s clear is that it contains a decent amount of content for a game of this type especially when you include the 30 collectable ‘Dream Bible Scraps’ and a handful of other collectable items
Dream is quite pretty and it’s also backed up by a great soundtrack. But the asthetic of the game is obviously made for a VR headset. This is especially clear in the rollercoaster side level that would probably be quite impressive if you were but on a screen was dull.
It’s difficult to make up my mind on Dream. On the one hand the puzzles for the most part were excellent, and felt like a grown up, slightly harder Professor Layton kind of thing. The small hints of depth in the world and varied locations were also great. But I keep coming back to one sticking point, it just took so much wandering around with no real direction to find what I was looking for. This is especially true in the third act where it took me about half an hour to even find one of the puzzles! There are some people out there will really really love this game, but for most of us I have to say it’s probably one that we’ll never get round to finishing it properly.

When I bought the game, I had the faint option of finding something similar to Yume Nikki or one of it's many fan tributes. As such, the fact that the game for the most part is a walking simulator where you sprint from A to B (and sprint you will) with only the occasional riddle or puzzle did not particularly bother me, and many parts of the game (such as a large park or a south sea resort built entire on offshore platforms) are nice enough to look at that you won't mind spending roughly half and hour simply running around in the place.
Unfortunately, the developer's approach to the dreamworlds the player moves through is rather conservative, especially if you consider how you could put virtually anything into them. This becomes especially sad when you consider that many of the smaller "side dreams" actually tend to be way more interesting than the larger main levels. But safe for one side dream that looks as if straight ripped out of a McEscher painting and another more abstract area with looping corridors and warping tunnels, the infinite potential a veritable dream has in terms of design simply is not fully used. Instead, the game largely relies on fairly generic landscapes with the occasional out-of-place object thrown in to remind you that you are still dreaming.
Add to this that the game's story is only seen in retroperspect, and that investigating the home of the player character for about ten minutes will tell you everything you need to know in order to predict the good and the bad ending,  and you will come to realize that the game simply lacks a strong source of motivation. You don't care about getting to know the story because you already know what happened and what will happen. You don't care about exploring new worlds because you expect them to be as bland as the first sand desert/ snow desert level. Even the music (which, for the record, is very well done) only keeps you going for so long.
Long story short, Dream is a game that had an enormous amount of potential, but lost much of it due to design choices.

This is a good game if you are learning Japanese.

As long as the developer keeps working on it, it's a WIP (Work In Progress) and should be viewed as such.
There is a reasonable number of kanji and all kana with the exception of the less common wi and we kana available for tests.
Charts to study for tests are available for kana only; these charts also do not display wi or we kana.
As of this review, there are no kanji charts though it has been posted as an upcoming feature.
Kana tests allow duplicate visuals, which I hope becomes an option in the future.
As of this review, there is no phrases, tenses, grammar, or dictionary.  For a touchscreen laptop about the size of a 10" tablet, this could be ideal for the 1st month of the 1st semester of a college Japanese class because of the kana charts in combination with the kana tests.  As the kanji charts are not there, I don't see it being useful for studying kanji from an efficiency standpoint.
If you have a summer of time to burn, and you really want to know Japanese, I recommend "Modern Japanese: A Basic Reader" Volume 1 and Volume 2 (Hibbet, Itasaka. Harvard University Press).  It's old and it's hard, but it's got all the kana and over 2000 kanji and a lot of reading in one course... assuming you survive, you could feel like you graduated a low end Japanese high school.  Seriously though, don't even think you can do that course in a month.  Get a ream of printer paper, a pack of pens, and copy the 60 chapters of vocabulary in Volume 1.  Then study what you copied.  Then copy the reading from Volume 2 and use the vocabulary you copied from Volume 1 as pieces to a puzzle until the puzzle is solved.  Repeat 60 times since there are 60 chapters.  Find three months and hit it hard.  Very hard.

This game is very simple.  It gives you a character from the Japanese language with many options to choose from.  This is helpful for memorizing and quickly identifying the characters. Also I found being quizzed and getting a little better over time, due to learning, oddly addicting.

Was very excited to buy it, but doesn't seem to go through all  of the Kanji for any particular level. Just picks some at random. You have no way to tell how good you're actually doing.

I really want to like this game... but I just can't. I'm now at the final stage and the only reason why I keep playing it is the couch co op feature (there simply aren't many story driven couch co op rpgs out there). But let's just list all the things I liked and disliked about Divinity Original Sin:
- Nice story at the start, the first map is beautiful
- Character creation
- Character classes and skills felt really good when I was low lvl
- The game doesn't hold your hand and feels like an oldschool rpg
- THE COUCH CO OP FEATURE, i wish more cRPGs would adobt this
- The story gets boring after the first map, I felt invested in the world maybe for the first few hours
- The game tries to be funny and witty at times, but mostly fails at that and just breaks immersion
- The character developement in terms of skills and gear gets boring after the first few hours - no new skills after a certain point (not even close to the ending), weapons are just the same few models with different effects, armor has a laughable amount of tiers and there is absolutely no variety in the look of different armor sets (1 lvl plate armor - just a simple breastplate, 15 lvl plate armor - the same breastplate as lvl 1, only this time with an oversized shoulder piece
- Enviroment effects are a nice mechanic in combat, but in reality they are more frustrating than fun - the fields are imprecise at best. For example when your character just slightly touches a firefield with the tip of his foot for a split second - that's it, you are on fire now.
- The combat was fun at first, but when you have to battle 10 guys - good luck waiting for your turn.
- The AI is quite stupid - for expample when I manipulate an oponent to fight on my side, they often just stan around doing nothing.
- The level design is aesthetically pleasing, but the hitboxes are plain lazy. Try shooting a fireball next to flag post or over a little stone structure - it'll get stuck on an invisible concrete wall 1 meter above the mesh
- The quest log is a f***ing mess - you'll never find out if you've finished a quest or if you have to do anything. It's more like a diary, in which your character writes every stupid thing he encounters.
- I've found the player home completely meaningless - I only returned there when the story forced me to.
All in all this isn't a bad game - it was fun to play in local co op. I would give it a 5/10 with a slight tilt towards a final negative score. if it wasn't for the fact that I can play this with my gf on one monitor I would've stopped playing 70hours ago and never touched this game again - especially when there are way better old school RPGs out now.

This is the first time I have written a review on Steam for any game so hopefully that will give you some indication how impressed I have been with Naval Action during beta testing and before the Early-Access release.
Although there is still much to be added to the game, there is already enough present to give you what feels like a complete experience, much superior to other games of it's ilk that have been released fully.
The focus is very much on simulation and the game is initially quite daunting and challenging. For example, you have to navigate properly between locations using just a compass and without your position shown on the map, whilst you have to manually aim your guns in battle (rather than letting the computer do the aiming for you as in other games). You have to learn to read the wind and sail properly (different for each ship) and the difference between a good sailor and a bad one (me!) is significant.
Although the game isn't easy at first (and there are no tutorials yet), this brings me onto one of the best facets of the game; the community. I have played more MMOs than I can remember but this is by far the friendliest and most helpful playerbase I have ever seen. Shout out for help or advice and players will quickly reply with what you need to know or sail to help you. I have had players capturing ships and giving them to me and the general chat is fun and interesting. Plenty of features are still being worked on whilst the mechanics of port-battles, boarding and much else are still being developed. Nevertheless, there is already so much good quality content present that I have no hesitation in recommending Naval Action even in early access - you won't be disappointed.
So, if you have any interest at all in the Age of Sail or warship combat generally, this is an absolutely must-buy game even at this relatively early stage.

Aka: OH GOD WHY DO I GET SO ANGRY WHEN I FAIL?
Bit.Trip Runner is the third in the Bit.Trip series, which makes a break from convention of the previous two. This time, you actually play as Commander Video in a side-scrolling platformer. The screen moves at a cracking pace while you run constantly in a 3D retro 8-bit inspired world. Your basic functions are to jump, slide, and kick your way around/through obstacles, while collecting gold and powerups, to reach the finish line at each stage.
While this seems simple enough, and it is easy early on, it quickly delves into devious territory, requiring the utmost attention and rhythm. As with the previous Bit.Trip titles, the gameplay is heavily dependent on the music. As you collect powerups, the music becomes more and more intense, so you know after a few of them (and when that glorious rainbow trails behind you), you’re close to the end. It’s often much easier to time your jumps with the music, rather than looking at when obstacles are coming up.
But if you fail; fall down a gap, hit a wall, etc, it immediately carries you all the way back to the beginning, and starts straight away in that dull pre-powerup music. It’s incredibly demoralising, to know that you were so close, only to go right back to the start music. Particularly on the longer levels (damn you, Odyssey).
Because of the instant reload times, much like Super Meat Boy (who also gets a sneaky cameo), it forces you to keep trying, and keep trying, until you finally triumph. And you will retry. A lot.
Only one other game has ever made me more frustrated than this (you’ll keep, Dark Souls). I’d have the final powerup, rainbow trailing behind me, knowing the end is near, only to miss-time an easy jump and go all the way back to the start. My desk is not fist-pound rated, but it should be. What makes it frustrating, is that on paper, it is so simple. All it is, is timing and reflexes and knowing the right inputs. There’s no other tactics that that. But the timing here can be unforgiving.
Makes it all the better when you do finally complete a level you were stuck on forever.
This is the best of the Bit.Trip series; if you want to start somewhere, this is the game to buy.

Yes, Gabe Newell Simulator is in Early Access. So bugs are expected. But the problems with Gabe Newell Simulator go far beyond what could be excused by it being in Early Access.
The image for this game alone sums up pretty well all the problems with this game. The entire games quality is poor. No quality control whatsoever.
Here's all the issues:
- Full-screen doesn't work. It changes were the cursor clicks by around 2 inches.
- The menu for the game looks like it was created within 3 minutes.
- The controls/how to play section was literally made in paint.
- Level menu lets you skip levels even when you've never played/completed them.
- Level menu constantly doesn't show levels.
- Text in the cut-scenes look like they've been made in Windows Movie Maker.
- The game is laggy and badly optimised, no matter the computer or graphic settings you used.
- Level layouts are very bare-bones and simple.
- The AI are so unresponsive you can run straight by them and complete each and every level.
- There's no audio in the entire game except the starting cut-scene and gun sounds.
TLDR;
Game is broken in full-screen. Game is sluggish. Menu is bare-bones. Cut-screen text is unreadable. Gameplay is mostly unresponsive and irritating. No quality control. Game can't hold your attention at all.
Thank Gaben for Steam Refunds.

One thing for sure the game's 'media' feel is fairly varied.
The Balance and the mechanics, whilst I played it felt broken to some extent, and vastly under-balanced.  The only real solution for me felt like 'kite'ing and killing at range, as AI accuracy vastly gets worse proportionally to range.  However some elites will hit you immediately at what ever range... There was also a legitimate instance of me 'kite'ing an elite, who can 2-3 shot kill me at sniper range with an AK assault rifle, who, when I ran out of his weapon range to avoid getting shot(5 seconds max, (not straight running in opposite direction i..e 'kite'ed)) respawned... Oh also, look forward to missions with intermittent checkpoints(viz. On one occasion keep dying and having to listen to the same garbage speech as you sit in a lift for 30 secs; one piece of dialogue then bugged and repeated on loop til i left the area...).

This game is really underrated here on steam. I expected much worse from this game. Bought it when on sale, definitely worth 7,50 euros. It's a survival game as you can imagine, and really piratey. The potential is huge and apparently they've been patching it, not sure how often, but they are working on it and the upcoming features look amazing. I'm pretty sure this game is gonna be better and better. There's also a raiding system that I really like because it limits griefing. Basically when you build a base you have to make a builder's desk to protect your building. The more you upgrade this desk, the longer it will take the enemies to raid your base. Basically once you destroy it, a countdown starts. As long as the countdown doesn't reach 0, the enemies cannot destroy or steal your stuff, but they can destroy doors and beds (respawn points).
I think it is a really cool features because we are used to survival games that basically become your main job if you want to succeed and keep your base safe, and even if this is the situation, you are not certain you gonna preserve it.
This game may use some better animations and sound effects, but not a huge deal honestly. You can build small boats / rafts in order to sail and explore. There are caves to explore in which you find minerals such as copper and iron in order to make better tools, better armors, better equipment in general. The equipment can also be made of bone which can be harvested by hunting animals and using a hatchet on their dead body in order to gather it, along with fat (used for torches), hide (armor and other gear) and meat. You can also plant crops, such as corn, but also small plants for fiber and berries, and mushrooms as well.
And, OMG, there are pirate clothing and weapons ^^. I like the environment. I actually needed something different and if this game gets more pirate stuff in the future, even better. Finally, something different (as far as I know).
I'm looking forward for a lot of features, and also hope that more of what I got in my mind will be added to this game.
Combat system is not bad. I actually like it. It's not as fast as it is in ARK, for example, and you can use different weapons and also shields in order to parry enemy attacks.
Overall, the game is looking good and getting better, so it's worth a try in my opinion. As I said, I expected much worse. It definitely deserve better reviews on steam, and apparently, lately, things are changing for the best.

After picking this game up as a huge survival game player (Rust, 7 Days to Die, H1Z1, DayZ, Miscreated, The Forest, etc) I wanted to try this since it was on sale.  I picked it up, streamed it on my channels for both Twitch and Beam and 5 hours later, I don't want to even quit and continue going it's so fun.  I love these types of games.
As an early access game is it VERY WELL put together with a lot of rich features for building, crafting, planting, hunting, fishing, and more.  The land is well put together with decent textures, lighting, ambiance, sound and more.  There is no tearing or issues with land masses like some early access games have with falling through floors or animals running through rocks without collision.  The amount of materials gathered is decent as well for each item durability.  The pace of the gathering is decent and it’s not a hard grind or overly unfriendly to game play.  It’s just right.  Also the animals in this game are diverse and thus far I ran across a Hippo, Rhino, Lion, Gazelle, and Zebra.  Most are cautious can hear you approaching like in any hunting wild-life game however, some as you would expect are dangerous and if they see you, decent line of sight/aggro, they will rush you!
The building is pretty impressive and fast working from the B letter and then off of your mouse buttons or numeric keypad which you get use to fast.  This is proximity as well so you can lock down certain areas where people can’t build next to you on onto your base.  There are concepts of ‘Clans’ as well to promote people in a guild-type fashion and give them pretty granular permission to either unlock doors, build, destroy, use of chests/crates.  There are also upgrade features to improve your structures from wood, stone, bronze, etc as you gather them across the lands.
The environments are very impressive.  So far I ran across nice breezes from the ocean, which by the way you can leverage fishing traps from, winds, rain, impressive lighting storms which flash your screen.  The sounds is spot on.
If I were to say anything negative, it would be maybe when you move your mouse off of the active game window you are playing it minimizes the screen to your task bar?  That is probably a feature incoming or maybe because I’m playing windowed mode?  Also, as far as I can tell there is no music which is fine by me because in survival games I never play it just keep the other sounds up to hear things approaching.
To me, this is an 8/10 game hands down and I look forward to continued improvements.

The actual core battles are fantastic. I'm completely addicted to the mechanics of the wizard duels. There is an incredible amount of risk management around the RNG rolls, so it's got a brutal learning curve. Think of Blood Bowl or the new X-Com games.
However, this game has a few major issues, even after launch:
1. It's primarily a multiplayer game, and the player base is miniscule and already dwindling
2. The adventure map mode called "Realms" is a just a poorly curated collection of user created content
3. The mechanics of the "Realms" are not in line with the rest of the strategy. Realms are a tedious race against a timer where the strategy is more about who can collect the biggest army before the actual battle starts. This gathering process isn't a fun mechanic at all and detracts from the real gameplay.
So while I love the core of this game, I simply can't recommend it in its current state.

You will become highly motivated to complete challenging scenarios in single player as finishing victorious is the only way to keep the weapon/armor upgrades you discover along the way. There are lots of interesting choices for varying playstyles.  You can upgrade your defense and melee skills and charge in or boost your magic power, hang back and sling spells.  Choosing from the large pool of weapon and armor upgrades to streamline your playstyle is definitely one of the strengths of the game.
Criticisms that the game is too random are fairly baseless as there are many tactical and strategic decisions revolving around spell casting order, area control and most importantly equipment loadout. You have several effective and varying ways to boost your spell casting chance and eliminate most rng.  People complaining about rng haven't learned the game mechanics well enough.
This game is why I game and a no-brainer recommendation for tactical game junkies.

You probably know that Chaos Reborn is a reimagining of a 1985 game, Chaos, by its original designer, Julian Gallop (also the designer of X-Com).
You probably also know that the heart of the game is arena battles between up to four wizards and their menagerie of summoned monsters, who summon and fight based on do-or-die percentages.
What you may not know is that the single-player component of Chaos Reborn, the Realms of Chaos, is largely created by players, either those who have risen through the ranks of combat to become Wizard Kings, or those who, well, bought the rank with real money. Within the realms, you can find equipment that has also been created by players who have leveled up to the Forgemaster rank or, again, purchased it.
The realms of chaos are worlds of magic that you explore and conquer over an overworld map filled with ruins, towns, enemy wizards, requitable mercenaries and monsters. If you win the realm by defeating the Wizard Lord who presides over it, you keep the gold and equipment you acquired in the realm. During battles, you may also be aided or attacked by other players.
I've only played a few realms so far, but they have been engaging and fun. I'm very impressed that they were created by players. When I look at my equipment, I can see which player designed it. It's pretty great.
The meat of the game, the combat, is exciting, polished, strategic, and fun. The surrounding context of realms and equipment, created by players, will only grow from here.
Truly an amazing game. Read other reviews if you want more detail.

So, I am not a platform gamer.  I get frustrated, confused and angry at constantly failing...and yet....while those moments did exist within this game, I never experienced the desire to give up.  I had to beat it, I wanted to beat it.  And beat it I did (in just under 10 hours, and I think less than 300 deaths...possibly....)  Now then, onto the game
Gameplay 8/10
Lots of fun, very responsive and overall feels like a well designed machine.  There are some parts however that feel a little to much like a "skill" shot experience, where if you make the tiniest of mistakes its over.  This honestly didnt bother me due to the save anywhere feature (unless I ran out of blues...then I cried) but I have to say, escaping the flooding tree was ridiculous.  It was so satisfying when it was over but my lord I had flashbacks to the Water temple from OoT.  YOu feel proud to have bested it but never want to go back.  I am not a platform gamer and the gameplay made me feel like one, so I think its great.
Music - 10/10
Guys....guys....I want a CD.  Seriously, please give me the CD for this music...The music so perfectly fits every zone you are in, and I actually love that while each zone is different, you can still hear the original song woven in.  Plus....ITS A REAL LIVE ORCHESTRA!!!  (IF you cant tell....this makes me excited)  I love being able to hear each instrument and pick out its part and the music...it makes you feel warm and happy, sad and forlorn, hopeful and determined.  Honestly it was the music that drew me to this game and I was not disappointed.  I found myself idiling in areas just to listen to the music.
Story - 10/10
While there is not much to the story in terms of dialouge, its really not needed.  The music and art do such a good job at telling the story, the little text that is in the game feels more like a bridge that connects what we are visualy seeing.  The story is both sad and yet hopeful that at times youll be crying, and others cheering.  I nearly cried within the first 20 minutes of the game....Any story that can be told primarily through music and action is a 10 in my book.
Art 10/10
Beautiful.  The game is seamless, although there are some lag and framerate drops at times but when the game is running smoothly, its gorgeous.  You feel like you are running through a painting and everything looks and flows seamlessly.
Overall 9.5/10

Let's start out with the three negatives I've found: the text can be really hard to read, so it can be tough to tell what's going on. The story is even more difficult to follow since there's no voice acting whatsoever besides NPC greetings (which I don't mind so much) to accompany the small text. Quests can be annoying to read the descriptions for and items on the ground can be hard to find for the same reason, but the game has so far been fun to play even without knowing for sure what I have to do at each step. Occasionally the text on some screens doesn't even show. The quests are also sometimes given to you after you've already completed a stage, so you have to go back and complete the stage again, but this is far more fun to do in C9 than it is in other games I've played, especially MMOs.
The screen looks cluttered and overwhelming a lot of the time, partially due to how many colors are used simultaneously, but it's not game-breaking; just takes a bit to get used to.
Sadly, last but not least of the negative things about this game, spambots are in tremendous number all over the servers, messaging easily a few times per second. This is tied with the small text as the biggest problem about C9.
Here's a neutral: the way your character starts off seems a little too advantageous, as you can wear one of three widely different costumes - each one increasingly conservative with the last one being a full suit of armor - from the very beginning. I started off with the most revealing outfit because it didn't feel right to be so armored-looking at the very beginning. Some of the clothing options include extremely impractical things like angel or schoolgirl miniskirts and lace stockings, but I don't always mind being a doll fighting monsters.
Now onto the good things: the customization seems pretty awesome; female faces are characterized by whether they're "alluring", "hardhearted", or "enchanting", which is a nice small addition. The tattoos are numerous and, though the available colors are a bit too saturated, they're still a cool feature. The choices of hair color seemed very dull and the hair meshes don't seem completely polished, but the different hairstyles look really nice and fairly original, surprisingly. This is an extra plus to me since I love being able to customize my character.
The music in the tutorial is an interesting metal/rock combination, which I haven't heard before in an MMO, so kudos to them for originality. After that, it's a happy, magical ballad, very dreamy and fitting for such a game. When you're in a busy area, there's even the sound of idle chatter.
Attacking is very fluid and makes me wonder why this game is free-to-play: things like this seem fairly polished in this game, so I'm impressed. The bounding boxes aren't ridiculously small nor far too large, either.
Ultimately, Continent of the Ninth Seal feels like a mixture of the fighting game Dead or Alive (for the attack combo features), Fable (for the previews of skills and the arrows on the ground to your destination), and D&D games and is pretty fun so far, even though my girl runs like an anime schoolgirl/ninny with her arms cast out to the side. :P

Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine Review
Few games make you feel as badass as Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine does. In Space Marine you play as Captain Titus a 7 foot tall, specially trained solder who can kill thousands of enemys with both gun and steel.
STORY: You are in command of a commando squad of Space Marines who is sent to the planet Graia to stop a hoard of invading orcs. That’s all the story is for the first half but quickly changes for the better during the second half, giving you a reason to care about the characters and to care about what happends next? The bad thing about the game though, is the sad fact that THQ went under, losing any chance that the clifhanger ending will be solved. So if you want and ending to your story, its not going to be here.
GAMEPLAY: Space Marines is a third person shooter/hack and slash. Think of something along the lines of Gears of War with a mixture of Darksiders put into the mix. It may seem like that’s a bad idea, but Space Marines pulls it off very nicely with only a few minor issues. The sword and gunplay feels very fluid during combat, allowing you to shoot an ork, then stab it with a sword with only the touch of the middle mouse button. The combos with the sword are easy to pull off, only requiring the use of two buttons. The bad thing about the gameplay is that after about 2 hours, its starts to feel repetitive, only giving you a few extra weapons to use. Along with the story, the 2nd half changes the gameplay. Suddenly making the game more enjoyable to play.
Final Thoughts: Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine is a solid game with good gameplay and a good story, although it takes 1/2 of the game to become good, it is still worth it. Space Marine is not worth $29.99 for its regular price, but is worth the price of $10.00 or less.

The visuals and performance of this game is pretty good too, considering the computer I played it on is pushing five years old and was nothing special at the time anyway. Often you are running through large open corriders opening doors along the way without seeing any enemies for what seems like forever. Gladly, though, when killing Orks starts to get boring, without spoiling anything for you, you are introduced to some new enemies, making for a progessive game. Having said that, though, the main difference between the Orks and these new enemies is (obviously their appearance, but) their strength and health. They play very similarly to the Orks but, seeing as though you get better armour and weapons as you go, it all just feels a bit repetitive.
But, like I said, I still enjoyed this game. It's a lot of fun even for people who have never even heard of Warhammer before. It's a tad on the short side and I didn't check out the Multiplayer for this game but I'd imagine it's a bit empty nowadays (you might want to check that though). I would say definitely get it when it's on sale, because it really is a great third person shooter. Enjoy! :D

Anime (Japanese: アニメ?, [anime] ( listen))[a] is Japanese hand-drawn or computer animation. The word is the abbreviated pronunciation of "animation" in Japanese, where this term references all animation.[1] Outside Japan, anime is used to refer specifically to animation from Japan or as a Japanese-disseminated animation style often characterized by colorful graphics, vibrant characters and fantastical themes.[2][3] Arguably, the stylization approach to the meaning may open up the possibility of anime produced in countries other than Japan.[4][5][6] For simplicity, many Westerners strictly view anime as an animation product from Japan.[3] Some scholars suggest defining anime as specifically or quintessentially Japanese may be related to a new form of orientalism.[7]
The earliest commercial Japanese animation dates to 1917, and production of anime works in Japan has since continued to increase steadily. The characteristic anime art style emerged in the 1960s with the works of Osamu Tezuka and spread internationally in the late twentieth century, developing a large domestic and international audience. Anime is distributed theatrically, by television broadcasts, directly to home media, and over the Internet. It is classified into numerous genres targeting diverse broad and niche audiences.
Anime is a diverse art form with distinctive production methods and techniques that have been adapted over time in response to emergent technologies. It consists of an ideal story-telling mechanism, combining graphic art, characterization, cinematography, and other forms of imaginative and individualistic techniques.[8] The production of anime focuses less on the animation of movement and more on the realism of settings as well as the use of camera effects, including panning, zooming, and angle shots. Being hand-drawn, anime is separated from reality by a crucial gap of fiction that provides an ideal path for escapism that audiences can immerse themselves into with relative ease.[8] Diverse art styles are used and character proportions and features can be quite varied, including characteristically large emotive or realistically sized eyes.
The anime industry consists of over 430 production studios, including major names like Studio Ghibli, Gainax, and Toei Animation. Despite comprising only a fraction of Japan's domestic film market, anime makes up a majority of Japanese DVD sales. It has also seen international success after the rise of English-dubbed programming. This rise in international popularly has resulted in non-Japanese productions using the anime art style, but these works are usually described as anime-influenced animation rather than anime proper.

My review - From my experience in the early alpha
First of all i wish to state that the community of the game has been amazing and the developers have been listening very well to us. I have been following this game ever since early 2014 and it's grown to a very enjoyable game.
PLEASE NOTE: This game is not made for the impatient
The game requires atleast a decent interest in ship combat and sailing, you need to navigate yourself, the combat is made realistically. It is not an arcade, note that if you just want to kill, kill, kill this game won't be a good game for you.
First of all, the graphics look fantastic. Probably the best looking game I've ever seen in the Unity engine. The Open world currently does look a little worse than the battles, but this is understandable for performance reasons. The game runs decently, haven't had any issues to achieve a solid 60FPS. Yet the dev's stated they would improve performance in the future so no worries about that.
The ships are beautiful and detailed, just look up the trincomalee in the game, and irl. It looks identical. Honestly amazing how detailed the ships have become. I hope to see more crew on deck in the future. More activites there would be nice.
The sound design is AMAZING, it sounds like you are actually in an 18th century sea battle, the smoke really adds to the battles aswell. Couldn't be more perfect.
Overall the battles feel very complete already, it is the open world which does require a bit of work. Of course, the UI can be confusing at first, and it does not look the greatest. It is not the priority, and we understand this. The UI is something to improve on definitely. Another negative thing about the game is that there is currently no tutorial. So finding out what to do can be a bit tricky at first. So please use the help chat in game, someone almost instantly helps you on there.
The open world is a WIP and that is clearly visible, and this is most likely where the developers will focus on in Early Acces, so you will mostly see that progress.
Overall, I bought the game on a Thursday and within a week I had played over 100 hours. A recommendation for sure, dedicated dev's, good communication with the community. Best Naval game out there right now!

I found this to be quite a good program. I agree, you don't learn Japanese from the ground up. If you want a program that does everything, you will have to look elsewhere and expect to pay a lot more money. However, this program compliments any form of book or online study that involves reading and recognition. Even at entry level this program is useful, because quizzing yourself is essential, if you hope to get anywhere.
When you launch the game, beginners can select hiragana and katakana quizzes. Once those are mastered, you can devote more time to the different grades of kanji. I don't know what constitutes a grade, but I find each one manageable and not overwhelming.
Each quiz is random, but if you repeat a quiz 5 to 10 times a session, you will notice the value of doing so. Some kanji repeats while others are introduced. I find it easy to take note of the kanji I don't know, study them in my spare time and do another session of multiple quizzes at a later time. I also look up words related to the kanji I learned in a previous quiz and expand my vocabulary a little. Kanji is intimidating. The game seems to take the confusion out of knowing where to begin, so it is a big timesaver.
I'm learning Japanese as a hobby, so I don't want to spend a lot of money on online classes or foreign language software. I use books, websites, and communicate with a few Japanese friends on Facebook regularly, so this program suits my needs perfectly. I highly recommend it to anyone in a similar situation. Sure, this program could use a few fixes and added features, but if you prefer something that compliments speaking, grammar, or an overall more comprehensive material like stroke order or background, look elsewhere.

The Age of Sail game that serious PC gamers have been waiting for.
It isn´t for casual gamers, the scale of the map is huge and navigation takes a significant amount of time.
The combat is excellent, and with each update every aspect of ship warfare is simulated with increasing fidelity.
There are a lot of people reviewing the game prematurely, or at least without any real understanding of the concept of early access, or certain decisions made with regard to the business model. 99% of these reviews are uninformed drivel. It becomes apparent very quickly that Naval Action is a labour of love, each ship is beautifully crafted in a way that honours the real world originals, the combat is intense, lumbering, yet somehow despite that slower pace is always edge-of-your-seat split-second decision making. Quite the feat really.
Most of the negative comments here come from the fact that the developers have decided to sell ´premium ships´ in order to pay for the very high capacity servers. Seems perfectly reasonable once you look at the details and reality, as opposed to simply get all hot under the collar because you want everything in life for free. The game world is huge, and to support that many players on one or two servers requires income other than the initial sales. The game is very reasonably priced, and there is no subscription fee. These ships aren´t pay-to-win. Stat-wise, they will be more or less the same as the normal ships, and unlike premium vehicles in other games it is possible to lose them (they can be sunk four times before they are permenantly lost). Seems reasonable enough to me.
Another reason some of the uninformed masses have complained here, seems to be the fact that there are no ingame tutorials or anything. It´s early access! All efforts are currently being directed towards creating and improving game mechanics. The UI, filler and content like more ship types will follow. Currently they are releasing minimum one new ship design per month.
If you understand this, then this game might be worth looking at in its current state. For all others, stay away from our baby.

It's interesting, it's pretty fun, but I can't recommend a strategic game like this where you can pay money to get gear in game. There is literally a King pack you can buy for $80.
Overall, the game feels mediocre. The gameplay is fun and simple, but it doesn't seem to have more potential than what it already is. It is what it is.
If you were dying for a random-number generator quick turn-based strategy game revolving around risk management where you can level up and get gear or pay $$$ for it, go for it! But honestly, how many out there want this?

Three layers of randomness killed this game for me. Your spells are cards, so what you have available at any one time is random. The chance to cast a spell is random. Yes, you can mitigate, but that kind of detracts from the game. You want to use your powers to beat up on things, not increase percentages to actually succeed at spellcasting. The law/chaos bar is feels forced and adds nothing to the game. The illusion mechanic is senseless and feels like another tacked-on mechanism to justify the casting success randomness. Finally, of course, you have the combat randomness. Overall, I was disappointed at the way the game's mechanisms were put together.
In addition, as of this writing Chaos Reborn has no single player campaign. Playing solo involves a generated instance where you grind trash to get to a big bad. There's no story involved at all. Finally, this is a loot grind. It's essentially turn-based Diablo 3, and it doesn't have anywhere near the appeal of that title.
Unless you really like randomness and playing odds, instead of feeling like a powerful sorcerer, I recommend passing on this game.

The game is a turn based tactics game with a heavy emphasis on risk/reward decision making.
In the game you play as a wizard, with the aim of defeating one or more opposing wizards on a small hex based board. You achieve victory by summoning minions and casting spells. Layered on top of this is a light meta game in which you can level up and increase your pool of available minions and spells.
You will be assigned a semi-random selection of minions and spells at the start of each match (out of the pool which you have unlocked from the aforementioned meta game) which you can cast in any order you wish. The successful casting of spells/summons is not a given, each spell/summon has a base chance to cast; with the lower tier spell/summons having a much higher chance than the higher tier ones. For instance, a weak minion will have a 90% chance to summon, whereas a powerful minion will have a 40% chance to summon. Each wizard can attempt a spell/summon only once per turn, so the player has to balance the risk/reward of each spell/summon in their pool before acting.
The combat works in a similar, chance based fashion. All chances are clearly displayed to the player before attempting any action so there is no chance of frustration occurring from hidden information. The combat chances are based of the stats of the creatures in question, details of any creature on the board (or in the players hand) can be found during play.
There are some interesting mechanical twists however! A player can choose to create an illusionary summon which will always have a 100% chance of success and can attack as normal. The downside of this is that an opponent can call your bluff and cast a spell which removes this creature from the board. If the opponent successfully casts this spell on a creature which was summoned as an illusion then they can cast another spell in the same turn! This creates a further layer of strategy which really adds a lot of depth and longevity to the game.
The core gameplay of fighting against other wizards (whether human or AI) is well designed and realized and the layered meta game is passable, if not exactly ground breaking. However, for the price point it's a great deal.
Now on to the less good stuff:
The UX design leaves something to be desired, there are several points where you end up in a menu with no way to go back. This is especially evident in the tutorial area where you unlock single player challenges. You will click on a challenge to find out what it's conditions are, but instead of opening a dialogue explaining the challenge and asking you to accept, it just loads straight into the challenge - requiring you to exit to main menu if you didn't actually wish to DO the challenge. These kind of UX decisions are prevalent throughout the menus in the game (but fortunately not in the battle menus!).
The graphics, while pretty, are not making it particularly easy to read the board. Units don't "pop" from the background and it's hard to tell each players units from one another.
The tutorial forces you to complete each stage before continuing to the next. I found myself failing a few times on a specific stage, even though I had learned the mechanic. I wanted to carry on and learn the next mechanic so I could practice in a real game rather than the spoon fed tutorial section, but it wouldn't allow me to until I completed the current section.
The sound is good, if not particularly memorable. I swear the sound effect when you receive a new card/press "escape" when focussed in the chat box is the same one I heard in Starcraft 2 somewhere, probably just me tripping though.
Finally, when I first entered the game (after completing the tutorial), I was met with a menu which linked to several sub menus. Some of these sub menus appeared to be micro transaction menus, although apparently they are not. One of the mechanics - forging your own staff and robe, is locked unless you pay $15... apparently though it's not at all required. So I am really confused as to the design decisions of this area. Also the Upgrade Tiers are really confusingly worded.
All in all, I'm happy with my purchase and would recommend this to anyone interested in tactics games, especially if you want to play them competitively online with leagues etc. Maybe buy the forge upgrade, but avoid the two upgrade tiers above this as they are purely cosmetic (I bought them thinking they added some mechanics, turns out it's just tiny cosmetic details, kinda regret it now).
To the devs: If you add further cards later down the line, consider making them a free DLC for people who upgraded to the higher upgrade tiers or kickstarted the game.

TL;DR - This game is amazing and well worth the $20 dollars spent on it.
Like many here, I will say this game is gorgeous. Beautiful. Awe inspiring. Many were the times I sat in the middle of an area just admiring the amazing view.
But you all knew that. The screenshots and video to the game showed you as much.
Ori and the Blind Forest did what many games have failed to do lately. It reeled me in and did not let go through the entire time I played it. It provided a great simple story. It grabbed at you with great gameplay mechanics. It stretches it's limits with amazing exploration.
The game has no Auto-save feature, which only adds to it's difficulty. If you are like me and get really captivated by the game, you will forget to create a save point, and you will have the ancients remember why their wrath is mild compared to yours. I did rage quit once because of my own inability to remember to save the game. Hint: When the game tells you you can create a Soul Link... By the love of all that is holy, DO SO!!!!
None of Ori's skills seem useless, so the game doesn't have you investing points in useless skills. In fact, each point spent on Ori's skills makes you feel how your survivabilty increases ever so slightly, tilting the tables in your direction.
The game is breath-taking. Literally. There are some very intense areas that make you question if you are dealing with the most difficult stage of the game. You will forget how to breathe. I mean it. I found myself pausing the game a couple of times just to regain the breathing thing that keeps me alive. What a doofus.
I did find some things that could be fixed but are not game breaking at all.
The game is not happy about sharing processing power with other games. Keeping two games opened normally sent Ori and the Blind Forest into auto-minimize and it would not come back from it. Even though I could hear the game still working. I fixed it by just creating a save spot and closing the game. Restarting it seemed to fix it pretty good.
There are areas where the particle effects are so many that it would suffer a slight drop in FPS. Nothing to the point of breaking the game. In fact, it made it look like it was running in slow motion sometimes. Not even too annoying.
Once I got a glitch in which Ori went through a floor and a wall, but he landed in an area that I could easily move back t where I was before, so I wasn't even mad about that.
There was also a slight graphical glitch that would render certain projectiles from enemies to look like its particles were not rendering properly. But again. Not game breaking.
Ori and the Blind Forest has been an amazing experience. It packs a punch. Hit the nostalgia button hard. Many times I kept saying to myself "This is what Metroid used to be... If Samus was a Mew with a slight parkour hobby".
Do yourself a favor and partake on the journey that this little gem takes you through. You wont regret it.
Also... Keep an eye out for all the numerous easter eggs the game holds. I saw so many references to other video games that were carved into the beautiful background, that I gave them ovations as I noticed them.

I'm torn between recommending this game and recommending against it. Ultimately, I recommend against buying it.
Pros:
- The game has a wonderful and cohesive visual and auditory aesthetic.  The levels convey a compelling liveliness and otherworldliness.  The obstacles, enemies, and background "creatures" are inventive and cool-looking. I wish I could go explore the background with Commander Video.
- The music is great.  I actually bought the album of the band that did the opening credits theme (Anamanaguchi) after hearing it in this game.
- The mechanics are pretty predictable. It's obvious when you need to jump, smash, etc, although sometimes certain elements can get muddled by everything else going on around it.
- It has achievements, and I like achievements, because I'm kinda OCD.
- It has Steam cloud sync, because it's 2014.
Cons:
- It's billed as a rhythmic platformer, but falls short on both counts. As a platformer it's dull and the controls are tight. It requires rote memorization in many places rather than reliance on reflexes.  As a rhythmic game it falls short because the beats of the songs actually throw you off and aren't very well-timed to what you're supposed to be doing.  Rhythmic platformers must be pretty difficult to design because they require absolute integration in the spatial and time dimensions, but when the designers fail it actually makes the game less intuitive and more frustrating.
- At times it seems like my character didn't actually collide with an object, but it registers a hit, sending me back to the beginning of the level. Seems like there's fudgy hitboxes. A game like this requires skintight hitboxes.
- Just because it's hard doesn't make it fun. The designers deliberately made the game very hard by the exclusion of checkpoints.  You could call this "sadistic" or say it's meant to attract only the most diehard platformer fans (of which I am one), but it makes the game inaccessible and artificially extends the playtime. It's a crutch you see used a lot in indie platformers these days. Super Meat Boy was exceptionally hard but had an enormous amount of depth. Bit.Trip Runner is actually a pretty short and shallow experience if you add checkpoints.
- Since this is a rhythmic platformer, a large part of the game experience is enjoying the music. But it's incredibly difficult to even get past the first world (of three total), and you don't really hear different music until then.  By the time I got there I was so ♥♥♥♥ing tired of the music in the first world I never want to play it again. Contrast that to Electronic Super Joy, 140, and Super Meat Boy, where I frequently go back and play levels just to hear the music.
- You have to focus so much on timing your movements that
- Autoscroll on every level kinda sucks in platformers. That's probably a controversial statement, but it's what I think. Oh, and while I'm at it, Metallica's "And Justice for All..." is their best.
- The boss battles are inventive, but by the 100th time I tried to beat the first world boss I was ♥♥♥♥ing bored out of my mind. I actually had to write down the order of what comes at me in order to beat it. This isn't Calculus. I shouldn't have to take notes.
I think the cons outweigh the pros, so I can't recommend this one. But, if you like really hard platformers with good music and don't mind nearly-endless repetition, you'll probably enjoy it.

Holy crap what can we say about this marvelous adventure and effort to bring it to consoles/additional content/controller support?!
One of the first things you'll notice, is that EVERY npc interaction is now fully voiced whereas beforehand only major characters were voiced (leaving the game feeling rather empty perhaps though it was supported by excellant writing).  All of that is now still there and it's certainly nice even interacting with a fish vendor or other minor entity that it has it's own voice.  Fantastic!  That alone would be worth buying the enhanced addition.
Quests have been reworked so they are more streamlined and additional quests have been added.  I was playing along the first major quest noticing a quest item had been moved here or there but it was essentially the same storyline.  Happy to report that keyboard and mouse working just fine - and PC demands were performing better with no visual hitching or bugs that I noticed.  I am not running the game on a 'state of the art machine' 12GB of DDR3 Ram, Quad Core Processor and only 1 GTX 680 (the other one died haven't bothered to replace it); so overall performance is optimized pretty damn well.
Next, after 2/3 of the way through the main first storyline (Mysterious Murdur) I plugged my controller in - a 360 controller and was immediately detected with a tutorial starting up as things came up to show how to interact with the world using it.  I found the transition seemless.  The radial menus are easy to navigate, and became intuitive after an hour or so.  Navigating inventory, a somewhat annoying task with mouse/keyboard I found to be a bit easier though you can certainly flip from mouse/keyboard and back to controller easily enough (ingame keybind) so choose which way you want to play.  Personally I found that sitting back and moving my team around using a controller much easier as I've often lately grown tired of clicking around etc so its nice to sit back on my couch thus using my 360 Controller.
Is this game worth a buy then?  It was with the unenhanced version and well, it certainly is now.  So what are you wating for?  I would buy this if you like RPGs, its a fantastic game with hours and hours of gameplay.  The added voice content and controller support offering more ways to play a great game.

The visuals are still fantastic, really capturing the dark and foreboding atmosphere of the 40k universe. While the story is straightforward enough for 40k veterans and laymen to understand and enjoy equally, that said the single player is somewhat short and the level design while beautifully detailed is restrictively linear at points. Unfortunately, with the collapse of THQ Space Marine will not be getting the two sequels it deserved leaving the cliff hanger ending somewhat bitter sweet.
I recommend this game to anyone be they 40k enthusiasts or just a fan of the hack and slash genre in general.
