** Comments are in regard to online play only **
Players may be offput by the game's close dependence on RNG values to determine success or failure, but I've found this focus on managing probabilities over more typical dmg/defense values to make every game (and often every turn) interesting and thought provoking.  These underlying mechanics give added importance to bluffing and reasoning out opponents' decisions from a more nuanced angle.
I find the art and sounds to be very well done.  I'm a fan of the more simplistic designs that were part of the Kickstarter's early days, but the added details and embelishments feel very thorough and consistent.
The inclusion of a Classic mode is great for those who want to do away with all of the fancy character customization and play the game on a more even footing.  That said, I've found the leveling and customizations to be well thought out and balanced.
The player's guide that's available ingame is excellently presented with accurate descriptions and illustrations.  Same for the readily available info cards.  All of the needed information is placed right up front which really helps make the game accessible to new and old players alike.
All in all, this is a great game to hop in for a quick brawl, but don't be surprised when you find yourself itching to play just one more game.

Chaos Reborn is a rework of a game created in 1985, so thirty years ago!!  The original game was written on the ZX Spectrum and called "Chaos: The Battle of Wizards".  It was developed by Julian Gollop who was also the creator of the original x-com which most people are familiar with.  I used to play the original "Chaos" game way back then in the eighties, so when I heard the news that the same developer was going to be working on the remake I was extremely excited!!
It plays like a conventional table-top game with dice rolls.  The game is played between two, three or four wizards that have a random number of spells at their disposal which are distributed at the start of the game, similar to a card deck.  The spells consist of creature summons, buffs, environment spells and magic-attacks.
The map is hex-based so looks a little similar to other turn-based strategy games but we have many differences in Chaos Reborn.  For starters there is no hit-point system.  A successful attack on one of your army means it will die.  The calculation takes into account the attack vs defence so you can still use your summons with high defence to block and tank but there is a chance that it could be defeated with a lucky shot.
Every action in the game has a percentage chance of success.  These chances can be influenced via a number of factors including mana, elevation, buffs, law/chaos alignment.  Spells are either aligned with Law, Chaos or are Neutral.  The more Law spells cast successfully, the more the world changes to become Law attuned and future Law spells will be given a buff to the spell casting chance, the same is true for Chaos aligned spells.  This means that a 20% success spell can, in the right circumstance get buffed all the way up to 100% casting chance!  So influencing these factors and casting at the right times can be a crucial part of your winning strategy.
Another important mechanic is the ability to cast 100% successfully when summoning a creature by means of opting for an illusion.  The illusion will function exactly the same as a real creature with the exception that your opponent can call your bluff.  They may cast a “Disbelieve” spell and if successful the creature will vanish and your opponent will get another casting turn.  If the creature is real then your opponent won’t get another chance to cast a spell until their following turn.
Your turn consists of moving and casting a spell, but you are completely free to move any creature in any order during your turn and you can also choose to cast at any point.  This opens up the tactics and makes it a lot less restrictive than most TBS games that have turn and movement phases.  Considering line-of sights and moving, positioning and casting in the most efficient order can be the difference between victory and defeat!
Games can be played live with a timer with options of between one and three minutes per turn.  Alternatively you can play up to twenty asynchronous games which can be played over a number of days or even weeks, taking your turn at your leisure.  If you find yourself enjoying the game you can enter into one of the many community leagues or tournaments organised outside of the main game.
During the early-access I posted regular screenshots to my steam feed and the most popular comments was how nice the game looked.  It really is eye candy and there are so many nice touches such as the backgrounds and lighting subtly changing colours depending on whether the world is law or chaos aligned.
The development team “Snapshot” continue to develop this game past its full release and we are expecting new features to be added such as new spells, in-game social features and more.
There really is no other game similar to Chaos Reborn with its eclectic mixture of gaming elements.  I’ve tried to describe the core game as best as I can to give you the clearest picture of what this game is.  If it even remotely sounds like your type of thing then I can highly recommend this purchase.

Huh... wow...
I've rarely been so blown away by a game, I don't even know what to write...
TL;DR version:
+ArtStyle
+Graphics
+Sound(-track)
+General quality
+Gameplay
+Controls
-Sometimes the screen gets crowded with stuff and it's no longer recognizeable if what you're jumping at is background fluff or a bloody death trap (doesn't happen that often though)
-haven't found any others, which makes me suspicious
Ok let me get started by what you may already have heard, it's astonishingly beautiful. The art design is superb, fits in every scene perfectly together and creates an immersion that i've rarely seen in any game. In fact, the magnificent graphics are part of the story and make you feel claustrophobic, slightly frightened, relaxed etc where appropriate without ever feeling over the top.
It's rapid gameplay and steep learning curve seem to be "unfair" at first sight, but... and there's a BIG but... it never is. It ramps up it's skills and abilities like it's nobody's business, makes you learn the moves then throws challenges in front of you that seem unsurmountable... until you actually figured out what the hell you're supposed to do with your fingers. Needless to say, the feeling of reward is immense and you get a boost for the next challenge.
And while we're at "gameplay": quite a few games have shown me how bad, laggy, unprecise and generally shity controls can be... not "Ori"... the controls are precise, do exactly what they're supposed to do and behave in a more or less logical way... the only thing hampering the controls are your fingers and your own damn hand-eye coordination.
There is (as laid out in the TL;DR section) however a tiny criticism that i just have to put:
Sometimes it's not very easy to see what is background and what piece of the scenery will hurt you dead. It's a small thing, really... emotionally it's quite a shock when you're invested in a game like this one and suddenly what you perceived to be some part of background graphics fluff makes you vanish into tiny sparks...
Well... there we go, just Wow... they took the media "Game" and made it right... thank you...

Since the amiga era I haven't had so much joy while playing a platformer.

They designed everything with almost no repetition and everything seems hand drawn.

BIT.Trip Runner is a rhythmic, side-scrolling platformer.
The player takes control of Commander Video, who will run endlessly until he reaches the end of each stage. You can have him jump and duck to avoid obstacles, kick certain obstacles out of the way, launch himself on springboards or deflect objects with a shield. If Commander Video impacts with an obstacle, the player is forced to repeat the entire stage from the beginning. The game consists of 3 themed worlds, each with 11 stages and a boss stage.
Aside from the main objective of reaching the end of each stage, the player can also attempt to collect all items within each stage (score multipliers that increase the intensity of the music and particle effects, as well as gold bars). Completing a stage with every item collected will give a "Perfect" score and grant access to a bonus stage in the style of an old Atari game. The core mechanic is mostly the same in that you reach the end of the bonus collecting as much gold as you can while avoiding obstacles. Collecting all the gold within a bonus stage gives a "Double Perfect" score.
Graphics are simple, most objects being composed of low-poly blocks with very basic textures. The overall visual aesthetic is competent, pulling off a retro-inspired look yet remaining in a 3D space, but the repetitiveness of playing stages consecutively undermines the appeal of the simplicity as there is very little visual variation between them. Audio quality is likewise competent and fitting to the overall theme, with the level designs reflecting the rhythm of the music to varying degrees, mixed in with suitable arcade sound effects. Unfortunately, this also suffers from monotony as you will hear a lot of the music repeated over and over as you progress, with only two unique songs for each of the three worlds (excluding boss stages, which again all share the same music) and none of the music is particularly good.
The controls are tight and responsive, each stage is mostly a fluid experience with each button press feeling natural in time with the rhythm. Mistakes will be made but they rarely feel unfair, but the game is nonetheless totally unforgiving in that any mistake that causes an impact with an obstacle will cause Commander Video to fall right back to the start of the stage and do it all over again. Later stages may cause players to give up out of frustration, even on easy difficulty (which isn't actually easier at all).
Completing a challenging stage gives great satisfaction and the motivation to carry on through the disappointingly bland presentation. It tests your skills and timing rather than relying on stats and/or making it too easy, but this will of course leave some people out of luck if they are finding it too difficult to continue past a certain point, because anything short of perfection will not allow for progression. Despite this, the difficulty curve is relatively steady from start to finish.
BIT.Trip Runner is a fun game to play in short bursts, but due to the monotony of the visuals, audio and level design, would probably cause headaches and frustration if played for much longer durations.

This game looks stunning.Environments ranging from the doors of the Manufactorum straight to the Titan Invictus itself you will experience some of the most well crafted settings you could ask for in a WH40K game.
Space Marine is a 3rd person shooter/hack and slash. The melee is some of the most satisfying ive ever seen in a game and it works incredibly well with the provided weapons. Hacking through your enemies with a power axe or ripping them to literal shreds with a chainsword you will not be disappointed with the melee system in place here. There's alse an execution mechanic that you'll be constantly using to replenish your health in the longer battles.The game isn't just hack and slash though. You also have a fair variety of ranged weapons including but not limited to,the Stalker Pattern Boltgun,the Plasma Cannon,and the Storm Bolter. All of the ranged weapons have a satisfying kick that you would expect from a 40K game.
Space Marine features a co-op "Exterminatus" mode.The mode itself features either chaos marines or space marines(depending on if you're playing the DLC or not) holding out against waves of enemies on one of two different missions sets,Assault on Hab Center Andreas or Escape from Kalkys Facility.The mission sets include 4 different arenas with 5 waves in each.Multiple small objectives are inserted every little while as well. The objectives are mainly just hold a point for 2 minutes or something like that. There's also challenges that pop up during gameplay such as "kill 20 enemies in 10 seconds" or "kill 5 shoota boys in 15 seconds".
I personally didnt care too much for the multiplayer.It gets stale rather quick due to there being only around 5 maps and 2 objective types.The maps make up in quality what they lack in numbers but still its just not enough to keep the gameplay from becoming stale.
This is more of a middle ground.The story wasn't bad but it sure was incredibly average and the story ended on a cliffhanger. That wouldn't be a problem if THQ hadn't gone bankrupt and the 2 other planned games in the series been cancelled. As it stands the story is just average. Average characters,average dialogue,and an infuriating ending.

-No romance options AT ALL for the protagonist until the very end, which is kept super minimal

Holy crap what can we say about this marvelous adventure and effort to bring it to consoles/additional content/controller support?!
One of the first things you'll notice, is that EVERY npc interaction is now fully voiced whereas beforehand only major characters were voiced (leaving the game feeling rather empty perhaps though it was supported by excellant writing).  All of that is now still there and it's certainly nice even interacting with a fish vendor or other minor entity that it has it's own voice.  Fantastic!  That alone would be worth buying the enhanced addition.
Quests have been reworked so they are more streamlined and additional quests have been added.  I was playing along the first major quest noticing a quest item had been moved here or there but it was essentially the same storyline.  Happy to report that keyboard and mouse working just fine - and PC demands were performing better with no visual hitching or bugs that I noticed.  I am not running the game on a 'state of the art machine' 12GB of DDR3 Ram, Quad Core Processor and only 1 GTX 680 (the other one died haven't bothered to replace it); so overall performance is optimized pretty damn well.
Next, after 2/3 of the way through the main first storyline (Mysterious Murdur) I plugged my controller in - a 360 controller and was immediately detected with a tutorial starting up as things came up to show how to interact with the world using it.  I found the transition seemless.  The radial menus are easy to navigate, and became intuitive after an hour or so.  Navigating inventory, a somewhat annoying task with mouse/keyboard I found to be a bit easier though you can certainly flip from mouse/keyboard and back to controller easily enough (ingame keybind) so choose which way you want to play.  Personally I found that sitting back and moving my team around using a controller much easier as I've often lately grown tired of clicking around etc so its nice to sit back on my couch thus using my 360 Controller.
Is this game worth a buy then?  It was with the unenhanced version and well, it certainly is now.  So what are you wating for?  I would buy this if you like RPGs, its a fantastic game with hours and hours of gameplay.  The added voice content and controller support offering more ways to play a great game.

Set in the Age of Sail you will captain your ship through the entire Caribbean in search of either the riches of the land or the blood of the enemy. You are able to rank up to command some of the biggest ships out there, like the 1st Rate HMS Victory, or build up your trading and crafting endeavours and rake in the big money.
There are a whole bunch of nations to choose from (United States, Denmark/Norway, Sweden, British Empire, France, Dutch Republic of the United Provinces, Spain and the outlaw Pirates), ranging in various difficulties depending on how many islands they start out with and their diplomatic capabilities. You can log onto a server (PvP or Player versus Player) where many of the ports can be conquered by other players of other nations and players of the different nations can fight it out in the Caribbean waters with each other as well, or you can choose to take it easy and sail around on the PvE (Player versus Environment) server where those things are disabled. Rank progression is shared among the two, money and assets aren't.
Even at this early stage the tropical world you sail in looks gorgeous and the action when battling looks breathtaking. That being said, it's not a game for the people that are impatient and with a short attention span. If you intend on exploring the Caribbean you can easily spend 30 to 60 minutes sailing without anything in sight but open sea before reaching land again. But it's worth picking up for those who played Empire: Total War for the ships and possibly familiar with Pirates of the Burning Sea.

Naval Action offers a borderline simulator experience with its age-of-sail combat gameplay. Take command of anything from a simple schooner to powerful Ships-of-the-Line. Travers a massive map of the Caribbean and experience beutiful sights and sounds of the Age-of-Sail.
In-depth naval combat mechanics means you control your yards and aim your cannons all while attempting to manuever and dodge gunfire yourself. Mistime or aim incorrectly and watch your broadside fly over the enemy's deck or hit the sides of a wave insted of the enemy's hull. Misuse your sails and you'll find yourself face-first to the wind and unable to move, am easy sitting target for your enemies.
This is NOT a pirate game. This is an Age-of-Sail game. While pirates are a playabe option, they are by no means easy to master. The game offres a challenge while still being fun. As is expected with Early Access, there are still a bit of impurities and imbalance, but even so, the combat system alone is very well honed and can offer some interesting yet not altogether lopsided battles.
This is a must for anyone who is interested in the Age of Sail.

I started playing Naval Action about a year ago. When I bought it, you could only play something called Sea Trails, which was only combat and no open world. I got a bit tired of the wipes, so I didn't play that much. That didn’t mean I disliked it, though. Naval Action does in fact beat all the games I've played about warships from the age of sail. I think it beats Assassin's Creed: Black Flag and Pirates of the Caribbean Online by a long shot, even though I played the crap out of them. That was true even a year ago, when the ship vs. ship action wasn't as good as it is now and there was no open world.
The visuals are amazing, too. Stern lights and the day and night cycle gives a really good atmosphere. When in combat, the muzzle flashes of cannons going off as well as the gunpowder smoke looks better than in any other similar game.
I have most graphic options on the lowest, but the game still looks amazing.
Naval Action already have a lot of different vessels ranging from fast 8 cannon sail ships to giant first rate ships of the line with up to 138 cannons and three gun decks (four if you include the weather deck).
If you have played World of Warships, you will recognize certain elements when it comes to shooting. For instance, you can shoot individual shots to make sure the full broadside will hit. It is, however, more difficult and in my opinion better than in WoWs.
Wind is an important aspect in NA, as all ships are using sails. Tacking against the wind can be hard for newcomers, but there are good tutorials out there that cover this.
Open world is something I haven’t really played that much, but I do like it. You can choose between the British, French, Spanish, Swedish, Danish-Norwegian, Dutch, United States navies as well as Pirates. You become a Pirate automatically when attacking ships from your own navy. The whole crafting and trading system may seem a little overwhelming to some, but it is something that should be learnt quite easily. Off course, there are tutorials for that too.
Ships can be crafted, and players can set ships for sale at a price they choose themselves. You can, for example, sell a cutter (The first ship you get) for 100.000 gold, but nobody will buy it as they can get it for free in the store. Also, each ship have 5 durability, which means that if it sinks 5 times it is gone forever. You can buy repair kits, but in combat you can only use one. That means that you will often find yourself running away if you’ve ended up in a bad situation.
Apart from from the placeholder UI, the only thing I dislike about the game is that after you buy it, there’s no way to continue supporting it through the game itself.
The game is not for people who are just looking for a relaxed and forgiving MMO experience, but if you're interested in warship games I can almost guarantee that you'll like it.
There is more to this game than just what I've mentioned, and I might add to this review when I've played some more.
10/10

*** Review for SINGLE PLAYER game ***
I liked this game!  The story, characters, and gameplay.  Loved "Ethan" (E3N) especially.
It held appeal because of the game's incorporation of "values".  For instance, the marines(?) commander's viewpoint toward Ethan changing over time.  The hatred for the people of Earth on the part of the Martian humans, and their collective, communal drive toward expansion and dominance via war ... it being their societal ethic.  Made me happy to bring 'em crashing to ground!  :D
The "Klingon in me" was glad to see sacrifical deaths of heroes.  Nothing new in that with CoD instalments, heroes going down in battle.  But
These sorts of things, for me, make satisfying endings to stories.
I found it both an interesting and a good addition to the CoD franchise to have the side missions to different parts of the solar system.  Missions to assault fleets or facilities using space fighter-craft or as ground assaults.  They added more content to the single-player experience.  I played them all through the first time.  However, they are optional ... at least in subsequent plays through.  I don't know if the "chance of mission success" figure for each side-mission had any bearing upon the difficulty of the main game's ending.  When I had my second play-through, I don't think I did any side missions.
The game controls seemed typical and thus natural and easy.  The character motion/animation was (imo) good.  Two-stage negotiation of obstacles such as walls with NPCs is probably fairly standard, I guess, being a bit of a cut-scene thing.  ** There's a game called "Warface", a free-to-play multiplayer FPS that uses two players to perform such two-stage manoevers!  First to boost one up, the second to pull the booster up.  Kudos to the Warface devs!  :D **
There was a satisfying variety of environments.  Most notable for me was probably the darkness caused by dust/smoke during one stage of the attack on Earth.
Heaps of weaps to pick up.  Customise your loadout for each mission if you want.
*** The bad ... ***
There was crashing ... and it wasn't just a few times.  I think it was mainly an issue with my PC setup though.  *Very* unimpressed with my GFX card.  It's been crashing for everything.  Most play was during the summer (southern hemisphere), so cooling issues really came into play.  Aimed some fans into my open PC case.  That *largely* resolved the issues.  I used a Gigabyte R390.  It was capable of displaying full HD but seemed unstable.  However, I had removed the OC Guru s/w and I think the result was that the fans weren't operating optimally because the OS didn't know the metrics.  My mistake.
*** Summation ***
I liked it.  Only played it through twice though.  This is typical for me on SP FPS's because, unlike action-RPGs (FPRPGs/RPS), they don't have the same depth of character customisation that encourages "a different approach".

Ah Bit.Trip. I like the entire series. Some games I like more than others. Void is a strange one indeed. But that's not why we're here! You're here to see what I like about the Wii ware turned Steam title that is Bit.Trip Runner! Well, It's good.
The games controls are simple: one button is to jump, another is to duck, another is to kick, another is to spring on platforms, and another is for blocking beats. five buttons. The game could've been played on an NES. That said, it is as hard as some NES games. You run at a constant velocity, jumping and sliding your way past obstacles. With each successful jump avoidance of said obstacles, a little note is played with the music. get a pile of gold, another note. Get a little + (they're called Mode Ups) and the music raises in intensity and your score multiplier is raised. fail to jump or hit something and you get sent back to the beginning. Collect all the gold and Mode Ups and you can enter an Atari 2600 style bonus challenge where the stakes are set even higher: You have one shot and one shot only.
While it seems simple and devilishly difficult. It's the way that the game is designed that keeps you hooked. As you play, you enter a zen like trance where you anticipate and react to incoming obsticales, all with the music pounding in your ears. It's something that really cant be expressed in words. So let this be a resounding "GET THIS GAME"
There's also cards for you card collectors.
The Music alone is worth it, If you can get it for cheap, go for it!

Dream is a game that makes you think inside-the-box in outside-the-box scenarios. I came across this game by accident: I wanted to find a newer game that was similar to LSD: Dream Emulator, a game I have never played, but want to play something like it. Dream did not disappoint that urge, but in its current state, it does have a few things I want to point out.
WARNING: The following will contain spoilers.
I decided to purchase this game recently after it had been sitting in my wishlist while I was broke. I wanted something new and different to play. This was a good choice, but some things still bother me:
REALISM: This game is set in a realistic scenario, where you play Howard, a British man who, should we say, talks to himself alot. The story comes from his abstract dreams which are supposed to represent the dreams (and nightmares) we have in real life. When playing this game, I don't feel like I'm in a dream at all. If we are being nitpicky, dreams are different levels of hazy, and are not always in perfect lucidity. I mention this because I want the game to feel like a dream, not just a series of abstract levels and puzzles.
LINEAR: In its current state, the game is very linear, Yes, there are small worlds in which you can explore, but each dream leads to the next, and the start of the game is always the same: Go to sleep, go to the hub world, go to a dream world. I can't help but feel a sense of repetitiveness every time I start the game up. I feel that the dreams should be random, and should randomly link to other dreams. I also think not every world should contain a puzzle. In the abstract worlds of dreams, most of the dream is exploring, or for some people, just letting your dream control you, tell you where to go, and tell you what to do, like a story.
PUZZLES: I've never had a dream with a puzzle in it. I also think this game puts too much emphasis on the puzzles, and not enough on the exploration. Puzzles, in my opinion, should be a rarity, not how you reach the next level. I think each level should be the result of picking up an item, or enteracting with a being.
PORTALS: I think the portals that are currently in use are unrealistic for the dream scenario. I also think nightmares should not be easily noticeable based on the color of the portal. Nightmares are not something that can be avoided when they start, so seeing a black portal would be unrealistic, and gives us the choice to enter it or avoid it.
DIALOGS: Between dreams, there are some dialogs between Howard and his uncle Ed. These dialogs seem to last for what feels like hours, and all I'm left to do is sit there and wait it out. If there's any way of making these dialogs a little shorter, that would be great. I want to get to the next level already.
I think this game could be better, but I would still recommend it to those interested in playing a game based on dreams. I do wish that there will be larger worlds, more exploration, and a more interactive story. I also hope that there is a better use of Howard's house. Currently it is only used for the Tutorial and the nightmares. I think it should have more use as a bigger part of the story, such as if Howard has a job, or people coming over, then Howard could also live a life during the day, and the game could use Howard's workplace for dreams and nightmares, and more exploration. Consider the state of this game as a prototype. It could use some polishing and added content. Looking forward to the development of the game, and its evolution.

This one came out as a gorgeous, engaging and fun explorer with some big annoyances, but overall worth experiencing. I'm not sure where I picked Dream up, but the narrative and dialogue hooked me right away, and the simple gameplay and gorgeous world were enough to keep me there and the weird and interesting rewards for exploring brought it up a level. Unfortunately it also frustrated the hell out of me and felt rushed and incomplete at stages, especially because of some jarring technical problems which are actively difficult to avoid in certain areas. Fortunately due to the non-linear nature of Dream and because of the casual gameplay, these problems are only as apparent as the sections they're found in, and can be mostly ignored if so desired.
Dream differs from most games in it's genre by not sticking to a linear path, and instead offering the player the ability to approach whatever they like after the initial segment. This gives a casual hands-off approach to exploration and puzzles that means revisiting the game lowers any frustrations it has, and keeps it pleasant. It's also a very good looking title, and the tone, atmosphere and theme for each section and subsection is done well. The clever writing help out too and all combine fairly well.
The puzzles are a mixed bag of really quite fun to bloody laborious and frustrating, but overall they're mostly engaging and with a fair pay off which again is helped by the clever writing and steady narration.
While there are some very minor issues I found with annoying level design or small graphical problems, they're all negligible and don't take away from the game at all and the only issue with Dream from a gameplay standpoint was that it was often far too ambiguous, vague or lacking in showing the player how to progress and I found myself looking up a guide or walk through rather than being able to deduce from my surroundings or steps so far how to accomplish something. I understand that the nature of the game is meant to be soft and ambiguous to fit in with the dreamlike nature, but when that makes it harder rather than easier for the player to establish a foothold on the games good points, it's simply bad design.
The main complaint however, is the technical problems, and it's a shame that it's such a meaty complaint that harms the game overall.
The one I had most troubles with, and probably the biggest complaint from the community involves a particular level where interacting with movement control hubs is either slow and misaligned or simply flat out broken. The cursor routinely disappears when interacting with computer terminals and causes issues. Oculus Rift support is all but an afterthought, and is currently completely broken. I ran into one instance where I jumped out of an elevator and found a secret hidden floor that I thought was a really cool setup for a level; instead after falling down a tunnel for 5 minutes I realized it was a level design glitch and I wasn't even supposed to be there, and there are countless other bugs and problems others have had I haven't approached.
There have been consistent updates from the developers addressing technical problems with Patch 1.1 in particular addressing keybindings, collision, menu items and more. It's just a shame there are still so many issues and that the time needed to polish and patch this game was never given throughout development.
At £12.99/15.99€/$16.99, Dream is probably fairly priced, but given the availability of alternatives and titles of the same ilk, it's not great value for money if you're weighing your options. Both NaissanceE and The Stanley Parable, for comparison, more linear but slightly similar titles with equally attractive visuals and more polish, and I'd argue much more engaging overall, are around 25% cheaper and so probably better purchases when choice matters.
The soundtrack is worth pointing out as being good, but like the game, it's quite mellow and ambient, and justifying half the cost of the game again isn't realistic. If on sale, it may be better value for money.

So this is a nice, short Metroidvania style game with a remarkable art style and a superb soundtrack. It's got some decently challenging platforming in it and some fantastic level design.
I've seen some people describe the game as 'hard'. It isn't. One of Ori's core features is the ability to create save points at any safe location, which essentially means that the game pretty much expects you to essentially go through its challenging platform sections with a bit of trial and error. You'll jump off a platform and get shot by one of the forests many death lasers, which kills you instantly. But that's okay! Respawn is completely instantaneous and doesn't break the game's flow, so you can live and adapt.
Mind you: A bit of quick thinking and twitch reflexes can get you through things in the first go for most of the game. However, in the 'escape' sections you can expect to have to go through them 6-10 times before you get it right. And that's okay! Learning patterns and executing interesting escapes is really quite fun. Especially since Ori gives you such a variety of different platforming tools to deal with any given problem.
Though honestly: The fact that the game is challenging makes me like it all the more. Games have gotten too accessible lately. I like the image of some hippy getting the game based on the art style, expecting some postmodern tale about the folly of man, and then getting spikes shoved up his butt. GIT GOOD SON.
Speaking of the story, it's actually pretty good, but ultimately a bit too happy go lucky for my tastes. Anyone that tells you that they cried at the beginning is probably the same kind of person that cries during Disney movies. Mommy dies, ♥♥♥♥, no one cares. Get a ♥♥♥♥ing hold of yourself, you're a ♥♥♥♥ing mess.
But in any case:
It's smooth, it's satisfying and it's beautiful. It's over in about 8-9 hours, but you'll spend those hours in a bit of platforming bliss as you admire the jaw droppingly beautiful art style.
Get it. You'll enjoy it.

When I purchased this, what I was expecting was a short, linear platformer with a few themed levels and scripted sequences. What I was not expecting was a fully fleshed out Metroidvania style game with an expansive overworld map, hidden power-ups, and dungeon structure. All of the artwork and music is consistently high-quality as it is presented in trailers, and every character is fluidly animated and hand-drawn. The entire soundtrack is recorded from a live orchestra of original music. The most satisfying aspect of this game, though, is the movement. You start out frail and restricted in your movement options, but you acquire new abilities as you explore more of the map and the game progresses. By the end of the first dungeon, you'll already be able to chain together jumping techniques to a degree that you can acrobatically somersault and fly through several rooms with ease without touching the ground. It has the most satisfying platforming I've experienced since the year 2007. You can assign accrued ability points to three different ability branches and set save points at any point you wish, barring a few restricted areas. The main campaign can be finished shortly, but the time I spent trying the different movement techniques and exploring the map for power-ups and secrets extended my play time to a respectable amount. There are three dungeon areas with a pre-dungeon for each to unlock them, and every area is filled with challenging platforming segments and creative puzzles. Depending on how emotional you are, you may enjoy the fairy-tale story that develops over the game. Events occur gradually and if you are not just doing backtracking and exploration, there is never a time where it feels like nothing is happening. The content of this game is very high quality, especially for the price. If you like 2D platforming, map exploration, or fairy-tale 2D animation, you can't go wrong. The most pleasant surprise of the year.

Space Marine is a spectacular game. The graphics beautiful and they clearly show the the people who moddled this game took a lot of time and effort on this game. In the campaign I liked to spend 5 minutes sometimes just to admire the scene.  THere aren't many games out their that have been given as much time and effort to make the background so inspiring and so real life. Not only it shows the Imperium of man in the 41st millennium have such skilled builders like described in the books, but also shows how much potential moddlers can achieve when creating the game people are going to play.
The combat system is amazing. When first I heard about a 3rd person shooter for warhammer 40k I first thought it was a mistake and it should of been a first person. But I'm gladly they didn't make it a first person shooter, because if so the game would of been completley different. Not only it allows you to see background the full scale of the war, but also the executions you just can't stop loving. Every close combat weapon have there own executions for different scenarios of combat and for both Orc and Chaos as well as the Chaos deamons.
The campaign is a thrilling adventure which you can't stop playing until you have to force yourself to take a break. Like some books that have such cliff hangers on every chapter you can't stop reading, for example: Percy Jackson. There are scenes which hold your breath because you don't know where the squids will come from (little Orc kamikaze peach dogs that go up to their enemies and explode in front of their face) as your in a tight spaced sewer that the Orcs use to get into places. You don't know if they'l go up behind you or not and if they do then they can make you jump resulting in you getting killed sometimes, (which happened to me a lot in one of the chapters). There are also very happy ending like you finnaly beating the Orc warcheif and stop having to fight with the orcs.
There are two bosses in the game: The Orc Warcheif and The Chaos Prince, who both have their own combat moves which you have to get fiqure out and make a plan how to counter them.
There is only one sidequest in the game: to collect all servo sulls. It's not necessarily quest because no-one gives it to you, but there are to achivements if you collect servo skulls. And each servo skull is reward. Hint: It's something to do with Imperial Guard the and the people when the Orc Invasion struck.
After you finnish the campaign, you really want to go and start playing online. There are 2 gamemodes: Versus and Exterminatus.
Versus contains different gamemodes where there 2 teams against each oother: seize ground, annihilation, capture the flag, and a dlc gamemode: Drednought.
Seize ground is where there are 3-4 control points and both team have to hold and defend control points from the enemy team whilest treing to capture the enemies. Each control point you hold gives you points unless the enemy have captured more control points than your team.
Annihilation is where both teams try to be the first to get 41 kills.
Capture the flag is where both teams have to defend their own flag and capture the enemies flag 3 times.
Drednought is where both teams battle out to be in control of a drednought. At the start of the game or whenever a drednought is destroyed there will only be on capture point. The team who capture it, one of their players will become a drednought. That team has to captaure as many points as possible until reaching 20 points, whilest the other team try to destroy the drednought and dfending the control points.
Versus also contains weapon and armor challenges. Whenever you complete enough weapon points for a specific weapon, you get a weapon perk for that weapon. If you complete enough armour challenges, you get different armour parts available to you for you to use.
Exterminatus is really fun. There are a max of 4 players in a single game, where they need to work as a team treing to survive waves of Orcs or Imperial guard or Space Marines. There are 2 exterminatus gamemodes and 3 maps. Each map contains 4 arenas and each arena contains 5 waves. The 4th arena however has a bonus round.
Classic gamemode is where your team are the Space marines and you fight waves of Orcs. On the Bonus round you fight a wave of Chaos marines and Chaos deamons. There are 2 maps for this gamemode.
The Chaos Unleashed is a dlc gamemode where your team are the Chaos marines fighting waves of Orcs, Imperial guard and Space Marines. The Bonus round is where you fight massive swarm of Orcs who have the help of Killa Kans.
You can customise your own character who can achieve you the maximum level of 41. Each level grants you a reward. The character is either Chaos or Space marine depending on the gamemode. You only have one online character who can equip different loadouts you can customise. There are 3 classes for online: Tacticle, Devestator (Heavy), or Assult. Each loadout contains a class you can pick. The options are yours. Use which ever weapons you like best for different classes and their perks.
You can customise how you Space Marine and Chaos Marine lookes as well. You can choose chapter set, or make your own set. Most armour parts will be locked until you unlock them in Versus mode by completing the armour challenges. But if you want something more Vertren then you can buy some skins, which are very cheap.
The DLC are worth getting. The Chaos Unleashed unlocks new maps for Versus and a gamemode for Exterminatus.
The drednought unleashed gives you extra maps for Versus and a new gamemode for Versus.
There are a whole selection of VErtren skins you can buy and customise your character with.
And there are 3 dlc weapons.
In my opion the whole game is worth the price and all of the DLC's. Although I recommend you buying only one Vertren Skin set for Space Marine and Chaos Marine since you can only use one at a time. But the choice is yours.

I like this game a lot. There is a wide variety of game modes that include coop, pvp, and invasions. The first two are self-explanatory but the invasions are similar to dark souls. You can invade another persons single player game and take control of one of the AI wizards. You can also volunteer to become an ally instead. Keep in mind you can disable this completely if you want to play without interruptions.
You control wizard(s) and cast spells in a turn-based format. The objective is to kill the enemy wizards. The gameplay is simple and well explained in the expansive tutorial; however, the point of contention is the RNG or luck. Everyone has 1 hit point and your spells have percentage chances to cast. This makes the game feel like a mix between Chess and Poker. The movements of the wizard and casted minions are strategic, but you must manage your RNG appropriately. You need to make the right decisions and try your best to account for mistakes. 1 HP means that any attack landing will be a death.
This is a remake to the classic game Chaos and it lives up to its namesake. You need to manage your luck, not control it and take your losses on the chin. There is a ton of replayability, between realms and the various pvp. The bar for entry is very low and not intimidating, so it's worth giving it a shot if you enjoy turn-based games heavily wrapped in luck. RNGesus take the wheel!

This is a new take on an old classic, keeping excellent gameplay but updating just about everything else to make it enjoyable by today's standards.
The premise is that you are a Wizard fighting one to 3 other Wizards, human or AI, and take turns in summoning creatures or casting damage spells, with the goal of defeating the other Wizards.
There is a good degree of complexity with the possibility to bluff hard to cast spells (cast illusions), and the opponent to call your bluff (disbelieve).  As you case more spells aligned to Law, other law spells become easier to cast, and vice versa with Chaos.
Although this is not a card game, I think people who like the depth offered by games like Hearthstone or Magic the Gathering, will be pleasantly surprised.  Although your list of spells is somewhat smaller, the option to boost them, bluff them, physically move and position creatures adds a new level of depth which is intuitive and easy to understand.  The tutorials do an excellent job of explaining the game mechanics.
All in all, an excellent turn based game.

Naval Action is purely a ship based game, no walking on land or walking around on the ships however this does not mean that boarding is not a thing, whether you are a pirate or you sail for any of the numerous navies you can capture enemy ships and either take her a prize, sell her or even just sink her and keep the possible loot for your self for trading purposes.
The game also features a crafting system which you can use to craft ships, however if crafting is not something for you you can buy ships from the stores or find a crafter which can craft a ship to your specifications, there are plenty of crafters out there.
Upgrades allow you to change the qualities of your ships, most upgrades have some short of downside which means that you have to pick and choose which ones best fit your style, you also have a limited amount of upgrades slots and if your ship looses all its durabilities(lives) you will loose the ship and all its durabilites
Positives:
-many beautiful ships ranging from the tiny lynx(schooner) to the giant first rate 138 gunner that is the santisima
-an open world with ports and plenty of enemies to fight
-Great visuals and amazing looks
-simple UI
-everything isnt done for you, navigation and such is up to you so you can get lost
-Both PVE and PVP servers so if you dont like PVP you can always be on the PVE server and be sure that you are safe from getting attacked by players, however if you like PVP join on in the exciting PVP on the PVP Server!
Negatives:
-UI although simple is not the most easy to use as it is very much work in progress and it does not look pretty
-the game can be very demanding on your system, you need at least a decent cpu and gpu to play the game thus stopping entry level systems from being able to run this game at decent(30 fps and above) frame rates
-No tutorial(there is a good beginners guide by me here though:
Neutral:
-The travel time on the Open World can be a bit excessive however depending on the person, it might be too fast or too slow, I find it personally fine where it is

There is another review on here that Ant has put up, with a lot of negative comments for it. Forlorne Hope wrote this in response, and had it spread over four comments due to a 1000 character limit. He opted to delete it, with no response. It is unsurprising he deletes any comments that disagree with him so that he creates this aura of agreement. It is a shame that Steam allows one to do so. Now, I edit my own review to let it be more widely known:
You have to wonder why someone would spend so much time bashing a game, instead of listing a review and moving on. The feedback could be useful, but, from what I gather, this user has decided to remove any the development team's direct feedback on the game, right here, rather than letting people leave their comments and have a productive discussion.
That said, this player has decided to try to do exactly what he accuses others of doing: Silencing those of differing opinions.
Let us address this review point by point:
He cites that there is nothing to due, as there are not enough people sailing around. Yet, it would be interesting to figure out just where this player was sailing. There is plenty of traffic in the Antilles. There is plenty of traffic around Cuba/Haiti. There are quieter zones as well, such as the Gulf.
He states that the massive grind is a huge turn-off, yet... there is no need to grind. Smaller vessels are viable, as are larger ones. The Lynx, the lowest ranked vessel in the game, is great for running down Trader's Lynxes, which are what people run their high-value cargo in (due to their high speed upwind).
Concerns of optimization and lack of UI are curious, as it is an alpha game, where optimization is towards the end, and UI will be worked on once the features themselves are in. The developers have said this themselves.
Content patches are generally monthly, with new patch notes for October already posted. New ships are regularly added, new mission types are in this patch, forts along coast lines are in this patch, land in OW battles has been in for some time, and land in port battles is still coming. A "lack of content" seems to me to simply say, "I want it all, and I want it now."
The playerbase has contracted from peak times when huge content patches were added. This is shocking to none. In a lull period between patches, the game still hovers around 800 players at peak hours, and 400 players at off-peak hours. In an alpha game.
As far as microtransactions go, I believe they are still working on that, with potential changes to come. I do not believe anything is finalized yet.
The ultimate concerns of this player comes down to the developer staff, and in particular, one person. Simply put, Ant doesn't like admin, and seems to have made it his goal to do a character assassination of him, and of the game. He still brings it up regularly, and tries to make an issue out of it. And yet, the key thing this player was complaining about is being added in this month's patch anyway.
Maybe this player wants to have an honest assessment of the game. Maybe he has the integrity to allow for a differing view. We'll know that he does if this response is still here in a week or two.
If he simply deletes it, well, then we know he just has an ax to grind, and should be given that level of concern.

Dream is a beautiful and twisted journey through the subconscious. You play Howard, a man with a over active imagination and recurring dreams. You guide Howard as he goes through these dreams and solves puzzles and begins to unravel the mystery of his own mind. What makes Dream so unique is that the narrative and path you take is up to you. There are many paths to choose from and each them weirder then the last. There are many details in the game that make it's story and universe rich. Along the same lines of Gone Home, you can pick up items and learn more about Howard and the houses former tenant. However, this is far from just some simple walking simulator. (even though I don't think that's a bad name/genre) There are several puzzles that keep you involved in the games story and makes you feel like an active participant, even if you don't know necessarily what is going on. Dream is gorgeous in design, music, and sound, it's game that must be experienced to truly understand. The tone of game can shift in seconds, as every dream, can be become a nightmare. This tonal shift keeps you on edge and makes the game feel suspenseful. I feel like I barely scratched the surface of Dream and there is  so much more to see and do in this journey.

I would give BIT. TRIP RUNNER a 5/10.
BTR is a music and rhythm game, where you must perform a simple set of platforming moves to music. As you progress through the level, you can collect gold pieces or bonuses that allow each gold bar to be worth more. Each of these upgrades adds new levels of musical melody and harmony, making the music more complex and beautiful.
Whenever your character that you control collects a gold piece, smashes through a box, or jumps over a cavern, the game reflects that by making a musical sound within the realm of the song. Your character, in essence, can add to the song, which is pretty cool. The music itself sounds great, an electronic, pulsing rhythm. You progress through 3 "worlds" each with a different setting, and each world has a dozen or so levels. Each world has similar style tunes, and each level within that world is slightly varied from the one before.
As cool as the levels are though, I still don't recommend this game. The main thing that is frustrating is that you can make zero mistakes throughout the course of the level in order to beat it. While getting gold pieces does make the music sound better and gives higher scores you don't have to get it. But if you run into a block that can't be broken or miss jumping a gap, at all, through the whole level, for each level, you must start over at the beginning of that level.
I am fine for having a difficult game, but some levels are quite hard and require precision, and sometimes the levels can have a lot going on to watch for. This can make it frustrating to practice the level a lot but see zero progress. Many of the later levels especially have a somewhat cheap mechanic at the end of the levels, that throw something random at you just as you feel you are near the end. Think you are done? Nope a random purple block with no leadup from the music or other channels after you are simply running on a flat path for 5 seconds takes you out and you start over, ending your perfect run.
Because of that I can't recommend it. If you get it for a good price and are up for the challenge or like rhythm and music games, it may be worth a shot.

<- n ->
[..........] ^
[--.......] |
[----....] n/c

I honestly wanted to write a review for this game a little further into it.  I do have more than 22 hours in game, maybe offline gaming does not count.. That out of the way;
I am pretty pleased with the overall scope and feel of the game.  It wouild be nice to have a higher population, but again, not too many people dedicate time into early access game like this one.
Population is a bummer atm.
Next I look to another part of games that clinch things for me, tho NOT honestly something you see as common place in survival games.. That being taming.  I like to tame.. plus.. your own pets just make better friends/group mates.  So. currrent lack of taming is another bummer.
Lastly for the things that bum me out.. The frequency at which you need to eat and drink. I  understand that this is a survival game, and thats all well and good.. But seriously. if I ate and drank this often IRL. I would be the size of my car.. tied into this issue for me, we have decay of food stuffs. I decided one day I was just sick of jogging up over the hill, and down the next, for my setlang sandwich, so I killed everything with a pulse, that even looked like it may go well with a slice of bread.. Had a nice fatty haul to trudge home with.. ONLY to get the food cooked, which I assumed would dramatically adjust decay rate, yet I find myself seeing by the timers, that I would soon be headed out to my local not so fast food joint for a bit of setlang.
The other thinig that isn't really an issue so much as it is a feature not yet dropped in, is my guess at least.  That issue being Way points that draw a rudimentary line to keep you focused.. They added markers, and I stopped.. well almost stopped.. well kinda stopped losing my base set up locations.. BUT.. travel lines of some sort, would be nice for when you have to circle mob spawns quickly, and need to keep your bearings.
The Graphics, that several have spoke of, and controls being slow or clunky?  Those are things that are fine to me.  My in game, in fact, looks very close if not exactly what the preveiws show.  Maybe a bit better even.  my FPS, honestly couldnt tell you, I am not lagging at all when playing for at the least 85=90% of the time, and since this is the case I see no reason for me to run searching for ping and FPS
As far as the controls causing issues.. I'm not sure what those issues could be?  For me, I like the freedom to remap any key to any other key. The poblem with that, is, again, more likely it just isn't dropped into teh game yet..
Harvesting and Crafting both work well.  There are numerous things to "munkey" around with. and you can get a fairly decent small base going without too many tears falling from starving to death.  No taming, which I cant say enough times  to at least try getting into the game.
The game runs very well for me on any of my 3 machines, but I do wish it could load thru the slpash screen much faster..
Overall the players are non toxic, something rare, as of late, in the gaming community.
I would buy the game without question at its current price, and while I may not burn up hours in it like I did MMO game titles. I log in and play at least once a week, and no doubt end up staying in the server, unaware the amount of time that has passed.
I use survival games as my break time from MMO gaming. This one does very well in the area of keeping me guessing, and with me finding out that mobs in games really do attack, and kill you.  Too often the mobs in MMO games and even survival games, are so toned down, that you can play one game with this hand.. and another game on the other hand, While watching tv or any number of other activities.   Now I wouldnt complain if there were more mobs, and if areas were pre developed  setting up several "destroyed" settlement type grinding locations.
I give the game a solid 7.5/10 with faith that it will continue to flesh out as it moves forward. TAMING woulda been an 8.. Just Sayin.
IF you are the type needing direction, or someone who needs the gfx you find in single player/console style games. OR if you need a lot of NPC quest guided interactions, and the bells and whistles you get with AAA developers. Then you may want to move along, this may not be your game.. However, in thinking about the survival game  genre alone. Many of them that push those graphic, fall way short in the area of FREE content. Direction for players, Support of their game, and so many other things.  This game needs work still. To my tastes, a good bit of work in needed. However, the whole concept of Early Access, is for players to jump in, play the game, give input, then rinse and repeat, every change.. or after each patch. which consistently comes rolling along once every week.
If you like being annoyed that you died from starvation, and on your server death = loot AND/OR skill. knowledge dropped plus you loot.. then jump in.  It's is beyond a doubt worth 10$.. even just to grab and keep checking in on the dev progress...

Although the story line of Major/Minor was not as lengthy and choice-filled as I had imagined, I was still on taken for quite the ride. Although it started slow, the ambient music, fleshed-out characters, and heart-breaking consequences kept me eager to follow the story to its end - and this is coming from a gamer who is usually more concerned about action than sitting down for a nice long read.
[WARNING: POTENTIAL SPOILERS]
Going through my first run and not getting the true ending left me with a lingering "but there's nothing else you can do" feeling. Don't get me wrong, I still enjoyed it for what it was, but I felt like everything that led up to it was almost of no effect and that the potential for a final decision - of what the
wanted to do - was overlooked.
Additionally, the guarentee of the character being erased from existence in exchange for saving what was left of it became an ironclad finale that was twisting my emotions apart. It arose moral questions and philosophy; "how will I truly know I saved everything if I'm going to vanish, prohibited by fate to see the fruits of my work?" I ached over the thought of just vanishing, and my fears of what lay beyond the void of death from when I was ten came rushing back to me that night (perfect time to view an ending like that, right?).
Then, seeing Acheron visit his sister in suspended time, but not knowing what happened was a major side-cliffhanger. As soon as the epilogue took that turn, I was upset, not knowing Maxine's fate - forgiven, erased from history, etc.
[END OF SPOILERS]
All in all, Major/Minor gave me the feels - the ones only a few certain stories can froce their readers to have. Even without much replayability, It was still worth its price to kill time and delve into the idea. If anything should be changed, it should be a quick-access menu for displaying the controls and shortcuts, as well as possibly a tree diagram showing the paths you've taken, so as to avoid repeats or for experimentation. Even if you're not a furry, this is still a good read. If you're strictly anti-furry, then go ahead and be stubborn - you are missing out!
9.6/10

The Imperial Forge World Graia is under heavy attack by Orks. Since Graia is a place where War Titans are constructed it has to be defended at any cost. Unfortunately there is no army close enough to react in time, so a part of the Ultramarine's 2nd company which happens to be closer to Graia is sent there. The Ultramarine's Captain Titus is the protagonist of the game. He and two other Marines - Leandros and Veteran Sergeant Sidonus - barely make it to the surface of Graia since the Orks are already controlling the planet's airspace. Soon Titus finds out that Graia holds something even more valuable than War Titans and that something even more dangerous than Orks is at work here.
Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine is a third person action game. It cannot really be called a third person shooter because melee combat is an integral part of the game. Titus has access to various melee and ranged weapons. He starts out with a knife, a bolt pistol and a bolter. Later, more weapons can be found. The pistol and the bolter are not swap-able, they are however later changed into a plasma pistol and a kraken bolter. Titus can equip two more ranged weapons and one melee weapon at a time. Those can be swapped out for other weapons freely. Additionally Titus can have up to five grenades with him. Space Marine flips turret sections the bird. Yes, there are mounted guns that you can use from time to time. But you can just rip those out and walk around with them. There are also some sections in which Titus uses a jump pack. While using one of those he is restricted to melee weapons, pistol and bolter.
Combat in Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine is extremely visceral and satisfying. All of the weapons feel powerful. One thing the game gets extremely right is conveying what a Space Marine actually is. He is not just a heavily armored soldier. He is a genetically enhanced super soldier carrying weapons that normal people would not even be able to use effectively. A Space Marine's armor is pretty much the finest one humanity is able to craft and only works because of the servos inside of it. The size difference between the Space Marines and the soldiers of the Imperial Guard is highly noticeable. Also you can kill weaker enemies by simply dashing into them. Titus' armor regenerates after not being hit for a few moments. Health however is replenished by executing stunned enemies. Some weaker enemies can be executed right away without even hitting them first, further conveying the actual power of a Space Marine. This is the single thing the game does best in my opinion: making you actually feel like a Space Marine.
The single player campaign is fairly enjoyable. It can drag a little in the middle part but it's not that bad. The only real gripe I have with the game is the final boss battle. In my opinion it is quite lazy and uninspired. It is also an unnecessary late difficulty spike since there is only one autosave during the whole fight as opposed to the other boss battle where there were regular autosaves between phases. Other than that the campaign is really fun.
The multiplayer is surprisingly well done. It features classic modes such as team deathmatch and capture the flag as well as exterminatus that is basically a horde mode. Players play either as Space Marines or Chaos Space Marines and can choose from three classes: Tactical, Devastator (Havoc) and Assault (Raptor). Tactical Marines are the most versatile character and can equip a variety of different weapons. Devastator Marines carry the heaviest ranged weapons but are the least mobile class. Assault Marines are equipped with jump packs and focus heavily on melee weapons. Players unlock more weapons and equipment to choose from as they gain levels. Multiple loadouts can be saved for quick access. Also, every character can have two different perks in his loadout. Actually you unlock the second perk slot at level 15 but it does not take long to get there. Different perks and armor parts are unlocked via challenges that work pretty much like achievements. Armor is just for the looks, so players can pick whatever they like best. There are several armor sets but you can also choose to mix and match parts of them together to your liking. It can take a while to unlock the perks you want but that is partially negated by the ability to copy the loadout of the person who killed you instead of taking your normal loadout on respawn. The only shortcoming of the multiplayer is that it is peer2peer based and therefore can be laggy depending on who is the host.
Long story short, Warhammer 40,000 is a really enjoyable game that is pretty much a must-have for warhammer fans but also worth a look for everybody who likes action games.

tldr: it's pretty good
=====Positives:
-Fun turn-based gameplay with interesting and varied mechanics: rune abilities, burning cards, mana boosting, height levels and lines of sight, pillars with passive effects, summoned obstacles and stationary creatures, law/chaos bar... the list goes on
-Fluid to play, good controls including camera zoom and rotation (important for this kind of game!)
-Multi-part tutorial explaining most mechanics (but not all, especially specific creature mechanics sometimes aren't straightforward and are learned with experience) with additional challenge levels
-Supports battles of up to 4 players, plus offline with the option of vs cpu
-Endless Legend-esque realms* are fairly interesting and give you permanent progress (levels, equipment and runes) for your character
*Realms are small missions or campaigns that feel a little like Endless Legend, with various points where you buy and sell equipment, hire mercenaries, and recruit or subjugate native camps. As of now it definitely feels like a huge part of the game and what most people would spend time in; even competitive players not interested in realms would likely play here for the rewards. Nothing as large and complex as endless legend games though
=====Negatives:
-Portals cost gold and are often the only way to reach different areas, which can slow progress down or leave people stuck
-Fee for joining realms in certain cases such as after abandoning the realm: if someone gets stuck and they are forced to abandon the realm or wait for a long time for a random volunteer match, they are further punished by this... abandoning forfeits all rewards aside from xp anyway, don't think we need this
-Equipment doesn't tell you exactly what they do, for example does a "creature" staff give you different cards from a different type of staff? Which cards specifically?
-There seems to be no way to truly customise your deck to what you like if you can only choose from "types", especially when you don't know exactly what's different about them apart from the small stuff they do tell you (deck/hand size, etc)
=====Meh stuff (stuff that's not that bad but could be better):
-Might not have enough variety for some people, with only a handful of units spread out over three categories (neutral, law, chaos)... we'll see how much content is added in the future and at what rate, right now it's still serviceable
-RNG CAN be an annoyance, but just like endless legend you can make your RNG better by playing tactically, checking enemy movement and attack ranges, using the terrain and manipulating lines of sight
-There are only a handful of realms as of now and it seems like there are little ways to get more realms... we'll have to see about this in the future
-Volunteer system lets you play in other players' realms, but only for one battle... nice but turn-based realms supporting multiple players would have been better
-fighters from villages can only reach a short distance from where they are based. not a huge problem but there should be some sort of indication as to how far they can reach as this is important when deciding whether you need control of the village or not to help attack an area
-ordering your villages around feels clunky, and the bubbles representing them on the map don't accurately let you know where they are. This becomes important if you're moving around while a marauder's chasing you, as they could be just out of your reach to join the fight
=====ALL IN ALL
there's a lot of annoyances and stuff that isn't explained well, but the gameplay has fantastic mechanics and plays well. Not something I would would spend a lot of time on per day, but still a good game!

I've barely scratched the surface of Chaos Reborn, but it's clear that this is a must-buy, must play for fans of classic turnbased strategy games like X-Com, Jagged Alliance 2 etc. Of course it's made by X-Com creator Julian Gollop. The tactical combat looks like HoMM but is much more fun. It compares favourably to my other favourite turnbased game of this era, the Kings Bounty games. But the game that this reminds me of most of all is another favourite, Disciples 2. This is coming from someone who hates and won't play Disciples 3.
Basically in this game you control a wizard on a hex grid. You will have  a few small units to assist you and the wizard summons more allies or casts spells. Each spell cast has a % chance to succeed, so there's a luck element too. The tactical combat is highly polished and enjoyable. Hell, even the tutorials were fun!
This game is mainly geared towards multiplayer, which I haven't even touched yet, but old school players like me need not despair. There IS a large singleplayer component. This is the Realms mode, bascially dev or user made maps that really remind me of the strategic layer of Disciples 2, which was so much fun to play 10+ years ago. I haven't found a game other than Disciples 2 and the Kings Bounty games that are this much fun to play on the strategic and tactical layers. Enough said!

In summary, 10/10. I would recommend.

I'm going to not recommend this game, but I'm going to do that with the caveat that if you read the positive reviews and think you will like it, you should probably give it a shot anyway.  The game is very pretty, it feels very fluid (no bugs or UI lag that I experienced), and it's definitely a different take on the squad tactics genre.  I have no problems with this game that aren't purely down to personal taste, but I feel like I'm an archetypical player of games of this type, so I feel like I should provide a "caveat emptor" for anyone like me that sanity-checks a game purchase with the negative comments before buying.
The "different take" part above was the part that I didn't like.  This game resolves every single action on an all-or-nothing basis.  Every monster essentially has 1 hit point; the only thing the stats dictate is the hit % chance.  Your spells are the same way; almost all the worthwhile ones have a base of 50-70% chance of success, and if you fail, you lose the spell from your hand, you lose your cast for that turn, and nothing happens except gaining a few points of mana that you can use up to get 3-5% higher chance to cast your next spell.
All this resounding success/abject failure stuff happening over and over makes this game INSANELY high-variance.  You can be rolling the opponent, and then he'll make a desperation summon of a couple 30% creatures and succeed, then proceed to dismantle your entire board state with them.  Of course, this happens the other way around too, but do you care, if you're losing that bad?  Wouldn't you like to win because you played well, and then a win like that feels dirty?  On the other hand, if you are playing well, doesn't it feel 10x more dirty when you lose because of something like this?
I'll repeat myself above that I don't think this is necessarily a bad design.  It definitely helps with any kind of matchmaking disparity if the underdog can pull out a spectacular win every now and then on a guy that should otherwise beat him 99% of the time.  I bet it also makes more of the games into memorable stories too, something they claim a couple of places on the Steam store page.  I'd probably welcome this in a casual card game that I might play with my 10 year old since it's fun for him to have a chance to gutterstomp me on draws or dice rolls, but I don't think that's the audience they're going for here, is it?
I think in some ways this is supposed to be mitigated by the illusion/disbelief mechanic, and maybe that works in games with people (which I didn't get around to because the tutorial took long enough for me that I was already past the point of eligibility for automatic refund), but it definitely didn't with the AI.  The reason it didn't I suspect might end up being valid in games with people too - the poke/counter-poke establishment of battle lines that everyone is familiar with in these games takes long enough that both wizards easily run out of spells in their decks in the games that I played.  When this happens, the only thing left for you to do with that phase of your turn is simply disbelieve all of your opponent's units.  That really cheapened this part of the game for me, because if you successfully get an illusion out that the opponent doesn't disbelieve immediately, then you can't play defensively with it, because eventually it'll fail the smell-check at the end of the match, and then your unit blows up and you don't have a spell in hand to replace it with.
I hate to be down on this one, but it is what it is!

BIT.TRIP RUNNER: A great little arcade game that is sure to challenge you in a variety of ways. BIT.TRIP RUNNER is a challenging game in it of itself and requires quick reflexes as well as patience. While it is simplistic the game offers a hidden layer of depth that is only marred by some basic design choices. Levels are fun…for a while, they become stale and repetitive since there is only ever one way to go and if you fail you must start over at the beginning of the level, so repeating the same sections over and over may not appeal to some and may frustrate even the most seasoned of gamers. Music and style are perfect for this game, it’s hard to imagine it looking nor sounding any different, the music has a great retro beat that suits the game well and the 16-bit retro style of the game gives it charm, as well as being creative and colorful which helps nail down the fast pace action it’s trying to drive.
Overall, BIT.TRIP RUNNER is a nice simple arcade game with fantastic music; it’s challenging and may seem unfair with overly long levels and may frustrate some gamers with having to repeat sections over and over. If you love a tough challenge, retro looking games or a game with great music for $10.00 USD it may be a bit much, however when on sale this game is easily worth it. You can also enjoy the game and support the developers by purchasing the awesome soundtrack that is also for sale. Either way BIT.TRIP RUNNER is certainly a game to consider adding to the collection of fun and challenging arcade games.
-Thumbs Up from Royial

I wish I could recommend this game. I am a fan of the survival genre, and have sunk over 130 hours into empyrion (sci fi survival) and when I saw this I was excited. It looked like a similar game to empyrion with better graphics.
The game looks good in 3rd person, I'll give them that (though the 1st person models and animations are just horrible), and the world is hostile, with plenty of mobs. It's far more action packed than most survival games, as you will find yourself fending off creatures with alarming regularity.
Now, if it was just dense packs of critters, I'd be less critical, but the respawn timers on those mobs are... short. Like, really, really short. A large part of survival games is gathering resources. When you need to stop gathering on a stone because the same mob respawns 4 times 3 foot in front of you... it's a problem. when there's then issues like the creatures not entering any space that overlaps with your base structure (which is to my mind an overly simplistic build technique which requires large amounts of raw materials to produce large structures in one go, everything seems template based which really limits creativity) allowing for easy kills if you dont venture from your base (you can retreat back to safety, upon which the mobs start runnung away, allowing for easy, 100% safe kills), respawning materials every time you log out and back in again, the dense packs of creatures and ridiculously fast respawns mean it's all too easy to fall into a trap of barely venturing from the base until you get strong enough and have gathered enough resources to build better weapons... which still suck. This can quickly feel more like a chore than fun.
To my mind, this feels like a survival-lite. It's limited building/crafting options will appeal to those who want to get up and running quickly, and maybe my problem was I was playing solo. It feels like it's designed for groups of people working together watching each others backs whilst one person gathers for the group. Even the base pre-fab was a huge area, seemingly designed to be populated by multiple people/buildings. The pre-fab designs and the constant, constant, constant respawns quickly got the better of me though, and I'm afraid I have requested a refund, and felt compelled to warn off like minded people.
One of the other reviewers has called this the best sci fi survival on the market. I'm sorry, but I cannot agree, and I'm going back to Empyrion for my sci fi survival fixes
