Really fun, really cute, lots of polish, and I honestly recommend this to anyone who enjoys fast-paced arcade style games, especially maze-style games.

.Story.
The campaign features the story of Carrie, a pink humanoid crab (I had to look at the Steam page because this isn’t immediately obvious) who runs a humble little diner alongside her red humanoid lobster friend, Calcia. The place is going under—no pun intended despite the aquatic theme—and it’s up to you to rake in enough funds to stop that from happening. You’ll have a week (and 20 stages) to do so. To complete a stage, all you have to do is make an assigned amount of money and avoid getting three warnings (more on this later).
.Gameplay.
The name of the game is speed and quick reflexes. You control Carrie via the arrow keys, making your way down the narrow aisles between tables and trying not to knock into your patrons while you serve food and collect dirty dishes. The little crab lass never loses forward momentum, so you’ll really only be making turns and twirling. You can tap spacebar to spin, which will allow you to move past diner patrons without knocking them over, or hold it to dash.
Your guests are nautical in nature and adorable to boot. They’ll walk, hop, and slither around, getting in your way at every chance before finally taking a seat and demanding food in the form of a word bubble with a picture of the desired menu item. It’s your job to speed your way over to the counter, where Calcia will place completed orders, still avoiding other diners who have yet to seat themselves, pick up the food, and bring it to the correct person. You do so simply by walking past them and you’ll deliver the dishes in the same way.  There’s no possible way to bring orders to the wrong patrons, either, because Carrie will only place it down in front of the diner who wants it.
After your diner has eaten, they’ll get up to exit and leave a dirty dish behind. This is your chance to make a little bonus cash as you can zip by, pick them up, and deposit them into a sink for washing.
I found this to be more irritating than anything because you can only carry dirty dishes
orders. If you happen to pick up a dirty dish, you are committed to carrying it back to the sink whether or not your patrons are getting impatient.
A lot of the times my guest ran out were a direct result of my having to run over to the sink because I had accidentally run past a cleared plate.
While this may not seem like a big deal, it swiftly becomes one once you take into account the fact that a patron leaving results in a warning. You know the old saying “three strikes and you’re out”? The same is true here: if you get three warnings, your run ends and you gather up whatever cash you’ve earned. This will prove problematic for those trying to get a high score.
If you run into three guests, that results in a single warning.
If you’re clumsy and slip on some of the obstacles that are introduced later in the game, you get a warning.
The game could have done without some of these elements as they hinder the speed and fluidity of a game that’s meant to have a frantic pace.
There are two difficulties of campaign: arcade and friendly.
Arcade keeps track of your score and allows you to complete challenges like “no warnings,” “collect all coins,” and “finish in x amount of time.” This version is for those who want to challenge themselves to the true arcade experience. There’s no room for errors because a warning will clear out your diner instantly and you’ll have to wait for more hungry patrons to file in. You’ll also be able to complete challenges for bonus score. Aside from that, it’s your typical three strike deal, after which your score is recorded and can be labeled in the classic arcade style—with your initials.
Keep in mind that there are no online leaderboards so you’ll only be seeing your scores listed under “high scores” in the menu.
Friendly is a little more forgiving, as getting a warning allows the business day to progress as usual. All of the other aspects are present in both modes, with one being a little kinder about mistakes and lacking challenges. This mode also does not record your score.
Finally, you have endless mode… Which is exactly as it sounds: you keep playing until you’ve had enough. There’s nothing more to it. You do get to choose a location, which is a nice way to mix up the appearance of your diner. More locations can be unlocked.
.Pros.
.Cons.
.Bottom line.
If you’re into arcade games and/or Diner Dash, this game is worth a shot. If you weren’t already a fan of like titles, this game probably won’t change your mind. It’s cute and charming and the cosmetic changes activated by the way you dress Carrie are a nice touch, but there are little things gameplay-wise that are more frustrating than challenging.

Easily the best arcade-style game on Steam. Absolutely worth the $2.99 price-tag; maybe even more.
While the game may seem simple on the surface, there are actually a little bit of strategy in delivering food to hungry customers. Not only do the variety of colorful customers add to the game's charm, they also have different properties. There are standard customers, fast customers (will walk down aisles VERY quickly and demand their food be served quicker, too), impatient customers (walk at a normal pace, but wil quickly leave if not promptly served their food), and large customers (walk very slowly down aisles and will deplete more of your spin). Having to deal with all of these customer types at once makes the game challenging, but never too frustrating.
There are only a couple things I don't like about this game: First, there seem to be a few minor bugs. Alternate costume unlocks were given to be before I had legitimately earned them, and on very rare occasions I can phase through tables (I think this has to do with taking corners while spinning past customers, but I'm unsure). At the time of writing, fullscreen mode looks a bit ugly on widescreen monitors, too; the big black bars along the sides of the game could've been replaced by simple wallpaper or tile textures. The positives vastly outweigh the negatives, though.

I hate to give this game a negative review since i've been waiting patiently for two years to play it fresh. Unfortunately this game cannot really be evaluated on its artistic merit due to numerous technical issues:
- Lots of graphical tearing, despite vsync.
- Several menu UI problems, many of them painfully obvious, such as inconsistent highlighting of menu options, confused/incorrect localization options, and even disclaimer text on the remapping menu explaining that it doesn't work correctly (!!)
- Several in-game control problems, such as apparently incorrectly labelled keybindings. "F", for example, pops a console message, rather than the stated function of "using" an object. Small things like the loss of the mouse pointer when using the catacomb computer can be worked around or figured out but are still rather rough for a finished product. Maybe this is just me but when I found an item to pick up and put it my inventory, I had no idea how to find it again. Collision boxes are also rather rough-and-ready.
- I had problems with the voice-overs. The initial house section seemed to "speak" correctly, but in the desert I was unable to hear any speech, although subtitles appeared from time to time. Even the subtitles had misprinted characters (possibly a localization issue? or related to the localization menu confusion?)
Other issues are possible since I stopped playing just after the maze/light puzzles; if patches improve the experience I'll be back to finish it off.
On the positive side I found it pretty good-looking and it definitely has an interesting concept, one I've long been awaiting. But despite the long lead time in early access, this game is not really ready for a true release, particularly at this price. If you're interested in purchasing, I would wait a for a few patch cycles to address some of these problems.

Major\Minor is one of those few games that I feel deserves to write a serious review for.
Let me preface this with two things: First, I don't play many visual novels. Second, I did not follow the so-called controversy with the creator nor do I care, I'll judge the game by its merits. Considering I've just finished my first playthrough it might end up a bit train-of-thought. I plan to give it a second go later and update the review, it's earned that at least.
Here Be Spoilers.
The gameplay itself is probably what you'd expect of a visual novel - I wouldn't know, I don't have many. Most of the time it's just dialogue and descriptions with the odd bit of input. It's not strictly terrible, but it's hardly DOOM. It could stand with a little more player interaction.
I personally found the plot to be rather interesting. I had no genuine clue where the next turn would lead, which is both a boon and a curse. Perhaps that's a good sign of bad writing, if so I was fooled until the final few acts when the inevitable explosition explosion is unleashed upon the player and it all came crashing down. The Velasquez, Federation and World Stone revelation was interesting from a setting point of view, and call me out if I'm wrong, but it felt fairly novel. It's just thrust upon you so quick it barely has any time to have any impact. I would have rathered you find this out yourself organically instead of just being told. The Terran plot is very much all over the place, with no real direction as to who or what is the antagonist. Perhaps that's intentional, but it doesn't excuse the sudden appearance of two new characters completely out of left field to serve as the "final boss" as it were. On the Earth side, it was a major disappointment that Max was caught off-screen. I would have loved for her to suddenly appear in the bunker for a final confrontation between her and Acheron, it would have been a great ending to the Earth plot.
The choices you make in the game don't seem to have a major impact on the story at a first glance, but that's something I'll discover in subsequent playthroughs. There are several minor things you can do such as whether or not Rook ends up with one of two characters, if at all, but I killed him in my game so I didn't get to see this (and also didn't have relationship points so his ghost just faded away before giving me his backstory exposition - I regret nothing).
However, the glaring flaw in Major\Minor is the writing itself, especially characters dialogue. Half the time they don't act like real people. They just don't. This is especially true with the Earth characters. They're almost too articulate, they have tendancies to have bizzare statements: "But now my curiosity is affecting me." is not something you bloody say out loud - Thanks, Lord Plair! Or they'll word their sentances in long-windedly. This is people talking to each other, they'll use contractions and slang. They get to the point, that's how people talk. Granted in writing you can't ever actually emulate real speech exactly - it looks wrong. This is the complete opposite of that. I found myself rewording a good majority of the sentances in my head as I went through the game so they'd sound much better. Myother issue with the writing is that I just can't tell many of the characters apart from the way they're written. Some, like Rook or Inumi, were distinct enough but frankly they were the minority. What I did like was the lack of focus on the "furry" aspect. Other than hands being referred to as paws there was next to no mention of anything "furry". No interplay of species relations or anything like that. The characters were just ordinary people. I like that. It felt appropriate.
That being said, I grew fairly attached to the characters. They were on the whole interesting to interact with, and each have their own backstories and do have some fleshing out to them. For a game with literally dozens of characters you interact with in quick succession I'm fine with that. It's a shame most of the time they give you that backstory in a cascade. I guess it saves time and considering the game isn't short is probably for the best. There are several characters that really didn't feel necessary (Dazz, Kabu, Trisha) and I'm sure that was because the creator had to work in creations from the backers, and the game did suffer for it in my opinion.
Continuing from that is the art. I like the character art. It's perfectly fine, but suffers from a lot of good old fashioned "sparkledog" (seriously, Kila and PB?). That's what you get when you let the fandom into your creation. There's nothing inherently wrong with it, but it does especially look out of place when your supposed fantasy-esque Terra has very modern-looking characters mixed with more appropriate ones. My main gripe with it would be the lack of diversity. You get one image for their first appearance in game and one for everytime thereafter. They dont move or change aside from being mirrored half the time. The backgrounds are equally lazy stock photos, which could stand to be more fitting, but that isn't very important.
Finally the music, which is decent. It will occasionally feel out of place but most of the time it's fine as a general background or mood-setting. Like the art it's not very diverse, which is a shame, however some are genuinely good. I laughed when I heard the predictable ShockerDazz duet over the credits because I thought it would be insanely corny. It wasn't. That made me happy.
I've probably written far too much already. It's a game with many flaws and some genuine redeeming qualities. I'll be frank, it's not
worth £14.99. Like any other Steam game, get it in a sale. It's a decent length and the plot will keep you interested through its number of twists and turns, and with the choice system it has some replayability.
Major\Minor might have some weird quirks, but there's some good in there too.

Chaos Reborn is what i have been wanting for a very long time, without realising it! Realising that the game is largely driven around RNG rather then healthpoints or other RPG troeps initially sounds unappealing, yet the game's art style and manner of managing combat makes the game a definite Steam gem which Gabe himself should take a look into!
+The art style and animations is truly wondrous to look at. I can not stress just how little credit the screen shots give the artstyle! In game i am both amused and awestruck by just how beautiful the renditions of the sprites are,
+Online offline modes leave to varied gameplay, as just ai would obviously be a bit of a bummer. AI are intelligent though and a good challenge to beginners, which i am at the moment.
+Staff abilities; when one has enough manner they gain the ability to gain a special card which, once played, can easily turn the tide of the skirmish, thus forcing players to reach for the gems mid board in an attempt to increase their magic pool.
+In game audio is well worth listening to, it is 'realistic', so no strange squeeks or grunts which ruin immersion from grunts.
+The Soundtrack is just fantastic, the music changes from a mellow calm undertone, to a heroic fanfare, spurring the most valient of Wizards onwards to victory!
-RNG could begin to grind on some people's gears, the notion that your entire plan could be lost due to a few
rats could be a negative to some who prefer 'safer' gameplay.
-Repetition? Whilst online games are varied in terms of the opponent you face, single player games (if you have bad internet) could be poor in terms of ai repeating themselves? I am clutching at straws here, there is really not that much bad about the game :P.
Conclusion: A Damn Good Game! 9/10. Definitely worth a buy, despite the relatively high price for an indie game.

What a fool. Space Marine is a bloody, messy, action-packed romp into the heart of the Warhammer 40k universe. A mix of good and bad.  Do I recommend this game?  I don't know.
The character creation is a bit bare bones.  Class customization is somewhat interesting, but you cannot customize starting gear.  You get what the base class has, and you don't know exactly what that is until you start the game (you can get a vague idea by looking at the character).
For a tactical turn based game, where precision is very important, the user interface is terrible.  Occasionally, clicking on a skill will not activate it, leading your next click to send your character astray.  The Esc key does not let you exit dialogue, meaning you cannot quickly exit dialogue in panic mode when your characters are rapidly dying (out of combat) and instead of healing your partner, you start talking to them, because when you clicked on heal, it did not activate.  If you do activate an ability, and then change your mind about using it, and click End Turn, instead of ending that character's turn, the character uses the ability at the area underneath the end turn button; very aggrivating.  Worse still, if you are attempting to melee attack, or ranged attack an enemy, you absolutely must hold down control and then click.  If you don't you run the risk of the enemy shifting around in place, causing your character to run up to or around it instead of attack.  I've had numerous occasions where my archer wasted his entire turn running to an enemy I was going to shoot because for a split second the attack indicator became a move indicator without me moving the mouse at all (especially noticable on the half eaten zombies).  On other occasions, I will click to melee attack only to have my character take a slow walk around the enemy, usually through fire taking ridiculous amounts of damage (as it ticks approximately 4 times).
The failure to activate a skill when clicking on it happens with characters as well, such as when I need to quickly change the character I am focused on, and nothing happens while I frantically click the character icon.  Sometimes I think I have clicked on a particular character, and then tell them to move, only to have the wrong character move - often walking them right through deadly traps, hazardous terrain, or right into a group of enemies I am trying to tactially position myself around.
When trying to move a character around a tight spot, such as to avoid a known trap pressure plate, navigate around hazardous terrain, or avoid stepping into a vision cone area, the character often randomly diverts from the given path running directly onto pressure plates, through large swathes of hazardous terrain, or directly into line of sight.  Other times, pressure plates are triggered without the character actually touching them, by oversized phantom hitboxes.  When playing this game, I am often shouting either in my head or out loud at my characters "WHAT THE HELL ARE YOU DOING?!"  Beyond that, party formation sometimes randomly changes.  For instance, in a recent battle I specifically selected a spellcasting character to move, put everyone in sneak mode, and put him in front, then cast the firefly spell, and when it actually cast, he teleported to the back, cast it from the back, and set my party on fire.  Which reminds me, it's often very difficult to determine if a given path will actually take you through hazardous terrain, or not, or when you are currently under a poison gas cloud (and the top down view is so awful I never want to use it).  Also the default run speed puts me to sleep.
So that's all of my griping about control precision.  Now for difficulty curve.
For context, I am playing this game in Honour Mode, the highest possible difficulty, where the two main characters dying = game over (even if the remaining character has a ressurect scroll?).  My first attempt, I narrowly beat the first battle where I was grossly outnumbered, made my way to some drunk legionnaires... decided to fight them.  How tough can two legionnaires who are drunk and only one level above me be?  The dog (also level 2) killed both of my characters in two rounds, there was no possibility of victory.  Basically 1 level of difference in this game is like 10-20 levels of difference in games I am used to.  Now I like hard games.  I do no death runs in Dark Souls.  I play Nightmare mode in American McGee's Alice... but this was just bull.  4 attempts later, I make it past the first fight again, make it into town, drag myself around the weird layout of the town for hours, eventually I am level 3.  I find some of the NPC dialogues to be quite entertaining, and some of them to be painfully boring and long winded.  I find myself two more party members, buy new gear... I'm feeling good about things.  I try to head west, near the beach, because I hear that is easier from NPCs.  The guards tell me I am too inexperienced.  I try various other gates, same warning.  After getting demolished by enemies one level above me previously, and being on Honour Mode, I heed the warnings... I have no idea where to go.  I search the internet.  There is a west gate in addition to a northwest gate.  It has level 3-4 enemies... so if I am lucky I will survive.  I nearly get obliterated right out of the gate by lightning zombies.  Scraping myself off of the ground I limp onward, fighting many harrowing battles where it is of dire importance that each action I take is deliberate and well planned out.  Several times, the controls try to get me killed by making my characters do things other than what I had attempted to command them to do.  I meet a dog, my witch can speak dog, and the dog says let's go beat up some wolves.  Sure, why not... The dog takes me to a completely new area (I was unaware of this at first because the only clue was that it stopped raining, little did I know that meant new area and not just a change in weather).  The dog immediately engages in battle with a whole pack of LEVEL 7 FREAKING WOLVES.  I quickly learn how the Flee mechanic works.  Back in town I recouperate, regroup, and head back out soon hitting level 4.  Hooray, progress.  I sneak up to an area and see a level 5 Ghoul surrounded by friends.  No thanks.  I find a well, go down it, there is a Rogue, but my party is full.  The area has level 2 enemies!  Damn, why didn't I find this sooner?  The fights are still hard, but they are manageable.  I've found a bunch of sweet loot, it's almost time for me to head back to town, identify things, sell things, buy things... What's this area?  I walk through a doorway.  Click.  Your party is dead.  Honour mode.  My save gets deleted.  Level 2 area, level 4 characters.  Apparently not taking that Rogue with you is not an option if you want to explore this level 2 area, even if your main character has the lightfoot trait.  So in closing, the difficulty spikes in this game are terrible.
Now for one last thing that grates my nerves.  NPCs with ambient dialogue.  They repeat it incessantly, over, and over, and over, and over, and over, and over, and over, and over.  It's horrible.  If you encounter an NPC that has only two lines of ambient dialogue, run far far away.  Do not barter with anyone near them, don't manage your inventory near them, just run.
Aside from those huge negatives, the game is alright I guess.  But I am only playing this game until March 8th.  I thought for sure I would fall in love with this game and play it for a very long time.  Not anymore.

Simply put, Extremely Satisfying!
First off the game offers so much to do and many ways to built and play your characters, Sometimes you may get lost chillin' in the city for a few hours talking to Npc's about quests and such and other times you'll be on an adventure outside the castle walls, every second fearing for your life. (Save often peoples...) The game introduces a very fun and unique conversation system, that especially shines when your playing with a friend or family member, Allowing you and your Co-op partner to make decisions on how you feel and want to do in the game world. (Even if your Co-Op partner is settled on always trolling and disagreeing with you just to start an arguement)
The combat is engaging and difficult, But not too much so. Although I will say it does matter what type of party you have set up, For instance, My party I have for my Solo playthrough is 3 different type of melee characters (One who can heal of course.) And a archer... Now, while its still fun, such a team is much harder to playthrough the game with then, I dont know, a team with only one melee character and 2 mages instead. But regardless it doesnt take away from the fun of the game.
Now for a few cons about the game... Personally I feel the game offers little in the way of actual character appearance options. You make two characters, But without being able to change your characters build what-so-ever if you make two of the same gender characters they tend to look a bit similar. Not to mention there is only 3 voices per gender and about 10 or hair style's and faces. Im not saying this is a big deal by any means, You can still make characters you'll enjoy playing, and I know alot of people would like to argue about how much your characters appearance matters in a game like this, But I honestly think the closer you can get the character to how you imagine your adventuring crew helps with immersion and feeling your characters more. Who knows, I might just be weird or something... Heh.
As for the other beef I have with this game is *Sigh* it kinda feels like your always pushed to do stuff in a certain order, No matter how much bragging goes on about the tabletop-like freedoms of the game, Simply put you will have to explore the world in "somewhat" a set order. The main reason for this is because levels on this game are a big deal at times. So say you set off for a quest that seems interesting at the time to find out that the enemys are 2 or 3 levels higher, Well your better off just walking away and doing a different quest or finding a way to earn some experience points before going back. And honestly, even when you do complete stuff 1 or 2 higher levels than you (Which isnt easy at all) That means you 'prolly just overleveled yourself for a different quest, Taking away from the difficulty of that quest. It isnt a huge problem honestly, because you still have some choices on what to do and when, but it feels bad when alot of things around you are too high of a level and you know theres only two or three quests you can do.
Overall I find the game EXTREMELY SATISFYING! No matter how much I said about the cons the game is still overwhelmingly good. The endless ways to build your team is wonderful, Tank healers, Two-handed sword mages, fire magic archers or even traditional type builds like pure mages or sword and shield... Basically anything you can think of! (Just make sure you spend your attribute and skill points wisely!) The endless ways of building your team helps keep the game fresh through multiple replays, Despite if you kinda go through the quest in a somewhat similar order. Also theres more than one way to do some quests, so that helps too. Bottom line, If you, and perhaps a friend, want a good turn-based rpg world to explore then look no further! Buy this game!

As with most of the more 'modern' HO games, The Lonely Hearts Murders is more of a puzzle/adventure game; the HO scenes are few. But that's to be expected these days.
The mystery (who is the Lonely Hearts Killer?) is cleverly-plotted; the story itself is lacking severely in common sense. You are an average British chap whose daughter has been kidnapped by the Lonely Hearts Killer. This is a sensible start, but there's no real reason for you to be involved in the search for the kidnapper. You are not an officer of the law, yet the resident police officer allows you to follow him around, contaminating crime scenes and breaking into houses and suchlike. The flawed logic here makes my teeth ache.
Also, be aware that skipping a line of dialogue skips the whole scene/conversation. this leads to unfortunate scene jumps, where you might miss pertinent plot information. The cut scenes are mostly clever and attractive, and worth watching perhaps once, but they do go on. And on.
Also, during the (very long) denouement video, your character starts to fall asleep, and the video goes blurry and hazy, before cutting out -- and then you wake up to listen to the others in the scene continuing to discuss the murders. And then the video goes blurry and hazy again. And again. And again. And yet, you can still hear everything that's being said. Yes, it's been a stressful few weeks for your character, but you're not that old; you shouldn't be nodding off like that. Seriously. Drink some coffee.
It sounds like I'm complaining a lot here, but this is not a bad game, all things told. It's pretty, and none of the mini-games made me want to tear my hair out. And I do like a good mystery.
Pros:
+ beautiful music
+ minigames/puzzles are logical and pretty straightforward
+ pretty graphics, smooth animations
+ clever mystery
+ bonus chapter is quite good
+ map, indicating puzzle locations
+ include extras, like wallpapers and music tracks
+ the kittens. meow.
Cons:
- can't skip individual lines of dialogue (although the tutorial suggests that you can)
- can't use the map to fast-travel
- can't skip individual lines of dialogue (yes, it was so annoying, I had to mention it twice)
Meh
~ voice acting is hit-or-miss. several anachronisms in speech (given that it looks as though it takes place in the late 19th C). some characters are whinging morons, but others are quite well-portrayed.
Ephy Rating: 8/10
Summary: Attractive environments and a clevery mystery make up for logic flaws in the story itself. The bonus chapter was probably my favourite part; I liked how it gave a subtle nod to their first game. Although I would have liked to have been able to use the map to fast-travel, the zones weren't so large that it was impossible to find one's way around. All in all, it's a good example of the modern HOG, and worth picking up, especially on sale.

Anyone experienced with Artifex Mundi's extensive oeuvre (whether developed or only published) will very quickly become familiar with certain hidden object game tropes. In fact, good as they are, it can sometimes get to the point where, from one title to the next, it can feel like a re-skin of previous outings. But what I really like about this and Magicindie's previous
game is that they're really trying to do something different.
Like with every other hidden object game, the structure makes no sense whatsoever. There's no good reason for a bunch of horrendously convoluted locking mechanisms barricading the world at every turn. Nor is there a shred of logic in having an item buried away in one location being used to unlock something or complete a structure all the way over on the other side of a town. The whole thing is fundamentally bonkers. But if you can look past that, what they lack in gameplay sense, they make up for in storytelling and characterisations.
There is an actual attempt being made here in trying to give depth and reason to the actions that are unfolding and the characters behind them. It's not winning any literary prices, but I still really appreciated the genuine, honest-to-goodness endeavour to entertain the player with something interesting. While the previous instalment was more of a thriller♥♥♥♥♥horror game, this time we're treated to a more traditional murder mystery as a man has thirty days to rescue his daughter from a serial killer who prays on "lonely hearts". Mileage may vary as the overall tone and feeling of both games are completely different, and your fondness for one may not wholly translate to the other, but I personally enjoyed the shift in styles rather than simply reusing an old, tried and tested formula.
Puzzles are rock solid, writing and voice acting are again mostly pretty good, though occasionally laughable at some points - as seems to be the inescapable norm for the genre by now - but one welcome improvement over the previous game is navigation. Last time around, the map was so large and called for so much backtracking that a sizable chunk of time was spent merely finding your way around more than anything else. But this time, while the overall content and length is roughly the same four hours, areas are laid out differently and are now broken up into different chapters each with their own smaller handful of unique locations to explore. It definitely streamlines everything and significantly helps improve the flow and pace of the game.
Technically this is a prequel to the previous Brink of Consciousness game, but the links between the two are incredibly tenuous, and if anything, they possibly feel a little shoehorned in for the sake of it. But as a result, you could easily play either one without having to know anything about the other and still enjoy them just the same. But while it does give and take in equal measure; this game being a more user-friendly experience, but lacking the compelling villain of the last game, provided you can find them at a discount price, I could easily recommend either of these for your enjoyment.

I must admit that I was positively surprised with the Lonely Hearts Murders. What is more I would probably place it among my top ten HOGs (not top 5 though), and that is quite telling since I didn’t really enjoy it’s prequel that much. Of course, I’d still claim that hidden object game is not the finest means of delivering a crime - oriented story, and that this game suffers from the typical goofs its genre is known for (repetitive searching for various items not even remotely connected with the intrigue while the murderer is on the loose,  objects needed to solve the puzzles being placed in the most improbable locations, or the fact that during the first few minutes of the gameplay, in the closet of the main protagonist, a proper, elderly gentleman, we find a feminine corset, shawl and a lipstick ). Nonetheless, if that doesn’t scare you off, this installment of Brink of Consciousness offers a very solid (although brief - 3 hours, together with the bonus chapter) experience.
Unlikely in the vast majority of the hidden object games, the Lonely Hearts’ story is actually worth mentioning for a few reasons. The game attempts to deliver a criminal plot without ever resorting to use any form of supernatural phenomena, and to a large extent succeeds (if you are willing to suspend your disbelief for a few ridiculously mood-breaking puzzles - but to be fair there are also a few really brilliant ones). There is slightly more dialogue to be listened to and a little more background behind the characters than on the average, and the plot twists are quite interesting. Finally, the bonus chapter offers a rather graceful connection with the Dorian Gray’s Syndrome (but does not require the knowledge of the Lonely Hearts’ prequel).
The game’s art and sound are both very good. The graphics are darker and more toned down than it is the case in the most hidden object games, but still manage to look elegant and detailed. It is also worth mentioning that the game allows switching on a film grain filter if that is to your liking. The music is moody, calm and plain gorgeous most of the time. Some voice acting is annoying though.
The gameplay is a competent HOG standard. The puzzles are rather on the easy side and the game offers hints and a guide so it is virtually impossible to get stuck. The map displays objectives, but there is no fast - travel between the rooms and there is one rather annoying little detail connected with that: far too often Brink of Consciousness requires you to travel from one end of the map to the other with just one item to solve a puzzle where you acquire another object and are forced to trek back all the way again. Rince, repeat. I’d even say as much that at least 30 minutes out of my entire 3 hours of the gameplay would be running back and forth between the objectives in each chapter.
As you see I have a few complaints about the Lonely Hearts Murders, all in all though I’ve enjoyed it more than its pre-sequel (it is a second game in the Brink of Consciousness series, but it’s events take place before the story of Dorian Gray’s). While it is a solid game I would not suggest buying it at a full price: if for nothing else, 3.33 euro per hour is an abysymal conversion rate. Still, if you manage to get it discounted, or even better, in a bundle, you should probably give it a try if you think you can turn a blind eye to the game's shortcomings.
Polska recenzja:
Przyznaję, byłem przyjemnie zaskoczony Lonely Heart Murders’ami. Co więcej, umieściłbym tą grę w  pierwszej dziesiątce (choć nie w pierwszej piątce) moich ulubionych gier z gatunku hidden object, a to już o czymś świadczy, jako że poprzednie Brink of Consciousness nie do końca mi się podobało. Jak i w przypadku poprzedniczki, stwierdzam że hidden objecty nie są  najlepszym sposobem na opowiedzenie kryminału  - gra cierpi na typowe bolączki tego gatunku (zabójca na wolności a główny bohater przekopuje się przez wysypiska przedmiotów w żaden sposób nie powoiązanych z opowiadaną historią, niektóre zagadki nijak nie pasują do nastroju gry, rekwizyty potrzebne do rozwiązywania zagadek są ukryte w dziwacznych miejscach, czy chociażby fakt że w szafie głównego bohatera, statecznego, podstarzałego dżentelmena, odnajdujemy podczas pierwszego HOGa damski gorset, kapelusz i szminkę). Niemniej, jeżeli to was nie odstrasza, ta część serii Brink of Consciousness oferuje bardzo solidne (aczkolwiek krótkie - 3 godziny, razem z dodatkowym rozdziałem) doświadczenie.
W przeciwieństwie do przytłaczającej większości Hidden Object’ów, historia opowiadana w Lonely Hearts’ach jest warta wspomnienia – i to co najmniej z kilku powodów. Przede wszystkim, w żadnym momencie gra nie odwołuje się do zjawisk nadprzyrodzonych i (jeżeli tylko dość mocno przymykać oczy i powstrzymywać niedowierzanie) warstwa fabularna okazuje się całkiem interesująca. Okej, bywają zagadki które zwyczajnie wybijają z rytmu i niszczą nastrój, ale jest też kilka naprawdę udanych. Dodatkowo, w grze pojawia się jakby więcej dialogów i postaci wydają się odrobinę lepiej zarysowane niż w przeciętnym HOGu. No i bonusowy rozdział zaskakująco zgrabnie skleja całą historię z wydarzeniami z Doriana Grey’a (poprzedniej części Brink of Consciousness – której, swoją drogą znajomość nie jest konieczna – nie książki).
Gra wygląda i brzmi bardzo dobrze. Sceny są mroczniejsze i bardziej przygaszone niż w innych grach tego gatunku, ale mimo to wyglądają estetycznie i są pełne detali. Gra pozwala włączyć filmowe „ziarno” i ,trzeba przyznać, wychodzi jej to na dobre. Muzyka jest nastrojowa, spokojna i najzwyczajniej w świecie boska (jeżeli pasuje wam pianino i saksofon) przez większość czasu. Za to głosy niektórych postaci irytują.
Sama rozgrywka to kompetentny standard gatunku. Wiadra przedmiotów do znalezienia, łatwe zagadki, system podpowiedzi, dołączony do gry poradnik – czyli raczej nie da się tu utknąć. Na mapie zaznaczone są cele, ale nie ma systemu szybkiego podróżowania między lokacjami. I tu przyczepię się do tego jak często gra każe nam biec z jednym, jedynym przedmiotem jaki mamy w drugi koniec dostępnej lokacji, gdzie oczywiście zdobywamy następny przedmiot , galopujemy z powrotem, rozwiązujemy – zdobywamy – biegniemy – rozwiązujemy i tak w kółko. Z trzech godzin jakie zajęło mi ukończenie gry spokojnie można ująć 30 minut na samo latanie w kółko po mapach.
Jak widzicie, mam trochę do zarzucenia Lonely Heart Murderers. Mimo to, muszę przyznać że podobała mi się bardziej niż jej poprzedniczka (lub sequel, zależy jak spojrzeć … mimo że jest drugą częścią, jej wydarzenia mają miejsce przed Syndromem Doriana Grey’a). Mimo że jest to solidna gra, odradzam raczej kupowanie w pełnej cenie – 3 euro 33 centy za godzinę gry to zdecydowanie paskudny przelicznik. Ale w jakiejś sporej zniżce, albo jeszcze lepiej w bundlu jest to pozycja jak najbardziej godna polecenia.

Aka "the adventures of Inspector Bloody Incompetent Von I-Make-Lestrade-Look-Like-A-Dozen-Sherlocks-Combined" and his friend "Protagonist McSUDDENLYSHOUTY".
An unexpected improvement over the previous installment in the series, actually. The gameplay is just about borderline adequate, and the story + voice acting are... well, see
by way of illustration (spoilers, obviously) but nonetheless, It’s kind of amazing how much of a difference a semi-comptent story, some basic gameplay improvements and being able to interact with NPCs can be.
The gameplay: Very basic HOG stuff. The map still doesn't allow you to teleport, and doesn't even tell you where you can use your new items, so follow the hint button / guide religiously. No explanations for puzzles by default - you still have to hit the "?" button to get those. You can't skip individual lines, only entire conversations, and NPCs love nothing more than relating entire volumes of dialog at you.
Positives - the different chapters are divided into separate gameplay areas that you don’t have to backtrack through. The sepia-tone has been scaled down to the point that the game looks depressing, but you can tell objects apart. Plenty of interactions with NPCs, and even some hint of a mystery regarding which one of them is the killer (the revelation came minutes after I figured it out, so I guess the mystery was
. The NPCs were singularly incompetent, and the game actually made a fairly neat meta-joke:
.
As always, it's nice to have the protagonist driving the plot instead of following a random series of instructions, and to have (useless) friends by your side as you play. All pretenses towards being a horror game are dropped, and that's a net positive. Inspector Ulysses Peruseless' voiceacting actually made his incompetence less annoying, and the protagonist being dramatically shouty even by the standards of an HOG protagonist looking for their kidnapped daughter was... interesting. It certainly didn't have any moments that rivaled "GO AWAY! LEAVE ME ALONE!" for sheer unintentional comedy value.
Recommended, if only for the sheer level of improvement from terrible to perfectly adequate.

Now onto the review; I would say that I had high hopes for this game since it had made "Anthro game of the year" on a furry site but it is anything but and cerntainly not worth the $20 that the dev is trying to sell it for. The major complaints I have on this VN:
The plot feels like a blantant rip off of Persona 3 (at first) but then ends up jumping all over the place and barely making any point other than 'this is this now'. Your choices BARELY matter in this regardless of what he says and when the dev mentions 'multiple endings' he just meant two... Which yes I know two can be multiple but it just bothered me. The writing is awful  and the main character doesn't feel relevant to anything that is going on in the story. Some parts of the plot tend to go on and on and on without having much meaning which I found myself skipping through quickly and still getting the idea as to what was happening.
The characters all speak the same and actually their faces all look the same - their portraits are all static with no change to expression with the exception of one maid cat. Not to mention that once you get to 'know' the characters a bit further they all have VERY similar sob stories... VERY similar which makes me wonder why the hell there are so many characters - feels very cookie cutter to me.
The artwork is all sparkledog basic furry. The characters themselves seem to miss match a lot with each other and their enviornments (clothing ect) which takes away from the immersion. A lot of gender confusion also happened with me in this as I'm not used to seeing so many fem boys in a game before. The backgrounds are also not hand drawn but taken from a commercial free website I believe. There is also no CG's to unlock in this game which is basic for a VN imo.
The characters are all Fursonas of people who paid to be in the game and people who worked on the game. The dev is also in this game which explains the sparkledogs but it seems a bit egotistical to me. Granted if I paid good money I would want my character in a game but it also feels like it cheapens the experience.  I also feel like I should mention that the Dev is also a popstar who could do no wrong which is ehh? No offense to Klace or anyone who has their fursona in this game but I feel this should be mentioned for those who are possibly going to buy this.
The true ending actually feels like the worst ending to me - I won't spoil anything here but it barely makes a difference if you get this one or the regular ending. Both are just bad.
I have read worse VNs and things but I have also played free VNs which give much more of a enriching experience than this; I am highly dissappointed since there is absolutely nothing worth paying $20 for in this game. It's Meh
I've heard lots of good things about this game, so I bought it during the Steam Winter Sale. I did not enjoy this game. At first, the game was pretty fun, and I liked it, though I noticed a delay from when I hit a key to when the game responded (I had no lag/framedrop during the time of play) so it made the game difficult to stay on beat, so I found myself starting over quite a bit. This could just be my keyboard, so I don't know. Also, there are no checkpoints. At all. So one little mistake, one little off-beat press of a button, and you are sent all the way back through that 5 minute level you just drudged through.
The game itself is a music/rythm platforming game, however I wouldn't call it a rythm game. It feels more like a memory game. Throughout the game, you must jump, kick, slide, bounce, and reflect to reach the end of the stage. The graphics made me felt like I was going crosseyed while I played, they look good, but they don't mix well with a moving foreground. It made it unenjoyable, and I got headaches from it. This, mixed with the whole jumping and kicking, made it nearly impossible for me to even see what was going on. The rounds would drag on, and on. So, I had to memorize the course, while the backround remains stationary with a moving foreground, with a delay on me hitting buttons.
Here is the most enjoying part. The music. I loved it, except, every time you die, you get sent back to the beginning. Meaning that the music starts over with it. So you will be hearing the same du-du-dun-dun-dun-du-dun ... du-du-dun-dun-dun-du-dun ... du-du-dun-dun-dun-du-dun over and over again. I know I said I loved the music, but I couldn't love it enough from the constant restarting. Also, a lot of the songs sound the same, the music is put together from you "staying on beat" with the music. Staying on beat is used loosely (see above paragraph). I liked this aspect, you were making the music as you played along. The music progressively got better and better as you played, unless you miss one of those power-ups that up you, and the music. That part bugged me, but it is my fault for not being good enough, it made me want to replay the level and try to hear the music to it's full potential.
The graphics, they are really good. It's a mix of a stationary backround and a moving foreground, which I hated, but even though I hated how they pulled it off, they looked very good. So credit where it's due.
So, to close this review, here are the pros and cons of this game.
Good music, good graphics, fun to play, bonus levels are repetetive, but fun, a bit of replay value in there.
Repetetive music, headache inducing graphics, late controls, lack of checkpoints makes the game very unforgiving, not a rythym but instead a memory game.

I only spent about 30 minutes on this game, and I understand that the point of an MMORPG is the long-haul/end-game, but there are some serious fundamental flaws here.
The controls are garbage. Why do I have to double tap a direction to move faster? Why not just move at a brisk pace at all times instead of sluggishly treading along unless I hit an arrow key twice? If there's an option to change this, then why isn't it just default to move fast? I don't even care to check if that is an option. It's poor decision-making either way. Why does the entire process of moving from one side of a map to the other feel like such a chore? Moving around should be the easy part of an MMO.
The introduction is weak and generic. After 30 minutes of playing a game, I should feel some sort of investment, at least. Instead, all I know is that I'm on some sort of adventure about me, a character I barely care about except that I made it, in a world I know nothing about except that there are tons of anime-looking characters and probably some magic or something.
I started with no weapon as a mage class, so I couldn't use any of the abilities I leveled up. I was left with no choice but to punch some wolves for 5 minutes before they died. If you are supposed to start with a weapon, then WHERE WAS IT IN MY INVENTORY, I LOOKED REAL HARD, OKAY?!
Graphically, it's not terrible, but it looks like a less endearing MapleStory. Perhaps it has nice visual effects as well, but I wouldn't know cause I COULDN'T USE MY SPELLS.
Honestly, this game does not seem worth playing for free, let alone spending any money on it. For those that have fun at end-game, more power to you. If you are willing to trudge through a mess of a game to experience the later game, then go for it. If you are looking for a well-made game with an immersive experience, just play something else.
Hell, MapleStory does a better job at being a game than this.

Now that the game is only ten days away from its release I feel like I have to post a review just to communicate one vital piece of information that the developer of Dream fails to communicate to present and future customers:
This game is listed as having "VR Support" - it does have the corresponding entry in the feature list.
However this game only supports the Oculus Rift DK1. The official position of the developer is, that they will implement support for newer VR headmounted displays as soon as the engine they are using gets updated ... and that's the problem: This game was made in UDK. Epic, the developer of UDK, clearly stated that UDK won't get any updates EVER again. The developer of Dream knows this and is thus, by not removing the "VR Support" entry from the feature list, deliberately deceptive.
The only positive thing that 'can' be said in this regard is, that the thread where I wrote about this problem months ago was not deleted or locked and I wasn't banned from the forums. So in some minimal regard they are better than some other developers of UDK games, who formerly planned to implement VR support, still want to use it as a selling point and actively suppress any statement of the impossibility of such VR support ever being implemented on their forums.
For me however the fact that the VR support tag remains combined with the genre of this game (releasing a 1st person exploration game in this day and age means, that VR support is practically mendatory) is enough to not recommend Dream, as much as I'd like to give it a positive rating, since it 'seems' to be a nice game. I however cannot bring myself to play such a game on a normal monitor anymore.

This game was simply stunning to behold and to play.  Between the breathtaking art style and some of the best music scores I've heard in a game, it felt as if I were in a Miyazaki film.
Before I even got to the real meat of the gameplay, the story had already grabbed my attention, and all but had me in tears in the first 5 minutes.  And from that point on, it was just a never ending ride of joy and tension.  I love a story that can be told with few or no words at all, and this game delievered beautifully on that.  (Though I honestly could have done with less exposition from the Tree of Life.   He would seriously explain something that was already revealed perfectly through the visuals immediately after it happened.)
I started out using a keyboard, but had to switch to a controller simply because there was no possible way to maneuver without a joystick.  The platform mechanics got rather complicated as I unlocked newer ones.  Sometimes I'd end up dying over and over again simpy because I kept mixing up how to activate certain abilities.  Thankfully, it was never a deal breaker.  Even during the long, no checkpoint escape sequences, I never end up rage quitting.  It was always that good kind of frustration, where if I just tried this one thing different, or jumped a little more to the right, I could make it.  Also, the music never restarted when I died on those levels. So that up tempo, heroic score was always encouraging me to keep at it, and it was SO rewarding when I finally succeeded.  (Though I did nearly snap my controller in half several times.)
In short, I loved playing this game, I loved looking at this game, and I loved listening to this game.  It was a fantastic ride, and well worth the price.
Others civilizations must know of this masterpiece too.

I rarely ever go to the steam greenlight, it's usually filled with trash, "simulators," and joke games, but a few months ago I decided to check it out for sh!ts and giggles.  While treading through the wave of filth, I stumbled upon this little diamond in the rough. I'll be honest, it was solely the game's art style that brought me over.  I was intrigued by the game's concept, it reminded me of Diner Dash, a Ds game I used to play a lot.  I decided to give this game my support, something this game was the first to receive from me, and currently the only game I've supported on the workshop.  After a few days, I completely forgot about this game.  A couple of days ago, I received an email from Steam telling me that this game was released, and you bet that I went and bought it...                                A few days later. What!? I'm a busy guy.  Carrie's Order up is visual porn, every little aspect of the game looks beautiful, from the retro-like cutscenes, to the little idle dance Carrie does, to the illustrations shown on the main menu.  It's obvious the artist behind this game has a large amount of talent and creativity.  The gameplay is similar to Pac-Man, with the player movie Carrie through a maze-like area while avoiding customers (ghosts).  What separates this game from Pac-Man is the fact that Carrie never stops moving, forcing the player to constantly paying full attention. Unlike Pac-man, however, Carrie can go past customers by spinning, but don't think you can get away with spinning past every enemy, as Carrie will get dizzy and eventually fall if you spin too much. The music in this game is also very well done, almost never getting too repetitive, and even if it does get repetitive, you can always change the music in the pause menu.  Despite all the positives this game has, there are a few negatives, but when I say few, I mean the very VERY little nitpicks I have. The voice acting in this game feels a bit unnatural and can sound a little strange at times, a few more takes could have helped a bit.  While the characters in this game are very charming, dialog between them can be awkwardly worded and feel a bit odd, but that will probably be a problem only I will have.
All in all I feel that this game is very addictive, fun and perfect for people who don't have time to play any major releases.

Fantastic little arcade-style game. Simple, fast, challenging, colourful play. If you're looking at this game and thinking this is yet another Diner Dash type game, you would be wrong. It's not a time management style game at all.
It's a challenging old school maze game that's suited for twitchy play. You need to avoid the path of the customers in the shop as you serve them, and must serve them the food they ordered before they get angry.
So think more like... Pacman's maze and enemy-avoiding gameplay (but executed much better imo)... crossed with the fast-paced grabbing-orders-from-wherever-to-serve-quick-to-anger-customers of Midway's Tapper, then crossed with the matching orders to customers and collecting dirty dishes from games like Diner Dash. I also find myself thinking of an old LCD game I used to own, called "Coffee House" by Sunwing.
Beautifully detailed cute retro art style, reminiscent of Taito arcade games of the late 1990s (think Puzzle Bobble 4). Your score when you get game over contributes towards unlockables, so that's a neat touch too. Full controller support, and it auto-saves.
Only problem so far with the game: it regularly crashes on exit. But hey, I was trying to exit anyway, so that doesn't matter too much.
And yes, I did get this game via a Steam key. The game was once part of a game bundle, and was actually the main reason I bought that whole bundle. I forgot about it and didn't actually play it until today, though.
EDIT - 14/09/2016: This game was crashing a lot during gameplay yesterday. So much that I was re-thinking my thumbs-up on this review, even though I really like the game. I sent a lot of bug reports to the dev, and so did some others, and it was patched within hours. Hasn't crashed during gameplay since then. It still crashes on game exit though.

This game is a very easy game to pick up on, and very difficult to master. Given the nature of the game, there is some dumb luck involved, but the game lets you choose where to where to lean that luck towards. It is primarily multiplayer but in 0.28 a single player campaign has been introduced that allows you to go on quests and fight wizards leading up to bosses and such. This single player mdoe does however have multiplayer elements, allowing you to request help from a fellow player at the cost of a small fee and half the rewards of the battle.
This game is very much a digital board game. You are a wizard facing off against one (or more in some multiplayer matches) other wizard, with an arsenal of spells in the form of cards. It is turn based tactics with percentage based spells, that you can increase chances of succeeding casting in a few ways. Creatures also have percentage chances of destroying other creatures, based on their respective stats. Meaning, yes, a rat CAN kill a Hydra, but it is very unlikely (6% chance if I'm not mistaken).
Each card has a base percentage that represents the chance you have of successfully casting the spell. The percentages can change based on the influence of the field at any given time. Each card is one of three types. Law, Chaos, or neutral. If a spell of either law or chaos is successfully cast, then the overall influence of the field will change in favor of that type. However, a neutral card will not change the influence one way or another. These cards are chosen randomly, tho evenly, with the exceptions being cards you have forced in your deck from talismans that can be equipped to your staff and robe, and two spells called Disbelieve and Dispel. The first is a spell that you always have, that you can use on an enemy creature if you think they are an illusion, and the second you can use to dismiss your own creatures for mana in return.

I cannot believe how many fundamental issues this game has that are blocking its actual content.
-Clickbox for enemies is FAR too narrowly defined, meaning instead of attacking your character will walk around them like a moron. On hard mode, this often means you'll have to redo an entire fight as every action matters
-Fire and poison. Where do I even start on this? Not only do both do an absolutely ABSURD amount of damage, but walking even one or two steps through a fire/poisonous area will both afflict them AND do additonal immediate damage for traversing the area.
-Utterly baffling mechanics. Zombies become poisoned when I attack them? This corpse randomly blows up for 85% of my health when I walk over it? This trap instantly vaporizes my guy, with no way to disable it or get around it? This person is healed by magic?
-Horrible skill system. Combat skills mixed with magic skills mixed with crafting skills, with at least half of them being useless. The same can be said for the "talents".
-Utterly pointless "sheath/unsheath" player states which exist for NO reason other than to punish the player. Accidentally have your weapons drawn and activate a dialogue option with an NPC, and then misclick the dialogue option? Hurray, they've now attacked you, and unless you can reload you can kiss any sidequests they are involved in goodbye. What awesome immersion.
The pacing is slow, the questlines are dull and obtuse, and are usually solved by accident rather than on purpose, as the game eschews any waypoint system. I can understand not putting waypoints for some kinds of quests, or leaving an option to turn them off, but forcing the player to wander needlessly? Stinks of lazy development.
Another game I wanted to like so badly, and when the combat works, it's great. But I don't want to play a game of "click the right pixel" and be more stressed about misclicking during a fight than the actual battle itself.
Overall, this game feels like a beta in severe need of interface polishing and game balancing. I can tell that there's some great stuff buried underneath these issues, but the fact that the game is in this state means I find it nearly unplayable.

In a few words--the best RPG I've played in a decade.
expounding a little further:
The good: Character customization. From an aesthetic standpoint, not so much, but in terms of build variability you have a LOT of choice. It's not quite Path of Exile, but I'd still venture to say no two players will have the same party composition between their respective playthroughs.
The great: combat. No RPG I've ever played has had combat with the depth and variety of this game's. I'd recommend playing on the hard difficulty setting, as it's very rewarding to finally figure out a winning strategy for some of the tougher encounters. Unlike in many other games, there is no single dominant rinse and repeat strategy you will find yourself using in every fight. Even with the same characters, different fights demand different tactics, and you'll come to appreciate your carefully-tooled character builds across your party as you explore this game's many nuances in successive battles. Each encounter is unique in this game. Of the many things this game did well, combat stands out the most. What Counter-Strike is to shooters, this game is to RPGs.
The not so great: voice acting. I left the game on subtitles only. The plot is also a little cheesy, but you're not going to care because it's really just an excuse to keep mauling zombies and orcs which, as exhaustively stated prior, is deeply satisfying.
Buy it.

Let me begin by saying that it has been ages since I've touched a 2D slider game. I have become tired of survival and fps shooters etc. La Tale has brought back old memories from a much simpler time from when I was younger.
The graphics are cute and anime-ly if you are into that kinda stuff. I do see a big resemblance to the more popular game Maplestory. One major difference I noticed was the combat. (Maple's combat is pretty much♥♥♥♥♥lol) The combat is still not Guild Wars 2, but it's as good as it gets on a 2D slider.
Starting the game was quick, we (me and my partner) were given free gears that seemed to have gave us the power to kill everything in one hit. I thought that was kind of weird since it took a lot out of the combat for me personally. We switched to regular beginner gears instead and continued our journeys. Leveling up is quite fast, the quests would give me a few levels at once. Perhaps this game is more focused on the end game like most of the other mmos' these days.
A flaw I noticed was that there doesn't seem to be a clear enough guideline to start this game as a beginner. I looked online but the few guides that were availible were mostly outdated. Lucky enough, we were invited into a guild and our guildmates helped us with all the questions and where to go etc. I highly recommend that IF YOU'RE NEW, JOIN A GUILD. I feel that there is so much hidden info on this game that it's essential to get help from older and more knowledgeable players.  So far my partner and I have just been duoing but there are many other new players around that are down to team up so partying up for stuff shouldn't be a problem.
Overall a fun and nostalgic game. I would recommend this game if you like anime style games with cute costumes or if you're looking to just get into a mmo with a welcoming community.
tl;dr
Fun game with cute anime characters, combat is smooth, and players are nice. Starting out could be confusing, so ask for help in game.

In my opinion I wouldn't recommend getting too invested with this mmo, however if you want to play and join a great friendly community feel free to do so. It was fun while it lasted; being about to re-visit this game and reminisce.
The only thing "Evolved" about it; is that it has a different publisher. Either than that the game is still the same thing as it was before during the previous publisher OGP. The only difference I could spot out between the two publishers is that the community is more lively and active.

BIT.TRIP RUNNER is an auto-runner. You have no control over Commander Video's movement speed, and your only interactions are jumping, ducking, kicking, and blocking objects that block your path.   The main difference between BIT.TRIP RUNNER and other auto-runners is that obstacles aren't randomly generated or placed in every stage, and instead appear in a set rhythm and melody to the music. As you collect gold bars and dodge obstacles, you fill in various bits of each stage's song, and the more power-up cores you find, the more intense the music gets and the higher your score will soar.
The game is HIGHLY focused on immediate reaction, and if that's not your cup of tea, then your pattern memorization skills will be put to the ultimate test. RUNNER has a relatively smooth start to try and ease you into the experience, but if you're to complete the game then your execution is going to have to be near-flawless. There are no mid-stage checkpoints to save you, and one missed jump means being thrown back to the beginning of a stage to try again. It's easy to get caught up in a flurry of "just one more try"s, but that satisfaction isn't quite the same as you'd get from something like Super Meat Boy or Rogue Legacy. RUNNER can be rote almost to a fault, and it'll probably take people that enjoy very specific types of linear challenges to enjoy it.
If there's one major issue with the game it's that there are some crazy intense swings and spikes in difficulty. Stage 1-11 - ODYSSEY will probably be enough to shut down most that aren't dedicated to trying to see the game to its end, and there are more than a few other bad apples in the bunch whose level of challenge can feel a bit excessive considering the game's lack of checkpointing. It's all doable with the right amount of practice, but again, if that kind of rote memorization isn't for you, it may be best to pass on this one. Otherwise, game on. It's a fantastic game with great music, a fun aesthetic, and engaging gameplay for those of us that like a little something different in rhythm games.

Stay away from this game. It's a good example of poor game design.
The core idea is fine; it's a runner-style game, not unlike others of the genre. The good distinguishing things that it has are the art style (it looks like an Atari game) and the music. As you evade obstacles and grab items, it adds to the music in interesting ways. Sometimes, you can use musical patterns to help you determine when you should jump. It's a nice, unique touch.
The problem is that the game demands perfection, and requires trial-and-error and memorization in order to achieve it. If you die (get hit by an object, run into something, or fall in a pit), you're sent back to the beginning of the level. There are a number of cheap deaths to be found, where you can't realistically be expected to foresee or react to a threat quickly enough to survive it. This means you'll have to die repeatedly while you discover these points and memorize them, until you reach a point where you can clear a level. Many of these spots require pinpoint precision, and a few levels are particularly infuriating for their great length.
Perfection's a fine goal, but it shouldn't be what's required in order to play or enjoy a game. If Rock Band ended a song as soon as you missed one note, no one would play it. That's essentially what this game does, and it ruins what could have been a pleasant pixelated romp.
(Note: The sequel is MUCH better, correcting most of the major problems that the first game had. If you're interested, go check that out instead.)

Dream is a very interesting game with a very captivating concept.
You play as a man named Howard whose uncle recently passed away and you
are a Dreamer. The majority of the game takes place in your (lucid) dreams.
These dreams involve exploration and puzzle solving, in a variety of environments.
Pros
+Graphically most of this game looks ok
+Outside environments are beautiful and very nice to look at
+Inventory system has a very simplistic design that is easy to use and understand.
+Voice acting is very crisp and clean, and nice to listen to.
+Music is very well done
Cons
-Howard's lines are very awkward and some things he says I think shouldn't be said explicitly
-Hitboxes on some things are god-awful, especially the rocks in the desert level (some places you need to crouch to get through even if there is a five foot gap)
-The "pop in" is terrible. The ground literally changes before your eyes
-(This is just my opinion) Exploration is very tedious, I found myself using sprint as much as possible (because there is a godamn cooldown for who knows why?) because I found walking just, well slow. However this might be a personal problem especially because I like going superfast in rouglikes such as spelunky.
-The four mazes in the desert level are very tedious. Doing the same thing four times in a row is just stupid. Yes the "perks" of each maze are all unique but it doesn't change the fact that it's just the same thing over and over.
-I really hate this- thepuzzles have all been done before. Correct me if I'm wrong but I didn't find a single innovative puzzle in the entire game.
-Player model is clunky and looks pretty bad, and shadows  are animated badly aswell.
Though I don't really want to play anymore of this game based on what I've played so far I'm still watching how this early access title will play out. This is their team's first game, so it will be interesting how they will work things out and fix problems. If the cons I listed even are problems, and not just my own displeasure. Anyway try it out, but buy it on sale.

Before going on to explain why I actually didn't like Thirty Flights of Loving, bear in mind that I enjoyed Dear Esther (an interactive story with no real gameplay).
Thirty Flights of Loving takes approximately 15 minutes to get through and by the end of it, you're left thinking what you just played. I won't call it a game because like Dear Esther, it is an interactive story. The story in Thirty Flights is non-linear, meaning you're told the story in the incorrect order and you're essentially left to piece it all together. While this is a plus, as it helps you take the story as you're required to pay attention and really think about it, the story is nowhere near long enough to be worth the amount you pay.
Typically, I would say that for every £1 (or $1) you spend, a game should give you one hour of gameplay. Now this game is £4, so following that system, you should get 4 hours of gameplay, but even with Gravity Bone included, you don't get that much gameplay, since there is very little replay value. I would say this is the kind of game you would find on a free games website, not something you would pay for. It's just not worth it.
Just to clarify why I liked Dear Esther and not Thirty Flights, Dear Esther actually has some level of replay value, since each time you play, the script changes. So in order to fully understand the story within Dear Esther, you would need to play it multiple times to get all the dialogue.

Overall, the story is cliche' and can be seen from 3 miles off by a blind guy including all the plot twists. This wouldn't be an issue, if not for the fact that the game seems intent on minimizing any of the interesting things within the 40k lore, you don't see any of the awesome armor of the Imperial Guard laying waste at range (yes, yes, I know, they were being overran, but then we should have seen Orkz with looted tanks, then, eh?), Space Marine mechs, or the tons of baddies and variants of the Chaos and Orkz forces. This felt less like a planet wide invasion and war than it did a strike force, and this is made all the worse when you see that even when Chaos forces are preparing to invade and wreck things, there are only the most minor of vehicles of the Guardsmen in any respect. Even when the Imperial fleet arrives, you don't see any vehicles really, aside from troop transport ships... This could be forgiven if the gameplay was amazing, but that is next.
The gameplay is repetitive, and I can already hear folks say, "Well yeah, you're a Space Marine, of course! You are meant to kill things over and over!". There is one major problem though... You feel invincible. Aside from 1-2 deaths from being cornered as I rolled into a wall, there wasn't anything to fear. The AI went to the Herpa Derp school of combat, and this is most clearly seen by the Chaos Marines. They seemingly forget that their most hated enemy, the Space Marines, were just shooting at them, only to have you step around and then look at you as they ponder if you'll be their friend. "Maybe this time we can frolic in the fields of bones and snuggle vorpal bunnies as the blood fountains start in the background!" I don't expect super secret tactics taught to only the most elite of forces, but I do expect more then move left, move right, then get shot, or to stare at you with their heads conveniently out of cover. Orkz should be more charging and melee (which I admit many of thier units are melee which is nice, but far too squishy for even the standard bolter). The Chaos forces are just sort of a joke, especially the Guardsmen, and even their marines are a simple headshot with the laser cannon, they feel less like a real challenge as opposed to being really "challenged". What's more, there is a lot of padding as you walk through various corridors of rubble, and without a jump feature (aside from some of the funnest sections of the game which are all too brief, and honestly the the only major redeemer in single player) it greatly limits exploration in a giant planet factory.
About 9 models for the Orkz which is sad given Orkz are not what one would call "organized" with standard gear aside from some having melee primarily, others ranged, you can't expect every Ork unit to be exactly the same.  It's even worse with Chaos, as the idea is these units are being warped into monsters essentially at random (as if Chaos wasn't a hint at that), clocking in with 8 models as well. These counts are including the Warboss of the Orkz, as well as the Chaos Commander of the Chaos forces. If I am off, the count is likely not off by more then 1-2 as I recall the units from memory. I'm not saying make every single unit look different, that would be an insane task when you have a swarm of Orkz coming down on you, but you do expect to see more then one model for every enemy (with the exception, perhaps, of the standard daemons of Chaos). This could have been achieved easily with something so simple as some minor palet and texture swaps on the faces, and 2-4 scars made for the Orkz to put on faces randomly upon spawn. Yeah, it wouldn't change much, but it wouldn't look as bland, and would take little work.
I'll grant you, Chaos would be harder to make have variants, because for all intents and purposes, the Chaos forces (the marine portions there of, and the corrupted Guardsmen) look the same as their Space Marine counterparts, aside from palet swaps of course for the most part, but that isn't to say you can't have tumors or something (again, 2-4 variations) to help liven up the roster so it doesn't look like you're killing a corrupted Guardsmen, and his 15 identical brothers who all so happen to work for Chaos too.

After playing through this game in its entirety (roughly 10hrs of gameplay for me - with a moderate completionist slant), I can say with 100% certainty that this game deserves every bit of acclaim it has been receiving.  It is everything the "metroidvania" genre should be and more.  It's so very rare that I run across a game of this caliber that holds my attention so tightly that I play it through to completion within a weekend - something I did with Ori and haven't done in a very long time prior.
You won't need me to tell you how beautiful the graphics are, you can see that for yourself in the screenshots and video previews.  What you see there is what you get, the whole way through.  What is more amazing is that the rest of the elements that make up a great game (audio, game mechanics, overall gameplay, balance, difficulty, etc.) are all as beautiful and perfectly crafted as the visuals are.
The gameplay in particular is so well done, and while very difficult, the game never leaves you feeling like you can't progress further because of it.  It is JUST hard enough to throw you into a bit of a frenzy where you aren't quite sure if you've reached your limit - but you just gotta try at least a few more times - and then you get it, and it feels magical.  Then the next challenge, and the next.
By the end of the game, you're performing tricks you would never thought you were capable of in the beginning, and that's part of the magic of Ori.  It guides you through a progression so perfectly smooth you don't even realize how far you've come in skill until you reach the end and compare it to the beginning.
It's within this progression and the journey that you really become drawn in to the whole ordeal, and finally reaching the end of all of these trials is a great relief and a feeling of supreme satisfaction.
If I had to say something negative about this game it would be only that after reaching the end I craved more.  Not because Ori wasn't long enough - it was, in fact, a very decent amount of content for the price and any more might have been too exhausting.
