So I just finished playing through Divinty:OS EE, and my final thoughts upon finishing this game are "Thank god it's over". But I can explain how I got to this stage of complete agony when trying to finish the game. Divinity utterly fails at making the UI a pleasant experience at playing the game. Furthermore the game makes astounding choices that make you question if anyone in the development process asked WHY ARE WE DOING THIS.
So to start things off I'll say some things that Divinity does that makes zero sense to me.
-There's no quick trading
If you have a ton of ingredients or items to trade to your OTHER character you have to move them ONE ITEM AT A TIME.
This is completely ridiculous to say the least, BUT the more astounding thing is that the game actually has a system in place to automatically move quest items from one characters inventory to the character that needs it. In other words? There is absolutely NO reason to ever have two seperate inventories like they've done in the game. Inventories should be "magically linked" 24/7 and capacity combined from the characters.
-Healing after combat
This is one that I think gets ruined for me after playing The Last Remnant. See the concept is that in TLR you fight every battle like it's your last battle so you are FULL HEALED after every combat. Divinity decided that you should be forced to heal yourself after every fight, which makes sense IF there was a system that worked around this. The problem is kinda covered w/NO MANA so skills can be used freely outside of combat to heal. However this takes hours because of the cooldowns. There's food that can be used as well which has no cooldown and can heal decently. But THE BEST HEALING can be done FOR FREE in a bed next to most Waypoints. So let me just ask if it makes more sense to either
A) Fully Heal the Party after every Fight
or
B) TP to a Waypoint and go lay down in beds to fully heal which takes a grand total of 2 minutes every time
When they both achieve the same objective which is HAVING A HEALED PARTY. Neither of them cost anything except for the second option which is a COMPLETE WASTE OF TIME.
PLEASE DEVS DONT DO THIS AGAIN FOR THE SEQUEL.
Either make Inns and Spells cost mana (which means healing COSTS something forcing the player into making choices about when to go back) or completely heal the party after combat, there's no inbetween.
-No Mana
Kind of covered previously but skills cost no mana in the game. Everything runs off AP in combat so outside of combat everything can be used freely as long as it's off cooldown. This seems like a good idea, and quite frankly I enjoy the thought of it. But to be quite frank, it made more problems than it fixed. Mage characters in the game easily benefit over this kind of stuff where spells could be used right before the fight breaks out at no negative to the player since nothing was wasted. The spell was cast and the player has no mana or ap loss since it was considered to be cast 'outside of combat'.
There is synergy that exists in this game which is beyond cool, but the problem is that the pay off for these synergies is waaaaay too much. These synergies (mostly the poison cloud explosion) do FAR too much damage and can be done even with grenades. I was able to kill most large mobs in a single turn with this combination, and it just felt cheap. Master level mage classes can do large AoE spells like Earthquake, Hailstorm, etc which also do copious amounts of damage. I get that mages would probably be weaker towards the late game but that's why spells should more heavily weigh off of the Int. level of the character.
-Invisibility and How it ruins the Game
You can go invisible and steal anything just sitting around without worry. A max leveled pickpocket can go to town with invisibility and bleed everyone dry. I was sitting on 200k gold when I finished my playthrough. There was literally nothing I could have bought to spend this money.
-Leandra
I don't know if this was the enhanced edition only or what, but the fight begins with Leandra surrounded by 4 Void Knights and Three demons. The fight begins by the three demons casting THREE INVULNERABILITY AURAS one of which goes to Leandra. I immediately off one of the demons and two rounds later (when the invulnerability wears off), the remaining two demons PLACE THE INVULNERABILITY AGAIN. I kill the next demon and yet again the process continues. Finally all of the demons are dead and I can go for the boss! NOPE. Physical Immunity aura and eventually places an elemental immunity aura as well. Now the problem with this fight was that it was entirely wasting your time. For 8 turns you have to sit there with characters being COMPLETELY INVULNERABLE. Now this makes no sense to me because the Void Aura is supposed to be able to get hit through as long as the character has a tenebrium weapon. WHICH DIDNT WORK. I had a weapon that required Tenebrium skill lvl 2 which APPARENTLY doesn't count as Tenebrium. Irremovable invulnerability is never a fun option to a fight. Especially not when this is one of three fights IN A ROW that you have to do at the end of the game.
-Crafting System and Blacksmithing
The crafting system at times makes absolutely no sense and Blacksmithing is simply worthless because you'll never make an item that's halfway decent. Seriously go look up the crafting recipes online, google Divinity crafting for a .pdf file that will be the first option. You can make fish pies, apple pies, pizza, and cheese bread from dough but CANNOT make a pumpkin pie. At first I was willing to go along with it until I realized how asinine the recipes were. A jar of mud combined with a fiery heart makes the most OP weapon in the game, a sword of planes. Take THAT blacksmithing.
-Identifying and Repairing
Merchants/Player don't have a Repair All or Identify All button. I don't know why.
-Perception
There is no reason this game should rely so heavily on this. It just feels cheap. If you don't level it you'll get stuck with no answers until you read online that your perception should be 10. You buff it to 10 and proceed on. There's only negatives to keeping this around.
-Puzzles
The puzzles were mostly for children which was the the practice of put the cylinder through the cylinder hole concept. When the game didn't rely on this, it instead quickly shifted to tiny buttons that are hard to see or find in large rooms. Tiny buttons are not puzzles.
-Teleport Pyramids
While I thought initially they were a neat idea, I quickly realized that it was a cheap fix or free puzzle item for the devs.  When in doubt get the puzzle to somehow incorporate leaving one character behind and having to use the pyramid to bring them back. Also I thought I would be fancy and leave a pyramid in an area I wanted to quickly return to. But apparently the devs think I'm stupid so the pyramid would get teleported into my inventory if I left it (Waypoint travel). This makes no sense to me BECAUSE as long as you have one of the pyramids it's absolutely impossible to lose the other one. I thought that was the point of the pyramids but I GUESS NOT.
-The First Town
Too close to the start, players enter and are given too much to do in the town which results in not leaving for a few hours.
Bugs
-Enemies just stare in combat and waste your time (The Fix? Combat skip to YOUR turn.)
-Icara (An essential NPC) died during one of the final bouts, her dead corpse kept teleporting to me but I had no way to revive her. I easily killed the boss in two rounds without this NPC, but it also affected the Ending where I was unable to ask Zandalor what happened to the Sisters, BECAUSE she was dead and I was never given an option to fix the Soul Forge.
I had more to say but WORD LIMIT
tl;dr It's okay but not a 9/10 game. Expect a 6/10 at best.

Eventide 2 is a bit too short, even for a hidden object game, but it offers plenty of hidden/fragmented object scenes, a standard but interesting story with decent voice acting, and nice scenery during that time.
The first Eventide was like an obnoxious child jumping around shouting: “look what I learnt from Slavic mythology!” Thankfully, the second game, The Sorcerer’s Mirror chose a more traditional approach in its storyline: evil wizard kidnaps niece, find a way inside his mansion through a village, cemetery, and some countryside to rescue her.
To the game’s credit, at least it tries to hide this old formula behind a few purely cosmetic story choices; but somehow I get the feeling that it was also a vain attempt of forcing replay value, as the game isn’t even two hours long (unless you get stuck on the marble rings puzzle).
Speaking of puzzles, Eventide 2 is a very conservative HOG, meaning it mostly features hidden and fragmented object scenes. Naturally, there are also conventional puzzles and the usual adventure game mechanics, but they are in a secondary role, making Eventide 2 a perfect game for more conservative HOG fans.

It's not as flavorful and rich as the first
, but it's still a good casual point-and-click adventure. Like the first entry in the series, it's rather short and easy. But it's still smooth as better and very pleasant.
This game introduces a “choose your own adventure” concept, but it's rather thin. Your choices don't make that much of a difference and hardly justify a replay. Still, it's a nice little touch.
Finally, thank you, devs, for supporting Linux!

It’s time to jump back into the world of Slavic mythology with
! This is a fun and simple hidden object game with casual puzzles and an interesting story. While this is a sequel, you don’t have to play the first installment to understand what’s happening. For myself, I preferred the first game. While this was a nice game to play it was a bit short and a bit easy, but anyone new to this genre may find it to be a good way to get their feet wet.
The story follows Mary from the first game, though nothing is mentioned about that adventure except from the cover a magazine. You’re out mountain climbing with your niece when trouble strikes and she is kidnapped by the evil sorcerer Tvardovsky... because she looks like his dead wife. You spend the rest of the game trying to free her as well as help the village he’s using to fuel his sick experiments by dangling the spirits of their loved ones in front of them. The story is interesting but I really couldn’t find anything Slavic about it unless I searched the internet for things and I’m sure I missed some points because I’m just not a folklorist. As a fan of the previous game I was disappointed how far removed it was from that title.
As mentioned before, this is a hidden object game. The game offers seventeen scenes, none of which you have to visit twice. They range from a list of items you need to find, to finding a certain amount of an item, like flowers. I enjoyed them and found them well made. The downside of this game, however, is the puzzles. They are just too easy. There was only one I had any difficulty with, everything else provided little to no challenge whatsoever. You have a map that you can use to teleport, however it doesn’t seem to have exact locations, just general ones. Like, if an area has three or four parts to it, it won’t show each individual area which would be annoying if you needed to use the map to see where your next action is. The game has three difficulty levels and one custom one along with plenty of collectables to find. The unique feature in the game is a choice system. The game claims that your choices affect the story, but they don’t. The changes are very minor and the ending is always the same. While I applaud them trying this feature out, it fell pretty flat.
The graphics are beautiful, the game has gorgeous scenery and the character models are for the most part well done. The hidden object scenes are rendered well, none of the items are blurry or too small. Everything looks great, and the music goes well with it aesthetically. The game is fully voice acted and overall this is also well done. I wasn’t a fan of all of the acting, most notably Yanosik, his audio quality also didn’t seem to match that of the other actors either. Overall everything is fine and tolerable.
tried a few new things out and that much I have to give it credit for, with so many casual games on the market it’s important for developers to think outside the box. However, this game is short and easy so I do recommend grabbing it on sale or in a bundle. This game has Steam cards and achievements which are easy to collect, you just have to play the game twice. Sadly, there is no bonus chapter in this game and since changing your choices barely changes anything in the game, having to play it twice isn’t a good enough replacement in my mind. It’s a good game, it’s accessible and enjoyable, but it could be better.

I find it hard to be choose between "thumbs up" and "thumbs down" for this game.
I really enjoyed the first of the series: it was just the right length, puzzles varied in difficulty (nothing too simple or too hard), you could unlock a cute short " continuation" of the story after you beat the game, the universe was great (I enjoyed the elements of Slavic cultural hertidee ) as well as the art. I can't say all that about Eventide 2.
I've still enjoyed the story, artwork and cultural elements but the whole thing was simply too short with puzzles that were just simply too easy to solve. I did like the newly added element of making choices which can lead to the story developing slighly different but the choices were too black and white for my personal liking. It was very clear which choices were "good" and "bad" which kind of defeats the purpose of the choice even being there (at least for me). At last whichever you ended up choosing made very little diffrence in how things play out. However, I was still excited about the prospect of this mechanic.
Overall, I'd still recommend the game if you really enjoyed the first one and don't mind the aforementioned downsides. The game is still fun. However, I bought the game during sale though, maybe I'd feel different have I bought it at full price.

I was pleasantly surprised by this game.  My library shows something like 15 Artifex Mundi HOGs, so I think there's some experience there.  It feels like this game was crafted with more care than others.  Towards the end it felt a bit rushed, but that is common.
The puzzles were (very slightly) harder (especially early in game) than in previous Artfex Mundi releases, and I really hope they find a way to offer harder puzzles for people who want them.
The idea that your choices affect your future is a common desire among these games.  To make that happen, a great deal of content has to be created that will often never be seen.  That is a roadblock.  But it was great to see the attempt at it.
It was nice that we were given a 'moral' choice several times through the game, but the actual result wasn't significantly different.  From a mechanics standpoint, it was a difference between how many tired/old/simple puzzles you had to play at the end to beat the boss.  Understood... everyone should be able to complete the game, but :(
Maybe, instead of sticks, offer carrots to those who choose to attempt the hard puzzles?
However, from a story standpoint, there were good differences.  Who had you befriended?  Who had you harmed?  Those choices come back in the story.
The publisher did add extra content for those who were willing to search for it, and that is good.

CONTRA:

- no bonus chapter

PROS
+ nice graphics & hidden object scenes

+ music

I knew about this game before even Artifex Mundi put it on Steam. Indeed, I was sent a beta copy of the game and played it till the sorcerer's manor.
You're again Mary, the heroin from the first Eventide but this time, you're on vacation with your niece Jenny. However, she's taken captive by the local noble and you discover that he has a certain hold on the villagers...
You're still in that universe of eastern and slavic world, however, now, no cute creature is allied to you: it's mainly humans and the only mythic beings are imps, used by the sorcerer. The story is inviting you to a journey of love (ultimately, all the hurt is coming from love, for the wrong reasons), of souls and of decisions. Indeed, Eventide is the first hidden object game by Artifex that use decisions as a way to change the story, although these are just impacting the final showdown and yet, this doesn't change the end: you're still beating the antagonist of the story. But I can understand the moral choices: will you lie or tell the truth? Will you be exiging something or be a kind woman?
The gameplay is pretty standard, apart for the moral choices: hidden objects scenes, puzzles, items to find, to combine, to use. The hidden objects scenes are quite easy and use the trick of real hidden objects in the scene (you have to open jars, move stuff, etc...). The puzzles are also easy, apart perhaps for one or two. You have also the hunt for the imp cards (like in the first Eventide with all the mythical creatures), the mirrors and the notes, achievements being the main target here.
The graphics are also quite good: alternating between outside landscapes (sunny) and the inside (warm when it comes for your allies but sinister when you're in the lair of your enemies). The soundtrack is also good, as usual with any Artifex Mundi published game.
I'm just being sad to see that the decision gameplay, while being a good idea, isn't impacting more the story, like the characters changing their behavior and changing quests, etc
Eventide 2 is a very good game, so don't hesitate!

An enjoyable enough action RPG that has a LOOOONG single player campaign (30 hours).
The graphics and sound are often excellent, but there are segments that are lacking in polish. Irritating gaming and pop culture jokes are everywhere in side quests and hidden collectibles which detract from the feel of the main story, as does some occasionally terrible voice acting.
The biggest issue is that while it is a competent Diablo-like, it really doesn’t have the endless re-playability of those games. Even with daily challenges, once you’re done once there's really no pull to come back to it again. The combat is a little spammy too, with hordes of monsters just milling around waiting for you to hit them with massive AoE attacks.
And the less said about the final boss the better. 3x battles against the same monster, taking about 30 minutes of kiting him around the arena… very boring. Many of the other bosses (especially early game) feel unbalanced and overly difficult, but as is often the case with these types of games, skill and character spec can have a dramatic effect on progress.
If this still sounds like your thing and you don’t need to play through multiple times to justify your purchase then this is recommended, otherwise look elsewhere at games such as Torchlight, or Diablo 3 which is still the best action RPG going around.

Graphics: 8.5/10
The graphics overall look great. I did notice a few... issues here and there. Although, mostly minor graphics problems with textures. It seemed to go away after swapping to OpenGL from D3D. My PC isnt exactly powerful graphics wise but, from what I can use, it looks great.
Gameplay: 6.5/10
Standard RPG gameplay. (As expected.) The User Interface/Menus works well. There are a few gripes I have about spells/controls but, they are managable. I have completed the game on casual and have started a new game on the hardest difficulty... I am regreting that decision... Which brings me to my next point...
The game difficulty is a bit brutal. You are basically expected to die a lot. I can't even imagine hardcore characters... Maybe on casual... Anything above that though, would be a challenge indeed... I have died so many times on fearless (and harder per levels.) that I lost count. I barely have any gold to buy stuff and whatnot. I think they game difficulty could use a rebalance. However, Casual is still fair enough. I did die a few times on it but, not as many on higher difficulties...
I also did encounter a(n) annoying flaw that I hope they fix at some point. Certain Containers/Boxes/Barrels/etc can cause the game to lag for some time. I am not sure if it's just my PC or the game. It really annoys me when it happens though. It rarely happens in the story mode. However, it happens more in the adventure mode.
Finally, I want to point out there are a lot of movie/video game references in this game as well. Made me laugh a few times. I kinda question its legal usage but, whatever.
Replayability: 7.5/10
There are a few different classes to play and many difficulty options to choose from. Even a Hardcore Character. There is also an extra adventure mode that is also fun. If you want to drive yourself mad, I suppose the harder difficulties is for you. Personally, I prefer the Casual difficulty.
Sound/Music: 9/10
I love the music in this game. Very memorable. The sounds are fine as well. My only complaint would be one of the enemies has a very loud and annoying shreak when it dies. It's the "ice tiger"? (IIRC.) All the others are fine though. The dialog between the protagonist and Katarina is interesting too. Well done.
Overall: 7/10
I do like this game. However, I feel like if they rebalanced the game and had less forced deaths, it would be perfect. Perhaps a smaller increase in hp/ap for the monsters. The scale is pretty high/insane as it is now. One of the highest being 9000% hp. That's just crazy. Personally, I would adjust the HP more than the AP. I am fine with the AP. It's mainly the HP. Then again... I did notice one thing while making a character... I tend to focus on one ability and not the others. Mostly because HP/Defence was pointless on harder difficulties. I focused on damage. I tried HP/Defence but, I just could not kill anything in those builds. Thankfully, there is a reset character stats in game... I was experimenting with it for some time... I still think the game needs rebalancing work for sure though... As for right now... I don't like it as much on higher difficulties. Thanksfully, Casual is pretty fair.

I do not care enough to ever review or recommend games. This would be the first I ever do.
Sentimentality is not something I do, either; however, here I am.
In Ori and the Blind Forest, you have the perfect unity of gameplay, mechanics, story, music and artwork.
The controls are smooth, responsive. Animations are complimentary to the style of movement. The game is challenging, offering harder areas to those who care, or just the main story for those who don't.
A typical metroidvania, you get the red powerup to unlock the red door, etc. Starting out, you're a fast, agile little white critter, doing flips and moving fluidly along the ground. Come near game-end and you're a nigh unstoppable flurry of moving energy weaving through the world with little to nothing that can stop you.
An emotionally charged story backed by utterly breathtaking painted and painstakingly animated visuals, and music that pluck at your heartstrings... this game leaves you with a knot in your throat, loosely holding onto your controller as the credits roll, unable to believe this amazing dream of light and wonder has come to an end.
I will miss you, little guy. And the brilliant world that Moon Studios crafted will call to me in my dreams for weeks to come.
GOTY 2015.
PS: yes, he totally looks like a pure-white version of me... does that make me biased? Pshhh.. nooo...

So after playing through the game about 5 times to get all the various endings, I feel confident in giving a review. There are many good things and many bad things, so I guess I'll give the pros and cons of it.
PRO:
Plot - It was pretty good. A lot of twists and turns. The first time I played through I honestly didn't know what was going on and was curious to see where it all would go.
Characters - It seems a lot of folk say the characters are badly written. Some are, I'll get to those in the Con section. But a lot of them are quite well written. I know people in real life who act like Shock, Rocker, Inumi, and some of the others. For most of the characters I did want to see what happened to them and was actively cheering for a few. A lot of folk seem to dislike this game simply because they are furries. I think that's sadly shortsighted. If you made everyone here a human male or female the story wouldn't lose it's impact. To me, the choice to make them all furries was simply a stylistic one (And the creator is a furry too so write what you know and feel comfortable with.) All the art was consistent too, even though almost all the characters are YCH (You Character Here aka pay to have them put in). Whoever did the final art was able ot make the characters consistent and none of them really seemed out of place.
Music - I was impressed. Very nice music. It's not going to be for everyone but then again what ever is?
Replayability/Achievement - If you like to achievement hunt, you got it. 136 to get, some require really screwy choices (Scumbag Saviour being the most obvious). While the writting is mostly the same, the choices you make do in fact alter a lot of dialogue and the two endings. You won't be logging hundreds of hours in this, but I got a good solid 17-18 or so.
CONS:
Characters - Some of them are written badly. Maxine Armstrong and Nagi come to mind. Both are very inconsistent in how they are written and while they try to make them sympathetic or relatable they kinda fail. (Sorry Nagi, you don't get to do what you did and claim the "I'm actually the good guy" card.) Others can come across as arrogant or stupid but generally the writing and the backstories (if you unlock them) make them a lot more relatable. Shock, Kila and Rook all fall into this category.
Art - Also some of the art is poorly chosen. Caylen and Kabu are the prime examples. They always look like beggers even when they weren't. Not sure why they didn't make more sprites. Also, that brings up the lack of different sprites. All the characters seem to have two. One you see the first time they show up, and then the forever default one. They rarely change between them. I think the story would have been helped if they had more sprites.
Some game mechanics: Ok the constant auto save pop-ups can suck an egg. Way to many of them and they sometimes break the flow of the story. You don't need 50 odd save points. Have 1 at the chapter's end and the option to save when you want to. Also, would it hurt to make stuff you've seen before go faster? It is doable, Blackgate has a feature that auto skips all dialogue you've seen, stopping for new dialogue, choices or saves. I do know if you hold the button down it does speed it up but 1) That's awkward to do sometimes and 2) the game doesn't tell you.
Wasted plot/Weird plot choices - This is a visual novel so this pops up sometimes. You'll never agree with everything the creator does and I was no exception. There were a few times I was going, "WTF?" but it was never game breaking. It was always, "I would have done X and not Y" or "Why isn't this a choice? it seems obvious." While I personally don't care about romance, a lot do and they lack of it is odd, especially seeing how Konrad is openly flirty with you regardless of your gender. I know Klace said it was meant to be open ended and use your imagination but dammit, sometimes I want to be told what happened!
Out of game drama - I don't like to comment but it does come up if you read forums and the like. Thankfully Klace has seemed to knocked off being a twit about stuff and that seems to have sorted itself out but it can and does leave a bad taste in ones mouth if you care about it.
OVERALL:
I would recommend it. While furries might not be your cup of tea, I think there's enough here to warrent an actual playthrough. The first time I got the true ending I was a bit misty eyed. So yeah. A game about fluffy cartoon furries made me tear up a little. That's doing something right. Give it a shot at the very least. I would try and get it on sale as it is a bit pricey and once you've seen all the ending there is no reply value worth mentioning.

I love this game! It could best be discribed as Magic the Gathering and Warhammer's love child. I say this as the core of this game is wizard vs wizard duels (both PvP with full tournament support and PvE) played on a hex based, procedurally generated, battle field with one hit kills for everything.
The matches start with each player only having their wizard, and a "hand" of randomly selected spells from your randomly generated (for the most part) spell book, which is your deck. Each player then spends the rest of the match moving around the battlefield summoning critters and monsters as well as casting spells in an effort to control the map and kill off the other wizards. Matches themselves, are resonably short lasing 10-30 minutes. A simple concept, I know but there is a lot of depth. As everything is killed in one hit there is no truly useless monsters, and as long as you play smart and have a little luck you can go from an almost hopeless situation to a win, or have your dragon get killed by that rat your rival summoned five turns ago and you forgot about. Another mechanic that adds depth to combat is the Illusion system.
In Chaos Reborn, in general, the more powerful the spell or summon, the lower the chance of the spell working, but summons have the summon illusion option at casting were you can create a fake monster that is just as potent in all ways as a real one and it will always work but with one potentally huge weakness. They can be unmade by a skill everyone will always have access to: Disbeleive, a skill that if used on an illusion, kills it and allows the caster to cast another spell that turn. If it was real; nothing happens and that doubter loses the ability to cast anything else that turn. Thus an illusion heavy army can be wiped out in one turn potenally, and if your willing to gamble on summoning a dragon on turn one, you can trick the other wizard to effectively waste a turn. The right bluff or call of one at the right time can and will win you games!
There is even going to be an ranking system out side of the traditional leaderboard ladders. In it you can have your wizard climb the ranks so that when you're out of game: you become a mid boss in the single player game, be the boss of a level you design (you get bonus exp and gold if they do well at these jobs,) or even be one of the gods that guilds (the game calls them Orders) sacrifice offerings to in hope you will grant them boons in the forms of various buffs or unlocking loot rich levels for them to pillage. Just be careful though, if you start playing poorly you will be demoted.

This is one of those games I feel myself to be in a good condition to review. I may not have completed it perfectly, as my friend and I did not quite have the patience for that. I got around 70% of the achievements and downed the final boss after over 100 hours of play. I can see it being very possible to do it quicker, but playing it slowly and enjoying it is definitely worthwhile with this game. There are probably better qualified reviewers still, but at least I would make a baseline qualification as an amateur. That aside, this game incorporates some of the greatest ideas in the genre of top-down, party-based RPGs. Here is a list, some of them sound dry and factual, but also contain experience and opinion:
1. It has a free-roaming co-op mode where you can separate and join as you please
2. You can write notes on the maps
3. The log book keeps a good track of the quests, which there are many
4. It has a competent levelling system where you have to make tough choices about how to level your character
5. There are five rarities of random loot to keep the rewards fresh for replays.
6. There is a reason to keep and use scrolls. They get around cooldowns and the spells limited to 1/battle
7. It has great non-combat encounters which involve diplomatic choices and interesting puzzles.
8. It balances between high magic an low magic in the setting by having a lot of magic, but few actual spellcasters
9. It has a good turn-based combat system with a calculation of AP for all actions that is balanced.

Divinity: Original Sin is a roleplaying game developed by Larian Studios. The game was also partially funded through Kickstarter. This enhanced edition of the game was released in October 2015 for PC, PS4 and Xbox One. It came as a free upgrade for everyone that owned the original game which was released in June 2014.
Gameplay in Original Sin follows a very classic RPG style of play. You control two heroes, and you take part in battles which are turn-based combat.  The game play is very tactical, and some fights can last up to about forty five minutes at times. Positioning, making sure you use potions and spells at the optimal moment all play a key role to success in Original Sin. The combat system can be considered to be slow paced, but I personally enjoyed the tactical thought you have to put into every action you take. The game’s tutorial system at the start of the game is done very well, and introduces all elements of gameplay in a satisfying manner.  A lot of the game is based in dialogue as well; I will say this now, if you aren’t one for reading masses amount of text (or listening to), then you will probably want to avoid playing this game, as there is a boat load of text and dialogue to be found here. There are times when you get to make key choices in the dialogue scenes, and also offers branches to find out more information about lore and plot as well.  Overall, the gameplay is really well done, and if you want to find a game that you can absolutely get completely lost in its gameplay, then you should stop here and just pick it up.
Graphically, Original Sin looks gorgeous. The enhanced version of the game improved the graphics quite a bit over the original release, and how managed to reduce the install size. The colourful environments and lush greenery just look amazing. This is one of the best looking games I have played in a very long while. The animations of all characters is done very well too; never did I see any janky looking movements or action, which helped at keeping me fully immersed in the beautiful world.
As with all RPG games, the story is crucial to the reception it gets. Original Sin does not disappoint here either. On top of the games over arching main story line, you also have the chance to branch off into other lesser side plots which can sometimes make you forget all about the rest of the game as they are so in depth. The side quests in this game would probably be main stories in another; that is how good the plot behind Original Sin is. You will of course have to be up for reading the text if you want to get the full effect out of it though.
The majority of Original Sin is voice acted – this helps a lot given the amount of text in the game, but there are parts, which are sometimes quite randomly selected, which aren’t voice acted. This is where you will need the patience to continue reading the dialogue to fully understand what is happening in the world. The sound effects and soundtrack are really good too; nothing seemed out of place so it fits in well with the game.
I found the game to be fairly tricky, I had never played the classic RPG games, I was just too young to understand them, and so I felt as if this game took me on a crash course of learning about them. I have to admit, I did have to use wiki’s and FAQs at times to progress and work out how best to tackle a few bosses; but that should be taken as part and parcel of the gaming experience with something of this size. Researching the best action to take for me makes the game all that more fun.
The world in which this game is set in, feels so alive and active. When you are in towns you can hear plenty of market sellers in the background selling their goods, you can find countless amounts of side quests, and plenty of items to interact with and loot. If you are looking for a game with almost perfect level design, look no further.
In total, this game took me about 54 hours to complete, this was with doing as many side quests as I could find and listening/reading to all the dialogue in the game as well – that is on single player. Where Original Sin gets above other games of its type, is that you can also play the game in co-op mode as well; that alone means you can probably hit the triple figures for the amount of hours on offer in this game.  There is an absurd amount of content to see.
Since this is the enhanced edition of the game, I didn’t find any technical issues. The game runs like a dream on 4k resolutions. Loading times are almost none existent as well. Like I said above, they have somehow managed to get the install size down on the game as well, which is something of a mystery given the amount of improvements they have added/changed. .
To sum up, Divinity: Original Sin is an absolute masterpiece of a game. The gameplay whilst slow paced is so well done, it will keep you interested and wanting more after you first battle. The plot is one of the best I have ever had the pleasure of seeing in any video game, and one that I will remember for a very long time. On top of all this, you the amount of content on offer is amazing. I cannot recommend Divinity Original Sin enough, even if you aren’t a massive fan of the RPG genre, this could be the game that changes that opinion for you.

Currently I am experiencing some kind of crash with the latest update so will enlighten on how I felt about the game last I played it (last review is deleted). For a while I loved DREAM and it still is a great game. Good enough that I still recommend it. The premise is a fantastic and unusual one for a video game: Lucid Dreaming. As a result this opens so many doors to how creative and fun the game can be. For its already existing good points, DREAM is filled with quality. The environments are stunningly detailed and beautiful and even more enjoyable to explore given the non-linear design of the game. Puzzles are varied and at times really challenging to accomplish. As you wander in Howard's dreamland your ears are bombarded with some beautiful and appropriate music. Added together, these things highlight significant promise for the developers' ambition. Overall, I commend them for taking a brave turn in development in this unique setting.
HOWEVER, there are a few negative points that really need addressing:
- I must be honest with the story. It's really not as good as it could have been. Though the premise is fitting enough, as it focuses on a lonely young man whose life seems futile and non-progressive, and depends on the ability to lucid dream in order to find reason to live. And that simplicity is completely OK if it can be executed well. You'd think it could given that it focuses on the psychological/dream world which opens the ability to produce so much depth and surreal interpretation for an otherwise basic plot. Unfortunately it doesn't utilize that potential. I know it's an indie game made by a very small and inexperienced team, but it still would have been nice to have more in the way of mystery and reason that is not all that well-developed. Things might change in the final release once the (various) endings become available but until then, I can't laud the story too much.
- Though it is an early access game, the controls are really terrible. It's easy to get stuck in weird places and it makes some of the already challenging puzzles even harder to accomplish. For the setting of an inner subconscious world I would expect one to feel more "free" in their experience and gameplay. I would have forgiven the clunky feel if the game still took some advantage of "freedom" like adding some flying sections (a large domain of lucid dreaming) instead of constantly walking/running around and doing too many physically basic 'waking life' routines. Additionally, the nightmares are a bit lacking. Though they have good atmosphere and some appropriately bizarre design they just feel more like anxious thoughts than actual *nightmares*. There is no danger to the player and they always take place in the same area which wouldn't be a problem were there more variation in added environmental designs. Given that the nightmares are the major point in the game's storytelling they don't provide nearly as much sense of horror and progression as I would have liked.
I applaud the team for tackling a project like this, particularly as their very first! And the game is still worth buying if you wish to support the game and developers. As excited as I am that there's a game that takes on the subject of lucid dreaming with a very ambitious focus, its current form makes it difficult for me to give a high rating for the time being (higher than 7/10). I'm sure my review will change as the game further improves. In fact, I still encourage you to get it if you are interested as it's full of potential! Just for the time being it hasn't quite reached it yet.

Overall, another fine release from publisher Artifex Mundi.  The game takes about 4 hours to complete, and if you like HOG's, you will like this one.
Pros:
- Custom difficulty allowing you to chose exactly which "helper" features you want.
- Ability to interact with some inventory items.  At times you can take them apart, and at other times you can combine them with other inventory items.  This added some nice additional puzzle solving.
- Moral decisions which change the story (this is a pro and con, see below).
- Nice graphics, animation, and voice acting.
- Crisp, clear HOP's that were not repeated.
- Two different object collections to find throughout the game (mirrors and imp cards).  Thankfully, neither is of the horrid phasing in/out type.  Both collections can be completed fairly easily as long as you bother to look for them in each scene.
Cons:
- There is an achievement to play through again, making different moral choices.  I did this and got no credit for this achievement.  This leaves me with one annoying uncompleted achievement. :(
- While it is nice that you can make decisions that effect the outcome, the ending video is exactly the same for all endings, and actually inconsistent with some of your choices.
- The map has one general square for each area consisting of 2 or 3 rooms.  Thus when it shows you an action is available there, you are never sure which room.
- The mini games are mostly the same puzzles re-skinned from other Artifex Mundi games.

You don't really play it as such, more like you move around to progress a story told through sparse fragments of interspersed scenes which suggest much but which never really outright state anything. Instead, it's largely left to the player to give context and meaning to everything, and therein lies its greatest strength and its greatest weakness. Some will breeze through the very brief experience with little thought, others might enjoy reading the world as they play through. A great curiosity without a massive amount of substance, I wouldn't necessarily recommend it outright as a must see, as even with the included, equally short prequel, Gravity Bone, there still isn't much here you couldn't really live without. But I certainly wouldn't discourage anyone from checking it out if the price was low enough to justify your intrigue.

You also have the interesting addition of Lady Katrina, a ghostly figure who follows you around and has her own seperate skill tree to assist you during gameplay. With this release of the Final Cut they have combined the 3 previous games into one mega game with the choice of six different character classes (Protector, Bounty Hunter, Elementalist, Umbralist, Philogistoneer, Constructor) that all play differently.
The game is a blast to play but unfortunately for those of you looking to play multiplayer the netcode really lets it down and every single game you play will result in a desync no matter how good your connection is, even if you are playing on the same LAN together. This makes the game impossible to finish in co-op without having to constantly leave and remake the game which causes the quests to quickly become tiresome chores.
Another thing to note is that you can only ALT+TAB from the game twice per session or it will crash when trying to bring the game back up, even if you are still on the main menu and not actually loaded into the game. I still recommend the game as it's fun but it's definitely not without its technical faults.

Codename CURE is a well made free to play zombie first-person shooter, the most common game mode is Plant The Bomb (and get away before it blows up), it has various unique maps, such as the Bunker, Office, Trainstation etc, and characters such as Pointman, Assault, Technician, Support and Sniper.
In order to complete every mission, teamwork is crucial, no one can just go Rambo and complete the mission right off the bat. There are 3 varieties of zombies so far, the most common ones are the limping zomies, the others being the agile but weak running zombies, and the 'bullet-sponge' but very slow, soldier zombies.
Each member of the team has something to contribute, Pointman being the spearhead, Assault being the main powerhouse, Technicians provide supporting fire with deployable sentry gun, Supports provide health, armour and ammunition (the supply box is also a great zombie-proof barricade), and Snipers take out Soldier zombies before they even reach your team.
In a nutshell, Codename CURE relies heavily on teamwork for the success in every mission. You can rely on your team to keep you safe, make sure they can rely on you as well. Do your part of the job, no man left behind, that is how Codename CURE should be played. Also, did I mention it is completely free?

The plot is good. The execution could be a lot better.
For anyone who is interested in Major\Minor, I urge you to be very careful about what you prioritize in a novel. If you value an interesting plot above all else and can look past flaws in storytelling, this game may be for you. If constant small nuisances get in the way of enjoying a story, please look elsewhere. We'll start off with the pros. It may be a bit shorter, but don't let that deter you.
The plot is teeming with potential no matter how you look at it. It is very widely twisting, intriguing, and manages to interleave characters together in a very nice manner where each character is impacted by others and impacts others meaningfully. There are very very few characters that stand out which don't add value to the plot, and the way it weaves feels very much like a TV drama. The method of which this was written can be seen -and I won't lie - care went into how the plot folds out. It's a 12 hour long story, but because of that, feels more like a short TV series. Characters are also pleasanlty rendered which, while is cliche in furry artwork, is never jarring to the presentation. It has this sort of feeling about it where you can tell the creators of this piece really wnated this to be big and amazing. And with all due respect, it's got charm.
That's not to say it's flawless. Sadly, there are many small flaws which add up en masse. I'll list them off first and explain the main problem with most of these flaws.
1: Self inserting author
2: Fursonas shoehorned as characters in the plot
3: Typos
4: Poor editing
5: Mild Fanservice
6: Misleading advertising
7: Lack of pause/menu/options
8: Cliche character profiles (Nerd. hothead, workaholic, etc)
9: Overuse of certain plot devices
10: Lack of variance in character emoted drawings. (most characters have only a single drawing)
While some are worse than others, it is not up to me to make that decision. What I can safely tell you is these hold 2 common problems. They break your immersion a leave a bad taste in your mouth.
Immersion breaking is very serious with this novel. Many writing choices feel out of place and will cause you to take notice of them. For example, a few chapters in, you'll be able to give pronoun preference. Even then, characters will once in a while refer to you as "they". This will immediately bring you out of the story and impair the experience. Problems like these are fine in small doses, but when they add up, it becomes a chore to keep yourself immersed. This is why I say the plot is good, but the story is bad. Too many instances while playing, would I be alerted to a poor design decision or unusual writing that I'd have to put it down for a bit. That is the true problem with this novel. It lacks the polish it needs to take it from being 80% done to a finished experience.
To those who read this, I hope you understand that this isn't a bad novel — it's got quite an interesting plot, in fact. It's just that it has a lot to go before being a complete, immersing story. So I say again. If you can look past the flaws for the equivalent of a bingewatch of a TV series, go for it. But just know it's not going to be what you fully expected. Enjoy.

Very much on the fence on this one, but I'm going to have to come down on the side of not recommending this game.
Bit Trip Runner is a scrolling rythm based platformer. The screen constantly scrolls to the right and as you run you have to jump, slide, kick and block your way through the level. It starts off great. Good music, tight controls, and bright colorful graphics put together an awesome presentation. As you pick up gold and "power ups" the music fills in and the your actions in the level fill in the background to the music. It's a cool effect.
That for me was where the good times ended.
Near the end of the first world, the game becomes brutally hard. There are no checkpoints in Bit.Trip Runner. One mistake will send you flying all the way back to the beginning of the level. You have no health so it's one hit and you die. With some levels over 3-4 min long, the constant act of being sent back to the start every time is annoying and gives you little chance to work on the one tough spot you're having a problem with.
And those tough spots? This game leaves very little to no room for error. You have to be precise. At least with games like Super Meat Boy, the level is very short. It lends itself well to quick deaths and restarts because you're working on the same area and you can go at your own pace. That's not the case here.
I finally did beat this game, but my feeling was more relief than triumph. If you're hardcore into platformers you may enjoy it, but there are better titles out there.

In this day of DLC-happy games, (unfinished in my eyes),  it's refreshing to see a game so complete, the details so well thoughtout.  This game is made and executed the way games like the Baldur's Gate series and the Elder Scrolls series are with an open world, a solid storyline and plenty of side quests to complete along the way.  I'm playing the single-player game in Adventuring mode which is the easiest one.  Some pluses I especially like:
1.  My two main characters affect each other through the choices they make which add or subtract to their abilities and to those of the rest of their team.
2.  Rift travel.   These are portals that are activated when approached.  Once activated you can step into any portal and travel to any other you've activated.  (There are more features but it would borderline on a spoiler to talk about it.)
3.  Teleportation:  You acquire 2 teleporter pyramids through a quest.  They are linked to each other.  You drop one somewhere you would like to return to, go on about your business, click on the pyramid in your pack and your team is transported back to the one you dropped.
4.  Lots and lots, and lots, and lots, and lots of armor, weapons and items to choose from.
5.  A great crafting/recipe system that allows you to make useful things without the grinding!  You discover the Recipes by placing items in the slots on your Experiment page or acquire a recipe book that teaches it to you when you read the book. (The crafting system includes cooking, blacksmithing, potion-making, tailoring and spell-making and others, all on one character).
6.  Dynamic and well-thoughtout dialogue.  (example:  My main character had purchased very expensive armor for her fighter.  After he put it on he commented how expensive it was and thanked her for it.)  It's little details like that that let you know how much the developers loved what they were making.
7.  You are not tied to the skill-set you chose for your character at character creation.  (example: My Wayfarer has her archery skills but now also has the ability to use wands and staves, as well as decent rogue skills.)
8.  Lots of companions to chose from to complete your 4-person team anyway you like, (single-player).  Some you can "rent", (one-time fee), others you meet along the way and invite them to join.  You can tell a team member to take a hike so you can switch him out for someone else and then put him back on the team when you need him again.  He is sent to a warm and fuzzy "rest area" with the other "Island of Misfit Toys" you've temporarily retired. You can adventure alone or with 2, 3 or 4 companions.
9. Using tools for crafting, mining, repairing, cooking and others weigh very little and, no matter how big, take up only one block each in your inventory. As well, all other items, armor and weapons take up only one block. A backpack is included in your inventory to give you even more space.
10.  Inventor:  It's easy to switch between characters.
11.  For all new players there is a cave/dungeon you are given a choice to enter to before you reach the first town.  It's a very clever and useful way to introduce you to the dynamics of the game and some of the trickier traps you will come across later on. Obvious things like water-beats-fire but it shows you a possible way to do it you may not have thought of, (Like one area where I was instructed to drag a candle over to a pool of oil under some skels to set the oil and the skels on fire). In other words...use your environment, look around you, there are different ways to accomplish the same task.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a great game with a few faults:
What I loved,
-The Art
It's almost impossible not the be in love with the art. Every single visual aspect is so amazingly crafted and represented, it's quite surprisingly how much effort was put into it.
-The platforming/controls
I didn't expect this would have such a heavy focus on platforming and precision. Many times the game requires you to pull off a lot precise jumps, with tight timing. It's very rarely frustrating. In a lot of ways it reminded me of Super Meat Boy in that regard.
What I liked,
-Metroidvania
It's not the most complex of it's kind, but I enjoyed the fact that a lot of the early upgrades are not accessible by your current abilities. I didn't feel like the game was holding my hand too much and there were plenty of reasonably hidden upgrades. I'm a sucker for this kind of game so it's easy to please. I would have liked if the game went a little more down this path
-Closed off platforming 'dungeons'
A few times in the game it sends you to a standalone area that is essentially a dungeon with specific platforming mechanics. These are where the level design tend to shine. During these sections the game is not limited to being interconnected as much and can simply be a platformer. These are usually where the game introduces the most difficult platfomring requirements.
What I didn't like as much,
-The platforming 'dungeons' are literally closed off permanently
When you complete these sections of the game, you can't go back. If you miss any collectibles or upgrades, they are gone forever. That's lame. In a Metroidvania, the one thing you should never do is restrict my access to the gameworld. Especially if it's going to prevent me from getting 100%
-Lengthy chase sequences that require perfection with no checkpoints
Maybe I should just "get good"? Later in the game there are some segments where you are being chased and are on a timer and have to complete sequences of platforming near perfectly. If you mess up you are instantly reverted back to the beginning. I admit they can be prett exhilerating but it's very easy to mess up and have to redo it over and over and over. And then it becomes frustrating. The final one of these were the worst offender in my opinion.
So looking it over, Ori and the Blind Forest has some faults but overall it's still a really awesome game. I'd recommend it to anyone who wants something super pretty but also is looking for something with a chellenge.

First of all, there is no inbetween with this game, you either hate it or love it. So before you spend that precious $1.24, let's evaluate if you will or will not love it:
1. Do you like point and click games?
2. Do you like heavily plot based games?
3. Are you into cinematography, graphic arts, and/or innovative story telling?
4. Do you value the EXPERIENCE of a game over what you can actually DO in a game?
If you answered "yes" to all 4, this is definitely the game for you. This kind of game is so different and wonderfully pieced together. I cannot believe how many emotions this game made me feel in under 10 minutes. It was heart-pounding and heart-felt. DO realize though that it's more of a visual novel and therefore your actions are chosen for you, you just are simply there to enjoy the ride. Which is exactly what I did, I enjoyed the ride.
AS A BONUS: you also get their first game Gravity Bone (can't find it? hit esc and click careers) which unlike this sequal allows the player to move and figure out what they have to do, which is much more interactive but still as fun as Thirty Flights of Loving.

Thirty Flights of Loving had a lot of hype surrounding it when it came out. It's non-linear, non-traditional, and very stylized -- what it does it does okay. It's interesting, but for me it was ultimately an unfulfilling experience. I didn't feel for the characters like the reviews said I was supposed to, and I didn't have any investment in the story or where it went. I appreciated the attempt to do something different, but I felt that it was all just too disjointed and unresolved. I played through a second time with the developer commentary enabled, and there was a lot of pretentious talk about the ambiguity of the storyline and characterization; I felt that it was all a failed attempt at justifying decisions that made little sense to me. There are weaknesses in the story, design and gameplay, and the developers are well aware of them. All told, however, I didn't hate it. What saved it for me was the inclusion of Gravity Bone in the copy I did purchase. It was longer, included puzzle elements, and offered the player more time as the character. I think this last point alone made me enjoy it more than Thirty Flights -- if only I had five more minutes to explore the heist and the relationship to the supporting characters, I might have enjoyed it more.

NOTE:  This review was given during the Early-Access phase.
So before I write this review, I want to say that I'll be listing all of the pluses and minuses of the game below, but unfortunately a very prosaic and annoying issue is causing me to give this game a negative review and give a "buyer beware" review.  Hopefully in the near future, the issue will be sorted and I'll be able to play the game.  In a nutshell, this game has a game-ending bug that the devs have known about for (at least) a year and a half, and there's an entire Steam forum thread dedicated to it.  And given that they're going to be giving out release copies for review in roughly three months, I'm slightly concerned for them.  It seems like it's going to go very, very badly for this game if they hand out review copies of this game to major reviewers and the only thing that they can say is "Yeah, I played it for 5 hours, it seemed cool, but then the game glitched out and I couldn't play anymore."  In spite of my current experience, I really hope these issues get resolved and that the game is successful.  It's the first game I ever paid any attention to on Steam Greenlight, and it's one of the few that I voted for to be Greenlit.
The game-ending bug:  So there's a part of the game (the Terrace Walkway sub-dream) where you need to turn pillars to solve a puzzle, and the glitch is that the pillars don't turn, they just wiggle back and forth and prevent you from solving the puzzle (and thus unlocking the rest of the game).  So... yeah.  This basically forces my hand, and I have to not recommend this game until this issue is sorted.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
A Review of the Game (the portion of the first world that I can actually get through)
So Dream is a game coming from a group of unseasoned but clearly very talented game developers.  The style of the game itself is not entirely unique (it's in this new genre of games like Lifeless Planet and Dear Esther, which I guess you'd call atmospheric explorer games), but the execution and game itself are quite original and the execution is, in spite of a few issues, quite brilliant.  I think a lot of people are going to rag on this game essentially because they don't like atmospheric exploring games, but I think that they should be ignored.  The game itself is extremely fun.  So I look forward to being able to play the game in May.
By the way, people have also been complaining about the puzzles.  I thought the puzzle of the head stones was really very clever, and it required probably two hours straight of messing around with it and a lot of logical thinking, which I thought was very fun.
Warning: SPOILERS.  I will say a few things, however, that probably should be changed (and quite possibly are, this is an early-access copy after all).
-- Although this game derives a lot of its uniqueness from sort of dropping you into a world and letting you slowly discover what the heck it is that you're supposed to be doing, there might be a little more of an idea of what's going on.  After spending an hour or two walking around aimlessly, the game starts to get boring, no matter how pretty the scenery is (but see my next point).  So would try to either make things a little bit more straightforward/logical or find some way to boost the player with at least a little bit of guidance.  I kind of feel like the beginning of the game needs to have a little bit more of a tutorial on what the game is about and some mindfulness of the fact that if they players get stuck in these large worlds, they're going to be bored.
-- The game is supposed to be a big, beautiful open world, but your first level feels constricting and often claustrophobic, particularly the mazes.  Also, as near as I could tell, the mazes serve no function, yet there are many of them, and they aren't really fun and it's not conveyed in any way to the player that they don't need to waste two hours bumbling aimlessly in the scenic equivalent of a straightjacket.  If I have to bumble around aimlessly, I'd prefer that I was doing it in a big, open world where I get to freely explore.  (The Terrace Walkway, by contrast, had none of these issues.)
-- You guys need to work out how to get the clicking of collectable objects more... functional.  I walked by the grass cutter to pick up the strange stone multiple times, and tried to press it multiple times to no avail.  You have to stand in the EXACT right spot the EXACT right distance, otherwise you'll never see that you can pick up the stone, even if you notice it might be something you can snag and actively try to snag it.
-- The sun is WAY TOO BRIGHT.  Holy crap!  You guys need to turn that down a bit, you might blind someone. It also makes reading signs really hard, and it distracts from your wonderful landscape in certain cases.
Again, I really hope I'll be able to play through this game in the future and give it a much more robust, positive review.  From an alpha stage, so far so good, but you guys are publishing this soon, so hop to it!  We want to see your game!

Bottom line: a hit point system must be introduced before this game will be anything other than gambling at a computer desk for nothing, except maybe players can pretend to be wearing wizard hats. The current "one hit point and done" state for all players and creatures takes away any scaling strength or defense and reduces the battles to hit %'s. In other words, the game is more often than not is not less about strategy and more about chance.
There's nothing less satisfying than winning or losing strategic games largely by chance. In the case of Chaos reborn, it could not be made more clear that chance is overwhelmingly more important a factor than strategy. This game is a 'One hit or nothing" style, where players and creatures alike have but 1 hit point, and hit chance is clearly displayed when making any move. This places the player who takes the first turn at an unreasonable advantage, allowing them to move toward objectives or higher ground before the opponent can react, as well as cast creatures which then may get the first attack. If a player manages to successfully cast a powerful creature early (you guessed it, spell casting it chance based), or even a ranged creature placed at highest ground on turn 1, the game is often already over. On the other side of the coin,  there will be many situations where one player has an overwhelming advantage, either through attrition or unbalanced luck of chance, and will be standing right next to the opponent with multiple powerful creatures, attacking with 50-70% hit chances, to have all of them miss, followed by all of the opponent's lower-chance spells and attacks hitting successively the next turn to flip the game upside down, all with no apparent strategy involved.

My original assessment of the game was that  it was far too arbitrary for the strategy element of the game to be enjoyable. However, credit to Mr Gollop et al, the development team have created an alternative play-model that removes a lot of the wild random swings from matches, and so I have spent the day reacquainting myself the game and thoroughly enjoyed it. As someone who's been a fan of Julian's games for nearly  four decades, I'm very happy to switch my 'thumbs down' to a 'thumbs up'. I think it also bodes well for the ongoing support of the game that the development team are obviously still very reactive.
I have included my previous grumblings from my original review below, but would just like to reiterate that they now longer stand as the developers have since put in a lot of time and work listening to their community.
"Very, very, very disappointed with this. Far too arbitrary and reliant on chance. It seems to have missed the great advances that board games and strategy computer games have made since the original days of Rebelstar Raiders & Laser Squad.  At its core, it's deeply unsatisfying to play; short games that rely heavily on wildly swinging variables. Everything I loved about Julian Gollop's previous work seems to have gone right out the window for this. There have been so many creative moves away from running games off badly-balanced dice mechanics (or their computer equivalent), I'm totally bemused at this massive step backwards."

It's entirely possible that I'm just not the target audience for this game, so please before taking my word for it, read some of the more positive reviews for it and see if they sound more in line with your expectations.
Personally, I couldn't get into it. I really wanted to because the concept seemed really interesting and the screenshots were absolutely gorgeous, but there doesn't appear to be any gameplay - or at least, I couldn't find any. The game offers no concrete direction about where to go, what to do, or what's important. You are given a character you know next to nothing about and a dreamworld for him to explore. After a couple directionless hours, I managed to find and solve one puzzle, go to a second...place that didn't appear to have anything to do, and grab a few collectibles which could just as easily be critical to the story and its progression as it is to be just collectibles.
I can get passed the lack of polish and the graphical glitches that make it run sluggish and jittery even on hardware above it's recommended specs, but I don't have the time or the patience to figure out what makes this game worth playing and what I'm supposed to do in it. I understand that the game is supposed to have a lot of exploration and discovery to it, and it does. The problem is that without a stated goal, exploration quickly turns into simply being lost.
Honestly a solid tutorial would go a long way to giving direction to the experience, but I imagine that if one was planned, it would have been implemented by now. If you like walking around aimlessly looking at beautiful scenery, this game has something to offer you. If you're looking for anything else, unfortunately, I think you should pass on Dream.

Farnham Fables Tape 1 is a really short story about a girl visiting the palace where she meets the king who tells her a story. It's a mix of a visual novel and a point-and-click.
The 'main part' of the game is a tiny point-and-click scene which uncovers the story the king is telling. The pnc user interferance is pretty crowded and complicated (several options to use on each item; correct order to click on things), but the written out functions make it simple to use. If you have played old school text command adventures, you'll feel right at home.
While the game is extremely short -- especially if you are really familiar with pncs -- it does come with plenty of character and small things to discover. Some of them will make you chuckle (just try combining stupid actions and things together), but this is not really a comedy. The writing is nice and there has certainly been effort put into making characters unique. My favourite was the doctor. ;)
Overall, the game has a strange feel of a bedtime story gone on a Saturday afternoon acid trip with friends. I'm not sure if I would recommend this for kids, but neither does it feel 'advanced' enough for adults. I'm still recommending it based on a positive feeling it left me with despite me being extremely prejudiced against furries and animorphic characters. Play if you got this in a bundle. Very short.

If you also start liking the characters like I did, the choices you make become progressivly harder to make. I will not say any spoilers as this novel is too good to be spoiled. Contrary to what it looks like you do actually get to customize your character after abit so don't let the lack of any options on your character off the start deter you. With multiple endings I strongly recommend you make multiple saves before each choice unless you want to experience the whole story per read changing things here and there. All in all I strongly recommend this visual novel even to non-furries for the story and soundtrack alone.

I love the game for the atmosphere that it gives me and the story it presents me with. The hub, which you'll see in the beginning, filled with white cubes, is absolutely astounding. Its a stupendous RPG that is literally everything I love about the genre! Gorgeous art and scenery, intricate story with frequent breaks for goofy jokes, and a soundtrack that I wish was playing all the time in real life!
Don't forget the combat! A deep, turn based combat system that frequently gets chaotic and kills all my characters because I made the slightest of errors! Most of the time I'm grinning like an idiot as I load my save game.
It has an environmental hazard system that makes perfect sense, for a fantasy world. Fire makes you burn for some damage every turn, but water spells put out the fire and make the floor wet and electric spells become area of effect in wet areas, but freeze spells make the floor slippery and everybody moving on ice can fall and lose a turn! There's also poison and oil, and most of them interact for mayhem!
Yeah, I'm having fun!
Fav part is the elemental combos.

Divinity the enhanced version is a solid turn based RPG.  Basing my viewpoint in contrast to past experiences with Baldur's Gate, Ice wind Vale, Neverwinter etc
The enhanced version is vastly superior to the original game in both function and stability
As a turn based RPG:
- innovative and immersive environmental impact of spells
- some measure of chess like turn based decision making
- compelling story, early game being stronger than end game
- some very interesting skill/class combinations, especially when combined with ennvironmental interaction possibilities
- overly easy to exploit, I'll not outline them here but self restraint once you figure them out is essential to enjoyment
- inventory management is horrid
- crafting system is fun yet horrid in design.  It actually became less usable with the enhanced edition
- graphics are pleasant but not ground breaking
- voice acting:  I turned off the sound, that pretty much covers it
This game was crowd funded at its start, the enhanced version refined many of those rough edges but beware you will still nick your self on the occasional bur.
If you are looking for a fun turn based RPG its definately one of the better ones of the last 10 years.

I've had this game sitting on my pc for ages now, (since the Blendo Games Humble Weekly Sale) not having the time to really go through any of my backlog of games. I really enjoyed both Thirty Flights of Loving and Gravity Bone!
Most people rate games according to stringent rule sets, going through a bullet point list of expected content or features, which in my opinion is wrong! Games always have a focus - sometimes that focus is a balance between gameplay and story, sometimes between systems and level design. Thirty Flights and Gravity Bone lay their focus upon the narrative, its delivery and the world they are set in. Both games are very characterful in every way. The narrative, visuals and music of both games are extremely charming, and in some ways reminded me somewhat of Tarantino flicks. Both games are short (though longer than 5 minutes as some have stated), but this is as a result of the focus on narrative, and trying to put the player in the right mood, at the right time, and telling the story in a way that makes sense (with a bit of fun along the way).
I went through both games, and the commentary version of Thirty Flights, and spent just under an hour.
I was recommended this game by a friend, and will definitely do similarly!

Two-dimensional indie platformer game which is weird but fun at the same time. A Review by
While the protagonist is asleep in the land of happy cows, a dark creature appears, thinks of an evil plan, and points its laser eyes at the cows in order to make them fly to space. Once the protagonist wakes up, all cows are gone.
He then starts his journey to free the kidnapped cows. The goal is to walk, jump around and collect a few hovering circles, in each level. Sometimes you will need to enter teleporters, which will lead you to a parallel dimension and backwards, to collect all of the availible rings.
Making a game with hectic gameplay be level-based, was a good decision, as finishing a level provides the good and regular oportunity to relax and take a break.
Both arrow keys and W/A/S/D can be utilized by default to play the game, but it also teaches that in tutorial levels with nonverbal instructions. They are changeable though, if desired. Another smart idea, since sign language makes a game playable for everyone that makes it through the main menu.
Yet Another World launches in windowed mode, but this can be switched in the settings to fullscreen, to use the full potential of a PC screen.
It comes with slow exotic background music, which is "enhanced" by farts whenever you press the jump key...but this does surprisingly not alter the reassuring effect of the music.
If you are looking for an agility game, which does a good job as casual timekiller, Yet Another World may be the right one for you. Since the game was made by an independent developer, the unusual price of $3.99 is acceptable, as it is justified by the high quality of this title.
One of the best 2D game, inside steam store, i recommend this game, if you want a 2D simple game.
