While it may look like a game that blends casual gaming with hard core, it is definitely anything but, this is due to some ridiculous thoughtless implements by the developer which make this game very quickly a chore, having to repeat the same parts of the level over and over again.
The game was developed by a single Russian developer which can be found here (
) The story is something that could have been drummed up in a kindergarten. An Alien has taken your assortment of colourful cows while you were sleeping, your job is to now get them back. The art style which is basically just squares placed at different angles, clouds, trees etc. I guess by everything made up of squares shows that everything in this world has a basic outline/concept to it. Delinquently basic, this is also demonstrated by your only super power to get the cows back is to fart. Yes by farting you can retract spikes, make boulders fall early which would have normally have crushed you etc.
Granted there is a single soundtrack which is relaxing, but soon this begins to play out like a soundtrack you get exposed to when you phone up a customer complaint line and get placed on hold. It soon becomes irritating as well. Everything in this game becomes irritating, like a cactus in your shoe. What is a cactus doing in your shoe? Is a strange question, just like it is when you’re forced to ask yourself 'Why am I playing this game which is causing me severe pain!! ?’
What makes this game such a shoddy form of entertainment? For one thing the learning curve goes from one extreme to the other. The first 5 levels consist of you finding 3 'o' rings these will open up the exit gate for you. After level 5 you’re given the option to simply find 3 or 10 'O' rings depending if you are a completion freak. You can also find one 'secret' per level after level 5 too. With 120 levels on offer here you would think that the game would have a gradual level of difficulty. Nope it goes from level 6 onwards into a Normandy beach massacre of having to try and retry. Evidently this game is not suitable for casual gamers which not only would make up a large percentage of the gaming industry, but also would be the ones most attracted to the art style and level design concept.
You see the platform your standing on becomes 'yet another world' as soon as you enter a portal and what was once the outside world becomes the platform. It's hard to describe but it does make the game interesting at first. Why does it not keep the game interesting? Because those portals soon become a hindrance. Every time you die, the portals spawn back even if you accomplish everything within that portal and now they get in your way from reaching where you want to go. This means you have to play the same parts of the level over and over again regardless to the fact you have already completed it. Also every time you die you drop a ring. This means more often than not that the ring gets dropped at a death trap where you have to try and pick it up again. Or that the ring dropped in an unreachable area like underneath the platform which causes you the need to restart. While it may not be so bad at first, it does become seriously tedious in later levels where you’re required to journey the length of the map to get to an exit portal. Hard core gamers will soon tire of this troll of a game. Yes you heard me right, this game serves for no other purpose than to be a troll. With no mid-way save points, with completed portals constantly reappearing and with rings being dropped constantly at inappropriate places. Any short amount of fun you get will be whisked away from careless design.
I honestly cannot recommend this to Casual gamers, and as for hard core gamers there are better products out there such as 1001 spikes, Airscape and Supermeatboy. These are examples of games that both cater for the Casual as well as the Hard core. A game by energy milk I seriously wanted to enjoy, but in the end the product completely tasted spoilt.

I really wish there was a middle ground recommendation button... But before you become too  judgemental about my negetive recommendation, I suggest you read it first. After my game lagged to  the point of crashing to desktop, I felt it was finally time I gave my word on this game.
Warhammer 40,000 Space Marine is a fun little hack n' slash style action game game which throws you  into the grim-dark world of Warhammer where you play as Captain Titus of the Ultramarines. The story  is about as good as you can expect for a Warhammer game with pretty decent gameplay for it being a  transition from Relic's normally RTS style play to a third-person shooter.
The campaign isn't terribly long but not terribly short either, with unlocks for the Captain as you  go. While it could have been done better, I suppose I can't complain about what we got. After your  7-8 (at most) hour story is over, you'll pretty much be done with the game which leaves you with  either completeing the game again on a higher difficulty if you haven't already. Or playing one of  the two multiplayer modes available to you. With a good to mediocre suggestion for the story thus  far, I'm sure you can see where this is going...
The EXTERMINATUS mode allows you and three other space marines to band together and fight the green  skin menace in a co-op mode where you'll be flung into an arena where you must fight through five  ways and continue to the next zone, confronting more and more difficult enemies as you go. I highly  recommend playing this with friends, as the public matches are completely random with who you get  paired with, often matching you with new or inept players or outright ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. You'll usually know  what you're in for when people refuse to help you, shoot at you whenever there's a lull in the  fighting, or swipe ammo from out beneath your feet. Which leads me to the next portion.
Multiplayer. Multiplayer can be fun. It can be frustrating. Too often it's frustrating. The  aforementioned people can be found most commonly here. I've yet to play a multiplayer game with a  'good' community, so I can't really hold this against Space Marine alone. Expect lots of weapon/perk  abuse with cookie-cutter loadouts and over-powered weapons with little hint to any actual game  balance to be found. Assault marines will darken the skies and tacticals will roll about the  landscapes, burning away everything with the one-hit wonder meltagun. Unless you plan on fighting  fire with fire, I suggest avoiding multiplayer. Feeling more reminiscent of Call of Duty, this  gamemode feels very 'tacked on at the last minute' than anything else in the game and offers little to  nothing new to the rest of the game apart from the ridiculous armory challenges which grant you perk  and armor unlocks for customizing your multiplayer character but unless you plan on grinding for a  very long time, they aren't something you can achieve in the short-term.
Latency... I've played good games. I've played bad games. I've played games with amazing  connections, and I've played games with bad connections. And then... I've played Space Marine...  Never in my life have I played a game with such pathetic connection ability, with frequent lag and  constant 'host migrations' (Which if you plan on playing multiplayer, be prepared to view this  screen:
A. Lot.) the lack of  dedicated servers and actual lobby browsing leaving you to the mercy of the the dice roll on whether  or not you get a good server from the two or three that ever seem available grows very tiresome very  quickly. This is the number one thing that suggests to me that multiplayer was just an afterthought  once the game was made.
Overall, I would indeed Recommend Space Marine to my friends who were interested or to any  Warhammer fan, if not for the story mode alone and possible co-op. Even non-fans looking for a fun  hack n' slash could possibly enjoy it. Though I leave with an actual POSITIVE recommendation, I  won't for the $30.00 dollar price tag this game sports. While fun, the shoddy multyplayer and lack  of being able to unlock things through exterminatus mode leaving you with a short, and underwhelming  campaign and ending leaves me wondering why this game is still so pricey. If you must buy it. Please  wait for a sale. $10-$15 dollars at most.
TL;DR: 6/10 - There's better, cheaper games out there, should prolly go play them insted.

Out of Reach is by far the best survival game i've played. I have almost 700 hours in game and have played the game for about 9 months. It is pirate themed game where you have been shipwrecked on tropical islands. Just like most survival games you have to gather food and resources to keep you alive and build up a base. Depending on the type of server you play your experiance will change.
PvE:
~ No PvP
~ Harder to find areas to build as there is no raiding
~ Good way to learn the game before starting PvP
~ Some players like to roleplay and trade
~ Players are more friendly
Standard:
~ PvP enabled
~ Raiding enabled
~ Hardest gather speed
~ Resources are more valuable
~ Base protection (depending on the resources invested) between 3 hours - 3 days
~ Slower paced in terms of development
~ More spaces to build
- Players will either attack you or help you
(My opinion the best type of server to play as I find it the most fun)
PvP:
~ PvP enabled
~ Raiding enabled
~ Easiest gather speed (up to x5)
~ Resources are less valuable
~ Base protection (depending on the resources invested) between 1 minute - 15 minutes
~ Faster paced
~ Usually very built up
~ You're most likely going to die alot if you havn't played the game before
This game is very unique to other games such as Rust and Ark. Yes it isn't as developed as these games or as popular but personally I have played Rust and would recommend this game over it. Rust doesn't give me the rush I have when playing this game. PvP in this game is a little glitchy and can have some improvements in terms of smoothness however it gets me really hyped and me and my group really enjoy PvP in this game. Whereas compared to Rust you could walk around and get one shotted from 100m away and not know where he was or have any way to fight back. However in this game you have to choose carefully what armour you choose and sometimes combine the different tiers of armour to fit your purpose. In this game you can be a slow tank walking around in metal armour or a fast archer running in leather armour.
Resource gathering is very painful, just like any survival game, the grind is hard but it adds more value to it. This game requires lots of hard decision making on 'Shall I bring this armour out?' 'Do I want to carry this must resources with me at once or shall I take multiple trips?' However with the animations when farming it can be very fun. Such as falling trees when they run out of use instead of vanishing like Rust. Or possibly the breaking  up of stones when rocks are no longer filled with stones to give you.
Crafting in this game is very unique. You require different tools and crafting areas to make tools. But what makes this game even more interesting is the fact you have to load an anvil with a casted part from your furnace and physically hit it with a hammer until it is shaped. Something I havn't seen any other game do.
And my favourite part, raiding. I have never felt so satisfied raiding in any survival game other than this game. There is a range of ways to infiltrate a base: trebuchet, glider, seige projectiles. Sometimes you have to use all of them to bring down a base. They all have their strengths and weaknesses and makes the game great!
One of the cons of the game is map size. The map can't really fit 30 or more players in it. There aren't many spawn points so you find new spawns running into eachother, one getting killed and then refunding the game. Although there are plans for new islands and improving spawn locations.
This game is heavily worked on and the devs are very open to the community on suggestions and advise. I have seen features I have requested implemented in this game and bugs I have reported fixed within a patch.
Lastly there is only one issue I have with this game, population, many people buy the game on sale and refund it without giving it a chance. Most just say 'rust is better' and leave within 5 minutes of joining. Or people get so mad that they lose a base and quit the game completely. I have seen this alot and it is sad to see as this is such a good game. Most just need to get over it and start again and improve what got them killed last time. That is the best attitude to have.
Honestly you should stop reading reviews and give the game a go, you will not be disappointed.
If you have any questions about the game add me on steam or would like some help starting out do the same.

My "short version" review:
As one of the first wave through the Closed Testing doors, I can say that if the pace is kept up for bug-hunting and content addition (which historically has been the case with ABT), their 6-12 month EA estimate may be longer than it actually takes to get out of EA.
Stability is terrific as I've seen myself and others without any trouble.
However, I do see some reviews here with crashes happening; With a wider testing audience now that all Repop owners have their keys, and others coming in this may be expected. Early Access (at the time of this review) is not yet a week old. My hope is that the users experiencing issues post in the forum instead of (or in addition to) "GG Uninstall" reviews.
As far as content goes, more is being added in terms of Art, mechanics, and new features.
There will be modding possibilities and other user-centric items / features beyond the already-planned updates. Check out the official forums for more information or to voice your input.
Some reviews I've seen refer to this as the game they were backing and ABT is making a cash grab. To this: Fragmented is not the game you were backing; That's true. Fragmented is a separate project that former Repopulation backers coincidentally get for free while The Repopulation is being made. It's a survival-type game with a Repopulation theme (simpler crafting, not as deep as Repop will be, etc.).
The Repopulation will still be a MMO; It will be its own game. It just needed to get off the Hero Engine which had issues unrelated to ABT. Development was stopped once ABT saw issues coming up with HE's development.
If ABT was trying to make a cash grab, they would not give backers copies of this game and would not continue developing The Repopulation. I haven't seen any indication that they've gone back on their word on anything they've promised so far.

While still rough around the edges, it is in early early access, I enjoy Fragmented a lot.  The devs are the best I have seen in any game I have played.  They listen to suggestions and are always working hard to get the next patch out as quick as possible.

Playing this game feels very basic. There's a decent variety of enemies and items and content, but there aren't enough meaningful decisions for you to make along the way during a given run.
Meta-game advancement requires the same currency (gold) that you would use to buy items during a run, so you're strongly incentivized against buying items during a run unless they're either extremely cheap or desperately needed, which only exacerbates the extent to which RNG controls whether you receive the tools you need to succeed. Furthermore, that meta-game advancement is quite grindy; some incremental upgrades take as much gold as you would accumulate during a whole good run, so it will take many hours before you feel free to spend gold on things that would help you during a run.
Randomness has always been a central piece of the roguelike genre, but good roguelikes balance it by giving players the ability to anticipate and adapt to the otherwise-unwinnable challenges they will face. This game has too much random determination without enough opportunity for the player to mitigate it.
There is almost an okay game here, but it's crippled by a few unsatisfying design decisions.

Dream is what happens when you have a designer creating a game who understands nothing of the topic they are trying to build an experience within and even less understanding of how to make a game which provokes any kind of enjoyment or emotion from the player. It is clearly aiming to be some kind of exploration into the psyche of the main character, called Howard, by trying to be something thought-provoking and intellectual. But it fails miserably to accomplish even that one simple task for two reasons.
Firstly, there is lack of creativity here that is so pronounced that even the designer felt that they needed to label significant things and explain them. Floating text frequently appears at key points-of-interest within the environments to explain what this thing you are looking at represents. There is also scraps of paper, supposedly from a Dream Dictionary, which you can find in places if you explore. What this reminds me of is when someone tells you a joke that is so lame that they have to explain it to you afterwards.
Secondly is the complete lack of anything enjoyable to do in the dreams, since most tasks are simply mundane puzzles which are only difficult due to how long they take as a result of setbacks from mistakes. You won't have any 'eureka' moments here since the solution to the puzzles are obvious. The Dreams aren't visually interesting either causing you to not really want to bother exploring and at other times they clearly aren't intended for exploration anyway. I'm not joking here, but there is a dream where you go onto a very slow roller-coaster ride around a smoky-grey room and do nothing for a good 5 minutes. Another is when you walk around an empty office building just looking for how to get out unless you happen to notice a pc you can access using passwords written on a clipboard from the ground-floor. This gives you some puzzles and rewards you with access to a "Nightmare" that is so unimpressive that I actually felt cheated out of the time I spent solving the puzzles.
If Dream is trying to convey that Howard is depressed, bored with life and has no sense of direction or purpose then it accomplishes this goal with huge success... because the game itself is also boring, lacking direction and creativity.

I don't know why a lot of people compares this to Minesweeper. Unlike them, though, I don't mean that as a compliment. You click squares in both games, but that's where the similarities end. Minesweeper is a logic puzzle where you deduce which squares to click based on available information. Each game is going to involve a few guesses, but the vast majority of the time you will know whether a square is safe before you click it. As you can read it plays alot Desktop Dungeons (DD). Contrary to DD, your goal is not to beat single dungeons one after the other, but to go as deep as possible in one dungeon (roguelike).
This game has no available information. You randomly click on squares until something happens, and at that point you have some strategic decisions to make. Once you've decided to fight a monster or go around, though, you're just back to random guessing. It also has the same problem as DD, which is deaths from accidental missclicks. but in this case it's not so bad, because you play to die anyways, and - contrary to DD - you make progress on the metagame when dying (you keep your gold and can use it to buy upgrades).
It's an simple, cute and awesome game, especially for that price tag.
From what I remember the entire game was based upon RNG -- and it's not really replayable... I wish people would stop falsely tagging "roguelite" on everything that has a little bit of randomization.

Starscape is a curious fusion of an arcade and a turn-based strategy game. The arcade component is in total domination, but as long as it is not backed by strategic advancements, it tends to become overwhelmingly hard.
The main feature of the game is addictive gameplay. Despite the simple idea ("collect resources to become stronger, but watch your back and take offensive actions to collect intelligence") the gameplay is extremely immersive. The whole stroy takes ~12 hours (or less on low difficulty levels) to complete. The storyline is not bad, but not too bristling with events.
From purely technical point of view, the game mechanics is trivial: the more resources you collect, the more powerful you get; and few things can prevent you from collecting resources. Whenever you save a game, it is always easy to load and avoid any serious danger you get into. It is possible to think of circumstances resulting in 100% death, but I have never encountered such a coincidence in practice. The only thing the enemies can do is substantially delay your advance.
plot is simple, but intriguing, graphics is nice, strategy is straightforward. But there is something in this game that makes it addictive and immersive. An insight into this game is highly recommended. Slightly overpriced (for a reason).

Killed some time with this back in college, but it's pretty meh.  Collect resources, upgrade your mothership and your fightercraft, research and build...but the mechanics don't come together, it feels shallow, the interface is a pain, and it doesn't do bigger than 800x600.  The concept isn't flawed, it's just too small: the mechanics would have been fine in a shorter game, a flash game, that kind of thing, but stretched out to full-game length it suffers.  This game doesn't need a strategic map, but you have to slog through it anyway.  Worst of all is that it caps what you're allowed to research pretty aggressively, so early in the game you're sitting on max levels of resources that you can't spend.  Way to identify the fun part of the game and then kick it like a puppy, guys.
I still have fond memories of this game though, mainly from one night when I heard the starbase alarm going off, said "Hey wait my mothership is still at full health", and realized it was my next door neighbor playing at full volume.
Verdict:  Go play Tyrian instead.  That's what you really wanted anyway.

More than a year after originally purchasing the classic edition, I got around to playing through the game on the enhanced edition. Clocking in at ~60 hours for that run, I have to say that, barring some poor design choices, this is an RPG of a quality I don't see often, high as it is.
Where it counts: in making decisions that define your character(s), in the engrossing combat mechanics and the outstanding world design, Divinity: Original Sin shines as a unique example of an RPG done right.
That said, the Diablo leanings the game has, in the inventory system most particularly, detract from what could've been an even more interesting experience. Fiddling with a massive inventory that keeps overflowing with prefixed and suffixed items, many of which aren't that good, was tedious.
Another minor bad point is the practical punishment for preparing for tough battles. The system doesn't let you down potions in advance, nor apply buffs. They don't last long enough if you initiate combat willingly. Food, it appears, under this, is useless.
But with all that said, I still enjoyed the game a whole bunch and can recommend it greatly.

There seems to be a lot of frankly unwarranted hate for this game, although I will agree the price might be too high in the face of the short playtime.
I'm going to address that hate. If you want to see the review of the game itself, scroll down to "The Game(s) Itself"
What I'm seeing mainly boils down to this:
As for the cost, well, this was previously featured in a Humble Bundle. So it was part of a package, where you had freedom to set a price. Currently, it's barely over $1 on the Holiday Sale.
Is the normal asking price of $5 too much? Well, I would say yes, actually. The two games to me are effective, but very quick and not very good on replay unless you wait a while between plays, so it feels fresh on the next playthrough.
I say a range of about $2-3 would be better, though a "Set your own" option would be perfect. (if that's possible on Steam...not sure.)
Now for the game length.
Unfortunately, the 1st game, "Gravity Bone", seems downplayed by not even being mentioned as available in the "About the Game" section, it just states that this is the sequel to it.
I played through the 1st and 2nd game. It's found through "Career" in your Menu. Altogether, I spent about forty-five minutes, mainly because I got stumped in Gravity Bone while...looking for some birds. I even had to make a savepoint.
Anyway, I found a great balance between the two:
Gravity Bone is focused on the gameplay. More about finishing "Objectives".
Thirty Flights is focused on story and emotion.
Played back to back, you get far much more of a complete feel. The character is also the same across games.
Playing Gravity Bone first is better, since Gravity Bone is not as big on story and introduces you to the mechanics of the game. Also, a character in Gravity Bone later makes a cameo in Thirty Flights.
If one only plays Thirty Flights of Loving, I can completely understand that one would feel a bit underwhelmed by the rapidfire pace. Gravity Bone helps set up the story.
For what these games are, I think both managed to be extremely effective. They present experiences well without dragging things out, without filler or fluff, and with virtually no dialogue, as far as I remember.
While playing these, instead of trying to rush through like you're speedrunning or something, it's good to at least let yourself get immersed in the games a bit.
Due to the nature of the storytelling, it's like placing yourself in someone's shoes for a while. What stood out to me is that by the end of each, you can come away from them feeling a good bit of connection to the story, especially in the case of Thirty Flights.
I personally think the way these games manage to present their stories well in such a short time frame is a great representation of what games can do. I would say I am quite proud that there is something like this that is challenging, even debatable (when considering the negative reviews) available to us gamers.
I eagerly await the next game from Blendo;  hopefully this time around with a pay-what-you-will option, or at least a lower cost.
NOTE: Two technical issues I did face. Gravity Bone crashed once while in fullscreen, I went to windowed, and never had that issue again. One small fix that would be worth the developer taking care of. Also my screen brightness seems to have been changed by the game, and I can't find out what specific system setting was altered. This does use the Quake 2 engine, so I may look into that...but I did manage to change it back through the brightness setting in the game until things looked calibrated again.

So, after playing a decent amount of levels on this, and spending around nine and a half hours on the game (at the time I am writing this) here's my overall impression of the game:
The story doesn't make a whole lot of sense, if you are looking for some immersive story-rich experience.  Some alien being has stolen your cows while you were sleeping, and you are on a mission to get them back at all costs.  I guess a lot of platformers can be kind of vague in this regard, with very limited story, so I don't really have much to complain about with this, but it is worth mentioning.  I don't really understand what is going on, but the idea is to collect at least 3 of the 10 "o rings" in each level in order to open the portal gate thing to get to the next stage, while avoiding traps, pits, falling objects, creatures, and other obstacles.  I've been working on collecting all 10 rings per level so far, and it is fairly difficult on some levels, partially due to the need to have a responsiveness adjustment for controller or keyboards.  Your lives are unlimited, but you will lose a collected ring from the level you are on with every death you incur.
I really like the graphic style, and the mood and setting.  The art is nicely done, in my opinion, and the Gameplay is pretty responsive, but for me, a bit too sensitive.  Music is light and doesn't overburden the experience.  I also like the small square gates you can enter in the levels that will take you to small subterranian tunnels to usually find an "o ring" or something similar.  They're  generally scattered around the levels as you progress.  I also like some of the small in-level objects you can "eat" or "use" to create other effects with your environment, whether it is cooling yourself to tolerate heat better for a limited time, eating various fruits that grow from the regular green trees that will cause farts when jumping, which I believe can potentially kill things.  I am not certain, but I think I might have killed a fish with one at some point, though I am not entirely sure at this point.  There are also some black root-like structures that will grow when you get near them which give you some explosive powers when you jump that will lower spike traps very temporarily.  I also like that you can find hidden bonus items in many levels that you can use from the menu that will help you temporarily as you progress.  They are limited, to my knowledge, so best used wisely!
While I like the art and style, a little more variety would be nice, as progression seems a bit slow at times, due to the fact that I am collecting every ring in each level, perhaps.  I have noticed water as I've progressed though, which is nice, and a few other things every 10 or 20 levels I move onward.  I've had a difficult time using a controller, since the sensitivity cannot be changed at the time I write this.  This can be a bit frustrating at times.  When I use the keyboard, it is much easier to do smaller movements left and right, but still not as easy as a lot of similar style games.  Some areas can be fairly difficult, where you need the smaller movements, which my controller overcompensates for, as does my keyboard - would be easier to play if I could lower the movement speed or sensitivity with a sort of in-game slider or something.
I haven't figured out one squirting button I noticed on controller, and I'm not sure what that does, or if it is useful for anything.  As far as bugs, if I hold down the squirting animation, and jump away from it, the stream will stay in the same spot, I noticed.  I also noticed you can hear jump noises, or farting noises if the game is paused, and this also happens if you die and try to jump over and over.  Also, if I exit the game, I have noticed that it will default me to the wrong page, rather than what level I was just on, so I will have to go back a bit to start over, if I completely quit to the selection menu.  Once or twice upon falling off the screen, my ring appeared in places where it would be impossible to retrieve it and still collect all 10 rings in the level, making me have to restart the level entirely.
Overall I do like the game, but there are some things I hope can be worked on with some time as it is developed and improved further.  In particular, I hope there will be a controller sensitivity slider that can be used because I find it moves a little too quickly for me with my controller compared to similar platformer-style games.  The glitches are fairly cosmetic, and have no real effect on gameplay, aside from the missing or unobtainable rings prompting a restart. So, I deleted my last review about this game because I dont think I wrote it well, so, here is my second try:
Major\Minor is a visual novel in a world of anthromorphic characters (Humans/Animals hybrids for dummies).
I cant really say much of the story because i'm afraid to spoil the story for anybody who want to play it.
The only thing I can say is its genre: mainly a You-are-the-hero story with a bit sci-fi and a bit of magic maybe? (Hey, the story is actually complicated to explain... I cant really say anything better...)
I personnally really liked the game. The story was told in a very unique way if you ask me, many views on one subject...
Also, it offers a different way of seeing the world, I personnaly questionned myself after playing throught the full game and I am still a bit confused beacause of this game... Yeah...
I went throught all sort of emotions when I played this game: from joyfull to full on anger! From neutral to very sad... (I even cried at one point in the game... That's how much I like some of the characters...)
The graphics are not the strongest point I must say... Yes, I absolutly LOVE the aspects of every characters, you can see by their looks what type of personnality they have and everything, but, the only problem is that it is only a still picture... Not much movement... (But, this is a visual novel, and not a hardcore FPS we are talking about here.)
The music is sometimes out of sync and also sometimes not quite matching the current mood the scene express, but, overall, when it was at the right place at the right time, I got chills on some scenes and cried on others...
I would recommend this game to anyone who like visual novels, its not for everyone, but there is no visual gore or anything (But in the text, there is some, so, parental discretion is advised a bit...). I also recommend this to people who like to think a bit more than average because, sometimes, characters talk about various deep subjects like the universe, some type of physics (I think it was Quantum mechanics actually, I not too sure...)

Ori and the Blind Forest is a 2D platformer created by Moon Studios where, after an apocalypse caused by a dark force causes the death of Ori’s adoptive parent Naru, the player must navigate a series of puzzles and fight enemies using a range of different abilities unlocked throughout the game to restore balance to the world.  The game takes places in a sprawling forest that includes caves, mountains and secret tunnels.
When the game begins all Ori is capable of doing to navigate the world is a basic jump allowing the player to reach some higher areas of the map, however they are still greatly hindered by the geography of the environment until more abilities are unlocked. The player is introduced the basic movement and jumping mechanics in an interactive backstory in which the player can control Ori and Naru for brief periods of time. This allows the player to become immersed in the story while naturally learning how to navigate the world. As the game progresses and new abilities are unlocked, similar tutorial sections are implemented. These will typically involve the current surroundings in the form of puzzles that let the player continue to progress while mastering these new skills.
As the number of skills available to the player increase, the difficulty increases quickly as player will find themselves requiring the quick successive use of different powers in order to conquer the challenges presented to them. Frustration in the player can grow greatly in sections like this where some puzzles can take many attempts in order to complete. Fortunately The Blind Forest includes a mechanic where a player can use their energy resource, which is usually spent on more powerful attacks, to create a checkpoint wherever they are so hours aren’t spent trekking back to puzzles from checkpoints like many other games. While frustratingly difficult, the immersive story of Ori and the Blind Forest is enough to force them to carry on until the end.
While primarily being a puzzle/action game, Ori and the Blind Forest also includes elements of collection consisting of upgrades to the player’s health, energy and abilities. Rather than just gather these items as the player moves through their respective locations, these items are often inaccessible to the player on their first trip through, requiring the use of abilities yet to be unlocked in order to acquire them. This encourages plenty of exploration from the player as if they wish to collect everything it will almost certainly require backtracking.
The aesthetics and sounds of the game are also a major part its charm as the atmosphere created by these elements greatly enhances the player’s experience and makes them want to spend even more time in the world. While player actions take place in only two dimensions, there is often movement going on in the foreground, creating the sense that you are in a three dimensional world.
Through clever use of mechanics, story and aesthetics, Ori and the Blind Forest is able to create a world which, while difficult to traverse, can keep even the most infuriated player immersed for hours on end.

A dungeon crawler RPG/roguelike that takes place on ~7x8 grids. You start with one tile revealed and then click to reveal more tiles. You'll find enemies, treasure chests, traps, devices, stores and more as you look for the exit tile to descend to the next level. Luck is very much a part of your runs although there are ways to make the runs more consistent.
When you level up, you pick from one of 4 stats: STR, DEX, INT, and STA. STR increases melee weapon damage. Melee weapons are the only ones that can be dual-wielded for an accuracy penalty. DEX increases damage of ranged physical weapons plus gives a bonus to accuracy and dodge. INT increases ranged magic weapon damage and magic damage resistance. STA is nice to get early because it increases the effect of hearts (which you use to restore hp and increase max hp).
Every so often you'll unveil an event tile that gives you a random multiple choice event. Results are often based on your stats and sometimes new choices appear if you had completed another event earlier in the dungeon.
You're going to lose a lot and early runs are really just to grind gold to unlock permanent upgrades, learn the game mechanics, and memorize the multiple choice results. I didn't bother spending gold for much except for especially good runs or for god starts. The treasure one wasn't really worth it (it cost hundreds and was pointless if you lost early) until you could make your runs consistent enough with the permanent upgrades.
While your runs will sometimes end early because of an impossible/bs level (like a high attack ranged enemy that spawns when you first enter a level), know that there are things you can do if you have the right items (such as the insta-kill ranged enemy item or by going for ranged weaponry). Sometimes, you just have to move on and skip the level (via item or worship penalty).
By the time I cleared normal difficulty, I found I had enough upgrades to just start grinding chaos difficulty for more gold for permanent upgrades. There's not too much to do after you clear the boss besides repeat on harder difficulties (or with penalties) and unlock permanent upgrades for future runs. The events were interesting but not enough for me to replay countless times hoping to get the right random events in the right order. I never figured out what certain event items were for.
Worth a look for those who like roguelikes and are fine with a lot of losing and gold grinding to make your runs easier and more consistent.
Other thoughts:
Great roguelike. If i only had more time  to play. Im pretty i will revisit this one soon.

An interesting puzzle rogelike.
While levels, loot and other rewards and threats are randomized like in a classic roguelike, each level/floor is abstracted into a tile grid you get to explore click by click. And like half the enemies play a passive role, too, limiting your exploration of adjacent to them tiles, but only countering your blows - though that doesn't stop them from harming your journey in some other way, such as inhibitting the collection of mana or soul (kinda like standard mana but for items and such, not spells) or buffing others.
There's some loot collecting involved, but it feels a bit off when it's pretty standard for RPGs whereas most of other game aspects are more casual, so you gotta manage the backpack contents and all that. Though, the items sometimes have interesting effects and abilities beyond stat boosts so that's cool.
And there are also single use items, and mana requiring abilities, and some objects like ballistas scattered around floors, so there's plenty of tactical options. Unfortunately the start may be bit dull, with a single, always same ability per character and cooler goodies showing up just way later on. Also it takes a while to unlock new characters, which is bit unfotunate as you'll be stuck with a single character for a while early on.
Anyways, this is totally worth a try if you're into puzzles and roguelikes, an interesting combo that surprisingly works.

Right now as this game stands, I would have to say avoid it until it's finished. I won't bother writing a full review until I have replayed the game after its release but here is a short breakdown of the notes I took along the way:
- Beautiful graphics and scenery, absolutely amazing to be able to explore
- Fun little collectables which express dream interpretations of things around you
- Have feet, always a bonus
- Little questionable but not entirely bad voice acting
- Non-linear game but the structure is a little lacking organisation wise

- Puzzles can be a tad frustrating and pretty unimaginative, lacking originality
- Got stuck on one level, left unable to progress any further because of a bug which hasn’t been fixed (Terrace Walkway)
Don't get me wrong, a lot of that is negative but I have high hopes for this game when it's fully released. Well, where to begin.  The game has been in early access for quite some time now and it was just recently announced that the game would be officially released at the end of this month.  Since the very beginning I have love the artwork and gameplay.  The artwork while being somewhat minimal in detail, does a great job for creating a uniqueness in the visual design.  The gameplay is turn based which doesn't seem quite as popular these days, but it is handled in such a manner that it doesn't feel like a con.  I should note that the original Chaos was also turn based so this one is as well in trying to stay somewhat true to the original.  In every turn a wizard and creatures (if you have summoned any) are allowed one move and one attack.  The wizard also gets one cast per turn.  Each spell has a given percentage rate of success which can be boosted by earning mana from failing spell casts, acquiring mana sprites, discarding cards, or killing enemy creatures.  Spells of either Law or Chaos alignment will also start to get increases to the chance of success depending on the alignment.  Alignment changes as spells/creatures of either Law or Chaos alignment are successfully cast.  There can be a bit of a learning curve in the beginning but once this is overcome the game is exceptionally enjoyable and in my personal opinion, very unique.  Something else to take note of is the community for this game.  It is by far the best community I have come across for any game I have played to date.  Whether on the forums or on the community site (
), everyone is extremely helpful and very pleasant to chat with.  Feel free to check out my Chaos Reborn videos here:
There is a variety of game modes to choose from.  1v1, 1v1v1 (3 person FFA), 1v1v1v1 (4 person FFA), 2v2 (team battle).  There is also the normal live match style or the asynchronous match style.  Asynchronous matches can be played at your convenience.  You could pop on and play one turn a day against your opponent if you chose to, but they can also be played live if your opponent would happen to be online at the same time.  It is an excellent choice if you are not sure if you will have time to finish a given match or want to have several matches going at the same time.
The forge system (an optional upgrade) allows you to create custom gear.  I like this one because you can customize the appearance and sockets to your liking.  The downside that has been noted here is that it could be mistaken for pay to win.  No one build will win them all and this is merely an optional tool for players to use if they are enjoying the game.   The forge does not offer any stat increases over already available equipment.  It also adds forge created items into the publicly available item pool, hence allowing other players to acquire them.  This is a pretty awesome feature!
The separation of classic chaos and RPG chaos (equipped mode).  Classic chaos allows you to go into a match against another wizard without custom equipment and it gives you a random mega spell.  This keeps players on relatively equal footing and seems to be the preferred method of play in early access.  Equipped mode allows you to earn gold by playing in the ranked matches or playing the single player.  You can use the gold to buy random equipment packs and also purchase items in the single player maps as you complete them.
The artwork is superb as I have noted above.  It provides a very unique aesthetic to the visual experience and I have found it very enjoyable.  This is one of very few games I find myself constantly coming back to and playing matches with others.
The community is exceptional.  If you happen to have any questions or just want to play against someone who will try to teach you the gameplay mechanics then don't hesitate to visit
or the community sites chat client at
(you will have to create an account and login on the main page ).  You can also check out this video from UnstableVoltage for some gameplay tips:
You can also check out this
by d00m.
The single player while being a nice addition to the game, can be very confusing at first and also at times possibly frustrating.  It does feel somewhat incomplete and is not nearly as enjoyable as the multiplayer aspect of the game.  I would easily say that if you are not interested in the multiplayer portion that this game may not be for you; however, I am sure there are some lets plays out there that play through some of the single player so it is just something to be aware of.  UnstableVoltage also has a video going through the single player realms here:
Server lag.  While this does not ruin the game since it is turn based.  It can create a delay in the execution of your moves leaving you feeling like the game just broke or something.  This one is just something to remember.  Chances are if you executed an attack or movement and it didn't happen right away that the server is experiencing lag and the action should happen within the next few seconds.
I don't know if this is really a con or more just bad luck but sometimes the RNG (random number generator) can feel somewhat merciless.  There are just matches where it will seem like almost every spell fails regardless of success chance (like a 96% success dwarf or something).  This will likely happen to you at some point but overall not really a con.
I can say that I would easily recommend this game.  It feels very well done even though there is still quite a bit more development ahead for the social features.  I strongly recommend joining the community for playing matches as it can be a lot more fun that simply using the match maker all of the time.  Please feel free to leave comments on this review.  :)

(I have not finished the main campaign, but have brought two characters to the third and fourth acts)
Companion and minion heavy, slow and teasing, but fun.
Most of the damage needed to progress and defeat enemies is provided not by the player, but by the companion and minions. The player character, Van Helsing Jr., seemingly always feels weak and depending on the class chosen, is. For example, the Constructor does not simply gain support from his minions, but relies solely on them. The Constructor attacks about once every 3 seconds and does immaterial damage.
When your companion, and/or minion army, dies, it is clear that the follower is more important than the leader. The amount of damage that your "team" deals sinks drastically and leaves you with excruciatingly slow enemy clearing. Also, it seems to take such a long time to gain experience for leveling.
The slow leveling adds to the teasing effect of the character's progression system. The skill system is divided into a 3-tier wheel. The first tier is immediately available, but the second unlocks at level 20 and the third, 40. Why this is a tease is because, of course, the seemingly most fun or awesome sounding and damaging skills are usually amongst the final third tier.
With this all said, it still is fun to build the character. This game also has a classic ARPG feel and look. The story is throw-away, but with a fun theme of the Van Helsing nature (hunting classic monsters). Some quests can be fun such as deciding whether or not to aid a character type that you've just killed dozens of. There are also several hidden and self-titled "Easter Eggs" throughout each act, which, along with quests, are clearly layed out in your journal when you uncover them and are tallied at the end of each act to show how many you've found and how many there were.
The individual acts were great, to have them all in one install is greater.
You will fall in love with this game. A brillant soundtrack and awesome visuals and artstyle, bit.trip will make you smile.

The game is very well balanced (in normal mode - which is all I've played), and each fight could go either way if you recklessly run into a situation. It is very enjoyable and the world, characters and quests are all expertly constructed.

Before finishing the game: This is worth the $20 ($15 if you catch the sale). Great characters, story, and artwork.
After: After playing this game fully and completing the entire story I'll give my full review about this VN.
I still do recommend the game for great soundtrack and story, but not for the characters throughout it. I'll list both the things I found problematic and pleasurable.
Spoilers:
Problem 1) The lack of emotions given to the characters.
Sure, this is your first game and it's understandable that characters are given a main sprite, but to have said sprite be the picture for each event that happens makes the story lose some of its feelings.
For example: Endymion's death. Both Konrad and Endymion depicted their same facial expression during and after all this had happened. It made Endy's death seem not as heavy as it should have be. Same with the deaths of Velasquez, Rook or Kila, Klace, Kabu, Phidget, Rocker, and anyone else I am missing.
Another: When Kila is threatened about why he came to the tour or when Inumi or Shock talks about how they are feeling (one sad and the other upset) or when Eclair is worried about Rook, Acheron is upset at Singe
Problem 2) Character has a sprite to show any change in actions/events. This may only be minor, but also major at the same time (See what I did there XD). Also not all are just about the characters' sprites.
I'll just list some here: Rook getting his tablet taken; Archeon and Reiyo grabbing a sword; Nagi having both swords; Velasquez having stabbed himself and both him and Nami getting stabbed. I know this is not a high age-restricted game, but when both blood and death are mentioned, they should at least be depicted in some manor (Vel having blood trail from his mouth or his spectre getting a splash of red, anything!); Rook and Kila being tied up and Eclair and the two crying/were crying.
Problem 3) Scene changes. This one isn't really a big one + the fact that it could be replaced by some above.
You could add some backgrounds to show more than one or two character on the screen doing said actions/even or depict the surroundings that everyone is in and give better insight of what is going on or how said action/scenery looks rather than the generic faded background. The deaths of both Endymion and Kabu could both be done with this as you could show Kabu on the ground bleeding out while Riley stabs Endymion or when Lord Plair kills Riley. Doing so could also better introduce new characters like when Inumi is in the front seat of the limo and quickly disappears or for when you 1st meet Konrad and Endymion or show the backstory of when Kila meet Righty and also Phidget's drawings. I would have love to see those.
So much could be added to this one that could improve the style of this which the story is being told
Problem 4) Not being able to buy the soundtrack! I MEAN WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥?! I loved everything about the music, especially during the ending credits and the scene with Dazz and Shock or any of it tbh. I saw that your Indiegogo was a fail but what if you put a price on steam for those who want to buy it seperately with/without buying normal edition or as a bundle for the ones who buy the complete edition.
Problem 5) Not being able to load/save at any point in time or the ability to skip text previously read...that's all
Now for what I actually liked:
Pleasure 1) The overall story was beautiful. Even though I've yet to read and achieve all possible outcomes, I enjoyed the adventure that I was lead through from beginning to end. Although, if one isn't well kept up on what is going on it can get very, very confusing.
Example: The constant switch between to and fro Earth and Terra; while on Earth, showing events happening on Terra; while on Terra, showing events happening on Earth.
Pleasure 2) The soundtrack was very lovely throughout the game. Original or not, but you should add them on steam for a price (Read Problem 4)
Pleasure 3) Having consequences that affect the story as a whole. This is the 1st VN that I have read that has done that (I know that there are others, but this is new to me). It makes choosing more challenging and making me want to go back through it to see all outcomes 100% more likely. With how many there are currently, I doubt I'd be able to get through them all without writing all my choices down somewhere.
Pleasure 4) Having death in the story and you only having a small role in the story rather than the entire/majority of it. Not everything is fairy tale perfect or about the creator, but also is there a choice to join Nagi in that last fight? Do let me know.
Pleasure 5) Getting to know what happened to Max at the end of the credits. Forcing someone to go through the unskippable cringe so they have a vague idea of what happened to Max at end of this
Pleasure 6) It's a furry VN...no. Not 100% true. The character designs are interesting to look at but only for so long. (Cue Problem 1 and 2).
But in all honestly, I did enjoy some of the character's like Righty, Velasquez, Riley, Inumi, Max, Archeon, Rook, and Eclair. I would add Nagi but for some reason having a perfect creation have a scar and possible blind eye doesn't make any sense since both him and Nami were suppose to made without flaws.
Pleasure 7) The way the story made me feel to the end. There were some parts where I couldn't take what was happening to its full extent due to certain things (Problem 1,2 and 3), but reading them and imagining all that was taking place helped me get into the events more.
I doubt anyone has gotten this far so if you did, I congratulate you for reading this out. I don't see this as a bad game, just one that has some highly needed fixes/thoughts that could be added to the next game

The final ship components cause all end-game ships to look the same, and the final boss has a stupid mechanic which requires you to either have a way more responsive ship than the game gives you, or to angle a shot in a way that gives you a generally unsatisfying win because you didn't do the high-agility maneuvers that it feels like you should do.  It caps the game off with not even allowing you to have a solid victory in the final "cutscene."
Overall, a good 75% of a game marred by an overly repetitive final zone.  If you don't mind this, and the late 90s graphics, go ahead and get it!  It's actually pretty fun, reminiscent of Asteroids with an upgradeable ship and uh, better graphics, though still a far cry from anything you'd call "modern."

TLDR:  A Space themed 1v1 MOBA with a unique style of resource management.  As of the time of writing this review the game is 100% Free to Play with absolutely no Pay to Win. Currently in Basic form, but still very enjoyable.
It's basically a 1v1 MOBA as of now, but what sets it apart is the style of resource management.  You take control of and build rings around planets which will in turn produce more units to go into your wave of minions.  There are also side objectives that spawn and can be contested over.
Your mothership will level up as the game progresses first unlocking the abilities you've chosen before the game, and then upgrading your ship itself (speed, attack speed, attack damage, hull, shield, something else i can't think of.)
There is more detail to go into about the production part (and hell all of it) but i don't truly understand it all yet.  Despite being in basic form, there are still abilities to experiment with and strategies to test.

There are slow periods during the PvP and frantic bursts of micro management.   Not alot of ships or abilities to choose from yet but if the developers give this game some love, time, polish, and content It could really turn into something great.
-AI is pretty simple, more of the tutorial than the ACTUAL tutorial(which doesn't cover much)
-Has a nice space theme that for some reason reminds me of Homeworld (though the two have little in common)
-Playerbase isn't much yet but it has to start somewhere.
-You are starting with the same pool of ships/abilities to choose from as everyone else.  (LEVEL PLAYING FIELD!)

It does look like when they add more ships/abilities/skins you will be able to unlock them with ingame currency earned through playing or probably buy it with real money.  If new content is balanced, this shouldn't become a problem.
All in all  I'm having fun, I think other people will enjoy this game too.  I really recommend giving it a shot.
Also there's a parallel queue, so if you don't want to sit around waiting for a match you can beat up on some AI and the game will let you know when your match is ready.

Would I recommend it? Yes. Why? Read on, because there are some pros and cons.
Before I bought the game I did some research as always. Just so I know what I would buy and if there’s a change that I would like it for more than a few hours of gameplay. By the time I write this review I have played this game for 17 hours and had a lot of fun.
I do like survival games as well as crafting and (base)building games. It lets me tap into my creativity and it’s more relaxing than other game genres I play. But what makes Out of Reach so interesting from other games? Well, for starters, you play on a server and you can choose the way you want to play (PVE, PVP or STD). I see a couple of people complaining about the fact that you can get raided by other players. That’s true and you will lose your base and or stuff. But that’s the fun! It’s a survival game after all.
Let’s look into PVP and STD (standard) gameplay. If you are unlucky and log into a server with grievers, the game would suck. Try to find a server where you can join clans and/or make your own. Build your own base or help a clan to build their base. Defend it and work together to maintain your position in the world. Explore together and make damn sure you have the right stuff for battles (like armor and weapons). I never take too much stuff with me. Because if you lose a fight and die, the raiders will take it all (obviously). If you’re lucky your friends will pick up your stuff and take it with them to the base so you can get it back. It’s the excitement of wondering around exploring the map and gather resources for your clan. If you have enough and if you think your clan is strong enough, set out to find other clans and destroy them.
The PVP servers are typical for PVP gameplay. It’s against each other and not much else. The environment is hostile as well but that’s just how the game is designed. The pvp extends the standard survival gameplay. It’s much harder to survive while fighting against other people than against the environment.
Standard mode gives you the best of PVP and PVE. You can do both. I started a server and I’m playing with a friend. We started out by playing together and work out the gameplay. See how the game feels and works. It’s a good way for new players to find a standard server with people who are willing to teach you how the game works (as well for PVE as PVP).
I think PVE gameplay is easy to understand. You against the environment and not against other players. It’s possible to build different clans but you’re not fighting each other.
Since it’s an early access game there are some bugs and possible improvements. I did not found any bugs that make the game unplayable. I have an ‘old pc’ and it runs fine. So the higher end pc’s shouldn’t have much issues.
The pros of the game are:
The cons of the game are:
In the end I recommend this game to people who like survival games and do want to support the devs in early access stages.
Where the game is heading I don’t know. I do hope that the game will be developed into something fun and with unexpected gameplay twists. It has a lot of potential, like a lot of other early access games, and I hope the devs see that as well and continue to work on this game.

Hey, so I've played a lot of turn based strategies (all of the advance wars, battle for wesnoth, and many many more), and this one is fantastic.  Most of what makes it great is the incredible diversity of gameplay and the dynamic battles. I don't think "opening theory" even has an application to this game.  However, it is a very niche game, so I will focus on it's idiosyncracies that may or may not turn people off.
1) Heavy PvP focus.  While there is going to be a limited sort of MMO style "PvE" from what I gather called "Realms", there is nothing of this sort yet, and I'm pretty sure pvp will still be the focus.  Single player is just a pvp vs a bot that will entertain you for all of 3 hours.
2)Heavy luck element.  Playing against the median player, the win rate spread for chess is about 2% to 99.5% depending on the player.  For advance wars maybe 10-90%, for battle for wesnoth 15-85%.  For this game it's a whooping 25-75% win rate against randoms.  Saying there is a heavy luck element in an understatement.  This is going to change some, but not much.  Don't get me wrong, there is certainly enough skill for a ladder be stable and make sense and have "best players".  But you will lose to newbies.  Regularly.
3)Imbalance.  This is not bad so much but things get tossed up like every few weeks as more and more stuff gets added to the game. So the game wont feel very balanced for a long time.  Such is early access ;)  Current example:  Undead can only be killed with attack spells, equipment or other undead.  Sometimes you have none of these.
4) The game is built around a deck of spell cards but you currently have no influence on the deck, and will only be able to influence maybe 5-20% of the deck in the future.  This is actually a good thing for the game, as it makes the game more about your full knowledge of all the cards, but it might turn some people off.

Currently best played as a multi-player game (single player vs. AI exists, but misses the point) either on-line or hotseat.
Battle is conducted by casting spells (somewhat appropriately for wizards...) that may: summon creatures, buff your wizard, affect the game board, or directly attack your enemy. Spells are (currently) randomly selected and allocated at the start of the game.
The strategy is affected by probability - each spell has a chance of success (and therefore failure) and a single successful attack will kill a wizard, therefore at each juncture you need to consider 'what if'?  Naturally, better spells are more prone to failing. This makes for tense games where you can, depending on your desire for comedy or awareness of tragedy, happily go for the 1,000,000:1 shot or situation permitting, attempt to amass an army.

I've only played the first eight or so levels but I think I'm ready to give my opinion. I can only describe it as a beautifully executed bad idea. The game is lovely, the graphics are lovely, the sounds are lovely, the animations are lovely, the implementation of the 2.5D is lovely, the controls are lovely. The game behind it all... well again the implementation is good with nice responsive controls and snappy resets to the start of the level that don't break up the flow when you fail. Unfortunately the core idea behind it all is actually pretty weak. The rest of the game is constantly making up for that but it can never quite overcome the fact that if you look behind the curtain at what is happening mechanically there isn't much fun to be had there. What is really annoying is that one or two minor changes would have made it sooo much better.
On the surface it looks like a standard auto-runner but these are set levels rather than anything randomly generated and they have ends that must be reached to progress and ultimately, if you have the patience, beat the game. The problem is that once you've learnt the controls and learnt to read the meaning of the obstacle you must pass (pit means jump, step means jump, high UFO means duck, low UFO means jump etc) then it becomes just an exercise in pressing the right sequence of buttons with the right timing. You can see what buttons presses will be required next just as surely as if they were presented as flying towards you as they are in Guitar Hero type games. So what is there left to do? Just mindlessly try and try until you succeed in getting the timing right. The music and visuals effectively distracted from the essential boredom of this exercise for awhile but ultimately life is too short.
Now how could it have been better. Well when you pass an obstacle it plays a certain little chime that combines with the background beat to make a little song and that is lovely. It would have been great to see that combined into the game somehow so that you could use the audio cues to help with the timing of your jumps. Or if the button presses had sounds associated with them that you had to insert into the tune at the right moments and thus complete the tune then I think the game would have really come alive. As it is the game is more fun to watch and listen to then actually play.
I do not recommend this game. The Cost vs. Enjoyment is not good. This is the definition of an early access game, I will expect something more promising in 1-2 years.

I really don't understand what people are fussing about. There is a little nudity in it, but nothing explicit, and it's not played for kicks. The lizard woman isn't naked. The lizard man is, but the game text hints that this isn't normal behaviour and his tribe only tolerate it because he's VERY good at his job. And yes, the lizard girl is naked. Briefly. But there's a perfectly reasonable explanation if you PLAY the game, rather than just look at photoshopped screenshots of it and believe all the stuff people make up about the content of it. NO, there isn't any sex. "Tickle fetish"? What? Yes, you can do that. To one character. You can also stab a boar with a sword, but nobody accuses the game of having a "Sword fetish". "You bring her back and ♥♥♥♥ her mother in front of her". Err...no you don't. That's just a flat out lie.
I don't get it. Frankly, if you think this game is furry or paedophilic, that says more about you than it does about the creator. At least they're prepared to stand up for themselves, which is a refreshing change. And there are THOUSANDS of games which features anthropomorphic animals. Come on...that was the standard for decades. Nobody accuses Sega of being furries because of Sonic the Hedgehog, do they? And as for the lizard girl...well, if you've ever been around young children, then you should KNOW that they revel in doing things that make you uncomfortable. Nine times out of ten if you bathe a young child, they'll do everything they can to cause trouble, simply because they prey on your anxiety...if you choose to sexualise it, then YOU are the one who needs help.

Thirty Flights of Loving is an indie art game which I found short, obtuse and largely uninteresting.
Speaking as someone who loved Dear Esther, and even Thirty Flights' developer's previous game ('Gravity Bone', which is included here as a free extra), I found myself thoroughly bewildered by Thirty Flights of Loving.
I was bewildered by the sloppy non-linear storytelling. The game hops, skips, and leaps, with all the grace of a big rig in a tutu. I've played through the whole game and read several summaries to make sure I wasn't missing anything, but even once I made sense of the story being told (a by-the-books tale of a criminal caper gone wrong), it didn't connect with me at all.
I was bewildered by the lack of flow within the gameplay. For such a short game, I was astonished to find myself stuck on at least two occasions. Normally I'd be the last person to call for such handholding tactics as blatant signposting or railroading of the player, but in this case the current state is completely at odds with the intended purpose. The developer obviously wants to tell a story, but I found it a trial just to get to the next part. This is not to mention the pointless interactions in the game which sometimes seem to serve no purpose whatsoever.
I was bewildered by the end. It came out of nowhere, and left me with the strongest feeling of 'is that it?' I think I've ever encountered with a game. I spent more time in the options menu than I did with the game itself. I wouldn't mind if it was some kind of masterpiece of storytelling, but it just wasn't.
Most of all, I was and am bewildered by the praise this game has garnered. 88% (at the time of writing) on Metacritic. Critical acclaim. Fans on the forums defending it to the hilt. I saw similar reactions to Dear Esther (which, as I said earlier, I felt deserved every bit of its praise), but I genuinely cannot understand it in this case.
Maybe I'm missing something huge here, but Thirty Flights of Loving was not an enjoyable, enlightening, or otherwise entertaining experience for me. I respect any developer who attempts to tell stories through games, but this feels like one of the more unfinished, unfocused efforts that I have played. Not recommended.

I truly enjoyed this game. The artwork was wonderful, the characters were defined quite well though the dialog, and there was never really a 'Black And White' situation. I found myself engaged and I felt like I was reading though a decently written Mystery Murder/Sci-Fi...which is what the creators intended. After 13 Hours, I finished my first play though and I am fully intending on playing though again and making different (better) choices.
The Ending gave me mixed feelings. I had a sense that everything moved a little faster than the rest of the story, but I didn't mind that too much. The Finale was wonderful, but I didn't have a sense of full completion, as there were a few things neglected that was unable to resolve on the first play though due to in-game choices. I loved how the end of the game showed the full extent of the choices made.
Now, as a GAME, there were a few major/minor (that is a pun...I'm not sorry) things that I found to be missing.
One of the most noticed (and commented) is that the characters facial expressions remaining static. I understand (somewhat) the difficulty of having the character portrait change, but the Game play would have been much more engaging if facial expressions could have been added, as it is a little out of character when someone is describing a traumatic life event and grinning like an idiot the whole time. A somewhat Minor detail, true, but one worth adding in my opinion.
Something that I would have LOVED would have been some voice files for the characters, just to add a little extra personality. Nothing grand, just a simple phrase or "hello" when the character is first introduced would have added more depth to the characters as well.
All and all, a very solid story that made me really question who the good guy was, and normally that is fairly easy to figure out. If you like a read and enjoy a fairly complex story with an interesting moral code, you will love this one.
8/10, will be playing again...and again...and, well, you get the idea. ^.^

I feel really badly about this, since I love furries and furry-related content, but, like, man does this game feel more like an emulation of a game than an actual game. The art is really static and nondynamic; all of the characters have the same smirkish facial expression on their face that totally makes them all identityless and, well, just plain boring to look at. What's worse is that they never ever change their facial expressions or, well, anything else about themselves during your interactions with them. They really aren't characters at all; they're just pictures on your screen attached to dialogue that is extremely cliche and - sadly once again - boring. What's worse (again) is that I wasn't even given any time to figure out the story for myself through the dialogue; instead the narrator basically straight up told me what was going on, so that I really didn't feel intellectually/creatively challenged at all. Somehow I was in charge of the main character, making decisions for him, yet he was also the one telling me how he felt about everything and what was going on. I really didn't feel important at all in the story or in the grand scheme of things, and I came to hate the art, story, and game as a result. This is a really bad game, and there are so many better things you could spend your money on that are more meaningful and, well, fun. Stay away; stay far, far away.

I wrote a review for this novel several months ago, giving it a thumbs up, but since then, my mind has shifted downhill. First, I have to admit the plot was actually kinda good. You're this average joe no one has ever heard of, minding your own business, and suddenly, you're the savior of a different world, trying to stop an evil force from completely destroying it. The plot has some build up, but that's about as good as it gets. As for the negatives, grab some popcorn, because this might be a lengthy read.
First off, the thing I noticed is that despite the various mood changes, the characters keep the same expression, as though they're frozen. I understand making different expressions for each character can take time, but trust me. It's worth putting the effort into. Even the smallest changes can make an impact on a product. It almost felt like I was staring at a frozen screen the whole time. The only things that changed were the backgrounds(which had a crap ton of blur, IMO) and the text dialogue when a character was speaking.
Second, I'm not sure if this bugs everyone else as bad as it bugs me, but a lot of the achievements seem to have the same icon(s). At this point, I was getting the feeling the developer wasn't putting in much effort to make the novel stand out as much as he wanted it to. It's a little sad, to be honest. I actually had high hopes for this.
Third, the music is easily forgettable. As a music maker myself, I can honestly say I almost fell asleep a few times just because of the music. It was very boring, even during the "build-up" scenes.
Fourth, and this is a big one for visual novels like this. Fourth, is the lack of choices your character  is able to make, at least when it comes to more important situations, other than which ally you want to tag along with. Seriously, I could care less about who I'd rather tag along with. We're all trying to take out the same guy in the end, right? And the worst part is, your character doesn't even get the honor of killing him. Your allies, who come out of nowhere, at random, kill him. Why? Why go through all that trouble to even get to that point when you can't even kill the guy yourself? The main character is supposedly the savior, so just let him finish the job, like the story says he's supposed to do?
My fifth complaint isn't really a big deal, but this kinda goes to show that not all furries are the same. When it comes to clothing, some of the characters are a bit underdressed. Just look at the character Rocker, for example. If the creator drew him with his pants being worn any lower, his dang crotch would be showing! And as for Sam, if her dress was worn any tighter, you could probably just say she's only wearing body paint, painted to look like a dress! I just don't understand why some characters are drawn the way they are. Sam is in the medieval looking scenario, so wouldn't she be wearing something to better suit that period, instead of wearing what looks like a modern day bar waitress outfit?
There's a few other things I wanted to point out, one including the creator's fursona being the most "important" character, but I'll just skip that, because according to other reviews, he seems to have had a habit for flagging such reviews as "abusive'. Whatever. Anyways, my first thoughts were "A nice game with an amazing story". After going through it a second time, my thought is "A bland, repetitive storyline, showing no emotion, in an effort to make one's ego popular. Would not recommend it. Will be uninstalling and removing from my library.
