First thoughts when seeing this in my inventory: Wtf is this? did I buy another game while sleeping (Apparently, ive done it once or twice)? After reading and finding out i got it for The Repopulation being canned (LAME. No other game would let me be a Robot-building Stripper/ Dancer... Seriously.)
First thoughts when seeing the video in the store page: Oh great.. ANOTHER survival game...
First thoughts when launching the game: Damn, is that a steady 60 fps? I doubt it, on my system, but it does run really smooth.
Lots of crafting to be done. From Stone axes all the way up to using Nanites ( no clue as to thier purpose).
-EDIT 4/28/16-
After playing a few hours of forraging and gathering logs and branches and fiber, and many Metimucil jokes later, I was able to start crafting a base. Heres where its broken. I spent the better part of 30 minutes chopping down all the trees i could see, only to make a giant "base", or a giant platform that you can build on top of- supposedly... I placed the base down and afterward was unable to build directly upon it. Walls dont link to edges, nor do they place directly next to the previous wall. They tend to always give the "Item is intersecting with another, cant place" error message. The most frustrating part other than that is the item has 3, yes THREE, colors when in placement mode. Green for yes place here, red for no you cant do that, and brownish yellow for no you cant place that here and let me tell you why, followed by the message of why you suck at life. The third color, being the most prevalent when making your base.
-End edit-
You start off in your underwear (cause thats how i would load up into an escape pod... in my skivvies) as in most survival games. This one Is more Sci-Fi based than most games, though i did have a feeling for a while that i was playing ARK, if only due to the Ambient sounds making me feel like there was a giant something just around the corner, looking to smash my face in.
The scenery is nicely done. Most of the environment can be harvested and used for crafting. Its a nice breath of fresh air to see more than just ONE type of item drop from any one type of harvestable (I.E. A bush will drop Sticks, Twigs, Berries, Fibers, Etc.).
It being just released out of Alpha, there are a bunch of things, I'm sure, that are not working/ in place. Like the base building.
What i noticed, from the hour i've put in: Creature animations are stiff, if there at all. I was smashing an "elk" type thing over the head with my pointy stick. It was just standing there looking at my health get lower and lower. The next one i killed actually attacked me, but then after a few kicks to my face, it too just stood there and watched my health deplete. I lol'd.
Some of the character animations are a bit funny. The pointy stick being the best/ funniest animation. Its a pointy stick, but you bash things with it instad of stabbing. Well, at least most of the time.
As long as you have an item equipped to the hot bar and have that number selected, but sheathed (hit the button once to pull out selection, again to put it away, Hands come back up), you can literally punch ore out of rocks, logs out of trees, Etc. This basically lets you harvest anything you want, even with a broken tool in your hotbar.
My favorite thing, for some reason, id to go into third person mode, and look down. Watching the characters wrists bend like they do... Its funny (hands are still tethered to the camera even though its now behind your head, so they bend a bit oddly).
All in all, i cant say i found anything too terrible in the time i ran around. It was a bit confusing to figure out that i level up and have to spend skill points in the inventory to unlock new skills/ craftables; without a tutorial of sorts. Some sort of exp meter would be nice on the HUD as well as the minimalistic one in your inventory.
-EDIT- 4/28/16 A little explanation of the leveling sytem skills: Every couple hundred exp you earn (early levels, thousands later on), you gain 4 skill points. These points can be used in the following catagories (Copy-Pasta'd from
:
* CONSTRUCTION allows you to create buildings, props, storage containers, and various types of crafting stations
*ELECTRONICS includes the creation of Electronic Devices, Turrets, Medical Scanners, or Robotics.
*MELEE provides bonuses in melee combat, as well as the creation of melee weapons and tools.
*RANGED provides bonuses in ranged combat, and allows creation of ranged weapons and grenades
*REFINING is used to refine raw materials, unlocks harvestables, and creates tools
*SUBSISTENCE reduces the effects of hunger and thirst, and allows the creation of foods, drinks or medical compounds. It will also include genetic engineering on the high end
*SURVIVAL increases your health and allows the creation of traps, torches, and campfires
*TEXTILES is used to create armor, clothing, and backpacks
-End Pasta-
As you level up, the amount of skill points required for the next level skill is the number of level youre trying to get to, I.E. you want to learn level 3 melee, you need 3 skill points for that, 4 for level 4, etc.

Biggest issues right now is that it's short on content for end game but that should take a decent amount of time to get to and the rate these devs are working I'd imagine we'll see more content for then before most users get to it. This IS NOT REPOPULATION or It's REPLACEMENT! It's a second project the Repop team has been working on that is set in the Repopulation universe it's also a great testing ground for them to work on porting over to the engine with Repop!

A game that could be brilliant if only a couple of things were re-designed.
There's no winning strategy - on one hand you have to click each tile to have a chance of getting the items/upgrades that'll be needed to progress, but on the other hand you are severely punished for doing so by unavoidable spike traps, poison traps, etc - which would be fine if there were a stretegic counter but there is not! (other than the ocasional trap detection item you may stumble across... but only by means of clicking tiles and risking traps!)
Look, rng is fine but not when it makes the purpose of the game (clicking tiles, fighting monsters, finding loot) result in random punishments that are not avoidable.
90% of my deaths are ultimately due to traps, so there's definitely a problem here.
Redesign the traps - add an inbuilt trap detection so a player only uncovers the trap when she really *has* to progress beyond a tile (thus strategic decision; hp loss for sake of exploration) or honestly just get rid of them - the game would still be extremely difficult due to the strength and abilities of the monsters you encounter.
It's a vote down until the death by trap syndrome goes away, as the mechanic literally kills the game.
Its a solid roguelike, but I don't feel like enough gets saved and moved over such that its not a massive grind.

1) The first 'world' is the least compelling and the hardest in terms of puzzles. Don't be put off by this, keep at it and you have some really incredible levels to look forward to.

3) This game is nowhere near being finished. There are clever bits, even a little personal branding going on, that make playing it feel worthwhile overall. For an early-development game, this is well done.

I've played this game for just under half an hour and I feel like i've experienced everything the game has to offer. In fact I felt like I had only 10 minutes into playing. It has some serious problems that make the game much harder than it should be and overall not enjoyable to play.
The premise of Tic-Toc-Tower is that you have 10 seconds to complete every level. To complete a level all you have to do is make your way to the exit door. These rooms are often filled with diffcult platforming and obstacles to avoid. Or at least that's the premise. In my experience it wasn't quite like this.
I'll just describe the arcade made to start since this is were the main experience is meant to be from. In this mode you have to complete as many levels as possible without running out of time. Levels are picked randomly from a pool of already designed ones. The majority of the levels though are way to simple. Some are simple enough to literally just running to the other side of the room. Others just have 1 or 2 platforms to jump on. There are few that have twists and turns, hard platforming and traps to avoid, but not enough. On top of this there isn't actually enough different rooms. I think i've experienced every room now multiple times.
Within this mode you can also pick up a time powerup. Although don't ask me what it does because I have no idea. It didn't actually seem to add any extra time and all it did that I could see was light up in the left.
There are a few other modes. These include hardcore, hell (harder version of hardcore), time-trial and co-op. They all seem to use the same levels though that aren't diffcult enough. Hardcore and hell do add a lot traps though which spices up the gameplay to be a little harder at least.
Heres the killer problem though. Controls are absolutely horrible. They are unresponsive and just don't do what you want them to. I mean I couldn't get my character just to jump a tiny way. If I just tap the button he still goes really far. This means you have to try and guess where the game is going to make you land. On top of this there seems to be a short delay on the character actually acting on your button press. These problems also exist with using controller. This is what I mean by the problems making the game way harder than it should be.
The other problem with making the game difficult was with the graphics style and spawning. Your character seems to blend in a little too much with the background. This means you often find yourself loosing your character. The spawning system makes this even worse. You never actual spawn in the same place so at the start of the level you have to search for where your character has spawned. These two issues combined together can you make you loose valuable seconds at the beginning of every level.
Another small issue but still worth mentioning is that within levels the text clips off the screen slightly so the resolution if obviously not set properly.
Aside from all of these problems the game does actually look really nice. The graphics style is simple but it works well. It has a pretty good soundtrack to go with this experience. The thing with the soundtrack though is that it only seems to get into it and sound good about a minute into gameplay.
So overall I can't recommend the game to people in the current state, not for the asking price at least. At the moment the games controls just don't work well and it is highly lacking in content. I have no doubts that if they act on this feedback properly the game would be an enjoyable experience. For now I would say wait until later in the early access period, or better yet release, to see if the issues I have stated are fixed.
Disclaimer: I was provided a free key by the developer to write this review.

I powered throught he complete edition and the story is still a sophomoric mess that left me feeling like I wasted a major chunk of my time. There's no real incentive to even replay it since unlike basically every other visual novel, this one is made in rpgmaker and the dev, Klace, decided that the usual conventions of a visual novel were unimportant and made trundling through his baffling display of making even what could be ~maybe okay~ plot elements plodding chores to get through. I won't lie; like I said, there are some interesting things about it, but the ideas are openly aped from various other games, and the inability to do seemingly simple, expected Visual Novel amenities - skipping already read text to choices, saving anywhere, a wide variety of facial expressions for the characters - really hurt any drive to want to play this game ever again. There ~are~ different portraits of most characters in the game, but only one other, sort of introductory portrait, and then you rarely if ever see it again in the game. There is a rare example of one entire character having a different set of expressions and they honestly should have been taken out because it simply doesn't fit.
There's a wide variety of reasons not to play this game, but I can't stop being fixated on how Klace chose to use RPGMaker's engine to make this instead of an engine made for visual novels. The "Command Remember" artifact from rpgmaker default menu options will probably remain there for some time. I believe before there was an "Always Run" option that was an artifact. Did Klace remove the latter and not the former for some specific reason? Who knows! Not being able to rewind text to review conversations, another staple of most VNs, is upsetting and unfortunate. Having ~save points~ designated combined with the fact that you speed through text you've already read to choices means that you'll sped a lot of time clicking textboxes or tapping enter and probably sighing and wondering if you really care about the game this much to go through this.
Do not waste your money on this. There are far better visual novels out there. If you are a furry and find some appeal in this visual novel because of that, don't!!!!! It's just not good.
Go play Analogue - A Hate Story or Hate+, its sequel. Or Digital: A Love Story. Or hell, play Saya no Uta or one of the many Higurashi visual novels that are on steam. They are all less of a headache than this.

A remake of one of the best Spectrum games of all time, Chaos, even in it's early access state, is the most fun you'll ever have with a gooey blob.
Created by Julian Gollop (author of the original and creator of UFO/X-Com, Laser Squad, etc), it's basically a turn-based strategy game that pits wizards against each other armed with a lottery of spells, and coupled with the best reason for a random number generator to exist - ever.
Playable either live or asynchronously (start a game, and each player takes their turn in their own time), the last wizard standing wins. The random nature of the game might not be to everyone’s taste, but it’s a game of managing the odds and knowing when it’s worth taking a risk that leads to an amazingly addictive game that, at times, will have you winning a game against odds that you didn’t think were possible.
As a remake, and as it stands at the moment, I have no hesitation recommending it, yet there are a lot of things planned for the future that drastically expand upon the original’s concept.
If you remember the original game, you need this. If not, give it a go anyway. Even if strategy games aren’t your thing, you might find this one a lot more fun than most.

I am another one of those old-timers who played the original Chaos game on the ZX Spectrum 30 years ago. To be honest I never stopped playing it. There have always been enough emulators and remakes on various devices to allow me to keep playing even when the Spectrum long ago retired to the attic.
Chaos is a mixture of poker and 3d battle chess, but that hardly does the game justice at all. You and your opponents each control a wizard on a hex map. Each turn you can summon creatures to fight for you, use direct magic attacks against your opponents, or create gooey blobs that spread across the map covering everything in deadly goo.
Even though there is an enormous amount of randomness that determines whether each spell or attack succeeds or fails, there are always strategies that give you the best chance of staying alive one more turn. It's always been a key feature of Chaos that you're never dead until you're dead. Last turn reversals are par for the course. The more you push for the win the more vulnerable you are to a lucky retaliation.
Julian Gollop is my favourite game designer bar none. I've been playing his games since 1983, from Chaos to Rebelstar to XCOM and beyond. I was absolutely delighted to back the Kickstarter last Spring 2014 and the progress that has been made since then has not disappointed in any way. The art style is unique. The animations are beautiful. The sound effects are top notch.
The thing about Chaos is it never gets old - unlike me. The replayability comes from the almost infinite combinations of randomness in the way the game can play out with bluffs, double-bluffs and triple-bluffs. I'd recommend the game to anyone who would enjoy chess if it were pretty and more... chaotic, or anyone who likes the randomness and bluffing in poker but wants more strategy. It's a unique genre all of its own in my opinion and I fully expect to be playing the game for years to come.

is a short episodic point and click style with pixelated old style graphics that sort of takes me back to some of the "golden age" games in this genre.  I should mention right off that there is some nudity in this game at a certain point, so that is something for one to consider.  I know some people might be more or less likely to want to play a game that shows anything which could be offensive, so it is certainly worth a mention.  The premise of the game is that Naigye and her niece Cally visit the castle of King Farnham, and meet the king.  He brings them into his throne room, and tells them a story, in which you reenact.  The style of the graphics and the overall feeling this game has is extremely reminiscent for me, bringing me back to those days where games were very simplified in some ways, but the text in this one really "speaks" to you, and this is one of the things I really really like in this game.  The price is great for the length of time, and I'm glad it is at a realistic level for the material involved so far.  I think this could become an extremely nice work once the episodes become available.
Graphics are done very well for the pixelated style, and they remind me of some older games I played years back with a similar style and feeling to them.
The story, while short, has a lot of different reading, if one explores all options.  I found this a very good plus, that so much care was put into every single character, and what they might think or say or do, given each selection.  Some games will have all characters sort of do the same kinds of things, but this game's characters really have a kind of personality that is reflected in their thoughts and actions.  All of the different narrative work is great, and the time and effort put into this is a real bonus if you like to experiment with your point and click style games just to see what will happen.
The way the screens are laid out is nice, with a map sort of near the bottom, and little direction arrows you can click on if you want to move to another location.  It's easy to follow, and I'm a big fan of having some sort of navigation or maps in most games I play.  The arrow will be greyed out more if you cannot go that way at the current time.  I'm really glad there's a map system, though so far it's not too hard to navigate since it is pretty short.
The work put into the game overall has achieved what I really like in almost "reliving" an older game from the days of the floppy disk.  I love the way everything is collaborated and molded together to create a really fine work of art.  Anyone who likes the older point and click games will really enjoy this I think, especially since there are more episodes to come.  In that regard I can excuse the shortness of the opener, almost like a small teaser to more on the way.
The price is spot on for the length of the episode.  I see other games that are pretty short and priced much higher than this one is.  It's a fair price for what you get, and like I said, old-school point and click people will love this!
Well, the short gameplay is one, since I would love to have enjoyed a bit more, but I can understand since it is an episode-based work.  I cannot wait to see what will happen as the game develops.
I would have liked to have done a little bit more with my surroundings, but the time and effort that has been put into the game already with what is said and thought by characters is pretty nice for the length of the game.  I think characters did not have enough chances to fulfill their roles.  I would have enjoyed a little bit more from each of them in their contrasting specialties and personalities as far as that goes.
The music was fairly charming, but I felt it was a little overpowering in some ways.  It definitely fit the genre and style of the game, but for me it was a little bit too much at some points.  I suppose I could have lowered the volume on certain things like that, and it may have helped though.  I was just going on pure defaults to give an accurate experience with as little changes as possible for my review.
I think I really covered most anything I'd put here at the bottom, but it's a game I definitely recommend, especially for somebody interested in older games niche, or somebody that loves a good point and click.  You can complete it fairly quickly, but more episodes are to come, which is great!  There were no bugs or glitches at all, so everything worked well.  All the time and effort put into the game alone makes it worth checking out.  I liked the vibe, and it really brought me back a bit in many ways.  I kind of already went over it for the most part.  I highly recommend checking this one out for almost anyone.  If you want to play some FPS military game with blood and gore, this is probably not a good one for you, but for the casual fan or point and click enthusiast, this one is a real hidden gem!

This is the initial survival game of The Repopulations UE4 port MMO that they are making, and it really has a ton of depth for a survival game, leveling, loot, a lot of different items to harvest and craft.
It's kind of like a sci-fi version of ARK in the sense that you level up and put points into different stats/skills to progress as you level, gaining new recipes. You will be using futuristic weapons and armor later on in the game, instead of taming dinosaurs.
Most of your time when you start will be consumed by not freezing to death, and eating and drinking, but I found after you get your feet under you, the exploring is pretty fun, it is a great looking world imo.
I'm not usually a big fan of survival type games, findin them too simplistic to really stay enjoyable, but with the added leveling and recipes and loot in Fragmented, it really does feel a little more MMOish and more depth/things to do then most survival games.
The game is a little laggy/buggy atm, but pretty stable for how quickly they got it out, and since the assets are being used for the MMO they are making, I expect there will be plenty of updates and additions as they progress on the MMO and add those items to this game also.

There aren't quite enough positive adjectives I can conjure up to express my feelings for Ori and the Blind Forest.
It's rare that a game will excel in nearly every single aspect, and transcend all that came before it so spectacularly. Whether it be the incredibly sharp controls, the extremely satisfying mechanics, the ingenious level design, the jaw-droppingly beautiful aesthetic, the soaring orchestral soundtrack, the touching story or the powerful atmosphere; these things all stand out as a testament to the sheer amount of love and creativity that was poured into making Ori. And when they all come together in perfect balance, in moments of sheer adrenaline and glorious fun, this game will grip you like very few modern games manage. And it will send shivers down your spine.
To summarise; if you're a fan of MetroidVania's, or puzzle platformers, or... well, video games in general for that matter, then I very, very seriously urge you to go and play this game.

That's not fair, Moon Studios.
That's not fair at all.
You can't do that to someone in the opening five minutes of the game. You can't make me experience so much joy and then so much heartfelt sorrow that I am completely inconsolable before I've even started PLAYING THE ACTUAL GAME. That's not fair. That's inhumane!
But I did it. I completed the whole game. And godDAMMIT you tore my heart out again and again and again with this game, unrelentingly. I completed it and spent five whole solid minutes crying my eyes out before I could even muster the will to close the game so I could get back to my real life.
Everything about this game is beautiful. From the beautiful hand-drawn art, the epic and deep storyline, the breathtaking music, the well placed and directed narration, the gameplay mechanics themselves, the challenge, the level design, the placement of secrets, the ingenuity of puzzles and that feeling you get when you work them out, even such tiny details like how well the controls are laid out and how intuitive they are, as well as particular lighting changes, and how a tiny, relatively flat area is turned into a sprawling multidirectional maze at one segment until you reach your goal there! VERY well done!! I put something like sixteen hours into this game, and could easily go back and play it all again to grab those last secrets and max out my ability tree, mostly just because of the achievements and that satisfied feeling of 100% completing a game that I love this much.
As for the story, I daren't say anything that might be a spoiler, but buckle up because you are in for a hell of a ride. As heartwrenching as it is, the game has beautiful moments of tenderness and warmth, and the ending is stunningly beautiful, even with so few words spoken.
The game has its flaws and if I'm going to be completely honest and fair I should mention those too. Firstly, after a certain point, your health meter is largely pointless. You basically die in one hit to environmental hazards (which nicely are very easy to spot that they are going to murder you in one hit even if you've never seen them before), or you can soak about four or five hits tops, if you max out your third skill tree and get the half damage power. Generally speaking though if you're taking that many hits then you probably aren't gonna make it through the segment anyway.
Secondly, there are what are known as "Escape Sequences". There's I think three of them in total? Now be warned, it's not exactly signposted when they're going to happen so as a result I missed a big chunk of one area because I didn't realise that was the 'exit' as it were, and then I was locked into doing it no matter what. Furthermore, these Escape Sequences throw a lot at you all at once. You have to have reflexes of a goddamn cyberninja or something to get through it in one go, ESPECIALLY on the finalé one. There's often very little if any clear direction of where to go and where to proceed, but that's forgiveable for a studio's first outing.
As a first game, there IS a bug that I have encountered and it was a doozy. Thankfully, not a game breaker as it turns out. After getting a particular "key" object aat one point in the game's third act, I found I was falling through the level geometry, which made the game uncompletable as I could never get back to where I wanted to, forever falling into other areas of the map or dying. Thankfully, closing and restarting the game fixed it, but it WAS very aggravating. Thankfully I saved just before that happened.
Everything else however is absolute solid gold... All the women and men of Moon Studios deserve every praise and accolade they get. This is a masterpiece, especially for a first outing. Well done, Moon Studios! Looking forward to your next game with great anticipation!

I just finished this Welsh point-and-click adventure game. You find yourself in a desolate farmhouse in Wales and get to investigate strange ghost-demon related activity there. Let's begin with the fact that it was fun at some times and some of the puzzles were enjoyable. Some moments of the story, too. On the other hand, many of the puzzles were very typical (find a light bulb to enter an unlit room etc.), some of the puzzles were randomly stupid. Many of the parts of the storyline are boring and they feel really random and illogical.
The game was made in 2008, but it feels like 1997. Graphics is OK at times, but most of the time it feels like a high school project, same goes with animation (but there isn't much of that). Music is almost non existant and when it's there, it feels like MIDI made by a single person over a weekend...
Rhiannon was made by a three person development team with Wintermute - freeware amateur software for creating point-and-click games. I got it in a game bundle, but I wouldn't recommend paying more than $1 for this game.
Also, there are bugs. Sometimes inventory items disappear. Sometimes menu buttons (MAP) disappear. If you save afterwards, you'll never get them back. It is a known and never corrected issue.
To sum up: if you ever played a point-and-click adventure game, you probably won't enjoy Rhiannon. If you haven't, you may enjoy it. I wouldn't recommend it though.
GRAPHICS: 4/10
AUDIO: 3/10
GAMEPLAY: 3/10
STORY: 2/10

A lovely but flawed hard adventure game. Would be especially attractive to fans of Myst/Riven.
The story is very engaging, and the puzzles are "realistic" in that they are never obvious. There is no hand-holding: it's very challenging. Not quite Riven-challenging, but you better take care to look closely at every clue. The puzzles are fair, but sometimes the clues are extremely subtle. For fans of hard puzzles, it would be greatly rewarding to solve them through patience and sheer perseverence. If you're looking for a casual point-and-click, however, this is definitely not it. With a walkthrough, though, it could definitely be a more casual experience.
The UI is annoying: many times you have to click in a very small area, but there is no indication if you get it wrong. Too many times I had the right idea, but thought I was mistaken because I didn't click at exactly the right place. That felt quite unfair.
Another problem is the rather weird pace. You would think that puzzles would get harder towards the end, but suddenly they become easier. It almost feels rushed. Well, except for the very last puzzle ... those always have to make no sense, right?

Dream is an indie first-person adventure game where you play the role as Howard Phillips, a man obsessed with his dreams, and,  just as the game's name and that sentence implies, you play as him in said dreams.
Dream is somewhate educational; throughout the game, you can find various bubbles with paper encased within them floating around. Upon interaction, they tell you random facts about objects and things that are found in your dreams, and what they mean if you see it in a dream. I thought this was pretty neat, seeing as I was once previously interested in such information, and I had to use a website to learn about that stuff. Well... now the game does that for me. xP
Dream is nothing extraordinary in my opinion, but it's good to play if you want to just relax and immerse yourself in some nice atmospheres, as well as not minding having to do some puzzles at times. The game also offers a very lovely soundtrack composed by Norman Legies, which compliments the game rather well.

Tic-Toc-Tower is a fast-paced platformer with some of the most intense yet simple gameplay I have ever experienced. The game revolves around overcoming an onstacle course within the span of ten seconds, or twelve if you managed to grab a clock on the previous level. The levels are randomly chosen from a batch of many different levels, each with their own clever twists and turns to keep you on your toes, always wondering whether the next level will be incredibly hard or pretty easy.
PROS:
-Extremely catchy and upbeat music
-Great Pixel-art
-Fun
-Addictive
-Has co-op
-Many different modes
-Intense gameplay
-Easy to learn, hard to master
CONS:
-Occasionally throws incredibly unforgiving levels at you
-The art style can sometimes be a bit distracting when looking for platforms which are actually jumpable
-Precision platforming is a bit hard due to the floaty nature of the movement
All in all, this is a wonderful little game at a great price, which, despite it's few flaws, is definitely worth picking up if you are just looking to sit down and have fun playing!
TL;DR:
Buy it, it's fun!

Art style, graphics, animation, itemization, classes/skills, setting/maps etc. Nothing is done particularly well, so the game constantly had me thinking "Instead, I could play another ARPG that is actually fun" and there are plenty of those.

If you like the genre and have some time to waste, by all means give it a try. If not, don't bother. You won't miss much.

Gorgeous & very addictive game with nice pixel graphics & hefty sound-effects.
Objective: Delve into the dungeon as deeply as possible.
You have to act carefully and manage your recources to reach the deeper levels of the dungeon. There you find new gods to worship, better equipment, "runes" and the opportunity to unlock new adventurers to travel even further during your next attempt. When you die (and you will die frequently, thereby loosing your precious equipment) you restart from level 1 again, possibly with a new character, worshipping a new god granting important boni. Fortunately you retain the skills you paid for during the whole game and the gold you earned with the previous character (I'm unsure about the tatoo's...). During your travel in the random levels you will find traps, treasure chests, special single-use equipment, shops with weapons and armor, teachers, rune-smiths, shrines, tatoo-artists and as a matter of course: many, many monsters and elite-monsters! All monsters are attached to their segment but have very nasty special abilities. Hence it's important to watch out for their interplay with the dungeon and the other opponents and to fight them in the correct order, killing ranged attackers first. Sometimes it's better to skip a fight - if possible - but in doing so, you loose the opportunity for important loot, that you might need later on. Some monsters even carry the key you need to get to the next level...
I especially like the feature that some dungeon levels have "sub-levels" that can be unlocked for more monsters and loot. Remarkable are the non-combat random encounter's during the game with different outcomes, depending on your reactions/answers - often conected with your intelligence-score.
Great game, absolutely worth every eurocent! = 9/10

Fragmented is the catalyst Above and Beyond needs to finish The Repopulation.  In case newcomers aren't aware, these developers left their previous server host, Idea Fabrik, over hosting issues and Idea Fabrik also running out of funds.  The whole story is a circus, but you can read up on it online.  Anyway, AaB decided to leave Idea Fabrik and go their seperate ways.  Since they need more funding, they came up with the idea of a survival game set in the Repop universe.
Survival games are THE thing right now.  Steam is saturated with them.  Fragmented uses the UE4 engine .About 90% of the game are the same asset's you'll see in the new Repopulation MMO. Fragmented needs alot of work on the animations and crafting list.  Right now, it's just a list of stuff whereas games like Ark and Rust, have departments you navigate to for crafting certain things.
Fragmented is a mix between Rust and Ark.  You can tell by the name of some of the food items.  They are pretty smiliar to Ark.  The big difference between these games, is that Ark is actually fun even in early access.  Fragmented is short on the monster department.  You have to actually go and look for mobs to fight in Fragmented right now.
Early on, you find plenty of materials to craft clothing and weapons.  This is a great move on the dev's part, but there aren't enough monsters to fight.  This makes the gameplay drag on for awhile.
How the crafting works is, you have a level system.  Every time you collect materials you gain xp, just like in Ark.  When you level, you gain skill points.  You have about 9 or 10 skills to level, and when you level those with skill points, you learn new recipes.  So if you want to be a combat character, you level up melee or ranged, and can craft better weapons.
Seeing as how Fragmented is just a catalyst to make more money to eventually finish Repopulation, I don't see the dev's putting in a lot of polish on this long term.  They will push this out of early access, hopefully sell a few thousand units, and make enough cash to finish Repop. That's what I hope anyway. I really don't care for Fragmented, I just want to eventually have a working Repopulation game that I paid $100 for.

So far I have seen many positives from Fragmented and the future looks even more promising.
Graphics
________________
As far as graphics go, they are a massive improvement over The Repopulation. This gives me great hope for what the new version of Repop will be like when its coded for UE4. There are minor glitches with weapons but that is to be expected from an early alpha release. The lighting is great and makes many of the familiar creatures look much better than they did previously. There is always room for improvement but they are on point for today's Survival Game standard.
Survival
________________
The basics are all there, food, water, health, energy. Resources were not super abundant, nor were they overly scarce, I was able to survive without dying at all on my inital playthrough of the game. There are a number of food items that can be upgraded into better food items or even drinks, at higher levels there is a farming system in place for growing sustainable crops for a settlement. The NPCs were easy enough to dispatch with the help of bandages and I reccomend stocking up on them because they are a life saver when you are starving or dying of thirst.
Crafting
________________
Crafting recipes are aquired as you invest points into a number of skills and the recipes get stronger as you advance. Right now even in the early stages there are lots of items to craft from basic refined resources all the way up to off road vehicles and large technological buildings. I have spoken to the developers and they plan on adding an in depth crafting system similar to the one that is being developed for their MMO The Repopulation. This  is huge news as it will make the crafting the most advanced and in depth crafting system of any Survival Game to date. I look forward to seeing this develop.
Combat
________________
Combat felt fluid and the animations were nice as well. There are ranged and melee weapons from basic rock knives all the way up to Laser Rifles and beyond. Bases/Building
________________
There are a log of prefab structures you can place on base platforms that you craft of varying levels of durability. You can make everything from small huts to large cities based on how many resources you have at your disposal. The interiors have easy to use placement for items you wish to craft for decorative or use puproses. The developers also mentioned they are importing a lot of interior items for both functionality and RP purposes.
My overall opinion of the game is high and it has lots of promise in the future. I look forward to following the development as it grows into one of the top Survival Game contenders.

However I have been following the development of this game for the last 8 months and am now certain that this game is the real deal and will be a worthy successor to the brilliant original.  Any feedback left of the forums is taken into account and any features that did not work have been changed or removed completely.
Some people complain about the RNG and how there is a degree of luck in the game but Chaos Reborn is all about successful risk management.  It is possible for a weaker player to be lucky and beat a stronger player but they would not win over a long run of games.  I actually prefer this system as it means no matter who you are playing or how far the game has swung one way there is still a chance you can win or lose.
Julian Gollop is the mozart of the gaming world and his games will be remembered as classics long after other games fade into history!  If you enjoy turn based strategy games then this game will entertain you for years and possibly decades.

This game is simply awesome. It's a turn based wizard battle game, with some very extensive future plans. The game also support asynchronous multiplayer (kinda like e-mailing a chess game, except the game servers do all the work for you. Simply an awesome game.

You start in an arena with one to three other wizards. You have one of several staffs and a plethora of spells. You can summon hordes of creatures and send them into battle while you support them with your magic. Or cast sword of law, hop aboard a manticore, and challenge the enemy wizards in personal combat. You can bluff by summoning creatures as illusions. Entrap hostile monsters with the gooey blob. Singe your opponent's eyebrows with a magic bolt. There is a great deal of strategy involved, but luck also plays a big role in the game, making every match unique.
Every spell you cast has a percent chance to succeed. Every attack you make has a percent chance to kill. There are no hit points in Chaos Reborn. An action is either wildly successful or a dismal failure. This makes for exciting swings in fortune! One moment you might be sitting on top of the world because you've cornered your opponent with a sapphire dragon, unicorn, and giant spider. Suddenly, your opponent's magic bolt kills your spider, your opponent runs the unicorn through with her sword, and your opponent's rat somehow manages to slay your dragon (an 8% chance!). Now you're on the back foot and have to do some fast thinking to salvage the situation.
The luck factor can create some ridiculously funny situations in Chaos Reborn. My most fun and memorable games have involved wild swings in fortune. That being said, careful planning is still a very important aspect of the game. You must be constantly aware of your chances, maximize your odds, and prepare a backup plan in case lady luck doesn't go your way. Bluffing can also help control the influence of luck. (See below.)
Although all spells have a percent chance to fail, you can choose to cast any creature as an illusion and automatically be successful 100% of the time. An illusion behaves precisely like a "real" creature: it can attack, defend, fly, and carry you around on its back if it is a mount. But perhaps an enemy wizard suspects that huge dragon you summoned last turn is an illusion. He casts Disbelieve on your dragon and it vanishes in a puff of smoke. That's the downside to using illusions. If the dragon had been real, the Disbelieve spell would have failed and your opponent would have wasted his turn! If you are a great bluffer, you can probably get away with summoning lots of illusory creatures. If you are a very perceptive person you can probably deduce which creatures your opponents have summoned as illusions and Disbelieve them!
I am a big fan of the graphics in this game. The art direction is distinctive and avoids the typical visual cliches associated with well-known fantasy creatures like unicorns and dwarves. Spells and creatures identifying with the concept of Law tend to have cool colors and a rigid crystalline appearance. Spells and creatures identifying with the concept of Chaos tend to have warm colors and an "entropic" aesthetic. If you like unique art direction, you will love this. If you prefer predictable visuals that you can easily associate with character models from other games, this will probably not be your cup of tea.
There is a great deal more to be added in the coming months. There will be a social rank system with orders (guilds), demi-gods, and gods. Have you ever wanted to be a God? Well start gathering your worshipers because you will have that chance in Chaos Reborn!
Some folks seem to be under the impression that this is a deck-building game similar to Magic: the Gathering. It really isn't. Chaos Reborn does not have thousands of spells to choose from, and you will probably never have full control over the "deck" of spells that you bring into duels.

Solid gane, but some issues may prevent you from enjoying it fully
Good:
Visuals are beautiful and make the game look like an illustration, with the actions flowing from frame to frame. Areas are varied and colors are bright and vibrant, with visuals happen in three different planes.
The story is simple, emotional, but well written. Backstory is told through a single viewpoint via the narrator. Each character has reasons for their actions that the observer can relate to.
Mixed:
Oddly enough, the music. While the music is beautiful and atmospheric, the only music that comes to mind when not playing the game is the main theme.
Controls are generally tight and responsive, but certain actions (at least when using keyboard) are loose enough that issues arise when percision/speed is required (escape/chase sequences).
Instead of different enemies for each areas, the same enemies are used for every area, which only slight visual changes based on area.
Bad:
Despite the areas of the game being inter-connected, the game has a very linear progression path that is tied to story and does not allow one deviate from expected order to get abilites or access new areas.
Once completed, you must to start a new file, as you cannot load your old save to go back to get collectables you may have missed.  This is compounded by the fact there are also missable collectables as well as certain areas become inaccessible due to story.
Multiple escape/chase sequences that have leave little to no room for error.  These events are also set up to progress at a constant pace that does not allow for players to get ahead of it.  These make the sequences feel more like a trial and error gameplay then a frantic attempt to escape
As enemy health scales based on area, as you progress it doesnt feel like you get stronger, which makes the combat upgrades feel useless.

Bought and jumped in to Ori without really knowing anything about the game. I saw a bunch of people were streaming it on twitch, it had a beautiful art style and seemed like something I should check out. I'm glad I did.
You control Ori, "an orphan once more", who adventures to bring back the light that is now gone from the forest. While platforming and fighting through various landscapes you learn new abilities and skills through the main story elements and other collectibles on the map. The basic gameplay flows great and improves more and more as you unlock more advanced moves and are able to traverse the terrain in a variety of ways whether it's your basic doublejumps or more advanced dashes through the air.
The big thing about the game is it's beauty in every single aspect of the game. The obvious one is the stunning artstyle and animation of background and foreground elements melding in to a cohesive landscape of beauty. The beauty however goes much further than that. It's an emotional and touching story presented largely through the music, sounds and art, and it excels at each of them.
From the moment you first open the main menu, to the moment the closing credits end, it's a damn beautiful game definitely worth experiencing. One of my favorite (if not the) platformers ever and an early leader for GOTY 2015. It's a damn near perfect game.

I wont be doing such a long review on this game because I can't really be bothered.
So instead I will give you a small taste of my review.
Major/Minor is a visual novel that revolves on the concept of Anthropomorphic animals. The characters are all astonishing to the eye but it seems to me that they particularly revealing when it comes to clothing.
For example Dazz (Reference: Dazz is the character to the left of the game cover [the purple husky with the gold hair]). The story takes place Japan (also transferring to different worlds throughout the chapters).
Soon after arriving in Japan you receive news of murders that occur during midnight, later on you are handed the task of having to investigate and find out what or who is commiting these murders.
Now at first for me I was pretty interested in getting this game, I didn't know what I was going to expect. As a furry I would have been biased about the opinion, but that's not the case for me and especially for some other furs.
First I would like to give props to the developers on creating a (visual novel) game based on anthropomorphic animals, which is nice to see. Some great games that include anthropomorphic animals as well are Ratchet and Clank, Dust: An Elysian Tale, Star Fox and much more.
Now why did I not recommend this game? Good question. Well the first couple of chapters didn't hook on to me so much, it didn't give me such a 'wow factor' to start off with... The game did leave me to wonder what was going to happen next after each chapter but after chapter 6 I was pretty much done with the game.
And no I was not being serious when I said Sakura Spirit is better than this game, it was pretty much just satire.
Looking from the reviews, I was seeing some sort of dispute between some person and one of the devs (Kyle Lambert). The reviewer in question did state that most of the characters in the novel are from other peoples fursonas and while doing research on it, it is well and fairly true. As a matter of fact one of the characters which is Rook commented on this review, and he is the owner of the fursona (I think, idk).
I'm not going to say that it was a bad thing to place others fursonas into the game but it just shows a lack of originality from the developers and possibly a sign of lazyness as they cannot even create most of the characters in the novel. But who am I to complain, i'm lazy as well.
I don't plan to continue from Chapter 6, I might probably come back to read the rest of the remaining chapters but for now i'll just leave the game sitting on my library.
And please don't be salty over my review, it is my opinion after all and you should respect it (even if its just a little bit of respect). Besides, the butthurt furries in the fandom are usually the ones who contribute to giving our fandom a bad name.
My Rating: 3/10.

Denny Crane here, and I cannot recommend this video game. Here are the reasons. These reasons will also stand for the first three versions of this one video game and shall be posted accordingly.
1. Sloppy copy and paste approach. The took the first three video games and just combined them "loosely" into one giant video game. The problem is, they changed a few things, but at the same time, left other things in that have zero affect upon this version itself that affected the original three chapters.
2. Your ghost lady companion is designed only half a-s-s-e-d. First, she stops gaining new levels after 60, which quickly makes her become obsolete later in the video game. She also has a tendency to just stop attacking enemies as if nothing is wrong. This makes certain parts almost impossible to complete unless the video game "decides" she should attack again.
3. When you design a mode of the video game that is only beatable by cheating, that is a bad design choice. There is a mode called "Hardcore." In this mode, if you die, the whole video game is over. You have to start fresh, anew, creating a whole new character. My office IT guy showed me away around this so that I can bypass the limitation. But that still means the only way to beat this mode is to cheat. There are COUNTLESS times when a simple swipe or random chance that kills your guy with one hit. Can you imagine being so far into this video game, only to HAVE to start all over again?
4. Spelling errors. I know this video game was not made in the good ol' US of A, however if you are going write for a video game English, get someone who knows how to read. There is a series of clothes that are named "Wicth Hunter..." and every time I read that, my head hurt.
5. The items in this video game do NOT scale well as you get further into the video game. Eventually, you just are unable to find anything that is better than what you are wearing... when you still have a 3rd of the video game to play. This could be off set if your ghost lady companion would still level up.
6. The same button to move your character is the same to attack. So when you are trying to attack something, you accidently run towards it and get yourself killed (have to start all over again). That is a terrible choice for controls.
This video game does have some nice things to it but not enough to make up for the frustrating playthrough. I will be posting this review on the other three versions seeing as they are just 1/3 of the same thing.

Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine, while quite underrated and unplayed, is quite a fantastic game. It's blend of genres make it quite unigue when it comes traditional Third Person Shooters ( I know there are other melee based TPS games like Bayonetta ). Though it is not without it's flaws, the variety of game modes means there is something for everyone. Want a great story? Play campaign, want some good team based action? Exterminatus is for you ( PLaying with randoms can leave you with  afeeling of RAGE!!! sometimes ). And of course there is the multiplayer, which in my opinion isn't the strongest part of the game.
The setting and sound design for some people might be considered a bit dull but for any 40K fan it could be considered some of, if not the best in any 40K game to date. The color scheme is a lot of browns and greys but that fights in nicly with the grimdark setting. We also finally have decent sounding bolters for once, they actually sound like powerful weapons they are supposed to be.
There are, as I said, a few things wrong with it. For traditional Codex fans there will be some small problems such as the obscene amount of damage you can take from even the weakest Orks and the use of Lascannons in an anti-infatry role. Such things are quite minor and shouldn't stop you from ejoying the game. Other problems can just be the extreme level of difficulty in both the campaign and Exterminatus. enemies can take quite a few shots before they go down and in return, as  i said before, they can take you done rather quickly if you don't play smart. In contrast to other TPS games, Space Marine has no cover system. As such you must use your mobility to your advantage, with the use of combat rolls, sprint and later on (in limited fashion) the jump pack.
In Exterminatus and Multiplayer, the game is actually a class based game, meaning that you can choose one of three classes to play. In these modes you play as either Space Marines, fighting for the Imperium. And the Chaos Space Marines, fighting for the glory of the dark gods. Both sides are exactly the same in terms of classes and abilites. The three calsses are: The Assault Marine/Raptor, Devastator Marine/Havoc and the Tactical Marine/Chaos Space Marine. Each class has different parks, abilities and weapons. The Assault Marine/Raptor is the master of close combat, is armed with a close combat weapon and a pistol and has a  jump pack. The Devastator/Havoc is a beast at long range, armed with the heaviest armor and heaviest weapons, he can however be beaten quite quickly in close combat without support. And the Tactical Marine/Chaos Space Marine is a very flexible all rounder, with neither the close ranged power of the Assault Marine/Raptor, or the longe range fire power of the Devastator Marine/Havoc. He does however have a lot of options and weapons that neither of the other classes has access to.
There are also an extreme amount of cosmetic customization options. you can have up to five saved custom marine appearences for both the Space Marines and the Chaos Space Marines. There are also a lot of different parts of your armor that can be customized from the helmet and chest plate, to individual legs, arms and pauldrons. Relic also released some DLC  specific sets of armor including: Blood Angel, Salamander, Legion of the Damned, etc for the loyalists. For the traitors there are sets like: Death Guard, Iron Warriors and Emperor's Children. these were not only colour schemes but had custom bits of armor like the Legion of the Damned skull helmet and the salamander shect plate with Drake hide attached. These were unfortunately unchangeable but the community did figure out a workaround.
There are a few over sights and missed opportunities, such a s a lack of vehicular combat. There are a  few turret sections in the campaign and there was a DLC released that let you play in a dreadnaught but that is largely considered unbalanced and is rarely played now. Also the absence of dedicated servers means that multiplayer is often plagued with constant latency issues. And the combat can be consdiered repetative.
tl;dr
+ fantastic campaign
+ setting and sound design
+ varied roles in multiplayer and Exterminatus
+ customization options
- repetitive gameplay
- general difficulty
- lagg issues
- lack of players for multiplayer modes
In summary: Just play it. Rent it, buy it, borrow from a friend. Just try it for yourself, it's still a fun game despite it's flaws.

I already have the Xbox One version of this game, as I bought it to play MWR, so that's how I've experienced the game.
So honestly, I was pleasantly surprised when playing IW here on Steam. Minus the 3-5 minute"pre-loading shaders" BS, the game was responsive, ran well on menus, and was generally a good experience. I didn't want to♥♥♥♥♥♥myself off playing a public match, so I booted up a multiplayer game with bots just now and I had a fun time.
I have a somewhat weak rig, (GTX 1050ti 4GB, AMD FX6300, 8GB RAM) but the game ran infinitely better than Black Ops 3. I had 50-60fps at all times, and I was playing on mostly high settings at max res, max internal res, etc. It is worth noting that I opted to use "optimal settings" and got these results, meaning the pc devs have seemingly put effort into this version. Black Ops 3 on this same rig runs awfully, because there's always stuttering, slowdowns, sluggish menus, etc. But as far as CoD goes, this seems to be a very good port.
I heard kill trading was removed as well, though it is an option in custom games which is nice. You'll find a lot of neat features and customization in this game, not with characters and guns, but how you want to play the game. So that's also nice.
As for the actual game itself, I can't recommend it. The campaign is better than what we've had in recent years. The characters have some degree of personality, and some features from BO3 such as custom weapon classes have been brought back as well. It was generally enjoyable, though my dislike for BO3's campaign may be blinding me from seeing IW's campaign more objectively.
The multiplayer... Where do I start. First off, everybody uses the NV4 or that laser SMG I keep hearing about. While kill trading was removed, the fact it even existed for a time feels insane. I'm the guy to yell from a mountain top about how CoD needs to fix their♥♥♥♥♥♥and stop rewarding players with the best/worse connection (aka MAKE A NEW ENGINE ADAPTED FOR TODAY'S STANDARDS) but kill trading is not the answer. The futuristic stuff is insane. Everybody is constantly flying around and everything is just hard to follow, and there's weird stuff like grenades that follow you around, stuff like that. It ultimately follows BO3's formula, so if you have BO3 you've already played this game. IW's multiplayer is absolutely nothing to get excited about. It's not all that fun. Infected can be a blast, but few people here on PC play it anyway.
As for zombies? Well I don't play Zombies. But the few times I've played the map it comes with, it's been good fun with friends. Also David Hasselhoff. It's not entirely different from Treyarch's zombies, and I'd imagine most religious zombies players are occupied with Chronicles, so I wouldn't buy IW just for this.
In the long run, I'll praise IW for being a good port as opposed to BO3, and having a nice weekend killer of a campaign. Also David Hasselhoff. Okay.  So.  Runestone Keeper.  You have a grid.  You click on a square on the edge of the explored area to search it.
Or click on an explored square to interact with it.  (Temptatriomn to say "Tap" not "Click.")  Each of these clicks takes a "Turn."
Your character is nowhere in particular on the grid.  Fights with monsters happen in a turn based order, but only when you click on them.  <Note, some monsters have a special ability to attack you any time you click anything.  Best to kill them sooner reather than later.>
"Interaction" with explored squares has various contextual outcomes.  It is how you attack monsters, open story dialogs, collect treasure, enter shops, worship at shrines...  There's a lot of options.
So you have monsters, loot, leveling, skills, upgrades, runestones... which do not get adequately described if you ask me... Stats, figured stats, more loot, and a whole lot of special monster abilities.  Including one that causes the monster to explode if you don't kill it quickly.  There is also something to do with gods.  But religion is bad for you so I'm avoiding them for the present.
Overall I do recomend this.  Though I think a $10 price tag is a bit high, I am notoriously cheap.

I knew when I grabbed this game for free as part of a package it probably wasn't going to be my thing. After playing it for a while I can confirm this game is too much like a cow-clicker for my comfort.
Runestone Keeper is a rogue-like dungeon exploration game where you advance by clicking on tiles and revealing whatever lies beneath them. You'll randomly get traps, treasure, monsters, exits, shops, or nothing. Within a session you can gather items and gold to enhance your character. Items you carry have a far greater impact then actually leveling up, so your ability to survive for extended periods is heavily influenced by the monsters and loot you encounter rather then your character. Also, your random ability to actually hit what you click on as attack successes are randomized.
The way your character grows is part of my problem. There is some skill in managing your resources, but it's far too easy to have runs were you both don't get very far and likely won't see any way to improve. There are permanent bonuses you can apply to your character that are supposed to help you, but I never really felt their effect. I also wasn't a fan of the starting character, and getting a more interesting character requires either a great deal of gold grinding or the right amount of skill and equipment grinding to get down to the low dungeon levels. Normally I'd be happy to try and see how low I can get into the dungeons, but when I started encountering monsters with ridiculous hit strength and health that not only regenerated but increased when you don't hit them I had to question why I would spend any more time with this nonsense.
If there was more to unlock that was actually interesting, and if the gameplay was less of a complete grind apparently for the sake of a grind, I might spend more time with this. However, this is just too much like a free to play game for me to recommend anyone actually buy it.

TFoL is... hmm... well, it's... umm... no, that's not quite right... gimme a second to think, here... uhhhhhhhhh... ok, so................. yeah. This game is kind of hard to explain. So I guess what I will say is that this is... sort of like a Quentin Tarantino film that's been super-condensed to a length of just 15 minutes and turned into an art experiment. There's no "gameplay" to speak of - it's a first person interactive story-slash-art-piece, nothing more. The graphics are as simple as can be, but it has some cool ideas and is worth checking out if you are open to these sorts of artsy game experiments. I wasn't kidding before, though - the experience is over in literally 15 minutes or so. So just keep that in mind as far as your personal "price vs. playtime" factor goes.
One other note: this game also includes its prequel, "Gravity Bone", for free. I recommend playing this first. To access it, click "career" in the main menu and select Gravity Bone.

This game is a very good ARPG. Easily holds up to Diablo 3, Torchlight 2, and Grim Dawn.
Pros:
-Combat is really fluid
-Skill Tree is really easy and fun to use. You are also allowed to respec as much as you want so you have a lot of freedom in how you build
-6 classes to play as with different playstyles and builds
-End game is really good. It is similar to Diablo 3's adventure mode, but still having it's own unique characteristics like faith points and being a lot more challenging
-Pet system is amazing. Out of all the ARPGs games like Torchlight and FATE with pet systems, this game has the best one. There is a lot of freedom in building Lady Katarina, and she is really powerful. You can build her to do her own thing like do damage or tank, or build her to just support Van Helsing. Regardless of how you build her she is very powerful.
-Campaign is really good. Comes with all 3 games put together with most of the DLC. Worth the money easily. The storyline is really good and Katarina and Van Helsing's banter is worth listening to. Voice acting is top notch no complaints there.
-Multiple difficulty options that can be changed whenever similar to Diablo 3's torment system.
Cons:
-Game balancing can make fights hard.
-Advneture Mode can get hard due to having limited lives or time
-You need online to play Adventure mode by yourself.
-No one plays the game so you might need to find your own friends.
If you plan to get this game, they have a promotion (Not too sure if it is still going) but if you own the first three Van Helsings you get Final Cut for free from Neocore's website. You can just skip those three and enjoy Final Cut since it has all the content and improved mechanics of the later games.

[Updated 5/5/15]
While recent updates have brought many improvements, including fun new spells, gear, leveling system, map improvements, and better textures, I must now also temper this recommendation due to some recent changes. Online battles (the only game mode really worth mentioning at the moment; single player is still basically practice mode and provides no rewards) are now skewed in several ways. Law has a superior spell set, and nearly everyone I've encountered is therefore playing law, which makes for boring matchups. The new system of wizard and gear leveling was thrown into all matchmaking options, so new wizards can expect to be frequently paired up against level 30+ opponents with bigger hands, bigger decks, and spells and talisman abilities that require a good deal of grinding to acquire. And yes, the game has become very grindy. There have also been some questionable changes to the line-of-sight formula, which is now driven by a ruleset whose results are frequently counter-intuitive, also to the detriment of new players; example:
Hopefully these are just growing pains, and the balance and easy-to-pick-up nature of the game will be restored soon. I still recommend this game to hex strategy and RPG fanatics based on its future features (development definitely seems to be on track), but I strongly suggest waiting out these kinks before taking your first plunge.
[Update for 12/22 patch]
The most impressive game project I've had the pleasure of backing on Kickstarter. Development is moving swiftly and productively, and the latest Steam Early Access version now includes an offline play option with support for up to 4 human or AI opponents in addition to the existing online multiplayer options. This is essentially a hotseat mode but is limited to free for all, with no team play option yet. This combined with the rudimentary but passable AI make it great for learning the game or battling it out with friends, but you'll still have to rely on matchmaking to scratch that co-op itch. This release also brings us some new spells, showcases a new environment skin, and adds some seasonal holiday details to some of the creature models. A handy play guide is now also featured on the launch screen to help get started, and is highly recommended reading for every new player.
The final feature set will be nothing short of stellar at this pace. The devs care about just about everything, and that is already beginning to show throughout. I'm focusing on quality and development here because the fundamental concept is already rock-solid: turn-based wizard hex strategy with spell decks plus all the usual online roleplaying frills (guilds, gear, pvp/pve) PLUS a social ladder in which you can become a king or even a god, design your realm, and act as an NPC opponent when you're offline (and customize, track, and be rewarded for your performance as such!). If you're not sold already, then you are definitely in the wrong place.
A few other points are worth mentioning here. The temporary, placeholder leveling system in use now doesn't take long to max, but will be fully replaced (likely accompanied by a stat reset). The game does not have native controller support, although it has been suggested that it may make the final feature set. It is rather easy to map with Xpadder or the like in the meantime.
All in all, if you have even the slightest love of roleplaying or strategy games, this is one you will want in your Steam library sooner or later.

While I believe this is a remake of an older game, I only have very distant memories of a game that may or may not be similar on the PS1. So my perspective is mainly that of a newcomer. I love strategy games, and while I watched a video of it on YouTube I still wasn't 100% sure what playing it would be like.
The game is deceptively simple in premise - you are a squishy wizard, and you can move, attack and cast a spell (which are generally to summon creatures or deal direct damage) during your turn, and likewise move and attack with any creatures, in any order. The other player(s) - up to 4 total - then take their turns. There is no health - there is just a percentage chance to kill based on the stats. While seemingly simplistic, the gamble is thrilling as you can only really tip the odds in your favour and reduce the risks to your own demise.
Creatures have strengths and weaknesses, and there are spells that provide tactical and defensive advantages as well.
One thing that does add an extra dimension is when you cast a spell, it has a % chance for success based on the strength of the creature you are summoning. You can choose to cast it as an illusion with 100% success, and it will be just as effective, unless your opponent uses their spell to disbelieve your summon for the illusion it really is. So there is an element of poker going on there too. Your chance to cast creatures depends on the current overall magic-o-meter, which can swing between law and chaos depending on what types of spells the wizards are casting. Neutral spells are not affected by this.
There looks to be future mechanisms to allow you to change the appearance of your wizard and introduce more RPG elements, but I ended up jumping into frays with experienced players and holding my own quite well.
The graphics are detailed and not overblown, as is the music and atmosphere, and the UI and overall feel is good and generally well executed - especially for an early access game.
Currently it's multiplayer (real time or play-by-mail-like) only at present, with single player to come but people seem friendly.
I'd say this game has a lot of longevity and you will find yourself wanting to come back to it time and again. Thoroughly recommended for anyone who wants a modernised and well polished version of old-school strategy at its best :)

Oh my this game is so good.  It's unforgivingly hard, even on Easy difficulty, but it's never unfair.  Every time I fail (and I fail over and over again) it never feels like the game cheated me out of victory, but that I needed to play better.  Further, I can't play this as a marathon play session.  After 10 or 15 minutes my concentration starts to break, I stop improving, and I have to quit for a while and come back later.  And I do keep coming back.
As to what the game is actually like, the trailer video is a good representation.  If you see that and want to play, you won't be disappointed.  If you see it and aren't sure, maybe just watch some perfect runs on Youtube.  Different genres appeal to different people.
The only difference between Normal and Easy is there are no coins to collect in Easy.  That's it, all the obstacles and platforming challenges remain.  In theory you could play through the game on Normal that way and just ignore all the coins to complete the levels more easily.  But there's so much to focus on that's harder than it seems, and removing the distraction does make a difference.
And the difference between Normal and Perfect is you have to collect ALL the coins and other scoring opportunities in a level to pass it.  This is actually really helpful.  When you're trying for a perfect run on a level you don't have to fail on purpose and lose your momentum if you miss something.
So the only reason to play the game on Normal is for the Braid achievement.  Otherwise I recommend switching between Easy to see the whole game (and make the Endure achievement easier) and Perfect for collecting all the things.  Beating a level on Normal doesn't feel quite as thrilling when you know you left some points behind.  (It still does feel pretty awesome though.  Just even more awesome when you get all the things.)
The only misstep in the whole thing is Odyssey (stage 1.11).  And it's not bad, it's as great as everything.  But it may be the hardest stage in the game, and it feels like a wall to get stuck on compared to earlier and later advancement.  It seems to be included as early as it is not because of a difficulty progression, but because as you progress you are taught new skills, and Odyssey doesn't require abilities and tricks that later levels do.
One final note -- other reviewers have talked about the artistic quality of the graphics and music.  But the level design throughout is art too, and a joy to experience.

Whilst I haven't played many games of the Point and Click genre, I do know that the game Scratches has a much bigger map than this one. The voice acting is good, and the graphics aren't too bad but certainly not top notch either. You may find the fonts used throughout the game (even on the main menu) offputting as they don't blend well with the game or interface in my opinion.
I bought it at a discounted price, but to be honest I am having trouble deciding whether or not it was worth that. The storyline was good but, leaves a lot to be answered as we never do meet the girl who is the 'damsen in distress' throughout the entire game. That being said though, it has an interesting theme and I did enjoy the puzzles for the most part.
As for the horror factor, there were a couple of parts that made me jump but it's not really a scary game. The music throughout was sub-par, but bear in mind this may have been made on a small budget.
In conclusion, if you like point and click games Rhiannon: Curse of the Four Branches has some tricky puzzles, and will be worth picking up at a discounted price. If you are looking for horror, this is very mild at best. And if bad fonts bother you, I wouldn't go for it. Still, I'd recommend it as I managed to finish the game and the story is fairly thorough.

TL;DR:  This is a great remake from the visual and audio standpoint, but it totally fails as a game due to bad controls and performance.
Clunky controls no matter what scheme you use, poor performance (in many areas I had 20-40 fps regardless of settings, and my CPU, GPU and memory were never at 100% or even 50% load), and a horrible camera. Going from 2D to 3D made it very hard to sometimes understand whether an object is on the background or blocking your way.
All of the above coupled with the fact there are many areas in the game where you have to act fast make the game not enjoyable at all. This is somewhat rectified by the ability to use quick save / quick load, but even with that function many areas in the game are very frustrating.
Another thing (that's also true about the original game) is that many areas feel identical, and you basically do the same over and over again. Remember and reproduce the password, evade the explosives, run&jump over bombs, etc. What was ok in the 90ies looks boring in 2010+. Whether you like it or not, games come a long way in 20 years.
P.S. The very last level is simply infuriating even with quick save/quick load. I can't imagine how it can be completed in one go: you have to go through 4 razor blades, jump around some mines and disarm 3 mines. All of this requires split-second timing, and needs to be done under 2:30 minutes. I hink in that one location I died more than in all Dark Souls combined. Did the developers think that is fun, seriously? The whole game is pretty hard, but they decided to add an insanely and unjustifiably difficult level in the end. This is NOT FUN.

This game is an amazing splice of morbidity and cuteness!

It has greatly improved since the first chapter came out and is definitely gonna be one of my all-time favorite visual novels. Pawzi Clawzi's art is amazing, the writing is absolutely stunning, and the cast of characters are as cute as they are enigmatic and charming.
The story delves into many situations that make you question the legitimacy of your morals and realize the indefinite consequences of your actions. The game isn't afraid to talk about serious and potentially controversial topics, and makes you question everything. Every character has 2 sides. There is no definite good or evil. The decisions you make determine who lives and who dies.
Unlike other games I've played, ALL the characters in this game actually felt as if though they had a purpose. Everyone had their own individual story that resonated with me. No matter who I met, I was astonished by the bonds that had formed between us. It actually hurt me to see some of them die and at moments I would tear up.
This game has definitely left it's mark on me. I had voted for this game on Greenlight way back when. Back then the writing wasn't pretty, rash decisions were made, and rumors and hate ran rampant. But I stayed with the game... and I'm glad I did. As the chapters came out one by one, I could see exponential imrpovement in both the writing and the game itself as a whole. Slowly, I watched as a masterpiece was made.
I'd expect no less from the highly talented Klace. I have been following this title since the start and I have seen seen his writing improve greatly over the chapters.
I will always remember the message of the story, as well as the journey behind it, and I can't wait for what Klace plans next.
10/10
Nearing the end of a fantastic journey filled with despair and chaos, knowing that we are so close to the end, I come to realize that I would never be the same and that the choices i've made will bear fruition to the outcome of my character.
