In this game, you'll play as a number of trained soldiers who are constantly outrunned and beaten to death by a number of half-decayed reanimated corpses. It takes about 2 shotgun blasts at point blank range to kill one zombie, yet punching them with your non dominant arm immediately kills them. With this tactic, it would be very easy to just punch your way out of the zombie apocalypse, but unfortunately, the survivors have some strange mental disorders. For example, if you're dual wielding pistols and go to punch a zombie, the survivor will immediately flip his guns out again, despite the obvious fact that he wields the fist of doom. This leads to a wierd situation in which you'll be trying to punch the zombies, but the survivor you're playing as constantly flips his guns around like a deranged circus performer.
Occasionally, and by ocassionally I mean all the time, you'll hear a roar taken from Half-Life 2, and a large amount of zombies will spawn out of thin air and rush towards you. Among these zombies are some infected soldiers, who wear body armor and require about 10 minutes of continuous fire to kill. These ones also hit a lot harder than the regular zombies. Hell, the idea that a scrawny, half-dead humanoid can flail its arms around and incapacitate a healthy soldier is dubious enough, so I'll just suspend my belief in pretty much everything and accept that these armor laden zombies can keep on their feet after having 4 rounds of buckshot emptied into their faces.
About halfway through each mission, there comes a point where you have to rip off Counter Strike and plant a bomb. After this, the only thing you have to do is hightail your♥♥♥♥♥out of there before the damn thing explodes. Just to make people aware, the Complete Edition is the exact same as the old edition, there is nothing different between them. Buying one should grant you both (that's how I got this 'free', by owning the original), but there's very little reason to start both unless farming for cards. I never quite understood why we needed 2 identical versions, and I still don't.
That aside, let's review the game:
+ 2 very interesting inter-connected stories
+ Very long for a visual novel
+ Large cast of interesting characters
+ Great art
+ Branching paths throughout entire game rather than just the end most VN's have make this rather replayable.
+ Developer listed to player feedback and is very rapid to fix any reported typo's
- Wording can be a bit odd at times, you still understand it, it's not VN Engrish that's so common, just feels a bit quirky.
- Since it's made with RPGMaker and not VN software there is no manual saving, fast forwarding or dialogue log. Going faster requires you to hold space or enter. Makes it extremely tedious if you want to go for 100%, which requires a few playthroughs or long sessions with specific savegame locations
- Only 2 art stances for most characters. One got more (and they look great) but sadly the "talk" is only shown once at introduction and then a single one is used throughout the game. Certain sections, like the sadder story-segments could do with another artpiece to reflect that just like Eclaire has.
- Despite it's long duration already it feels like it doesn't spend nearly enough time on Terra as I wanted it to have.
I came into this game with a bit of worry that it would just cash on the characters (which, true, also was how it catched my eyes), so I am very glad that initial fear turned completely false and this is one of the better more interesting VN's you can find on Steam. If your interest in VN's is in dating rather than plot you should steer clear though, none of that is in this game, it's pure story. And what an enjoying one it turned out to be. Looking forward to the next games of this developer!

After playing Sara is Missing and hearing about Simulacra through that purveyor of all things horror-related, Night Mind, I decided to check it out.  I was pleasantly surprised.  The story is much more developed compared to SiM, and I enjoyed exploring Anna's phone.  The concept of the game was much more interesting than SiM, though I feel like it could still be better developed and hope the devs continue with this idea.  While the text speak used by the main "players" of the game was perfectly realistic, I felt that the primary antagonist of the game
would not have the spelling errors I encountered in that character's texting.  For instance, the character used "lead" instead of "led" and "it's" when "its" was intended.  I know, I know, others might not have noticed or been affected by this, but I felt that the character would not have made those errors.
Overall, the characters were better developed than SiM, definitely.  Anna was three-dimensional, and so were the characters we encountered.  Omitting Iris
, was a good decision.  I don't know if the plan is for DLC or sequels, but I look forward to a continuation of the Simulacra and/or Iris story-line, in this world where technology has a mind of its own.
For the devs:
All that being said, I do hope you continue and would love to play any other games set in this world.  If you appreciate nothing else from my review, let it be: less is more.  Subtle horror is better than overt horror.  The idea that somebody might be in the room with you, where you're holding that phone, or the idea that you might lower the phone and see, I don't know, a floating disembodied head, was so much more effective than momentary flashes of the screen turning into something scary.  And if
It's the suspense that gets you, not the actual scare.  You don't have the suspense before the jump scares on the phone, just an image shift.
Nevertheless, public who have reached this far (or TLDR), I do recommend this game.  It isn't a long game, but I've spent...7 hours in it so far?  And intend to spend more unlocking achievements.

This is a decent action RPG that wears out its welcome after a while.
Good stuff:
+ Great gothic/steampunk atmosphere with just about every trope from Eastern European folklore and old horror movies tossed into the mix. If you liked that Van Helsing movie from a few years back (an underrated classic) or if your favorite DnD setting is Ravenloft, you'll appreciate this.
+ Good dialogue between Van Helsing and his ghost companion, Katarina. She gets better lines than any other sidekick in an ARPG I've played.
+ There's a surprising number of mini-games available in your home base, including a Tower Defense game that is way better than it has any right to be and some odd soldier assignment missions that feel like they're out of a mobile phone game.
+ The ability tree is huge and reminded me of the Sphere Grid in Final Fantasy X.
Meh stuff:
- There's not much variety in the look of weapons/armor. Making your character look cool is a huge draw of ARPGs, but aside from sporting a sleeker hat, my endgame Van Helsing looked pretty similar to my beginning Van Helsing.
- The endless array of nerdy easter eggs is cute at first, but gets tiring over time.
- Enemy AI isn't very good, and the game's entire gimmick revolves around throwing bigger mobs at you, which becomes old after the 20th hour.
- I know that this is three games in one, but I feel like there's almost *too much* content here. My favorite part of Van Helsing: Final Cut was the first game, which features just the right balance of Romanian-style forests and Victorian cityscapes. The later two games start including more filler sections that weigh the whole experience down.
- Apparently the multiplayer function is broken, though I wouldn't know as I only played solo.
Anyhow, I can't compare this to similar gothic fantasy ARPGs like Victor Vran or Grim Dark, since I haven't played those yet, but I will say that as a single player experience, I found the game more engaging than Torchlight II (if only for the superior story) and for a time even liked it more than Diablo III, though Diablo III has much more replay value. Get it if you like classic horror themes, but be aware that it lacks the polish of similar titles and may get boring over time.

Dream is a good adventure game filled with lots of puzzles. Currently, the game suffers from quite a few bugs, but the game is still in its alpha stage for a reason. The game's mood swings from being relaxing to moderately scary. Scary enough that you start to get goosebumps, but not so scary that you want to turn off the game, which is good. I have yet to find anything in the game that can 'kill' you, though there is at least one enemy in the game.
Despite being a good game, it does have flaws.
The game's biggest flaw, I'd have to say, is that the game never gives you any idea as to what you're supposed to do. This does have some upsides to it for fans of exploration, though players trying to simply get on with 'the main quest' (if one even exists) will find themselves a bit annoyed. Also, it'd be nice for there to be a part of the map that tells you where you are right then and there, so you don't get lost.
As for its strengths, it has plenty. Personally, I enjoy listening to the protagonist. He has a good sense of humor, and allows some of the darker parts of the game to be a bit more bearable. Also, the surreal environments are just gorgeous. Also, the game never holds your hand, which is also a very good thing.
Over all, I'd say if you like surreal environments, exploration, don't mind just a touch of horror, then this game will be worth your money.

As of v0.22:
Chaos Reborn is a game about tactical turn-based duels of wizards.
Grab your wizard, spawn on the battlefield and use your spells and summons to defeat the competitor.
The game was designed by Julian Gollop - a father of original X-com game - so, it has some very interesting mechanics and they can assembly into pretty complex strategies even though they look pretty simple.
Do you want to summon a real creature or trick the opponent with an illusion? Do you want to go for a quick kill or take it slow and steady?
You will have to consider a lot of things during the game. And once again - don't let the simplicity of a rules and mechanics trick you - this game is not an easy one.
At the moment game only features the multiplayer mode, so if you want the AI and single player, it's better to wait a bit.
But if you enjoy some pvp action and/or have some friends to play with - this game is pretty fantastic.
More detailed look in the video:

Already one of the most enjoyable tactical games out there. The fantastic thing about this game is every person has 1 health and if you get hit, that's it! You can use mounts to keep your wizard alive but if that mount gets hit then you're on the ground and have only one more hit to take!
The way defense vs strength vs agility and magic resistance works in this game is that changes the percentage chance you have to hit. The height of your units also plays a role in the percentage and you can use mana to boost spells as well. You can either sacrifice cards to get mana or you can pick up one of the mana sprites that spawn in the maps.
Right now it's just multiplayer, but it really is a blast. Definitely proves once again that Julian Gollop knows what he's doing. I am currently backing this at the lord level and will soon be upgrading to king.
Chaos Reborn is the bomb.
It has instantly become one of my favorite games of all time.

My Let's Play featuring four-person Free-For-All Multiplayer can be found here:
My Review:
Turn-based tactical RPG featuring wizards who use cards to cast spells.  The game mechanics work in such a way that you can move, cast, and attack all in a single turn.  Many of your spells are summons that bring in other beasts and baddies to fight for you.  They, too, have their own turn cycle within your turn.  A sub-turn, per summoned creature, if you will.
Depending on the value of the card will determine if you can successfully cast it or not.  The chance of success is clearly shown via a percentage (%) amount on the card itself.  You can increase your chances by investing mana crystals either found on the level itself, signified by the bright glowing plants or by discarding cards.  For 100% chance at casting your spell, you can instead opt to have your summon be an illusion. But you need to be careful, summoning something too powerful early on will be a VERY easy tell that you summoned an illusion and can be easily dispelled.
The multiplayer portion worked without a hitch and even offers an asynchronous mode, so you can play with friends even if you can't align on a time schedule.
Visually speaking, everything is top-notch.  Exotic deadly plant life, lumbering giants, manticores, everything looks amazing!
Really I'm surprised this game is considered Early Access at all.
Kudos to the Dev Team on a stellar Early Access Launch.

NOTE: This review was made for an earlier version of the game and I haven't kept up on the progress of it, so this review may be outdated in terms of current game content.
I don't really understand why the game is getting the reviews it is. I understand it's early access, but there are a lot of things that should have been done from the get-go from a design perspective.  Here is a list of problems I have with it.
- One of the first things I noticed is that there's no infinite loop checking, and you can easily lock up you game by making one. Well, at least with JS, and on that note it could just be a JS issue that Blockly detects but I honestly can't be arsed to check. That not being implemented (for the JS, at least) really shows what kind of game these guys are making, one focused on final results rather than code implementation. For me, this is a big red flag, even though it might seem trivial or nothing at all to someone else. If it is in this state because it was released too early, then
. I am entirely certain that some prodigious beginner programmer has at one point crafted a beautiful spell just to have it be destroyed with a game-freezing accidental open loop that they can't fix.
- Even if one does get far enough into the game as to be able to freeze it like that, the UI feels... unresponsive. I found it difficult to find specific functions In the Blockly editor, and what little time I spent with the interface felt unintuitive and haphazard. Orb creation isn't even called that, rather it's listed as casting another spell... While this makes sense logically based on how the game works (one orb per spell), my first instict was to look for "Create orb" or similar. Even Multimedia Fusion does it better.
- The JS editor is okay, and has a number of simplistic IDE-like features, such as syntax highlighting, simplistic realtime syntax and error checking, and the occasional autocomplete, but the clunkyness and unresponsiveness of the UI still really hampered the experience. Also I wasn't able to find any select all option, to copy it into something that didn't suck to edit, and the mouse selection works when it wants to. To boot, there was no proper error console for all I could find; errors would just pop up at the bottom of the screen, with a surprising lack of information related to the error. Having an actual console like
would be nice, guys.
- There is a code converter that converts Blockly code blocks into JS... This leads me to believe the code blocks actually just generate JS on the fly, which makes me wonder why you can't do the reverse (i.e. JS to Blockly). You also can't edit the generated JS without making a new spell and copy-pasting it. There isn't even a button to do this on the code generation pane, so you'd have to repeat that process for every spell you want to add a little JS flair to.
- There is a distinct lack of proper low-level documentation. Sure, there are some help prompts [in the Blockly interface] and plenty of explanatory beginner spells [also mostly in the Blockly interface], but all of that is just as haphazard as the rest of it. There is no documentation for a number of JS functions that, according to numerous spells posted on their forums, a number of people use regularly. There is no one central place to read about how these functions work, and one of the functions relies on understanding of the underlying Unity framework (it evaluates UnityScript) and how the CodeSpells world is set up programmatically (you can access the game scene from the US scape, which isn't that super unsafe???). At least if you don't want to use those functionalities, there's not a ton of different things to learn and the beginner spells keep it relatively simple, so a new player won't feel overwhelmed...? I guess??
- Mana (right? that's what it's called? I forgot already) drain doesn't really make much sense, and there's absolutely zero feedback on what takes what mana and by how much. You can't mix together mana usage very well, either; too little of whatever primary source your spell is assigned to, and it just flat out won't work. You can't change the type of a spell without -- again -- copy-pasting it into a new spell. Nothing but clunk. Maybe this was meant to introduce some challenge and mystique into the game, some guesswork on what will work and what won't. However, code doesn't work like that and will either yell at you or crash silently if you do something wrong. I doubt the game will hold your hand when you try to make this awesome spell to find that it takes way more mana than you even have available to you, and it hurts more knowing that it could have helped you out earlier, saying "hey this costs 100 so don't use it more than twice", but that doesn't happen.
Aside from the programming, I also have gripes with the presentation of the game:
- The game world is incredibly tiny. The edges of the world fall into what appears to be an endless void, and there's no indication other than falling to your untimely death that anything is wrong. I thought it was just a cliff for a moment, and was prepared to create some water with a spell to cushion the landing. That landing never came, as I was just teleported back up to a random position on the map.
- While the fluid simulation is
nice, it's incredibly jagged, and really needs some visual polish.
- Heating things up doesn't really make as much sense as I'd have expected. Instead of being able to light individual objects on fire, you instead increase the heat of the surrounding area until it gets hot enough for things to burn. Maybe I missed something, but that seems really silly (though having both abilities available would make for smashingly good design). Heating water to create clouds and humidity to create rain (if I was reading that right and it wasn't just random luck) was really awesome, though.
TL;DR it has promise, but generally falls flat due to clunky, disjointed interfaces and lack of proper documentation. It tries to be simple and easy to understand, but complicates this by not having a very solid foundation to build on. I certainly wouldn't want anyone to try to learn programming using this tool, especially not my children or anyone I care about.
I won't be requesting a refund or anything like that, mostly because I never have and don't want to go through the effort, but I doubt I will be playing this again until these issues are addressed. Yes yes early access blah blah, but not making sure your core gameplay mechanics are fully functional (or at least better alert your buyer that they are still undergoing development) is a downvote from me. The currently implemented features and functionality are done so poorly and there's no excuse for that. Regardless of my personal feelings on the matter, it's certainly not worth its hefty pricetag. Not yet, at least.

We have all seen big men, wearing big armor, wielding big guns and doing manly stuff from previous games (like Gears of War or Star Craft), but have you ever wondered who started it all?
Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine is a Third Person Hack, Slash and Shooter game developed by Relic Entertainment who has constantly delivered quality work when dealing with the Warhammer 40k universe.
You play as Captain Titus of the Ultramarines, along side his friend Sidonus and the newly initiated Leandros, all of whom are sent to the forge world of Gaira with the objective of protecting a Warlord Class Titan from being looted by a full Ork Invasion. Unknown to Captain Titus, however...other forces are at work there.
+
-This game boast beautiful cut scenes, epic scenery, massive buildings and intense combat. Model and Animation quality are very well made which is complemented by its superior sound quality. The violence in this game is extreme and oddly very satisfying.
+
-From the soundtrack to the footsteps and  bolter or lasgun fire, Relic has performed admirably on the sound assets which greatly improves the immersion experience. The voice acting delivered by Mark Strong as Captain Titus is great and complemented by the performance of the supporting cast.
+
-The game offers a linear story progression which contains enough lore to satisfy the old school and long time fans of the Warhammer 40k Universe, but at the same time, is easy enough to comprehend and understand for the new comers. Story is around 8 to 9 hours long, and 6-7 if you have already played it once. The difficulty level of the game does merit a replay.
+
-I normally don't consider multiplayer because I'm a singleplayer oriented gamer but I was able to substantially play the multiplayer mode of Space Marine and was impressed. Multiple game modes and heavy customization really is a big bonus here.
-
-Although I said that visuals AS A WHOLE is good, the texture quality of this game is quite inferior. It may have looked good on the console versions but on the PC on 1080p, one can see that the textures used was only low res. The poor lip syncing was also a minor annoyance for me. The Artstyle is great but it does not excuse low resolution textures specially on the PC.
-
-This game should have had a more extensive PC settings instead of the generic preset of “low-medium-high”. I feel that devs who does not put effort on the settings are not fully utilizing the capabilities of the PC as a gaming platform. On the up side, at least gamers with not so powerful systems can still enjoy the game and have fun.
-
-A certain boss fight for me was very disappointing since it was more or less a quick time event and mini-game than an actual fight. The fight in itself was still badass and manly as hell with regards to the story though.
GREAT GAME, extremely fun and satisfying to play with a very enjoyable singleplayer and multiplayer experience.
The game is well worth its full price for not just the fans of the Warhammer 40,000 universe but fans of 3rd person action games and new comers to the franchise alike.

is a great and innovative tactical Roguelike, very unique and addictive. Instead of controlling a character, you click on tiles to reveal what's behind the mist. Your ultimate goal is to reach the 20th floor and beat the boss, and that's a hell of a ride! Traps, bombs, monster with a variety of skills and a lot of curses awaits you, and you'll need a lot of thinking and planning to get through.
The greatest beauty of this game is that, despite everything being randomly generated, there's almost no luck involved. Your skills count more than your luck for the most part, but don't be overwhelmed, you can unlock permanent buffs (which also increases the difficulty a bit) and passive abilities especially for your next run.
Pixel art in this game is absolutely gorgeous, and the minimalist and atmospheric soundtrack helps to keep you calm and focused. There's 10 characters in total (one starting hero and nine unlockable heroes), and a lot of combinations (from monsters to runestones, abilities, gear, etc), so the replay value is awesome and the game is still intriguing after you beat it for the first time (I did it today by the way).
Last, but not least, I can't recommend this game enough, specially if you're a fan of Roguelikes and/or would like to discover a new kind of minesweeper experience with a lot of features added.

Overall, wonderful game. One of my personal favorites now. I like being able to take the time to think things through and still have fun.

I got some mix feelings about this so bare with me.
The music overall is... decent, but tries too hard to be DOS-music, I guess? I don't know. Some of it just didn't sit well with me while some I was okay with. I do wish more work was put in for the music. I can't find anymore words to comment on this.
The story is simple and short (less than 30 minutes), however the setting I'm confused; medieval, tribes, and modern socity as one? Sounds like an interesting idea on paper, but execution needs to be planned very well, and this sorta went half-way on it. Good attempt though, I'll give it that much.
The story alone feels like it's aimed more toward younger readers, however visually toward a mature audience, so unsure what target audience they were going for with this game. That's where most of my mix feelings come from, while partially from the music.
The artstyle (I refuse to call it graphics for this game) is pretty simple as it can get for an old-school-esque adventure game. Took me a bit to understand the UI. However, I didn't like that I had to use a UI window to go in a direction than just simply click on it. That was the only issue I had with it that I found odd and inconvenient for me.
I felt a bit stuck near the end, however noticed something peculiar with a bush that had a black hole in it the 2nd time I went by it.
Sure there is nudity (which is not even a real focus I may add) but it's the more artsy kind of nudity (aka non-sexual aka non-fanservice, etc.), like drawing a live model in art class in college or the ancient greek sculptures. It usually fits well with tribal worlds than anything else so it sat very well with me.
If people get that easily offended just by the sight of breasts or anyone nude in a non-sexual way, that's purely on them and their own problem for getting worked up about it. I fail to see how that can be the dev's fault.
I did take a few minutes to try silly combinations and see what would happen (and this will really add up the game hours to find them all). Gotten a few chuckles but didn't explore every combination yet (good excuse to do while waiting for the card drops). Wanted to get the story done first to get this review up properly.
This game isn't perfect, but isn't bad either. It's average more towards good. Worth the $0.99 though as I didn't see anything that I found disturbing as some people were exaggerating about, with zero technical issues to boot, and overall found it alright for the price. I did notice some grammar issues I would like to point out to the dev if I can, though, in private.
So, yeah, not gonna ask for a refund just because I finished the story under 2hrs as that'll be abusing the refund policy since I did enjoy it and gave it a chance from start to finish.
P.S.: I was, at some point, expecting the CG that's displayed on the steam store to show up. That would've been great. A mother reunited with her child that got lost in the forest after wondering off to it. ^_^ Guess it's not possible with this game. Shame, really.

You can explore people's profiles on the dating app and strike up a conversation with someone inconsequential, you can read comments on posts on the social media app, you can read spam emails. The characters (while the voice and visual acting can be a little hokey) each have their own distinct personalities through texts and messages, the writing there is spot on, plus you can interact with them in so many different ways it feels like your voice really matters to the plot.

I've been with this series since the beginning, and it has been a bumpy ride.
The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing was excellent. Despite the fact that multiplayer was bugged and unplayable at the beginning, Neocore resolved the issue quickly. The first game was an excellent example of what ARPGs could be.
The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing 2 was extraordinary. Everything was improved upon and the added end game content was thrilling.
The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing 3 was... Terrible. Necore tried something new, and good on them for putting themselves out there, but it was like watching a one legged pug trying to climb stairs.
The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing: Final Cut is all three games in one, including a massive skill redesign and the ability to play the same character through all 3 games. Most of the negative reviews here are about online character saves. As a programmer, let me tell you that dealing with anything serverside is a nightmare and expecting a small gaming company to get it right on the first go is arrogant and childish.
Is this compilation perfect? No. But if you are a fan of Torchlight, TQ, and Diablo, then give this a try.

BIT.TRIP RUNNER is a game that hails to the pre-NES gaming era. This game has the player performing well timed jumps, slides and other moves, usually in a rhythmic fashion, to collect gold bars and avoid obstacles. BIT.TRIP RUNNER was a well received game and it seems that this game has a lot of indie cred but my experience playing this game contrasted to what I hear in the reviews has me wondering if I'm playing the right game or if I need to drill down into an option menu somewhere to enable the good content. The art style is distinctive and appealing and the game itself does have it's moments, however it forces you to endure quite a bit of tedium to get to a meager portion of enjoyable gameplay.
BIT.TRIP RUNNER is a game that requires very price timing and rythmn and a single half-second delay will mean restarting the level in most cases. The first 20 seconds or so of each level will insult you by being boring and unchallenging and due to the nature of this game that first 20 seconds of gameplay will be what you experience most as any mishap will transport you back to the beginning. I'm not advocating making the game easier as I appreciate a challenge but I don't appreciate being forced to repeat uninteresting gameplay several times over.  Many levels seem to be laden with challenges that can be fun at first but are repeated ad nauseum and end up feeling like a gimmick (for instance there will be a staircase in almost every level that requires consecutive jumps). These challenges quickly become tedius and only serve as a mechanism to return you once again to the boring part of the level. Levels can get quite long too so the chances you'll be repeating uninteresting gameplay is quite high.
I've read comments about the game's soundtrack and the menu options do feature Anamanaguchi in the menu and credits the actual game's music is boring most of the time as it requires progress in the level to become interesting. I wonder why the game's music didn't feature Anamanaguchi as well.
If you're looking for a game that's challenging and requires a high level of precision and quick reactions, although the format is different, other popular indie titles like Super Meat Boy and VVVVVV do a better job. Super Meat Boy's short levels and VVVVVV's room based format allow these games to respect the player's time.
Score: 5/10

For me, THQ nailed the visuals and the sound for the Space Marines, Orks included! I can't stop slow-walking, just to listen to that steady clump-clump of my Marines' boots as he walks LOL! The power of the holy Bolter resonates beautifully, with amazing smoke trails off the shell. I do feel like I am firing a Godwin pattern Bolter. As with the proportions; I'd have liked the scale of MArine - Human a little bigger, but I am not disapointed :)
The background scenery is some of the most beautiful I have seen in a shooter. Grand towers and ornamented architecture that soar high into the Industrial World's air, the sunset and fluffy clouds are very screenshot-worthy. The navigable scenery is very clumpy and I can tell I am playing a console game. No havoc engine destruction, no craters that remain...a PC could handle that, but a console cannot, so I do not like the reminders that I am having to compromise on gameplay yet still pay full price. It does get repetetive. I find myself having to constantly re-try checkpoints for some silly bit that I just can't get past - HOWEVER, after practice, you will find yourself succeeding.
The main problem I find is the complicated controls. For a start, I cannot re-bind them. Secondly, to perform certain manouvers like simply throwing a grenade, you HAVE to read the rapidly appearing and disapearing prompt FIRST TIME, or else you have to play 'let's hit every key till we get it' game as there is NO controls menu (can you believe that???) for anything other than firing the gun and swinging the smashy smashy.
Furthermore issues I have with the controls is that to perform tekken-style moves in order to regain your health is probably THE most annoying feature of this game. I want to conduct myself as a soldier, on a PC, not a tekken or streetfighter gamer on a console. This does smack of streets of rage in places I'll warn you now. But there is something slightly satisfying about taking down 6 orcs in one slash of my Chain Sword. Mounted weapons do not respond to the 'E' interaction move which I actually class as an in-game bug, (you'll see what I mean). However there is the option to tear the mounted heavy Bolter OFF it's mount! >:D This does not mean that you have acquired a new heavy weapon however, as he drops it after about 60 seconds or so. So make the most of them :) The inventory menu is based on 4 slots ONLY, whereby a more powerful weapon type REPLACES YOUR OLD ONE - which I found very upsetting, I cried.
Again, with all linear shooters, this game can be completed in an afternoon <sigh> but I think you all have become accustomed to that eh? My advice, buy this in a sale. It is good fun, and if you want your Ultramarines brought to life somewhat beautifully, it's worth it for that alone :)

The idea of crafting spells through a visual language is both fun and rewarding.  You have to work to make your spells work, and that makes any spell you craft feel much more awesome than if you just made it with a predetermined effect.
There is no tutorial and little documentation as of yet, so I reiterate strongly only buy this game if you are intrigued buy the idea.

A bare-bones roguelike with a legacy system. To progress, you reveal tiles on a square grid, which can hide monsters, traps, usable items or various shops. Your character does not have an avatar, and monsters do not move around; attacking an enemy is simply done through clicking it. This results in fast-paced gameplay, which makes the game surprisingly addictive. There are loot drops, a magic system, gods to worship for various bonuses, and random quest events, which are always a series of dialog choices that can result in good or bad outcomes.
I do recommend the game, but caution that it contains some very strong RNG. There's no way to avoid all the traps, and some levels are just paved with toxin traps that will quickly build up to a lethal does, and you will die. Sometimes there are ranged boss monsters with as much attack as your health that will literally oneshot you no matter how healthy or well-equipped you are, and if you dont happen to have an instakill item, you will die. Those elements taint an otherwise tough, but relatively fair game.
For those of you that have played Gmod or Half life this game should feel right at home asthedic wise.

Very few games culture the feeling in me that I just can't stop playing.  This one does it big-time!
There is a very high return of fun for the minimal purchase price.
While the game-play is outstanding, the graphics are absolutely masterful.  I am generally not one to point out good graphics before I point out good game-play, but here I am just blown away - I can't stress that enough.
To my mind they are so masterful they should hold a place of their own in the progression of the craft of game art.  (The artist has employed a "dual-resolution" pixel graphic technique I have never seen before, and it works to absolutely breathtaking effect).
Buy this.  Buy this game.  Buy it and play the *BLEEP* out of it
-------------------
edit:
In the interest of expanding my review into specific likes/dislikes:
This game is, at it's core, a very innovative grid-based puzzle and resource-management game.  As you reveal tiles the play field evolves, and the player is required to continually evaluate and re-evaluate what is their most optimal move at any given time or state of the play field.
Every foe on the battlefield affects the other foes in interesting ways, and there are a wide range of upgrade branches for the player in terms of stats/skills/equipment.  There are Gods to worship, shrines to socket, buffing tattoos, runestones to hoarde/upgrade, etc, etc, etc each with a unique effect and pro/con the player needs to evaluate.
It's really fun for me because I enjoy thinking deeply about my moves in a game, but also in maintaining the certain fluidity of thinking that this game requires - because new elements are continually entering play.
At first blush the interface itself looks like typical "pixel" graphics which are all-too-common these days and can -sometimes- be a red-flag indicating bad game play covered up with nifty retro slop - well this is not the case at all with RuneStone Keeper.  I find the graphics are masterfully and intentionally designed to be looked at for long play sessions without requiring too much focus or strain on the eyes.  The instant, and I mean instant you look at a tile you can recognize it and remember its effects.  A studious eye will notice multiple visual layers in the UI and see where the artist has actually "broken the rules" of pixel art and changed resolutions with larger/smaller stroke(s).  It is effing genius because it works on an emotional "looks beautiful" level and also on a gorgeously-functional level.
[[ That's enough of my personal feelings on that subject but the last thing I want to say is that I feel many discerning UI lovers would get a real pleasure from seeing and interacting with this game besides the fact that the mechanics are also brilliant. ]]
There are some minor flaws that I hope are corrected.  At times the left/right clicks required for actions like closing dialogs are not efficient or intuitive.  Sometimes elements like scroll lists are very hard to "grab" and scroll you have to find just the right pixel to click.  Some of the icons for the one-time use items are very un-intuitive - three of them look nearly identical and I forget their effects constantly for that reason.
But all in all this game for me and my preferences, will remain in my top 20 of all time for a loooooong time I think.  Win!

I had a complete different idea of the game going into it, thinking it was going to be a quick and casual romp through the levels to be easily completed in a few half hours. Ohh! Boy was I wrong, I immediately died on the first level and to boot had no idea why. After playing an hour, I realized that random clicks of tiles was not going to lead me anywhere. This game requires strategy and carefully planning of any of your resource. I died a lot during the first hour, a lot and all this in a game where you just click a path through a dungeon that is layed out in a grid.
The game has a number of RPG elements, with 4 different stats that shape the way you play. You can play as a mage, as a warrior or as a ranger, or a hybrid by filling up INT, STR and DEX. STA takes care of the way your health is replenished. You have three main resource pools, a health pool (which if emptied, you die!, Surprise!), a mana pool with which you can cast spells and a soul pool, which is the main resource pool to use items you possess or in the battlefield. A great loot drop system with a number of slots to fill helps you augment more your game, together with other elements such as worshiping gods, a runestone system that can sacrifice and use runes, and random events that provide bonuses or handicaps.
But when you die, all bonuses, god worships, items and loot disappear... except for you gold can be recycled to upgrade your character in town or buy items to prepare for your next journey. Gold is the only link between each game and it is also awarded at the end of every round.
Finally, the game is hard, very hard and can sometimes be very unforgiving, piting you in situations where you cannot survive or fight it out. Each level has to be planned, how to use certain items, or to use ballistas (one shot heavy damage weapons), how to use your resources pools and how to kill each monster after each other. Monsters have certain abilities and effects, such as redirecting their damage to other monsters or healing others, and these abilities together can either be used in your favour or a combination of them putting you in a bad situation that will drain your resources. The game will not hold your hand, and you are expect to die until you get better at it.
Yes, Recommended

Very good art on this game, built upon a minesweeper-esque tactical game turn-based premise that seems like it would be compelling. I've had major comebacks that turned into run completions due to good desicion making, as well as great desicion making that just fell flat on it's face. Such is the roguelike. It fits the bill. I'm a roguelike ♥♥♥♥♥, so of course I bought it.
Alright then, so why the downvote? Let's ignore the lazy UI, typos, ambiguious stats, and uncompelling quest events for the moment.
So when a designer anylizes a game that they've made, they don't always ask themselves "what's the design space of this game?" and subsequencially, "At what point am I forcing players to play the 'grindy' part of my game to reach milestones before the design space caps out?"
This game attempts to milk playtime out of the user by making them farm gold and runestones, running the dungeon over and over again to accumilate these scarce resources in hopes to make future games better (and options accesable). On the whole, I'm not in disagreement with this playstyle, but using these resources is a total crapshoot. You can blow the entirity of your runestone payload on a playthrough that slams you at level five for reasons beyond your control, leaving you feeling cheated for making a desicions that not only had very little impact on play, but were not meaningful choices, just things you farmed up in between.
This drop rate is just not satisfactory compared to the content the game actually has to offer, and is a lazy design choice, and the limited design space does given much room for gameplay expnasion. The solution should not be 'farm'. This isn't an MMO; It's minesweeper. You can only milk so much gameplay out of it. If you're going to make a score attack mode, don't make people farm for the opportunity to play that mode, just have them unlock the option once.
Now add in all that stuff up top that I said to ignore, ya know, stuff that should be implimented in alpha and, at the very least, beta tested fixed. Keyboard controls. Documentations on those controls. Icons for crucial monster abilities. What the ♥♥♥♥ the luck stat does. These are 2-10 minute fixes a peice.
No, I do not recomend this game, especially not for $15. This is a $5 game, $2 during steam sale.

This is the best taxi driver simulator I've ever played: it perfectly captures the existential crises endemic to urban life. Welcome to a populous yet barren and surreal world. You pilot a shopping cart painted like a taxi cab with the inertia of a battleship along the hidden bumper-car lanes of urban development in a quest to gain the favour of silent invigilators ("fares"). Main features include: ghostly, collisionless pedestrians ("hey! I'm walkin' here!") and blind commuters, no soundtrack (just like IRL), constant brake screeching sound effects and more. I particularly liked the complete lack of roadsigns and constantly looping cars. My first actions as uber-auto-pilot were to try to drive through the park. Sadly this was not die hard 3 and an inivisible wall halted my progress with the sound of crumpling aluminium foil.

Undeterred I picked up my first fare; my cab lurched into 5th gear and barreled down the generously wide lanes of NYC at 115kmh towards a green-dot, lurking like a spider, in the peripheral of my routeless GPS. After many false turns I arrived at my passengers "destiny" (according to the in-game help) and was paid in insults. I swore to improve and picked up a tourist who wanted to go to two different featureless street corners (maybe they were a corner-spotter).

This time I tried to obey the speedlimit (which consists of tapping the up arrow every few seconds) and the few existing road markings (arrows on the lanes) and quickly found myself trapped in an infinite loop along with the other cars. My mind began to shut down as I crawled along the circuit of start-stop traffic. I longed for the glaring sun baking the tarmac to set so I could get out of the sweltering cockpit. I thought about my body-odour wafting around me as I stewed in my own juices on my beaded seat-cover and absently watched my ancient air-freshener dangling from the rear-view mirror. My eyes were dark pits. I had become a taxi driver.
All that broke my immersion is the low pedestrian density and absence of constant horn honking.

A metroidvania game done right in every possible way. The story, graphics and gameplay are all amazing. It is a bit short (7-10 hours), but there's still a lot of fun to be had, especially considering the price.
The story/setting struck me as sort of like the zelda-universe, which is always a bonus in my book (the three main dungeons reminiscent of "temples", and so on). Without spoiling it: It follows a creature called Ori as you try to fix everything that has gone wrong. Not insanely original, but it's delivered extremely well.
The graphics.. well, just take a look at the screenshots. They're really well done. The different abilities and attacks are animated beautifully, and I never encountered any weird issues.
The gameplay is really tight. You unlock plenty of abilities, and there are also a lot of progression involved. There is a skill tree which boost your efficiency in different ways (from unlocking a second double jump, to making your weapons more powerful). New abilities serve to gate content, as you need to find them to access new areas. You can also save pretty much anywhere if you have the energy to do so, so you never feel like you can't take a break if you have to (that said I finished the entire thing in two sitting because I was hooked). There are some exceptions, like if there are nearby enemies, or you're not standing on solid ground. If I have any complaints it would be:
1) that the boss battle isn't extremely well executed, it's essentially just a timed run-for-your-life. Nevertheless, it serves its purpose at delivering a great story, but I would have liked to see some cool bosses with unique mechanics.
2) I played the entire game with a controller (which works amazingly well), but I did encounter an issue. There is an ability which lets you slingshot by grabbing onto an enemy or projectile, and if I did this while holding the stick in a direction the slingshot direction would be locked. When you are on a time limit during certain points in the game (like said boss battle) this could be infuriating.
Bottom line, if you're remotely interested in the genre, this is a must-buy. If not, it is probably still worth taking a look at.

Onto the actual review.
The plot is relatively generic, being that you are trying to defeat a dark monster that is hounding the forest that is the realm of the dark father tree thing. Regardless, the game is very enjoyable and the basic plot and simple characters gives way to a breathtaking world that, despite the actual map consuming a relatively small area, still manages to feel like a sprawling world with beautiful scenery to match. A lot of people describe the game as metriodvania but I am far too young to understand that so I'll just call it an RPG platformer. You only have three rows of customization but that saves you the time that would otherwise be spend scrolling through seventy different stats trying to divide your points into insignificantly incrimenting the damage of your attack. Ori gets to start off unarmed and undefended and ends the game able to rain fire and brimstone upon anything that looks at you funny. The music is also quite nice. Not very distincitve, but nevertheless atmospheric and calming when it needs to be and fast paced when the game demands it.

This game is a stunningly beautiful work of art.
The visuals are glorious – masterful. No stone, no leaf, no dark corner of unimportance will you find lacking in artistic detail.
Audio is great, though the re-use of the central melody got old for me, but this is a minor gripe.
The total length of play is short, but given the work of art which this game is, it's still worth it. The game isn't any longer than it needs to be. I finished it after three days of intermittent play. For most people, this will be a 3-7 day game, depending on how many hours you put in during each session.
I have read that some players found certain challenges to be too difficult, but I did not have this problem. I was challenged sufficiently, but this is no Super Meatboy. You can save almost anywhere at almost any time instantly, so losing progress due to death is mostly dependent upon your own failure to save.
Play style and features don't offer anything new that hasn't been done elsewhere, but it's all implemented well here.
I did run into a few minor control bugs and music which would not start after resuming from a game save in a certain area, but nothing that hurt the game too badly. I expect these issues will be resolved in the future.
The narrative is a simple tale, and easy to get into. Be warned that the story gets a little dramatic and depending upon your emotional fortitude, you might want to keep a tissue box handy.
Overall, this game is a masterpiece and the release-day price is an easy value given such.

This review may contain light spoilers. The TL;DR is that I would recommend it, it's about 3 hours of gameplay, but is quite hand-holdy in parts. Don't go into this expecting a cerebral game where you need to figure everything out for yourself. Also, don't expect the choices the game forces you into making to make any sense, either.
I quite liked it. It's definitely an improvement from the last game, but there are a few things I noticed.
For instance, there's a few grammar and spelling mistakes in the phone's interface through the game, and most notably the 'BUSTED' chatroom, after it's just 2 people left in it, turns into 'BUSTED' is typing, as if the contact name was called 'BUSTED' and this wasn't actually a chatroom.
The knocking, gasps/breathing 'outside' the phone (This game could also be titled "Millennials don't answer the door simulator 2017") were also unneeded. It wasn't that scary and took away from the game, if you're going I was expecting a jump-scare, or some kind of mechanic where I would need to move around my house to avoid various hostile entities from 'getting me' while I solved the phone mystery.
It was also a bit too linear and railroady for my tastes. The auto-suggestion mechanic needs a lot more work because I felt like I was constantly being railroaded in the dialogue sections down a path that there's no way I (as a person) would have done or said. I wasn't a fan of the two 'supposed-to-lose' parts, either - I spent a good half an hour on one, hunting around and going into every app and going through every bit of information I had so far trying to get more information.
The story felt very one-track also. If you compared this game to a visual novel, which is pretty much what this game is, a standard VN player would be very dissapointed with the lack of branching paths, different dialogues, and small amount of endings.
I really want to emphasize that the 'free-roam' hunting for information was the best part of this game, and the dialogue elements forcefeeding you stuff you figured out 10 messages ago was the absolute worst. If the devs want to keep on making games like these, the dialog absolutely needs more work. Additionally it seems like the developers really wanted to characterize these people but in the process of haphazardly sprinkling photographs in there were serious inconsistences. Players are going to be combing through this stuff trying to find precious information and the last thing they need is to be misled due to a mistake.
Overall, though, I recommend a buy if this is the sort of game you like. This is a vast improvement upon the last game and I look forward to this studio's next game.

Simulacra is a simulated mobile phone method of delivering a horror game. It is based on the disappearance of a young woman named Anna, and the protagonist (you) has discovered her phone on their doorstep. From there, you delve into the secrets of her phone to find all the information you can, and try to locate--and subsequently save--Anna.
From a mechanical perspective, the game is pretty solid. There's no skeleton or standard out there for "Phone application based horror", making Simulacra a rather noteworthy pioneer and sequel to the developer's predecessor. Applications are sound, mimicking their real-life counterparts exceptionally well. The interface is smooth, and the methods for accessing the different pools of data prove acceptable. My only real complaint is, while the "data restoration" mechanic was easy enough to use, it felt ultimately meaningless and proved only to be a minor time sink. It was an interesting concept, but executed poorly. Perhaps, in later editions, the method for restoring and recovering data might make a more central point in the story.
However, in a game like this, the story is what really holds the fiber and and strength of a game. Hoo boy, does Simulacra tell you a story. The deeper you delve, the closer you get, the more stressful the game will become. Information will consistently surprise the player, and force them to make intensely difficult decisions. While they do have some effect on the ending of the game, the limitation to four significant endings does, to say the least, cause some level of dissonance between decision making and results.
Overall, for five dollars, it was a surprisingly binge-worthy experience.

For a long time I wished for a game where mages could be much stronger than mere jugglers. In many books a mage is a man who has monstrous powers and abilities. It’s takes no effort at all for him to crush half of a world into ruins or to get powers by sacrificing kittens. He can raise armies of undead or elementals, summon spirits and demons. But all we see in present-day games is just hilarious hocus-pocuses. Well known “Magicka” that gave us a lot of fun in one’s time, noticeably gone much far away with its arcade spell constructor.
And here comes CodeSpells. A new milestone of a games-about-magic evolution, where you can make spells starting from hocus-pocuses and eventually ending with destruction of the world. All you need is to build your very own, very powerful, hyper-destructive spell! MUAHAHAHA!!!
And there you find your first problems. If you do not understand at least basics of programming (loops, conditions, variables etc.) it will be either too hard or you couldn’t make something at all. Yes, this game for developers first of all: novice or skilled – no matter. However, even for me as a programmer it was very difficult to understand controls pile of the spell constructor. Moreover, even a simple spell looks like hell in the spell-constructor, as in code viewer it has just five rows of JavaScript in two Unity3D methods: OnCreate and OnHit. You can’t write your code inside the game, but it could be more comfortable as for me, and I see at CodeSpells forum that I’m not alone in this opinion — people want to have a JS editor inside the game. And it could be possible to have C# compatibility because the game made using Unity3D.
But what could do those, who has never tried to program something and even can’t imagine how that works but nevertheless wants to dip to the world of boundless magic? Unfortunately, it’s the only way for now – you have to gain an understanding of all that stuff. In fact, I want to ask developers to make more user friendly (for more casual gamers e.g.) spell creating tool. For example, possibility to draw different lines which could give different effects depending on curvature, intersections, length etc. Perhaps, there is much more interested people could be found.
As a whole, the idea is great and perspective, so I give it a like. If developers are willing to improve the game, it could be a true bomb. But for now it’s not a game; it has a sandbox where you can’t understand what to do, except experimenting with spells, and there are a couple of mini games, where you need to complete tasks in time to test yourself, your abilities and knowledge of spell constructor.
I hope that there will be serious product closer to the release date, which planned in a year, not only for programmers but for different categories of players. Good luck!

Note: My low hours comes from the time I spent designing code on the website simulation which I sadly havent found in game,
A really fun game where just about anything is possible, and there are infinite ways to do so. Harvesters for example, do you go with multipurpose workers who mine and carry like traditional RTS harvesters or stationary harvesters who leave carrying to other worksers? This is just an example of one of the decisions you can make but you can choose how you want to run your won code.
Since there are infinite possibilities for a given situation you can do things in any way. Although there are countless ways to do different tasks, some code is objectively better than others, this creates different levels of play and ultimately introduces competetion, this does not make the game any less fun however as you can easily improve your code based on past mistakes.
For those who do not want to do a pvp experience, and would rather an empty sandbox or PVE I would open a private server, here you can customize the game to your every desire, you can add or disable bots that are added by the game, adjust tickrate, or even tweak any in game variables like creep lifetime if you know how.
The only bad thing I can think of is that if you do not know how to code javascript your for all intents and purposes screwed, this does not mean you cannot play the game however I cannot reccomend playing in multiplayer until you understand at least some coding basics about coding and have developed colony scripts. Until then you basicly are dead in the water PVP wise and should stick solely to the simulations and private servers. If your willing to learn to code however I can definately reccomend this game to you and it is great for learning to optimize and upgrade your code.
I would like to emphasize something from my last game, THIS IS NOT A TUTORIAL, if you come here expecting one other than a typical walkthrough that tells you what to do you will likely be disappointed but that is because you simply need to learn how to code elsewhere at first. Once you have done that, definately come here.
My biggest complaint is that the in game code editor makes debugging a slight form of hell, I would love it if it highlighted the point of any contention in red or at least the error message spit out something that was more specific, and easier to read and understand. As of now it does not, it only gives you a generic javascript error that makes it confusing to understand. Another point of contention is the autocomplete is very buggy, it decides when it wants to work and generally doesnt work at all, this makes guessing some of the code you can use and reference tricky unless you know what to look for. Often you cannot autocomplete code in lines and as of such have to make a fake copy out of a code statement in order to try to coax the autocomplete to work. Although these points can be nullified by the game's support for an external code editor, it does not make the issue any less prevelant in game.
Overall this game quickly became one of my favorite games for coding practice, here it can teach you debugging, optimizing, and even upgrading your code. Once youve set up your initial code you can move from the initial stage of developement and initial debugging into a live test which will highlight any issues and exploits that your code preasents to others. In this game your failiures will make you sucessful, and that is something to keep in mind. Great job on this game.

You want depth? You want strategy? You want unexpected token errors 73 lines down in your harvester code? Then this is the game for you. This game is both educational and engrossing if you're the type of person that enjoys combat programming and ultra-high skill cap RTS gameplay at a snail's pace.
If you're not that type of person, then don't buy it.
Running someone else's code is boring, and the game's glacial pace will put you to sleep if you're not using all that downtime to improve your code. The meat of the gameplay is literally just coding the logic that your creeps will follow, and the "game" on-screen where your colony grows and fights other colonies just serves to give you concrete objectives and goals to reach for as you code.
Once you're done coding and you feel satisfied with what your colony can do, then the game runs on autopilot. The goal of this game is to automate everything your colony does so that you don't have to play it anymore. Nidhogg is a side scrolling fighter with a unique combat system. Basically, you move your sword to different heights in order to attack in different ways or to be in defensive positions against your opponent. There seems to be just enough  moves to allow surprising your opponent if you’re cheeky, while also being predictable enough to be fair.
The combat works well strategically, but more notably can produce some hilarious moments. Ridiculous attack sequences of back-and-forth fumbling, sword throwing, punching, diving, etc. actually manage to be really funny sometimes.
I played this game mostly without someone else. It works… fine… like this, but I strongly recommend finding a friend to play with early on.
If this game has a flaw, it might be it’s simplicity causing people to lose interest too quickly.
I haven’t played loads of Nidhogg II yet, but so far I prefer Nidhogg. I think Nidhogg II’s slight increase in variability makes the game less predictable and therefore a teeny bit less skill-based. The kinaesthetics of it felt a little off for me, but only because I’m familiar with the original: I’m probably judging the sequel a little harshly for that reason. I actually like Nidhogg II’s art direction (aside from the characters).
I’d recommend finding out more about Nidhogg II to see if you might like it better, it’s also pretty solid. The sequel is probably better for someone that would be willing to devote more of their time to playing.

Truly a fun roguelike. And I consider it unique and certainly worth it's money.
However the gameplay is stiffling.
It's not a true roguelike, as some elements carry over between runs, namely runes, gold and shop unlockables.
Main problem are the runes, any rune collected and not used carries over to the next game, they are very powerful and rare. The key to success is to use the runes wisely. Additionally, many gamemodes (look up runewords) cost runes to play (most notably the endless runeword)
after your death, you can spend your gold in the shop to get passive upgrades to make the game slightly easier.
So what you end up doing is grinding. Grinding gold and runes in order to pay your expenses in a serious run, where you may want to play with a certain runeword, have prepared runes for certain gods you intend to worship and get tatoos from, and stock gold for certain items you hope to find in shops.
So when you do have a good run, you might not want to go all in in and spend your runes on the much neded tatoos in case you mess up and loose your entire investment.
What I want to recommend is a true roguelike, where every run is a chance to play it big, where you can play all in whitout having to grind for it on countless runs in advance.
Things this game regrettably isn't.

I personally read only the top two possitive comments and about five negative comments just to make sure that I know any flaws in a game. I'm thumbing down this post not because I would not recommend buying the game. Buy the thing, it's awesome! I'm just leaving this here so that people who are reading for reviews get all of the information they need.
This game is beautiful as you can see in the gameplay trailer and screenshots. Unfortunately for someone like me with a crappy machine that graphic comes at a cost. The lag on a mid range laptop is insane and there is no function to tone down the graphical fiddelity and therefore you WILL be forced to play on max graphics even if you have a 300 dollar netbook. Are we clear on that? Great!
Onto the actual review.
The plot is relatively generic, being that you are trying to defeat a dark monster that is hounding the forest that is the realm of the dark father tree thing. Regardless, the game is very enjoyable and the basic plot and simple characters gives way to a breathtaking world that, despite the actual map consuming a relatively small area, still manages to feel like a sprawling world with beautiful scenery to match. A lot of people describe the game as metriodvania but I am far too young to understand that so I'll just call it an RPG platformer. You only have three rows of customization but that saves you the time that would otherwise be spend scrolling through seventy different stats trying to divide your points into insignificantly incrimenting the damage of your attack. Ori gets to start off unarmed and undefended and ends the game able to rain fire and brimstone upon anything that looks at you funny. The music is also quite nice. Not very distincitve, but nevertheless atmospheric and calming when it needs to be and fast paced when the game demands it.
Now the rest of the complaints. I do hate to complain about a game that imediately established itself as one of my favourites but I am a jerk and I am quite bored and I should try to at least balance out the gushing. The main problem I had is simply my problem with my own hardware which, though it is my fault, does leave me wanting to turn down the lag a little through scenes of conflagalation and watery death hot on my trail. The game, I also feel, sometimes falls victim to its own stunning art. The fireball primary attack looks good like everything else, but on higher upgrades the light was just so bright and intense that it was hard to know when to stop firing. The neon-esque color palette can also make it difficult to see Ori throughout the scenery.
Despite my complaints: I loved the game. It was both fun and beautiful. Quite cheap as well. Buy it.

This game is a stunningly beautiful work of art.
The visuals are glorious – masterful. No stone, no leaf, no dark corner of unimportance will you find lacking in artistic detail.
Audio is great, though the re-use of the central melody got old for me, but this is a minor gripe.
The total length of play is short, but given the work of art which this game is, it's still worth it. The game isn't any longer than it needs to be. I finished it after three days of intermittent play. For most people, this will be a 3-7 day game, depending on how many hours you put in during each session.
I have read that some players found certain challenges to be too difficult, but I did not have this problem. I was challenged sufficiently, but this is no Super Meatboy. You can save almost anywhere at almost any time instantly, so losing progress due to death is mostly dependent upon your own failure to save.
Play style and features don't offer anything new that hasn't been done elsewhere, but it's all implemented well here.
I did run into a few minor control bugs and music which would not start after resuming from a game save in a certain area, but nothing that hurt the game too badly. I expect these issues will be resolved in the future.
The narrative is a simple tale, and easy to get into. Be warned that the story gets a little dramatic and depending upon your emotional fortitude, you might want to keep a tissue box handy.
Overall, this game is a masterpiece and the release-day price is an easy value given such.

So, the server migration took a bit longer than expected, and the community goes absolute butthurt over it. Lot of recent negative reviews, and that's the ONLY reason most of those reviews are negative. But enough about that - let's get to the actual review.
At first glance, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing doesn't look like much. A static world with a limited pool of mobs and "the usual clickfest aRPG" elements. But before you even get to the first quest area, you'll notice something different about this game - the atypical voiceover banter between Van Helsing and his "partner" Katarina. That right there adds a lot of entertainment value.
The "class" selection and pool of skills, spells and equipment varies significantly based on your selection. Many other games in this genre offer variety, but this game seems to excel at it. Your first choice - creating a character - will determine pretty much everything about how you play through, giving the game some replayability.
Where the game really shines, though, is in the secret lair, where you have several mini-game options from tower defense to strategic loot acquisition through generals and your pet - I like to call him Fluffy.
The full game - the Final Cut version - offers a much longer play experience, and takes you through several Acts as you attempt to establish order in Borgovia and the surrounding area. The environments vary just enough to give you a feeling of exploration, and aren't too far off from those you might find in any Diablo game. Load times aren't too long, visuals are pretty much on par with most recent titles in the genre, and missions make sense. There are even several missions that can have multiple outcomes, and choices made can have an impact on later missions.
Overall, I enjoyed the game for what it was, and the "difference" factor between this and other aRPG games exceeded my expectations. Granted this game is way better playing it with friends than going solo, but either is a viable option. Now that the network has been patched and everything is working again, if this is your type of game, and considering the 75% off sale, there's no reason not to pick it up and give it a shot.

Anyway I want this to be brief: The game itself I love. The visual style, the characters, the story, the dialogue it is all quite good and enjoyable. The combat is fun and intuitive and I love the musical score.
The online aspect has indeed been fixed and you can once again login with your neocore account to hop on...and for those solo players like myself you can play solo offline no issues as well.

At the time of its release, I was kind of obsessed with Sara is Missing. The style was fresh and new, and what a great idea! Finding a missing person through their phone is already such an interesting mystery, a look at how much of our lives are stored in this technology with a personal touch. However, in the end, I had too many questions that went unanswered, and ultimately felt unsatisfied.
SIMULACRA, on the other hand, has so far fixed all of these issues. For clarity sake, I have only achieved two endings at this time, and have more to go. For the same reason, and to give my respect to the developers, I will say I found this game through NightMind's video. This was one of the very, very few times I actually paused in the middle of a video to go out and buy the game myself - I will admit however, the low price was a factor in that. I was expecting more, but this game was more than worth my money.
There are a few silly little mistakes - Some of which add a level of realism and are undoubtedly intentional, like the varying type styles and occasional grammar errors and misspells... And some which are just a little funny, but in the end, the writing and acting won me over any time I was distracted from the experience. The mystery this time around is far more fun and rewarding to solve, the characters are largely likable (UNLESSANNAWHEREARETHOSEDATAREPORTS) and believable within this context.
The whole theme of using someone's phone to dig through their identity is played with far, FAR more effectively here, and the paranormal aspects (cmon it was obvious) offer some commentary, as well as another interesting character I wanted to explore.
The fact that the game doesn't allow multiple save states to allow choice-scumming for the desired result was at first a bit annoying, I want to see what they would all say if I said this or that, but it does add a certain weight to each choice - If you slip up and don't want to see it through, you have to start over.
There are a few other fun little distractions, if you need a moment of relief from the spooks, such as replying over and over again to the home security bot, replying to other people's tweets with memes, editing Anna's Spark profile the moment you have access to it so that it shows the lyrics to Feel Good Inc. and a picture of her cat, and etc. And even if you do choose to mess around a little it, you can still progress the story whether or not Anna's profile name is now Snart.
While I can't promise poo your pants horror, and the scares will be subjective, it's a fun little game even if you only want to pretend to be another person and gain everyone's trust, or immediately tell everyone you meet that you're not Anna. Or call 911, call her friends, read her texts and emails, waste her phone battery, and etc.

I was pretty impressed with Sarah is Missing when it came out, though it definitely had its flaws. With Simulacra, the developers have clearly built on criticisms of their first game and made for a way more unsettling and entertaining experience.
The game does rely a bit on jumpscares at times, but not to an excessive or obnoxious degree. Far better is what the game does with subtle ambiant spookiness--things that happen in the background that don't really draw attention to themselves but definitely left me feeling unsettled.
There are still some things that didn't work for me. The corrupted images and messages were fun, but a little bit too easy, and often didn't really give a satisfying payoff. The voice acting could be kind of hit or miss at times as well, though generally the game was very well acted. But on the whole, it was a great experience, and one of the scariest games I've played this year.

So, I've been a fan of Blendo Game's stuff in the past.  I have put an absurd amount of hours into Atom Zombie Smash, and enjoyed my time in Flotilla.  I more recently discovered that another Blendo Game, Gravity Bone, was available on free from the studio's website, and after playing it, decided to throw down the $5 to play Thirty Flights of Loving.
I'm not sure it was worth it.
First thing's first: 30 Flights is really short.  I played through the game once normally and again with "developer commentary" on, and it took just a bit over a half hour combined.  I know it shouldn't be a factor, but as someone with a small amount of free money, I have to think about time value.  While I had fun with 30 Flights, I'm not sure I had $5 worth of fun.
That said, 30 Flights is fun.  It isn't a game, really...more of a short story told from a first person view.  It's a pretty wild ride, shifting from quiet moments to in-your-face intense moments with jarring smash cuts that fit the tone of the game well.
If you are curious about the game, I'd recommend giving Gravity Bone a spin first, which is available free at the Blendo Games site.  If you like it, go ahead and play 30 Flights...but I'd recommend waiting for a sale.  Even if I enjoyed it, $5 for 15 minutes is a hard sale.

This game is awesome, and it's got me more into Javascript than I've ever been. I normally write things in C# when I can, whatever else, with JavaScript being relegated to client-side web page adjustments, as little as possible.
Now I want every excuse I can find to use JavaScript, because I'm about to start running attacks on AI, and while the documentation is great and simple, the best ways to organize code and make everything happen are constantly evolving for me.
I'm playing on a local server I'm running and focusing on improving each step of gameplay. I have no reservations about restarting because at some point I want to join the MMO portion, and I want my code to be strong out of the gate.
If you like dabbling with code, you'll love this game, but you'll want to get a job as a JavaScript developer after buying it. You do NOT need to be awesome at JavaScript. I often have to search up syntax on things, and read about the language as much as the object model.

One can tell that there was so much more planned for this game. It appears that there were two parties, the one aiming for the teaching aspect and the one aiming for the gaming aspect. The teaching aspect is just just sufficiently represented, while the gaming aspect is also just barely adequate. There are many hints that both wanted to putr more in the game, but neither had the time to. I will stress it feels like a deadline and not a lack of desire, becuase what is here is very well polished and well presented. It is just shallow.
To draw a comparison to Kerbal Space Program, this game teaches you every science mechanic upfront directly (Unlike KSP where one figures it out and LEARNS), there is fairly strong penalty early on for screwing up (KSP at least has sandbox mode for learning early blunders), and there is really no progression in learning, the game just gets more tedious.
For example, there are player upgrades for speed, but no timed events. There are competitons for plant breeding, but they are no more difficult or challenging than the normaly plant orders. The ability to directly and decisvely influence the punnet square outcomes makes the game trivial  to start, it should have been an ability earned later.
It really could be so much more challenging, but it falls too flat for me.
