Sometimes the winning move is not to play. At least that's the feeling I get when I try to get through Runestone Keeper. As an adventurer, you must brave the depths in order to accomplish a thing. A lot of the story is in the background, and tends to crop up in random events. So you'll explore, find treasure, die, and repeat until you get bored.
I was planning on ignoring this game. Can you blame me? Just look at it. It's a rogue-like. When it comes to game-design, perma-death has been ran into the ground harder than zombies. Every freaking game wants to see me dead, my stuff taken away, my level reduced to 1, and my progress wiped away like it never ever happened. It's freakin' obnoxious, and yet I continue to play rogue-likes, because obviously I hate myself. As a bonus, this rogue-like resembles Minesweeper. Problem-solving! Strategizing! Clicking on stuff until you lose! It's all so terrible I want to vomit out of my nose.
As expected, it took me about a dozen hours of Runestone Keeper, just to figure out how much I hate it. There are some lovely aspects. The music is nice and atmospheric, the art is effective, and the simple click-to-explore interface removes a lot of the tedium. Also, unlike a number of rogue-likes, there's a shop where you can purchase permanent upgrades. The catch is that these upgrades increase your chances of something good happening. So after several play-throughs and investing hundreds of thousands of gold, your chances of survival might go up 2%. Thanks I guess.
Inside the dungeon, there are multiple floors. Exploration is as simple as clicking on a darkened tile. These tiles will reveal items, traps, mysterious shrines, monsters, shops, and other random events. Monsters are interesting in that they don't actively attack, unless you choose to fight them. The exceptions are the ranged monsters, who attack everytime you move. You could search the immediate area for items to help you deal with these evil denizens, but you run the risk of spawning creatures that boost stats, or cause any number of other problems. This aspect is pretty neat, as it forces you to weigh your options. Do you kill everything as they appear? Maybe you should explore and hope to stumble upon a healing item or a rare piece of armor.
I have nothing nice to say about traps in this game. Each floor is filled with them, and they will chew through your HP at a constant rate. There are items that reveal traps, but they're too infrequent. Most of the time, all you can do is click on the tiles, and pray you don't lose too much HP to spikes, falling rocks, bombs, poison, and so on. Sometimes I'll luck out and acquire a piece of armor that restores HP with every explored tile, but that's luck.
RNG is easily the most dominant force in this game, especially on the harder difficulties. While you have options such as spells, items, the gods you worship, and the stats you raise; they mean nothing when RNG decides to screw you. While exploring, I ran into an Overlord. The properties of an Overlord are random, but well let me just explain this particular jerk. This Overlord was a skeleton archer. His ability was that his attack level was equivalent to my HP. Once this guy appeared, I was♥♥♥♥♥♥out of luck. There are tools for dealing with this situation (like throwing knives, which insta-kill any ranged enemy), but I couldn't find anything of the sort. As I mentioned earlier, archers attack everytime you move, so they can't be avoided. Since the game is entirely turn-based, I had all the time in the world to think about how much I hate RNG. Along with a gigantic middle finger, I recieved an achievement entitled "WTF".
WTF indeed.
Even if Lady Luck blesses you a hundred times over, you'll still have to contend with the end-boss. I've managed to reach him once. Apparently there are multiple end-bosses, and this phantom is the easiest of them. He has a big fat wad of HP, and after I hit him a few times, he split into four (WTF), and quadrupled his number of attacks. Since I can't beat him in a straight fight, I considered that it'd be a better idea to find certain items that could even the odds. At this point the problem becomes: "I need these items, but I also need to survive long enough to reach the boss, and I also need a lot of HP, plus some great equipment if I really have to fight him." Basically, I need every star to align and Pegasus to arrive on a rainbow made out of gold.
Runestone Keeper does a lot of stuff right, and it can be very addictive. However, you have to account for the massive amount of RNG. Plus it's got the perma-death aspects and I...I just can't take it anymore!

Before moving on, i will say that supply boxes in these maps sometimes give smg and shotgun weapons to bots when they're supposed to give a pistol and ammo during the first waves. The classes are basic enough. You got Assault, Pointman (who is basically just a different version of the assault class), Support who places a supply box which gives ammo and health when necessary as long the class has enough charge for it (Could be tweaked to discharge faster), Sniper who really serves use only on damage side since the maps take place mostly indoors and closed areas, and Technician who drops down a sentry to mow down zombies. Problem with the sentry and supply classes is that they can place their stuff inside other players causing them to be stuck. You can bet that trollers and bots

I hate it.
1. The combat is clunky and boring. It's turn based, but like every turn based RPG ever, it really isn't. Enemies just take turns whenever they feel like it, sometimes acting twice before you get to go once. You spend most of the time watching enemies move and attack while you do nothing. Every minor fight takes at least 10 minutes, often longer. There is a bar at the top that shows what order turns will be taken in, but its accuracy is laughable. You'll look at it, plan out the entire turn, and then watch as enemies take extra turns and yours probably gets skipped.
2. There are too many enemies that heal and revive each other, with no warning that they can do so. Expect to spend 30 minutes mopping up enemies only to find out that the last guy left has the ability to revive every single one of them in one turn. Hope you had a quicksave before the fight started.
3. Everything from the battle system to elemental interactions to crafting, trading, repairing, and identifying items has a complex system behind it that isn't like any other game. Sound cool? Maybe it is, but good luck figuring it out because the game doesn't tell you how anything works. This has to be the most user-unfriendly game I have ever played.
4. There are quests that you can miss forever if you do the wrong thing.
5. You have "choices" in quests, except you'll often be harshly punished for choosing wrong.
6. There are a ton of side quests. Again, sounds cool right? Except there are literally a TON, with no indication of what order you should try to tackle them in, whether or not you can even resolve them at the moment, and whether it is a side quest or part of the main story. Your quest log will have 17 active quests in it. 9 of them will be impossible to complete at the moment, but you won't know that, you'll just run around wondering how you complete them. 3 of them will be possible, but you will eventually find out you are way too under-levelled to do them. 2 will be the main story, and 1 will be a sidequest that you are the appropriate level for. Good luck figuring out which is which!
7. The story sucks. Just a bunch of generic fantasy stuff. Every character you meet has to blab a novel to you, and eventually you just start skipping all of the dialogue, which leads to even more confusion on quests.
8. There are really important quest items that are very easy to miss and can be sold to vendors, dropped on the ground, etc. etc. with no indication that you will need them later to progress the game.

I played this back on PS1 and was utterly mesmerised by the world of Abe's Oddyssey. But damn was that game rock hard,
I bought the original again on Steam a few years back but found the difficulty a bit too much and didn't spend more than 10hrs with it: the frustration was outweighing the fun that came from solving the great puzzles, exploring the world and of using the charming gamespeak mechanic.
I was therefore not too keen on a straight remaster. However, the recent Humble Bundle presented a compelling deal so I went for it.
And, overall, I don't regret it; there are so many good things to say about New 'n' Tasty.
So let me say them:
- Amazing, beautiful, captivating art design. The original looked great but was a low-res affair; this brings the game into 3 dimensions without disrupting the fundamentally 2D game design or the superb aesthetic. If a film was made of this game I would watch it.
- The music is beautiful and mysterious, mirroring the original
- the puzzles remain excellent. Really fun to figure out in the main
- The gamespeak is as charming as ever
- I love the story. It's a classic, with tragedy and ample comedy throughout
So it is then with a heavy heart that I'd score this game about a 7 out of 10.
Why so low after all that praise?
It's the way Abe controls. He doesn't do what you want him to do. And when there is precision platforming and split second timing involved, my controller was, more than once, on the cusp of flying out of my hands right into the TV. I don't mind hard games, and I have put in the hours with the likes of Dark Souls and Super Meatboy: both challenging games that offer a massive emotional payoff when your conquer challenging stages. With Oddworld, rather than getting satisfaction and euphoria from beating a stage you struggled with, you get a jaded sense of "I'm glad that's over". No emotional payoff at all. What's the difference? In Dark Souls and Super Meatboy, you always feel that you died because you screwed up. In Oddworld, it's often you find yourself saying "No, I did NOT want to do that!!!"
I still like it though. There are so so many good things about this game. But for me, that one huge sore point of frustrating controls brings the whole experience down considerably.
Final word: Abe should to be revived as an icon of videogames. He is a brilliant character who deserves a few more games about him.

I have been playing for a couple hours as of the time I'm writing this. I'm not typically someone who takes chances on alpha games and usually don't bother to write reviews.
That being said this game's concept is amazing, and if pulled off well, I would like it to become a staple of all magic games. As someone who loves magic in games, some part of me is always dissapointed when I find myself climbing a skill tree, looking around and seeing every other player doing the same. This game allows the gamer the opportunity to literaly create his/her own unique spells, forging one's own prefferences and style.  Even at alpha stages they have provided impressive diversity. It is obviously not perfect, but it's imperfections amount to little at this stage in it's development. Since everything is based off of code I even feel like I'm learning a little, but not to the point where it is like a lesson (though if I did study code I could probably kick butt in this game!).
The number 1 thing new players will find defficient is the lack of any guidbook. Though it is said to be coming soon, you are thrown into the game with complex spell making based on coding and no manuel. At first this really anoyed me, I wanted instant understanding and the ability to craft mind-blowing spells! However it appeared I had to dissect the starting spells the game gave me to determine how they worked. As I said, I wasn't happy at first, but after trial and error for around a whole 20 minutes, I was rewarded with my first semi-original spell! Talk about feeling the rush and emersion in the game! The feeling of having worked and earned it, something being yours. Being able to use the spell and think of how you had put it together, how the idea had come to you! That is all worth it in my book.
Conclusion: Good game. Not great yet, it's too early, but definately a project I would recomend supporting.

CodeSpells is an interesting and unique game. The power to devise your own magic, limited only by the physical rules of the universe and your own imagination, is a truly unique experience.  The art style and music are very charming and draw you into the world from the start.
The first time you wander around and use a simple push spell to launch a little red dinosaur into the sky, you will feel a sense of awe of the possibilities. Then you get a spark of an idea and bring up the spell menu.  At first, you may be a little daunted by the Block-based language used to construct the spells. But after some guess and test and a little bit of practice, you will soon be creating all kinds of magic! From jumping on a rock and causing it to float and lift you off the ground, to building structures and terraforming the world around you, to changing the ebb and flow of water around you, to manipulating the elements around to ignite massive fires.
I have been playing/tinkering with CodeSpells since its earliest Kickstarter Alpha release and have seen it evolve a lot since then. Currently, there are a limited number of options of what you can control in the world around you, primarily:
These may seem very basic and trivial, but the combination of simple logic and these abilities provides an enormous amount of variability in the awe and potency of your magic. One of my favorites is a very simple spell that leviates boulders and allows you to fly around in style
Pros:
Cons:
Despite the few issues of the game, the development team has been extremely receptive to ideas and suggestions by users and there have been many improvements as a result of backer feedback.
Overall, I highly recommend CodeSpells.  No other game gives you a charming world that is both fun and engaging for creating your own magic. As an added benefit, you will learn/improve basic programming skills that are directly transferrable to the real world.

TL:DR; If you're interested in programming with javascript as a hobby, for school or work, this game is a must have. If you're not into programming and need a GUI to place objects, don't buy it and don't leave a negative review.
Play the demo on the website to understand the basics, then buy screeps on steam. I would suggest to play on a local private server first to create a "AI" yourself or use one of the many
provided repositories **before** you active the 30 day free subscription on the server. It takes a couple of days before you get the hang of the game and get a script up and running.
You start with one room, which grows slowly and steady and as your Room Control Level gets higher, you get access to more and more structures. Towers to defend against and heal creeps and to maintain other structures, terminal to trade resources and gain in-game credits, labs to use those resources and boost your creeps.
Once you reach a higher Global Control Level (based on upgrading the Room's Controller), you can own more rooms and have a higher CPU limit (allowing you to take more time while executing your code). It all comes down to your code: how is it designed (room based, creep based, task based, operating system), how efficient is your code and how are things prioritised. Some areas are more hostile, which requires some extra defensive measurements and offensive capabilities to survive / expand.
Unfortunately, the tutorial doesn't cover much more then the tower and spawn structures and you'll have to figure everything out yourself. On the plus side, this can be interpreted as an incentive to read the docs (and API docs), read blogs from others and check out thousands of public repositories on
.
Subscribtion is paid, but it's possible to buy in-game subscription tokens with in-game credits. This could take a while tho. The same tokens are also sold/bought on the Steam marketplace.
All in all, 10/10 recommended to anyone with an interest in programming with javascript. The game combines thinking about the general design of your code, with actual programming, PvP/PvE battles, alliances (LOAN!) and an active/chill community.

Desktop dungeons style "roguelike" (click on tiles to uncover stuff, you have no player sprite). It's quite nice, fun, with a variety, pleasing graphics and effects.
What I don't like is the coin system. As you play you gather gold: this can be used to buy both one time upgrades which give you a permanent advantage every run going forward, and also temporary boosts which you have to buy again each time if you want them. I would prefer it if the game were balanced around the idea of starting from scratch each time.
What can you do though? Sensing, rightly or wrongly that mainstream audiences don't like the lack of a feeling of progression in permadeath games they essentially removed the permadeath by having a persistant "character" that exists at the level of the main menu so you progress each time despite dying over and over.

A novel, pocket-size Rogue-lite that might once have been titled Minesweeper Quest; a feature-complete dungeon crawler conveying the full suite of CRPG trappings with originality and insight. Save for some slightly stilted event dialogue, the presentation is excellent, ably negotiating between gratuitous low-fidelity and unimaginative modern rendering. A thoroughly interesting way to engage with a well-worn (and profoundly frustrating) genre concept.

"Runestone Keeper" sounds a little like "Minesweeper." That's because the games follow a similar format: click on tiles to reveal what's under them. In Runestone Keeper, however, those tiles can have monsters on them, or traps, bombs, helpful items, poison pits, or any number of other things to keep things interesting.
The game requires just a little thought, but not much. It's mostly just clicking, but the effects of various equipment and items picked up can be taken into consideration to turn around an unfavourable board, or just help you avoid certain tile types in order to find the exit that much easier.
It's a good game to kill some time with - made to be difficult, a single "session" is usually very short before you die and have to start over again. Gold carries on, however, and you are able to buy upgrades to make subsequent trips into the dungeon easier. Eventually you'll find yourself reaching new depths more easily.

I've played through this game twice so far, once when it came out and again in Enhanced Edition, both times in 100% co-op.
I have to say that the second playthrough was pretty fun. Knowing how to game the system, craft really powerful items and create a well balanced party that can smash through obstacles is pretty fun. The last boss just completely folded like a wet noodle in just over one turn of combat (it would've been less than a turn, but alas we cast some buffs that we didn't need). I had a particular amount of fun carrying a stack of oil and poison barrels in my characters inventory and throwing them out at bosses before/at the start of fights so that my ally could blow them up with meteors. KABOOM.
The 'Enhanced Edition' doesn't change much for most of the game, but does spruce up the ending quite a bit. And it's free anyhow, so what are you even complaining about? Unfortunately however, the game's approach to making puzzles is not enhanced. It's still 'go find this stupid switch that we hid between six levers' or whatever. Ugh. No thanks.
In any case, I'm quite looking forward to the sequel with it's competitive questing business. That will take a bit stronger storytelling than what they've been doing though. The story is already hard to follow with two people plugging along at different rates. I can't imagine how confusing it'd get when everyone's trying to kill each other or what have you.
But well, that's something for the future.  For now, this is a good game that people should play.

CodeSpells is currently in a very early alpha. Don't buy it if that's not your cup of tea. Aside from that, the premise of the game is one that practically everyone has wanted since they were little kids: you're a wizard and you make your own spells. And it is AWESOME.
The game's physics system is impressive, allowing players to create rock-tornados, unleash torrential bursts of water, part seas, and - of course- hurl fireballs to and fro. Spells can are created with programming logic: a few predefined functions give players a place to start (OnCreate and OnHit, for example) and effects can be added by controlling certain variables (spell movement, lifetime, etc) and logic (if then statements, loops, functions, etc).
Is there a lot of content? No. Is it a cool game? Absolutely. The concept is amazing and the execution is impressive. If you want to see the game's development progress, I highly recommend buying it now. If you don't want to chance it, check back every so often and see how it's grown! It just might win you over later on.

Being a big fan of the Oddworld series sure took me a while to play this remake. However, this is far from being just a remaster like many others nowadays. As compared to the original it has several technical differences that pretty much changes the entire gamestyle.
The original Abe's Oddysee worked with prerendered 3D graphics, making most of its levels work arround screen transitions. Since New N Tasty is full 3D, is easier to predict what's coming next in the area rather face the unexpected (There's still some surprises but most of them easy to prepare against). This new version also eases the experience with quicksaves, checkpoints, and a health bar (although there's still tons of instakills) so is not that punishing to retry puzzles and challenges compared to the original. Overall, Easier is the keyword but that doesn't mean that lost the appeal of the original's gameplay.
If anything, the transition to 3D wasn't perfect and has a few problems. Some of the areas and cutscenes lost the charm they had in the original game, although quite minimum and just when in comparison. When a character dies instead of rotting away they'll ragdoll and thus losing the immersion if starts glitching a bit. Then I had some audio issues where some sound effects didn't play at all, specially from a new mechanic appearing at the very last portion of the game.
Despite some small flaws, New N Tasty still is a great rebuild of one of the jewels from the 32-bit era. Abe's Oddysee is still available everywhere if you prefer a harder experience, but along New N Tasty are wonderful games in both their differences and similarities.

The old classic puzzle platformer made for new generations, friendly for casual players like me, and providing new challenge for hardcores (speedrunning the game without quicksaves on the hard difficulty seems like a challenge).
I've never beaten the original version (Abe's Oddysee), which I know since I was a child, due to lack of quicksaves (yes, I know, I'm a n00b) and hard difficulty, but I was always intrigued by the story, the atmosphere, and the gameplay itself, which is quite original as I've never seen anything like the "gamespeak" before in any other game.
You have 8 keys for communicating with other characters throughout the whole game. For example, in order to save your fellow Mudokon, you must participate in an iconic dialog: - Hello! - Hello. - Follow me! - Ok. The 4 last keys are for whistling and... farting. They seem useless until later in the game, when whistling in proper order is kind of a "password" to let you through. Farting is always funny though, when you fart in front of other Mudokons they always laugh :)
Also, the important part of gameplay and puzzles is chanting, which lets Abe to open portals to save Mudokons (or himself) and to literally control mind of an enemy Slig. And guess what, you can use the gamespeak feature for them too (- Yo! - Waddup!). You can order the Mudokons to keep heads down so you don't kill one accidentaly while shooting to other Sligs. Or you can "talk to" to your good boy dog Slog and shout "Get 'em!" so they kill another Slig (or a Mudokon, you monster).
Each level is like a puzzle, but there is sometimes more than one solution. Generally, you need to do things in right order to get from A to B while saving as most Mudokons as you can (or not, if you're aiming for bad ending, you monster), sometimes you need to have good reflex as well, and you need to know what you can do (although the game gives a lot of hints, except in secret areas) and use it to your advantage. On easier difficulties, even more strategies work as you don't die instantly so you have a bigger margin of error. I like the level design of this game, it makes you think, it's not obvious and the game doesn't hold your hand, so there is a lot of satisfaction involved in not only figuring out how to beat the level but also in executing it properly. It also never gets boring, each level is different and the game introduces a lot of gameplay elements even after half way through (motion detectors, Shrykull power, grenades, meat, rocks, mines, Elums, ..., with new kind of enemies as well), and you need to use them in a creative way in order to progress.
Regarding the story, I was not dissappointed. The Oddworld is really odd, creatures are well designed, scary yet funny, the atmosphere is dark and yet the game can make you laugh and have fun from dying. It's like a dark cartoon. I like that you're not a hero*, you're just an employee of the year being in wrong time and place, simply wanting to get out of Rupture Farms, a food corporation which already made several species close to extinction just for profit and uses Mudokons as slaves, now planning to slice even them into new 'n' tasty meat as well. Also, there is basically no interface, everything happens in the game world, which is another great plus for the level design.
This is an excellent remake, although it's a shame it doesn't work on my old notebook, but the game looks great, like the original game (which has quite an amazing graphics despite being old) but in full high resolution 3D. Controls are smooth and the overall feeling of the game is amazing. I recommend this game, its game design feels fresh and good even after all those years after the original Abe's Oddysee was made. I'm waiting for remake of the sequel, Abe's Exoddus.
* I mean, Abe is a hero (if you're aiming for the good ending) but he didn't ask for his "destiny" and he's clumsy af, which can be seen especially in cutscenes and his funny animations in the game when for example you run into a wall.

I had to take a little break to say that I'm really enjoying this game so far, but that's mostly because the original was a masterpiece. Some areas are a little different and there's also a whole lot of side areas I've never seen. They've also changed some mechanics and added some features -for instance; you don't need to crouch to pick up bombs anymore, and Abe can now throw bottle caps. (no idea where he gets the infinite supply of caps from but w/e)
Graphics are nicely re-done, Mudokon's talk a little more and character voices are a little different but still just as charming.
Controls and movement are ♥♥♥♥ed up just like before, but I guess that's what makes it challenging in one way. This is no super mario platforming.
All in all it's a great game. I just wish they'd make a completely new Abe's instead.

Runestone Keeper is an interesting mix of Minesweeper, an RPG and possibly Magic: The Gathering with a pixelated art style. It's fairly simple to learn, but definitely harder to master. Worshipping different gods, as you "collect" them, has different effects on your character, both positive and negative. You gain mana from clicking open tiles and sometimes by defeating enemies. Some enemies attack at a distance and you have to have a distance weapon or spell to reach them, otherwise you take damage every turn as you have to be in a tile adjacent to theirs. Some enemies come back to life when killed. Some buff other on-screen enemies, or get buffs as each other on-screen enemy is killed. Some have a shield bonus that you have to take down before you deal damage to the enemy. However, items that benefit you are dropped or can be purchased with gold received from defeating enemies. You also get a point upon gaining a level that you use to increase a specific stat (strength, dexterity, etc.). Sometimes you have to look at the enemies' stats and plan a strategy on the order in which you must kill them, and/or use items you have collected to defeat the enemies easier. You may have buffs, abilities, or bonuses from your stat points, items and weapons you are wearing or using, or both.
All in all, this game is, as the saying goes, easy to learn but difficult to master. Each floor you descend contains stronger and more difficult enemies, as well as different events (marked by "?") that could help or hurt you depending on the choices you make. How many floors are in this dungeon anyway? A lot. A whole lot. Try to get to the bottom!
There are a few bugs here and there that will probably never be patched.  But, for $10, this is an excellent time waster.

Although the game is certainly rich both in interesting interactions as well as design flaws, it is hard not to recommend Runestone Keeper at its price point, which is set perfectly.
I will state this first: the game will repeatedly put you in positions where you are set to lose, without any possibilities of recovery. You will often look back from that point and realize that there was nothing you could have done to save yourself. It is expected that this does not frustrate you as you still "progress" by spending the collected gold on upgrades afterwards.
As it currently stands, Runestone Keeper is a very accessible rogue-lite game that offers challenging experiences ranging from 10 to 30 minutes. It is alright at everything it does, your play sessions will sway rapidly between mild fun and curiosity and slight annoyance. Its distinguishment comes from the fact that even with its current flaws, it is very close to a very polished and satisfying experience.
The main weakness is balance and polish, numbers don't seem to work well with eachother which makes a few of the in-game systems and interactions useless. Your main source of continuous progress is gold - still the game asks absurd prices for single-use items, synthetizing runes and mediocre equipment - thus rendering all three almost useless. The "gold-making" upgrades and gods are also mostly a waste, either never being able to return its own cost or taking too long to do so.
The starting class is bad when compared to the other two, still it matters not much. Most losses come from impossible scenarios - although your first deaths will most likely be to bad planning - where suddenly a "winning" run stumbles upon special rooms designed to kill you unless you meet very specific criteria, which are often simply not a possibility.
Overall it is a decent product, for a good price, and very close to being something satisfying or perhaps even great.

My only gripe, and it's a very small one, is that it's subscription-based. However, you'll always be able to play if you got it through Steam, albeit with limited 'CPU'. Even if that's not the case, the cost for a sub is very reasonable.

This game is unlike any other I've seen or played. It gives you the ability and training to make your own autonomous colony, and become a global superpower! Although, with no central goal of the game being forced on you, this is really whatever you make of it. Private and community servers allow you to play with your friends or just away from the main group. The only true downside is that you should pay for a CPU subscription. It allows you to run more creeps and effectively have larger colonies, but it is not required. Without a subscription you have a mere 10 CPU, but you can work through that with a little bit of ingenuity and reasonable persistence. I myself have been working on scripts that work under 10 CPU, in fact.
There is one major issue I should address, but it's not with the game. If you're the kind of person who lacks adequate attention span, one who doesn't like to do anything that's somewhat difficult, or one who doesn't like to learn and grow as a human being, this game is not for you. I firmly believe that anyone can learn to code, but if you tend to give up at the first sign or resistance, then you should probably look elsewhere for a good time. Now on a more serious note, the game provides a tutorial on how to play and on writing code, not to mention you can play the sim mode without a CPU subscription. It's also important to mention that the 30 days of CPU subscription don't start until you've connected to the main server, so worry not about wasting it before you really grasp the basics of the game.
All in all, this is a wonderful game for anyone who is willing to sit down and take the time to really get into it. If you're looking for something easy, or something that is fast paced, or you just really don't want to have to learn something new, I can't recommend this. But if you have some patience, by all means take a look at the free demo at
and see if you really want to buy this game.

Thirty Flights of Loving is Blendo Games short, similar, follow-up to their prior release of "Gravity Bone".
Thirty Flights follows the same style and make-up of the first game, with the same kinds of punches and surprises, but stylised in a nicer manner, with more focus on "the story" (what little of it there is) than "the game" (such as Gravity Bone).
The game is incredibly short. 15-20 minutes long, but succeeds in delivering you a firm understanding of an interesting story in that time, using dynamic scene changes and blends.
It's okay. I enjoyed it. For the price of £3.99? Not worth it. £0.99? Definitely worth the play. The game also has a "Developer commentary" mode, similar to the Portal 1 developer mode, where you can activate text-points throughout the game for more info on the scene, but whenever I ran this mode the game crashed within 1 minute of activating the dialogue boxes, so I was unable to complete it at all in this mode, sadly.
A decent injection from Blendo, but I expected more, from their clearly very talented team.

Thirty Flights of Loving is a first-person interactive story. The story's incredibly short, and can be experienced in about 15 minutes. The story itself is told in short, disconnected segments requiring you to fill in the blanks yourself.
30 Flights is definitely an arthouse game. It has an interesting approach to interactive storytelling that may be worth seeing, but unfortunately, the story it tells is unremarkable. From what I could tell, there just isn't much substance there. What's much more interesting is playing with the developer's commentary on, so you can see some of the thought that went behind the experience.
The game's prequel is also included, and while it's a longer game with more gameplay elements, it's designed clumsily, and you might be left with no idea where to go.
This game has a very niche audience, and to them, this game will be worth far more than the asking price. It wasn't for me, though, and I get the feeling that it's not for most people, especially because the price doesn't pay for much content. It's worth experiencing if you have a few extra minutes, but I wouldn't pay over a dollar for this. If this looks interesting to you, I'd recommend checking out The Stanley Parable instead.

I've played through this game twice so far, once when it came out and again in Enhanced Edition, both times in 100% co-op.
I have to say that the second playthrough was pretty fun. Knowing how to game the system, craft really powerful items and create a well balanced party that can smash through obstacles is pretty fun. The last boss just completely folded like a wet noodle in just over one turn of combat (it would've been less than a turn, but alas we cast some buffs that we didn't need). I had a particular amount of fun carrying a stack of oil and poison barrels in my characters inventory and throwing them out at bosses before/at the start of fights so that my ally could blow them up with meteors. KABOOM.
The 'Enhanced Edition' doesn't change much for most of the game, but does spruce up the ending quite a bit. And it's free anyhow, so what are you even complaining about? Unfortunately however, the game's approach to making puzzles is not enhanced. It's still 'go find this stupid switch that we hid between six levers' or whatever. Ugh. No thanks.
In any case, I'm quite looking forward to the sequel with it's competitive questing business. That will take a bit stronger storytelling than what they've been doing though. The story is already hard to follow with two people plugging along at different rates. I can't imagine how confusing it'd get when everyone's trying to kill each other or what have you.
But well, that's something for the future.  For now, this is a good game that people should play.

Without spoiling anything this game is a great example of what happens when you do really well at one thing and half♥♥♥♥♥everything else.
The Good sides!
The characters and the leveling system are well done, the skills are useful and varied and each type of abilities feel fleshed out and useful. Intelligence based characters have way more options than strength or dex characters as one skill is tied to strength, two to dex, and a whopping five to intelligence for some odd reason. The levels are fleshed out well, they look great, the enemies are challenging and the boss fights are interesting.
The Bad sides!
TRAPS
The game is completely littered with traps, literal traps, that will kill you and your entire group in maybe two hits if you are lucky. Half the time there is no way to avoid these traps, and there is no way to disarm them (save expensive single use items and they don't do much when there are six traps in one hallway). You just trigger them and then very slowly walk around them trying not to die and having to heal yourself over and over again while your tankiest dude takes all the explosions. The amount of traps is just insane and it doesn't add to the gameplay it really just slows it down to a crawl. Some of these situations you will find yourself in will make you scream in rage at the sheer unfairness of the situations the game forces you into, like spawning a giant minefield all around you for pushing a button you have no choice but to push for example.
The crafting system...
It makes no sense whatsoever. You need blacksmithing to make armor and weapons out of metal, crafting for everything else. You can't even improve armor without the crafting skill, which makes no sense seeing as how you make it with blacksmithing. Crafting does literally everything else in the game that involves making things. Downsides you cant find resources after you go through an area once, so there are a finite amount of things you can find. Add a system that gives  you stats randomly on items you make and you have a session of crafting and reloading again and again to try and get decent gear. By the way you have no choice in this since crafting makes better gear than you will ever manage to find since random drops are horrid most of the time. I found a legendary weapon with 1 durability point and couldn't be repaired... why even have it?
The story
It's pretty bland, magic using bad guys are bad, you kill bad guys. Nothing really standing out here,
The biggest problem with the game by far, the most unforgiveable thing they did that makes the game damn near laughable..... NO TIMED AUTOSAVES!!!!
Read that again NO TIMED AUTOSAVES.
You think its not a big deal till you lose yourself in a string of fights, get insta murdered when a moron character walks into lava for no reason, and then realize that because you havn't gone somewhere new in the past hour you never had a single autosave. It's downright insane that an open RPG in this day and age doesn't have timed autosaves. That's pretty much standard nowadays and the lack of one here is a real pain since you have to constantly remind yourself that you need to save. Add in the BS trap-a-palooza of instant death and you have a good recipe for frustration and rage.
The enemy spawning
Something else the game loves to do to you is spawn enemies seemingly at random. Go open a treasure chest? enemies magically appear, kill a specific enemy, more enemies magically appear, and the best part is when this happens, they tend to be suicidal enemies that explode for massive damage... No way to prevent it other than to already know when its going to happen.
The game is decent as rpg's go, and the closest thing to an updated dungeons and dragons game I've seen in awhile, but the flaws the game has just make it not fun to play. Save yourself the trouble and find something else.

Crazy Plant Shop is a pretty cool game while you're still figuring out the mechanics. Mixing plants and understanding how the dominant and recessive traits work in your favour (or against you). After you do understand, however, the game gets very monotonous.
Every mission is just someone asking you x number of plants with x and y traits. So you mix your plants to get the desired result. And that's about it. Some light management aspects to it, knowing when to buy a plant or mix them, etc., but those aspects don't make much of a difference, overall.
It also gets very dull to have to repeat the same procedure over and over and over again. Click here, click there, wait for the menu to pop-up, click here, open menu, close menu, etc. etc.
It would definitely benefit from a pipeline mechanic, like in SpaceChem, so that you could automatize everything. But that would be a different game altogether, I guess.
I'm not too keen on the educational aspect of the game. I mean, it's still sistematic/mechanic learning. You're not exploring, digging, investigating anything through trial and testing, for the most part. Which would be the real joy of learning?
Like this, it's following a textbook in videogame form. You're still just going through the required motions without ever being surprised. They don't give you a fairly obscure objective that requires you to explore the mechanics until you figure out a possible path to the solution. Instead, you're just kind of memorizing what you need to do, and then you're done. Which is unfortunate, but not unexpected...
Not my kind of "educational" game, but it may help with middle/high school tests, I guess.

This game is neither fun nor educational. Each day you can breed a limited number of plants and the game is 13 days. This discourages you from experimenting with the genetics and forces you to fill orders as efficiently as possible. The punnett square is a joke. You put plants in a machine and select which trait you want to result. All of the traits have one dominant and one recessive gene, so you can keep two heterozygous plants and breed any result needed. The customers have quirky dialogue but there's no sequence to it. I had one character complain I sold plants to another character I hadn't met. By the last day, almost all of the dialogue was repeated.

If you liked what you learned in Genetics or Bio I, you'll really enjoy the "strategy" to this game.  It's very simple with only one criterion to continue your jourmey: have 10g to pay your rent each day.  Other than that, just get heterozygotes for the plant you're working on and upgrade breeding power early.  Simple and relaxing, but no replayability if you win first time.
You can tell that the creation was pretty simple.
I recommend it if it's on sale or you have a child that wants to learn about genetics or likes plants or shop games.

It's fun for a while, although after a certain amount of time I got bored. It's really cute, and does something to teach about how genetics work. Not sure how correct it is, since I didn't do so hot on that topic in high school bio class, but that doesn't change the fact that I think I learned something while playing this game! Highly recommended for kids, people learning basics about genetics, or both!

It does look amazing and the graphics are just great. When i first got into it, it felt like a combination of a gorgeous painting and an animated movie (If you can describe it that way). There is so much to see and there is so much variation in the terrain.
The animations are also wonderful and especially for cute little Ori :3 but also for the surrounding vegetation which makes everything feel more alive when you pass through the forest for example. There is always something to look at and it's beautiful.
It is among the most beautiful music in a game i have had the pleasure of listening to. The composer has done an amazing job and has a certain theme for every area. At one point of the game it was so challenging that i got pretty frustrated and was about to leave the game for some time till i had calmed down, but the music was so good that it kept me playing till i beat the challenge.
Other sounds also adds to the atmosphere of the game as the different noises in the jungle, the splashing when Ori dives into the water or the deep breath she takes when she comes up above the water surface again. All in all, the sounds are relaxing, realistic, cute and atmospheric.
The gameplay is fun as it is challenging where you have to think to solve puzzles but it also feels rewarding. Like most games it gets harder as the story and Ori progresses and the game will not autosave for you so always remember to SAVE! LoL.
It also has the ability tree where you can spend your ability points that you get through killing enemies or finding special items. Im glad that there is an ability tree in the game as that makes the player free to choose what upgrade Ori will get next.
The story is also something very nice about the game as you immidiately get feels for Ori in the beginning of the game. One of the reasons that i bought the game was because of the feels i got when i watched the intro of the game on YouTube. You know it's a good game if it evolves a connection between you and the character.
You get to see some small parts of lore when you scout the wilderness and as Ori continues on her quest, but as i am one who likes lore a lot, i think there could be a little more to it. This game is greatly underappreciated.  It perfectly matches the atmosphere of the Warhammer 40k universe.  The game takes place over a short period of time during which the action and importance of what is going on quickly escalates.  Playing as one of the Ultramarines provides a great look into the world of 40k by allowing the players to become a seemingly unstoppable weapon as you fight hordes of enemies. This is a great game for Games Workshop, offering strong gameplay and a nice long campaign which covers a small selection of enemies to the Space Marines from the 40K Universe. Though the generic Ultramarine chapter has been designated for the SP campaign, the MP game allows for infinite chapter colours as well as some great DLC chapters. Acquiring all the achivements can take some doing as there are some very specific demands for a lot of them in order to gain bonuses, whereas levelling up to 41 is simply about playing for a long time. The MP co-op is pretty good fun, against the Orks, in a Left4Dead fashion you have to face wave after wave of hoardes of greenskins with a few specialist troops thrown to make things tough. There is also a Chaos version offering a variety of Chaos themed foes. The voice acting is good, gorefest is high, the AI can sometimes be quite tactical and tricky to overcome. There is a strange grenade launcher, original to the game and not a GW concept, it takes some getting used to, though to be fair the most fun comes from using bolters and the chainsword in melée. During MP get used to annoying players who spam metagun and plasma or lascannon attacks, as they are instant kill weapons which generally require less skill than the rest of the armoury. MP's biggest weakness is the lack of an open server list, you are thrown into the lobby of a match the game decides on and that's it.. shame, as this game could easily have attracted a bigger player base had it been more flexible with regards to offering hosting options.

Runestone Keeper is a great game.
Until this was put on sale, I had on idea that such a game was in development. And now suddenly, it is proclaimed as the best made-in-China game of this year (and you could probably count in a few years before), to which I intend to agree. In that light, this game is a reason to celebrate, because for long I've doubted the abilities of any Chinese producers to make a decent game at all, let alone a roguelike game, which is of a quite modern concept that is much less established in the Chinese game indutries than in the western ones. But somehow, the developers succeeded to pull off this genre, and brought us Runestone Keeper.
RK still has its defects, e.g. imbalance of skills or equipments (some being too powerful and desirable, while some being totally expendable); relying heavily on luck to progress into deeper floors; and certainly we need more new monsters and mechanics to contantly overcome the unavoidable repititiveness. But overall, RK could nonetheless score at least an 8/10 from me, and many other players as well, I believe.
Having said all this, I'd put a "recommend" label on RK as a conclusion, which is deserved without any doubt. And worth saying, the reason would not be "made in China but not cheap quality", but "this is a good game after all".
I hope the developers keep up with their efforts. As should many other Chinese developers, too.

Here's all the reasons why you should, or shouldn't play Screeps:
If you like coding, or want to improve your JavaScript, this is a great place for it. This game allows you to build up from nothing into an RTS extravaganza to fight against other players for their territory, or to defend your own using nothing but script. They make it easy to do basically everything with their api and documentation.
Here's my list of
for this game:
+Game API & Documentation
+In-Game Scripting & Saving
+Transpiled Language support
+Open-source
+Private Servers
+Scripts are easily accessible and saves on file system.
+Scripts edited on file system are immediately updated.
+Tutorial
+Game is free on Web Browser (with 10CPU to start with)
+Steam account can be played on Web Browser when bought.
+In-Game Output/Console
+Simulation / Sandbox mode
+Built-in Path finding
+Memory caching
+Progressive Gameplay & Rewarding
+Still runs while offline
+EMail Alerts (Being attacked, etc)
+Room replay
+Devs Constantly Updating
+Your Global Control Level is saved forever
+Nukes
+Becomes a total RTS game made from your own code later on.
+Nukes
With all the good comes the ugly. This game is loads of fun to play for me, but there's a bunch of things that might be off-putting to a good amount of people. One of them might be the tick rate. All your code runs per tick, and each tick runs once every 1-5 seconds (depending on the server you join).
This means, at the start of the game when you create your first unit (called creeps), you have to wait the tick duration of the server for that creep to move 1 space in the direction it needs to go (Note: The amount the creep moves will change the further you get).
Another thing is that there is no "run once" portion of your code, you have to do that part yourself, because all your code runs on a loop. I wouldn't even really call this a flaw or a problem, it could just be a little frustrating for some that are just getting into programming.
Here's my list of cons for screeps:
-Tick rates on servers can feel slow, and can be up to 5 second intervals.
-Learning curve
-Not many structure options until late room levels
-New players need to pick their spawn wisely, or they can be easily destroyed if safe mode is not enabled.
-All email alerts appear with the subject "Screeps game notifications" regardless of severity. (I/E: The subject for both the coding error and the hostile units in your room alert will be the same.)
-Output in Simulation can be confusing sometimes, and can make testing difficult. (Thus it's easier to test in the main game or in a private server)
-You can only own 1 room as a new player. A separate level (GCL; Global Control Level) determines how many rooms you can control. Which is much like a leveling system for a game, except leveling up takes a huge amount of gameplay. Each level you get grants you 1 extra room you can control.
Here's some varying aspects of the game:
-/+Slow gameplay & progress
-/+New players need to face huge threats later on
-/+Subscription based (You can play free with 10CPU)
-/+Intimidating surroundings
Overall I rate this game an 8/10!
I thoroughly enjoy playing this game and I believe it has a huge amount of replayability.
I look forward to how much further it can go, and hope the devs keep moving forward with it.

If you are interested in storytelling, how tales are told and put together, independent or small team games (just one man), or things that are unique I recommend it wholeheartedly. Thirty Flights subverts the tropes of first person games intentionally to create a game that is different for each player depending on the baggage, or lack thereof, they bring with them.

Without spoiling anything this game is a great example of what happens when you do really well at one thing and half♥♥♥♥♥everything else.
The Good sides!
The characters and the leveling system are well done, the skills are useful and varied and each type of abilities feel fleshed out and useful. Intelligence based characters have way more options than strength or dex characters as one skill is tied to strength, two to dex, and a whopping five to intelligence for some odd reason. The levels are fleshed out well, they look great, the enemies are challenging and the boss fights are interesting.
The Bad sides!
TRAPS
The game is completely littered with traps, literal traps, that will kill you and your entire group in maybe two hits if you are lucky. Half the time there is no way to avoid these traps, and there is no way to disarm them (save expensive single use items and they don't do much when there are six traps in one hallway). You just trigger them and then very slowly walk around them trying not to die and having to heal yourself over and over again while your tankiest dude takes all the explosions. The amount of traps is just insane and it doesn't add to the gameplay it really just slows it down to a crawl. Some of these situations you will find yourself in will make you scream in rage at the sheer unfairness of the situations the game forces you into, like spawning a giant minefield all around you for pushing a button you have no choice but to push for example.
The crafting system...
It makes no sense whatsoever. You need blacksmithing to make armor and weapons out of metal, crafting for everything else. You can't even improve armor without the crafting skill, which makes no sense seeing as how you make it with blacksmithing. Crafting does literally everything else in the game that involves making things. Downsides you cant find resources after you go through an area once, so there are a finite amount of things you can find. Add a system that gives  you stats randomly on items you make and you have a session of crafting and reloading again and again to try and get decent gear. By the way you have no choice in this since crafting makes better gear than you will ever manage to find since random drops are horrid most of the time. I found a legendary weapon with 1 durability point and couldn't be repaired... why even have it?
The story
It's pretty bland, magic using bad guys are bad, you kill bad guys. Nothing really standing out here,
The biggest problem with the game by far, the most unforgiveable thing they did that makes the game damn near laughable..... NO TIMED AUTOSAVES!!!!
Read that again NO TIMED AUTOSAVES.
You think its not a big deal till you lose yourself in a string of fights, get insta murdered when a moron character walks into lava for no reason, and then realize that because you havn't gone somewhere new in the past hour you never had a single autosave. It's downright insane that an open RPG in this day and age doesn't have timed autosaves. That's pretty much standard nowadays and the lack of one here is a real pain since you have to constantly remind yourself that you need to save. Add in the BS trap-a-palooza of instant death and you have a good recipe for frustration and rage.
The enemy spawning
Something else the game loves to do to you is spawn enemies seemingly at random. Go open a treasure chest? enemies magically appear, kill a specific enemy, more enemies magically appear, and the best part is when this happens, they tend to be suicidal enemies that explode for massive damage... No way to prevent it other than to already know when its going to happen.
The game is decent as rpg's go, and the closest thing to an updated dungeons and dragons game I've seen in awhile, but the flaws the game has just make it not fun to play. Save yourself the trouble and find something else.

If you're like me, you and a buddy will spend hours combing through Steam or whatever to find "that game" that is exactly what you're craving. DOS: EE was that game for us.
It plays like Baldur's Gate II back in the day, and despite some clunky controls and pathing (sometimes your followers decide to walk through fire instead of around it), the combat and skills are immensely satisfying, the class setup and dynamism are refreshing, and the story is, as a whole, interesting. Reminiscent of your weird buddy's decision to DM a tabletop that just goes crazy out of nowhere, there are plenty of side quests to keep you entertained. Plus you can take a talent to talk to animals.
My buddy and I are nearing max level and the close of the campaign, but it's been a wild ride and a great 60-hour investment. If you enjoy dungeon crawling and mild puzzle themes, you'll probably like this one.

Cons:

I picked this game up during the winter sale, it looked amazing and others were saying good things about it.  The game is still in early access, so things I mention here may not be true in the future.
From the get-go, the game looks, feels, and sounds amazing.  I am big on music in games and the soundtrack blew me away when you enter your first dream, it is absolutely beautiful.  The graphics aren't top notch but they still look amazing, I find myself wandering around through the different dream sequences just taking in the design.
Now as far as playing the game, basically you are exploring different dream sequences and solving puzzles within them.  The puzzles so far are really good, they may seem ambiguous at first but they are easy enough to understand once you start doing them (Sometimes listening to the main character speak will give a hint to the puzzle).  They still take some time to complete though, but I'd discourage using guides to solve the puzzles, it feels really good to solve one on your own :D.
Given that the game is still in early access, there are some thing that I feel could be improved upon.  Although I discourage a guide for solving the puzzles, it almost seems necessary to use one to find your way to the next one.  Figuring out where to go is a nuisance, it's cool running around and taking in the scenery but it gets real boring after a while and you just want to move on with the game.  "Moving on" with the game though isn't always clear though, what I mean is, for example, there was one point where I finished a puzzle, then it just brought me back into the bedroom, it was as if I completed the puzzle but nothing happened!  No indication that anything had changed, no indication of where to go next, nothing.  Figuring out where to go would probably be a lot better if the opening the map wasn't such a chore (It's almost as annoying as Zelda's Adventure for the CDI, if you watch AVGN you know what I mean), a simple hotkey that pops open the map would be much better rather than going through your inventory...at least if there is a simple way to open the map I haven't figured it out yet, adding to the game's ambiguity right now.
There were two bugs I encountered in this game, one was during a puzzle my character got stuck and I wasn't able to move, causing me to have to "wake up" in the menu and have to start the puzzle over again.  Another was when I had moved through a portal into a dream sequence, the game crashed.  I didn't lose much progress though.
Even though there are a couple bugs and the game is pretty ambiguous, I would still highly recommend it to everyone, it is a great game with huge potential and I know it will only get better.  For all I know the ambiguity is intended, after all, how many dreams have you had that weren't ambiguous?

I had a fever for roguelike or roguelike-like or roguelite games - whatever you name it - (Just FYI, I have had 100% achievement completion of many other roguelite titles, which at least proves that the following opinions are not from a noob's perspective)
The charm of roguelite games, in my opinion, is how to improvise under different random scenarios (tough ones mostly), and overcome them with all the strategies and skills you have learned from countless previous failures.
Yes, death is everywhere in roguelite games, but in good roguelite games, every death can provides you a sense of improvement, you (as the player not your in-game character) will actually learn alot along with every death. New strategies, skills and tricks will be gradually learnt to overcome all those seemingly impossible situations generated by bad luck. You will realize that there are always multiple ways to avoid it after each death, it is yourself to be blamed instead of the RNG itself.
But such sense of improvement is absolutely absent in
, and there are always more improperly designed mechanisms I'd like to blame than myself.
Now we are talking about
, of course luck is essentially involved in all roguelite games, so I tend to use a "Luck ration" when evaluating roguelite games, which is "How many percentages of luck will be needed for a decent play session (unnecessarily completed)".
In those best also the most well-known roguelite games, for example,
,
,
, this “Luck ratio” is definitely lower than 20%, and that’s why it is even possible for skilled players to do a low% run in those titles.
Among those less good roguelite games, like
, this ration might be around 50%.
What’s the difference?
Firstly, for example, in
, even the most powerful items will turn into craps when combined with wrong ones, while items with negative effects can occasionally become totally overpowered when combined with the right ones. There isn’t an absolute good or bad item, they were just “different”. Oppositely, in
, there are only useless items, good items and awesome items, no strategy was involved in the decision, all you need to do was just stack more and more items as no bad consequence will result anyway.
Secondly, most random elements in
can be manipulated or influenced by player’s action, e.g. the spawn chance of demon room and angel room. Such sense of subjective manipulation is also absent in
.
That’s why I think
is a better game than
, for it has two things that
doesn’t have: One is Strategy, including resource management, subjective manipulation on RNG etc. The other one is “Play Style”, which is also something fundamental in most classical action games, like
.
Well, let’s come back to
, what’s the “Luck Ratio” in this case? More than 85% even conservatively estimated, I would say.
Strategies only play a very limited role in
, and most of them were quite superficial and obvious that can easily be comprehended by any player in the first 2 hours.
After that, all you can do is just keep restarting again and again, until you’re finally lucky enough to grind out all the right combinations (equipment, items, traps and enemy settings) at the right times.
While bad luck only means a harder time in other roguelite games, it usually guarantees a certain death in this game. There was an excessive amount of unsolvable facepunching death trap in this game, Yes, I know, I know, they are still solvable somehow with either skill A or item B or equipment C or ABC combined, however, acquiring those ABC stuff (at the right time) requires nothing but sheer luck as well. And there is nothing you can actually do about its RNG besides praying.
A good game is all about experience, but the gaming experience provided by
was consisted solely by three things: Praying – Clicking – Restarting
This is why I think this
is more a gambling than a game. There is no doubt that gambling is still an addictive and engaging activity, but I don’t think anyone would agree that gambling is a good example for video game design except some mobile game developers.
So, as a conclusion: if you prefer gambling more than an actual game, and tend to rely more on your luck instead of skill, this
might be your thing, otherwise, there were just way too many better titles in the roguelite category.

Charming, utterly different game experience to anything else I have ever played. I only have very rudimentary coding knowledge, but thanks to the tutorial and the community I have managed to create a small flourishing economy.
While coders certainly will get more out of it than myself, the early challenges the game provides are interesting in their own right. I now have many different drones scripted to harvest, transport, defend and control. I need to keep track of production costs, harvest speeds, transport speeds and build priorities. Pretty much like in a regular RTS, but the beauty of Screeps is that you need to solve the puzzle of "how" while solving the puzzle of "what".
The tutorial throws scripts at you without explaining all the elements of the scripts, so it can be difficult at first to stray from the provided examples. If you're into creative problem-solving and don't mind a bit of internet research, you'll accept this as part of the game. If your frustration tolerance is a bit too low for this, go to the slack group and ask someone to explain it to you (certainly faster that way).
Have I actually learned programming now? Well, I've learned you can't just add two arrays together. Or that two drones with one task each are easier to debug than one complex drone with multiple tasks. I have also learned that after getting wiped by a NPC invader, having some of those complex multi-functional drones left is very valuable (no point harvesting if there is no one to collect). Or that simple conditions like "is this full, then to that instead" are stupid if the state of condition can fluctuate from second to second.
There is a ton of good design theory you'll pick up playing Screeps and a sense of achievement you will not get from grinding-based games, so give it a try!

Right from the getgo all the way until the very last scene it knows how to build you up and make you feel taller than ever before. It knows how to make you feel like you're on air and how to give you an overdose of adrenaline. In equal measure it also knows how to tear you down. It has the ability to play with your heartstrings and it will. (This is a good thing, it's executed phenomenaly)
I could continue to gush on everything that makes it so great, but I feel that instead I'll point out what is actually wrong with it (of which there is very little.)
1. The game doesn't quite explain 'why' some story events happen. They're very small things, small enough that you could easily get away with just assuming what the reasoning behind it was and likely be right. It can just be a little annoying at times.
2. Non-rebindable Keys. This isn't SO bad as the layout they have is decent. Holding the shift button while you move with WASD can be fairly strenuous but other than that all 3 different layouts are very good. (I recommend controller though. Mouse + Key layout has the Shift + WASD issue and the Keyboard layout limits you to 8-directions which can be annoying for some of the powerups)
3. The enemy types get reused quite a bit. They may have slightly changed gimmicks, powerups, or other slight alterations, but there are really probably no more than 15 enemy types in the entire game (Not counting variations.)
4. It's a bit short. This isn't so bad really. Quality over quantity, though I can't help feeling that it ended 1 dungeon too early. (Admittedly I didn't 100% the game or anything. I did a decent amount of exploring, backtracked a couple times to search for some powerups. I got like 66% completion I believe and that took me about 7 hours.)
That's literally it. I have no more complaints. All of these are so minor to begin with anyway! The music is absolutely stellar, the development of the characters is suprisingly in depth considering there is only 2 vocal characters in the entire game, neither of which ever speak to one another, and the gameplay is so polished and well made and blends with the aesthetic and story perfectly.
Something that truly needs it's own special mention is the abillity for the game to continuously vary up the gameplay and how it never stops doing so. Maybe about once every 30 minutes or so a new powerup is introduced that completely changes the way the game is played (shoutouts to Bash, probably the most fun ability out of every video game I think I've every played.) New movement options are constantly being added, meaning that while at the beginning you are limited to run and jump, at the end of the game you have a plethora of ways to move around the map like a badass (Triple jump, Wall cling, Wall jump, Directional air dashes off of projectiles, Super Jumps, Gliding. You name it, It's probably there.)
I cannot state enough how fantastic this game is. Just... just listen to this music:
If you have even a passing interest in MetroidVania style games, I recommend you buy Ori immediately. What are you doing? Why don't you own it yet? I own it. You should too!
(I saw some people on the discussions boards complaining about crashes, but that never happened to me. You might want to make sure it will run correctly on your computer first lol)

It's really more of a contest admission than a game. It really disappointed me, having read lot of positive reviews and opinions. I'm not even talking about shockingly short length (measured in minutes), which I was aware before buying. Maybe it's a fault of the hype around it, claiming that there's more to that game than there really is.
The game does features some original ideas. The story is told achronologically, conveyed only through pictures and to put all the pieces together you will have to play through it couple times to notice things after seeing whole picture. If only story would be more absorbing and had less holes in it (it's derp, it's open ended!!!). Why would you play narrative game if not for the bloody story? In result there's not much incentive to put all the pieces together (you're not going to connect all the dots anyway, so why bother).
The graphics is OK (for a Quake 2 modded engine that is) and the music is quite nice. What's most annoying is that it's a barely a game, your actions don't matter at all. Leave guns and ammo? Nobody cares. Take different direction, game teleports you! That's just lazy level design (or lack of it). Goes without saying that you have no effect on the ending. It does say something about the game if "credit hall" is the biggest level in game.
In the end it's neither good game nor good story. I don't think it will make much difference in story-telling department as well. I'm glad not much developers charge for proof of concept projects. It's of course important to experiment and explore what games can be and become, but it shouldn't be an excuse. That's the hardest part, turning brave and new ideas into working and absorbing games, not just leaving them be and packaging it as a game. I enjoyed "To the moon", this not so much. Maybe it would worked more as a Interactive Fiction? Spare the money, watch it on youtube.

where to start ... i guess i'll start with the pros
Pros:

I find that this game, while certainly not bad, is overrated. I've played all of the Divinity games, but I'd rate this the lowest alongside Beyond Divinity.
The game has decent combat, audio and graphics, but is, in my opinion, lacking in most other aspects.
My main interests in RPGs are mainly story, interesting character/locales, dialogue and optimizing builds/stats. The game doesn't satisfy on any of these areas. The story is a generic and farily lackluster fantasy tale that doesn't serve to invest you into the game. The characters, with a few exceptions like Arhu and Jahan, are forgettable. The locales are standard fantasy fare without anything standing out. There's also a lack of a world map to put the areas of the game into any sort of geographical context which is really hurting immersion into the gameworld.
The writing is mostly decent, but with an unfortunate focus on "funny" dialogue. I know that Larian loves to put humour into their games, but I feel this game is too far over the edge. The character generation and leveling process is nothing special, certainly not particularly unique in the RPG genre.
Another thing about the game that has puzzled me is the reference to the game being "old school". There is nothing old school about the game apart from the turn based combat.
I'd suggest Pillars of Eternity for a much more satisfying, deep and old school experience.

Crazy Plant Shop is an edu-tainment management/simulation game in which you use Punnett squares to selectively breed silly plants and produce offspring that conform to your customer’s specifications.
(As someone who has spent many years teaching Punnett squares, I’m aware that I’m probably not the target audience of this game, so that’s probably worth bearing in mind in the context of this review.)
I generally enjoy management/simulation games, and the idea of one centering on using biological concepts for fun and profit was very appealing to me. I was under the impression that this was a cute, casual management sim, but unfortunately, this game is pretty clearly intended more as edu-tainment to reinforce the concepts of Mendelian genetics than as a real game. The management aspects are trivial, the game progression is very linear, and determining the correct crosses to produce the required offspring is not very challenging.
I can see this game appealing to parents who want a fun way to introduce their kids to important biological concepts, and maybe to those who don’t remember much about basic biology and want a fun-ish refresher. Beyond its educational merits, though, I really don’t see any reason to play this game.

Dream is a first-person exploration game that is in it's very, VERY early Alpha stages and as such it is hardly playable. Since the story of Dream is still a work in progress, I'll overlook it and describe the aspects of the game that I was capable of gathering in my sporadic attempts to play the game for more than a 10 minute period.
Dream has extraordinary graphics complements of Unreal 3, which makes Dream just wonderful to look at and is complemented by an absolutely breath taking soundtrack. Because of this; Dream is very appealing to the visual and auditory senses and creates such an attractive potential for a spectacular experience. From what I could gather in the tragically short amount of time the games current build was willing to yield to me, you explore the dreams of the protagonist which begin in a central hub of his inner mind, travelling to different dreams through gateways which always crashes for me whenever I attempted to enter.
Aside from the crashes, Dream also needs work in multiple other areas as well. The afformentioned hub is difficult to navigate on account of it's monotonous white colors and lack of shading, being just short of a solid white screen.
The main menu also lacks control binding, which is relatively minor in an exploration game like Dream but is just something I personally prefer to glimpse at and tweak with prior to playing.
So while Dream has such amazing potential, it's current Alpha build isn't exactly in a very fit state to be sold and I'm honestly curious as to why the developers released it as it is (I am very skeptical of the applications for Steam's Early Access program).
If you're interested in picking up Dream, I suggest you simply keep it on your watchlist until it is complete.

The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing is a solid ARPG title with an unique setting, but it's not flawless.
The Steampunk atmosphere of the game is brilliant. The music, the design of the location and enemies ane the great art style all create a great experience. The 'Ink' is an intereting concept as well and nicely integrated into the game.
One of the smaller problems of the game are the additional game play elements that get introduced later in the game. They feel tacked on and managing them often feels more like a chore than an interesting diversion. Another minor issue is the fact that some of the level feel rather dragged out and get boring rather quick.
The presentation as mentioned before is great. Graphics and music create an amazing Steampunk setting. The voice acting is very good too and your companion never fails to put a smile on your face with her comments. While some of the easter eggs and references feel forced, overall they make you search all the areas thoroughly.
It's not a perfect ARPG, but with it's unique setting and mostly fun game play, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing gets my recommendation. I would wait for a sale to pick it up though.
