This is an awesome game, and one I really enjoy.
Upsides include:
- Deep gameplay (how much AI can you write in an RTS? Have you thought of everything?)
- Surprisingly good initial tutorial (you don't need to know a lot of javascript to play this, any experience scripting will do)
- A simulation mode that lets you test things out without risking your live empire
- Multiple worlds (shards) you can play on
- Co-op and competitive multiplayer (just make sure any allies start the same time you do), with alliances
- Slack channels, wikis etc, and a very complete API reference mean you can usually get the answer to your question
- Real sense of progess as you watch your empire develop - even more so if you've got the AI you wrote making its decisions and agree with them.
- Beating another player because your AI is better than theirs is an amazing experience. So, too, to a lesser extent, is watching your AI systematically dismantle NPC invaders.
- The community of players IN GENERAL is smart, knowledgable, and nice. Exception: the players near you are quite likely to try murdering you in your sleep using tactics you never thought possible. This isn't because they hate you, though. This is just because you're mining resources they want.
- If you want practice writing JavaScript, this is an incredibly fun way to get that practice.
- The ability to write JavaScript is an incredibly useful skill, so even if you aren't attracted to the game for the sake of practice, the practice will still probably be valuable to you at some point.
That said, there are some downsides:
- This is a subscription game, in an era where there's essentially no such thing anymore as a subscription game. There's a good argument for it (your scripts run 24/7 even when you're offline), ways to play without paying a subscription (buy it on steam once, get a small amount of CPU forever), even exchange game currency for subscription time. But, ultimately, you are either paying with money every month, or you're paying with time. For some people, the fact it is a subscription game alone rules it out.
- Combat can be brutal as a new player. While I have been doing fine, the outright majority of players I've seen start in my sector have either been murdered or abandoned their game within the first few days. TIP: if you start playing this, DO NOT start near a well-established player, as doing this means you have little chance of fighting back if they decide they want your resources for themselves.
- It is very easy to make almost game-ending mistakes. Not got any defense AI when invaders start showing up? Aggress a player you can't handle? Left a bug in your code that causes it to fail to run properly just when you need it? Empires can fall due to tiny mistakes like these. While the tension is sometimes great, some people will find it insufferably annoying that they can lose huge chunks of progress just because of a misplaced ';' in their code. These people should probably not play this game. You have to have some patience for debugging.
- The tutorial approaches scripting your AI from the wrong angle. While it is somewhat inevitable, given that it is aimed at new players, that it would take the simplest approach, it leads players down the path of having each unit make its own decisions. This works when you have 1 unit. Or 5 units. Or 10 units. It does not work when you have 100 units. At a certain point, if you follow this approach, you will realize that what you need is a sort of 'director' AI that assigns tasks to your units/creeps. This is a whole new level of AI programming that you will have to be willing to engage in to make real progress in this game, and the tutorial never mentions it, which is a major omission.
- The main server, shard0, has a tick rate of about 5 seconds. This means that units only move or otherwise act once per 5 seconds. There is a second server, shard1, which has a MUCH faster tick rate of about 2 seconds. As well as newer players in general. If you are starting out, you almost certainly want to start on shard1.... but shard0 is still the default, for some reason. This might seem like a nitpick, but it actually makes a huge difference to the game to play it at half speed. Whenever you're waiting for anything... you wait twice as long.
- This is a 24/7 game. Your empire exists 24/7. Your code runs 24/7. You can be attacked 24/7. There are few things as annoying as getting game alerts telling you that your empire is being wiped out while you're at work, or otherwise busy. Or even worse, seeing them in the morning after you wake up. You can script your AI to deal with this somewhat, but you also have to be prepared that it might, at times (rarely) interrupt your life to push you to deal with some crisis - or you might come back to an empty wasteland next time you sign in.
- You MUST be willing to read the documentation. You MUST be willing to read a lot in general. There are some things about the game, seemingly minor (like the fact that rooms beyond a certain level attract MUCH stronger NPC attacks) which aren't mentioned in-game, but are on the wiki/API documentation. If you've read the docs well, you will know them. If you haven't, you can get blindsided when the enemies you face are suddenly 4x stronger for no identifiable reason. That's just one example - there are many others.
- The longer you play, the less your empire changes on a day-to-day basis. You still have work to do, but progress is clearest in the first few days, where you're expanding more quickly. After that, it becomes ever more incremental until, eventually, you will probably settle into a position of relative stability - unless you are willing to go to war with a neighbor to expand further.
Who should/shouldn't buy this game:
- If you want practice writing JavaScript, or enjoy scripting things in general, definitely DO buy this game.
- If you don't like the idea of writing code, hate the idea of debugging, or aren't willing to read around, DO NOT buy this game.
- If you're not sure if you enjoy writing code, but are an RTS fan, I still encourage you to pick up this game and try to learn to write code - its a valuable skill and it will give you HUGE strategic and tactical insight you can use in other games. Not to mention teaching you a valuable skill in a fun way. Plus, frankly, I find it more satisfying to write the code to handle attacking, defending, etc, than I do micromanagement. If you're big into micromanagement (a la StarCraft) maybe this is not for you. If you're big into big-picture thinking, automation, etc (a la Total Annihilation, Factorio, etc) then this may well be for you.
- If you're not sure if you enjoy RTS games, and have no experience writing code.... play another few RTS games, and try writing some other code for something, before you try this.

I had previously given a thumbs down because of the constant NPC chatter, but there's a mod called A Quiet Day On The Market that turns that down rather substantially, and with that, the game becomes quite playable.  I've been having wrist pain lately from excessive mouse usage, so I've only been playing games with gamepad support, and when you don't have an XBox controller, these games are really hard to find.  It seems that most games these days list "Full Controller Support" yet only support the XBox controller, and literally nothing else.  Divinity is not one of these games.  I can play it just fine with my PS4 controller.  It doesn't recognize my other controllers, so I still wouldn't consider it to be "Full Controller Support", but at least it works with one of my controllers, so I can play it.
One thing I didn't realize they did was, when using a controller, the GUI changes entirely.  It is fully optimized for gamepad use.  There are a couple places I think it could be better, but overall, it's better than most games.  My primary complaint is that the combat log disappears before I can read it.  Five sentences pop up, and then 2 seconds later it turns invisible again.  There should be some sort of option for that.  I'd rather it stay up until combat is over.
The voice acting is still cringe-inducing more often than not, but with the aforementioned mod, I don't have to turn the voice volume to 0 (which I don't think was an option when I first tried to play it).  And, since it isn't at all painful to play with a gamepad (so many games just control so bad with a gamepad), which is something Larian far exceeded my expectations for, I've decided to change my review to a positive one.  Also, I've noticed that they made a bunch of improvements to the game since I last tried it.  I also found another mod that ups the difficulty notably, so I'm quite enjoying it.

This is a top-tier RPG for the RPG enthusianst.  The added controller support is excellent and extremely intuitive, and the split-screen/local co-op is aboslutely fantastic.  I know this had online co-op support in the original version, but I cannot think of another game that really plays off the co-op elements as well as Divinity does.  Quests can be tackeld in numerous ways depending on your build or affinity.  The fact that there are two heroes can be EXTREMELY entertaining when playing with a friend with a different attitude or moral outlook than yours.
The battle mechanics work well.  It's turn based, so it may be a turn off for some, but I found the combat very entertaining and satisfying.  Very, very deep skill system with your comman stats like STR, DEX, INT, etc., but also borrow a bit from fallout as you can gain "Talents" every few levels that are very similar to Fallout's Perk system.
Graphics and sounds are top notch.  Fun factor is off the charts for any classic RPG lover.  Story is goofy, whimsical, adventerous, and serious all at once.  It strikes a really great balance between all those tones.
Couldn't recommend the game more.  As you can see by my hours clocked I've spent a lot of time with it.  Must buy for any RPG fine IMO.
This has re-established my faith in the RPG genre.   Thank you Larian for your constant efforts on this and making such a great game.

Ori and the Blind Forest can only be described as a rollercoaster of emotion. Right from the getgo all the way until the very last scene it knows how to build you up and make you feel taller than ever before. It knows how to make you feel like you're on air and how to give you an overdose of adrenaline. In equal measure it also knows how to tear you down. It has the ability to play with your heartstrings and it will. (This is a good thing, it's executed phenomenaly)
I could continue to gush on everything that makes it so great, but I feel that instead I'll point out what is actually wrong with it (of which there is very little.)
1. The game doesn't quite explain 'why' some story events happen. They're very small things, small enough that you could easily get away with just assuming what the reasoning behind it was and likely be right. It can just be a little annoying at times.
2. Non-rebindable Keys. This isn't SO bad as the layout they have is decent. Holding the shift button while you move with WASD can be fairly strenuous but other than that all 3 different layouts are very good. (I recommend controller though. Mouse + Key layout has the Shift + WASD issue and the Keyboard layout limits you to 8-directions which can be annoying for some of the powerups)
3. The enemy types get reused quite a bit. They may have slightly changed gimmicks, powerups, or other slight alterations, but there are really probably no more than 15 enemy types in the entire game (Not counting variations.)
4. It's a bit short. This isn't so bad really. Quality over quantity, though I can't help feeling that it ended 1 dungeon too early. (Admittedly I didn't 100% the game or anything. I did a decent amount of exploring, backtracked a couple times to search for some powerups. I got like 66% completion I believe and that took me about 7 hours.)
That's literally it. I have no more complaints. All of these are so minor to begin with anyway! The music is absolutely stellar, the development of the characters is suprisingly in depth considering there is only 2 vocal characters in the entire game, neither of which ever speak to one another, and the gameplay is so polished and well made and blends with the aesthetic and story perfectly.
Something that truly needs it's own special mention is the abillity for the game to continuously vary up the gameplay and how it never stops doing so. Maybe about once every 30 minutes or so a new powerup is introduced that completely changes the way the game is played (shoutouts to Bash, probably the most fun ability out of every video game I think I've every played.) New movement options are constantly being added, meaning that while at the beginning you are limited to run and jump, at the end of the game you have a plethora of ways to move around the map like a badass (Triple jump, Wall cling, Wall jump, Directional air dashes off of projectiles, Super Jumps, Gliding. You name it, It's probably there.)
I cannot state enough how fantastic this game is. Just... just listen to this music:
If you have even a passing interest in MetroidVania style games, I recommend you buy Ori immediately. What are you doing? Why don't you own it yet? I own it. You should too!
(I saw some people on the discussions boards complaining about crashes, but that never happened to me. You might want to make sure it will run correctly on your computer first lol)

Crazy Plant Shop is a fun edutainment game inspired by Mendelian inheritance and Gregor Mendel's famous pea plants.
The premise of the game is similar to other shopkeep games (e.g. Recettear) in that you must earn enough money each period (one business day) to pay the rent and stay in the black through the entire game (13 in-game business days.) You can end an in-game day any time you want, but for the best results you should wait until you are unable to complete orders. Orders continuously stream in, but you are limited in the money you have and the number of plants that you can breed in one day; I have never run out of open orders. The game is short--a full run through will take about 1-2 hours depending on how much thought you put into each order.
The theme of the game is plant breeding and Mendelian inheritance. You will buy plants from a catalog and breed them for traits desired by customers. Each trait has a dominant and recessive expression and up to five different traits. One plant is asexual and comes with only one dominant trait expressed. You can choose to fulfill orders by breeding or ordering directly from a catalog. Ordering from the catalog results in a net loss--customers always pay the same amount for each breed of plant and this amount is always at least half the cost of buying a plant. Breeding is limited to 9-15 times per day, depending on upgrade level. This is limiting factor where strategy is required.
The power-ups are difficult to afford in the beginning and, aside from increasing your breeding power and shelving capacity, the upgrades provide little benefit to gameplay. You can take as much time as needed for any order and there are no bonuses or penalties for performance. The pacing and difficulty of the game is relatively static since there are few options for earning money faster.
In all, this is a relative short, fun, low-pressure game that might educate young botanists or entertain casual players. There is no New Game+ or Leaderboard and no record of progress aside from achievements, so the replay value quickly vanishes, despite its brevity. I recommend this game for casual gamers and fans of the genre, but if you like a challenge, look elsewhere.

Overall, a fantastic metroidvania. Moving story that will cause some tears. Beautiful visuals, music and animation. Very nice routing of the player, retraversal of previous locations in new ways and with new abilities. Not too heavy-handed on the puzzles. Save mechanic creates some interesting tension during the first half, but becomes more convenient later on, which is necessary as the difficulty ramps up harshly. Upgrade system felt meaningful enough to encourage currency collection.
Some negatives - over-use of spike hazards, some sections of the game feel like you're playing Operation. A few forced-progression sections requiring rote memorization and death cycles. Ori is sometimes lost in FX spam. Some non-deterministic elements to timed sequences - you can be playing well and still simply get unlucky. A little too much pixel-perfect platforming for a floaty player package, as well as occasional edge-case jumps - i.e., "I made that jump but it didn't quite feel like what I was supposed to do... am I going the right way?"
All of the above negatives are washed over by the high quality of the experience in general. It says a lot when I'm willing to die cheaply 50 times in a row just to see what's next. Buy this game and keep going - you will be rewarded.

[This review made after getting two bad endings out of 5 possible endings]
I like this game and I would recommend it, first and foremost, to players that are interested in STORY or, at least, world
building. The game is not difficult: picture puzzles, word arranging, and some light fact searching comprise the bulk of the challenges. The meat of the game is in the dialogue choices, and this is where the replayability come from. You don't really get locked out of most options when taking/talking different ways, so you can express your moral flexibility without fearing that you'll reach a dead-end. As for content, they did a decent job of fleshing out with stuff that makes it feel like a "lived with" phone. The game does a good job of simulating smartphone usage with the apps, pics and their poses, vids, and social media content. A nice touch, is that there is a checklist of tasks that would help the truly clueless and serve as a guide for those looking for certain keystone events to play around with on subsequent playthroughs. This checklist is out of the way though for those who don't want hints on what to do next.
On the negative side, some of the voice acting, for me, was off if not "unsuitable". The delivery of the voice only lines truly felt and sounded "rehearsed". The VOs not sounding natural kind of sticks out like a sore thumb amid the aptness of the pictures and videos to a phone setting. The worst offender of this, sorry to say to the voice actor, is the Greg character. Truly, to me, it sounded like he was voicing a cartoon character instead of making a call, and it kind of took me out of the general mood of the game.
I think, the ending, will be pretty hit or miss for some people as well. I want to liken how the ending progresses to one of the scenes in a movie, but that would probably spoil it a bit. It's just that most people that saw it back then went "Wait what was that again?" Don't get me wrong, I'm fine with the endings I got (two bad endings), but the way to the climax was tedious, especially since I don't know if there is a message skip button for when you are doing a replay and you know what is going to be said. A note on the endings I got, it seems like you get locked to a set of outcomes after some threshold. I know my choices at the end didn't end up changing any of my final options.
All in all, a decent casual horror sim game with some replayability, a fleshed out setting, hit or miss voice acting, and an endgame sequence (not ending, the stuff leading up to the ending) that'll make you go "excuse you? whowherewhenhowwhywhatnow?".
For now, at full price, it would depend on your affinity for games like these to buy it for around a 5 hour single playthrough (worth it if you go with the $1 per hour of gameplay mindset). It is a decent recommend to buy if it ever has a sale at some point though.

If pixel-art, rouge-like, dungeon RPGs are your niche then this game is 100% spot on. I'm a big fan and avid player of many games that are a combination of or all of the mentioned genres and in particular the duneon genre games are beginning to blend together, making what had initially been a fun concept become bland and overdone repetitions.
This game may *seem* similar but it's a fairly simple, straightforward and, most importantly, a refreshing take on dungeon rpgs. Particular emphasis on simplicity, I never once felt like I was grinding through a floor or felt as though I had too much equipment to choose from. No option "overload" with countless varieties of weapons/armor/shields with only slightly differing abilities nor endless labyrinths of areas to explore; it's quick, it's satisfying, and it forces you to make decisions.
Easy to get into and although difficult to master, you are mostly rewarded for your efforts. However there are plenty of "luck-of-the-draw" situations, so if you're the type to enjoy strategy over games of chance - you may be a bit frustrated or enraged at some of the randomization mechanics.
Learning curve is a little tough at first: keeping track of buffs, equipment stats, realizing that you accidentally sold back the equipment you just bought, finding out that trying to buy equipment after clearing the 1st floor is a waste of your reward since you can't use/afford anything, etc. Despite the initial confusion you learn the ropes quickly after dying a few times.

Overall an excellent game, worth every penny.

This is a different little game, a tile clicking/exploring game if you will.
You simply click unrevealed tiles on a dungeon level to reveal what's there.  It might be a monster, a trap, loot, health, or a great number of other things.  You continue searching each level trying to find both a key and a door to move down to the next, harder level of the dungeon.
Play continues like this until your health points run out and you die, at which point you see all your final stats including number of baddies killed and your final score for the game.
Because of the procedural generation, the Endless and Abyss modes that can be unlocked by beating the normal default game, this game offers a lot of value for the price it would seem from this early point in my experience with this game.
There are also shops and skill screens that can be unlocked which seem to offer more randomness and what is available to purchase when you unlock each of these by spending gold.  One you hit level 10, 15.. and so forth, you also open up new heros to explore the dungeons with.
All in all, it looks like a fun little game that doesn't require a ton of focus, doesn't require quick gaming reflexes, and offers a completely different game every time you'll play it.

This is a top-tier RPG for the RPG enthusianst.  The added controller support is excellent and extremely intuitive, and the split-screen/local co-op is aboslutely fantastic.  I know this had online co-op support in the original version, but I cannot think of another game that really plays off the co-op elements as well as Divinity does.  Quests can be tackeld in numerous ways depending on your build or affinity.  The fact that there are two heroes can be EXTREMELY entertaining when playing with a friend with a different attitude or moral outlook than yours.
The battle mechanics work well.  It's turn based, so it may be a turn off for some, but I found the combat very entertaining and satisfying.  Very, very deep skill system with your comman stats like STR, DEX, INT, etc., but also borrow a bit from fallout as you can gain "Talents" every few levels that are very similar to Fallout's Perk system.
Graphics and sounds are top notch.  Fun factor is off the charts for any classic RPG lover.  Story is goofy, whimsical, adventerous, and serious all at once.  It strikes a really great balance between all those tones.
Couldn't recommend the game more.  As you can see by my hours clocked I've spent a lot of time with it.  Must buy for any RPG fine IMO.

First, a caveat: my only experience with this game is on a private server I run on my VPS.  Playing on the official servers is a whole other ball game, I'm sure.  I'm probably not going to mess with that for a while.
I'm probably going to update this review eventually once my friends and I start getting more into the competitive aspects, but, suffice to say, I recommend it for anyone who knows how to code, appreciates strategy games, and wants a nice break from the sort of click-heavy, fast-paced titles that dominate the RTS genre.  The API is a little clunky and javascript is a poor choice of language for this type of application, but, once you get used to the environment, there are a whole host of interesting mechanics that make this game insanely fun to play.  It's complex, to be sure, but not so time-consuming as you might be led to believe---often, you don't have to do more than a quick check every now and then followed by a short bugfix or livecoding sprint to introduce a new unit type or behavior.  It's easy to get sucked into it late at night, but, other than that, pretty low-maintenance overall.  I could see playing this game with a full-time job and kids, which is not something I'd suggest about most games on the market today.  Again, that doesn't necessarily hold true for public server play, which requires payment of a large subscription fee I suspect the experience isn't worth.
If you don't know anything about code whatsoever, I'd learn that first.  This is not primarily an educational game.  That said, expertise with javascript /per se/ is optional; it's more important to have a basic understanding of how the game logic works, and ---I cannot stress this enough---to have read the manual and played the tutorial.

Moving to 3D ruined this game.
Instead of being tile based like Abe's Oddysee, the game uses modern floaty granular movement. If you've played the original, you'll remember how important crouching right next to something dangerous like a meat grinder and moving quickly is. In New n Tasty, pressing left doesn't just turn you around, it moves you slightly in the direction you pressed. For a game based around precise movement, this totally ruins the game.
Take, for example the first secret area, whre there are a series of meat grinders and a lever to control how fast they move- standing next to the lever, if you pull it, crouch and turn left to face the meat grinder, you then die as Abe moves slightly into the way of it.
Using the steam controller was also frustrating, as the default config refused to work until I switched to a community one and back and enabled an Xbox config option in steam's big picture settings. Having analog movement where you start moving slowly as soon as the analog stick is moved even slightly mean getting under the fast meat grinders in the first secret area is pretty much impossible, too.
Only a few minutes of my time were actually playing the game, most of it was trying to get the controller working. Long enough to decide I'd much rather play the original.

I'm not a huge fan of platformers and I bought this game on a whim. Glad I did.
The game looks gorgeous. All the colors are vibrant and pleasant to look at and the game has a pretty cool visual style that is reinforced by the use of mixed-mediums. The graphics are good as a whole and all the models, effects, backgrounds, enemies and so on look pretty good. Despite the myriad effects, I did not feel any strain on my computer.
The action is fairly fast-paced. There is a recommendation on Steam to use a controller and that does seem to be the better option. I am playing on my keyboard and it definitely is playable but there are a bunch of sections that feel as if a controller would have been better.
I am not too far into the game yet so I can't comment much on the story or characters as a whole. It seems to be a fairly simple story but it does what it does well. The first five minutes have brought tears to my eyes, which I very rarely get from games (or films, or books or etc...). Part of me would like to know more about the world but I think that would be detrimental to a game like this. I have to mention it that Ori is ♥♥♥♥ing adorable.
Many of the negative reviews I read complained about difficulty and yes, it is difficult. Unforgiving and prone to trial-and-error at places. But I wouldn't put that as a negative. However, there are some parts that *will* frustrate you. However, I have given up on other games for far less wheras I stuck with this one and this tells something about it.
The checkpoint system (which is effectively a create-your-own-checkpoint system) alleviates most of the frustration that comes from difficulty. It costs energy to create checkpoints but with the right perks, you can make them reusable and cost less. As a whole, this helps the pacing a lot.
Some of the reviewers also mentioned bugs. Haven't had any bug issues so far (about midway into the game). As a whole, this feels like one of the more stable games I have played.
Definitely recommend it.
Edit: Now that I completed it, my main points stands for most part. Definitely going to re-iterate my comments about keyboard VS Controller. The latter seems to work much better.
Story is simple but what it does, it does well. The ending was tugging at the heartstrings just as much as anything. If one critique, we didn't see much closure between Ori and Naru, which is a shame, given how much effort the game took to build their relationship.
One serious issue I have is in regards to the instructions received in the game about new abilities. Once a new ability is received, how to use them briefly flashes on the screen and that is it. Normally that is enough but when a move has multiple methods or uses, this gets problematic. I did not discover a certain way to use one of the abilities until near the endgame upon which I could have used it to get into couple areas I could not enter, leaving powerups behind.
The second critique I have ties to the first in that there were sections of the map that were disproportionately hard to get to. Breakable walls are one thing but some sections of the maps were blocked off by unbreakable walls that had to be opened via a switch or some other special trigger. Problem is, a lot of these were very well hidden. Couple of them I discovered by accident, one by educated guess but the rest, I could not locate. Again, it kept me from a %100 completion. Now, I don't expect this game to spoonfeed people. It seems to take pride in its difficulty and that is ok. But I pride myself an attentive player and I spent a lot of time around each blockade, slamming, dashing and charging at anything I could find before giving up. Similarly, there were sections in the game where I could see a powerup through the wall but nowhere to get to, even when I investigated each portion of land surrounding it. I suppose it would be less source of frustration to have a few more indicators on how to reach such places.
Still, my recommendation stands. This game is definitely worth playing.

A very interesting, unique, deceptively simple game.
Pro:
_Nice, clean art style: Looks good with its own art style. Nice character portraits as well. Isn't really bombastic, but does look unique and coherent.
_Unique: The gameplay is something else altogether. It's hard to align this to any specific genre.
_Satisfying gameplay: It's very simple stuff, but clicking on tiles to explore them feels satisfying in the way that popping bubble wraps is satisfying, if that makes sense. It's like fapping, it's hard to explain, but try it for yourself and you'll see immediately why it's so great.
_Rogue-lite: It's a Rogue-like with persistent upgrades that effects your future runs. That was fun in Rogue Legacy, it's fun in here.
_Difficult: It's hard, but never truly feels unfair.
_Deceptively simple:  It's deceptively simple, but with an underlining devilishness that is very, very rogue-like. The game isn't afraid to troll you.
_Great pacing: Short runs (Lasts about 20-30 mins on average), but you'll be playing it over and over. It's really easy to lose track of time playing this game.
Cons:
_Could use more art assets: The art is nice, but there's not enough of it... I'll be honest, I'm just nit-picking here. I can't really think of anything negative to say.

I really wanted to give a thumbs down to this game, but sadly there's no rating system because I would definitely give it average score because the game IS average as average as it goes.
-After playing Torchlight and investing more than 200 hours in Grim Dawn. I was looking for the next best ARPG, but the search still continues at least for me. My main issue with this game are sound effects, they are so plain, dull and boring. It feels like straight out of a 90s game. None of the attacks or magic spells/skills have any pleasing to ears sound effects, they are barely audible even when the boss attacks like the drill boss at the end of chapter 1 doesn't make any sound.
-Now lets talk about the skill tree, and I have to say that Grim Dawn did a far better job at this. Everything in this game is limited to 3 from passive equips to rage upgrades till skill's upgrades which really frustrates me, and to top on that there are hardly any passive skills or active skills. I can count them on one hand, as a guy who prefers active skills over the spamming skills, this game turned out to be quite a disappointment.
-The inventory system is one of the most basic and tedious thing that you will only see in the starting days of ARPG genre.

There's barely any different between the rare items and the epic items and it is just so easy to get them all when you play on Heroic or above difficulties unlike in Torchlight or Grim Dawn where it is actually quite a feet to get legendary loots that makes a hell lot a difference, and the worst of all there isn't any set equips or items which gives you huge bonus stats when you equip them as a set.
:-Doesn't have any replay value for me. There's nothing else in this game that provides something fun to break monotony! Hopefully, the creators next time will learn something from Grim Dawn, Torchlight or titan quests like games from next time!

I never, ever dreamed I would be giving this game a negative review. I'm incredibly hard to please when it comes to games, but disliking this one comes as a complete shock to me because I
the first Van Helsing game from this company, and was a good chunk into the second one when I heard this back-to-back series of the three games, done as close to "seamlessly" as was possible, was coming out. Once released, I finally got this game, started over since I couldn't transfer my save or anything, and hopped to it. I'm going to break down each of the three parts of this collection/game as follows:
The first game's (I'll call it "Van Helsing I" for brevity) content was great. I expected a garbage Diablo clone with a ghost following me around that wouldn't say anything and would be useless in regard to gameplay; just serving as a stand-in for a co-op partner because the game's balancing wasn't made for single player. Boy, was I wrong. That ghost companion is my favorite thing about all three games. Her name is Katarina, she's wonderfully voice-acted, is the best character in all three games, and she is snarky, funny, and great to have around for gameplay purposes, as she has three separate skill trees and levels up on her own. You can boost everything from boosting your hero's critical hit chance, to your Magic Find (item drop quality), to her own damage output, to her own HP, etc. She takes scenes that would be boring in any other game and injects personality and humor into them which make them either enjoyable or less unenjoyable than they would be without her. I cannot properly express how much I like Katarina. If I were given heaps of video game characters to pick from and could choose her, I dare say she would be in my overall top 10 favorite video game characters list.
With Katarina out of the way, the environments in the first segment of Van Helsing I are all outdoors, looking nice with rocks, grass, snow, swampland, trees, etc. It wasn't horribly exciting, but the sheer competence of the combat for a "Diablo clone" took me by surprise. The maps were huge with plenty of monsters to fight, loot to pick up, hidden treasure and a fair number of side quests. By the time I finished the first big leg of Van Helsing I, I was getting a little tired of the outdoor areas. So what does the game do? It goes full-on
. The guns and a few clockwork-soldier-looking-dudes in the wilderness had that vibes, sure, but I never expected a steampunk city with Van Helsing as the hero, but a ghost sidekick, monster allies, and scientist villains. It was cheesy and the vampire ally is practically a cartoon character, but it was all so lovable and fun. There were a significant number of references to movies, film, games, etc., but they never felt like "too much" to me, and added some levity to the game. The third act was more steampunk city, but the classier end of town, so it felt fresh.
The final boss to Van Helsing I was pretty easy, but I'd rather have easy than insufferably hard, because I'm here to have fun, rather than prove something to myself or others. The ending is a to-be-continued sort of thing, but not a cliff-hanger by any means. I thoroughly enjoyed Van Helsing I, and have played through it in its original release, and in this version of the game, both in solo play, and in co-op with a friend, and it's excellent. I would play it again, even, and am certain I likely will.
This is still a good game. However, the maps don't stand out/wow me like Van Helsing I did. I played through most of the game in its original release, and through its entirety in this version. You get a pet chimera, which sits in your base and you can send it to search for gear by clicking a map for it to go to. You never see the chimera except at our base, and he takes 10 minutes per trip to return, but you can reduce the time to 4 minutes if you find enough special items to equip on him. I only found 2, and he took 6 minutes to come back. He levels up, but it took a long time for me to get him to level 5. Leveling him up just means you have better odds of getting items when you send him out, and I never got anything jaw-dropping. It's a fun little minigame of sorts, but nothing incredible.
That's the biggest change between Van Helsing I and Van Helsing II in the Final Cut version of the game. Other than that, the story was decent but nothing amazing, the movie/TV/game references got a little carried away, but it didn't push me too far, and I actually thought the final boss fight was really well done for this sort of game. It was better than the
boss fight of any Diablo game (Diablo III butcher was done pretty well), in my opinion, as you are going up against two bosses leading two armies, both of which are all trying to kill you! You show up in the middle and can take the armies' qualities into account to help decide which side you should "aid" in winning before taking that side out last. I wish more action RPGs with this camera perspective put anywhere near this much effort into making boss fights fun. The villain was kinda meh, and there's a character who you will look at and say "This ally character is obviously evil" the moment you meet the character. Still, it's a pretty decent game; not great as the first.
If you tend to like most games, then you might like this one. However, if you have a discerning taste in games, Van Helsing III is the metaphorical turd in the punchbowl. I never could have envisioned that this series would sink this low. While there are a handful of really cool maps, the story devolved to "bad guy is bad, go to point A, now go to point B, fight a forgettable fight, go to point C, go back to base, repeat, ad nauseum." I understand many,
games are like this, and that this can be a slippery slope, but almost every quest in this game felt like a chore. Aside from learning more about Katarina's past, finishing the game, and one mission where you are sent to rescue an ally, I did not care about anything in this game, and cannot even remember most of the story, events, where I went, etc. I don't recall seeing any new features coming up in Van Helsing III compared to what's available in the Final Cut version of Van Helsing II, either.
The health on enemies in Van Helsing III seems to be ramped up higher than in the previous titles, to such an extent that you chip away at a normal-sized enemy's health for what feels far too long before it will die, which I found less enjoyable. No, this wasn't when I upped the difficulty several settings to give that a try, either. The enemies actually died a lot faster with something like 6x their max HP in Van Helsing I than they did with their normal HP in Van Helsing III. Changing the feel of the combat to just take a lot longer was not for the best, as large numbers of enemies with quick kills is what makes this kind of game fun for me. Diablo games' medium-sized enemies tend to die easily enough, but they can be deadly. The way to make battles harder is to ramp up each enemy's damage output to make them deadlier to compensate for shorter fight time. Van Helsing III did not do this, instead choosing to make fights take longer instead of being tougher, and this made a game that started to feel boring actually feel like a drawn-out chore. The final boss is no exception to this rule: huge max HP value, not an inventive fight like Van Helsing II's boss, and not short and sweet like Van Helsing I's boss.
I'm out of room, so in closing, I'll mention that the movie/game/TV references in this game came in sickeningly high amounts compared to the first two. I love references, and it got old super fast in this one. If you see this Final Cut on a good sale value, get it and play through the first two games, because the first is great, and the second is decent, but the third was
fun.  =/

The Adventures of Van Helsing is a phenomenal series, when I first played it I was using a crappy laptop to play it, mind you with a pathetic framerate, but even so I felt at home straight away.
Final Cut is a culmination of the past 3 games merged and improved as a final release [explains why it is free for owners of the past games]. At a fairly bulky price you get a base campaign of ~50 hours playing on a Normal difficulty, but there is endless replayability. A primarily single-player game for me, it does include multiplayer options but due to the immersion factor and campaign design it really is a game you want to play by yourself to get the full experience.
Gameplay is extremely solid, and ability range is wonderful with excellent sound design, well written script and a very challenging difficulty curve this is definitely one game that is worth every penny. There is a lack of contact in how combat feels but that is a very minor gripe as every other part of combat and connected gameplay makes up for it.
A Recommended purchase for Diablo 2/PoE veterans and ARPG fans alike.

If you have any intention to play this game multiplayer then I cannot, in good conscience, recommend it. There are serious issues with it that will block progress.
The game itself is fun, mechanically works great and looks pretty decent on its max settings. It has great humour in it and decent basic backstory. If you want to play single-player, go ahead and enjoy it.
The issue
----------
In multiplayer mode with friends, this game is fine up to about the ending of Chapter 6 and start of Chapter 7 but completely broken beyond this point for us. This is around the ending of the 2nd game and start of the 3rd game we think. There is an issue with simulation freeze that introduces major connection issues and game engine problems as your damage numbers increase with your level and abilities.
It seems the game stuggles to handle all of the combat data and it becomes bottlenecked. Occassionally, if you're attacking a small group and only put in a few attacks to kill them, you can see the game finally catch up with the numbers, kill all the mobs and then resume like normal. But against any decent sized mob (which is practically every combat situation), the game just freezes and becomes unplayable for anyone but the host - if you hover over their portraits the pings increase by thousands.
As a multiplayer group with 3 people with a GTX 1080, GTX 980 Ti, and GTX 750, we should be able to handle the game. We have tried changing hosts, changing graphical settings to low, putting FPS limits to 30, changing CPU Sync to GPU, changing to DX9, etc. Nothing fixes this issue at Chapter 7. We have done test over the last 3 weeks with the same recurring issue. The game is now broken and unplayable for us and we cannot progress.
However, if we make new characters and do a test in Chapter 1, the issue doesn't exist - which eliminates the possibility of any of us currently having local connection issues. Not to mention we play other online games just fine.

Well, damn, I am learning while playing a video game...Crazy Plant Shop is a game based around the idea of breeding and growing plants to tell to your customers in your "Crazy Plant Shop". This game is actually used in school based environments because of the benefits and information it provides for teaching.
Essentially you get a customer who has a request for a certain plant. You then have to either purchase the plant out right from the plant catalog or you can breed the plant with your Super breeding machine "out back". When using the breeding machine you have to take into consideration dominant genes and recessive genes, as well as different genotypes and phenotypes combinations. While doing this you also use the Punnet squares, something which I have not seen since my secondary school days.
I can see why this game is used in  schools, because there is so much information, each word that you may not be familiar with comes with an audio definition recording.  I actually learnt quite a bit from this game, science wasn't exactly my strongest subject at school, and boy could I tell when playing this. I haven't managed to complete it. The aim is to actually buy all of the plants in the catalog within a 13 day time frame and not go bankrupt through paying rent everyday. I really struggled around day 8 or 9. You have to be really good at your breeding, and try not buy as many plants just to sell outright, at least that's what I figured out would be the best solution.
The graphics are very cute; the game can be played in a browser which I suppose is for the school environments that don't want Steam being installed on all their machines (understandably) , so we are not talking revolutionary graphics - it does its job to a very high standard.
The game actually has amazing voice acting; every character, and there are tons, have an awesome voice actor. It's actually on par with some AAA games if you ask me. It's amazing how good voice acting can have such a positive impact on any game.
Difficulty; like I said, I didn't finish Crazy Plant Shop, I am terrible at science so that didn't help. If you put a lot of hours into this game you will eventually beat it. I have seen people ten plus hours on this so it does have it's own fan base out there. Along with some very handy community made guides in the hub.
There are no technical problems which your regular player will run into really. The only issue I had was that I was not able to take screenshots either using Fraps or Steam, I assume because it doesn't use any DirectX engine behind it so it doesn't recognize it, who knows.
In conclusion, do I recommend Crazy Plant Shop? Well I suppose the best way of putting it is that I "don't Not recommend it". The game does it's job very well, it serves a purpose to teach the younger audience about breeding, genes etc, and it will do that! I will actually be showing this game to my partner who is a teacher to see whether it would be used in a classroom environment. I am not going to down-thumb this game because its not bad, it's just not going to be everyone's cup of tea who will be on Steam.
If you found this review helpful, please consider giving it a thumbs up. You can also find more reviews over at

Compared to Divinity: Bless its Soul, Almost Perfect Edition, Divinity: Someone Kill Me, I Need Professional Help Edition not only increases the difficulty significantly between the two normal difficulties of the games with archers that almost never miss and damage hiked so far up you need a high powered telescope to begin to make out how ♥♥♥♥ed you are and even making Phreak say "that's a ton of damage" to adding things that make no sense and make you feel as though you're playing the game where you took the Dungeon Master's girlfriend and burt down his house a few years ago and this is his chance to wreak his horrible vengeance on your puckered ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, like hard-shelled crabs that soul sap you (reducing all stats by 2 and resitances by 50%), cast AoE disease, have ranged attacks, and 4 shot tanks in groups of three or more with archer support.
Imagine you're playing Final Fantasy 8 and fighting Ultima Weapon, Now imagine that you're actually playing the "enhanced" edition, and now you have to send one of your party members away for 8 turns to operate some silly giant crossbow that can't be aimed to even have a chance at winning. You win, but your entire team is dead except for that one person. They go to loot the battlefield and find phoenix downs (because in the "enhanced" edition there are hardly any) but they get murdered by a pile of sentient gil. I know what you’re thinking. A serious review on this game? That is a recipe for disaster, kinda like electing Tony Abbott. ‘World’s Fastest Pizza’ is a high speed rogue-like comedy game about delivering pizza to the hungry customers of a sleazy fast-food restaurant. Developed by Oscar Brittain, you play as Tortoiseman, who also works under the alias of Cornelius Pretorius. Aside from winning the naming lottery, the game’s protagonist also has the prestige of working at fast-food restaurant in the outbacks of Australia.
Upon booting this game up, my first reaction was to immediately draw comparisons between the aesthetic in this game and Hotline Miami. They are remarkably similar, Hotline Miami has you deliver justice to the masses of Miami, this game has you deliver pizza to some customers who well, just want pizza. This is often trickier than expected when you include the fact that the rest of Australia seems hell bent on ensuring you don’t deliver the pizza. The soundtrack in this game also reminded me of the halcyon days in Hotline Miami. The menu in this game is quite simple, you can either do the simple tutorial, view the credits, or jump straight into the game. I did not sight an options menu, and as a result, I believe this game is locked in full screen.
The game play in this game is simple, you use the directional buttons or WASD to move your character. In my one and a half hours of play, I wasn’t required to use any other buttons. You frantically navigate through the levels to deliver your pizza to a bulls-eye that is painted on the ground in every level. The faster you delivered the pizza, the more money you received. This seemed quite simple until you realize that the game throws a spanner into the works by setting this game in Australia. Suddenly, you are dodging bullets, running past lizards, breaking through windows and trying to run away from a guy called ‘Doug’. I asked my mate in Brisbane, and he said this was quite realistic. So props to the developer for taking their time to add realism to this game. Your character is a bit thick skinned, which I imagine is necessary to survive in Australia, and as a result can survive multiple hits during his run. At the end of each run you regain full health. After 3 runs, you are taken back to your restaurant to take another order of pizza. It is at this point where you are given the option to spend some of your money to purchase ‘not so superpowers’ to help you survive in suburban Australia. You are able to hire a flash mob, a parrot, a time machine, and even a koala to help you in your quest to deliver the pizza. I was mildly disappointed that you are unable to call in the help of Malcolm Turnbull.
That said, the game does have a few niggling issues. My character sometimes got stuck in an object and jerked around until he was free. This was a bit annoying as it broke away from the otherwise fluid game play. The game could also benefit from a wider variety of levels, but I guess it is a bit difficult when the setting is Australia and 95% of it is desert land and the other 5% is New Zealand.
Overall, the game is quite fun for the price you pay. Costing only $2.99 USD, the game is good for a few hours of cheesy puns and slapstick comedy. The game’s crust is just filled with memes and Australian pop culture references. Definitely pick up this game if you are planning on moving to Australia as it gives an accurate representation of life in the country. For the small price you pay, it is a fun, albeit short, rogue-like game with very fluid movement and full controller support. It will be interesting to see if this developer decides to continue supporting this game in the future.

Infinite Warfare is a delivering package. I have owned this title on PC and Console. I have beat the campaign and have played the multiplayer on console. My favorite thing about Infinite Warfare is its singleplayer campaign mode. Campaign will might be your favorite part of infinite warfare. The story is that in the future Earth's recources are depleted and the people of earth had to find a new source for materials so they can sustain their society. The people of Earth turned to the stars and started mining other planets and celestial bodies in the solar system. Soon colonies were built and people started to be born on ther planets. There was a lot of debate on who controlled the planets of the solar system so the entire Earth united under the UNSA. However on Mars there was a group of colonist that saw the UNSA as greedy and lazy as they milk the Martians of their resources and labor while sitting comfy in their empire. This group saw themselves as the true inheritors of the solar system and they deserved it. This group soon formed the Settlement Defense Front and successfully broke away from the UNSA. After several years of conflict the UNSA acknowledged the Settlement Defense Front's sovereignty and independence. However the Settlement Defense Front still wanted more as they raided colonies on other planets and celestial bodies. They eventually attack Earth by suprise in an event reflecting Pearl Harbor where the Settlement Defense Front's Navy and airforce bomb the UNSA ships and attack Geneva. You step into the shoes as Nick Reyes, a Leutenent field promoted to Cammander in the wake of the attack. The campaign is innovative as like Mass Effect you can pick your missions. There are even side quests you can go on. Each quest will reward you with new weapons so you can fight better on the main missions. Also like Mass Effect you can explore your ship and interact with it. You can go to your office and browse your computer and you can even go to the living quarters and watch television with your crewmen. I love campaign and if you are a call of duty campaign fan, I'm sure you will too. Now on to multiplayer. Sadly multiplayer is a copy and paste of Black Ops 3, but downgraded. What I like about Black Ops 3 is the map design as you can have cover to cover firefights and tactically flank people with your advanced movement. Infinite warfare copies the movement system, the pick ten system, and the specialist system, except the maps have little to no depth and zero gunfight opportunities. It is a twitch shooter. Unlike black ops 3 where you have gunfights where you lay down shots on eachother intensley in a firefight due to you two being behind cover, Infinite Warfare has no cover to alow this. If you see someone in Infinite Warfare it will most likely be a baren space and one of you will be dead within a fracture of a second. However with all of these flaws to the multiplayer it is rather addicting and I don't know why. The multiplayer is the equivalent of a food that is disgusting, and yet I can't stop having it. Maybe it is because of the Salvage system. I do find myself grinding for salvage so I can craft new weapons. The salvage system is great because it is rewarding and keeps players playing. When I spent hours working to earn salvage in order to get a gun and I finally get it, it feels rewarding. I can never get board of weapon I spent hours to get. that is the best part of the multiplayer in my opinion. Now onto zombies. Zombies is very fun and arcadish. It is very fun trying to get to high rounds and unlock weapons to improve your survival. Overall I would give Infinite Warfare either a 6, 7, or an 8 at best. The game is ok.

Brilliant game. Others have dwelt on the programming aspect, but the game design itself is superb. Like all the best games, it takes a small number of simple elements and combines them to create huge possibilities.
There are constant hard choices to make: do I spend energy on infrastructure, expansion, defence, upgrades...? There is never enough cpu, memory, energy, or other resources. Do I write a sophisticated algorithm to better exploit resources - but then I'm low on cpu - and so on.
You can spend as much time on this as you like. There are always tweaks and optimisations to make, new ideas to try. Alternatively you can walk away for a month, come back, and see how your AI is faring.
The feel of the game is a bit like EVE Online. It's a brutal PvP world where potential disaster is constantly lurking. There are 'real' consequences if you screw up. But when some code comes together and you emerge triumphant - it's a rush! Even getting wiped out is kind of fun. How did that happen? What was the other guy doing that I wasn't? How should I improve my code base for the next attempt?
Once up and running you don't need to spend a lot of time on it if you don't want to. However I recommend setting aside most of a day for a first run as you need to get your empire to a certain level before you can let it run unassisted. You need to get basic harvesting, production, and defence online. From scratch that can take a few hours.
First few hours are learning how to find food, build, etc. There are different game modes for different kinds of players: PvE, PvP, Standard. Give the game a try, so far I like it.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a top-notch platformer in every aspect.
Built with the Unity engine, the game is visually stunning. It's detailed, colorful, and vibrant. There's a lot of attention spent to animations and interactions. For instance when you do a ground-slam move, a lot of the foilage shakes. When you go to the status screen it shows you all of the collectables and world events with animated sprites; they didn't need to be animated, but they are. The movement and controls all feel very precise... tuned better than most platformers out there... with a controller at least.. I can't speak to using a keyboard.
The audio and music in this game is superb, and you really feel the effects during the intense moments of the game. It never feels repetitive, but you'll find yourself appreciating how good it is.
The world is one big map, sectioned into different environments. Each environment feels cohesive and tend to offer unique elements. As you complete more of the game you unlock more abilities which opens up options to explore more parts of the world that you couldn't reach before. The abilities all work well together and give you a lot of traversal options. There are a ton of hidden collectables that make backtracking and exploring fun, although they are pretty important as you need them to increase your maximum energy/life/ability points. Ability points are spent on 'perks' that improve gameplay... they're not required, and you are able to unlock them all by the end of the game.
The story starts off exceptionally sad (probably the saddest intro I've ever seen), but slowly becomes more uplifting as the game progresses. The characters are cute but a bit mysterious, as it's not explained what any of them are; they're only referred to by name. There's very little dialogue ever spoken, and most of it is by the narrator, but there is plenty of communication through character body language and movements. Overall, the story is satisfying from start to end, and is very emotional.
My only complaint in the entire game is that the save system doesn't really suit the type of platformer that this game is. The platforming is insanely well designed, but is occasionally insanely difficult during a first play-through. There are RARELY auto-saves (only usually after a cutscene), and very few "save wells" that restore your life and energy while also saving. Most of the time you have to put down your own save points, and early on you can't do it that often. Most of the time I'd put down a save spot when I thought a section might get hard. I'd get through that area no problem, but the next area turned out to be difficult, causing me to die.
The result of this design is that I'd play through the same sections multiple times because I saved at the wrong spot, or just died randomly. It's pretty frustrating, and in certain parts of the game the platforming is so difficult that not having automatic checkpoints can often make you just rage-quit the game. These moments are rare, but if you have a harder time with precision platformers, you may have even more of an issue than I did early on. Also, even though you have a lifebar, many things will just instantly kill you, so there are a lot of unforseen deaths... which makes manual saving such a pain.
To summarize... this game is fantastic and took me around 10 hours to "do almost everything." There is absolutely zero filler in this game, and even the areas that I found interesting but tedious were short enough to be enjoyable. If you were to do a second playthrough of the game it would be much, much quicker and you could breeze through it. If you enjoy platformers and don't mind the occasional frustration, then I highly recommend this game.

Quick Summary: Van Helsing Final Cut is all three Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing games combined into a single cohesive game (including the DLCs). I only played the first 2 games before playing Final Cut, but with this edition I don’t need to buy Part 3 since that story is packaged in there with the first 2 games. Since Final Cut is not as long as playing all three games back to back, obviously some of the content must have been removed. However, I played the first 2 Van Helsings a while ago and I can’t really think of anything significant that has been removed, so the game developers must have done a decent job of taking out only unmemorable stuff.
You play the monster hunter Van Helsing, visiting the cursed land of Borgovia with Lady Katarina, a ghost who is bound to serve the Van Helsing bloodline. The game’s environments have a gothic, steampunk feel, and a lot of the abomination enemies are fairly original. For example many of them are combinations of clockwork machinery and mutated biology (basically Frankenstein creatures). Many of the supernatural enemies are based on European folklore like Pied Pipers, werewolves, and various woodland spirits. As you’d expect from a game called Van Helsing, there are also vampires, but this isn’t really a vampire hunting game. It’s a kill everything game.
As an Action RPG, the game is played in third person isometric perspective like Diablo, Torchlight, Path of Exile, Victor Vran, etc. You control Van Helsing with your mouse + keyboard, while Katarina runs around supporting you depending on how you set her behavior (aggressive, defensive, etc.) Town portals are free, potions are free, and dropped loot is highlighted for you on the ground. The game is definitely a loot grind, with randomly generated equipment dropping along with tons of money for you to spend on even more gear. You’ll need to pick up that cash too, because the end-game gear is hideously expensive. Like many ARPGs Van Helsing has a Hardcore mode as well, where dying in game is permanent for that character. But in Final Cut, the enemies scale to your level, which means you cannot “overlevel” your character to make things safer in Hardcore. The enemies will just get stronger too. I didn’t even give Hardcore a try because I see how often I die in normal mode, and I don’t hate myself that much.
You should buy Van Helsing Final Cut if:
+You are into ARPGs with interesting characters and a wide assortment of spells/skills. The story is packed with pop culture references similar to the Magicka series.
+You enjoyed playing the original Van Helsing games, but maybe you don’t own one or two of them. Final Cut uses the 6-character classes from Van Helsing 3, and you can play through the stories of all three games using the same character. With the original games you could import your Van Helsing 1 character to Van Helsing 2, but part 3 had its own class system which couldn’t accommodate importing save files.
+You like to play the hell out of one game over and over looking for better and better loot and trying out all the different character classes. As I said earlier, the game scales to your character level so you could conceivably beat the game anywhere between level 30 and 100 depending on how much you like to replay areas grinding for gear/experience. You can actually finish a lot earlier by running through most maps avoiding enemies, but the “good” spells and skills get unlocked at level 40 (and you’d miss out on a lot of bonus skill/stat points and quest rewards).
You should NOT buy Van Helsing Final Cut if:
-You are looking for “randomized” levels or quests. Unlike Torchlight or Diablo, the layouts of specific maps are exactly the same every time you play the game. You’ll know where all the quest items and NPCs are hidden after playing through one time. This actually makes it easier to run through areas if you want to finish at a low character level.
-You want a quick, linear, 10-hour game to play once and then never touch again. After you beat the game’s campaign you can move on to the “adventure map” which has quests with randomized challenges, where you are rewarded with “Fate” points. Fate points are mainly used to purchase end-game gear such as “set” items and “god-like” items (ultra-rare random drop). Unlike the previous Van Helsing games, set items no longer seem to drop randomly from slain enemies. Instead they’re all level 100 and all awesome. They can only be consistently bought from the Pigasus vendor (a DLC vendor from Van Helsing 2) and they cost an arm and a leg.
-You hate grinding (replaying the same levels over and over). Once you’ve beaten the campaign it’s all grinding from there. The maximum level is 100 and I got to level 96 before I gave up. At that point it was taking over an hour to level up each time and who has time for that? Apparently you can go past level 100 into “glory” levels. Your character would remain level 100 and instead of “leveling up” you get small bonuses that affect all your characters, kind of like Baddass points in Borderlands 2 (+1% weapon damage, etc.)

Really wanted to like this game. Had high hopes coming into it. Came out a tad bit disappointed.
So the Final Cut is a compilation of all 3 games that went out in a "Episody" fashion, from what I understood. And this really shows... and not in a good way.
***Might be some spoilers ahead, but I tried not to disclose anything particular and keep all the details abstract***
Let's start with the positives. It feels kinda nice when you play through the first episode - it's refreshing, interesting, has some fancy mechanics, and a quirky way of storytelling. So far so good. Since this is a compilation I did feel too overwhelmed by the overabundance of options and features which would have made sense if they were introduced in batches over different episodes as per original intent. But by the end of the game I think I did touch most of them.
The everpresent companion at first seems like a good addition: has an ability tree of her own, cracks a joke once a minute and serves as a good shortcut to the item shop for selling all the loot. So, if the game ended where Episode 1 ends, it would be a Good game. The final battle would have been a bit underwhelming, the game would have felt a bit short but it would have had left a nice aftertaste in my mouth. Sadly this is not the case.
Here is where things start to go south... After Episode one you realize there is more.. a lot more... of the SAME. And everything out of the blue is presented in a totally different fashion: out of nowhere you start getting ugly looking cutscenes which serve no real purpose and don't add much to the game. They just sort of sit there like a cat sits by the couch after a hearty dinner.
You get an anthagonist you don't care about one bit; everything storywise seems disjointed and incoherent; you start to get sick of the same combat: get to a mob of enemies, cast all your spells, run around till they're off cooldown, try to amuse yourself by getting the biggest mob possible by combining a group after group down the road...   rince...and..repeat......again...and....again....and.....again....; the every-minute-like-a-clock spewed jokes of your companion starts to get old and thin: the best I could get was a disgusted grin of "here we go again with this sh***". You arrive at the boss; you don't care about it any more than any other mob; you kill the said boss, and you get to a sudden realization: there IS MOOORE....
The dreaded episode three. At this point I was sick and tired of everything in the game. Decided to push through as I always do. Now you get an OK'ish nemesis, the cutscenes are gone (like a cat after it pondered why it was just sitting there before after it's hearty dinner insted of taking a nap on the coach in the other room), but the annoying puns and combat continue stronger than ever. Now once you hear a joke from your now annoying companion or get ANOTHER reference to a movie or a game or whatever (oh, didn't I tell about those? oh boyeeeee....) you get triggered into a fit of annoyed rage.
Just try to focus and press on. Enemies start to become bullet (arrow?\magic?) sponges, just adding to the frustration. The new items feel same; introductions of "important" characters and environments feel the same as if you were introduced to your old broom in the closet; and everything just drags on to infinity.
There are nice spots here and there, don't get me wrong. There was this level. What was it called? Spectral Provinces? That one is beatiful. No, not just beatiful, actually Gorgeous. Masterfully crafted, just gives off a really different feeling not just to Van Hellsing game: the RPG games in general. Once I was there I was really hoping it would be like this further. At least 2-3 more levels like that, pretty please? Gues what? OFC NOT! I would have not minded if the whole game had that feeling and a bit weird perspective the whole way  through, I would definitely have had fell for it.. Sadly it's not the case here.
Once you finish with episode three with really boring and tedious end fight, you just feel one thing: relief. You will never have to launch this game ever again... unless you feel masochistic.

BIT.TRIP RUNNER is an indie game that, like most indie games, will leave you either wanting more or wanting your money back.
The game was developed by Gaijin Games for the Virtual Console on the Nintendo Wii in 2010, but was released on Steam in February 2011. BIT.TRIP RUNNER is a rhythm-style action plaformer that consist of a protagonist, Commander Video, on a 2D plane. The player controls Commander Video as he runs along the set track from left to right and controls when the character jumps, slides, and kicking. As you progress through the 36 levels in the game (three worlds, each consisting of 11 levels, plus a boss encounter stage), you collect powerups that increase the quality of the music that plays through each level.
The game is notable for it's unique soundtrack, retro feel, and it's frustratingly difficult gameplay, as the current level is started over each time Commander Video runs into an obstacle that the player failed to acknowledge. The game forces a trial-and-error style of play, and in the end, it can hurt the experience. I myself found that I would get particularly frustrated on nearly every level that I played, as I would have to start the level over simply for pressing a button to early or too late. However, the game exceeds in rewarding the player, as the sense of accomplishment that comes from beating a particularly difficult level is unrivaled by most games that are released on the market today.
BIT.TRIP RUNNER is a unique game that can be extremely rewarding, or absolutely crushing. Be warned: the game is not for everyone. While I didn't particularly enjoy BIT.TRIP RUNNER, it continues to be a game that is loved by the Indie community and the games that follow it only stand to be a testament to their devotion.
A 5 out of 10.
Authors Note - I, personally, did not enjoy BIT.TRIP RUNNER. I felt that it was too difficult for me and that it simply wasn't my type of game. However, I do highly recommend this game to any and all gamers that have yet to play it. It's a challenging experience that harkens back to the older days of retro gaming, and for that, I can honestly say that everybody should play these games, at least once.

The first installment of BIT.TRIP RUNNER is great, original indie game that will pass the time of those who are determined to reach the finish line of each level without fault.
However, if you're easily irritated, and don't like to waste time while getting nowhere, BIT.TRIP RUNNER might not be for you.

Brilliant game. Others have dwelt on the programming aspect, but the game design itself is superb. Like all the best games, it takes a small number of simple elements and combines them to create huge possibilities.
There are constant hard choices to make: do I spend energy on infrastructure, expansion, defence, upgrades...? There is never enough cpu, memory, energy, or other resources. Do I write a sophisticated algorithm to better exploit resources - but then I'm low on cpu - and so on.
You can spend as much time on this as you like. There are always tweaks and optimisations to make, new ideas to try. Alternatively you can walk away for a month, come back, and see how your AI is faring.
The feel of the game is a bit like EVE Online. It's a brutal PvP world where potential disaster is constantly lurking. There are 'real' consequences if you screw up. But when some code comes together and you emerge triumphant - it's a rush! Even getting wiped out is kind of fun. How did that happen? What was the other guy doing that I wasn't? How should I improve my code base for the next attempt?
Once up and running you don't need to spend a lot of time on it if you don't want to. However I recommend setting aside most of a day for a first run as you need to get your empire to a certain level before you can let it run unassisted. You need to get basic harvesting, production, and defence online. From scratch that can take a few hours.

This game is a programing game, and a programing game only.
So it comes with all its advantages and disadvantages, for example the relief and accomplishment feeling if something works as intended but as well if something goes horribly wrong.
If you do not fix your mistakes, either because you can't find them or don't have the time to do it, this will slowly have an impact on your colony, as creeps die approx. every hour (on shard1) and you lose controller level if no creep upgrades it resulting in fewer construction possibilities as well as no new energy to do things if no creep harvest it.
You can always rehab from this as your scripts stay and you always have a base energy you can work with to spawn simple creeps, so there is that.
Everyone who programmed, knows how frustrating it can be to not find an error in your program or something does not behave like you want it to do. You will have that. A lot. Like always in programing, so keep that in mind. For me, the advantages of actively seeing my steady improving code in a live environment visually outvages the disadvantages heavily.
If you ask yourself, can i program in this game with javascript? Can i learn with it?, i have an answer for you. It depends solely on you. You see reviews where people complain this is not for learners, others say it is easy to get into.

And i can well maintain my colony, you just need to understand logic to program, programing language matters little as you have some code snippets in the api where everything is well enough explained (i used it almost always for everything) as well as more and more users releasing some of their starter scripts where you can copy it, use it, and then improve it to your advantages. So i would say: Go for it, go and buy the steam version without subscription in the first place. But if you know yourself you struggle with simple coding (no matter what language) or just hate to be frustrated because of syntax or non-syntax errors, as well as never haven't programmed even something basic yourself, you may as well be better without it. This game is great in many, heavy aspects, and falls short on a few light ones. The negative aspects of it are more a matter of taste rather than being poor game design. Since so many negative reviews are written by people who think the game's too slow, I'll give a fast review so that you'll have time to play it sooner.
Pros:
- Great game design.
- Beautifully crafted world with a competent graphics engine.
- Great soundtrack.
- Combat is highly tactical and multifaceted. Planning and having a variety of strategies matter. (I recommend playing on Tactician Mode)
- Profound character creation, that actually matters in gameplay.
- Dialogue choices (sometimes) matter and help build character traits.
- Humour and pop-culture references.
- Lots of secrets.
Matters of taste:
- Very unforgiving to: Inexperienced RPG-players. Unskilled tacticians. People with bad dice rolls. Those who can't properly use Google as a last life-line. People who bought a keyboard without the F5 and F9 buttons. Sufferers of amnesia.
- Slow, sometimes painfully slow. A beverage or friend to accompany you through some parts of the game is highly recommended.
- A bit too few "in combat" tracks.
- Arhu is ♥♥♥♥ing everywhere.
Cons:
- Repetitive character auto-reactions to world effects. ("Feeling a bit hot under the collar!" "On the mend!" "What a deluge!" etcetera)
- Unnecessarily slow animations and queuing outside of combat.
- A little too uninformative quest log.
- Some quests/parts of quests are downright uninteresting.
- As with any game of any publisher, a few bugs here and there.
