Divinity: Original Sin is basically two things. First and foremost, it is a huge beautiful game that combines charm and depth in a way that most other role-playing only dream about. After creating your own characters, take control of its two main characters and one or two companions that are either mages, assassins, archers, knights, healers, mercenaries or other fantasy cliché encountered in its path.
One is unleashed in a world where every square meter is packed with neat design and good atmosphere. The music sets a great atmosphere through the whole experience, and jokes, obscure pop culture references and the ability to talk to animals gives the game quite a frivolous tone that only stops at the right times.
- Outstanding tactical combat
- Engaging quests
- Complex systems that make even the smallest actions feel meaningful
- Beautiful world that makes every new area a treat to explore
- Story and dialogue are full of wit and drama
- Rock-paper-scissors conversations strengthen the role-playing possibilities

- Cumbersome interface
- First few hours drag

After going through the entire game for the third time (Currently on my fourth playthrough, aiming for the Immortal achievement) and crying my eyes out over and over again, I have finally decided to write my very first review dedicated to the wonderful and magical, yet
challenging game that is Ori and the Blind Forest.
This was the very first "Platformer Metroidvania" style of game that I've played and I must say I was not disappointed in the least from my Ori experience, from the moment I set my eyes on the first trailer I was pulled in. The visuals and soundtrack alone made this game a must buy for me and when the time of release finally came out I found myself succumbing to the beauty of this gem more and more with every steps I took in the forest of Nibel together with the lovable and kind light spirit that is Ori. Some may say that I am "Biased" but honestly I knew nothing about what kind of game this would be besides what I've seen from the trailers, I had high expectations and for me they were all met.
Perhaps this style of game won't appeal to you as it did for me but If you are one of those who enjoys a game that can provide the feels, a good story, breathtaking visuals and soundtrack, along with a good challenge?? Then Ori is for you~ It has a lot to offer for 21,99$, personally I feel that it is nearly given away at such a low price for the quality it offers. Four years in the making is nothing to scoff at and this gem deserves all the attention it can get.
You may find yourself dying repeatedly in certain parts of the game specially If this style of game proves to be more challenging to you (Or If you lack a controller I cannot fathom how difficult playing this game on a keyboard would be), I did as well on my first playthrough and completed the game with well over 280 something respawns If my memory is correct. But remember this: Practice makes perfect~ If you have the will to see this game through to the end I guarantee you shall not be disappointed by the experience. The difficulty of this game may not appeal to all but it is well worth the purchase, that is without a doubt. <3
This concludes my review of Ori and the Blind Forest~ I doubt my review will have any sort of impact on your decision to buy the game or not but I certainly hope it has made interest towards this game grow within you. Lastly I wish to give my most heartfelt thanks to those who made this game come to life, you've given us all a masterpiece to enjoy and cherish~ I look forward to your future projects Moon Studios. |_|-Limit Out-|_|

This game has ALL of that.
Depending on how you define spoilers, the following may be lightly sprinkled with spoilers, but no story reveals:
1) Story:
This game has the kind of opening that is reminiscient of The Last of Us. If you don't cry in the beginning of the game, you are a monster. It was beautiful and within 15 minutes I was so heavily invested that I just didn't want to stop. I WANTED to succeed, if only for that little white dragon lemur thing. She is the sweetest, most adorable little thing ever and I love her and I want one.
2) Soundtrack.
HOLY HELL this game needs to be selling its soundtrack because jesus on a STICK it is beautiful. It literally makes me cry. Doing a playthrough of this game on youtube and the music alone sometimes makes me stop playing so I can seriously admire it better. It is so ARTFULLY written and so professional.
3) Gameplay.
This game is the essence of video gaming and platforming as it should be. The difficulty level is high and unforgiving, and it is a difficult game. You will get frustrated, and that means you should put the game down and come back later. It is brutal- but it is INCREDIBLY rewarding. That feeling when you succeed and get past a particularly difficult area is a wonderful feeling. I hate that I can see a counter showing me how many times I died- we all know I'm terrible at Platforming, does the game seriously need to tell me?
In all, I love the gameplay. The leveling system somehow makes it perfect, like I'm progressing and like I'm actually a child learning all of this for the first time, as Ori is meant to be. The little sprite thing, Sein, is perfect too- not a single ounce of Navi-syndrome.
Cutscenes are to the point, quick, and somehow heart rendingly beautiful. This was made in Unity I believe (or Unreal, for some reason I can't recall), and it uses the power of either of those engines to its fullest. A 2D sidescroller that feels and looks 3D is something you shouldn't scoff at- despite only one field of depth that you have to worry about, the illusion of depth is there and very very strong. You feel as if there is a world around you, a world outside of this simple [x, y] axis- like there's a Z axis and you just don't need to explore it yet, but it's there.
My favorite part has to be the fact that the game revolves around its gameplay. The story is beautiful and heart warming, but the fact that tutorial is explained artfully and skillfully and without stopping your forward motion or your ability to keep going is absolutely fantastic. I feel like I'm constantly moving forward.
In all, a wonderful game. 100/10.

Tail Drift is a nice, promising racing game, in early access, but looking fairly complete. It uses the unity engine, but (because of the multi-platform release maybe?) looks a little bit like a flash game. You don't really drive, but you fly around a (magnetic?) pipe that represents the track. You can't fly off the track or get your plane to explode - if you hit a wall you're slowed, sometimes significantly, and that's all that matters.
As a mobile port - you need to gather stars to progress in the game, while you gather coins on the tracks to upgrade your plane or buy a new one. There are quite a few coins on the track, but I think there is a cap on the reward you can receive upon completion (250, 350). The music is reasonable, but, I think, I only heard like 2-3 tracks, so there is a room for improvement. The controls are fine, I used keyboard, and it worked great. Maybe an option to rebind the keys might be useful, but the default keys work just fine.
The gameplay modes are nice - the classic race is "ok", as the opponents are not the brightest, but Time Trail and Time Extension is where the game shines in my opinion, as you can always try and do better. A steam leaderboards for those modes will greatly benefit the game.
At the moment all available planes are the same tier, so I don't see a reason for buying a new one, instead of upgrading your plane with the money you get, but more planes and tracks are coming, according to the developer.
What I personally really dislike, is that the game spins up all your available hard drives before start, and I find that really pointless and super annoying.
Coming off a Halloween sale and into a Christmas one, I really can't recommend the game for the full price tag, but then again I really do enjoy it, so I feel this dire need for a "wait and see / wait for sale" review option in Steam. Once the VR support comes and other cool features, I'll probably rework my statement.

This is an educational plant genetics game where your landlord is Mendel. Just saying. That’s charming. And charming’s the main descriptor I’d use for Crazy Plant Shop. Yeah, I can talk about maybe some of the stereotypes aren’t the greatest thing to stick in a game for kids, but I’d counter myself with how diverse the cast is, and in general, the thing’s just so darn cute. Especially the kid voice actors. Cuuuuute. And there’s hot dog plants and chompy plants and … and! It’s a neat way to explain homogenic and heterogenic / recessive and dominant genes. Also encourages a little critical thinking (I don’t have the right plants to get the combination the customer ordered, but if I breed these two together, and breed the resulting plant with the first plant … ).
Unfortunately, Crazy Plant Shop has a couple of major problems. First, the UI is a little muddy. Tool tips or a more involved tutorial would be nice. For example, it’s not immediately clear you can choose what alleles a plant inherits.
Second, and related, the game handles awkwardly. I swear I spent half my time wandering around and switching plants with plants. You have to pick up a plant to see its alleles. I do understand that you’ll never have enough pedestals to encourage that critical thinking again (do I need four plants to create all variations of this species? No, I just need two), but even if you narrow everything down to just what you need, the shelf space never stops feeling crowded and hard to organize.
So, gimme more informative UI and plant-wrangling that doesn’t involve wandering back and forth, and this is fair fantastic science edutainment for youngsters.

I really wanted to love this game. I mean, I really, really, really wanted to love it.
But I can't.
I absolutely adore the art style.
I love the concept.
And the plants are adorable.
But the gameplay sucks any chance of fun out of it for me.
The idea of the gameplay is exactly the kind of game I usually love.
But some of the decisions the designers made on how the game should work were foolish and they ruin the fun of the experience.
You buy plants from a catalog and sell them at a huge loss.
If you breed the plants it's free, but your machine only has a super limited number of uses per day.
So you basically can't actually experiment and play around any and if you make even one tiny mistake, you can screw yourself over completely.
The result is that the game is more stressful than was necessary and the idea of a shop owner selling their plants at a huge loss from the acquisition cost seems hugely immersion breaking and frankly, I think it was done as a way to artificially increase the difficulty, and that sloppy design shows.
If they had chosen instead to make the catalog orders a break-even scenario, you could play around, try things out, learn about plant genes in a lower-stress environment and have fun.
In fact, even with various difficulty levels, that would be nice. Low difficulty, break even on catalog orders. Medium, small loss. High, the default loss currently in the game.
As it is, I think it's incredibly cute to look at and it refreshed me about how genes work very minimally... but I can't recommend it as a game because I didn't enjoy it. :c

Nidhogg- a simple game that looked to have so much potential but in the end, delievered too little.
It's a tug of war style fencing game featuring two pixel art fencers fighting to make their way from one end of a long room to the other.  Featuring one hit kills, fast respawns, and a rock, paper, scissors style stance system, Nidhogg at its core is a fun, great concept.  It's easy to pick up and play, and honestly could be a great time...
...If you have someone next to you to play with.  If you're looking for an enjoyable single player experience you won't find it.  The single player features are anemic and feature just endless room after endless room.
I was unable to test the online netcode...because it appears dead.  Even during peak hours, I simply could not find a match.
What I was left with was a game that played well but had literally zero features.  The AI suffered from either being a complete push over to Atreides like prescience.
The art direction, which I enjoyed at first, quickly became vomit enducing in the second or third stage.  Literally, the colors hurt my eyes.
In the end, if you have RL buddies to play with, I'm sure it's a great game, but with literally no single player features and dead online, there's nothing to see here.  Perhaps it was better at launch, but clearly the overly simple gameplay didn't have the legs.
3/10

Crazy Plant Shop by Filament Games explores the concepts of genotypes in plants. You own a plant shop and your job is to provide customers with plants that have the properties/phenotypes that the customers request. The game has adorable artwork and, as there are no quicktime events but is strickly turn-based, is very relaxing.
You buy plants which you can “breed”: You select (using a punnett square) which genes the offspring should have. I found the breeding very easy which in turn made the game very easy, but on the other hand I am probably not the target audience. For kids learning about dominant and recessive genotypes, this would be a great way to introduce them to these concepts.
Other than that, there is not much gameplay to the game. New customers enter, you fill their order, you breed plants until your “breeding machine” runs out of energy, and then you close the shop for the day. Completing orders will make you unlock new types of plants. You win if you have unlocked all plants on the end of day 13.
A great game for anyone who wants to learn about genotypes and inheritance.

Got this in a Humble Bundle and figured I'd try it. The target audience is obviously people still in primary school - the game itself is trivial to break (get two identical plants of each type that have both the dominant and recessive gene for every trait and you can breed any combination) and it's nigh on impossible to actually lose (there's no time limit). While more plants are added as you progress, the mechanics remain unchanged throughout the game; it's the exact same game but with some different images for the later stages. I can't even really recommend it to teach simplified genetics because the game does a poor job of explaining how to breed plants.

I bought this game just because I thought it included punnett/punnet squares and mendelian sampling. It does and it does so in a way that isn't hard to learn either. I even bought this game for my nieces to play. This game and it's developer bring relatively hard concepts, even for some of my collegues, to a basic level and introduces them to children; Or the children at heart. I'll be going into my third playthrough soon and I'm only on 14.8 total hours. I could run through this game pretty quickly, but then you'd be missing the story. The story is...decent, not great but decent. You are the proprieter of a plant shop and your landlord is Gregor Mendel. He makes you pay 10 bucks every night for rent. You have to make enough money to stay afloat while also trying to breed plants for customers orders. A third but optional objective is to ender the local flower show and move through the local, state, and national levels before trying to win at the worlds fair. These are all pretty easy as long as you have two heterozygous plants ready to breed for anything. The hard part is turning away people when you don't have enough (breeder) power to breed plants for a customers order. Eventually the game will realize you have a spare fauxglove and give you a customer who wants that specific plant and only one. Other times you just have to keep it for the night and try again tomorrow.
I would strongly recommend this game for anyone who loves genetics to even the genetic outliers. (haha, that's a joke.) It will be hours of fun and it's not a game that you have to play for hours to get into, but you certainly can.
Hats off to Filament for this one.

Pros-

I have thoughts on this game.
I never played the original Oddworld, so I hold no nostalgic fuzzle-wuzzles for the source material. So this review is strictly of Oddworld as its own entity.
What it gets right, it gets really,
right - the colors, sounds, and story, even including the hackneyed, trite Captain Planet themes and forced rhyming couplets, are charming to the point of absurd. It's clear that Oddworld is a masterclass in the grotesque cuteness that Jhonen Vasquez and Danny Elfman were also tapping into around the time of the original. And that charm and feel has to carry this game, because the gameplay, updated it may be, does not.
Oddworld is a stealth puzzle platformer. This means lots of slow, precise movements. Oddworld's controls, however, want to be Crash Bandicoot or Sonic - all momentum and buildup/running. While the running animations are impressive, they're useless. You have next to no control over poor Abe as you will have him skidding off ledges, into bombs and on top of armed Sligs all game.
Coupled with stingy checkpointing and awful "load times" (entirely artificial, as you have to watch Abe regenerate), and a quicksave that requires, no kidding, going
to quickload, means if you don't get the long sequence right the first time, you have quite the wait in front of you to retry.
This is unacceptable. Poor Abe doesn't deserve what is done to him by you in this game, mostly because you are not trying to do it - it just is faulty controls. If you have the patience of a saint, or the willingness to approach a late-90s PSX game as an artifact, not a modern toy, you can get your fun out of it. I did, but I didn't finish because I just couldn't keep going back to the same room and reloading again and again to fail at the last jump.
If Oddworld were released today, it would come with a full rollout of Hot Topic gear for the kids, little plush Abes and Paramite Pie keychains. Sadly, its moment has passed.
Godspeed, Abe. May you find your gameplay in the next generation.

I was really excited when I heard that Oddworld was getting a remake, so I bought it a while back so I could play it when I finally got a PC to play it on. I was expecting everything from the original, plus even better visuals with today's new tech. All I got was a let down.
I played for an hour, then unistalled because of how inferior this rendition felt. First off, the animations are stiff and sluggish. Abe's movements used to have fluidity and weight to them, but he moves like a character in a SFM Youtube video in New n' Tasty. Then there's the game's atmosphere, which went in the opposite direction. The world of Oddworld used to give off a dark, oppressive feeling, with its shadows, grit, dirt, and bland colors. Now everything's bright and colored in bloom effects that only serve to burn my eyes. Even the Mudokens don't seem all that oppressed anymore. They're constantly making annoying side comments about being slaves, rather than being scared for their lives. I don't care how clean that foot of floor will be, you've said it 6 times already. All it does is make it more annoying when you have to retry a puzzle because the new controlls are awful. Seriously, there's no more grid movement, there aren't individual screens to determine enemy awareness range, there's no option for classic controls, and every action abe performs is slow and unresponsive.
Don't buy this game, just buy the original instead. Man, It hurts that I can't even get a refund for this.

Divinity is a turn-based , Co-op, adventure, strategy, indie, RPG.   (Jesus Christ)
The thing with Divinity is that it is , even the enhanced edition , is pretty unintuitive and still decently buggy. Minor flaws mostly but they do add up. Unable to shoot an enemy although you cleary should be able to , your co-op partner being stuck in a doorframe or doing funny animation buggs when using a bed , audio bugs etc.
Well this would usually put every sane person off the game , so what makes me forgive the game its flaws?
The reason being is immersion and fun , immersion can make up for alot of bad design choices. See how Assassins Creed I and Silent Hill 2 were games with many bad design choices yet many still loved them because they were able to suck you in so well like (almost) no other game could? It made you overlook these small flaws because you were having a great time. And this is how playing Divinity with a friend feels like. You will have a rough start early wondering around town aimlessly and being put into place by either guards or the ridicioulously strong monsters outside the city walls. But stick with the game here and explore the city , talk to NPCs for potential side quests , ( steal everything that you can fit in your pockets >:D) , venture down the main story line a bit and when you get stuck or when it gets too hard just do something else and come back later. Soon you will find yourself immersed in the world of Divinity and become extremely invested in your characters , level-ups feel meaningful due to many things you can invest in and you can have conversations with your co-op partner to (,to a certain extend,) shape your characters' personality.
As (in my humble opinion) the game lives off of co-op interactions, playing the game alone is not nearly as enjoyable and I would honestly even go as far as to recomend against buying it if you have nobody that is willing to play it with you. Don't get me wrong the game is great but it is infinitely better with a friend to enjoy it with as , as previously mentioned , one is more willing to overlook the games' flaws.
Grab a friend and give the game a shot , stick with it and you will find yourselves immersed in a beautiful role playing wonderland.

I have used the SKSE program since I first discovered Skyrim.  Note that I am not a programmer, and don't have complete mastery of the files, from a technical standpoint.  I do have a couple of comments, to make.
First, SKSE adds great dimension to the game, and allows for things could possibly done with loose files, BSA's, and whatever those things are.  But it does it in a very user-friendly way, in the MCM.  I am eagerly looking forward to its incorporation into the Skyrim Special Edition.
Second, this is a warning to everyone who is thinking about using it.  It uses scripts, to make certain things happen.  The real danger of doing this is that ... during a playthrough ... the user will add other script-based modification to game, and the result will be the infamous "Save Bloat", i.e., saved games become so bloated that loading times, and even quicksaves, take long times to happen, and can result in CTDs and frozen screens.
I have learned, by hard experience, to NEVER add a mod to the game, unless I use a tool called LOOT, to establish the proper load order of all of my plugins, and at least once per week clean any files that need cleaned.  This will seriously help to end trying a "Quicksave", while in the game, and having that process take 4-5 minutes!
With simple precautions, SKSE is a great way to expand your gameplay experience from the vanilla version.  I recommend using this utility to everyone.

Screeps is an amazing game for anyone interesting in programming, logic, and strategy games. It's got a long but smooth learning curve as you grow from managing a couple of miner-workers to building out custom roles & automating your bases, expansions, war and more. You'll go from small scale planning to optimizing the efficiency of your burgeoning hive empire in a few months.
This game offers something great for beginner coders and experienced professional developers. The community around it is one of the friendly and helpful I've seen for any game or online coding experience.

Screeps is a really fun programming game that is basically all about efficiency.  Early on you have a lower CPU limit that you are unlikely to hit.  However you need to get your room up and running as quickly as possible.  Later on you have a CPU limit that you'll need to manager, a memory limit, while making sure that multiple rooms are being managed optimally.
This game is not intended for someone who doesn't know or want to learn code.  It primarily uses javascript and without using code you can do nothing.  Every aspect of the game from spawning a creep(your units) to making a tower attack or a creep do anything has to be coded by the player.  The game's UI allows for some things to be setup without using code, buildings' construction sites can be placed, your initial spawn can be placed through the UI.  You can select a unit and see it's memory pretty easily as well.
Even though the online game is running 24/7 and the game is made to use code that is constantly automating your units you will likely always find something to do and if not you probably aren't being creative enough.  My code has gone through multiple optimizations and will likely always be getting improved.  You can also play on a dedicated private server as well.  A lot of fun seeing a slow start at the beginning and then starting on a new map and seeing how much better the new code runs and how much easier the game is with my newer better code.
If you like to code, love a lot of flexibility along with sensible limits you'll love this game.  While at it's core it's a coding game, the online gives it a bit of a RTS feel as well!

I play far too many games, the vast majority of which I find to be dull rehashes of other games I've already played. In such an over-populated genre as the ARPG genre then it is suprising to find a genuinely interesting and somewhat different game.
Companions are pretty common and often, in games like Torchlight, they feel underwhelming and do little to combat the feeling of isolation that can come with one-person-army type games. Katarina on the otherhand is genuinely powerful and I enjoy her characterisation; her constant snarky comments and brief moments of kindness make the game feel more alive and less isolating. If she is specced right she can be monstorously powerful, she also scales with difficulty which is especially useful and it means she always remains relevant. This being said she doesn't make you feel underpowered, even in the harder difficulties, as long as you play your class right.
On that note playing your class right is a big deal, each class is very different to the next and they often require completely different approaches to levelling. The Constructor, for example, you are most powerful if you get at least 1 point in all the minion-type abilities ASAP; if you do this even on the hardest difficulties (Fearless and then the increasingly difficult Inhuman Ordeals that unlock later) the Constructor is probably the most powerful class.
That being said in endgame, if you experiment enough, you will find the Philogistoneer can become effectively invulnerable and roughly 8 times more powerful than any other class (due to a unique and specific way you can combo it's skills).
As you'd expect most other classes benefit more from focusing on less skills and just making those individual skills as strong as possible but they all still play very differently which makes multiple playthroughs actually bareable which (for me) is a rare thing.
All in all a genuinely good ARPG that has all the necessary ingredients, lots of monsters, good loot, good power progression, good voice acting, interesting story (the middle gets a bit stale but the beggining and end are good) and the learning curve is smooth and well spread out except for a gap that covers all the 'third game' chapters and then starts again with adventure maps.
Also love the dev's sense of humor, the secrets are a huge part of this game, find all that you can and enjoy the references.

The Final Cut of the IAofVan Helsing series brought the multiple games together into a single seamless narrative; which is a huge kudos to the developers and the people who worked on this game.
Overall I found the story to be engaging and fun to play through. The mix of quests and hidden content made the world worth exploring - and the fact that a lot of the hidden content were related to teases about other popular games or references to popular culture made each one a joy to discover.  Additionally, I found the music quite enjoyable for Van Helsing. On most games I turn the music off and I did not feel the need to with this game. The voice acting was also very well done - with each character having their own unique voice and none of the actors sounding bored or tired in the delivery of their character's dialogue.
Gameplay is conventional towards any other Action RPG in the genre of Diablo. Point and click, fire abilities, kill packs of things, watch the loot rain. Speaking of the loot. I believe that was probably one of the drawbacks to the game. While the loot is plentiful I found that it was difficult finding gear to upgrade into unless I was hitting level gaps between pieces of 20+ or more. There is a limited crafting system here but it only works for normal and the highest tier magic items, leaving two tiers to be nothing more than sales fodder junk. The gem style upgrade system with Essences was a unique way to handle gear customization and helped with the lack of consistent gearing upgrades.
If you like ARPGs and Diablo style games. I recommend picking up the Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing and giving it a playthrough. Well worth the time investment to play this game to completion.

Overall I found the game to be entertaining for a day and would recommend it to science/plant enthusiasts.

Think you're good at rhythm games? Think again. This retro-style rhythm-them-up puts your mind inside the music and has you pressing the different keys at the right time to dodge the oncoming obstacles. The soundtrack in each level is different and incredibly funky.
The levels are all predetermined so you can be sure that when you fail, your immediate cry of “♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t!” is not at all justified. After a few levels of pulling off some sick moves, you can really check out your skills it BIT.TRIP RUNNER, and reaching the end of a tough challenge is very rewarding. There are gold coins to pick up along the way that naturally increase your score and clearing a level of gold will send you to an bonus challenge. Here you get no backing track, so you have to face the music (LOL) and make up the rhythm in your head, which is difficult even on the early bonuses.
The best thing about this game is the steadily intensifying backing track, and each time you collect a special pickup it gets louder and more involved. It’s also a great way of knowing if you’re near the end of a level, because of the intense bass after all those pickups.
Whether you’re tone deaf or fancy yourself as a bit of a musician, this game will keep you raving (and raging) all day long. And no, it’s not better than Rhythm Paradise.

Some may say this isn't a big deal, but the levels get quite long and so you quickly realize the smallest flaw killed you mere feet from the finish line.
The soundtrack is what truly makes this game standout though. Music is of course a subjective thing, but the gameplay mixed with the semi-chiptune soundtrack made this an engaging experience.

The choice is to either walk around while touching, talking to, and trying everything, or consulting the walkthrough. If taking the time to talk to everyone, touch everything, and try all approaches appeals to you then go ahead and buy this game. If you want to stand even a remote chance of getting it right without help then look elsewhere.

You can't just walk around and level up until things become easier. That's mainly because the starting town is surrounded by certain death on all sides. Players are forced to complete things in a very specific order to progress in the game and there's no rhyme or reason to the order so players are forced into time consuming trial and error.
Imagine being stuck in a large trap and being given a choice of doors and behind the doors is another set of choices. You have to go to door three, then door one, then go back to start and choose door one, then door five. It just keeps going that way. You can't just figure out a way.
You have to play rock, paper, scissors with psychic NPCs to win some arguments and it's totally lame.
Things like crazy design and dialogue decisions(really, Scarlett? Can you please be more consistent? Are you naughty or nice?!), nearly impossible difficulty, and completely nonsensical chronology with regards to the quests make me not recommend this game at all. It's such a shame, too! It's like a modern Baldurs Gate that is a massive pain in the butt to play. I really want to like it but I literally have to either walk around until I figure out what I'm supposed to do(not going to happen) or consult the walkthrough(not fun at all).

Overview:
Excellent game for Programmers.
!!!!!!Free version available via web browser!!!!!!- check that out before you commit to buying anything!!!!!
Would recommend beginners use TypeScript. Languages other than JavaScript are supported. See below.
Warning: building from scratch is time consuming.
First I have enjoyed this game a lot.  Good enough that it is the first non-work programing I have done since college.  Like most good programs however this will take time, especially in getting the basic framework up and running.  Not necessarily a bad thing in my opinion but still a hassle.  If you can find someone’s code that you can understand and figure out how to modify after you get a hold of the commands and API I would recommend finding someone else’s already built basic functions code and modify it to your tastes.  There are lots out there and even fully automated complete ones.
Basic functions include: harvesting energy and minerals, auto build basic buildings, auto repair, auto basic defense with at least turrets and 1 unit type available,  and auto spawn units/ hopefully with a priority que or similar.  Bonus if it includes building, pathing, and harvesting in other rooms.  From there you can tweak the code for optimization all you want and build your custom units/defense and plan your expansion/domination.  It takes a bit of the fun and challenge out of it but it will save your countless hours.  At the time of this writing I’m 75 coding hours into my session and i have only managed to do basic harvesting of energy, build, repair, and poor spawning method without a que yet.  I have much planned and could probably spend the same number of hours optimizing the pathing and functions of the units I have without even getting to defense or attack.
Second, I bought this game without realizing that it has a free version which disappointed me as, more than a week in, I have not passed the free 10 CPU limit on the main server so I’m pretty much wasting the extra CPU I paid for.  Check out the free version, get your basic code setup, as soon as you are happy with the basics move on to the main server.  Honestly I’m not even ready for the main server yet but I wanted to give it a go anyway.  you can do almost everything in simulation with unlimited cpu without paying so I would suggest you do that and then if you want to go to the main server and you need the extra CPU buy it them.
The game is written in JavaScript.  The steam client version has a built in IDE for JavaScript but it could be a bit better.  That is mostly JavaScript's fault however.  I would recommend looking up articles about TypeScreeps.  It shows you how to code in your own IDE with TypeScript for screeps which is a lot friendlier for programers, especially beginners.  There are setup instructions and everything out there.  More importantly it supports some other languages via conversion and even a portion of c natively for pathing and some other stuff so if you would rather use those then I would recommend it. Honestly the steam client version vs acess via web browser is that there is no setup on your computer to do.  It has its own premade environment with easy to use commit, branch, and change active code functions.  Very nice but probably doesn't make up for it not being a professional/your favorite IDE.
Cheers.

The biggest isue with the game is the combination of a high learning curve tied with a subscription plan. Individually they are not a big issue but combined they leave you with a bad game experience. You get a 30 day plan with the purchase of the game but after that you need to pay to continue this plan or are downgraded to a limited CPU. This is a problem with the steep learning curve the game has. You need to learn javascript. For a new player it can take well over 30 days to learn the mechanics of the game and the language. Unlike traditional online games with a subscription those games are at least playable while you "use up" the subscription. But the glaring issue with SCREEPS is while you are learning the basics of the game your 30 days subscription is being used up. By the time a player has learned enough to play the game your plan is over and you need to spend another 15$
The game needs to offer the option to start the upgraded CPU plan at will and give the players the limited CPU from the start. Once they have learned enough to actually play the game they can join the online community and then the players can start the 30 day upgraded CPU.
I wanted to learn the game at my pace without being rushed to beat the 30 day time limit or having to pay another 15$ but this game just doenst offer this.

It's not often that I actually enjoy a game enough to get off my♥♥♥♥♥and write a review on it, so here goes nothing.
Platformers have always been a guilty pleasure of mine. Be it 2D, 3D, or some sort of other sort of D, I've always been a fan of it. I bought this game on a whim based on a recommendation Kudo Tsunoda gave me on Facebook, and it is easily one of the best purchases on Steam I've ever made.
I've played more platformers than I would like to admit, and like any medium of entertainment, they eventually get stale. There are only so many variations you can make on a single genre over the course of several decades without running out of ideas. So a common issue that many modern platformers have today is they focus more on having some new gimmick than they do on having a fundamentally sound game that is actually enjoyable to play.
This is exactly what Ori does right. It doesn't give you some weird mechanic that is barely ever used yet is forced down your throat like. It favors ideas and mechanics that have been tried and true, and then perfects them to a point. This is easily on par with Super Meat Boy in terms of fluidity of controls and the implementation of mechanics.
Progression systems in platformers are always a bit hard to pull off. Often times you'll see a power up behind a wall that you think you can break, or a health orb on a ledge just barely out of reach, and you know that you'll eventually have to come back to this area later in the game once you get the needed ability to make the jump or smash the wall. This can lead to a tedious experience that almost discourages initial explanation of the map. What Ori does that helps this is the gradual evolution of the map. As you unlock and learn to use different abilities, various events take place on the map that allow you to better utilize the abilities you've just unlocked, and gives you a reason to go back and explore areas that you've been to before.
The story is great, and honestly I don't want to spoil it so I'm just going to leave it at that.
9/10

Absolutely stunning! A must-have for every gaming enthusiast out there!
Pretty much everything in this game is spot-on.
Let's take about the visuals first.
The overall Artwork is just lovely. Several layers add a lot of additional depth to the game although it is "just" 2D. The world you are about to enter aims right at your heart and it sure won't miss.
All the different parts of the environment vary enough to make it intresting and yet not feel completly out of place.
The soundtrack, as the rest of the game, is pure gold. Since there is very little dialogue the music gets even more important but Gareth Coker did a fantastic job at capturing the beauty of the world and characters within his music.
Characters and story are also top-notch. Although your main character does not speak at all and your little companion only says a few sentences throughout the game they still have lots of character and charme. I'm not even mad about them not speaking. The story is mostly told through visuals and music which is more than enough to make this game a wonderful journey.
The short introduction into the world and its inhabitants is enough to make you feel connected to them. Personally I really cared about the world, the characters and their destiny.
Controls are on point. Nothing more to say about that. Whether you play with keyboard or controller. Everything works just fine and you always have 100% control of what's happening.
The difficulty and pacing of the game are perfect. As usual it gets more difficult the further you progress. The game slowly but surely adds additional challenges by giving you access to new abilities. Areas you couldn't reach before are now open for you to explore. The player is forced to make use of his newly learnt skills and has to combine them all to reach the goal. Once you learn something new the game will make sure to slowly get you used to it and then speeds things up as it gets more challenging. Don't get fooled by the lovely arts tho. Some areas of the game can be quite tricky to beat. It's challenging, yet never gets frustrating.
For the price of 20€ you will get about 10+ hours of gameplay. An overall incredible value.

This is a relatively simple twin-stick shooter with limited depth but fast-paced gameplay and plenty of polish for its price. PC performance was good, and stayed mostly steady at a solid 60 FPS except for a brief moment when Windows decided to remind me for the seven-thousandth time that there was an update and I should really, really install it right now.
An average run took me about 5 minutes (to be fair, I'm not great at games like this, so more skilled players will probably do better). There are 5 power-ups: a triple shot, a side shot, a shield, a rotating one-time-use laser beam of doom that basically clears the current wave by itself, and a freeze item of some sort that I didn't quite get to use before dying to the one of the homing missiles that chase you down like a dog after the local mailman.
The game's vibe reminds me a lot of Geometry Wars, both in terms of gameplay and in general aesthetic. It's not the type of game that you will look back upon as groundbreaking, or a game you'll remember decades down the road as one of your favorite games of all time, but it is a great little game to sit down and play when you have a few minutes to kill.
For $1.99? Absolutely worth it.

The incredible adventures of Van Helsing Final cut is a hack and slash game developed by NeoscoreGames . What makes this game so unique is the fact it is three games combined into one, aka Van Helsing, Van Helsing 2 and Van Helsing 3 along with all the dlc with some continuation that links all the game together. Van Helsing is one of the rpg games that could have been great but failed due to technical issues and some frustrating mechanics.
In terms of graphics, the game does an acceptable job for its presentation without any fps drop. The developers also released recently a high definition pack which makes the game even more beautiful than before, particularly when it comes to the cyberpunk atmosphere.
The sound is amazing and it fits perfectly in the context of the game which further increases the realism for the cyberpunk theme presented so often in the game.
The incredible adventures of Van Helsing is essentially a hack and slash game filled with a lot of unique features and a lot of Easter eggs. The is in fact filled with Easter Eggs from the likes of Monty Python up to Jekyll and Hide references. The game uniqueness also consists of many mini-games and features which are not available in most hack and slash games. One of them is a tower defense game which consists of defending a portal of monsters coming in waves and building towers at strategic locations. Another feature in the game is the elite squad quests where you can send captains on missions and receive powerful items and gold when they succeed. All those extras just help enrich the Van Helsing universe and make the hack and slash experience a lot more bearable.
The game also has an amazing system with the companion. Your only companion throughout the game is Katarina, a ghost that served your family for generations. Katarina can either attack in melee, range or become ghost form and not attack but cast spells and give you a damage reduction. The beauty of the companion system is the amount of customization that can be done thanks to the Skills. There are three trees and each is very different from another which gives a lot of combinations.
Another system that impressed me was the unique classes. The game essentially has all the classes found throughout the three Van Helsing games and each is more unique than the other. I personally tried the constructor, the engineer with minions and a massive platform following which can be upgrade to deal tons of damage and equip extra weapons. Overall, each class will give a unique experience to the player which gives a lot of replayability value.
The story in game is not extremely great, but it has a certain originality attached to it. The game is also long due to the combination of the three games.
Another excellent feature I liked about Van Helsing final cut is the deal NeoGames did. The players owning certain parts of the game on steam could get it much cheaper depending on how many games they had, and would get it for free if they had all three games.
Once you finish the campaign, you can try the adventure map where you can attempt different missions with your character and acquire currency to open chests to get more loot.
The game also has an interesting crafting system however it is quite detailed. I personally skipped it but I will most certainly look at it in the feature.
Unfortunately for the game, there are bad points concerning Van Helsing, bugs and crashes coming into my mind for one. On my win 10 laptop I could start the game and hear sound but would only have a black screen. I could find a solution concerning the situation while looking on google but unfortunately it removed me from the online part which was annoying since it also de-activated steam achievements. The problem I had next was crashes while trying to go in a portal to get to a different location. To solve this issue, I had to re-verify my cache and tweak some settings in the regedit area. While the process was not extremely hard nor long, the issue might not be that big, but it can still annoy players considering the fact this bug was also in Van Helsing 2. It will also hinder the players that are only aware of basic features on a computer and cause them massive frustration.
The bugs are also very annoying concerning this game since some quests will end up bugged sometimes because of it. I personally had two quests bug during my playthrough which made me unable to complete them.
Overall, Van Helsing final cut is a fun game if you can cope with the bugs and if you enjoy having a lot of extra mini games in a hack and slash game. The game deserves a 7/10 and it is a nice addition to any hack and slash fan.

Very good ARPG with fun elements and dialogues. Played about 40 hours to complete the story.

A rather solid ARPG in a steampunk-eastern-european setting. Graphics are pretty, story is good, banter between heroes is funny, loot is plentiful - you get the picture. There are 6 classes, and although sometimes they do fall into the cliche "warrior-rogue-mage" categories, two of them - constructor and phlogistoneer - did surprise me, the former being a summoner/engineer type with turrets and drones, and the latter an exoskeleton-clad weapons master, throwing bombs, planting mines, launching rockets and burning foes with napalm. There are also 10(!) levels of difficulty and some after-story activities resembling rifts from that Blizzard's failure of a Diablo 2 sequel, so you won't get bored too soon after beating the final boss.

It was a great experience, but your fun largely depends on what you are getting it for.
If you want a Diablo-like ARPG that you can progress through, enjoy it's story, always progress forward and explore a new area and just go with the flow, this is definitly an excellent choice for you. However if you want it to just "be done" with reaching max level as soon as possible, then go for the loot grinding and build swapping like you do in Diablo, this game is definitly not for you. It has little to no replayability even though the developers desperately tried to implement it with daily missions, tower defense game mode and whatever more, it's just not that interesting of a game to explore it more than once, and the RPG progression system is kind of boring too - I played a hunter on heroic difficulty from start, finished the game after 33 hours on lv87, the last 20 levels I didn't even care to use my skill points. Got a movement speed buff "for fun" when I needed to backtrack a little to explore every little corner on every map, but without that, make that 30 instead of 20.
What's special about it, is that it is overwhelmingly full of easter eggs from Batman to Half Life, from W40K to Hugh Jackman, all kinds of references to hungarian and székely culture (really a special treat for us!). Comparing it to other ARPG-s, it's closer to Titan Quest than Diablo III, if that's good or not, decide for yourself. Personally I wanted to Diablo-like game that I can play with constantly progressing forward in the world and story instead of getting pulled in to the lootgrind. I got that, I absolutely loved it (amazing boss fights, beautiful world - be sure to download the 7Gb texture pack from the store as free DLC!).

Crazy Plant Shop is a botanical genetics lesson disguised as a casual time management game (without the time management).
Though it aspires to be something of an interactive entry course on plant genes and reproduction, its educational value never goes so far as to attempt to beat you over the head with the fact the game is trying to teach you something. It gets its points (for as hyper simplified as they are) across through gameplay hooks rather than walls of text, and it's a surprising amount of fun. It essentially boils down to cross breeding plants while taking into account dominant and recessive genes to produce the traits you need to fill a customer's rather exact and bizarre orders.
It sounds incredibly dull, but in this case breaking things down to their utmost basics actually works in Crazy Plant Shop's favor. Traits are distinct and easy to recognize, with the biggest thing you need to keep tract of being making sure you spreed enough recessive genes around to be able to breed plants with those traits. The lack of any time limit or penalty for refusing orders you can't focus on allows you to take as much time as you need mixing and matching plants, until you've found the right combination and feel like an insane plant matchmaker.
Where the game unfortunately trips over itself a bit is the unexpectedly punishing economy, which I wouldn't hesitate to call broken in most respects. You begin with a limited, finite amount of money to start your botanist career, and ordering plants is expensive and almost never fully compensated by the amount you're paid for fulfilling orders. If you aren't meticulously micromanaging your inventory and making full use of your also limited power for using the breeding machine, you're going to find yourself stuck with no other option but to start the game over. Aside from there being a bit about how breeding plants is cheaper than buying them outright, it was never made clear to me just how exact I needed to be with my orders, and how closely I needed to watch the number of power I had left if I wanted to succeed which led to me being forced into a corner several levels in on my first playthrough with no way out.
Crazy Plant Shop's oddly restrictive monetary systems make playing in it a little more stressful than I was looking for. I wasn't allowed room to experiment because I was so scared of losing all the progress I'd made because I bought one too many plants, and this really hampers and experience that seems designed as a more lighthearted way for people to learn about plants than a typical textbook. Once the game opens up a bit in the later third and puts less pressure on your every decision it was a lot easier to see it as one of the more creative forms of edutainment I've seen. It's just a shame that I'm sure a lot of people won't get that far.

Blood, gore and ridicolous amounts of violence. All in a day for a space marine. If you've ever had the dedire to play as a walking tank or demi-god, then this is the game for you. 40k fans would be rewarded by Relic's attention to detail but multiplayer has no dedicated servers so games might crash midway. If you can bear with that, then why not try it?

Unlike the strategy games of the 40k universe, this game truly captures how awesome it is to be a space marine. Be forewarned: this is a gorefest of chainsword ork-decapitating mayhem. If you enjoyed the sheer brutality and grit of the Gear of War franchise, then you will feel right at home with Space Marine. The camera perceptive and controls are similar. You can diveroll to avoid enemy blows and grenades. However, there is NO COVER system, which may take some getting used to. Even the level design is fairly open to force you out of hiding and into the fray. There is NO HEALTH REGENERATION (at least in the singleplayer) either; instead, you must eviscerate your enemies with a brutal melee finisher to regain health. Unfortunately, the game can get a little repetitive when you are using the same moves over and over in the same brown, drab environment, but the game does surprise you with some new, tougher enemies halfway through the game (I won't spoil it for you). Also, the multiplayer survival mode, Exterminatus, could use a few more maps. Fans of the 40k universe may be disappointed by the lack of certain weapons and armor sets (No terminator armor? No power fists? Dreadnoughts are DLC? Heresy, I say!) Overall, this is a well executed (pun intended) game with solid gameplay and an enjoyable multiplayer, offering a very satisfying (if at times simplified) Astartes experience.

I never got the chance to play the original Oddworld but when I was younger I played Munch's Oddysee and found it very interesting, so I decided to give this game a try.
This is so terribly disappointing...
For starters, this is a controller prefered game, and it originally did not work with my controller whatsoever. I bought an Xbox One controller and now it works, so if you have an Xbox 360 controller, or a third party controller, it probably won't work. The keyboard controls are abysmal, I wouldn't reccomend even trying to play the game with them.
This is a puzzle game based around trial and error. If you're a completionist, then you're going to want to rescue all of the Mudokons, which will require a lot of quicksaving because the game specifically tricks you into killing them all over the place, even during the tutorial. Didn't quicksave? Too bad, they're dead, now you have to restart from the last checkpoint. People have claimed this is brilliant game design because you have to pay attention to which buttons and levers do what, but I think it's not, especially because now the game is rendered in 3D and hints which would clue you in on what the buttoms and levers do might be not be on camera, or they'll be obstructed by foreground decorations. Sure, it's a puzzle game, but looking at the color of a button and then looking at the screen for other objects that same color isn't a puzzle. That's just basic color recognition.
The big problem with quicksaves arises from the fact that the game erases your quicksaves on a level transition, but level transitions aren't clearly labelled. If you didn't save all the Mudokons and you accidentally go through a level transition, you have to do that entire level from scratch again because you can't load your previous quicksave. This is so utterly stupid it hurts. Either have a warning message when going through a level transition or keep my quicksaves. Period.
Visually, the game is pretty appealing. It's nice to see creatures from previous games in HD, but the bloom is extremely overbearing. Way too much bloom. I'm sure you can turn down post-processing in the graphics, but I have the hardware to play the game on Ultra, so I want to play it on Ultra.
If you're a fan of the first two games (Oddysee and Exodus), you'll probably like this! If this is your first game in the series, I can't recommend this game. Although it's a very different game, I think Munch's Oddysee is a better entry point for beginners if you still want a more puzzle oriented game.

Approx. playtime: 10 hrs, single complete playthrough with controller
TLDR:
Pros: Beautiful graphics and sound design, challenging but not unfair, engaging story, reasonable price tag for duration and quality.
Cons: Harder to control with a keyboard, controllers are definitely recommended. Also, prepare to die quite a bit.
At times, it is the rare unexpected gems that stand out among the masses. As a person that doesn't play many platformers, I initially didn't pay Ori and the Blind Forest much mind. However, as word got around I decided to give it a spin, and what a pleasant surprise it has been!
Though it has been said by literally everyone now, the art style in this game is absolutely beautiful. From the way background objects sway when Ori walks past to the animation quality, this game oozes visual polish. Combined with an outstanding soundtrack, the game immediately draws you into its well-crafted world.
From the get go, the game starts off with incredible amount of emotion; I can say that I have never been so invested in a purple and black blob before, and that's literally within the first few minutes of the game! For such a simple story, it was impactful and very well presented despite having no voice acting and little narration.
I am not an experienced platform player, and at times, I was frustrated by the 'escape' sections that involved a lot of death and repeats. However, after finishing the game I feel that the gameplay while challenging, isn't unfair. While at certain sections it may be difficult to tell where you should go or what to avoid, the hazards in the game are generally well telegraphed and avoidable. It is worth noting, however, that a controller is HIGHLY recommended, as the keyboard controls are known to be clunkier.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game for those interested in a beautifully crafted platformer with a reasonable degree of challenge. For the price tag, this is a fantastic game that completely took me by surprise and will remain in memory for a long time to come. Bring a controller for a better experience.
I haven't been sucked into a platformer like this in a very long time.  Very highly recommended.

Overall, I give Screeps a positive review. I've been looking for a programming based MMO ever since I was introduced to a game called Asheron's Call (now shut down) and the ability to use plugins to script bot control. It was rudimentary, but fun.
Screeps is near exactly what I've been searching for, but it isn't without its caveats. I've been growing, testing, and refactoring my code for some time now, and I can say that it is worth its full initial price, though I happened to pick it up on sale. The API is well documented and thought out.
What needs to be said though, is that in its current state, you are better off testing by running in simulation mode, than on the public server (you could also run your own private server for testing). The average tick time on the public server is around 4-5 seconds, where in simulation mode, 100% speed runs at 1 second per tick. As you can imagine, this could make it hard to iterate your codebase.
There are some plans that have been made public to upgrade the servers, so only once those plans come to fruition would I reccommend purchasing a subscription for extra CPU - if you need it. You may find that if you only plan to expand to 2 or 3 rooms that the free 10CPU you get with the game is enough to sustain you, if your code is efficient enough.
Overall, its a unique game you won't find anywhere else, it is truly in a genre in its own. That can't be said for many other games today.

Screeps is the first and best game I've ever found for programmers. I can get absolutely lost in the gameplay for hours (I.E. writing code) and you can even play the game from the website with no download, so I find myself checking in and making slight modifications to my scripts throughout the day on my mobile phone. The API is very well documented so it's incredibly easy to jump in, and building up your code base can be extremely gradual or very quick, so it's great for experienced coders and for those learning.
I go to work and program in PHP, HTML, and JavaScript for 10 hours a day and yet when I get home, I find myself able to continue programming JS for Screeps for another 4+ hours; just can't get tired of it! This is an absolutely wonderful game for both experienced and nooby programmers. I highly recommend it!
Since this is a review after all, I'll give my one criticism: they do run your scripts 24/7 on a server, so there is a subscription fee for the game. This makes it feel slightly pay to win, because if you play for free you get way lower processing power for running your scripts. I understand why it is this way, but that doesn't mean I have to like it. The initial purchase of the game does include one month for free, however, so try it out and decide if it's worth subscribing or not after a month.

This is a good game. I like this game. The gameplay involves you and your partner, moving around the map, killing monsters, leveling up, gaining skills. It's not turn-based, it's real time. Let me talk specifically about what makes playing this game so enjoyable.
When you're fighting these monsters, you're strong. You can defeat almost any non-boss enemy in only several hits. However, you also typically fight monsters who come in mobs. It's up to you to make sure you use the right strategies to defeat these mobs of enemies. It feels really good seeing an enemy horde waiting, planning out your attack, and then striking - and winning.
Is it repetitive? Some players will think it is, some players will think it's not. Enemies don't have drastically different attack patterns and movement, but for me it's good enough, coupled with the other things in this game.
The banter between the main character and his partner. I've been playing this game and being generous, helping everyone to get that sweet sidequest exp, and the partner has berated and mocked me, on more than one occasion, for that.
The graphics are pretty good. My computer is bad, so I can't tell you what the graphics on the best settings are, but I can still say that they are pretty good. Same with sound.
Lastly, leveling up, learning new skills and perks, equipping new items, having a laugh at the various ridiculous parts of this game even though the story is all about killing monsters and being good at it.

So, what is this game? It's basically 15 minutes of story time, in which the author(s) weaves together a quick series of flash shots together. The minimalistic method is interesting, and entertaining enough for a one-time playthrough.
It's not great by any stretch of the imagination, though. The story given does not provide much literary merit, and is not nearly long enough to provide substantial "proof" for its concept. All it appears to be is a vehicle to demonstrate the potential of a unique storytelling concept to the video game medium. It works, but I would have liked an expansion on this idea beyond a 15-minute demo reel.
Your impact as a player is nonexistent. There are no choices to be made. Failure is impossible. Your sole purpose is to tag along for the ride and see what Thirty Flights of Loving has to show you. At this point, there is no reason why this shouldn't be a short film instead, which is a perfect medium to make itself right at home.
Is it art? Yes. But is it a game? No.

Just played through Thirty Flights of Loving and then the director's commentary. Inspiring. Anyone at all interested in narrative in games - go play it now. Best 15 minute lesson in level design and storytelling techniques in games you're likely to have.

OK, now I'm not saying go out and spend your dosh. But I will say this. I'm not sure what just happened, but I think it was art... and it was... interesting. I liked it. I think.... This is like one of those films where you're never exactly sure whats going on... and afterwards you feel unsettled for a bit.

journey ain't got nothin' on thirty flights lovin'
An awesome experiment in perspective, in story-through-environment, in developing characters without dialogue in the course of 13 minutes, in what's possible with video game storytelling and where it can take us.
The only problem I found with the game's open-ended interpretation: Most of the theories that make sense--the best stuff--is shattered by a note in the developer's commentary, where a forced design decision (i.e., boxes to block a doorway) doesn't seem to follow character motivations.
I hope Chung sticks with Citizen Abel stories in the future; Gravity Bone and 30 Flights are above and beyond the rest of his output, IMO, and despite its length, I found the game well worth supporting with a handful of dollar bills.
The game comes with a copy of Gravity Bone (freeware) accessible from the menu, and, as mentioned, a developer's commentary that's definitely worth checking out. Both GB and 30FoL ask to be replayed at least once or twice. You'll notice a load of new things each time.

Recommended only if you want to support the creators of Citizen Abel: Gravity Bone, or if you want a more stable, better version of Gravity Bone (which is included). Gravity Bone is better: the story is better, the game is more fun and it makes more sense.

As a newcomer to the series, I have serious doubts that fans of the original Oddworld are happy with this one.
I was aware that New 'n' Tasty is a puzzle platformer with very atmospheric art and anti-hyper-capitalistic message and I certainly got what I was expecting. When this game doesn't distract me with it's flaws, it a quite an enjoyable piece of interesting setting, likeable plot, characters and good puzzle design. Unfortunately, there are some major problems with this game that forces me to kindly decline the offer to join the cult following that this series generated around itself since the PS1 era.
The controls are the major problem. They are a suprise contented for the worst controls in the platforming video game I ever had a chance to check out. While Abe's Oddysey isn't a Sonic the Hedgehog and it focuses on puzzles, enemy manipulation and stealth, even for the slower paced gameplay those inputs are absolutely atrocious. Basic jumps, hops, climbing, operating levers and elevators, stealthing or even moving - all of Abe's possible actions feel sluggish unresponsive and suprisingly hard to perform in the heat of the moment. They are extremely frequently the core reasons for player's deaths. Even the simplest platforming sections become overbearingly frustrating, forcing me to constant guessing over the inconsistency to of my commands.
Puzzle and level design is an another nuisance. While half of the world is actually pretty neatly planned out with consideration for player's ingerention and possible actions, the other half just wrecks my nerves. Abe isn't an armored fellow, enemy guards are armed to the teeth, wildlife is constanly after your pound of flesh and explosives are at every corner. This all makes a compelling setting, but as for gameplay, this will often result in a dreaded trial and error that will make you chant in thanks for the inclusion of Quick Save feature. Neverless, some levels require nearly Buddish amount of patience in avoiding danger, trying different approaches and finding the "correct anwsers". Those latter are often time elusive, unintuitive and requiring knowledge of all the subtle game mechanics that the game throws at you. Guesswork is also involved especially in regards of the range of sight for guards and other machinery present in Rupture Farms.
All of this ends at it's worst with the moments where you can be stuck in a room without means to advance. This happened to me once in Zulag 1 revisit. The unfortunate placement of checkpoints, quick save and a special lock that requires enemies that you just defeated. This resulted in the restart of the chapter. As a completionists, I was also annoyed by the various hidden rooms, that were easily missable and pretty much required to get the 100% Saved Mudockons on the save file. I like looking for secrets, but those often weren't telegraphed quite well.
All in all, I'm not really interested in revisiting this series, or this game in particular, anytime soon. I could turn a blind eye on the controls and level design in the old version because of it's age, but this remake was a great opportunity to make Oddworld an more inviting place for the newcomers like me. In my opinion, some oddities should be kept in the bygone era, because the the final effect unfortunately ends up in the meat grinder of the modern times.

If you're looking for a simple, straightforward sim game with a slightly morbid theme then this is for you. You run an undertaker's (shocking, I know) and you'll have customers attend your shop regularly. You'll have to help them pick out coffins, headstones and flowers for their dearly departed.
Different customers have different budgets and some will have specific requirements. Customers that are satisfied with you, increase your reputation, which reduces the time between customers arriving so you can make more sales. Customers that are unhappy or who you turn away, can do the opposite. I found that to start with, it can take a while for customers to appear, at least until your reputation increases. Over time you can take on staff members, such as a secretary, who can help you identify the needs of the customer, and build other shops so you can make your own stock.
Overall, I found it quite straightforward to play once you work out what everything is and I have enjoyed playing it. There are flaws with it - the instructions at the start weren't especially helpful, the graphics could be better and it can be a bit slow to switch between buildings in-game. However, I like that it's an unusual theme, the game was easy to pick up and it's something I can chill out with. I liked being able to make my own items to sell.
Some of the other reviews have mentioned feeling that getting particular staff, such as secretaries, was unbalanced. Personally I didn't find this at all - I've had to wait 2 in-game days for a stonemason but that's been the worst of it and I haven't had any other problems like that even though I've set up shop several times by now.
I really hope the developers continue to work on the game as it is different to games I've played before and I think there's a lot more that could be done with it. It's a good starting point and I would consider other games they make if they're anything like this one. For the sale price, I've been very happy with it and I've been really enjoying this game.

Most have a childhood game or movie that still leaves them unnerved and anxious, and the first two Oddworld games will always remain that to me. Playing through the original
and
, even in my 20s, still leaves me feeling rattled and uncomfortable. The grotesque environments, often brutal difficulty, and nightmarish worlds are rarely seen together in other games.
And
is no exception.
In what simply looks like cashing in on nostalgia,
takes what
did well and sweeps it off to the side to prioritise outright questionable features:
• Areas are no longer divided into individual screens, but are mostly long scrolling expanses. While it works great for action platformers like
, not being able to see so far ahead and not knowing enemy boundaries really isn't a great idea for stealth games.
• Movement is no longer gridded, even though it's a platformer. In the originals, right moves you a step right, hop makes you leap three spaces, and even ending a run makes you skid two spaces. This time, all movement is totally free, making the simple act of deactivating a mine a precision act of gently tiptoeing and hoping you don't hit the collision box.
• Environments are cartoonish and excessive, with the punchy and dark environments flat out replaced with overwhelming noise. Where a distant barrel conveyer could be seen now there's a sprawling expanse with miles of vehicles heading into giant furnaces. Sneaking between shadows is now standing vents puffing out black smoke that prevent you from telling where characters are or even if you're hidden. Simple metallic walls and drills splattered in gore are now cartoonish replacements.
• Lack of tension. Escaping from the original RuptureFarms was tense and terrifying, as the game refused to hold your hand and instead left you to try and escape the nightmare as best you can. The remake is a frustrating exercise in unsatisfying trial and error, through a flashy cartoon factory that is ugly in all the wrong ways.
Honestly, it's worth saving your money. The orginal has terrible controller support, screws your aspect ratio, and trying to play on a computer made after 2005 tends to make the cutscenes screwy, but even then you won't be stooping this low.

First of all, thank you, Hyeson, for providing me with a free key to your game. :D
Undertaker's is a fun and cute little business management tycoon game by indie developer Hyeson.   You buy your funeral supplies and sell them to the bereaved who come to you to bury their loved ones.  Some have specific things they want, other's don't care, but all have a budget.  Eventually, you'll be able to build your own buildings to produce your caskets, headstones, and flowers, but will still need to purchase the materials from the local store.  The hand drawn graphics are colorful and charming.
There are just a couple of things that I find frustrating about the game, but they're not deal breakers for me, they just make it a bit harder.  The first one is the lack of storage. You start with 9 spaces and can build a storage building for $2000, but it only gives you an additional 9 spaces for a total of 18.  I've not seen anyway to upgrade that amount.  Items DO NOT stack, so if you buy 5 cherry wood caskets, it takes up 5 spaces.  If you buy one of every prebuilt funeral item (casket, headstone, and flower), there are 15 total, so that leaves you with 3 spaces.  But once you get your production buildings built, from what I've seen, they use the same storage space, so you'll be doing some inventory juggling.   Luckily, you can leave your customer waiting while you run to the store if they REALLY want something in particular and you don't have it.  Keep in mind, that sometimes, what you might want is NOT in stock and if you don't give them what they want, you can't complete the contract.  There is no negotiating for something else.
The other issue is the graveyard plot/trash mechanic.  You start off with 18 plots.  Once someone is buried there, they're there for 10  years (each game day is actually one year).  You get the cost of the plot in rent each year.  After 10 years, the plot is freed up for another dearly departed.  There are more zones you can purchase for burials.   If you don't have a plot available, your only option is offering to toss the dearly departed into the trash, which most customers don't take kindly to!  You lose reputation for suggesting it.  So, if you don't have a plot availabel, you have to kick them out, which results in more reputation loss.  If your repuation gets too low, you lose.  It would have been nice to see this handled a bit differently, such as sell them what they want and then secretly try and dump them in the trash (mini game of some sort) and try to not get caught.  But, this situation may be intended as part of the juggling/management that you need to do.
Overall, the game is enjoyable and I do like it.  I recommend it if you like business management tycoon games.  I'll be continuing to play it, trying to build all my buildings, fill up every plot in the graveyard, and see how much cash I can amass!

Let me start by saying that Oddworld is and will stay my favourite franchise ever, but only Oddysee and Exoddus, not the others in 3D. The reason I don't like them is the same reason I don't like New 'n' Tasty : it is not the same in 3D.
I know that Munch's Oddysee and Stranger's Wrath are not meant to be like Exoddus or Oddysee, but the 3D universe in those 2 games didn't really fit for me.
I think that the main thing that made me love Oddworld in the first place when I was a kid is the universe made out of boards. Each boards were unique in their own way (by the colours, what's happening in the background...) and even though I was so damn hyped for New 'n' Tasty, at the end I am truly disappointed. I am disappointed because this is not the same at all. The principle of boards disappeared, the sounds are totally not the same (I don't feel the magic in Abe enchantment anymore, and Scrabs sounds weird...), some scenes that were beautiful for me are so much different now, the gameplay is not the same with this 3D universe...
I kind of lost all the landmarks I had while playing the original, and I thought I would need a lot to lose them because I can't remember how many times I've done the Oddysee (on PS1, on PC, on PSP...), but I sure know some parts of the game by heart.
Now, I'm not saying that New 'n' Tasty is bad in itself, that they didn't put any effort in it. The textures are great, the lighting is impressive, the background is rich, the Mudokon's voices are funny (not Abe)... but for me, the 1997 version is way above.
I'm sorry if I sound like an elitist (especially with my profile picture) in some way, but I had so much hype for this remake and I kind of feel let down because it's too different from the original. It's not the same magic that in Oddysee, not the same gameplay (because the boards are gone. In the orignal, you could hide from a slig just by running from a board to the other).
I truly love Oddworld, I can confirm that this game made me love video games, but I can't love this remake and I have read that some people are exactly like me. I'm happy that they have done it though, because it allow people who didn't know about Abe to go on an adventure with him.
Should you buy this game ? Yeah you should, it is a well made platforms game.
