This game is an excellent, though fairly simple shooter. At least at first glance. Based on the omni-directional shooting mechanics of Descent, this game has you placed in a wheel-like, radial cyberspace map filled with allies and enemies. The story is also very uncomplicated, to the degree where I'm not too aware of what it is. It seems that you are battling malware entities in a cyberspace environment, but I could be very wrong.
The keystone for this game is the combat, which is very good. There are a wide variety of weapons, ships, and special modules for said ships, making customization nicely nuanced for your speedy little fighter whizzing across the map. There is a strightforward progression system, where your engines, shields, and fuel expand continually through mods you gain from killing enemies. It's very old-school Diablo in its loot-based gameplay: Kill enemeis, get upgrades, kill bigger enemies.
The combat ranges from flying through cyber-tunnels while blasting enemies with a lightning gun to engaging with intense dogfights with four or more foes in enclosed, contsantly shifting arenas. It feels excellent, and the game tracks your stats with every inevitable death, allowing you to track your skill as well. The ships UI is also really cool, letting you customize it to a very fine degree. Also, you can chnage your ships, and the environment's colours any time you want. That had to be mentioned.
The flaws are few, and given this game's early-access status, still potentially resolvable. First, the lone map, though generates the locations of bases and "cities" with every load, can get repetitive rather quickly. More maps, or a larger map, would go a long way to making this game last much, much longer. Secondly, having more missions, goals, tasks and objectives in between the awsome combat could help elongate the experience too. Misisons do exist, yes, but they are few and far between, and I had trouble finding them.
To recap:
The game has an exccelent visual style, excellent combat and progressions, decent sound design and insane levels of customization.
However, the lone map and few objectives make the game feel a tad empty, though both could be fixed over time with little problems.
Overall, This game is awsome, and deserves way more attention than it's getting.
EDIT: The map scenario isn't too bad when you consider the arena challenges, after playing some more.

I found this game a refreshing change from all the clichéd games around. It's an interesting change to the way you have to solve puzzles.
The biggest criticism I have is with the level design.
In a game that relies on you to solve puzzles by thinking them through logically, there are many times when the only way to proceed is by taking a leap of faith into the unknown and hoping that you land on something. Unfortunately, if you make the wrong decision, you invariably die and have to start the level all over again.
This tends to get very frustrating because there's no skill in pure dumb luck, so you end up repeating the level until you just happen to make the right guess.
If the level designers could eliminate all these "leaps of faith", this game would become much more enjoyable.

I felt that there was a lesson to take from playing this game. "Just because it's free to play does not mean that it's worth your time." I had some hopes for this. I admit platform games are not my favorite, but I grew up with Sonic the Hedgehog and liked the idea of color manipulation. However, this game only left me frustrated and happy that I thrived through it. My first issue is with having my fingers cramped up at 'z', 'x', 'c', and 'v' over the space bar so to jump. I couldn't quite get around to developing an instinct for which key goes to which button, and I figured that I could get the option to rearrange the key, yet no such option was available. I stuck with it to the end more so for the review so that I could have something more insightful than "this game sucked".
The character seems to possess the ability to effective ignore an obstacle of a specific color and I do mean ignore. This accounts for mobile and quasi-living obstacles. Some of them simply change colors on you so that the moment you think you don't have to deal with it, you do. More importantly, it's still there. Sure it behaves as though it's absolutely gone while it's color is select, yet the moment that you change the color, it's back the same as ever. This means that you cannot take on any opponents. None.
The story line. It's around somewhere. They definitely start you out with one, but the only evidence that you have one throughout the game is random one-lines or complete sentences with lots of "they" whoever "they" are suppose to be, and "it" whatever the "it" is that the "they" did to cause whatever wraith of un-described. What that in mind, you receive no notice that you're even going anywhere. I never thought that I would actually ask for a cut-scene or more but this needed something to indicate character development. Who are you playing as. Just some vampire I guess. Fangs. Fedora, tall lanky body, and a dark trench coat seems to point in that general direction. Why does he care? I don't even know what he's trying to stop, or why he even cares about a world wide light out of the world. Not only are we lead to believe that he's a vampire, but he wears blindfolds throughout the entire game. He probably doesn't see with his eyes anyways to begin with, so how is a sudden lights out going to hurt him? Did he have a loved one? Do people actually mean anything to him than food? I also feel that the games mechanics faltered in what elements could be taken advantage of such as the hat. Whenever you die mid-air you're left free falling horizontally with the character holding onto the fedora. Just let the fedora fly off. If someone is dead, there's no way that the fedora would be so much in their mind that their hand reflectively holds the hat in place.
The fact that the game instantly saves for you is both a good thing and obnoxious. I don't mind having to start all the way back at the beginning as punishment for obviously not getting use to the controls. If I'm having trouble with that then I might genuinely have to start from the beginning to refresh and re-familiarize myself with the functions. I died countless times in game and that had been part of my frustration and what relieves part of that is that there's no way you can know where to go unless you die on that level once you get maybe 5 stages into the game.
I feel that covers it, if anyone disagrees or feels that I missed something feel free to comment, because I might have missed something. I didn't bother to do any note taking through my game play experience.

This game is no longer wretchedly awful as it was at release about a year or so ago. Even if the legion of fanboi's who supported its development at the time, swore up and down, violently confronting anyone who didn't join their blind, fantatical praises that it was the best thing since sliced bread. It no longer feels like a half baked, rushed tech demo developed by Iceland's CCP with a hacked on multiplayer element.
It feels more like the Divinity RPG games that came before it. Years before it. The reason? It finally -knows what it is- and functions well enough. The initial amateur hour rushed development elements seem mostly tended to. There are issues and echoes of old school gaming, and not the good variety. To list them all out would be hair splitting however. A tiny UI issue here, a mild graphical glitch there and so on.
If this game is missing one critical thing it is a true character level view point that can be played from full time, be it 1st person or 3rd person. See KOTOR's camera view options for reference. Yet critically, i suppose that's personal taste and not an outright fault of the game.
In closure before buying this game, be extremely sure you know what you're buying into. Personally i still loathe this game. If i could have a steam refund tomorrow i'd take it in a heartbeat. But it's not a bad game any longer. If you understand what the game is, buy it, play it with a friend and enjoy. It's finally worth a look.

Tick rate is too slow for the game to be exciting to watch like it is in the crazy sped-up promo videos, which are very misleading to how the game actually plays. Instead of the 10 moves a second you see in the videos, the official server runs at more like one tick every 4 seconds.

Note: I am not associated with the developers in any way, I've just been playing a lot recently.
Screeps is a game for programmers.
But it is possible for someone without any previous programming experience to learn it with enough dedication, though I recommend at least learning some basics of programming/JavaScript from somewhere like codecademy first. And try the free tutorial before you buy the game (I am still running code that started out based on the tutorial code, 2 months later).
The game has deceptively simple visuals, but a lot of increasingly complex systems that you gain access to as you progress within the game, providing interesting challenges for your programming ability. How complex it ends up getting depends in part on how much of it you end up wanting to automate. Pretty much anything you can do, you can get your code to do for you.
Like most programming, you are going to want to look things up in the documentation, which covers all the different elements your code can interact with, and has examples for most functions.
I also highly recommend joining the excellent and helpful community on the Slack chat.
I recommend that new players spawn in the green novice areas around the edges of the map, so that any combat you get into is at least with someone of relatively similar power to you, instead of getting wiped out on a whim by an established player. You will want to get a tower and some defensive code up by the time your safe mode ends, and remember you can activate another safe mode from your controller if you have any available.
Your main progression is your continued improvement of your code, most players respawn a few times.
As for what I think of the game, I love it!
This game has really reignited and fueled my passion for programming unlike anything before it.
The learning curve may be a bit steep, but that is part of the fun/challenge.
The community is great, and I spend a lot of time chatting on Slack and helping people with their questions and figuring out problems with their code. :) (helping people is optional of course, but I enjoy doing that)
The developers are pretty responsive, and are continuing to improve the game, and fix issues that may be raised by the players.
I find the subscription model fairly reasonable, and it is even possible to fund your subscription through your in game activities if you are reasonably good/developed. Though some choose to take on the additional optimization challenge of playing without a subscription and the additional limitations that gives.
Buying the game on steam also gives access to private servers, which is an alternative/additional way to play the game, and is a good place to test your code before deploying it to the live server.
Edit: A year later, I'm still really enjoying this game. It continues to get updates, and even some pull requests submitted by players get merged. Recently I have been enjoying implementing more complete automation in my code to participate in community-arranged bot arenas where players spawn into a small map with all interaction disabled except for the initial code upload, and the code has to do everything on its own and try to beat the other players' code at what ever the goal may be for the round. :D

2/15/17 Update: I can no longer recommend this game. $20 is a bad price for this, but might be worthwile at $5 - $10. Fun game, but Forced and Gauntlet offer a lot more value at the moment compared to Overlord: FOE. Also, devs have killed any support. Game has Day 1 bugs still that they never addressed (only local host/player 1 gets progress saved and some network issues).
First, this is not Overlord 3 or a Diablo-like game. This is a hack 'n slash, multiplayer game. The tech tree and item loot are minimal at best, but on par with a Gauntlet style game. If you like Gauntlet style games, I recommend waiting for a sale on Overlord: FOE. Both Forced and Gauntlet offer better 4-player co-op for the price point.
I'd say this game most closely resembles Gauntlet: Dark Legacy. This game has the same humor as the previous Overlord games, BUT the minions take a big step back in regards to their utility. If your absolute favorite feature of Overlord was being a Minion Master, then you will not like the minions here.
However, if your favorite part of the Overlord series was killing people/animals/elves/etc. with your Overlord and being followed by a parade of tiny, evil cheerleaders, then you should enjoy this. Think of the minions as the pet familiars from Gauntlet: Dark Legacy. They are somewhat useful, but don't contribute very well to the game.
About the minions: Minion spawners are more frequent than the single-player Overlord titles, to compensate for how expendable they are in Fellowship of Evil. Browns are the only minions I keep out around me, as they stay near you and attack like the previous Brown minions (deal and take damage for you). Blues can only heal you, they do not deal any damage. Greens are better melee damage-dealers against foes, but disappear from your Minion control after they have slain their target. Reds have been completely changed. They are no longer ranged fireball-casters; instead, they are suicidal bombers that run in a straight line towards whatever you were facing and self-destruct on impact.
The game took me roughly 7 hours to beat, in a 2-player co-op session. I doubt the number of players would change this completion time.
Your Overlord has 4 attacks to play with: light attack (fast dps), heavy attack (slow strike with knockback), a charged heavy attack, and a special attack (strongest attack but tires your character for a few seconds and has a cooldown).
Each Netherghul character plays different from each other in how their attacks work, but all aren't different enough to get attached to any of them.
Final review (TL;DR) : This is a great couch co-op game to play with controllers (I use Xbox 360). If you only played the Overlord games to be an evil Pikmin Minion Master, then this is not a game for you. If you like multiplayer, hack 'n slash games in the style of Gauntlet, then you might enjoy this spin-off of the Overlord franchise.

As stated by the producers: It's not Overlord III, and should not be expected to be similar to previous Overlord games, which is exactly what a majority of the people are whining about.
That being said, I'm not saying it doesn't have its issues and whatnot, but it still pulls its own weight to a certain degree to be a decent game.
Pros:
+ Storyline is good
+ Dialogue is still as snappy as ever
+ You're not stuck with one type of character; you can pick from 4 which suits your playstyle
+ The environment has been rendered quite nicely. I especially liked the town with the zombies.
+ You can kill your allies with humorous results
Neutral:
+ New minion system. While this is one of the cons for many, I file this under Neutral due to simply the mechanic balancing itself out; as an intended multiplayer game, 4 people swarming minions tactically will be too overpowered. Instead, what they've done is decrease minion control while also making minions more cheap and expendable, in the form of easily harvestable cubes (and can be spammed in Cryos' case if you have the right weapon)
+ New Hub layout
+ Lack of a map
+ The style of how the characters look like haven't changed, and are still as cartoony as ever while managing to look serious at the same time.
Cons:
+ Still fairly buggy at certain points, but I do find it funny when one of the enemy soldiers just suddenly float off without any absolute reason
+ Not a lot of enemy unit variation so far: Standard Soldier, Big Sword Soldier, Shield and Sword Soldier, and different elemental Mage variations. But then, the previous Overlords did have this too.
+ Not a lot of attacks per character; we could do with more spells.
Overall, it's a decent enough game to play if you're a fan of the Overlord series for the storyline, but if you're looking for similar Overlord gameplay I'd advise waiting for Overlord III. For new players yet to be introduced to Overlord, it should prove decently playable if one can get hooked on the story.

I'd recommend this game...with quite a lot of reservations.  The TL;DR version?  If you're a fan of the Overlord world and story, buy it during a sale.  If you're like me and you really, really like Overlord and need your smashing sheepies fix, then maaaaaybe it's worth buying now.  YMMV.
First, the good.  The story is funny, with Pratchett's humor put to good use.  The minions are entertaining, as always, and the dialogue is cheeky and fun.  The world designs (especially the Netherdeep hub) are quite neat.  The Netherghul designs are fantastic, and it's fun to be able to play a variety of characters.  It seems obvious that Codemasters put a lot of love into the game.  The minion upgrades you can purchase were also pretty useful and unique compared to the previous games.  The voice acting is fantastic, and I really liked the new characters as a whole.  It was pretty cool to see the remnants of the old Overlord's empire, too, such as statues of the minion wolf riders and Fay.  The animated cut scenes had a really interesting wood-cut kind of style, which was unique and kind of neat to see in a video game.
Gameplay wise, I liked the fact that you could "carry" minions in reserve and use them when you needed them, rather than have them trail along behind you, inevitably getting lost or stuck somewhere.  The minion hammer was really useful.  I loved the fact that my blues could heal me.  The gameplay mechanics with the Golden was also pretty interesting, and it was very satisfying to finally be able to burn it back.
And now...unfortunately...on to the bad.  I really, really wanted to love this game whole-heartedly.  I love Diablo, and I absolutely love the Overlord universe.  It would have been really, really easy for this game to win me over.  The fact that it didn't really speaks to its flaws.
First of all, it's very, very short.  I was hoping for something a bit meatier.  I was hoping for more backstory.  The ending was very ambiguous, and while they're obviously setting up for a sequel or DLC of some kind, I'm just not sure if that's going to happen based on all the bad reviews.
The game play feels, as others have mentioned, very "clunky".  You're not able to recall your minions, which leads to a lot of them running off and getting themselves killed, which is annoying.  You also can't sweep them or plant them on a marker.  Yes, I know, you're a Netherghul, not an Overlord, but story shouldn't get in the way of good gameplay.  The reds were suicidal, which yes, was the point, but also massively, massively stupid.  They seemed to have no targeted mechanic whatsoever.  I'd point them at an enemy, and I'd be a *few* degrees off, and they'd go sweeping past the enemy to blow themselves up against the wall.  Ranged units would have been much more helpful, to be honest.
The attacks and battles are quite frankly boring, and this is coming from someone who once lost fifteen pounds over a summer spent playing Diablo.  I was hoping for a spell tree that I could use to do different attacks, at the very least.  The battles last too long, the enemy attacks lack variety, and the whole time I spent fighting just felt like a grind.
The traps were irritating.  I had trouble controlling my character (Inferna) using a keyboard and mouse, and often found myself blundering into something I thought I'd gotten out of the way of.  The time trials were honestly just really annoying, and didn't serve much purpose.
I would also have liked it if I'd been able to visit previously-conquered stages again to gather more loot.  The game was linear to a fault.  I'm terrible at maps, and often have trouble finding my way around complex stages, and even I found the linear nature of the game to be dull.
I don't regret my purchase...I love the Overlord universe, and I love Rhianna Pratchett's writing.  That said, I feel like this game had so much potential, and could have been so much more.  Hopefully the next installment will be (if not a proper Overlord 3!) a bit better...and cheaper.

Below you'll find both a written and video impression on the game.
NeonXSZ takes flight gameplay into an open cyber punk world, with tons of upgrades and customization. The game can be challenging, with a robust amount of upgrades for the player to experiment with for a long long time. With excellent flight controls, exciting dog fights, and lots to explore, NeonXSZ is a game with a ton of "meat" and depth. There is a small learning curve to get over, but once you get the hang of it, the game opens up. NeonXSZ is also incredibly impressive with buttons on your ship's hud actually functional, to the overall visual and sound effects. I felt as though I was in the ship piloting my enemies destruction.
The Aesthetics and sound is well suited to the overall theme of the game. Though the textures are rather basic, the lighting, design, and style makes up for it. The sound of course is full of beeps and boops, and robot voices, as you would expect from a cyber punk game. It's done well, and works with the game's theme.
To sum how the game plays out in a nut shell, you go around, exploring your environment, hunting down enemy ships, blow them up, and collect their valuable. Then you take those valuable and make new upgrades for your ship. Rinse, find new space stations, and repeat. The game is quite grindy, and I would even argue that it's designed around the grind. People like myself who don't mind the grind as long as it's well designed will welcome this, but those who are more sensitive to grindy games, it's worth your time to do a little more research before committing to a purchase.
Overall NeonXSZ is an enjoyable exploratory flight RPG, with lots of customization. Even though it is pretty grindy in nature, the game is deep and versatile enough to hold my attention. I recommend NeonXSZ
Pros:
- Deep and varied amounts of customization
- Challenging gameplay
- Easy to understand flight controls
- Very immersive
- Has that "addictive" quality
- Cyber punk your brains out
Cons:
- Lack of graphical options
- Lack of side features
- People sensitive to grinds may be put off

There have been quite a few attempts at recreating the 6DoF formula as of late, and none of them really do it for me with their attempts to over-complicate the core elements and make things "modern".
is the first game of its kind in a long time to really hook me in with its potpourri of elements that we know are fun and addictive, and have withstood the test of time. It combines the freedom of movement and perspective of
and the edge-of-your-seat twitch action of
or
with the addictive leveling and persistent loot of increasing rarity of an ARPG like
, all combining for what is absolutely the most addictive and replayable shooter of any kind in years.
The game places you into a vast and complex computer mainframe with a very open and free-form approach to exploration. There's a great in-depth tutorial to read at your own pace getting you into the motions, but you are more-or-less thrown into this world blind with no hand-holding involved and a great deal of content to discover on your own accord. While there is no hand-holding the game does not ever feel tedious or hard to get into even for the newest of players, as you are always being guided the right way thanks to the Appropriate Hostile function which will highlight on your map the best spot to hit next for your newest dose of weapons and upgrades. This makes exploration of the almost overwhelmingly large Station quick and accessible, as you are still lost but pointed in the right direction.
The objective of
is discovery and total domination, as you vie for control and power over the various hubs spread throughout the world in all-out territorial war. Despite the open-ended form of gameplay,
is ridiculously easy to get into for players of any skill level thanks to an approachable and flexible learning curve. This is gained through giving the player full control over which enemies and hubs they tackle on, giving the ability to scan hostiles for their level before deciding to engage or flee. As you fight higher leveled enemies you start to feel more confident, you'll return to bases with your hard-earned loot and become even stronger leading to newer and more challenging areas. The amount of content you have to explore is massive and already offers a minimum of 30 hours of feature complete gameplay with more to come.
I had already drifted around the computerized world for a few good hours exploring, taking on low leveled hostiles, and playing around with early equipment before I discovered the challenge arenas at the center of the Station in a massive sphere. This is where♥♥♥♥♥♥gets serious. Instead of analyzing and picking off single similarly leveled foes like in the main world, I was suddenly thrust into a large and complex series of challenging areas being bombarded by difficult but manageable enemies. Each lovingly detailed room was blocked off by a shield and every one of these persistent opposing ships had to be exterminated diligently in an intense and explosive battle in order to advance. The loot you get is of game-changing quality (depending on the level of the arena) and in high quantities, and defeating an arena allows you to claim territory on that Station for an allied side of your choosing.
Leveling up your tech level isn't as simple as gaining experience points or grinding mobs of same-y enemies like in other games, in
leveling up is determined by the quality of parts you're discovering and equipping. In order to grow strong enough to take on tougher foes, you'll need to outfit your ship with a select choice of higher leveled upgrades all dependent on the players' own playstyle. The range of different parts and the effect they have on how the game feels and plays is insane, and allows you to be anything from a slow, hulking tank with tons of shields and firepower to an agile and lightning-quick smaller ship that avoids all damage with ninja-like reflexes in the hands of the sharp-witted.
Weapons are another integral part of
and just like upgrades add a huge layer of player customization and personal technique to how combat is approached. You start with the standard pea-shooter in classic shootemup fashion, but are quickly presented with plenty of choices in how you take on your combatants. For the nimble and stealthy pilots who like to sneak up and get in close there's the Lightning Gun which packs a serious punch but drains your energy like crazy, and a Flak Cannon which spreads out for a wide shot but shreds anything in its direct path. For the sniper-minded you have the Railgun which requires the the most accuracy but disintegrates enemy ships almost instantaneously. There's Inferno Guns for taking your foes down in a firey blaze and Laser Cannons that deliver a shocking blast of energy from afar, all weapons I've discovered only in my first 25 hours of gametime and with more to be found. The arsenal in
is remarkable, and will keep the most seasoned action veteran captivated for hours.
The heavy mechanical beats and ambient dronings of the background music do an excellent job of keeping you engaged in the atmosphere of the cybernetic and neon-tinted highways around you. In general the sound design to me is very engrossing with its muffled sound effects and outside explosions giving you the feeling of truly being inside the cockpit. Some people might not be huge fans of the ships speaking A.I. system dubbed 'Betty', but personally I feel it adds to the retrofuture aesthetics of the setting and the authenticity of the interactive and immersive cockpit you become all too familiar with. Perhaps with just a bit more variation in speech, Betty would be welcomed by more players.

If you're looking for lightning-quick combat, huge series of interconnected arenas, and ludicrous amounts of customization then look no further,
is your next addiction. It's an already feature complete game with many hours of solid content, loads of replayability, and an amazing amount of polish. The games' state in Early Access is merely a sign of the tremendous amount of additional potential for an already mind-blowing shooter experience.

All this and much more is possible for you and your enemies to use! Then there are all the weapons and ship hulls that also each require it's own tricks, loadouts and playstyles. You don't need to qommit to one style throughout the game, instead you can switch at any time! You carry all your weapons at once and can switch out your whole loadout as often as you want even while on a hunt for loot deep in enemy territory, just dock in a garage!
If you don't feel like hunting down enemies in the open world and setting your own goals then you can now fly to the world hub/fighting center sphere (figurativly and literally) where there are prescripted challenge arenas with moving parts and level design handcrafted for the enemy waves and the loadout you meet in there.  Each level is a very unique experience and might require you to learn new tactics. The reward for completing the arenas is good enough that you can progress through the game mostly by these linear levels if you want to, or you can just ignore them whenever you feel like flying through the open world.
Though the challange arenas are a part of the open world and you can fly from them to any other place without any loading screens at all. Whenever you want to do something you fly to the appropriate place and just do it, you never have to select what to do from a level select screen.
NeonXSZ feels great, looks great, is fun and addictive. They aim, move, utilize tactics and gadgets based on their personality and they design different loadouts. Since they are playing by the same rules as you it's possible to even learn from them and pick up tactics that they use.
If you like 6DOF FPS games that requires some skill (though there's at least 4 ways to adjust the difficulty to suit anyone) and want to avoid boring grind then this is The Game! Fun from the start!

This game mashes together every single thing classic Nintendo RPGs offered back in the 90s - Good story, cool and nemorable characters, amazing humor with tons of references and spin-offs on modern culture, simple and responsive controls mixed together with a unique evoland twist.
The game puts you in place of a character that wakes up without any memories of himself and involves a plot that includes time-travel via magic artifacts. The unique twist is that the overall graphic style changes depending on the "time-period" you travel to.
So, when the story takes you into the plot past - the game becomes a 8-bit nintendo classic, as you move through the story so does the graphics. From 8bit, to 16bit all the way to modern 3D. The game feels as some of the best Nintendo titles like Zelda and Super Mario (you switch game types from birds-view RPG to 2D action sidescrollers to 3D arcade throughout the game).
Game's soundtrack accompanies the action perfectly which makes Evoland a real gem of a game.
Tl;dr - It's funny, it's cute, it's quirky, it's FUN!

Wow, just... wow. I liked the first Evoland (even it was short and every two second you had to fight), but Evoland 2 is something totally different. One of the most unique gaming experience in recent years and much more polished than the first game. Evoland 2 is mostly a zelda-like game, but it is also so much more. Evoland 2 is a really unique game. In fact, it is several types of games all rolled into one adventure. The majority of the game plays like Zelda, with some elements taken from Secret of Mana and Final Fantasy.
But then there's a part where you fight a boss like Megaman, or traverse a dungeon in Bomberman fashion. Or how about the part where you lead an army like a Fire Emblem game? There's even a gem-based game thrown into the mix.
The point is: this is a game that EVERY gamer can enjoy. There are references everywhere, the story is fun and interesting, the characters are likable and there are engaging ways to power up your party.
Evoland was a great game, but this sequel is heaps and heaps better in every way. I highly recommend this game for just about anyone, but especially if you grew up with NES, SNES or even early PS2 RPG's. You will absolutely love it.

Don't let Divinity: Original Sin's grim title and poster fool you -- this is a charming CRPG that is absolutely bursting with personality. The dialog and situations are often hilarious, and the turnbased combat -- while challenging -- is ridiculously fun. Your choices matter and the game frequently encourages you to really think about consequences and how to solve problems, whether it be a troublesome NPC that you'd prefer not to murder or a pesky foe that just won't go down.
Regarding the new Enhanced Edition -- I'm still fairly early into it, but it already feels like a major improvement over the original release. Between the extra polishing, performance improvements, and new features, the game feels much more "finished". In particular, I'm seriously loving the new dual-wielding mechanic, and wands are a blast to use. I could be wrong, but I think I've even encountered new quests that I never ran into in the original edition.
A couple of quick notes for new players: Leveling is much rarer than is typical of modern RPGs. You'll want to give careful consideration to how you allocate your skill and talent points, because a few bad choices early on can really screw you over and may even warrant starting over. If you find yourself wanting to improve a skill but the game won't let you, then that means you don't have enough skill points; you'll need to level up once or twice more to increase your pool of points. (Unfortunately, the game doesn't explain this at all.)
Also, if you're playing with a mouse and the camera controls feel clunky/uncooperative, I recommend enabling edge panning in the Options menu.
Other reviewers have done a better job at detailing the many cool aspects of the game (and I've yet to mess around with co-op mode), but if you're looking for a challenging RPG that's brimming with fun stuff to do and still manages to never get stale, then this is definitely for you.

An excellent fencing game with the perfect formula for fast, free, and strategic dueling the likes of which haven’t been seen since the Jedi Knight series.
Nidhogg is a side-scrolling 2D fencing game about beating enemies in 1 versus 1 duels.
First, the narrative: There isn’t one. You are plopped down in the center of a long arena with your foe and each of you has the goal of reaching the opposite side to be eaten by the glorious worm Nidhogg. The campaign consists of something like ten opponents you must defeat in different arenas, each more difficult than the last. The game gives you the time it took to defeat each one, and your “score” is the sum of all ten. There is also multiplayer, which functions in the same way as singleplayer.
Second, graphics. The game is very low fidelity, with jittery pixel art that seems to vibrate. Despite this, it has a very suitable style with interesting color schemes and level scenery. I would never call it beautiful, but it is attractive and psychedelic, very much suiting a game about fighting to offer yourself to a divine eumetazoan.
Third, combat. This is the strongest aspect of the game and the driver behind my recommendation. At the start of the level, you and your opponent drop down into the center armed with rapiers and ready to fence. You can hold your sword out at three levels (low, middle, and high). If you and the enemy are within range and your swords are at different levels, he who stabs first kills the other. Only one stab is needed to kill the player or the opponent. If the swords are held at the same level when an attack is made, you clash swords. If one fencer raises his sword up into the bottom of a sword on a higher level, he disarms his opponent, sending the sword flying backwards. Unarmed players can melee fight, but they have reduced range and can no longer instakill. Additionally, players may divekick or swipekick to knock opponents over, who must press the “up” button to stand back up. If a character snaps the neck of a fallen player before they get up, it’s an instant kill even unarmed. Characters may also throw their sword an infinite distance, though it is easy to block if armed and facing the proper direction. Killed characters have to wait a few seconds to respawn in the path of the opponent, during which that opponent may run towards their goal end. The level is long enough that, from the center out, a player may have to kill their opponent three or four times to get to the end even if they are never killed. You can jump over the opponent and make a break for the other end, but they can impale you in the air, throw a sword in your back, or simply respawn in front of you if you get too far ahead. There are also opportunities to do flips off walls, hang on ledges, and perform other impressive maneuvers if one knows what they’re doing.
This game is a lot of fun. Each fight keeps you on the edge of your chair, and you will have times where you are just outside the edge of the map before being beaten all the way to your own side. Things change quickly and the enemy is often just as skilled and smart as you are. This one is a deep deep discount game. It plays kind of like a janky greenlight game with good enviromental art.
Positives:
Minions loot things. And they they occasionally say, 'For youuuuu' as they run back to give you your loot.
Art of the caves generally very good. The golden is very well done as well.
Minions smash things like small picket fences automatically.
Puzzles are not really puzzles, since this a combat game. But the puzzles and races do a good job of breaking up the tedious combat.
Negatives:
Combat:
Waves of enemies that teleport in from nowhere.
Played Malady first. Very boring. Basic strategy was use charged heavy attack over and over again. No reason to play an entire game holding and releasing the heavy attack button until the waves of enemies are dead.
The amazing decision of players not being able to hold down the quick attack button to shoot continuously. You have to press it every single time.
Teleport has no visible cooldown, you just have to guess. There is a noticeable cooldown as well, probably to prevent a huge speed advantage in the race sections vs warriors.
Tried Fire warrior. Looked lukewarm in the lobby. Lethargic sword swings with weak visual effects and animations (except for their ultimate).
In general, enemies, minions and you don't look like you are fighting. More like you are brushing up against each other and one person falls down when their hp runs out.
Words to summarise combat: Floaty, Weak, Slow, Repetitive
Minions:
There is no way to track how many minions you have, or what the maximum amount of summoned minions is. You can only see how many minions in reserve you have.
Minions are very stupid. Especially around the 'golden', an instant death field. Minion AI do not perceive the golden and will walk right into it at the drop of a hat.
Also, since enemies are not effected by the golden, minions will try to attack enemies in there and die immediately.
This is an issue, since you can't easily restore your minions.
Minions need colour coordinated 'power cubes' to summon. This makes no sense. It makes you slow down and waste time, since the primary method of acquiring cubes is to attack a cube fountain. Which usually spits out random colour cubes, so you hit it and hit it until the correct colours have come out, then you run around collecting the cubes. A better method would have players attack it once and it fills up all the colours it can distribute. Then put some in combat limiter on it if the fountain exists in a combat area.
The only boon to the cube system is enemies can drop them, bolstering your supply mid combat. But maybe a different system of restoring minion charges over time if they are under a specific quantity might have worked better. You could have even added more upgrades around maintaining a minimum supply of minions.
Red minions are suicide bombers, so they are less desirable to upgrade as they only work once. Also, you have to aim them, since apparently they do not have eyes. They damage explosion is weak looking and weak in terms of damage.
Green minions are the same, except single target.
This leaves the bread and butter of all fantasy combat. The brown minions who are the tanks and blue minions who are the healers (you are the damage of the holy trinity).
Red minions should at least attack normally, and then explode when they die. They should probably attract enemies to attack them as well, since they are so brightly coloured.
I don't know what role greens have. There is an upgrade to make them stick around after one attack, but I already have brown minions who do that without upgrading.
Upgrades are very bare bones:
There are 10 minion upgrade levels per colour. However only 2 or 3 stray from + 1 minion cube or increased damage/healing.
I guess at least there are multiple colour minions you get to choose to spend points on, so your character will have a different balance of minion strengths.
It is a small relief that you can switch between the different minion hives by only visiting one. Both sets of hives are sort of out of the way.
There are many (8?) hero upgrades. But they are all minor. And every second level is the ever boring "more health and damage" upgrade.
Since there isn't any point in splitting your resources between heros, because you can only play one at a time, you should not have to spend resources to upgrade. There is game mechanic called an xp bar. And when you pick up crystals, it can fill that bar and you can level up automatically.
XP would be superior to you running to an out of the way shrine in the lobby area to spend crystals on a linear underwhelming upgrades track and then finding out you don't have enough crystals when you get to the shrine.
Weapons upgrades are more interesting, since they all appear to be sidegrades. Everything except one or two costs 50 [weapon currency].
There is an issue of choice though. There are 10 or so different weapons with apparently equal power. Do you get the one that sets people on fire or the one that poisons? Who knows? Is there any point? Both will do damage right?
Lobby:
The lobby is basically a menu system. So why wasn't it a menu system?
You can't sit in any of the seats, customise the look of the lair (that I have seen) or interact with anything other than popping up menus.
As an example. The game Warframe has your personal spaceship act as a menu system, but each 'menu' is only a few steps away. You can go from the pilot seat to the loadout console in 3 seconds. And EVEN THEN, you can use the main menu to teleport from console to console.
Bugs:
Minions get stuck behind fight doors after you enter. You have to move away from the door to teleport them to you.
Enemies get stuck outside the fight door (only happened once, possibly a goldened minion?). You can still kill them though, just hard to find them.
Minor bugs such as enemies floating up into the sky beyond the camera. With minions following them up to attack. Quite funny.
After playing single player, the continue option does not appear on the main menu until you restart the game. Made me think I lost all progress.
After loading my save, picked a different character. Story progress carried over between characters but there are no statues to upgrade my new character from.

Evoland 2 took the interesting mechanical concept of the original and made it a fully full game. It's delightfully clever, both in the ways that it combines and references classic gaming forms and IPs, and in its own story that it has to tell. Every mechanic of the original game was improved on, and the story is compelling, deep, and stands above the average time travel story in terms of intricacy. It makes excellent use of foreshadowing, and is rife with Easter Eggs. Despite what the glitched play time says here, I've probably put at least 30 hours into the game. The Review:
Color Symphony is an interesting puzzler where you platform throughout the 50 levels using your ability to change the world's 'color', You switch between cream, blue and green to get through the somewhat challenging puzzling levels. Along the way you will encounter, crows, dogs and cogs which are all trying to take you down in their spectrum of colours.
While the game is good and rather intuitive, it also suffers from messy hitbox detection, sometimes cogs or birds will hit you even though there is a gap between you. Some of the puzzles require you to completely guess the distance you travel, which will lead to many deaths. What is also aggravating is when you switch colours if any part of your body is midway through a newly 'appearing' platform you will die and have to restart the level again. Some of the later levels require a lot of precision jumps in enclosed areas which can mean this gets aggravating.
Overall it is a fun and pretty unique platformer, not too long as it's only an hour or two in length. Especially as it's free to play it's at least worth a go if you are looking for a quick puzzler.
Not bad for a free game.

Hello everybody, Shaun Meyers (Kyo Akiara) here from Universal Gaming Reviews to bring you an overview of our review for The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing: Final Cut. If you'd like to read our full in-depth review for the game, you can find it here:
The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing: Final Cut is the culmination of all 3 original releases in the Van Helsing series, combining them into one humongous experience.
We've had the opportunity to experience each game over the years since the first incarnation back in 2012 and it's been a great journey seeing the series evolve over the years.
The game is beautifully detailed, especially with the high-resolution textures, but it also features a very entertaining, and often humorous, storyline.
There's a ton of great features to discover ranging from the extensive list of unlockable skills, the tower defense mini-game that spawned the excellent game DeathTrap, and numerous other features.
The game isn't without it's share of bugs though and many of them surface in multiplayer and while trying to play with some friends the game often crashed for them in the middle of the game (It didn't do this for myself, but it hindered playability greatly) and the requirement for a neocore account to play online may be a bit off-putting for some as well.
Outside of this, the single player experience is as solid as ever and have had few issues playing by myself.
An excellent starting point for those that have yet to play the series yet and the improvements over the original releases make it worthy of replay for veterans to the series as well, 8.3/10.

This is how you do a remake!
The original
was quite possibly the greatest 2D platformer of the late '90s, not to mention one of my favorite games of all time.  It was an odd duck, to be sure, but it executed every weird concept it presented with startling finesse, quickly cementing its cult status.  Abe the Mudokon couldn't fight one-on-one, or take more than a single blow before dying.  He was clumsy, fragile, flatulent, and so naive that he thought the slave position he was born into "a good job" -- until he discovered that the meat processing plant he labored for would soon be turning his species into an exciting new line of processed meat-pops.  This revelation launched Abe on an adventure full of open-ended puzzles, daring rescues of fellow Mudokons, and stealthy escapes.  What everybody remembers the most about the gameplay, though, was Abe's awesome ability to spiritually possess the gun-toting Slig guards, sending them on murderous rampages among their own kind, or using them to solve puzzles, and then exploding them into meaty chunks when their usefulness was done (whereupon Abe always emitted a chuckle as chilling as it was goofy).  I won't go into great detail regarding the setting, but the blackly humorous milieu of Oddworld earned the game just as much attention as its fine and varied mechanics; it succeeded handily as a not-too-preachy satire of corporate greed, but went further, becoming a fully fledged science-fantasy world that we all wanted to explore.
takes everything we Oddworld fans adored about the now fuzzy-looking (but still eminently playable) classic and makes it
for a whole new gaming generation.  All the classic gameplay is there, even more fun now than I remember, and what mechanical changes have been made are in the way of improvement.  Most notably, the modular movement of the original (every discrete button press resulting in a perfectly measurable step, etc.) has been replaced with a more organically flowing system; it initially makes things a little tough for even
veterans, since an accidental twitch of the stick can make Abe jab his toe into a mine, but it results in a player-character who feels as alive as the person gripping the controller.  Having to take a little extra time in mastering Abe's lifelike inertia intensified my connection to the Mudokon savior, and in turn fed my sense of immersion into Oddworld at large.  But for those who absolutely can't make the leap to organic motion (and I highly recommend you try), JAW has graciously inserted a "classic" movement option.
Graphically and aurally, this has to be the best remake I've ever seen; the in-game assets are so impressive that they outstrip the (quite impressive) cutscenes.  From the redneck-ish muttering of the Sligs to the posturing of the feral beasts to the mechanical rumble and blood-spattered steel of Rupture Farms itself, no game in the too-long dormant Oddworld series evokes such a strong sense of place.  Lorne Lanning and company are deeply passionate about their bizarre alternate universe and know just how to make it come alive!
TLDR:  Classic gameplay and setting + new organic movement system + top-notch graphics & sound = game that you should definitely play unless amazing puzzle-platformers give you seeping hives

It's rare to find a multiplayer cooperative zombie survival game that is actually free. Even though in Early Access, this game manages to shine in several different aspects, providing a light-hearted experience for most players.
At first glance, the game has rather horrid graphics (the developers said they would create HD graphics to replace them soon), a lousy soundtrack (which is actually really horrible) and a rather poor crosshair for the first-person shooter genre. It does make players' experiences really unpleasant, and furthermore, the tutorial is rather incomplete, rather teaching only basic movement, shooting and utility options. Aesthetically speaking, the game is really horrible; newcomers might be distraught as they eventually get mauled by zombies after leaving the training lab. Even shooter game veterans may be unsastified by how poor its presentation can be.
In fact, this game's potential doesn't lie in the aesthetics, though I will agree with most people that graphically speaking, it is one of the most gruesomely-looking games in this age. The soundtrack can be very distressing. While it does manage to create some dread among the players, it's generally very repetitive.... and hollow.
But once you get past the visual and audio barriers, and be patient to learn the way of zombie survival (the hard way) through one to two hours of community server gameplay, you'll find that the game is forgiving to both newcomers and veterans alike in the gameplay area, while also providing suitable challenges to allow players to enjoy the game even further. With realistic zombie movements, and headshot mechanics, playing this game makes you feel as if you're actually in the mission. Speaking of missions, the game currently offers 2 game modes (more will be implemented by the developers in the future), which are objective, in which you have to plant a C4 in a specific area like in CS:GO, and then escape out of the bombsite like James Bond, and survival, in which you have to endure multiple waves of zombie hordes. Guaranteed, it might take long for you to finish a mission, but it never loses its fun when you play with a bunch of random people online, or your friends.
You see, this game promotes multiplayer cooperation to a large extent: going lone wolf won't get you far. You have to rely on your team's multiple abilities (depending on which classes they choose) to break through, and this also requires some form of communication, like Skyping with friends, or sending voice lines to randoms. There will always be frustration when playing online multiplayer, but it's definitely a much more welcoming experience than playing alone.
The spotlight of this game is how the team has to work together, each with different (possibly, as the class limit is 2) utilities: The Pointsman is your all-rounded fast shooter; The Assault holds an inaccurate but powerful assault rifle; The Sniper takes down bulky targets and burns others; The Technician who can deploy a sentry; and The Support who can heal, provide armor and ammo. With a coordinated cooperated team, all may stand against the mightiest of the mindless monsters; but without the communication and teamwork, one can barely get past, heavily wounded.
The game's potential is where how it's core gameplay is so amazing. It's no random fan-made game that has terrible graphics, audio, gameplay or whatnot. In the near future, the developers have promised to upgrade graphics massively and even allow classes to change to alternate weapons.
Don't judge a book by it's cover. Don't judge a game by it's graphics. It's worth playing and supporting, and I'm willing to support this booming seed. When the next big update comes, the game will prove all negative reviews wrong. Of course, that's if the developers can fix the large bugs first (personally please don't fix them, they're fun, which is the other reason why I support the game).

Literally the single best shooter I have ever played. The netcode is horrendous, and the game is Peer2Peer, resulting in a frankly hilarious amount of lag, but the lag compensation usually makes up for the massive lapses in connection that occur. There are also a few unbalanced weapons, which have a tendency to break the game if people use them en masse. The campaign doesn't tell much of a story, which is disappointing, but to be expected from a game where the focus is chainsword enemas. The leveling system is reminiscent (as in, a carbon copy of) the old Call of Duty games, which is aggravating because if you want to use a specific weapon you have to play for a significant period of time before you get it.
But aside from that the game is beautiful. The game plays like one would expect a Space Marine game to play; EVERYONE is overpowered! Assault/Raptor marines can traverse the entire map in a few short bursts from their jump packs, Tactical marines can level an entire room with some careful thinking and the right weapons, and Devestators can murderize anything that they can see in a matter of seconds. To this end, Space Marine is one of the few "Super Soldier" games that makes you feel like you are an actual Super Soldier. The combat is stellar, tactics and careful thinking pay greater dividends than being able to shoot well; this might be because everyone has a gigantic hitbox and the aim assist is practically palpable, but for me that's a good thing. Sneaking around your enemy and doing hit-and-run attacks are far more effective then just waltzing into a room and using your 10-years honed aiming skills to get 1337 360 headshots on everybody.
Overall, this is a thinking man's shooter. I played it for about a week before I was able to pick that up, and realized that even with the most basic gear and perks (I still use the starting weapons), I could steamroll the entirety of the opposition with a few deft maneuvers. The campaign is more of an after-work/after-school thing, same goes for the Exterminatus gamemode; for those days when you just want to exert your views on religiously justified genocide. The multiplayer is the real gem with this game; a shooter where thinking is more important than skills.

With little story, strong gameplay, and beautiful work in music and art, this game delivers a strong package for such an unknown title. Honestly I heard nothing of it till the day it was released, and when I started playing it, I was surprised I hadn't heard of this sooner. It hit me much like Dust did when I first tried it.
A heartfelt story that will tug on heartstrings for those who like the emotion of the light story will be hit at the very start. The story is light, but very intwined with the entire game. Starting off as meek, with only able to move, you'll feel very vulnerable through the start, but as you progress, you'll start to feel truely progressing through the story. Like a castlemania game, you'll backtrack often to use your abilities to explore hidden spots you missed, but be warned, be diligant in explorations as some sections will be cut off from you as you progress, so if you're a completionist, be ready to explore every inch.
However its more than exploration, every area will keep you on your toes as elements of the place will push you to use your abilities. However, don't be discouraged by this 'Super Meatboy'-esque style, as the game has a evenly paced learning curve, and manages to keep itself challenging without going into maddeningly hard, leaving you with satisfaction for completing an area, without missing a few patches of torn out hair. There will be moments you feel every second, every motion, every direction you take matters, and to a point, its what makes the game so thrilling, only to slow down, giving you a moment to breathe so you can explore.
Audio and visually stunning, the art and music are two elements in this game that jump out at you instantly. The amount of work that went into both will grab you the moment you start. Thankfully the Devs didn't make it the only priority of the game, but they did put extra care in making it all stand out.
All in all, for the asking price, the initially unassuming game delivers the quality you want at a $20 game and perhaps a little more. Well worth the price.

Co-operative play adds a surprising amount of depth and lets you fully engage in the duo hero scenario the game is built around, being able to have two humans debate choices as an actual game mechanic, and letting you split your party into two to explore and investigate. It's really a special game, with brilliant writing and amazing depth.

This game has everything you could ever want in a sci-fi survival game. You start out crashing onto a planet in an escape pod with limited supplies to utilize in order to survive. Overtime you construct your base and explore the many interesting locations on the planets surface such as abandoned mines, fortresses, other players, abandoned research outposts, and plenty spooky facilities that you may want to take a buddy with in order to get out alive. Once you've explored your planet you can construct a ship and fly to dozens of other planets in the solar system each one offering extremely different environments than the last. You never run out of things to do in this game and that's what makes it super addictive.
The only con is that this game is really only enjoyable playing multiplayer with friends and randoms. With multiple player-made factions fighting each other it adds an interesting twist to things. Exploring with your friends is also much more fun than by yourself.
At the end of the day if you're looking for a solid cooperative survival game, this one is perfect for you.

I know this is incredibly overdue, but I put this game on the shelf to focus on Fallout 4, and a few others titles since this game is filled with enough bugs to make The Witcher 3, and Fallout 4 seem great in comparison.
Neocore Games pushed this game back twice to make it "a better experience" for us, but it's still as buggy as previous Van Helsing games.
The Great:
Gameplay:
Van Helsing has always had really great gameplay. It's the best part of the game by far. If you love games like Diablo, or Path of Exile you'll love the way this game plays. Neocore has refined the game, but made it easier then previous titles in my opinion. I had no problems steamrolling through this with my bounty hunter.
Sounds:
Everything sounds really great and that comes as no surprise because all of the Van Helsing games have amazing soundtracks, dialog, and voice acting. Van Helsing sounds great, Lady Katarina sounds great, and the supporting cast all sound great. Some of the best tunes I've heard this year has come from Van Helsing.
Graphics:
Van Helsing has always looked really good when compared to other games in it's genre. Final Cut is no different. When everything is maxed out this game looks incredible. The environments are rich with detail, and the character models look good. They're not great, but for this genre they look really good when compared to Path of Exile, and Torchlight.
The Good:
Classes:
I'll be honest here. I preferred the three original character classes over the six that we have here. The original Van Helsing class is gone. You can no longer be a hunter in this game. He's been split into three different classes and I still don't understand the decision behind it. The other two classes have also been split into multiple classes to make it seem like we have bigger, deeper classes to choose from when in reality we don't. What we have is more character classes to choose from with half of what made the the original characters so great in the first two games.
All of the classes aren't bad though. I did enjoy playing as a Bounty Hunter, but he can't compete with my old Hunter class from Van Helsing II.
Story:
If I would have never played Van Helsing III the story would have been in the great section, but Neocore dropped the ball towards the end of the game. The whole final chapter in this series is just bad. There's no other way to describe it. Van Helsing I, and II were really good games while part III is forgettable and since this game merges all of them together I was forced to experience part III all over again... or at least I would have if a gamebreaking bug didn't prevent from advancing in a quest.
There's also a lot of pacing issues with this game. Some cutscenes were removed and instead me seeing the beginning scene of Van Helsing II it just starts me off where part I ended. It was confusing because I thought I would get a cutscene.
The Bad:
Skill Tree:
I think the most important thing in a dungeon crawler is the skill tree. They can make or break the game and they don't do either of those things in this game. The skill tree here is just... meh at best. I skipped the majority of the skill tree with just about every character I played as. The skill tree here just didn't appeal to me because it was broken up between six characters. Skills that the original three classes had were split up between six characters. I don't care what excuse the devs have for this it's unacceptable. The new skill tree is a big disappointment. I'm limited in the ways I want to customize my character because half of the skills on my skill tree is completely useless.
It's Not Better Than Previous Installments:
Van Helsing I, and II are the best games in this four game series. It's only gone downhill from part II and it's a shame. I understand wanting to change your game, but changing them this much is confusing to me. Don't fix what's not broken because you risk breaking it and that's what happened here. If you want to play a great game play Van Helsing II. It's the best game in the series by far. I like the changes that are in this game, but I don't like most of the new character classes that were introduced in part III and I really don't like the new skill trees.
It Has A Ton Of Bugs:
The bug that made me quit playing this game made it impossible for me to progress on a quest. I had a level 30 something bounty hunter and I was stuck in the beginning of Van Helsing II. I refused to start a new character and I never got a fix from the devs. They actually just ignored my post on Steam. No one gave me answer so I quit and moved on to another game. When this game is firing on all cylinders it's pretty good. It's not a terrible game and I do like it more than Van Helsing III, but that's not saying much because that game is all kinds of terrible.
I don't understand how you can push a game back twice and not fix the exact same bugs that were present in your first three games.
Animations:
The gameplay in this game is great, but the animations are just bad. They feel cheap and if you can ignore that, it's hard trust me, then you'll have some fun. Don't go in expecting Diablo kinds of quality because this studio doesn't have Blizzard's wallet size.
Replay Value:
At one point I considered Van Helsing one of my favorite games to keep coming back to. That changed after part III and it's no different in the Final Cut. Once all of the bugs are fixed I know that might change, but right now it has no replay value for me at all. I couldn't even give away my extra key because no one wanted it.
The Verdict:
The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing Final Cut isn't a terrible game. It's actually pretty good if you can ignore the bugs, and the fact that it was ten times better a few years ago. If you've never played this series then you'll probably really love this game. I've been playing it since the beginning and it's changed a lot since then and not for the better. Once the bugs are fixed I'm sure that I'll enjoy it a lot more, but I doubt the skill tree will ever change and I know I'll never be able to use my level 60 hunter ever again and that still bothers me because I worked hard on that character.
6/10
For $44 this game is not worth it. Go buy Diablo III instead. You can both Diablo III and Reaper of Souls for $20 a piece.
Final Cut is an inprovement over Van Helsing III, but it's literally filled with bugs and I can't recommend this game in this condition. It was fun, but I still prefer the first two games in the series and I recommend you go check those two out instead of buying this one right now.
My verdict might change in the future once the bugs are taken care of. If you can find this game for about $20 I'll recommend checking it out because there are many games that'll give you this much content for that price, but for $44 you'll be better off buying anything else for around the same price.

It's a real-time strategy game where managing resources and units becomes more and more important. It's part of a 4X strategy game, where exploration, exploitation, and extermination are things you will have to do. It's an exercise in software engineering and problem solving.

Designing ants body parts to handle a certain task. These ants are called Creeps. The creeps only do what you tell them to (by coding their behavior).

This fantastic, post-apocalyptic RPG is two decades old at the time of writing this, and it has aged impressively well. This is a great introduction to the universe of Fallout and must have been quite an ambitious project for its time, especially given it was the first in the series. It's a solid RPG where your character's stats, words and actions have an impact on the world around you. What you choose to do or not to do, not only has an impact on the outcome of quests and how other characters react to you, but affects how the world develops after completing the game. The role-playing is accompanied by a turn-based combat system that, although not very tactical, is good enough and even rewarding at times (e.g. by critical hits and satisfying animations).
This game is also quite unforgiving. Whether this is a good thing or not probably depends on your expectations and experience with older games. I was unable enjoy this game my first time through; it wasn't until playing some other older games I developed the patience and could appreciate this one. It is highly recommended to at least have read parts of the manual (located in your local files folder of the game) before beginning your first character. You are given few directions and are expected to explore everywhere and talk to everyone in order to possibly extract hints of where to go next. This is also where some of the flaws of the game starts to show. For instance, the dialogue system does not update properly or as you'd expect. You will often read the same dialogue and choose some of the same responses in order to get further information out of a character. There are of course other things that demonstrate the age of the game, and which could be considered flaws even by the standards at the time of the initial release, but I will not bother listing them - just know it's perfectly fine to use Google.
I completed it for the first time tonight and it was just awesome to experience the game that started the whole series. I'm installing the second one immediately.

It's an interesting concept and all, but the game wasn't designed very well.
For one, the game doesn't look that good. The animations are a little dull, and a palette of 6 colors doesn't leave much room for creativity. While I understand the reason for the choice, It's just boring to look at. The colors also mean that the walls you control disappear entirely when you get rid of them, which leads to annoying and unneccesary trial and error. You know where to go, you jump, you have no reference as to where you are in the jump, you cross your fingers and bring back the walls, and you clip into the wall, dying.
The game would have worked much better if the obstacles faded out instead of disappeared.
Two, the various RNG and practically unavoidable obsticles. Like the idea of objects randomly popping in front of you, leaving you no time to react? Do you like the method to get rid of them to be randomized. This happens TONS in this game, and it is extremely annoying having to constantly die and start over to get around them. A puzzle game shouldn't have you rely on luck.
Oh, and the hitboxes kinda suck too, and there are times when you can completely skip over areas.
Three, the game expects you to be psychic. There are far too many instances of the game putting the path out of your viewing range, forcing you to jump over a put to find out where to go. There are also cases where you fall down and have to dodge blades, and again, not knowing where they are and where to land. Not. Fun.
Four, the music. 1 track, looping over and over and over. The game is far too long to have just 1 track, especially with the constant retrying that you will have to do. Same for the SFX, as you are going to have to listen to the same jump grunt every single time you jump. Very repetitive.
Five, the story. He is blind, was sent to hell or something, and now controls colors for some reason. That's pretty much it.
There are also various other issues, such as the sometimes unresponsive controls and the weird health mechanic, but those are minor issues IMO.
In the end, I think it's a good concept, but poorly executed and just not fun to play. Unless you have some fetish with the color control concept, there isn't really a reason for you to play this. I wish I could say better, but it's not a game that anyone should bother playing.

New 'n' Tasty is a very difficult yet satisfying puzzle platform which stays mostly faithful to the original Abe's Oddysee's intense slig-dodging action. Additional choices of difficulty are available, with the hardest mode being on par with the original's difficulty (which i would recommend to anyone who has played the original).
The graphics are vastly improved, although nothing special, with various flashy effects and lovely meaty mudokon deaths when you inevitably slip into a mine or roll happily into a grinder.
Movement, on the other hand, feels fairly sluggish and a noticeable delay can make the more difficult moments of the game frustrating. This is most evident during later stages of the game involving vertically moving sawblades which offer incredibly short windows for safe passage.
It's worth adding that these sawblades seem to move at an unpredictable rate when the framerate exceeds 60fps, locking the framerate to 60 fixes the issue but the obstacles are still remarkably difficult to pass due to the aforementioned movement delay.
These flaws, though, are only minor drawbacks to the experience as a whole. New 'n' Tasty conserves the original's gritty tone and enchanting charm while updating it with all the bells and whistles one has come to expect from a modern release.
Highly recommended for those who enjoyed Abe's Oddysee or fans of difficult puzzle platformers in general.

is a complete HD remake of
, a cinematic platformer originally released in 1997 for the PlayStation and PC. In this game, you play as Abe, a Mudokon slave working for RuptureFarms, the biggest meat processing plant on Oddworld. RuptureFarms is known for their delicious snacks made from live animals. One day, Abe stumbles upon a corporate meeting held by his bosses, the Glukkons, and discovers that Mudokons would soon be slaughtered and turned into another tasty treat. Our unlikely hero abandons his job and attempts to escape RuptureFarms and rescue all of his Mudokon co-workers from captivity, unknowingly fulfilling his destiny in the process.
As Abe, you must run, jump, climb, avoid enemies, and solve puzzles through many varied environments along your quest. Abe's controls are just as responsive and fluid as they were in
The game is playable with a keyboard and mouse, but I suggest using a gamepad. The original game's unique GameSpeak system has returned and it is better than ever. GameSpeak allows Abe to talk to his fellow Mudokons to help them escape the facility. However, Abe can now get multiple Mudokons to follow him at once, a feature that was first introduced in
This makes quite a few sequences in the game far less tedious to solve while not making the game too much easier. In addition to this,
has increased the number of Mudokons to save to 299, instead of the original game's 99. In order to save everyone, you will have to search high and low for the various secret areas hidden throughout RuptureFarms and beyond.
has implemented many new features to keep the gameplay fresh and more accessible for new players. Abe now has a health system and loses health whenever he is damaged, rather than instantly dying like in
To make up for this, the game now has three difficulty settings: Easy, Normal, and Hard. Easy and Normal let Abe take a bit of damage before dying, whereas Hard Mode retains the original game's one-hit death. Difficulty also affects the number of throwable items that Abe can hold at a time and how fast enemies will react in certain situations. For returning Oddworld fans, I definitely recommend Hard mode. It provides a much more challenging and rewarding experience than the lower difficulty settings. However, if this is your first time venturing through Oddworld, you may want to try out Normal before diving into Hard. Checkpoints have returned, but they appear more frequently throughout the game. Quicksaving, another feature introduced in
, has been added to
, allowing you to save anywhere at any time.
Since this is a remake, all of
's graphics and sounds have been completely remade from the ground up. The remastered soundtrack sounds great and stays very true to the original. Graphically, the game looks absolutely amazing compared to
All of the cutscenes have been updated and there are even some brand new cinematics as well. However, the look and feel of many places, specifically RuptureFarms, have been changed somewhat. Several areas in the game have been altered to look more bright and vibrant compared to
Whether you like these changes will depend on your personal preferences, but I don't really mind them. The game still has its own unique style that is nothing like any other game out there.
In short,
is an amazing game. It retains most of the elements that made
great while adding several new components to improve upon the original. If you are a fan of the
series, you are sure to enjoy this game. If you've never played an
game in your life, you should definitely give this a try. This game is worth buying at full price, so be sure to pick it up if you find it on sale.

A good game.  The single player campaign is very well made, and the whole aesthetic matches the 40k 'verse to a T.  The multiplayer is a mixed bag.  I don't do pvp much, but you can do 1 v 1 private match to gain all the perks you want so that balances.  The Co-op multiplayer is good - Exterminatus is very fun, but you need 4 people.  At present, the multiplayer pool is essentially dead.  The only way to do co-op or vs in Space Marine is to meet up with one of the dedicated 40k gaming groups (of which there are a good number) and schedule with them, or to have personal friends to play with.  PUG grouping is non-existant nowadays.

You can play as the freaking Adeptus Astartes, what is not to love? Though, seriously, I am friggin' sick of the goddamn Ultramarines...
Beyond that, the story is forgettable and the characters flat. Single Player doesn't really have much to offer aside from the beauty of WH40k rendered with loving detail. The grandness of the universe is well represented; everything is huge, and even the towering Astartes feel small.
The multiplayer, both cooperative and adversarial, is much more interesting than the SP.
Exterminatus, though very flawed, is a fun take on Wave Survival/"Horde Mode". With more polish and care, it coud have stolen the show, but as is, it remains obviously what it is: a tacked on extra.
Versus, on the other hand, it extremely fun. Yes, Peer 2 Peer across oceans is lagtastic. Yes, it could use some balance. Yes, the maps are stale after 2 years. But it's still the most fun I have in gaming, and it's the only game that lets me play as the Adeptus Astartes. I can't help but love it.
In all, the game is a wonderful first step for Relic into the Third Person Shooter genre, and is amazing for the studio's first ever action game, but whether or not they will continue this trend under SEGA remains to be seen...
It should be noted that the animation quality in Space Marine is top notch, AAA, 5 star, all that and bag of chips. As a person who appreciates aesthetics in motion (i.e. good animations), I find it an absolute joy to watch.
