DISCLAIMER: I'm currently a lv.98 constructor and still playing, and this review is compatible with 1.0.4, namely the most recent patch on Nov.24. Several reminders to new players or someone who wants to play this game, you could treat this review as an incomplete guide. I'll update this review after each big patch as long as I'm still playing this game, you may want to keep an eye on this:
1. There are bugs, not major ones, but don't expect this is a bug-free game already.
2. Officially 50 hours game play in campaign mode, but actually for me, it's around 20 hrs (100% map exploration, monster respawn disabled, casual difficulty)
3. You should expect your characters are weak before lv.40, at least for some classes.
4. Put gold in your stash whenever possible, you'll need tons of golds in end-game (5m for a set piece, just give you a general idea), and you'll lose 10% of golds you CARRY IN YOUR BAG when you die.
5. Use essences whenever possible, you can keep both the gear and essence when you take essence out.
6. Unbalanced dmg between melee and ranged attacks for monsters, be careful. (fixed, see 1.0.4 EDIT2 below)
7. Keep all the epics, when you combine them, you can get level-matched epics no matter how low-level epics you used (This is useful before lv.100, not useful at all when you hit lv.100)
8. Arena gives you tons of EXPs, make sure you do it at least once a day
9. Adventure mode strategy: Do whatever missions till you get 20-success buff (300% epic drop rate), then take advantege of this buff by killing every monster in each mission (not to lose this buff by choosing the difficulty you feel comfortable with). But don't feel too upset when you lose the buff, actually you almost can't feel the difference, 300% is a small number in this game
10. You can buy keys using fate points near the trophy table, and also use five different kinds of essences to call Pegasus (Set vendor) near the trophy table
11. Fate point daily limit is a PITA, so try to finish challenges ASAP (possible reset after patch), will give you lots of fate points, but try to save them when you hit lv.100 for gold chests (see 1.0.4 EDIT3 below)
12. Buy cheap essences from vendors, because you'll need those for Chimera and Pegasus
13. Try NOT to change affixes before lv.100 (but feel free to enchant), too expensive
14. You can increase essence capacity by 20 at maximum, meaning that gears below 30 essence capacity are at disadvantage (godlike items can possibly have essence capacity beyond 50, wait to be tested)
15. Perks level is maximized at 15, Katarina is maximized at lv.60
16. You can only drop set and godlike items at lv.100 (from gold chest only, confirmed by devs)
17. Multiple characters are encouraged, because you'll see some daily quests requiring particular class to finish
18. So far in my opinion, proximity mine is the most difficulty affix to deal with, try to avoid by rerolling (costs 25 fate points)
19. Forget gamble before lv.100, not worth it, forge your epics instead
20. There are at least two types of monsters or skills you should be careful: one, the female mage's ice rain; two, the death circle of champions or elites with certain affix. Sorry for the confusion, but you'll recognize them. (may not apply to 1.0.4, haven't got a chance to test)
21. The best mission in adventure mode: boss hunt, because you could possibly kill the same elite and champions three times at most
22. Something about Chimera: before lv.7, choose the one with the most exps, after lv.7, choose lowest one (forget the name), FYI, you'll get her around Chapter 5, I believe
23. Yellow and below quality items are completely useless unless you treat them as a gold source in end game
24. As I mentioned before, epic drop rate doesn't help much, but you can see a significant difference when you choose a mission with three affixes
25. You should expect the leveling speed slow down after lv.95 and of course also after lv.100
As a final note, the drop for godlike and set items has been fixed in 1.0.4 possibly, but I personally expect further change to that, also there's a mod in discussion tab that potentially would fix this issue outright, but I haven't had a chance to have a try
26. In adventure mode, you can stack at most five daily missions.
Solid game overall, but don't expect too much advancement from VH 1-2-3

*UPDATE* I've read the corerules and found something about the fumble rule + some miscalculations in the review... This is a hastily written 'review' *UPDATE*
The real reason why I’m writing this review is because of the hit chance percentages. EVERYBODY COMPLAINS ABOUT THIS. For everybody who doesn’t know The Dark Eye ruleset this is indeed very confusing. A 100% chance of succesfully hitting someone  doesn’t give you a 100% chance of doing actual damage, and I think the percentages are misleading, also, the rules aren’t explained anywhere and the rolls aren’t shown in the battlelog. I don’t really know how you can have 100% for certain in the game.
I’m going to explain it a little bit with the actual rolls of the core rules. This is by memory and to be honest I haven’t played the actual P&P game so far. But I have read the core rules some month’s ago:
THE ROLLS BEHIND COMBAT:
You want to hit an enemy with your sword! You have two actions. One is moving toward the enemy, the other one is swinging with your sword trying to hit him. Your PC has an attack value of lets say 8. Your Rapier has an Attack Value of +1. The Rapier’s special attribute is agility, for every 3 points in agility above 8 you get a +1. You Agility is 14. 14-8= 6. You get a +2 to hit. This means you have to throw lower than 11 with you 20 sided die.
This means you have 55% chance to hit. (This would be a starting level character btw).
If you hit, the following happens.
Your enemy can parry or dodge with his parry or dodge skill. His parry skill is 13. Which is calculated by his DEX. Now he can use every 3 points above a base value 8 for agility. He has an agility of 12. 12-8= 4. So he gets a +1. Which is 14. Now he tries to parry with a short weapon against a medium weapon. He recieves -2 on his parry. He has to roll lower than 12. He has a chance of 60% to parry the weapon.
He can also dodge the attack. A Dodge is your agility divided by 2. 12/2= 6. But he has a skill body control which gives him +1. He has a dodge of 7. Which is too low to use.
You have 55% to hit and the defender 60% chance to defend himself. Which gives you less then 33% in total to hit. But the game will show 55%.
I think the percentages shown ingame are your own hit percentages. Because you can’t know your enemies stats.
THE FUMBLE RULE (IN TDE IT'S CALLED A BOTCH )
Now why still miss when a 100% hit percentage is shown? Two reasons. Probably the game rounds up. Lets say if you have to roll lower than a 19. But if your enemy lies on the ground, this gives you an advantage: making your *chance* 100% to hit: this can even go over 20. Lets say you have to roll lower than 23 to hit. This means that if you roll a 19 + a random disadvantage of + 2 making a 21 still is a hit. But the fumble rule still applies. If you roll a 20 it’s still an instant fumble (or botch as they call it in TDE, fumble is a DnD term) and norally in the P&P the gamemaster may get creative and invents a random failure. An archer misses on 19-20 rolls. So there is always a 5%-10% chance you fumble, and a 5% chance you crit (on rolling a 1) .
(If you played Drakensang, the first game wich uses the same DSA ruleset, there you can even fumble on picking up a flower.)
So in the original P&P, lets say you are in a house with a low ceiling. Your enemy lies unconscious before you on the ground. Let’s kill him in coldblood! You swing your sword full of rage. Outgame you have to roll a d20; let’s say that everything except a 20 hits. You’re unlucky: you roll a 20. The DM decides what happens: your swing your sword above your head in full rage and your sword gets stuck in the ceiling.
ABOUT THE GAME

Really encouraging that in this age of preorders, DLC, season passes, and microtransactions, a studio takes the time to greatly improve their game and releases it for free!
I played ~30 hr in the original version. It was quite good, but did have a few gaps here and there -- for example, crafting was very unintuitive. (Not even asking for hand holding, but I couldn't figure it out even after reading guides.)
EE polishes these rough edges to a shine, and adds in a bunch of new stuff, for example voiceovers of just about everything, and TACTICIAN MODE, which is a higher difficulty level for combat. And it isn't just giving all enemies double health or something cheesy like that; they actually went through and redid the mechanics of all the fights. I'm only about 4 hours into EE, but so far this mode seems fairly challenging, but not over the top. Most fights require some thought, and then tend to leave my party with about 1/4 health. In regular mode, most fights are pretty trivial if you've figured out a few tricks, and I was often able to get past them with >50% health on everyone without really trying. There's also Honor mode, which is Tactician mode + permanent death. I'm not crazy enough for that one, but it's nice to know Larien is keeping the ultra-hardcore players in mind, and is willing to spend time on something only a small percentage of very dedicated players will fully experience.
Looking forward to playing this a lot more and eventually getting the tactician mode achievement!

This was a wonderful little game.  It felt very reminiscent of those harder levels from older platformers that you just can't seem to beat.  It took me roughly an hour and a half to beat it while dying over and over again.   Now here's a bit of a summary:
Pros:
That wonderful platformer feel
Innovative game mechanics (filters)
Engaging Introduction
Short and sweet
Sufficient challenge
Interesting music choice
Cons:
individual levels rely on trial and error on occasion (gears changing colors after a jump)
Surprise deaths (traps appear out of nowhere right near the exit of a particularly difficult level)
Story becomes less-engaging and grows vague as the game progresses (I was personally hoping for the story to blossom a bit further)
Hit-boxes (my biggest complaint, you're controlling a ragdoll half the time)
Jumping (occasionally couldn't double jump in the air after switching filters)
As someone who has formerly worked for a video game company, a bit of advice to the creators would be to clean up the hit boxes and jumping, and maintain patterns with color changing objects (e.g. maintain the same colors for surprise traps regardless of the current filter).  Seeing as though this game is free however, I can honestly say that it was a fun experience, and that I'll be recommending it to each of my friends.  I'll also be looking forward to any other games that these guys are working on.

At first when I saw this game I thought to myself "Wow, it's a new twist to puzzle platformers".
Then I regret downloading it.
First of all, it's not that the game is hard. Just incredibly cheap when it comes to killing you off and wasting your time. Here are some of the issues I have with this game.
1. The birds that chase you around have far too much range, some even chased me halfway across the map before leaving me alone.
2. Problems with the edge. Try walking off an edge and jumping. More than half the time, you will fall off instead of jumping. Now you might think to yourself. Well, that's not so bad, just jump before you get to the edge. WRONG. There are so many jumps in this game that REQUIRE you to jump right before you leave a platform, and so many of these are right near the door, so it's doubly frustrating when you pass a difficult part only to fall off the edge. Which brings us to....#3.
3. There are no checkpoints within each level. Just passed an incredibly difficult part of the puzzle and almost there? Whoops you accidentally slipped off the edge instead of jumping. Now restart the whole goddamn thing.
4. No idea which direction you're supposed to go. There are no indicators for you to have any idea where to go. No map whatsoever. So if you happen to stand on a platform with nothing in sight, you usually have to jump in a random direction to see if there's anything there and you have to do it for ALL THREE COLOURS. Usually resulting in your death in finding the next platform. This results in an endless cycle of death and rebirth just to find the next step.
5. Changing colours while something (usually a platform) is behind your character will result in your death. And there are so many damned "puzzles" involving this, you're certain to die several times over just for one platform.
6. There are no indicators that there might be platforms in a certain colour. This game would have been so much better if they put a border/outline around areas with platforms. At least you'll know when to change colours, instead of guessing and relying on random chance.
7. The Hidden Gears. These randomly coloured gears will pop out only if you're close enough, usually placed so that you have to jump before seeing them, giving you about a 0.3 second chance to react before getting hit. Again, you have to rely on luck to be able to pass levels with these.
If you're looking for a fun platformer with some puzzles involved, you came to the wrong place.
If you're looking to do some repetitive jumping followed by constant deaths and wanna test you luck without requiring you to think or solve anything, then this is the game for you.

Remasters and remakes are nothing new in video games. In fact, it’s been quite the popular trend dating back to the God of War HD collection for the PS3 in 2009. Since then there have been numerous and, one might say, too many remasters and remakes.
The criticism of “too many remakes, not enough new IP” is quite fair. That said, very few if any of the remasters/remakes out there show the level of care and reverence that Oddworld: New ‘n’ Tasty exhibits.
My first exposure to the Oddworld series dates back to 1997 and the release of Abe’s Oddysee. Now, while I never played the game I distinctly remember the ads in EGM and Game Pro. Along with Soul Reaver no other game during that time had such striking and wonderful ads. I saw a dingy and strange world that looked unlike anything I had seen before, and the prerendered backgrounds looked breathtakingly realistic. The first time I actually got my hands on an Oddworld game was the wonderful Stranger’s Wrath HD. The world-building and unique characters stuck out as something derived from a fever dream and the setting was unlike anything I had seen before. When New ‘n’ Tasty was announced I knew I had to jump back in to the franchise.
Playing New ‘n’ Tasty for the first time was quite a joy and I see why this franchise (especially the first two) are so beloved, it’s smart and inventive puzzle platforming. You play as Abe, the bungling unlikely hero, out to rescue all of your fellow Mudokon’s and overthrow the evil Rupture Farms. Oddworld is a dangerous place and Abe must use his brain, not his brawn, to solve puzzles. The levels are thoughtfully designed and provide a sense of accomplishment upon clearing a room. Enemies can kill you at the drop of a hat so patience is best used instead of trying to brute force a puzzle.  Luckily, you have the ability to quicksave anywhere in the game and reload just as fast which makes getting shot by a Slig much more tolerable.
As far as the quality of the remaster, many of the levels appear to be a faithful reimagining with some small tweaks here and there. The game itself looks quite stunning and I found myself pausing when presented with beautiful background vistas to enjoy the view. This is not a simple coat of paint but rather a complete rebuilding of the first game, quite an undertaking but one that seems to be well worth it. The excessive bloom and lens flare may distract some but I quite enjoyed the overall aesthetic of the game and it seemed to keep the grungy, lived-in feel of the original.
As a platformer and mechanics go, the fairs pretty well but is not without its faults. The jump button in particular seemed to be a hair off in some spots resulting in a frustrating death. This small bit of latency (although not always present) can undermine great level design and layout when I push a button and Abe doesn’t react accordingly. Luckily these control issues are not ever present and only rear their ugly head every so often.
Oddworld: New ‘n’ tasty is an excellent jumping off point for those looking to get into the series and what should be good nostalgia trip for fans of the originals. With the next game, Soulstorm, in the works it’s good to see that we will be getting more out of the Oddworld series as it truly is one of gaming’s most unique and bizarre settings.

I played through the original Evoland, and it enjoyed the 3-4 hour experience. I was expecting this to be a little bit longer, but I was caught by just how large this game really is - I put 25 hours in and ended up at 90% completion.
This plays with genres and eras of gaming to a significant degree, as you pass through three distinctive time periods (eventually being able to switch almost at will) to complete the era-spanning story.  It features many of the classic RPG tropes, for both good and ill (the lack of a quest tracking system is the biggest weakness to my mind).  That part's good.  It also includes as many as a dozen other genres in smaller or larger aspects (including a card mini-game that's pretty good).  That variety is both good and bad - if you're not well versed in all of them, you may get stuck for a while trying to get past the Match-3 or the turn-Based strategy sections. And the vertical SHMUP section has some slowdown issues that made it pretty hard to finish.  But that's the only real weakness - for fans of gaming in general, this is a surprisingly good, surprisingly large game.

if you enjoyed chrono trigger, the first evoland, and video games in general then you will absolutely love this game!
I will start by saying it is much bigger and more difficult than the first game. It is a chrono trigger like game taking place across multiple time periods - and the graphics change according to the time period you are in.
You will encounter multiple types of game styles throughout the game - it is mainly an Hack n Slash (sort of Zelda-ish) but it features (but not limited to) Fighting, ATB Battle, Bullet Hell, and Megaman battles.
There are three difficulty levels. I am playing the Arcade (normal) difficulty and it is quite difficult at times. Many of the bosses can be unforgiving - but there is a strategy to them all.
The atmosphere and music is also a huge plus. There's one area you get to go to which you'll wish you could have access to in real life.

Evoland 2 is an amalgamation of countless genres and game mechanics throughout video game history. The issue is, it has no time to make any of those gameplay loops
or
. It's a mediocre platformer, a barebones RPG, it's a Donkey Kong clone for all of about 15 minutes, it's 8-bit and then it's 16-bit and finally 3D. Yes, it's all of those things and more, and yes I played it for nearly 18 hours but - I never felt like I was playing a great rendition of any of those genres or any of the games it was trying to emulate.
The turn based RPG part of the game is so easy because it has no time to introduce items or spells that it gives you them all at once and its "difficulty" comes from the screen flashing every 2 seconds and when the screen is dark you have 100% miss chance. These are the shortcuts Evoland 2 makes. It becomes tedious and repetitive. I had mixed feelings about Evoland 1 because I saw a lot of references and ideas but it had no time to expand on them. I went into Evoland 2 expecting it to be more fleshed-out and engaging but instead it just adds 30 new ideas, each with a run-time of about 10 minutes to an hour. It reminds me of those 40-in-1 game packs where you get a bunch of average games and you're reminded - "Hm, I could probably be playing one really good game that knows what it wants to be".
I know why it has such good reviews; it's very polished, it has some really great music, as well as a lot of neat references. But for every fun 30 min shoot em up section, there's an hour long awful Bomberman section or a 40 min epilepsy inducing RPG section.
Evoland 2 is a game that tries to be too many things and excels at none of them. It looks and sounds great and it can be wonderfully nostalgic but eventually becomes tedious and run-on. I almost always try to 100% games like this but it just started to wear at my patience, traversing between eras was taking longer than the actual gameplay sections and I was seeing nothing new or interesting in the end-game, other than Donkey Kong inspired platforming and a Bejewelled section that I didn't care for.

The Good: Addictive 2D platforming at its finest, charming visuals and audio, responsive controls, great level design
The Bad: Can be very frustrating in later levels, only one audio track, casual gamers may quite early on
Rhythm games may not be all the rage anymore the unique ones really stick out. You can’t pick your own songs, there’s no fancy instruments, it’s just you and the controller/keyboard jumping to make a good techno beat. The idea of the game is to get through each of the three worlds through 12 levels each while jumping, kicking, and sliding your way through the level. If you get hit just once you reset back to the very beginning. While on the early levels this is fine the later ones take up to 4 minutes or more to complete so getting reset is so frustrating.
Obstacles range from blocks you have to jump over, low hanging objects to slide under, stairs that require quick taps, and even some stop to fool you like a bouncing cube which one you slide under and one you jump over. There are spring pads and other obstacles to block your path, but precise timing will be required to get all the gold blocks to get to the bonus stages which are 8 bit variations of the 16 bit/3D levels. It’s very unique, charming, and extremely addictive and fun. I am currently stuck on 1-11 and have been for weeks, but I keep going at it because I just want to play every level.
The music is pretty good and full of life despite it being the same track through each level. During parts of the level you will pick up a giant plus sign that will add tracks to the beat and it also adds to the visuals. BIT.TRIP is really a game for casual players and hardcore platformers who miss the days of the 16/8 bit era. The game has brilliant level design that adds a lot of challenge while still being manageable. I haven’t really played a 2D platformer this addictive in years.
The visuals are stunning with wonderful 16 bit to 3D translation and the game has a wide color palette that sticks to the 16 bit and 8 bit era. Everything is made of blocks, but is built in 3D and can really be a mind trip some times especially when you first start playing. Don’t let the hard levels keep you from playing because being able to play the later levels is rewarding and challenging. I highly recommend this game to any 2D platformer or even for someone just looking for a fun arcade game.
--Score: 8.5/10

Really encouraging that in this age of preorders, DLC, season passes, and microtransactions, a studio takes the time to greatly improve their game and releases it for free!
I played ~30 hr in the original version. It was quite good, but did have a few gaps here and there -- for example, crafting was very unintuitive. (Not even asking for hand holding, but I couldn't figure it out even after reading guides.)
EE polishes these rough edges to a shine, and adds in a bunch of new stuff, for example voiceovers of just about everything, and TACTICIAN MODE, which is a higher difficulty level for combat. And it isn't just giving all enemies double health or something cheesy like that; they actually went through and redid the mechanics of all the fights. I'm only about 4 hours into EE, but so far this mode seems fairly challenging, but not over the top. Most fights require some thought, and then tend to leave my party with about 1/4 health. In regular mode, most fights are pretty trivial if you've figured out a few tricks, and I was often able to get past them with >50% health on everyone without really trying. There's also Honor mode, which is Tactician mode + permanent death. I'm not crazy enough for that one, but it's nice to know Larien is keeping the ultra-hardcore players in mind, and is willing to spend time on something only a small percentage of very dedicated players will fully experience.
Looking forward to playing this a lot more and eventually getting the tactician mode achievement!

This opinion is based on the singleplayer player vs AI campaign. I haven't played it with friends yet, but if I do I will update the review telling my experience with it. If you want a quick review: don't buy this game for the singleplayer: it's buggy, unrewarding, unsatisfying and extremely unfair and irritating.
The first 40 minutes of this game completely fascinated me. It was fun, enjoyable, and the AI difficulty was correct.
But, as I was winning the rounds and making progress in the singleplayer campaign, the difficulty started to be extremely annoying. You know when you're playing mario kart, and you're in first place, and suddenly, eight frickin' blue shells come along, a couple of bombs explode near you and you're hit by a guy who has the rainbow star, and all this happens just before you reach the finish line? Well, that's the way I describe the level of difficulty that this game takes after you beat the first 5 or 6 levels of the singleplayer. It's horrible. The AI starts doing the strangest things, you can't do annything, and best of all, when you die, the respawns are awful! The thing is, when the player who is winning gets to the end of the screen, he triggers an invisible switch that makes the next screen appear, and that happens even if the other player is alive and could kill the player, so that way you can skip all the encounters by jumping over your opponent and not getting hit in the process. I personally don't do it because it takes all the fun in fencing, but the AI uses this strategy ALL THE TIME, and that's what pisses me off most, because when the AI kills you, you want to kill it so that you can stop it from advancing more and eventually winning, so you try to kill the dude but the ♥♥♥♥ing computer just keeps jumping over you and you can't do anything.
The core mechanics are great, I find a lot of depth in them, and there are a lot of strategies that could be useful, but don't  buy this game for the singleplayer. It has three maps in that mode, they don't change at all, so that's not much. There is one song in each map, so due to the many times that you'll die you will eventually get tired of them.
It's buggy and lags constantly, even though my pc is more than capable to run it perfectly (gtx980, 8 ram, i76700k), for example, if the player and the AI die at the same time, the screen starts shaking and it won't stop until one of them dies again.
So, in conclusion, this game has a lot of potential, and I hope they do a better job in Nidhogg 2, I hope in the second game they polish a lot of the problems that this game has and that they add more content. But most importantly, they ought to improve the learning and difficulty curves.
Again, I have not played the multiplayer, and probably it's fun to play with friends.

Color Symphony is... okay. Given a bit of polish, maybe a little bit of difficulty added, a graphics overhaul, maybe change the story a little bit (read: start story from scratch), and this would be something I'd expect to see somewhere like Armor Games, New Grounds, or Miniclip. As it is, the game has a plot that doesn't make sense, graphics and story that try to come off as edgy (and fail, hence aforementioned graphics overhaul), and a soundtrack that doesn't suit the game. On the other hand, the controls are simple and easy to master for the most part, and the colour change concept is actually pretty clever.
However, it could have been implemented a little bit better. Enemies are reasonably easy to dodge, and if you hit one, you simply have to avoid it until your health regenerates, reducing the difficulty level. the erasure of multiple colours is confusing, and not needed after that tutorial level. There isn't a life system, so you can start from the start of the level as many times as you want. It also takes ages for the character to recover after being hit. Also, falling off screen is insta-death, which is annoying, as I feel like it should teleport you back to where you fell off, and reduce your health, although that would still be a slap on the wrist due to the regenerating health.
So, in other words, if I was developing the game, I would not have released it yet. The price of the game is an accurate reflection of how enjoyable it is (not very, due to rather quick boredom onset). As such, feel free to have a go, but don't be dissapointed when you get bored as I did.
Also, as a side note to the devs: I don't exactly know how you came up with the name of "Color Symphony", but the symphony part doesn't exacly fit the game.

When I played Quake for the first time I can't really say that I fell in love with it at first sight. I guess it's because I was expecting something more "realistic" like Wolfenstein (yeah, I know, at least for the most part of it). Either way, that was because so far I never had the experience of playing anything online. Back in the day I had this friend who eventually convinced me to give it a try. After I started, it didn't take long for me to get hooked on it. Time passed by and someday Quake II was released. Then again, when I tried for the first time I felt kinda disappointed with the game and can't deny that I still feel somehow like that after all those years (I guess it's because I missed that "medieval environment" touch from the first one). Anyway, when I first heard of Quake III, I didn't quite know what I should expect. I just read about the premise that the game was developed to be focused on the multiplayer experience. The irony was that although this title had exactly that concept in mind, that was the only one that I never had the chance to play with other people. Hmm what is there to say? For me it felt like a polished version of Quake II's multiplayer and later it wasn't hard to compare it with Unreal Tournament (which I won't deny that I liked better). Besides that, back then there were some really interesting mods involving the game's engine, like for example "Bid for Power", which had some DBZ characters and levels to play on. Overall, it's not a bad game, you can even play it casually if you're not in the mood to go through a whole set of matches.

Honestly one of, if not the best 3rd person shooter I have played in a while.  To any fans of the Warhammer 40,000 (WH40K) universe this is the action game you have always wanted.  To all fans of the "Over powered super soldier in sapce"  Kneel before the first Space Marines.  the WH40k Space Marines are literaly demi-gods geneticly engeneered super soldiers made by the God Emporer of Mankind.  The game series has been around for 20+ years so technicly everyone else is copying them.
This is the first real action game that holds decent weight to it and so it does take a lot of game play elements from other action games. At first glance that seems like ripping off Gears of War, but again WH40K is the great grand daddy of Gears...  That being said, the game is great.  The combat is bloody, fast, and very in your face.  Your armor is literaly covered in blood the more mele kills you perform, and you will do that a lot.  The visuals of the game perfectly represent the WH40K universe.  With the Vaulting Towers and foundries of an Imperial Forge world, Everything is in a hyper styalized Industrial Gothic scene.  The enemies are relentless.  Orks, in various forms and difficuties, Daemons with unholy speed and strength, and even worse Chaos Marines.  Once your brothers in arms, now they serve the dark forces of the Chaos gods...
PROs
--The graphics, its hard to over state just how good this game looks.
--Combat.  Glorius bloody combat.  In total there are 17* weapons to choose from all have thier own advantages and weakneses and fit different styles.
--The challenge, this game is hard.  WH40K is hard in general but this game tells you in the difficulty settings that you WILL die, even on easy.**
--Story line/plot.  Ill try not to post spoilers however, the story is pretty damned good.  Not the best litirary work ever but still holds it own.
--Multi-player, make your own Space Marine and Chaos Marine with near endless customization in looks.  Game modes are a bit sparce but its the classic deathmatch and Hoarde modes, as well as special DLC versions of each
*4 melee, 9 Ranged, 4 mounted Turret (these have limited ammo when removed from the turret mount)
**Remeber the Deamons I mentioned above?  They only use Melee attacks but they can teleport and on normal 3 of them can kill you in 5 seconds.  And they are some of the weaker enemies.
CONs
--Combat, Hard is fun, but this game is also unforgiving.  Ammo is spaced out regularly however you can only use each ammo box once, and they wont always fill all of your ammo reserves
--Healing, your shields regenerate if you dont get hit for a few seconds, your health can only regen if you perform a Melee execution, most enemies need to be stunned first, and the higher up enemies (garunteed 100% heal) need to take a lot of punishment before you can even stun them
--The game world/map  There is NO mini map, however the world is very linear, so transitioning from one area to the next is very dull, however these sections are often short and the figts and combat take place in large open areas
--Multi-player if you are a late comer of the game expect a lot of boots from online matches. and when you do get it, expect to be the cannon fodder.  I suggest leveling your online stats in the co-op maps first as those players are a bit more forgiving

I was a bit hesitant to start playing this, what with the very mixed reviews, but I ended up quite enjoying it in the end. Blackguards is a straightforward, simple RPG with short battles that are easy to complete in a short time frame, so that's already a plus. There's something about the setting that's nice too - the world is nicely presented and portrayed, considering the budget the game was clearly under.
The combat and RPG elements are mostly pretty entertaining. There aren't any levels, just experience points you can throw into any part of your character development more or less whenever you want, though you probably won't have points to max out everything you want for each character. My only complaint would be that there are a lot of key skills locked to certain trainers in the world who can be hard to find, and it's never clear who trains what without individually mousing over skills while visiting them.
Combat is pretty typical tactical fare, though it has the usual RNG problem of attacks with very high percentage odds seeming to miss half the time. I think this is because the game displays your base chance to hit, but doesn't factor in your opponent's chance to dodge or parry - bad interface design for sure if that's the case, and in any case it's annoying how often your attacks miss. On the other hand your opponents' attacks will miss a lot too, so it's kind of a wash. Still, basic but fun combat here. Sometimes neat stuff happens, like the time my dwarf knocked back an opponent and he flew past two of my spearmen, each of whom attacked him spontaneously using their attack of opportunity as he flew past, killing him before he stopped moving.
A note about the marketing - the game is trying to sell itself as being a dark and violent game about criminals, but it's really not much darker than any other fantasy RPG. The main characters are mostly criminals, sure, but they're more the loveable rogue type than actually repulsive people - there's a mage in particular with a hilariously over-acted voice who's really fun to listen to, but even the dreamweed-addicted elf and the arsonist dwarf are more quirky than anything. And the game's story is still a typical save-the-world plot, despite a bit of grit thrown in. Go in expecting typical fantasy with a slightly darker edge, and your expectations will be met.
All in all, a fun if not particularly remarkable RPG. Worth a look!

I have taken the time to get to know this game better so I am updating my review. First is my updated review, followed by my original, first impression, review, unedited.
Being an Oddworld fan since the original, this game was a blessing, a disappointment, and a redemption of sorts (see original review). After playing a few more hours, I have a new found appreciation for this updated game.
First, attention to the original. At first, I was put off by how many minor changes there were from the original. That said, I've increasingly noticed how many nods to the original there are. A lot of the puzzles are even the same. While the controls and the mechanics are a little different, overall, it's true to the spirit of the original.
The graphics are on part with what I would expect. Obviously the better video card you have, the better they will look.
My only real suggestion/complaint is regarding the controller. If you want the feel of the original game, use a well established controller (read: Xbox USB controller). Keyboard/mouse feel wonky for this game, and generic controller has really iffy support in game. If you have a good controller, it makes a world of difference for this game.
I am changing this to a "recommend". Coming in fresh, it's a great game. Coming in already an Oddworld fan, it takes some getting used to, but I think one will still enjoy it.
---
Original review:
I love love love the original Oddworld. It was the main reason I bought my Playstation (original) back in 1997-1998ish. I have played it through so many times and it is fantastic. The controls are great, the story is great, the challenge is great.
So fast forward a couple decades and I hear they're "remaking" Oddworld. COOL! I bet it's the same game with better graphics and maybe an expanded story.
Was I ever disappointed. They seem to have put so little thought into the controls of this game that it makes it unplayable. If you accidentally change your input device from keyboard to gamepad and you forget to bind any key, you're screwed because the keyboard just turns off and you're stuck.
Oh, and the controls are nothing like the original game. They've dumbed it down and remapped the controls into weird spots.
I wish I could even say the graphics are better, but they just don't seem a whole lot better. I mean, I know the difference between Playstation and modern PCs is a lot, but it seems like they could have done them SO much better on this game than they did.
I think if you don't have a strong background in the original game and you come at this fresh, it might be enjoyable. But if you're hoping for something that will do the original justice, you're going to be let down. It's hard for me to recommend or not based on that, so my "no" will reflect the latter.

Its one of these games that you really should play. It nails the execution of building a living and moving world that is gorgeous to look at, it has some seriously tight platforming sections that thrill without frustrating due to its clever checkpoint system.
The abilities you get to play with unlocks rapidly, and each newfound power stacks so nicely with the previous ones that by the half-point of the game you have a plethora of ways to move around and react to enemy encounters. I can praise the gameplay, atmosphere and the wordless cutscenes from the main cast of characters that evoked serious emotions.
My personal gripes with the game is that the early game feels a bit sluggish, and enemy encounters during that time are cumbersome and actually designed for the set of skills you get later on. I am also a bit saddened that there's no way for me to know more about the world itself through reading, or having spoken interactions with NPCs. Its elegant in its current form - for sure - but I would have so much wanted more nuggets of lore to spice up my immersion. I've found some scribbles on the walls though in hidden areas, so I could very well be just wrong, but they seemed inconsequential at the time I played and not really cohesive enough to form a narrative I could follow.
All in all, just get this title. You'll be challenged, you'll get a bit teary, you'll be blown away by the visuals and you'll master the gameplay intuitively using some of the most fun platforming abilities I've had the joy to use in a game of this type.

If you weren't around for the release of Quake III, you might be shocked at the furor its announcement kicked up. In the wake of heavily story-driven FPSes like Half-life, Unreal, and even Quake II, the successor of one of the biggest franchises moving to multiplayer-only was seismic. Despite the doom-saying and gnashing of teeth among series fans, Quake III proved to be an instant classic for online FPSes and helped establish the multiplayer-only genre as legitimate. But how does an online-focused classic fare nearly 20 years after the fact?
I want to make fun of Quake III's story, but it's honestly about as much of one as Quake I has. Some bunch of space ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s called the Vadrigar have been grabbing badasses from across the universe to mash together in their own little lethal playhouse. This means you can play as the venerable Doom Guy, grunting wonder Ranger from Quake I, luckiest space marine ever Bitterman from Quake II, and a bunch of cooler dudes like a neon skeleton and an eyeball on legs. There's upwards of 30 characters to choose from, but honestly after Party Skeleton they seem kinda superfluous.
They're put to good use though in the game's campaign mode. See, there actually IS a single-player mode in Quake III, but it pits you against bots across seven tiers of simulated deathmatches. Starting you out one-on-one against slow-moving opponents in small arenas, the game soon expands to fragfests with half a dozen foes across industrial complexes and eldritch hallways floating in the void. As predictable as they can become, the bots provide a solid challenge at each of their five difficulties so it's actually not a bad place for newcomers to learn the art or veterans to practice their technique.
The weapons are simple enough to come to grips with as well. I don't know why the Quake series is so content to have incredibly generic arsenals, but it makes it easy to keep track of here. You start with a standard low-damage machine gun and can locate shotguns, rocket launchers, railguns, and plasma guns around the map, each with its own color-coded ammunition. There are health and armor pickups as well, along with a few stand-by powerups like quad damage. This pickup system, common in the Quake era, makes matches more about map control than anything else and can be a welcome change from modern loadouts and class systems.
This isn't going to matter a whole lot if you can't find actual humans to play with, of course. All the games of the Quake series still have fanatics playing them but they are just that, fanatics, which means they are limited in number and absurd in skill. It's not reasonable to expect newbie-friendly servers or anything other than pros to spar with so be prepared for that if you are diving into the scene solo. On the other hand, there are few things more sublime than some classic deathmatch with your closest buddies so if you have others you can take the plunge with this is an easy sell.
Barring any graphical weirdness (which for me was remedied with disabling the Steam overlay) Quake III remains a very clean and polished experience, from the sharp if simple graphics to the tinny, growling announcer. Your weapons feel thick and threatening, the gibs gush freely, and the low electric growl of quad damage taking hold never gets old. Without a story-based singleplayer to work through this one does threaten to wear out its welcome. However, a little courage and effort diving into the online community that persists will reveal a world of wonders you might have thought died long ago.

i had a TON of fun with this game. so much so that it immediately became one of my favorite games i've played in awhile. the characters are likeable and fun, the story kept me itching to know more, constantly finding myself playing for hours on end just to get to the next part to see what i'd discover next.
the game constantly keeps things fresh, no two areas felt alike. it gets really clever with its time travel mechanic, and the graphics changing ways on how the puzzles can be solved (sylph forest, while tedious to some, was my favorite part of the game for this reason). even backtracking for the collectibles didnt feel too much like a chore, i simply was just happy to be able to walk around everywhere again. the visuals in the game are beautiful no matter which part of the game you're in. while some have nagged on the 3d models, i find the simple chibiness of them to be too adorable!
soundtrack is amazing, the ghost forest in particular. grabbing the bundle myself which came with the ost, i find myself listening to it at times because of how enjoyable it is.
story falls on its face at the end. i can't say i enjoyed the final part of the game as much as the rest, even with how fun the final boss fight was. the part leading up to the boss dragged on and on, which i feel killed a bit of the immersion for me.
because of the games gimmick of constantly changing things up, and introducing new styles of gameplay, it becomes a double edged sword. there's something for everyone. but there's also something to hate for everyone. for me personally, i HATE side scrolling beat em ups. i didn't enjoy the entire section with the pirates at all, but it was mandatory to continue on with the game.
there were times when the controls simply got frustrating (prophet fight). keep in mind while evoland 2 is also a jack of all trades, it doesn't master in any of them. it doesn't make them any less fun, (the constantly changing genre was a selling point for me after all, and i LOVED it to bits) but each minigame had its problems.
---
despite its few flaws, evoland 2 was an amazing experience that enjoyed to bits. definitely recommend this game if it even slightly interests you, you'll be pleasantly surprised.

This true and exceptional implementation of the proof of concept Evoland laid out.
If references to other games and culture are your thing, then this is a prime game for you.
It is true to its' difficulty levels across all myriad of sub-genres/games within the game that mainly come out as defined by the part of the map you are doing.
The game has three difficulty levels from a true casual experience to what would pose a reasonably difficult level for the average player. There will be times where one will want to change the difficulty, and the game will not provide a veteran of a certain genre a great challenge.
The sub-genres have been doctored in places as to provide a more casual/decently-paced experience.
There are three main time periods in which you travel between, each of which providing a different set of gameplay mechanics and character dialogue for the time period.
This game has sub-genres (a non-exhaustive list):
Bullet Hell
Street Fighter-esque (fighting game?)
Turn Based Strategy
- Early Final Fantasy Style
- Troop Movement Grid Style
Puzzles
- Match 3 (Candy Crush)
- Non-difficulty affected analyze the area and interact - Labyrinth Style and otherwise
Card Game - Collect them all dumbed down Hearthstone-esque
Retro brawler (jump kick, jump spin, punch, and well... walk across the screen)
Donkey Kong
Hack n' Slash
Forced Sidescrolling
- Runner with some combat
- Flying, shooting, avoiding
Many Boss combat situations across the generational time periods (main game styles)... albeit the final boss is the only one that spans across varying genres of gameplay.
This game is an easy 5/5 despite having a genre I dislike in it... danged match-3 candy crush saga-esque gameplay... at least they added a little flair to that.

Here is what you get from Blackguards by Daedalic Entertainment.
Linear story based
Pre-made heroes (characters)
Skill based characters (not class based)
Spell caster or non-spell caster class (all skill available except spell type for non-spell caster, spell casters have a one time use of AP(Adventurer Points) in the beginning when creating your character)
Close range weapons : Dagger, Sword/Saber, Axe/Mace, Rapier/Foil, Staves, Spears, 2-Handed Sword, 2-Handed Mace
Long range weapons : Bows, Crossbows, Throwing weapons
Left/Right hand slot : One-hand weapon + shield, Dual wield, 2-Handed wepon, or bare-fist (not recommended)
Armor slots : Head, Chest, Legs, Hands, Feet, Waist (for belt to put items usable in combat)
Attributes : Courage, Cleverness, Intuition, Charisma, Dexterity, Agility, Constitution, Strength, Vitality, Astral-energy(mana), Magic resistance [Each attribute points contribute to Base Values]
Base Values : Vitality, Attack, Parry, Dodge, Ranged combat, Initiative, Magic resistance, Astral Energy, Speed
Talents : Body-control, Will power, Perception, Traps, Street-wise, Survival, Animal Lore, Warcraft, Treat Wounds
Special Abilities : from Power Blow, Tripple Shot, Dual Wield, to Astral regeneration. 16 main abilities, 39 including sub-abilities (for example Dodge 1->Dodge 2-<Dodge 3)
The goods
1. "The complex rule system". All these stats doing all sorts of different things! A must for the sophisticated(?) nerdy RPGer.
2. Equipment changes the character outlook (even made me use a lesser equipment just for the looks that I prefered)
3. Each hero (or should I say villain) has a unique touch of personality in the story
4. Graphics/Animation of skills shows the effort of the developers.
The bads
1. Not-so-good-working "The complex rule system".
If I see a 60% hit chance, I expect to hit 6 times out of 10 tries, or 3 out of 5.
But I miss most of the time.
The game is a liar in this sense and no one likes to be lied to.
2. Limited AP (Adventurer Points) to level up your characters.
No random mobs. All encounters are pre-decided.
3. Some encounters are almost impossible if you level-up incorrectly due to the limited AP.
Makes you restart the game because you cannot go any further.
So don't think of making a jack-of-all-trades bard-like character...
Your frustration level will rise to max gauge.
4. Receive same amount of set Experience points (or Adventure Points) for each encounter, no matter how many opponents you fell. There are some encounters where you will meet infinite (respawning) mobs. If you down 1 mob and finish the objective, it will give you the same reward as downing 100 mobs before finishing the objective.
It almost felt like a puzzle game more than an RPG because some (if not most) encounters had specific methods to win easily. Other methods, not so easy or impossible (to me).
Personally, I like to farm/grind, especially when I cannot beat a certain area but not with Blackguards.
Perhaps you will survive better than me but comparing the enjoyment to the frustration level, Blackguards is not recommened.

Exceptional game within its genre. Fundementally what you'd expect from a survival/sandbox/crafting game in terms of gathering resources, managing several stats to stay healthy, crafting bases and weapons, unlocking new tech, etc. The ability to create your own vehicles, however, is really something exciting. Paired with the Steam Workshop, you can find vessels for anything, and often of any style you can imagine, allowing you to really have ships tailored to your tastes. I would recommend to anyone on the fence about this game to have a browese through the Workshop and see some of the possibilities for yourself.
Pros
-enormous possibilities: Build what you want, how you want. While there are limits on size, those limits still allow massive ships.
-Lots of replayability. The core scenarios offer a wide variety of planets to explore, but the steam workshop allows players to upload their own solar systems so you can always find a new adventure.
-Very proactive devs. The game is always growing and expanding, with new things happening every few weeks at least.
Cons
-Dependency on block-based construction can leave the game looking very primitive, despite the decent graphic options.
-Block-based construction with no options for placing objects ON blocks often limits how you can build, forcing awkward situations like needing a whole block worth of space to put a tiny sign on the side of another block.
-No way to walk around on a ship that's in motion, though the devs seem to be interested in fixing this some day.
-Planets are pretty small and are basically a 2d map wrapped around a sphere. Devs also seem interested in fixing this some day too.
-On-foot gameplay is pretty limited, with basically just the ability to walk, sprint, jump(pack), and shoot.
Consideration: The game IS still early access and is changing constantly. The devs are very proactive in both communicating with their players, and implementing changes on top of growing the game. Many things may still change, and even by next year the game could be very different. The above mentioned cons about the planet size and moving on a ship, for example, are both topics that have come up in feedback subjects from the devs, so they are aware of the issue and engage with the community about it.

TLDR: "Good game, still in development but in CONSTANT development; actually fun at the present stage; 8,5 - 9 / 10"
Of course I recommend this game. Lets try to make it simple and practical:
Graphics: they're nice. Not the cream of the crop ones, but not a pixelated retro game either. I'd say it goes around 8.5/10. The good point: easy to have a nice performance in not so powerful graphic cards (like mine, somewhat old and not fancy), and updates tends to bring some improvements here and there. The environment is fully 3D, increasing immersion. So, if you take off in a small vessel and point it to the moon, as soon as you enter orbit (no loading screens, but a slight jump lag), you'll be indeed facing the moon when you reach orbit (a different "playfield", as they call it). I once built a huge Capital Vessel (CV) in low orbit and I could really see a small sky dot when I was on planet's surface. Same goes to ingame NPCs orbital stations, which can be seen as peculiar "stars" from the planet's surface.
Gameplay: total freedom (10/10) and nice immersion (8/10). As a sandbox, this game needs you to stablish goals for yourself, since if you don't, you'll be bored once you achieve the most obvious ones (like building yourself a CV). Don't be fooled, though: getting to the point of building yourself a CV takes some time. Not a painful grind, but a good useful ingame time. This is the most obvious goal, but after achieving it, you must have a proper mindset to keep playing the game (as in every sandbox), finding yourself longterm goals: would you "pacify" your planet (there are enemy NPCs and factions), or go exploring and colonizing other planets? Would you do all ingame quests (quests are still in development, but they are there and are accessible through your UI)?
Sound: nice. Not awful, but not THAT great. General sound effects are nice, not annoying and make for a great experience. Weather effects (sound included) are beginning to be good, but still need some love (a lightining sound, specifically, is crappy and needs to be changed - it sounds like "stock sound effect from internet" -, but it is an exception to the overall picture). My rating: 7 out of 10, which is a bit poor to my standards.
Development: this is an early development game. There are frequent bug fixing updates and less common content expanding ones - less common doesn't mean "rare". The devs tend to listen to player requests and they usually ask for feedback
about bugs, balance and content "enjoyment / fun" degree (they seem not to care enough for Steam forums). Some features, though, are still kept ingame untouched, even though players have been asking for more than an year for overall improvement, like "repairing ships to blueprint" and "removing polar force fields" (walls added to keep us from going into poles since there are terrain rendering problems in their 3D spherical planets. I'd go for a 8,5/10 in this item, but only because I'm eager to see faster and more frequent development - a personal related issue, and not related to a real Devs lack of speed.
These are my impressions. Honestly, this game has charmed me out of Interstellar Rift - a very good game too, but lacking "out of ships and stations" and "planet landing" aspects. Here, you can EVA, walk on a planet surface, dig your own mine, build bases, hovercrafts, ships and Capital Vessels, forging your own adventure. I recommend.

Short review: 10/10, best game I've played in as long as I can remember
If you're like me, you have dozens of games in your Steam library that you've never played, or that you've played once and never went back to. Let me assure you right now that this game is not going to be one of those games. "Ori and the Blind Forest" is so good that you will want to keep playing even after battling a difficult sequence for five, ten, fifteen times.
I'm going to describe this game using a word I've probably never used to describe a game before: sublime.
The graphics are simply astounding. The setting of the game plays perfectly into the art style. The animations are seamless and everything controls fantastically well. The soundtrack is equally excellent. Combined with the gorgeous look of the game, there are many times during moments of relative calm where I found myself simply taking a moment to admire the fantastic atmosphere within the game that these two come together so perfectly to convey. Story wise, the game gives you exactly what you need. It doesn't bore with lengthy dialogue, it lets the actions in-game tell the story in a more powerful way. The few instances where dialogue takes place are steamlessly woven into the game itself while you continue to play, so the pace is rarely if ever broken. The gameplay matches this perfect pacing. New abilities are unlocked at well set intervals, and every time one becomes available, new paths in previously crossed zones become accessible, tempting you to return to grab that one extra powerup or discover that just out of reach cavern.
I can not give this game enough praise. If your views of the gaming industry have been disillusioned by the yearly rehashes we see in FIFA, Madden, Call of Duty, Battlefield, etc. then please please please do yourself a favor and buy this game, because it will remind you of what a wonderful game truly is. Ori and the Blind Forest is quite simply one of the best games I have ever played, and I hope you give yourself the opportunity to try it so you can discover that it reawakens an awe for games that you may have once had but lost.

An incredible game indeed!
Obviously, the most notable things here are visual style and music. Colorful, oozing with sort of comfy atmosphere, every level is a pure joy to lool at! The game is 2D, but the backgrounds are always moving, adding multi-layer depth to every scene. And most of the levels change visually in a big way as you progress through the game!
Gameplay-wise, this is a platfomer. There is nothing revolutionary here, but everything is very well put together and in the end the usage of every mechanic feels natural and really satisfying. Controls feel really tight, which is important in a game where precision is required.
There are no loading times and no separate levels - you have a single big world divided into zones thematically. You can not freely run around every zone from the start - in most cases you need a certain ability to fully explore this zone or the other (in metroidvania fashion). Generaly I do not really like games that do this, because this means you will have to backtrack a lot. In this case that never happened to me because of two reasons. Firstly, as I mentioned before, most zones visually change in a big way during the main story. Secondly, newly gained abilities often give you means to cut through the old levels much much MUCH faster then before. All in all, I never felt any problems with the metroidvania-esque natura of the game.
Ori And The Blind Forest is 6-8 hours long and does not outstay its welcome in any way. You will be stunned by the visuals, you will be charmed by the simple, but touching storyline, and you will enjoy yourself while jumping, climbing and flying in the most stylish ways possible. This game is not only worth the money, it is a must buy.

Thumbs up with a couple of reservations:
This feels like neither a game for beginners nor a game for advanced programmers.
It doesn't claim to *teach* programming, mind you, but I feel like it could be - with just a few more really well-thought out defaults, some more automatic instant feedback, and probably lots of good interactive tutorials. The goals/problems it sets are super appealing, and the naive solutions are *almost* easy to come up with for a highly motivated beginner, but I think still just out of reach without being motivated enough to spend hours reading through documentation when you aren't even sure you can figure out the documentation.
For advanced programming, I have a couple of gripes:
- No actual CPU profiling/detailed feedback on CPU usage in a game whose main constraint is CPU usage.
- No (built-in) ability to make your own interface elements in a game about JavaScript programming. I want to make graphs and custom UI elements for my own crazy creep-management logic.
- Lots of small annoyances that get in the way: The autocompletion and other Ace editor defaults; the number of clicks to access useful information; the strange choices the game makes about whether to email you about your runtime errors (if it came from the console, I'm pretty sure I know about it already!); the lack of documentation for simple things like: how much stuff costs to spawn; how the resource economy operates; what the frigging constants are that I'm supposed to use in places where a constant is a parameter to a function (e.g. FIND_*).
But what's really cool about this game is that it *is* integrated with many open-source tools, and hopefully/probably standard JS libraries? so I imagine if I really wanted to, I could work around a lot of these.

This is one of the most fascinating games I've ever played.
Screeps is basically a 24/7 MMO-RTS game where you write the AI of your force, and fight against other players' AIs. A large part of your AI is the management of your economy, which becomes progressively more challenging (respawn creeps, build roads, exploit other rooms, settle other rooms, combine minerals, and so on). The mechanics feel very fun and polished, and the devs have plans to add more challenges for experienced players.
At the beginning, you control just one room, and start in a novice area where you fight for domination with other new players. The area opens up over time, becoming part of the whole world over 30 days, where you compete or trade with all other players,  and build an empire spanning more than 30 rooms. Even if you're wiped out, you can quickly reach your old strength, as the number of rooms you can settle never decreases.
As this game is one of its kind, there are a few things to consider if you want to play it:
Almost all interaction is done by writing JavaScript modules, so if you don't consider programming fun, you won't enjoy Screeps. You can start even as a complete programming novice, but you will need to invest a lot of time if you want to go beyond the basics.
Also, if you spawn close to a more experienced player, she will kill you easily if she wants. So if you're unlucky, you'll wipe repeatedly until you know how to defend your base, and where it is safe to spawn. This will be challenging and frustrating, so be prepared for that.
A third point is that the progression of the game is rather slow; you will build only a few buildings each day, and settle a new room every week (up to a month later). A single organized attack takes 1-2 hours at least, and taking a well-defended room will take days.
Addictive I am recomedning to programmers and NON worth the money.

Hey everyone and this is my review about the game!
This is a RPG(RNG) Turn based strategy game.
There is a difficulty level settings available.
You are able to toggle the tutorial.
There is a master volume slidebar available and it is also % based.
There is a music volume slidebar available and it is also % based.
There is a effect volume slidebar available and it is also % based.
There is a voice volume slidebar available and it is also % based.
There are some different resolution sizes available.
Before you are able to play your game, they will ask you if you do wish to be a Mage, Hunter or a warrior. Each class has their own advantage and disadvantage. This game is borderline... Well let's say uncreative. You click on a map location and that level will start. You are either fighting against an enemy or you are in a town. Once in a town you are able to buy/sell items at a shop, Rest to recover the stats, Talk to some people or even doing quest activities. Whenever you are fighting against an enemy the combat rules are pretty simple (It's like Heroes of might and magic). The battlefield is on a Grid and each unit take turns for their action. The character speed is known as "initiative" and the higher number, the faster a character is able to perform again in a battle. Sadly enough the game suffers from "Random number generator" in fights (Such as X-Com) which means, Even if you have a 95% attack chance against an enemy. Well jokes on you, The 95% is not really 95% as you are still missing pretty often. Your character is able to level up and they are able to learn new spells, talents and other things. They can be equipped with items to make them stronger in battles.
Subtitles are voiced over. You are able to skip and fastforward it.
Great Graphics.
Turn based Combat.
Decent story.
Random number generated % based in battles.
Character has some customiziation.
There is a rules control overview.
Alot of ingame tips/explainations.
It has dialogues and cutscenes.
The random number generator in turn based games is simply NOT WORKING and will always ruin the game. Xcom is a good example (MY OPINION) as the enemy always have a higher hit chance than you will ever get.
So in short words. "Combat mechanic is unfair towards the player as it is happening too often"

The first world is not too hard, but the later levels provide much pain yet also a refreshing change in appearance and music. I've had issues with a couple tough levels in all 3 worlds but muscled through to the end. In addition to simple running and jumping, more complex commands and obstacles are added to put difficulty and spice to the mix. The toughness of the game may be a turnoff, but the graphics and music create a love for the older era of games.
Everyone loves the bit trip runner, he is a terrific athlete.
I recommend this game to any person who loves diablo, PoE, and titan quest.

Van Helsing final cut contains everything that made Van Helsing 1, 2, and 3 great. This rerelease of the franchise is a bundle that contains all three of the original games with added in content.
As if you had read the comment to this review, you might have seen that previously the end-game content was locked to online only, well as you see, Neocore actually cares about what players think of their products (something that is lacking in the games industry as a whole) and have introduced changes to the game to have the same content (minus the online interactions, such as daily events ect) made available to everyone should either parties internet go down for whatever reason.
I can whole heartily recommend this game as the storys itself is well written and has a good length to it. The gameplay is exactly what you would expect from an isometric ARPG, as in it plays flawlessly. The end-game content (known as scenarios/adventure mode) offer unlimited replayability with randomized missions for you to play through.
The only two downsides that I can think of at this time of writting this review is that there are some balance issues but those are to be expected, as well as the seperation of online and offline characters (which has not been done before in the series). While I see its use and purpose, I still see that as a drawback but now that all content is equal across the board, it is hardly an issue to even mention.
There are some bugs as well but as I can only speak for the ones I have encountered and they have not been many, or game breaking in the time I have spent playing (in both online and offline).
If you want a numeric score I give Van Helsing Finalcut a 8.5/10

Short review: 10/10, best game I've played in as long as I can remember
If you're like me, you have dozens of games in your Steam library that you've never played, or that you've played once and never went back to. Let me assure you right now that this game is not going to be one of those games. "Ori and the Blind Forest" is so good that you will want to keep playing even after battling a difficult sequence for five, ten, fifteen times.
I'm going to describe this game using a word I've probably never used to describe a game before: sublime.
The graphics are simply astounding. The setting of the game plays perfectly into the art style. The animations are seamless and everything controls fantastically well. The soundtrack is equally excellent. Combined with the gorgeous look of the game, there are many times during moments of relative calm where I found myself simply taking a moment to admire the fantastic atmosphere within the game that these two come together so perfectly to convey. Story wise, the game gives you exactly what you need. It doesn't bore with lengthy dialogue, it lets the actions in-game tell the story in a more powerful way. The few instances where dialogue takes place are steamlessly woven into the game itself while you continue to play, so the pace is rarely if ever broken. The gameplay matches this perfect pacing. New abilities are unlocked at well set intervals, and every time one becomes available, new paths in previously crossed zones become accessible, tempting you to return to grab that one extra powerup or discover that just out of reach cavern.
I can not give this game enough praise. If your views of the gaming industry have been disillusioned by the yearly rehashes we see in FIFA, Madden, Call of Duty, Battlefield, etc. then please please please do yourself a favor and buy this game, because it will remind you of what a wonderful game truly is. Ori and the Blind Forest is quite simply one of the best games I have ever played, and I hope you give yourself the opportunity to try it so you can discover that it reawakens an awe for games that you may have once had but lost.

An incredible game indeed!
Obviously, the most notable things here are visual style and music. Colorful, oozing with sort of comfy atmosphere, every level is a pure joy to lool at! The game is 2D, but the backgrounds are always moving, adding multi-layer depth to every scene. And most of the levels change visually in a big way as you progress through the game!
Gameplay-wise, this is a platfomer. There is nothing revolutionary here, but everything is very well put together and in the end the usage of every mechanic feels natural and really satisfying. Controls feel really tight, which is important in a game where precision is required.
There are no loading times and no separate levels - you have a single big world divided into zones thematically. You can not freely run around every zone from the start - in most cases you need a certain ability to fully explore this zone or the other (in metroidvania fashion). Generaly I do not really like games that do this, because this means you will have to backtrack a lot. In this case that never happened to me because of two reasons. Firstly, as I mentioned before, most zones visually change in a big way during the main story. Secondly, newly gained abilities often give you means to cut through the old levels much much MUCH faster then before. All in all, I never felt any problems with the metroidvania-esque natura of the game.
Ori And The Blind Forest is 6-8 hours long and does not outstay its welcome in any way. You will be stunned by the visuals, you will be charmed by the simple, but touching storyline, and you will enjoy yourself while jumping, climbing and flying in the most stylish ways possible. This game is not only worth the money, it is a must buy.

Absolutely gorgeous game. The score is breathtaking. The gameplay is what you expect from a competent metroidvania type game. It is responsive and flows quite nicely. With plenty of combinations and high speed gameplay you get a real sense of achievement when you get through an action sequence after several tries. And this is where things start to fall apart for me.
The gameplay flows so smoothly and quickly you do not have time to study all the work that goes into the background. At least at no point does it feel distracting - not to me anyway. But when everything goes by so quickly, stopping to study the backgrounds and looking at the environments breaks the flow of the game and a nice pace comes to a screeching halt. And there are a lot of details.
As for the story, it is what it is. I did not find it a deep narrative. And at a few points I do feel the game condescended to me as if I was too dense to follow the story. Keeping it spoiler free the worst offender was after a cutscene that showed the motivation of an antogonist. After the cutscene the same motivation, that was clear as day and shoved in your face, is told to you in text explicitly within the game. The rule "show, don't tell," is thus not followed, and it feels like the game thinks the player is that dense.
I get the central themes of it all, but it is delivered so explicitly with a lot of repitition to ensure you absolutely know what is going on, that it leaves nothing to the imagination. The game's puzzles served as the only motivation for me personally to move forward, just to prove to the game that, yes, I am smart enough to do this. And I do not believe this is what the game sets out to do. It delivers a narrative and I find thet delivery stunning, but the narrative mediocre. And I personally do not find the narrative that deep and engaging. Call me jaded if you like.
Not to mention that the ending was heavily prompted. No surprises and that left me disappointed.
To sum up, I recommend this. For what it is and the price I feel I got the value in return I expected. It is a beautifully presented so-and-so narrative. This is not looking to be a GOTY contender for me. Not even close. 7/10

Oddworld: New 'n' Tasty... seems fans either love it or loathe it. I'll try to clear up some important distinctions on why:
This game is NOT a 1:1 remake of the original Abe's Oddysee, it is more of a re-imagining. It takes the core ideas from the game, the aesthetic, the story, and packages them in a way that seems comfortingly familiar until you start to realize... this isn't the same game at all!
Perhaps some fans were expecting that, just a remastered audio/visual upgrade, but please come in knowing that while it may look like the same fish, swim like the same fish, it's actually a whale (that's a mammal).
The gameplay is very similar to the old-style game, thankfully with some of the innovations from the sequel thrown in like being able to address multiple mudokons at once. The game also plays in the same 2D Platformer left/right style despite being presented in full 3D
The graphical upgrade to full 3D is a lot more than it may seem, instead of having a fixed camera like in the original, the camera moves dynamically to scroll with you, this actually makes it impossible for certain "gamey" aspects the original had from being possible. Those hidden areas that were so conveniently hidden behind a barrel in the foreground, or the shadows you crept through no longer work in this new style, and have been replaced with new puzzles, steam vents, and an complete overhaul of the level design of many areas.
The level design seems familiar, that elevator is still where you expected, that platform with that slig above that mudokon is still there, and so is that bird portal where you expected it to be. However this isn't the level you grew up with. There are now 299 Mudokons to rescue (vs. 99 in the original game) and they are not always hidden the same way, or require the same puzzles to be solved.
This is still an Oddworld game though through and through, and has just as much charm as the original did. The same humor is there, the same atmosphere, the same story and interesting visuals are all there. The game is still challenging and is very much a puzzle platformer with great and memorable moments and characters.
The change in puzzles and level design is actually a huge plus for veterans of the series as they are basically getting to experience the game new again, since the bulk of the challenge is in solving puzzles, getting to solve tons of new puzzles is a lot of fun and makes the game worth playing for new players and veterans alike.
Go in expecting an Oddworld game with familiar mechanics but a complete new redesign and you won't be disappointed, if you go in expecting the Abe's Oddysee from 1997 with just a new coat of paint well then you may be scratching your head a bit.
