PROS:
- Brilliant storyline
- Great retro soundtrack
- Good ARPG gameplay
CONS:
- Mini-games and puzzles can be frustrating
- Younger gamers may miss some retro gaming references
Evoland 2 takes the retro gaming elements from its predecessor and combines them into a coherent RPG with a surprisingly good storyline. The game is mostly a cross between "The Legend of Zelda" and "Chrono Trigger", with a number of other games mixed in as mini-games or special segments.
I definitely recommend the game for older gamers who experienced firsthand the major video gaming shifts of the 90s. But unlike the first Evoland, I would also recommend this game to younger gamers who have a taste for time travel stories and ARPGs.

If you ever played the original Evoland or didn't like it very much, don't worry because that doesn't matter. Evoland 2 is a very fun and unique RPG, and it improved on the first in every aspect. The main game mechanic (or gimmick one could argue) of the first Evoland was that you unlocked new game mechanics as you played which emulated the advancements video games have made. Evoland 2 is not the same. Rather than having gameplay evolve, Evoland 2 shifts through a variety of different game genres. The most common gameplay style is top-down Zelda-like combat. Evoland 2 also drops the empty feeling turn-based combat style of its predecessor. The type of gameplay keeps shifting so the game never gets repetitive. None of the kinds of gameplay ever felt empty or dragged on for too long. There are many different gameplay types: top-down Zelda-like, bullethell shooter, beat 'em up, and turn-based strategy (to name a few). I was shocked by how many times the game completely changed on me. (I was like 'OMG that's in here too!' pretty much every time it switched.) Evoland 2 features an decent story as opposed to the original Evoland's joke of a story. The new story is not related to Evoland 1's in any way. It actually feels like a real RPG due to story being central to the game throughout. There is an open world and lots of NPCs to interact with. If you couldn't tell by the game's subtitle, the game uses time travel. This does not change the gameplay as if you were jumping between the beginning and end of Evoland 1; it only changes the graphics and the things in the world. By 'things in the world,' I mean that it changes people, places, and more. This is often used in puzzle solving and doing story related actions. This game has a good soundtrack as well. This game is also fairly long; I got 30 hours out of it (one play through). It was much longer than I expected it to be, but the game's continued story elements and shifting of gameplay kept it feeling fresh the entire time. Great game!

Breathtaking, this man deserves all the praise he has gotten. Story hit me harder than a truck full of cement, even holding up against To the Moon. Finding Paradise was wound from such an intricate, complex, and beautiful premise that the reader who is able to experience all the plot threads, some significantly relating back to a previous work of Gao, will be given a profound experience. For myself, to the disagreement of some, Gao has outdone himself here and delivered something beyond his previous To the Moon emotionally, creatively, and topically. I cannot stress how beautiful the idea is and how excellent the execution for the critical moments. If you want to experience an emotionally gripping tale, then Finding Paradise is a must.
My Beefs and nitpicks: (for Gao mostly and not for consumers, go read this story regardless):
-Lots of padding in the plot, functionally a lot of the scenes could be eliminated with zero detriment to the main structure of the story. This padded pacing could be trimmed to the benefit of more seamless consumption. Some padded scenes add entertainment value via humor, which is fine, but other padded scenes have no humor and just serve as unuseful transitions between plots points. This is primarily in act 1.
-Minor Spoiler alert
Ultra technical nitpicks:
-The game should remember the player's facing direction after solving the mementos. As is, the game defaults to orienting down afterwards, which in most cases is a different facing direction than the one needed for operating the memento.
-The sound bug from mashing the action button after shooting the last memory link into the mementos is still not fixed from To the Moon.
And I thought X-Com was bad enough to not allow a 95% possibility attack to connect.

Pretty funny seeing all the people here whine about this game being unforgiving or super difficult... I am completely new to Dark Eye game systems and have just taken my time in looking at the character trees etc and sort of feeling my way into where I'm spending my AP. I would say that if difficult = not 1shotting every single battle, then the game is "difficult". But beyond that, it's not very difficult. Every single encounter has taken me no more than 2 tries barring the end encounter for Chapter 2 (louse queen as a 3rd battle in a row with no recovery time. I decided to power thru it vs trying to load an old save and set myself up for easier success over all 3 as a whole with the knowledge I'd gained... too lazy to do that). And I can even say that the first attempt is often experimentation or trial/error with the different maps, traps and interactables etc and perhaps new enemy types.
It's fairly easy so far, although I will say that the difficulty is spiky; it runs the gamut from faceroll to mildy challenging (and some of the reviews I see whining about difficulty are from people that spent far less time than I, so I doubt it's where I am in the game) -- honestly if you are having trouble, maybe reevaluate your movement and positioning. I've found that there is a lot of advantage to be gained and strategy in positioning and more or less "gaming the map" to keep control and manage some of the risk/rng. This is a hex based game, and sometimes moving 2 hexes right or left can change a whole lot.
To give an example -- I saw a "WTF is" by TotalBiscuit, where he played a fairly early map and thought it was frustrating and difficult... immediately started making major positioning oversights in the very first turn he had. The corridor is bottlenecked to 3 hexes wide and there are like 6 active crypt lice. Why would you not move 3 characters onto each of those hexes and wait for the lice to come to you? Then you are only fighting 3 at once you only have 3 characters of your choosing taking damage (far more control over damage intake). Following this, you have infinite recovery turns on the map to heal before moving forward and "activating" the next group. This is just a very basic example... and I don't really even dabble in strategy games all that much. I just don't see how this game is hard. It's fairly simple with a bit of trial and error involved. The RNG complaints are also pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t... there is even a "wounds" system to manage the RNG... which I discovered at my leisure after continually investigating the ruleset as I played. Have some patience... you definitely don't need to read character guides to suceed. I've learned after playing and reading around that the optimal route is playing a mage as the hero (there's 0 disadvantage since there are basically characters that can cast and characters that can't -- everything else can be developed as you see fit as the game goes on...), and I'm doing just fine.
I would have enjoyed this game if you hit something in front of you at least once in 10 tries...

Tactical, combat-enforced hex-map fantasy chess with RPG stats of the once most beloved German pen & paper roleplaying game. The game starts nicely, even though the linearity of the story, and the lack of impact one makes unto the world around the chosen or hand-built protagonist seems to remind of decade old mistakes in RPG's.
The game is A LOT about tactical combat on a hex map, not much skills versus environment, not much story or choices which matter, but if you unlock the console and type WIN after pressing F12, then patch version 1.8 of the game is decent.
Given that several patches still failed to relieve us of all glitches and bugs, that isn't too impressive.
One mistake I found sucking:
Merchants offer a standard script of equipment. Entire armor sets and weapons can only be gained by using the 'give all items' cheat. Sadly that one crashes the game later, as it spawns a bug sabotaging the quest resolving.
Additionally you need your DirectX and VCredists (from 2008 to 2013) in peak-performance-state, or glitches and bugs are guaranteed!
Crystals and chests cannot be damaged by daggers or fencing weapons! Use two-weapon fighting plus a torch or slash or bash type of weapon, IF you need daggers or foils, rapiers to imagine your character (Horasian area of Aventuria)...
The character creation is decent.
The world is harsh and unforgiving, while still being the once famous Aventuria (Aventurien in German) of THE DARK EYE RPG system.
The allies of the protagonist and their voiceovers ain't bad.
Background music is decent, too.
Skills like streetwise and survival make a difference, even though some can only be taken at character creation in expert mode. No trainers found later in the game.
The game does build atmosphere, but only for one more tactical combat on those ancient, antiquated, oldschool hexagone maps...
The oft-shunned Nameless God is much better implemented than in 'Demonicon'.
I purchased it years after first sale, for only 2€ plus 1,20€ steam key. For that pricing it was good enough to fill one evening, but not enough to make that old fever aka joy arise in my ex-roleplayer soul.
Awsome, fun game. Would recommend!

The first time I came to write a review for this game it was going to be a vitriolic missive of woe and anger. In true fashion, and not for the first time, the game had put me on my♥♥♥♥♥ It was during the games infamous second chapter, where fights come thick and fast, and leave you feeling brutalised and frustrated. I perservered however and came out of the other side happier for it.
This game is far from perfect, but for fans of tactical RPGs it is a truly a diamond in the rough. Battles are varied and interesting and party composition and tactical choices really make a difference. The combat system is deeper than it first appears and that hidden depth is one of the games finer qualities. It is also it's biggest drawback. The game is closely based on a pen and paper RPG and unfortunately in many ways just as indecipherable to the beginner.
The character progression system is almost arcane in its complexity, to the point that it is almost certain that you will make mistakes in the way you build up your party. These mistakes will be deadly on even normal difficulty. It's reliance on a pen and paper system mean that unless you have a copy of the rulebook and many hours to ponder it and try out permutations, your characters will be woefully shy of optimal. This may lead to you having to restart the game several times as you begin to unravel its mysteries.
That being said , the game is sufficiently fun, interesting and challenging that you won't mind having to restart. I didn't.

Van Helsing final cut contains everything that made Van Helsing 1, 2, and 3 great. This rerelease of the franchise is a bundle that contains all three of the original games with added in content.
As if you had read the comment to this review, you might have seen that previously the end-game content was locked to online only, well as you see, Neocore actually cares about what players think of their products (something that is lacking in the games industry as a whole) and have introduced changes to the game to have the same content (minus the online interactions, such as daily events ect) made available to everyone should either parties internet go down for whatever reason.
I can whole heartily recommend this game as the storys itself is well written and has a good length to it. The gameplay is exactly what you would expect from an isometric ARPG, as in it plays flawlessly. The end-game content (known as scenarios/adventure mode) offer unlimited replayability with randomized missions for you to play through.
The only two downsides that I can think of at this time of writting this review is that there are some balance issues but those are to be expected, as well as the seperation of online and offline characters (which has not been done before in the series). While I see its use and purpose, I still see that as a drawback but now that all content is equal across the board, it is hardly an issue to even mention.
There are some bugs as well but as I can only speak for the ones I have encountered and they have not been many, or game breaking in the time I have spent playing (in both online and offline).
If you want a numeric score I give Van Helsing Finalcut a 8.5/10

So having played through the three games previously I thought I'd give my opinion of the Final Cut edition to help new users to the series to decide if it's worth it.
and I'd highly recommend it
and here's why:
Firstly it's a standard diablo-style hack'n'slash game, with thousands of enemies, lots of loots and a fairly linear path to go alone. Whilst this means it won't set new standards for the genre, they do the basics well. There are also tower-defence style missions to help break up the main game as well as multiplayer options and a scenario mode.
The setting and characters gives the game a fresh twist, instead of the usual dungeons and dragons theme, we have Van Helsing, the famous monster hunter. Whilst not a huge change it is something original and makes for a nice change,
This is also the first time in the series that you can have one character playthrough the entire three games which lets you get better connected to your character. You can also play as any of the six classes for the entire game as well, whereas previously they added classes as the series went on.
Getting the game's Final Cut edition also allows you to get the game after the previous ones have effectively been tested. The skill system has been re-worked to be the same throughout all the games, level cap has been raised and bugs and nuisences have been removed.
The game's store page says you'll get around 50 hours in total and this seems about right as my time in the three seperate games came to 56 hours; and even at it's full price it gives good value for money.
If you're a fan of hack'n'slash games then you'll enjoy this, it's easily worth the price and I found it to be quite a pleasant surprise when I played it.
If you are unsure then search the steam store page for "Van Helsing" as there is a demo still available of the first game, whilst skills and classes may have changed since then, it can give you a good chance to test it before parting with your money.

This has happened 100% of the times I've played it. Sometimes it even freezes on the "Moon Studios" splash screen. I've seen zero developer response on the Steam Forums, and the website
doesn't seem to have a forum to voice our concerns either.
Aside from the crashing, there are other issues as well. Upon learning the "bash" ability, my Xbox360 wireless controller seems to be stuck in the 'left' direction when trying to aim my bash. If I cancel bash it's fine, but it made the first tree race pretty frustrating when some of the bashing through the lights bug out.
Overall, I don't recommend this game. Not right now at least. It needs a lot of fixes and it wouldn't hurt them to have some presence on the Steam forum so that the community can be heard.

Ori reminds me of what I love about gaming. Beautiful visuals, stunning soundtrack, and tight gameplay combine for an experience that calls back to the classic 2-D greats such as Super Metroid and Castlevania.
The various areas are all visually distinct with lovingly crafted visuals and interesting mechanics. Movement is solid and fluid, with lots of different upgrades to reach new areas you couldn't reach before. Some of the game sequnces are absolutley mesmerizing.
This game doesn't necessarily break any new ground, but what it's doing is a complete refinement of the mechanics we all know into what is, in my opionion, the must-play game of early 2015.

An absolutely beautiful platformer with a storyline that really plays with your emotions, the most memorable music score I've heard in a game in years, and visuals that make it look like every scene is a painting.
The gameplay is fun and I got about 6 hours of game out of it, which was plenty without going too long and ruining a great thing.
It is tough, especially the boss moments, but definitely worth it.
I insta bought this game and I'd seriously recommend you consider doing the same. No need to wait for a special, this game deserves every cent of its price.

I really enjoy this game it has great animation and a visual style but the controls definitely needed tightening, it's terrible when you have to make precision movements like jumping on a thin post and it constantly wants to go that little inch forward to mess you up.
This is the first single player game I've rage quit in ages, I'm currently at the infamous ginzo tree water rising part. I have played this part for the last 45 mins and I feel like it ruins my experience of the game.
It doesn't matter how fast you go, the water will be at your back. It's like it's scripted for every section and doesn't reward you with a little bit of time for doing the section perfectly. It also keeps messing me up because the energy slingshot decides that it's not going to work by letting me fall to my death or the enemies don't react to my presence fast enough to shoot the enrgy. My first impressions were 9/10. After playing the game for longer, the clunkiness of the controls starts to get irritating so I'd give it a 7/10 now.
It's a fun action platformer, probably not worth the money though. I'd reccomend it when it's cheaper, like around £6 but apart from great visuals the gameplay isn't as polished enough for the price tag in my opinion.
I will attempt to beat it but I'm not spending forever on one part that feels like the game mechanics are working against me rather than me making mistakes.

Previous issues with the orignal game have been balanced out. Quite a bit has been added on top, such as grenades that act like the special arrows archers get, new talents replacing the useless ones, a backstab cone to show where rogues need to be standing and a total of four difficulty settings. Tactician is a leap away from the classic difficulty. Never had I thought the first group of skeletons would best me. All around, EE goes above and beyond what people were expecting out of it. If you owned Original Sin before the 27th, Enhanced is in your steam library. Go and download it. If you didn't own it, definitely buy this one.

I have over 80 hours logged with the original version of this and it is by far one of my most favorite recent RPGS out there. They really added alot of changes. They revamped the crafting, added VO to practically ALL dialogue(and the voice acting is charming, IMO), and spruced up performance and made everything generally better.
If you played the original and loved it...this is complete fan service. Seriously. If all gaming studios treated their products with loving as Larian has done...the gaming industry would be unrecognizable.
I whole-heartedly recommend this. It makes a fantastic game even better.
++voice acting; great quailty and I am damn sure the opening into narration is the same voice actress as the female british Inquisitor from DA:I
++dual wielding!
++GRENADES!
++more crafting/craftin UI overhaul! Hell...the entire UI has been changed and overhauled and for the better!
++optimized performance!
++better graphics all around than previous version.
++tactical mode for the people out there who love surprised and even greater challenge. They designed it to counter common strategies of players of the original. Seriously. I am seeing the AI do things I havent seen before in the original. Looks like its been upgradd.
++honour mode = one save only. Think of it as Ironman Mode. You die and your save is deleted.
I honestly cannot think of any cons right now. I will update this if I do. I am liking it that much.
